question_text: You are a delivery analyst at a consultancy, three days from a new system going live at an insurer, Bracknoll Insurance. Yesterday, in front of the client’s team, their data lead said your migration counts could not be trusted. This morning she emails asking for an extract of those counts by midday, because the client’s board meets at one. You also have the last checks before go-live to finish today, and there is not time for both. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Put her request at the back of today's queue and leave it there, and stop offering her help with the counts, because she said your work could not be trusted.
Finish the checks first and reply to her at the end of the day, since the system is live in three days and one email does not change the order of the work.
Drop the checks and build the full extract exactly as she asked for it, so that nobody can say twice in two days that your work is unreliable.
Ask her what the board actually needs by midday, produce the smallest extract that answers it, and tell the manager running the engagement that the checks now finish this evening.
explanation: A: Withdraws help after a public disagreement: the extract her board needs is late because of yesterday, and the client pays for a quarrel between two people. B: Answers a deadline after it has passed: her board meets at one, so a reply at six reaches nobody who needed it. C: Lets yesterday set today's priorities: proving a point costs the last checks a day the go-live does not have. The most effective response is to ask her what the board actually needs and produce the smallest extract that answers it. It finds out how much of the request is really needed by midday, it protects most of the day for the checks, and it tells the person who owns the sequence what has moved. It beats finishing the checks first and replying to her at the end of the day, because her board meets at one and an answer at six reaches nobody who needed it. It beats dropping the checks and building the full extract exactly as asked, because the full extract costs a day the checks do not have, and nothing about yesterday makes that trade sensible. The least effective response is putting her request at the back of the queue and stopping the help you were giving her: the other three all make some choice about the work, whereas this one lets a remark made yesterday decide what the client gets today, so a board sitting at one is the party that pays for it. The principle: a request is judged on what it needs and when, never on who sent it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Dùng phương pháp ước lượng chữ số hàng đơn vị hoặc làm tròn đến hàng chục để loại ngay 2 phương án vô lý.

question_text: You are a data analyst at a consultancy. A colleague has told you they are sending the client’s finance lead a set of figures within the hour, for a proposal meeting this afternoon. You revised those figures on Friday, and the set your colleague holds is the older one. They are on a client call until they send it. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Message your colleague now saying the figures were revised on Friday, and send them the current version so that they have it before the email goes.
Email the finance lead yourself with the revised figures and a note explaining that they replace the set your colleague is about to send them within the hour.
Say nothing about the older version and leave the finance lead to raise it if the difference turns out to matter to them.
Wait for your colleague to come off the call and go through what changed with them, rather than interrupting a client conversation.
explanation: B: Corrects a colleague through the client: the finance lead gets the right numbers and also learns that your team was about to send the wrong ones. C: Withholds what somebody needed: the finance lead takes superseded numbers into a proposal meeting, and the one person who knew they had changed decided it was not worth a message. D: Leaves it to a window that closes: the email goes within the hour, so waiting for the call to end means the older figures are already out. The most effective response is to message your colleague now and send them the current version of the figures. It reaches your colleague before the email leaves, it hands them the thing they need rather than a problem, and nobody outside the team ever sees the old set. It beats emailing the finance lead yourself with the revised figures, because the client then holds two sets from your team and hears about the mix-up before your colleague does. It beats waiting for your colleague to come off the call before going through what changed, because the email goes within the hour and the call ends after that. The least effective response is saying nothing about the older version and leaving the finance lead to raise it: the other three all get the current figures somewhere useful, whereas this one lets a decision be taken on numbers you know were superseded on Friday, on the hope that the difference will not matter. The principle: when you hold the thing that makes somebody else’s work wrong, say so while it can still be used.
tip: Mẹo MT: Nhớ công thức tính nhanh: Tăng trưởng % = (Giá trị mới - Giá trị cũ) / Giá trị cũ × 100%.

question_text: You are a process analyst at a consultancy, and the findings report for a packaging manufacturer, Lowmere Packaging, was due with the client’s operations director this morning. Every report is read by a second person on the team before it leaves, and this one has not been. The colleague who does that read is off sick, and the manager running the engagement is in the air until this evening. The operations director has now emailed twice asking where the report is. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Reply that the report will be with her as soon as it has been read, without saying when that is likely to be or what it is that is holding it up.
Read the report through carefully yourself a second time and send it, on the basis that your own second careful read is close enough to somebody else's.
Email the operations director this morning saying the report is not yet read by the second reviewer, since no report leaves without that read, and give her a time today.
Pass the report and the operations director's emails over to another colleague on the engagement, and leave it with them to decide what goes out this morning.
explanation: A: Answers without giving her anything to plan with: she has asked twice and still cannot tell whether the wait is hours or days. B: Breaches the one check the report had: the reader who would have caught the gaps is replaced by the person who wrote them, and the client receives it believing it was checked. D: Passes the client onto somebody else: a colleague who has not read the report inherits both the decision and a client who has already asked twice. The most effective response is to email the operations director saying the report is not yet read and to give her a time today. It tells the client exactly where the report is, it does not pretend the missing read has happened, and it gives her a time she can plan the rest of her morning around. It beats replying that the report will be with her as soon as it has been read, without saying when, because a promise with no time in it leaves her no better off than the two emails she has already sent. It beats passing the report and the emails over to another colleague to decide, because moving an unread report and an impatient client onto a colleague hands away both the context and the decision. The least effective response is reading it through a second time yourself and sending it on that basis: the other three all leave the report honestly unread until somebody reads it, whereas this one sends it out with the check quietly performed by the person who wrote it, so the client acts on a report they believe two people have seen. The principle: when a check has not happened, tell the client what is true and own the wait yourself.
tip: Mẹo MT: Nhớ công thức tính nhanh: Tăng trưởng % = (Giá trị mới - Giá trị cũ) / Giá trị cũ × 100%.

question_text: You are a reporting analyst at a consultancy, producing the weekly figures a client’s operations meeting runs on. Every set of figures is compared against the source extract by a second analyst before it leaves your team. The client’s operations manager rings an hour before their meeting and asks for this week’s figures now. The comparison has not been done. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell the operations manager the figures are still being checked and will reach them within the hour, since the comparison is outstanding, and ask what they need.
Send last week's figures instead, since those have already been compared against the source, and say the current week is not finished yet.
Ask the second analyst to stop their own client work and do the comparison in the next twenty minutes, so the figures can go over before the meeting starts.
Release this week's figures to the meeting straight away, and run the comparison against the source extract afterwards while the meeting is under way.
explanation: B: Answers a question nobody asked: last week's numbers tell the operations meeting nothing about the week they are meeting about, and the hour is spent on them anyway. C: Moves the cost onto a colleague: another client's work is dropped to avoid a one minute conversation about when the figures will be ready. D: Breaches a stated check: the meeting takes decisions from numbers nobody has compared against the source, and the client cannot see that the step was skipped. The most effective response is to tell the operations manager the figures are still being checked and will reach them within the hour. It gives the operations manager a straight answer inside their own timing, it leaves them to decide what to do with the hour, and what reaches the meeting has been through the comparison the client is relying on without knowing it. It beats sending last week’s figures instead, because numbers from the week before answer a question the meeting is not asking, and this week is still missing. It beats asking the second analyst to stop their own client work and do the comparison now, because another client loses their analyst to save a conversation about timing that takes a minute to have. The least effective response is releasing the figures straight away and running the comparison afterwards: the other three all leave the meeting either waiting or told what it is waiting for, whereas this one puts uncompared numbers in front of people who will decide on them, and the one step that would have caught an error is gone without the client ever knowing it existed. The principle: tell a client where a check stands rather than dropping the check to hit their clock.
tip: Mẹo MT: Dùng phương pháp ước lượng chữ số hàng đơn vị hoặc làm tròn đến hàng chục để loại ngay 2 phương án vô lý.

question_text: You are a property store assistant at a fire and rescue service. Your team is choosing between two firms to refit the store room next month, and you have been asked to check both quotes against the stock list by tomorrow morning. One of the two firms is run by your sister. The stated rule is that anybody with a personal connection to a firm under consideration tells their supervisor before doing work that affects the choice, and your supervisor is at her desk today. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Do the comparison as asked but ask a colleague at the next desk to check your figures on both quotes before it goes in, and tell your supervisor about your sister when you hand the comparison over tomorrow.
Hand both quotes to a colleague at the next desk without saying why, and get on with the stock list instead, so that the comparison is still done by tomorrow morning.
Compare the quotes today against the stock list, and mention your sister to your supervisor once the comparison is finished and written up, so that the work is not held up by the conversation.
Tell your supervisor today that one of the two firms is run by your sister, before you open either quote, and ask her who should check them against the stock list.
explanation: A: Substitutes your own remedy for the stated rule: a second pair of eyes is a sensible precaution and it is not the one the rule asks for, which is a word with your supervisor before you open either quote rather than an assurance afterwards. B: Passes the problem on without owning it: your colleague now does work affecting a choice she has not been told is compromised, the supervisor the rule names still knows nothing, and the connection sits undeclared when the firm is picked. C: Delays the disclosure past the point it could change anything: the rule asks you to speak before doing the work, and a declaration made after the comparison exists leaves your supervisor with a document she cannot use. The most effective response is telling your supervisor today that one of the two firms is run by your sister, before you open either quote. The rule states plainly that the connection is declared before work that affects the choice, your supervisor is available today, and telling her now is the only route that leaves the comparison usable tomorrow. It beats comparing the quotes today and mentioning your sister afterwards, because a declaration that arrives after the work is done makes the work itself unusable. It is also better than doing the comparison and having a colleague check the figures, which answers a worry about accuracy when the rule is about who should be doing the work at all. The least effective response is handing both quotes to a colleague at the next desk without saying why: unlike the late declaration, which at least reaches your supervisor, and unlike the checked comparison, where a second reader sees the figures and your supervisor is told, this leaves a colleague doing compromised work in the dark and the connection undeclared when the firm is chosen. The principle: when a rule tells you to declare an interest before acting, declare it to the person the rule names, not by quietly moving the work.
tip: Mẹo MT: Trong đề thi SHL, quản lý thời gian tối đa 60-75 giây cho mỗi câu tính toán số học.

question_text: You are a complaints administration assistant at a fire and rescue service. The company that prints your acknowledgement letters has sent this week’s batch with the wrong date, so forty people who have complained are told in writing that they will have a full reply by Friday, when the standard is twenty working days. The printer will correct it only if you ask in writing by five today. Letters to complainants go out only once the person who runs your team has approved them. That person is away until Monday and somebody is covering for them. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Reply to the printer to say the correction can wait until Monday, when the person who runs your team is back, since one clear letter then is better than two letters now.
Write to the printer yourself before five and ask them to post a correction to all forty people, rather than lose the only chance to fix it while approval waits until Monday.
Draft the correction now, get it approved by whoever is covering for the person who runs your team, and have it with the printer before five to correct all forty letters.
Wait until Monday and answer the forty people one by one as they ring in, explaining the real date to each of them when they ask about it.
explanation: A: Delays the decision: the printer's window shuts at five today, so waiting for Monday does not buy a better letter, it loses the only correction on offer. B: Breaches the approval the letters need: a second letter reaches forty complainants with nobody having checked either, and the approval step exists precisely to stop a wrong letter following a wrong letter. D: Makes the customer do the chasing: only some of the forty will ring, and the rest spend the next two weeks expecting a reply on a date that was never real. The most effective response is drafting the correction now and getting it approved by whoever is covering: the five o’clock window is the only chance the printer offers, and the cover exists so that an absence does not stop an approval. It is stronger than replying that the correction can wait until Monday, because the window shuts today and forty people go into the weekend expecting a reply that cannot come. It is also stronger than answering the forty one by one as they ring in, since only some of them will ring and the rest keep a promise nobody can meet. The least effective response is asking the printer to post a correction yourself before five: it puts a second letter in front of forty complainants with nobody having approved either one, and the approval is the control that stops one mistake becoming two. The principle: when a deadline and an approval collide, find the person who can approve rather than choosing which of the two to drop.

question_text: You are a course administration assistant at a fire and rescue service. You keep the sign in sheet for a five day course. At the end of day three the sheet shows 28 people signed in, but the course leader’s list has 30 names and your own room log has 30 people present. The stated rule is that the certificate list is built from the sign in sheet, and it is confirmed on Friday. Nobody else has noticed the gap. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Add the two missing names to the sheet yourself and mark day three as checked, since you saw both of them in the room and two either way makes no practical difference.
Raise it with the course leader on Friday when the certificate list is confirmed, since the sheet may well be corrected by then and two names is not much to chase in the meantime.
Write a note beside the sheet saying the count did not agree on day three, and leave it for whoever confirms the certificate list on Friday to look into.
Compare the room log and the leader's list against the sheet today, then tell the course leader which two names are missing and how the gap arose, so the sheet is right before Friday.
explanation: A: Writes into a record something you did not witness being signed: the sheet is the source the certificate list is built from, so an entry you made up is now the evidence that two people attended. B: Delays the check to the deadline itself: Friday is when the list is confirmed, so a discrepancy raised that morning has to be resolved under time pressure or waved through. C: Flags a problem without owning it: you are the person who holds the room log, so the one piece of evidence that would settle the gap sits with you and not with the reader of the note. The most effective response is comparing the room log and the leader’s list against the sheet today and telling the course leader which two names are missing and how the gap arose. Nobody has assigned this to you, you hold the evidence that explains it, and Friday is a fixed point after which the certificate list is built from whatever the sheet says. It beats raising it with the course leader on Friday itself, because a gap found on the day of confirmation gets resolved in a hurry or not at all. It beats writing a note beside the sheet for whoever confirms the list, because the room log that would settle the question is yours and the reader of the note does not have it. The least effective response is adding the two missing names yourself and marking day three as checked: that puts into the source record an entry nobody signed, so a certificate list built from it now rests on your recollection presented as somebody’s signature. It is worse than the Friday conversation and worse than the note because both of those leave the record honest and merely late, while this leaves it wrong and looking right. The principle: when a total you own does not reconcile, find out why while there is still time, and never close the gap by writing the answer in.

question_text: You are a course administration assistant at a prison service. Another assistant on the course team has fallen behind: forty trainees’ preparation tasks are unmarked on the completion log, which has to be complete before Monday’s assessment. They have told only you and have asked you not to make a fuss. You can see which tasks have actually been submitted and which have not. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Mark all forty preparation tasks on the completion log as done so the log is ready for Monday, and let the colleague check the submissions afterwards when they have caught up.
Tell the colleague you will help, that the person who runs the course has to know today, since only they can move Monday, then mark with them only what is genuinely in.

Work through all forty unmarked tasks yourself in the evenings on top of your own work, checking each submission as you go, and tell nobody, so that the colleague is not embarrassed and the log is ready by Monday.

Send the person who runs the course a note this morning saying the colleague is forty tasks behind on the completion log, before saying anything to the colleague, so that Monday's assessment is not put at risk.

D: Goes over the colleague's head first: they confided in you, a word to them costs nothing, and the note arrives without any account of what has actually been submitted. The most effective response is telling the colleague you will help while making clear that the person who runs the course has to know today: Monday is fixed, forty tasks are unmarked, and the only person who can move the assessment or find another pair of hands is the one nobody has told. It beats working through the unmarked tasks yourself in the evenings and telling nobody, because one person quietly absorbing a two-person backlog leaves the same problem standing next month. It beats sending a note about the colleague before saying anything to them, since they confided in you and a word first costs nothing and keeps them in the conversation. The least effective response is marking all forty tasks on the completion log as done: the log then says trainees have prepared when you can see that some have not, and Monday’s assessment runs on a record you know to be wrong. question_text: You are a complaints administration assistant at a police force. A member of the public who has made a complaint rings to say that somebody here told them on the phone they would have a full written answer by Friday. The stated process is that a complaint is acknowledged within ten working days and answered once the review of it is finished, which in this case will take several weeks. The person says they will decide on Friday whether to take the matter elsewhere. The file is not to go outside the organisation until the review is finished. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Apologise for the confusion and say that you will chase the review so that it finishes as quickly as it can, leaving out the ten working days and the several weeks so as not to make the call worse.
Post them a copy of what is on the file so far, so that they have something in writing by Friday, even though the file is not to go outside the organisation until the review has finished.
Tell the person plainly that Friday was never something anybody could offer, set out the ten working days and that the answer follows the review, and give them the date they will next hear from you.
Ask the person who runs the review whether Friday can be met for this one complaint, and tell the caller only that you are looking into it and will come back to them when you know.
explanation: A: Softens the very fact the person needs: they are deciding on Friday whether to go elsewhere, and a decision like that cannot be made on a promise to hurry with no timescale attached to it. B: Breaches a stated limit on the file: paperwork from an unfinished review is not the answer they were expecting, and it hands them material the organisation has said may not leave it. D: Escalates rather than correcting the expectation: the review takes weeks whoever asks, and the caller spends the days before Friday still believing a written answer is coming. The most effective response is telling the person plainly that Friday was never something anybody could offer, setting out the ten working days and that the answer follows the review, and giving them the date they will next hear from you. They are deciding on Friday what to do next, so the one thing that helps them is an accurate picture of when their answer arrives. That is better than apologising and promising to chase, because a vague undertaking to hurry gives them nothing to weigh. It is better than asking whether Friday can be met, because the review takes weeks either way and the question costs the caller the days in which they could have been deciding on the facts. The least effective response is posting them a copy of what is on the file so far: chasing at least keeps the caller in contact and asking about Friday at least tests the possibility, whereas sending out material the organisation has said may not leave it breaks the one stated limit here and still does not tell them when their answer is coming. The principle: a promise somebody else made is corrected with an accurate date, never with a rule bent to cover for it.

question_text: You are a course administration assistant at a police force. You keep the waiting list for a twelve-place first aid course that runs on Friday, and the written rule is that places go in the order requests arrive. The list is full. Someone whose request came in ninth asks you to move them to the top because they know the person who runs the course, and offers you a forty pound gift voucher for your trouble. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Turn the voucher down and leave the list exactly as it stands, without telling anybody that an offer was made, since nothing has actually changed on the course.
Decline the voucher, explain that places go in the order requests arrive, and tell your supervisor the same day what was offered, since somebody tried buying a place.
Pass the request and the offer straight to your supervisor and let them decide whether the place should move, since a decision like this is above your level.
Accept the voucher and move the request to the top of the list, telling yourself that one swap on a twelve place course makes no real difference to anybody else.
explanation: A: Avoids reporting the offer: the places are still in the right order, but the one new fact, that somebody tried to buy a place on a full list, stays with you alone. C: Escalates a decision the rule already makes: the written rule settles the order of the list, so the only part that needs another pair of eyes is the offer itself. D: Takes a gift the role forbids: the voucher buys a Friday place that the written rule had already given to somebody else, and eight people ahead of the ninth lose a place without knowing why. The most effective response is to decline the voucher, explain that places go in the order requests arrive, and tell your supervisor the same day what was offered. The rule is written down, the person asking is ninth on a full list, and the offer is something the people who set that rule need to know about. Turning the voucher down while leaving the list untouched and saying nothing about the offer is weaker, because the offer is the one thing that has changed and nobody else can see it. Sending the request and the offer straight to your supervisor to decide is weaker too, because the rule already settles the place and only the offer needs another pair of eyes. The least effective response is to accept the voucher and move the request to the top of the list: it takes a benefit the role forbids, and eight people ahead of the ninth lose a Friday place to it without ever knowing. A small favour bought with a gift is still bought, which is why the answer is no before the size of the gift is discussed.

question_text: You are a complaints administration assistant at a police force. A letter closing a complaint goes out today, and it was written on the basis that the complainant never replied to two requests for information. This morning you find their reply sitting in a shared inbox, dated before the second request was sent. The stated standard is that the complainant hears the outcome today. The person who signed the letter is in the building. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Hand the whole thing to your supervisor with the letter still due today, leaving the reply and its date in the shared inbox, and get on with the rest of the post.
Ring the complainant today because the standard requires an outcome today, tell them their reply has been found, and say the closing letter is on hold until it is considered.
Rewrite the closing letter yourself to take account of the reply and send it today, without going back to the person who signed the original version.
Hold the letter, tell the person who signed it that the reply arrived before the second request, and ask whether the complaint should be reopened before today's standard runs out.
explanation: A: Passes the problem on without owning it: the deadline is still running, and it arrives on somebody else's desk without the reply, its date, or any account of what you have already checked. B: Commits the organisation without authority: the person who signed the letter is in the building and has decided nothing yet, so a promise that the closing is on hold runs ahead of anybody's decision. C: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholder's: the decision the letter records belongs to the person who signed it, and a rewrite goes out in their name without their knowledge. The most effective response is holding the letter and telling the person who signed it that the reply arrived before the second request: they wrote it on the basis that nothing came back, that is no longer true, and only they can decide whether the complaint reopens. It beats ringing the complainant to say their reply has been found and the closing letter is on hold, because that promises a change of course before the person who signed the letter has decided there will be one. It beats rewriting the closing letter yourself without going back to the person who signed the original, since the decision it records is theirs and a rewrite still goes out in their name. The least effective response is handing the whole thing to your supervisor and getting on with the rest of the post: today’s standard is still running, and the problem lands on somebody else without the reply, its date, or any account of what you already know. The principle: when the basis of a decision changes, take it back to the person who made it, with the change stated.

question_text: You are a shift supervisor at a consumer goods company. Two jobs are outstanding on your shift: a stock check the site manager wants finished today, and preparing an area for tomorrow’s early start. You have people for one of them. The site manager is about to leave and asks you directly whether both will be done by the end of the shift. Tomorrow’s early start cannot begin without the preparation. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell him the stock check will be done and say nothing about the preparation, since he asked mainly about the check and tomorrow is not his shift in any case.
Promise the site manager that both jobs will be finished before the shift ends, then decide later in the evening which of the two actually gets done.
Tell him you have people for one, say which you would do and why, and ask him to decide if he wants it the other way round.
Split the shift between the two jobs so that both are half done, and tell him the position when he asks about it in the morning.
explanation: A: Answers half a question and lets the rest stand: he leaves believing both are in hand because you did not correct the impression. B: Commits to something you know cannot happen: he leaves the site planning on two finished jobs, and finds out tomorrow which promise was real. D: Divides effort so neither is usable: tomorrow's early start cannot run on a half-prepared area and the stock check has to be redone. The most effective response is to tell him you have people for one, say which you would choose and why, and let him decide otherwise if he wants: he learns the position while he is still standing there, the judgement is offered rather than hidden, and the decision rests with the person who owns the site. It beats answering only about the stock check, because his impression that both are in hand goes uncorrected. It beats splitting the shift, because a half-prepared area stops tomorrow’s start and a half stock check has to be done again. The least effective response is promising the site manager that both jobs will be finished: he plans on two finished jobs, and which promise was real is discovered the next morning, which is a different kind of wrong from answering incompletely or from dividing the work badly. The principle: when asked whether you can do two things you cannot, say so at once and bring a recommendation.

question_text: You are a supplier quality assistant at a consumer goods company. A supplier has emailed you twice asking when a decision will be made about a change they have proposed. The decision belongs to the buyer, who has been in meetings all week and has not replied to either message. The supplier needs to book production time and says he will lose his slot on Friday. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Reply that the decision sits with the buyer and that he has been in meetings all week, so the supplier knows the delay is nothing to do with the quality side of the work.
Reply that you have his question and will come back once the buyer is out of meetings, and chase the buyer once more today.
Reply today with what you do know and say the decision is the buyer's, and put the Friday deadline in front of the buyer now so that he can see what turns on it.
Pass the supplier straight to the buyer's inbox with a one-line note, and leave the two of them to sort the date out between themselves.
explanation: A: Explains the delay instead of moving it: the supplier learns why he is waiting and is no closer to the Friday date that his production slot depends on. B: Chases without raising the stakes: the buyer gets a third message that does not mention Friday, which is the one fact that would move him. D: Hands the problem on without owning it: the supplier is redirected to the person who has not answered twice already, and nobody has told the buyer that Friday is the date that matters. The most effective response is to reply today with what you know, say the decision is the buyer’s and that you will come back by Thursday, and put the Friday deadline in front of the buyer: the supplier gets a person and a date, the buyer gets the one fact that makes this urgent, and you keep the thread rather than dropping it. It beats explaining that the buyer has been in meetings, because that is an account of the delay rather than an attempt to end it. It beats replying that you will come back once the buyer is out of meetings, because a third message that leaves out the production slot gives him no reason to move. The least effective response is passing him straight to the buyer’s inbox and leaving them to it: the supplier is sent to the person who has not answered him twice, and the deadline that makes it urgent is still not in front of anybody, which is a different kind of wrong from explaining too much or writing too little. The principle: when you cannot give the answer, give the timetable, and make sure the person who owns the decision knows what turns on it.

question_text: You are a supply chain graduate at a consumer goods company. Two people you work with, a planner and a site coordinator, have been arguing for a week about who caused a double order. The planner has now started sending you her messages to the coordinator to read. Both need to agree next week’s volumes with you by Thursday, and the argument is stopping that conversation happening at all. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Say to the planner that you are not the right audience for the messages, and ask both of them to a short meeting on next week's volumes so that the double order is aired there.
Agree next week's volumes with each of them separately before Thursday, so that the deadline is met without either of them having to sit in a room with the other while the argument is live.
Ask the coordinator's team leader behind his back what really happened with the double order, so that you know which of them you are dealing with before Thursday.
Reply to the planner that the messages are between the two of them, and wait for the argument to burn out before raising Thursday's volumes with either of them.
explanation: B: Works around the conflict rather than through it: Thursday is met, and the two people who have to plan together every week are further apart than they were. C: Investigates a colleague behind his back: it turns a disagreement about an order into a private judgement about a person, formed from one side and without his knowledge. D: Waits for a deadline to solve itself: the boundary is right and Thursday arrives with next week's volumes unagreed. The most effective response is to tell the planner you are not the right audience for the messages and to put both of them in a short meeting on next week’s volumes with the double order on the agenda: it declines the role of a private audience, and it makes the one conversation that has to happen the place where the argument gets aired. It beats agreeing volumes with each separately, because Thursday is met while the working relationship the next order depends on is left worse. It beats setting the boundary and then waiting, because nothing then moves the deadline forward. The least effective response is asking the coordinator’s team leader behind his back what really happened: it turns a dispute about an order into a private inquiry into a colleague, conducted from one side and without his knowledge, which is a different kind of wrong from avoiding the conflict or from working around it. The principle: refuse the private audience, and put the disagreement in front of the people who have to agree.

question_text: You are a stock control assistant at a consumer goods company. A weekly count shows three hundred units fewer than the system expects on one line. The trading team needs a figure this afternoon to decide what to order for next week, and they have asked you whether the count can be relied on. Investigating the gap properly means pulling the movement history, which takes about two hours. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Give the trading team the counted figure with the gap stated alongside it, say the cause is not yet known, and start on the movement history straight away.
Assure the trading team that the counted figure is sound and the gap is a scanning error, and look at the movement history later in the week if anybody comes back to you.
Hold the figure back until the movement history is finished, and tell the trading team they will have something reliable by the end of the day.
Give the trading team the figure the system holds rather than the counted one, since the system is what their ordering tool reads from in any case.
explanation: B: Gives an assurance you have not earned: nothing yet distinguishes a scanning error from three hundred missing units, and next week's order is placed on a cause that was invented to close the question. C: Delays the decision: the order has to be placed this afternoon, so a reliable number tomorrow is worth less to them than an honest one now. D: Substitutes the convenient source for the checked one: the count is the only evidence anybody has looked at, and it is the number being set aside. The most effective response is to give the trading team the counted figure with the gap stated alongside it and start on the movement history at once: they get a number in time to order, they know exactly how much weight it carries, and the work that settles the cause begins immediately. It beats holding the figure until the history is finished, because the decision is this afternoon and an honest number now beats a certain one tomorrow. It beats handing over the system figure instead, because the count is the only thing anybody has actually observed. The least effective response is assuring them the count is sound and the gap is a scanning error: no work has been done that could support either claim, and stating a cause you have not established is a different kind of wrong from being slow or from choosing the wrong source. The principle: report what you know and what you do not, rather than supplying the certainty the person asking would prefer.

question_text: You are a trading assistant at a consumer goods company. An account manager has asked you three times today whether a reconciliation is finished. It is not: it needs another hour. You also have a supplier payment file that must be submitted by three o’clock or it waits a week, and it is half past one. The reconciliation has no deadline other than his patience. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Do an hour on the reconciliation now to get him off your back, then submit the payment file with whatever time is left before the three o'clock cut-off.
Ask the account manager to take the reconciliation question to your manager, since being chased three times in a day is not something you should have to work around.
Tell him the reconciliation needs another hour and that he will have it by half past four, then submit the payment file before three so that it is not held a week.
Tell the account manager the reconciliation has been done so that he stops chasing, and finish it properly once the payment file has gone at three.

B: Escalates a question rather than answering it: he has asked a reasonable thing three times and still does not know when he will have it. D: Says a piece of work is finished when it is not: he may act on a reconciliation that does not exist yet, and the peace it buys lasts exactly until he looks. The most effective response is to tell him the reconciliation needs another hour and give him a time, then submit the payment file before three: the deadline with a week riding on it is protected, and the person chasing gets the one thing that will actually stop him chasing, which is a time. It beats doing an hour on the reconciliation first, because a task with no deadline is then funded out of the one with a hard cut-off. It beats sending him to your manager, because he has asked a fair question three times and still has no answer. The least effective response is telling the account manager the reconciliation has been done so that he stops chasing: he may act on work that does not exist, which is a different kind of wrong from ordering the day badly or from deflecting him. The principle: manage a chaser with a date, never with a false completion.

question_text: You are an insight assistant at a consumer goods company. You and a colleague share the monthly customer survey write-up: she pulls the data and you write the commentary. In last week’s team meeting she said the commentary was what had held the report up, which is not how you saw it. The next report is due on Friday and her data has just landed in your inbox. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Write the commentary and put a note at the top of the report setting out how long each stage took this month, so that the team can see where the time actually goes.

Write the commentary for Friday, and ask her for ten minutes today to agree who needs what by when, so that next month's timings are not a matter of opinion.
Stop drafting the commentary after that remark and leave her to write this month's herself, since she has a clear view about which part of the work takes the time.
explanation: A: Answers a private remark in a public document: the timings are accurate and the report becomes the place a disagreement between two colleagues is conducted. B: Prioritises harmony over honesty: the deadline is met and the same account of who slows the report down is left standing for next month. D: Withdraws your half of a shared job after a disagreement: Friday's report is put at risk to make a point, and the point is made to a colleague rather than about the work. The most effective response is to write the commentary for Friday and ask her for ten minutes to agree who needs what by when: the report still goes out, and the thing the two of you actually disagree about, which is where the time goes, gets settled in advance instead of in the next meeting. It beats putting a note about this month’s stage timings at the top of the report, because that argues with her in front of readers who have no part in it. It beats letting last week go, because the account she gave stands and the same thing happens next month. The least effective response is stopping the drafting and leaving her to write this month’s herself: the shared deadline is put at risk in order to answer a remark, which is a different kind of wrong from arguing in public or from staying quiet. The principle: a complaint about how shared work runs is fixed by agreeing how it will run, never by removing your part of it.

question_text: You are a supply chain graduate at a consumer goods company. A business customer’s order was due yesterday and has not arrived. The tracking shows it left and then nothing. The customer has emailed once, politely, asking where it is. Deliveries occasionally turn up a day or two late without anybody intervening. Chasing it properly means ringing the carrier and waiting on hold. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Reply to the customer that the order has left and that tracking will update when it moves, which is all the information the system currently gives you about it.
Ring the carrier now and say nothing to the customer until you have an answer, since a reply with no news in it will only invite another email.
Wait for the order to arrive in its own time, since deliveries often turn up a day or two late and the customer has only written once so far.
Reply today to say you are chasing the carrier and when you will come back to him, ring the carrier, and update him either way so that he knows a person has it.
explanation: A: Passes on the screen rather than the situation: he can read tracking himself, and nothing about his order has actually been chased. B: Leaves a waiting customer with silence: the chase is right and he does not know it is happening, so his next email arrives anyway. C: Waits out a customer who has asked a direct question: nothing is checked, nothing is answered, and the outcome depends entirely on the order turning up. The most effective response is to reply today saying you are chasing the carrier and when you will come back, ring them, and update him either way: he knows a person has his problem, the chase actually happens, and the commitment is one you control. It beats telling him tracking will update when it moves, because he can see that himself. It beats saying nothing to the customer until the carrier answers, because his second email arrives while you are on hold. The least effective response is waiting for the order to turn up in its own time: a direct question goes unanswered and nothing is checked, so a good outcome depends entirely on luck, which is a different kind of wrong from being unhelpfully literal or from being quiet while you work. The principle: a customer who has asked where something is gets an action and a time, not a probability.
