question_text: You are a customer care assistant at a consumer goods company. A customer is asking for a refund that is larger than you may approve. Refunds above your limit need a manager, and the manager is in a meeting for another hour. The customer is polite, has waited a long time already, and says he needs to know before he leaves for work. The refund itself looks reasonable to you. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Approve the part of the refund that is inside your limit now, and tell him the rest will need a manager's decision that you will chase this afternoon.
Tell him it is fine to expect the full refund and that nobody senior needs to look at a case as clear as his, which you have not actually checked.
Tell him the refund is above what you can approve, put the case to the manager with your recommendation as soon as her meeting ends, and give him a time you will ring back.
Interrupt the manager's meeting to get a decision on the refund now, since the customer is leaving for work shortly and has already waited a good deal longer than he should have had to.
explanation: A: Settles the easy half and leaves the substance: he gets part of an answer and still has to wait for the decision he actually rang about. B: States as settled something nobody has decided: he leaves for work believing the money is agreed, and the manager may see the case quite differently. D: Escalates by interruption: an hour's wait for a call back is a smaller cost than pulling a manager out of a meeting for a case that is not urgent in that sense. The most effective response is to tell him the refund is above your limit, put the case to the manager with your recommendation as soon as she is free, and give him a time you will ring back: he knows exactly where his case is, the decision goes to the person who owns it with your view attached, and the call back is a commitment you can keep. It beats approving the part inside your limit, because the decision he is waiting for is the rest. It beats interrupting the meeting, because an hour is a smaller cost than that. The least effective response is telling him it is fine and nobody senior needs to look at it: he leaves for work believing the money is agreed and nobody has decided anything, which is a different kind of wrong from half-answering or from escalating clumsily. The principle: say what is decided, by whom and when, rather than what the person in front of you would like to hear.
tip: Mẹo MT: Nhớ công thức tính nhanh: Tăng trưởng % = (Giá trị mới - Giá trị cũ) / Giá trị cũ × 100%.

question_text: You are a trading assistant at a consumer goods company. A large account has queried a charge on last month’s invoice. You have pulled the figures and can see the charge is correct, but the reason it changed is a contract term you do not fully understand. The account manager is out today. The customer wants an answer before the end of the week, and it is Wednesday. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Reply with the figures you have checked and what they show, say that the contract point needs the account manager, and book time with him for tomorrow morning.
Explain the contract term to the customer as best you understand it, and say you will confirm it with the account manager tomorrow.
Send the query on to the account team without the figures you have already checked, and let them start the contract point again from the beginning.
Reply to the customer that the charge is correct and leave the reason for the account manager to explain when he is back in the office tomorrow.
explanation: B: Answers outside what you actually know: an approximate account of a contract term is the thing most likely to be quoted back at the business later. C: Passes the problem on stripped of the work already done: the account team starts from nothing, the day you have spent on it is wasted, and Friday is two days away. D: Answers the easy half only: the customer did not ask whether the charge was right, they asked why it changed, and that is the part being deferred. The most effective response is to reply with the figures you have checked and what they show, say the contract point needs the account manager, and book time with him for tomorrow: the customer sees progress and an honest boundary, the checking work is used, and Friday is still comfortably reachable. It beats explaining the contract term as best you understand it, because an approximation about a contract is exactly the sentence that gets quoted back later. It beats replying that the charge is correct and leaving the reason to the account manager, because the reason is what was asked. The least effective response is sending the query on without the figures you have already checked: the next person starts from nothing, a day of work disappears, and the deadline is two days out, which is a different kind of wrong from over-reaching or from answering only half. The principle: escalate the part you cannot answer, with the part you can attached to it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Nhớ công thức tính nhanh: Tăng trưởng % = (Giá trị mới - Giá trị cũ) / Giá trị cũ × 100%.

question_text: You are a stock control assistant at a consumer goods company. A recount you asked for turned up a mistake in your own figures, and the colleague who did it said, in front of two others, that he had wasted an afternoon on your arithmetic. It stung and he was largely right. The next count is due on Thursday and it needs two people, one of whom is normally him. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Ask your supervisor to put somebody else on Thursday's count, since working alongside him this week would be uncomfortable for both of you after what was said.
Refuse to work with him on Thursday's count after the way he spoke to you, and say you would rather do it on your own or not at all.
Acknowledge to him that the figures were wrong and say what you have changed, and do Thursday's count with him as planned since the count needs two people.
Say nothing about it, do Thursday's count as planned, and let the remark fade rather than reopening something that was fair comment anyway.
explanation: A: Redesigns the rota around one awkward afternoon: the count is harder to staff, and the two of you have to work together again the week after in any case. B: Withdraws from a job that needs two people after a disagreement: Thursday's count is put at risk to answer a remark made about an afternoon. D: Lets an unrepaired working relationship stand: the count happens and he has no reason to think the mistake will not simply repeat. The most effective response is to acknowledge that the figures were wrong, say what you have changed, and do Thursday’s count with him: the criticism was largely fair, saying so is what restores the working relationship, and the count that needs two people gets them. It beats asking for somebody else on Thursday, because the rota is rearranged around one bad afternoon and you will work together next week anyway. It beats letting the remark fade, because he has no reason to expect anything different next time. The least effective response is refusing to work with him on Thursday: a count that needs two people is put at risk to answer a remark, which is a different kind of wrong from avoiding him or from staying silent. The principle: when the criticism is fair, own it and stay in the work with the person who made it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Nhớ công thức tính nhanh: Tăng trưởng % = (Giá trị mới - Giá trị cũ) / Giá trị cũ × 100%.

question_text: You volunteer as an assistant manager in a charity shop. Sorting donations you notice that a batch of electrical items has been put straight onto the shop floor without the safety testing the charity requires. Nobody has asked you to check this. The shop manager is on holiday for a week and the area manager covers by phone. The shop is open and the items are priced and on display now. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Ring the area manager to report that untested electrical items are on sale and ask whether she wants them removed before you touch anything.
Take the untested electrical items off the shop floor now and ring the area manager to tell her what you have found and ask how testing should be arranged.
Leave the items on display but attach a note to each saying it has not been safety tested, so that customers can decide for themselves whether to buy them.
Leave them as they are, since a volunteer putting stock out is not your responsibility and the manager will sort out the testing when she is back next week.
explanation: A: Delays the decision: the phone call is right and the items stay on sale while it happens. Removing them first costs nothing and is reversible if she disagrees. C: Passes responsibility to the customer: the charity's testing rule exists because a buyer cannot assess an appliance's safety from a label. Disclosing the gap does not close it. D: Fails to escalate a genuine risk: untested electrical goods stay on sale to the public for a week because the person who noticed decided it was not her job. The reason for silence is precisely why nobody else will catch it. The most effective response is to take the untested electrical items off the shop floor now and ring the area manager to tell her what you found: untested electrical goods on sale are a risk to whoever buys them, removing them is immediate, reversible and within your reach, and she needs to know so testing can be arranged properly. It beats ringing her first to ask whether she wants them removed, because that leaves the items on sale during the call and afterwards, when removing them costs nothing and can be undone if she disagrees. It beats attaching a note to each saying it has not been safety tested, because a label does not make an appliance safe, and it moves the judgement onto customers who cannot make it. The least effective response is leaving them as they are until the manager is back next week: it leaves untested electrical items on public sale for a week on the basis that someone else put them there. That is worse than ringing first, which reports it, and worse than labelling them, which at least warns buyers. The principle: when you find a live risk, remove it first if removing it is cheap and reversible, then tell whoever owns the process.
tip: Mẹo MT: Luôn kiểm tra kỹ đơn vị tính (Triệu VNĐ vs Tỷ VNĐ, Tháng vs Năm) trước khi tính toán.

question_text: You are a sales assistant at a garden centre. Your manager asked you this morning to price and shelve a delivery of spring bulbs before you finish at 5pm; the bulbs are not on promotion and no customer is waiting for them. At 2pm the till supervisor tells you the card terminal on the main till has failed, a queue is building at the single working till, and you are the only other member of staff trained to open the second one. Your manager is running a planting workshop outside for the next hour. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Open the second till straight away to clear the queue, then go back to the bulbs and let your manager know afterwards that the pricing may run past 5pm.
Carry on pricing the bulbs because your manager asked for them personally, and leave the till supervisor to manage the queue without mentioning that you are trained on the second till.
Serve at the second till between trips to the stockroom, pricing a few trays of bulbs each time the queue drops, so that both jobs keep moving through the afternoon.
Interrupt your manager's planting workshop to ask whether the bulbs or the till queue should come first, and wait for her decision before doing anything else.
explanation: B: Hides the problem: you hold the one fact that would fix the queue and you withhold it, so the supervisor cannot solve a problem she does not know is solvable. That is concealment, not a priority call. C: Splits effort so nothing finishes: customers are waiting now and the queue only clears if someone stays on the till, so stepping away repeatedly leaves the queue growing and the bulbs still unpriced. D: Escalates prematurely: a queue at the only working till against unpriced stock nobody is waiting for is a call you can make yourself, and interrupting a customer workshop costs more than it settles. The most effective response is to open the second till straight away and tell your manager afterwards: customers are waiting now, the bulbs are waiting for nobody, and the pricing deadline is internal and movable while the queue is neither. Telling her afterwards keeps her informed without pulling her out of a workshop. It beats serving at the second till between trips to the stockroom, because serving in bursts never clears a queue; the till needs someone sitting at it, and dividing yourself leaves both jobs half done. It beats interrupting her planting workshop to ask which comes first, because this is a straightforward call between a waiting customer and a task nobody is waiting on, and it does not need a manager pulled away from a customer event to make it. The least effective response is carrying on with the bulbs without mentioning that you are trained on the second till: you are the only other trained operator and you keep that to yourself, so the supervisor is left unable to fix something you could have fixed in seconds. That is worse than serving in bursts, which at least serves some customers, and worse than asking your manager, which at least surfaces the clash to someone. The principle: when one task has people waiting on it and the other does not, serve the people, then tell the person whose deadline slipped.
tip: Mẹo MT: Nhớ công thức tính nhanh: Tăng trưởng % = (Giá trị mới - Giá trị cũ) / Giá trị cũ × 100%.

question_text: You are a scheduler at a double glazing company. A customer has taken a day off work on Thursday for a full house installation booked eight weeks ago. On Tuesday the factory tells you three of the eight windows are the wrong size and will take three weeks to remake. The fitters could install the five correct windows on Thursday. The customer is contactable. Your operations manager is available today. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Send the fitters on Thursday to install the five correct windows, and tell the customer when they arrive that the other three will follow in three weeks.
Ring the customer today, explain that three windows are wrong and will take three weeks, and ask whether she wants the five fitted on Thursday or the whole job moved.
Cancel Thursday without explanation and rebook the whole installation for three weeks' time, since it is simpler to fit all eight windows in one visit.
Ring the customer today to say there is a problem with the order and that you will come back to her tomorrow once the operations manager has decided what to do.
explanation: A: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholder's: it decides for her that a partial installation is worth her day off, and tells her on the doorstep when she has already committed the day. C: Hides the problem: a customer who has booked a day off eight weeks in advance is cancelled with no reason given and no choice offered. The silence about why is what makes this worse than the other options. D: Delays the decision: it reaches her in time and gives her nothing to act on, when you already know precisely which windows are wrong, how long they will take and that Thursday could still be partly used. The most effective response is to ring the customer today, explain that three windows are wrong and will take three weeks, and ask whether she wants the five fitted on Thursday or the whole job moved: she has committed a day off, Tuesday still leaves her time to change her plans, and only she can decide whether five windows are worth the day. Giving her the facts and both options is what makes the day off recoverable. It beats sending the fitters on Thursday and telling her on the doorstep, because that takes the decision about her own day out of her hands. It beats ringing to say there is a problem and that you will come back tomorrow, because you already know everything she needs, so withholding it serves no purpose. The least effective response is cancelling Thursday without explanation and rebooking the whole installation: it cancels a day she booked eight weeks ago with no explanation and no alternative, purely because one visit is tidier for the company. That is worse than fitting five, which at least fits five, and worse than the holding call, which at least makes contact. The principle: when a failure affects a day someone has already committed, tell them at once, tell them the whole of it, and let them choose.
tip: Mẹo MT: Trong đề thi SHL, quản lý thời gian tối đa 60-75 giây cho mỗi câu tính toán số học.

question_text: You are a course administration assistant at a probation service. Another assistant on the course team has fallen behind: forty trainees’ preparation tasks are unmarked on the completion log, which has to be complete before Monday’s assessment. They have told only you and have asked you not to make a fuss. You can see which tasks have actually been submitted and which have not. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Mark all forty preparation tasks on the completion log as done so the log is ready for Monday, and let the colleague check the submissions afterwards when they have caught up.
Tell the colleague you will help, that the person who runs the course has to know today, since only they can move Monday, then mark with them only what is genuinely in.

Work through all forty unmarked tasks yourself in the evenings on top of your own work, checking each submission as you go, and tell nobody, so that the colleague is not embarrassed and the log is ready by Monday.

Send the person who runs the course a note this morning saying the colleague is forty tasks behind on the completion log, before saying anything to the colleague, so that Monday's assessment is not put at risk.
explanation: A: Records work as done that was never checked: the log then says trainees have prepared when you can see that some have not, and Monday's assessment runs on it. C: Avoids the difficult conversation: one person quietly absorbing a two-person backlog gets Monday through and leaves the same colleague in the same position next month. D: Goes over the colleague's head first: they confided in you, a word to them costs nothing, and the note arrives without any account of what has actually been submitted. The most effective response is telling the colleague you will help while making clear that the person who runs the course has to know today: Monday is fixed, forty tasks are unmarked, and the only person who can move the assessment or find another pair of hands is the one nobody has told. It beats working through the unmarked tasks yourself in the evenings and telling nobody, because one person quietly absorbing a two-person backlog leaves the same problem standing next month. It beats sending a note about the colleague before saying anything to them, since they confided in you and a word first costs nothing and keeps them in the conversation. The least effective response is marking all forty tasks on the completion log as done: the log then says trainees have prepared when you can see that some have not, and Monday’s assessment runs on a record you know to be wrong. The principle: help a struggling colleague by getting the right people involved, never by making the paperwork say something that is not so.
tip: Mẹo MT: Dùng phương pháp ước lượng chữ số hàng đơn vị hoặc làm tròn đến hàng chục để loại ngay 2 phương án vô lý.

question_text: You are a security analyst. A project has finished and left eleven unused software licences that nobody has asked about. Two colleagues have already taken one each for personal machines and told you it is normal. The licences cost the company four hundred pounds each per year and renew automatically next month unless somebody cancels them. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Cancel the nine that are left before the renewal and say nothing about the two that have already gone, so that the money is saved without anybody being named.
Take one of the licences for your own use as the others have, and cancel the rest before the renewal date, which still saves the company most of the money.
Tell whoever owns the project budget that eleven licences are renewing next month and that two are already on personal machines, so that they decide what happens to all eleven.
Raise it with the two colleagues and ask them to hand theirs back, then cancel all eleven before the renewal without involving anybody else in it.
explanation: A: Solves the cost and buries the rest: four hundred pounds a year is still walking out on two machines and the practice is left described as normal. B: Takes an advantage the role forbids: you are the person who saw the licences, and the saving does not buy you one of them. D: Settles it privately with the people who took them: it may work, and the budget holder still never learns that eleven licences nearly renewed unnoticed. The most effective response is to tell whoever owns the project budget that eleven licences are renewing next month and that two are already on personal machines. The renewal is a real deadline, the budget holder can act on it, and the two already gone are part of the same fact rather than a separate accusation. It beats cancelling the nine that are left and saying nothing about the two, because two are still being paid for and the practice goes unexamined. It beats asking the two colleagues to hand theirs back and cancelling all eleven yourself, because that may resolve today without anybody learning that eleven licences sat unnoticed. The least effective response is taking one of the licences for your own use as the others have: it is worse than either of the other two, because both end with you holding nothing, while this has the person who spotted the problem taking a share of it. The principle: when you find something valuable that nobody is watching, the finding goes to whoever owns it, and finding it earns you none of it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Trong đề thi SHL, quản lý thời gian tối đa 60-75 giây cho mỗi câu tính toán số học.

question_text: You are an account coordinator at a translation company. A client needs a contract translated for a signing on Thursday. On Tuesday your specialist legal translator falls ill. A generalist could produce a draft by Thursday but it would not carry the legal certification the client asked for. A certified version is possible by Monday. The client’s counsel is contactable. Your operations director is available. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Have the generalist produce the draft for Thursday, and tell the client's counsel it is uncertified when you deliver it.
Tell the client's counsel that the translation will now be ready on Monday, since a certified document is what was ordered and an uncertified one would not meet the requirement.
Ring the client's counsel today, explain the certified version cannot be ready before Monday and an uncertified draft could meet Thursday, and let them decide.
Deliver the generalist's draft on Thursday presented as the completed translation, since it will read correctly and the certification is a formality that can follow afterwards.
explanation: A: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholder's: whether an uncertified translation is usable at a signing is counsel's judgement, and telling them on delivery leaves no time to decide otherwise. B: Delays the decision: it offers only the option that misses the signing, and withholds the existence of a Thursday draft that counsel might well find useful. D: Misrepresents the work: presenting an uncertified translation as the completed certified document is a false statement about a legal deliverable, and a signing may proceed on a document that does not carry what it appears to. The most effective response is to ring the client’s counsel today, explain the certified version cannot be ready before Monday and an uncertified draft could meet Thursday, and let them decide: certification is exactly what was ordered, only counsel can judge whether an uncertified draft is usable at a signing or whether the signing should move, and Tuesday leaves time for either. Giving both facts is what makes the choice real. It beats telling them the translation will now be ready on Monday, because offering only that hides a Thursday option counsel might prefer. It beats having the generalist produce the draft and disclosing that it is uncertified on delivery, because that presents the decision as already made. The least effective response is delivering the generalist’s draft as the completed translation: it passes off an uncertified document as the certified one, so a contract may be signed on a paper that does not carry what it appears to. That is worse than the other two, which choose badly but describe the work honestly. The principle: when you cannot deliver what was specified, put the real alternatives to the client at once and never let a substitute be mistaken for the original.
tip: Mẹo MT: Trong đề thi SHL, quản lý thời gian tối đa 60-75 giây cho mỗi câu tính toán số học.

question_text: You are a finance assistant at an engineering company. Yesterday you emailed the monthly departmental spending report to six department heads. Today you notice a formula error pulled last month’s figures into two columns, overstating several budgets. The department heads hold separate budget meetings tomorrow morning, where they will set spending plans using your report. It is now mid-afternoon and you have already prepared a corrected version. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Plan to explain the correction in person at the start of tomorrow's meetings rather than emailing today, so the department heads hear it directly from you with the right context.
Replace the report on the shared drive with the corrected version without telling anyone, since anyone who opens the file again before their meeting will see the right figures.
Email all six department heads now, state plainly that yesterday's report contained an error, attach the corrected version, and highlight which columns changed so they use the right figures tomorrow.
Tell your own manager about the error first and wait for their advice on how to word the correction before contacting any of the department heads.
explanation: A: Delays the message: the department heads may prepare tonight using the overstated figures, and with six separate meetings running tomorrow morning you cannot be in the room to deliver the correction at every one. B: Hides the problem: silently swapping the file conceals that an error ever existed, and anyone working from yesterday's email or a saved copy keeps the wrong figures with no warning. That is concealment, not just a slower or clumsier correction. D: Tells the wrong audience first: briefing your manager is sensible, but waiting for advice before contacting anyone leaves the six people who actually rely on the figures uninformed while a simple factual correction sits ready to send. The most effective response is to email all six department heads now, state plainly that yesterday’s report contained an error, and attach the corrected version: they are the people relying on the figures, the correction is ready, and an email this afternoon reaches all of them before they prepare for tomorrow, highlighting exactly which columns changed. It beats waiting to explain the correction in person at tomorrow’s meetings, because that leaves the heads working from overstated figures overnight and depends on you being present at six separate meetings you cannot all attend. It beats telling your own manager first and waiting for advice on the wording, because a straightforward factual correction needs no approval, and waiting leaves the affected people uninformed for hours when you could simply copy your manager in. The least effective response is replacing the file on the shared drive without telling anyone: unlike correcting it in person, which does eventually tell everyone, and unlike checking with your manager, which at least starts an open correction, it relies on people happening to reopen the file and conceals that a mistake was ever made. The failure is the concealment, not the speed. The principle: when you have sent out wrong information, correct it quickly, openly, and directly to everyone relying on it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Luôn kiểm tra kỹ đơn vị tính (Triệu VNĐ vs Tỷ VNĐ, Tháng vs Năm) trước khi tính toán.

question_text: You work in a field sales team and process your colleagues’ expense claims. A colleague submits mileage for a client visit on a day you know he was at the regional office, because you saw him there. The amount is small. He is popular and has just had a difficult quarter. The expenses policy is clear that claims must reflect actual journeys. Your sales manager is available. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Process the claim and mention to your sales manager that the mileage looked unusual, so that she can look into it if she thinks it is worth it.
Go back to the colleague, tell him the claimed journey does not match the day he was at the regional office, and ask him to correct or explain it before you process it.
Reject the claim in the system with a note that the journey could not have taken place, and let him take it up if he disagrees.
Process the claim as submitted, since the amount is small, he has had a hard quarter and querying it would be awkward and probably damage your working relationship.
explanation: A: Passes responsibility to others: it pays the claim first and raises a vague concern afterwards, so the money has gone and the manager is given a hint rather than a fact. C: Escalates prematurely: a formal rejection recorded against a colleague is a serious step taken before he has been asked, when there may be a simple explanation such as a wrong date. D: Breaches process to protect a colleague: it knowingly pays a claim for a journey that did not happen, because the sum is small and the conversation would be uncomfortable. That is dishonesty by omission, not discretion. The most effective response is to go back to the colleague, tell him the claimed journey does not match the day he was at the regional office, and ask him to correct or explain it: the discrepancy is a fact, there may be an innocent explanation such as the wrong date entered, and the person who can settle it in a sentence is the one who made the claim. Asking him first is both fairer and faster than any other route. It beats rejecting the claim in the system with a note that the journey could not have taken place, because a formal rejection on his record is a heavy step before he has had the chance to explain a possible typing error. It beats processing it and mentioning to your sales manager that the mileage looked unusual, because that pays out first and passes her a suspicion instead of a question that could already have been answered. The least effective response is processing the claim as submitted because the amount is small and querying it would be awkward: it knowingly pays for a journey that did not take place, which is precisely the reasoning that makes small false claims routine. That is worse than the other two, which act clumsily but do not knowingly pay. The principle: put the discrepancy to the person who created it before either paying it or recording it against them.
tip: Mẹo MT: Nhớ công thức tính nhanh: Tăng trưởng % = (Giá trị mới - Giá trị cũ) / Giá trị cũ × 100%.

question_text: You are a sales administrator at a car dealership, responsible for recording confirmed orders. Monthly sales figures close at 5pm today, and staff bonuses are based on them. Priya, a salesperson you get on well with, asks you to record one of her deals as a confirmed order even though the customer has not signed, saying the customer will definitely sign early next week and that the deal would take her past her monthly target. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Record the deal as a confirmed order, reasoning that the customer is very likely to sign next week and a few days' difference is unlikely to be noticed by anyone.
Tell Priya directly that you cannot record an unsigned deal as confirmed, and suggest she asks the sales manager whether the almost-completed sale can be recognised another way.
Put Priya off by saying you are too busy to update the system this afternoon, hoping the 5pm deadline passes without you having to refuse her outright.
Report Priya to the sales manager for attempted fraud straight away, on the basis that she has probably inflated her figures in previous months as well.
explanation: A: Falsifies a business record: entering an unsigned deal as confirmed misstates figures that bonuses are paid on, and makes you personally complicit in dishonesty, a different kind of wrong from the weaker but honest alternatives. C: Prioritises harmony over honesty: inventing an excuse to avoid refusing a friend dodges the falsification but never addresses the request, and leaves Priya free to ask someone else before 5pm. D: Acts on assumptions without checking: escalating a single request as probable repeated fraud treats suspicion as fact. The immediate situation needs a clear refusal and a legitimate route, not an accusation built on guesswork. The most effective response is to tell Priya directly that you cannot record an unsigned deal as confirmed: it refuses the request honestly, explains the real reason, and points her to a legitimate route by suggesting she ask the sales manager whether an almost-completed sale can be recognised another way, so the record stays true without wrecking the working relationship. It beats putting her off with a claim that you are too busy this afternoon, because that hides behind an invented excuse, never addresses the request, and leaves her free to try someone else before the 5pm close. It beats reporting her for attempted fraud straight away, because that turns one improper request into an unevidenced accusation of repeated dishonesty when a proportionate refusal resolves the situation. The least effective response is recording the deal as a confirmed order: unlike stalling, which falsifies nothing, and unlike going straight to the sales manager, which is heavy-handed but honest, it makes the record itself false and misstates figures that pay is based on. The category failure here is dishonesty, and it makes you complicit. The principle: when loyalty or convenience pulls against honest records, decline clearly and point to a legitimate route instead.

question_text: You are a commercial finance assistant at a retail chain. Two colleagues you work with, one in trading and one in supply, have fallen out over a promotion whose cost came in well above plan. Each has told you separately that the other changed a number without saying so. Both have asked you what the other said. The figure has to be explained in Monday’s review, and you are the person who holds both versions of the file. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Ask each of them separately to walk you through their version of the change, then decide yourself which account the file supports and take that to Monday's review.
Write up what the file shows and send it straight to the reviewer before Monday, leaving the two of them to sort out between themselves how the change happened and who made it.
Tell each of them what the other has been saying about the change, so that both know where they stand before the review on Monday.
Put both versions of the file in front of the two of them together and say what changed and when, so that they agree between them what Monday's review is told about the cost.
explanation: A: Substitutes your own judgement for theirs: you arbitrate between two colleagues in private, and whichever way it lands, the loser hears the verdict at the review. B: Avoids the difficult conversation: the number is explained and the working relationship the next promotion depends on is left exactly as it is. C: Personalises the disagreement: it turns a question about a figure into a question about two people's accounts of each other, and does it in the way least likely to survive either of them repeating it. The most effective response is to put both versions of the file in front of the two of them together and ask them to agree what the review is told: the disagreement is about what the file shows, the file is in front of everybody, and the people who have to work together next month settle it themselves. It beats writing it up and sending it to the reviewer, because Monday is covered and nothing between the two colleagues is. It beats hearing each version separately and deciding which the file supports, because a private arbitration by the most junior person present leaves one of them told they were wrong by you. The least effective response is telling each of them what the other has been saying: the argument stops being about the promotion cost and becomes about what each said behind the other’s back, which is a different kind of wrong from ducking the conversation or over-reaching in it. The principle: put the evidence in front of both parties at once, and let the disagreement be about the thing rather than about each other.

question_text: You are a customer care assistant at a retail chain. A customer says she rang three weeks ago and was told her order would be replaced free of charge. You can see the call on her record and a short note that matches what she describes. Replacing it free now would cost more than your team usually allows, and the colleague who took that call has since left. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell her you can see the call and the note and apologise that nothing followed, and put the case to your team leader today since honouring it is above your own limit.
Tell her you have no record of the earlier call and offer the standard remedy instead, since the colleague who took it has left and cannot be asked what was said.
Tell her the note exists but that a free replacement is above what the team allows, and offer the standard remedy as the most you are able to do today.
Tell her you will look into what was said on the call and come back to her next week, since the colleague concerned has left and the note is brief.
explanation: B: Denies something you can see in front of you: the note is on her record, and she is told it does not exist by the one person looking at it. C: Treats your own limit as the end of the matter: the promise was made by the business, and nobody with the authority to honour it has been asked. D: Delays behind an inquiry that cannot happen: the colleague has gone, the note is all there will ever be, and she waits another week for the same facts. The most effective response is to tell her you can see the call and the note, apologise that nothing followed, and put the case to your team leader today: the evidence is acknowledged, the decision goes to somebody who can honour a promise the business made, and it happens now rather than next week. It beats saying the note exists but the cost is above your limit, because that treats your own authority as the last word. It beats promising to look into the call next week, because there is nothing more to find. The least effective response is telling her there is no record of the earlier call: the note is on her record and she is told it does not exist by the person reading it, which is a different kind of wrong from under-reaching or from stalling. The principle: never deny what your own screen shows, and take a promise you cannot honour to somebody who can.
tip: Mẹo MT: Nhớ công thức tính nhanh: Tăng trưởng % = (Giá trị mới - Giá trị cũ) / Giá trị cũ × 100%.

question_text: By what percentage did the North region’s revenue increase from Q1 to Q2?

Reading the £36,000 increase itself as the percentage gives 36.0%; the size of a change in pounds and the percentage it represents are different quantities.

question_text: A distribution centre splits 4,900 parcels between three depots in the ratio 3:4:7. How many parcels does the largest depot receive?

The other two depots receive 3 × 350 = 1,050 and 4 × 350 = 1,400, and those three figures sum back to 4,900 as a check. Answering 1,050 or 1,400 means reading off one of the smaller depots, and answering 350 means stopping at the value of a single part instead of multiplying it by the 7 parts the question asks about.

34.0 litres
40.0 litres

question_text: A supplier invoices €4,680. The exchange rate is £1 = €1.17 and the company’s bank adds a 2.5% conversion fee to the sterling amount. What is the total cost in pounds?

Multiplying by 1.17 instead of dividing gives £5,475.60, and stopping at £4,000.00 forgets the fee entirely. question_text: What is the total gross profit across all three products?

Widget C: (32.50 − 21.00) = £11.50 × 640 = £7,360. Total gross profit = 6,600 + 7,650 + 7,360 = £21,610. Total revenue alone is £62,800 and total cost alone is £41,190, and the difference between those two confirms £21,610. Adding the three unit margins on their own gives 5.50 + 9.00 + 11.50 = £26.00, which is the profit on one of each product rather than on everything sold; each margin still has to be multiplied by that product’s units.

question_text: Three printing machines produce 7,200 flyers in 4 hours. Working at the same rate, how long would five machines take to produce 13,500 flyers?
options: 1.5 hours
4.5 hours
5.625 hours
7.5 hours
explanation: Find the rate for a single machine first: 7,200 ÷ (3 machines × 4 hours) = 600 flyers per machine per hour. Five machines therefore produce 5 × 600 = 3,000 flyers per hour. The time needed is 13,500 ÷ 3,000 = 4.5 hours. The three wrong options each come from a specific slip. Reading 7,200 ÷ 4 = 1,800 flyers per hour as one machine’s rate and then multiplying by five gives 9,000 per hour and 13,500 ÷ 9,000 = 1.5 hours, but 1,800 is the output of all three machines together. Dividing 7,200 by the three machines and forgetting the four hours gives 2,400 per machine and 13,500 ÷ 2,400 = 5.625 hours. Leaving the fleet at three machines gives 13,500 ÷ 1,800 = 7.5 hours.

question_text: After a 12% discount, a maintenance contract costs £30,800. What was the price before the discount?

Adding 12% to the discounted figure instead gives 30,800 × 1.12 = £34,496, which is wrong because the 12% was taken off the larger original amount. Taking a further 12% off gives 30,800 × 0.88 = £27,104, which discounts a price that has already been discounted. Reversing the discount correctly and then adding the 12% back on top counts it twice: 35,000 × 1.12 = £39,200.

question_text: What is the combined value of the three invoices in pounds?

question_text: A team of 24 people earns an average salary of £38,500. Next year headcount rises by 25% and the average salary rises by 4%. What will the total salary bill be?

question_text: You work for a tour operator. A group of twenty-four is flying out on Saturday on a walking holiday. On Wednesday the mountain hut booked for two nights closes after a water supply failure. An alternative hut is available but is four hours’ walk further on, which changes two days of the itinerary. The group leader is contactable. Your operations manager is available today. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Rebook the alternative hut and send the group leader a revised itinerary, so the holiday is secured and everyone knows the new plan before they fly.
Wait until the water supply position is clearer later in the week, since the hut may reopen before Saturday and a change of itinerary would unsettle the group unnecessarily.
Let the group travel as booked and have the guide explain the change of route when they reach the mountain, since the alternative hut will be arranged by then anyway.
Ring the group leader today, explain the hut closure and what the alternative would mean for two days of walking, and agree the plan before anything is rebooked.
explanation: A: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholder's: adding four hours' walking to two days changes what the group signed up for, and some members may not be able to do it. That is the group leader's call, not a booking amendment. B: Delays the decision: the alternative hut may be taken by another group while you wait, and the leader loses the days in which walkers could have prepared or withdrawn. C: Hides the problem: twenty-four people are told on the mountain that two days now involve four hours' more walking, when some may be unable to manage it and none of them can do anything about it there. That is concealment with a safety dimension. The most effective response is to ring the group leader today, explain the hut closure and what the alternative would mean for two days of walking, and agree the plan before anything is rebooked: four extra hours on two days is a material change, some of twenty-four people may not manage it, and only he can judge that for his group. Wednesday leaves time to prepare, adjust or withdraw. It beats rebooking the alternative hut and sending a revised itinerary, because that presents the change as settled when its acceptability depends on the group. It beats waiting until the water supply position is clearer later in the week, because that risks losing the alternative hut and burns the days the group needs. The least effective response is letting them travel as booked and having the guide explain the change of route on the mountain: it tells twenty-four walkers the route has lengthened substantially at the one point where nobody can opt out. That is worse than the other two, which decide or delay but do not spring it on people in the field. The principle: when a change affects what people are physically committing to, tell whoever speaks for them while they can still choose.

question_text: You are an operations coordinator. A cabin crew member is waiting at an airport away from base to find out whether she flies home tonight or stays in a hotel. The decision depends on a meeting that will not finish for about two hours. She has asked twice already and has been given no answer either time. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Wait until the meeting has finished and the answer is certain, then call her with the decision so that she is told once and told accurately.
Tell her the decision has been made and that you will send it through shortly, so that she has something to hold on to while the meeting finishes.
Send a message to a colleague at that airport asking them to let her know the decision is still a couple of hours away, so she hears it from somebody nearby.
Call her now, tell her the decision is about two hours away and why, and say that you will ring her back as soon as it is made either way.
explanation: A: Waits for certainty at somebody else's expense: she sits for two more hours not knowing whether to look for food, a hotel or a flight, and the silence is the part she has already complained about twice. B: Invents a decision that has not been taken: she stops waiting and starts planning on the strength of it, and the meeting may yet go the other way. C: Relays a simple message through a third person: it depends on a colleague being free and passing it on accurately, when the call would take a minute from here. The most effective response is to call her now, tell her the decision is about two hours away and why, and promise to ring back as soon as it is made: she cannot plan the next two hours without knowing that they are two hours, the call costs a minute, and a promised time replaces uncertainty with a wait she can manage. It beats waiting until the meeting has finished so she is told once and accurately, because the silence, not the decision, is what she has already complained about twice. It beats asking a colleague at that airport to let her know the decision is still a couple of hours away, because relaying a simple message adds delay and a chance of it arriving garbled. The least effective response is telling her the decision has been made and will follow shortly: it says an answer exists when it does not, so she plans around something that may still go the other way. That is worse than the other two, which are slow or roundabout but tell her nothing untrue. The principle: when somebody is waiting on you, tell them what you know and when you will know more, rather than waiting until you can tell them everything.

question_text: You are an operations coordinator on a day of heavy disruption. An evening flight has been cancelled and its thirty passengers need rebooking onto the last service of the night, where seats are being taken by other cancelled flights as you work. You also owe your manager the delay report for this morning, which she needs by the end of the day. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Write the delay report first while this morning is still fresh in your mind, then turn to the rebooking with whatever seats on the night service are still showing as available.
Ask your manager which of the two she would rather have finished tonight, and begin whichever she names once she has come back to you with an answer.
Rebook the thirty passengers onto the night service straight away, then write the delay report afterwards and send it to your manager before you finish for the day.
Rebook the passengers whose journeys look most complicated, then write the report, and come back to the remaining rebookings if there is time before the end of your shift.
explanation: A: Spends a contested resource on a fixed one: the report can be written at any hour of the day, while the seats disappear as you type, and the passengers who lose them cannot be told why. B: Hands back a decision you can make: the seats are going while the question sits in her inbox, and nothing about the choice needs information you do not already hold. D: Splits effort so nothing finishes: the passengers left until later are competing for the same shrinking seats, and are no less stranded for having simple itineraries. The most effective response is to rebook the thirty passengers onto the night service straight away, then write the delay report and send it before you finish: seats are being consumed by other people while you decide, and the report is due at a time of day rather than at a moment, so the rebooking is the only task that gets harder every minute you leave it. It beats rebooking only the passengers whose journeys look most complicated, because that still leaves the rest chasing a shrinking pool, and simple itineraries do not make a passenger less stuck. It beats asking your manager which she would rather have finished tonight, because she has no information you lack, and the seats go while the question waits. The least effective response is writing the delay report first while the morning is fresh: it spends the contested resource to protect a deadline that was never in danger, so passengers lose seats that were there when the shift started. That is worse than the partial rebooking, which at least books some of them, and worse than asking your manager, which loses minutes rather than the whole night. The principle: when one task is competing for something that is running out and the other is not, the scarce thing decides the order.

question_text: You are an administrator in a pension scheme’s benefits team. Checking a routine calculation you notice that the formula used for a group of about thirty members appears to apply the wrong revaluation rate, which would mean they have been underpaid for several years. You are relatively new and the calculation is complex. The scheme actuary reports quarterly. Your benefits manager is in the office. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Work through the whole group's calculations yourself over the coming weeks so that you can present a fully evidenced case rather than a suspicion.
Take your workings to the benefits manager today, explain which rate appears to have been applied and that the calculation is complex and you may have it wrong.
Raise it with the scheme actuary at the next quarterly report, since the revaluation rate is a technical question that falls squarely within the actuary's remit.
Leave it, since the formula has presumably been reviewed and audited over the years and you are new enough to be misreading a calculation you do not fully understand.
explanation: A: Delays the decision: weeks of solo checking on a complex calculation postpones a possible underpayment to thirty pensioners, when the benefits manager could confirm the principle in an afternoon. C: Delays the decision by choosing the wrong route: the actuary is the right technical authority and the wrong clock, and the benefits manager is the person who can involve them now rather than in three months. D: Fails to escalate a genuine risk: thirty pensioners may have been underpaid for years, and the reason for silence is that others must have checked, which is the assumption the error itself disproves. Being unsure is a reason to ask, not to say nothing. The most effective response is to take your workings to the benefits manager today, explain which rate appears to have been applied and that you may have it wrong: you may have found a long-running underpayment to thirty pensioners, you cannot confirm it, and she can either dismiss it or escalate it to the actuary within the day. Saying plainly that you may be mistaken is honest and costs nothing. It beats working through the whole group’s calculations yourself over the coming weeks, because that postpones a possible underpayment while you build certainty someone else could reach far faster. It beats raising it with the scheme actuary at the next quarterly report, because that is the right expertise on a three- month delay. The least effective response is leaving it because the formula has presumably been reviewed and audited over the years: it lets a possible multi-year underpayment stand on exactly the assumption your own check calls into question. That is worse than the other two, which are too slow but do act. The principle: take an uncertain but serious finding to whoever can confirm it, promptly, and be open about your own uncertainty.
tip: Mẹo MT: Nhớ công thức tính nhanh: Tăng trưởng % = (Giá trị mới - Giá trị cũ) / Giá trị cũ × 100%.

question_text: You work in the accounts office of a small manufacturer. A supplier’s representative drops in with a Christmas hamper addressed to you personally, saying it is a thank you for prompt payment. The company’s policy requires gifts over a nominal value to be declared to a manager, and you are involved in approving that supplier’s invoices. Your finance manager is in the office. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Take the hamper home without mentioning it, since it was addressed to you personally, it is only a seasonal gesture and it will not change how you handle the supplier's invoices.
Accept it provisionally, declare it to your finance manager today given that you approve this supplier's invoices, and follow whatever she decides.
Refuse the hamper on the spot and tell the representative that the company does not allow suppliers to give gifts to staff.
Put the hamper in the staff room for everyone to share, so that no individual benefits from it and nothing needs declaring.
explanation: A: Breaches confidentiality or process: the declaration rule exists precisely because the recipient cannot vouch for their own impartiality, and taking a supplier's gift home unrecorded while approving their invoices is the conflict the policy is written to catch. C: Applies the rule without using it: the policy provides for declaration, not blanket refusal, and turning it away at the door resolves it without the record that the policy exists to create. D: Acts on assumptions without checking: sharing it changes who eats it, not whether a supplier gave a gift to someone who approves their invoices. The declaration is still owed and is now less likely to happen. The most effective response is to accept it provisionally and declare it to your finance manager today, given that you approve this supplier’s invoices: that is exactly the situation the declaration rule exists for, and she is in the office and can decide whether it is kept, returned or shared. Declaring it puts the decision where the policy intends. It beats putting the hamper in the staff room for everyone to share, because that changes who benefits without removing the conflict or creating the record. It beats refusing it on the spot and telling the representative gifts are not allowed, because that is well meant but skips the declaration, so nothing is recorded about a supplier offering gifts to the people who approve their invoices. The least effective response is taking it home without mentioning it because it will not change how you handle the invoices: that assurance is precisely the one the policy exists because nobody can give about themselves. That is worse than the other two, which handle it imperfectly but do not conceal. The principle: declare the thing the policy asks you to declare, and let the person it names decide what happens to it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Nhớ công thức tính nhanh: Tăng trưởng % = (Giá trị mới - Giá trị cũ) / Giá trị cũ × 100%.

question_text: You are an accounts assistant. A department head asked for a breakdown of his costs by project. The system can only split them by cost centre, which is close but not the same, and he will notice. Producing it takes two hours. He needs it on Thursday. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell him today that the split is by cost centre rather than by project, explain the difference, and ask whether that is still worth two hours of work.
Spend the two hours mapping cost centres to projects by hand so he gets exactly what he asked for, without checking whether the approximation would have done.
Produce the cost centre breakdown and send it on Thursday without saying that it is not the project split he asked for, since the two are close enough for most purposes anyway.
Reply that the system cannot produce a breakdown by project at all and simply leave it there, so that he can decide for himself what he wants to do about it from his end.
explanation: B: Buys precision nobody asked the price of: a hand mapping may be unnecessary and it is the slowest route to Thursday. C: Withholds the one difference that matters: he asked for projects, receives cost centres, and nothing on the page tells him they are not the same thing. D: Reports the obstacle and stops: the cost centre split is close and may well serve, and he cannot judge that without being offered it. The most effective response is to tell him today that the split is by cost centre rather than by project, explain the difference, and ask whether that is still worth two hours: he learns what is actually available, understands the gap, and decides whether the work is worth doing. It beats replying that the system cannot produce a breakdown by project at all, because a flat no withholds something that probably serves. It beats spending the two hours mapping cost centres to projects by hand, because nobody has established that the approximation would not do. The least effective response is producing the cost centre breakdown and sending it without saying it is not the project split he asked for: he uses cost centres believing they are projects. That is silence about the difference rather than an unhelpful or over-thorough answer. The principle: when what you can give is not what was asked for, say so before you build it.

question_text: You volunteer as an assistant manager in a charity shop. Sorting donations you notice that a batch of electrical items has been put straight onto the shop floor without the safety testing the charity requires. Nobody has asked you to check this. The shop manager is on holiday for a week and the area manager covers by phone. The shop is open and the items are priced and on display now. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Ring the area manager to report that untested electrical items are on sale and ask whether she wants them removed before you touch anything.
Take the untested electrical items off the shop floor now and ring the area manager to tell her what you have found and ask how testing should be arranged.
Leave the items on display but attach a note to each saying it has not been safety tested, so that customers can decide for themselves whether to buy them.
Leave them as they are, since a volunteer putting stock out is not your responsibility and the manager will sort out the testing when she is back next week.
explanation: A: Delays the decision: the phone call is right and the items stay on sale while it happens. Removing them first costs nothing and is reversible if she disagrees. C: Passes responsibility to the customer: the charity's testing rule exists because a buyer cannot assess an appliance's safety from a label. Disclosing the gap does not close it. D: Fails to escalate a genuine risk: untested electrical goods stay on sale to the public for a week because the person who noticed decided it was not her job. The reason for silence is precisely why nobody else will catch it. The most effective response is to take the untested electrical items off the shop floor now and ring the area manager to tell her what you found: untested electrical goods on sale are a risk to whoever buys them, removing them is immediate, reversible and within your reach, and she needs to know so testing can be arranged properly. It beats ringing her first to ask whether she wants them removed, because that leaves the items on sale during the call and afterwards, when removing them costs nothing and can be undone if she disagrees. It beats attaching a note to each saying it has not been safety tested, because a label does not make an appliance safe, and it moves the judgement onto customers who cannot make it. The least effective response is leaving them as they are until the manager is back next week: it leaves untested electrical items on public sale for a week on the basis that someone else put them there. That is worse than ringing first, which reports it, and worse than labelling them, which at least warns buyers. The principle: when you find a live risk, remove it first if removing it is cheap and reversible, then tell whoever owns the process.

question_text: You are a production planner at a commercial bakery. Tomorrow’s production schedule must be in the system by 5pm today; without it, the overnight shift bakes to last week’s quantities, and this week’s wholesale orders are noticeably different. This morning the owner asked you to prepare a costing summary he needs for a bank meeting at ten tomorrow morning; he is driving between suppliers all afternoon and cannot be reached. It is 2pm, each task takes about two hours, and you start at 7:30 tomorrow. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Build the schedule now so it is in the system by 5pm, then leave the owner a message that his summary will be ready before his ten o'clock meeting, since the schedule's cut-off is fixed and the summary is not needed until mid-morning.
Keep trying the owner's phone before committing to either task, so the person whose meeting it is chooses what comes first, and start immediately on whichever he picks once you get through.

Spend the afternoon making the costing summary as strong as it can be, adding the comparison charts a bank is likely to ask for, since the loan decision matters more to the bakery's future than one night's baking quantities.

Rough out both pieces of work in the time available, entering a part-finished schedule before 5pm and drafting the summary's headline figures, then complete whichever still needs work when you arrive at 7:30 tomorrow.
explanation: B: Delays the decision: asking the owner would normally be right, but he is stated to be unreachable all afternoon, so time spent waiting for an answer burns down the one window in which the 5pm schedule can still be completed. C: Gold-plates one task while the other burns: the summary has until mid-morning tomorrow, yet this option spends today's only remaining hours adding unrequested extras to it while the single fixed deadline (the 5pm schedule) is knowingly allowed to pass, sending the overnight shift to bake the wrong quantities. D: Splits effort so nothing finishes: a part-finished schedule still leaves the overnight shift guessing on the lines you did not reach, and the drafted figures gain nothing from being started today, since the summary can be finished tomorrow morning before it is needed. The most effective response is to build the schedule now and leave the owner a message that his summary will be ready before his ten o’clock meeting: the schedule’s 5pm cut-off is the only deadline that expires today, a whole shift bakes from it overnight, and a 7:30 start tomorrow still finishes the summary comfortably, so the defensible call is to protect the fixed deadline and say exactly when the rest will arrive. It beats trying the owner’s phone before committing to either task, because the stem says he is unreachable all afternoon, so the waiting itself is what puts the 5pm cut-off at risk. It beats roughing out both pieces of work and finishing tomorrow, because a part-finished schedule still leaves the overnight shift guessing on the unentered lines, while starting the summary early gains nothing that tomorrow’s spare half-hour does not already provide. The least effective response is spending the afternoon polishing the costing summary and adding comparison charts: unlike chasing the owner, which at least tries to get the right person deciding, and unlike roughing out both, which at least gets most of the schedule entered, it knowingly abandons the only fixed deadline to add polish nobody asked for to a task with hours of slack, so the whole overnight bake runs on wrong quantities. The principle: when a stakeholder is unreachable, protect the deadline that cannot move, make the defensible call, and communicate it. Waiting or polishing is a decision too, just an unowned one.

question_text:
【Ngữ cảnh】：The appeal in Larkhill against Brindle Manufacturing was heard by three judges over two days in March. The court allowed the appeal on one ground and dismissed it on the other two. It substituted a declaration for the order the judge below had made, and remitted the question of costs. The judgment was given by one judge with whom the other two agreed. It has been published on the court’s own site and runs to twenty-six paragraphs.

【Câu hỏi】：Based only on the information in the passage, is the following statement True, False, or Cannot say? Statement: “The appeal was heard by three judges.”
options: True
False
Cannot say
explanation: The statement is True. The passage says the appeal “was heard by three judges over two days in March”, which is the statement in the same words. The rule: a statement the passage states outright is True. The most tempting wrong judgement is False, because the passage later says the judgment was given by one judge, and a reader who reads that as the whole court will halve the bench.
tip: Mẹo MT: Trong đề thi SHL, quản lý thời gian tối đa 60-75 giây cho mỗi câu tính toán số học.

question_text: Based only on the Kestrel Logistics data shown, is the following statement True, False, or Cannot say? Statement: “Kestrel Logistics revenue rose by 10% from 2024 to 2025.”
options: True
False
Cannot say
explanation: The statement is False. Revenue went from 105.0 to 113.4 GBP m, a rise of 8.4 on a base of 105.0, which is 8%; the 10% figure belongs to 2022 to 2023, where 84.0 rose by the same 8.4 to 92.4. The rule: a percentage change is measured against the earlier year’s own base, so an identical absolute rise is a different percentage in different years. Here a correct percentage has been attached to the wrong pair of years.
tip: Mẹo MT: Dùng phương pháp ước lượng chữ số hàng đơn vị hoặc làm tròn đến hàng chục để loại ngay 2 phương án vô lý.

question_text: Based only on the Kestrel Logistics data shown, is the following statement True, False, or Cannot say? Statement: “Operating costs equalled 85% of Kestrel Logistics revenue in 2022.”
options: True
False
Cannot say
explanation: The statement is True. In 2022 operating costs were 71.4 GBP m against revenue of 84.0 GBP m, and 85% of 84.0 is 71.4, so the proportion is exact. The rule: a share claim is checked by taking the stated percentage of the named base, here revenue, rather than by eyeballing the two figures against each other. Both values are read from the 2022 column.
tip: Mẹo MT: Trong đề thi SHL, quản lý thời gian tối đa 60-75 giây cho mỗi câu tính toán số học.

question_text: Based only on the Kestrel Logistics data shown, is the following statement True, False, or Cannot say? Statement: “Kestrel Logistics revenue will exceed 120.0 GBP m in 2026.”
options: True
False
Cannot say
explanation: The statement is Cannot say. The table stops at 2025, and no row carries a forecast, a target or any statement about future trading. The rule: a percentage change describes the years it was measured over and does not license a claim about a year the table does not cover. Extending a trend forward is an assumption, not a reading.
tip: Mẹo MT: Nhớ công thức tính nhanh: Tăng trưởng % = (Giá trị mới - Giá trị cũ) / Giá trị cũ × 100%.

question_text: Based only on the Kestrel Logistics data shown, is the following statement True, False, or Cannot say? Statement: “Kestrel Logistics averaged 70 GBP of revenue per delivery in 2024.”
options: True
False
Cannot say
explanation: The statement is True. In 2024 revenue was 105.0 GBP m against deliveries of 1,500 thousand, and 105,000,000 divided by 1,500,000 is 70 GBP per delivery. The rule: when numerator and denominator are stated at different scales, millions against thousands, both must be put on the same scale before dividing. The average is named per delivery, so deliveries are the divisor.
tip: Mẹo MT: Nhớ công thức tính nhanh: Tăng trưởng % = (Giá trị mới - Giá trị cũ) / Giá trị cũ × 100%.

question_text: Based only on the Kestrel Logistics data shown, is the following statement True, False, or Cannot say? Statement: “Kestrel Logistics revenue exceeded operating costs by 16.8 GBP m in 2023.”
options: True
False
Cannot say
explanation: The statement is False. In 2023 revenue of 92.4 GBP m less operating costs of 77.0 GBP m leaves 15.4 GBP m; the gap of 16.8 belongs to 2024 and again to 2025. The rule: a difference claim has to be recomputed for the year it names, because a gap that recurs in other years is easy to accept without checking. Reading down the 2023 column is what settles it.

The Standard was amended last year to add two questions about outsourcing, and the Office publishes a template alongside it each January. Firms may submit the return through the Office’s portal or by post.

options: True
False
Cannot say

The rule: a stated obligation is a fact about the rule and never a report of what a firm did. The most tempting wrong answer is True, because every element of the test is supplied except the one that settles it.
