question_text: You are a course administration assistant at a traffic enforcement agency. You keep the sign in sheet for a five day course. At the end of day three the sheet shows 28 people signed in, but the course leader’s list has 30 names and your own room log has 30 people present. The stated rule is that the certificate list is built from the sign in sheet, and it is confirmed on Friday. Nobody else has noticed the gap. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Add the two missing names to the sheet yourself and mark day three as checked, since you saw both of them in the room and two either way makes no practical difference.
Raise it with the course leader on Friday when the certificate list is confirmed, since the sheet may well be corrected by then and two names is not much to chase in the meantime.
Write a note beside the sheet saying the count did not agree on day three, and leave it for whoever confirms the certificate list on Friday to look into.
Compare the room log and the leader's list against the sheet today, then tell the course leader which two names are missing and how the gap arose, so the sheet is right before Friday.
explanation: A: Writes into a record something you did not witness being signed: the sheet is the source the certificate list is built from, so an entry you made up is now the evidence that two people attended. B: Delays the check to the deadline itself: Friday is when the list is confirmed, so a discrepancy raised that morning has to be resolved under time pressure or waved through. C: Flags a problem without owning it: you are the person who holds the room log, so the one piece of evidence that would settle the gap sits with you and not with the reader of the note. The most effective response is comparing the room log and the leader’s list against the sheet today and telling the course leader which two names are missing and how the gap arose. Nobody has assigned this to you, you hold the evidence that explains it, and Friday is a fixed point after which the certificate list is built from whatever the sheet says. It beats raising it with the course leader on Friday itself, because a gap found on the day of confirmation gets resolved in a hurry or not at all. It beats writing a note beside the sheet for whoever confirms the list, because the room log that would settle the question is yours and the reader of the note does not have it. The least effective response is adding the two missing names yourself and marking day three as checked: that puts into the source record an entry nobody signed, so a certificate list built from it now rests on your recollection presented as somebody’s signature. It is worse than the Friday conversation and worse than the note because both of those leave the record honest and merely late, while this leaves it wrong and looking right. The principle: when a total you own does not reconcile, find out why while there is still time, and never close the gap by writing the answer in.
tip: Mẹo MT: Luôn kiểm tra kỹ đơn vị tính (Triệu VNĐ vs Tỷ VNĐ, Tháng vs Năm) trước khi tính toán.

question_text: You are a course administration assistant at a traffic enforcement agency, and you send out joining instructions for training courses. A person booked onto next month’s course was told in writing that they would have their joining instructions by the 12th. It is now the 19th, they have rung twice, and they have travel to book. The person who prepares joining instructions is away until Thursday and nobody else can produce them. You do not know why the 12th was missed. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Ring the person today, tell them the joining instructions are not ready, explain that the person who prepares them is back on Thursday, and promise a date by Friday, since they must book travel.
Reply by email that their query has been logged and that somebody will be in touch about it, giving no date, so that you are not committing anybody else to a promise you cannot keep.
Assure the person that their joining instructions were sent out last week and will reach them shortly, which buys quiet until Thursday and saves them a third phone call.
Wait until Thursday and put it to the person who prepares joining instructions the moment they are back, so that the caller hears the real date from the person who actually owns the work.
explanation: B: Answers without the one fact they need: the person has travel to book and has already waited a week past the 12th, so a reply carrying no date leaves them exactly where the missed date left them. C: Gives an assurance you have not checked: nothing tells you the instructions were ever sent, and the person may book travel around a course date that nobody has confirmed to them. D: Delays the reply for a tidier answer: the caller has waited a week past the date they were given and has travel to book, and two more silent days is what the tidier answer costs them. The most effective response is ringing the person today to say the joining instructions are not ready, that the person who prepares them is back on Thursday, and that you will call again by Friday with a date. That is better than replying by email that their query has been logged with no date attached, because the caller can do nothing with an acknowledgement and still cannot decide whether to book travel. It is also better than waiting until Thursday to put it to the person who prepares them, since the caller spends two more days with no word at all. The least effective response is assuring the person that their joining instructions were sent out last week: you have not checked that, the assurance stops them chasing, and they may spend money on travel for a date nobody has confirmed. Waiting at least leaves the caller free to keep asking, and a dateless email at least tells them nothing untrue. The principle: when you cannot give somebody the answer they were promised, give them the truth and the next date, never a comfortable version of the truth.
tip: Mẹo MT: Luôn kiểm tra kỹ đơn vị tính (Triệu VNĐ vs Tỷ VNĐ, Tháng vs Năm) trước khi tính toán.

question_text: You work on the forecourt of a petrol station. Part of your role is recording the daily fuel dip readings, which are used to detect leaks from the underground tanks. Today’s reading is a hundred litres below what the sales figures predict. Your colleague says the dipstick is unreliable, that this happens most weeks, and that you should write down the expected figure so the paperwork is not queried. The manager is in tomorrow. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Record the actual reading, and ring the manager today to tell her the dip is a hundred litres below the expected figure so she can decide whether the tanks need checking.
Write down the expected figure as your colleague suggests, since the dipstick is known to be unreliable and a queried reading would only create work for the manager tomorrow.
Record the actual reading and take a second dip yourself at the end of your shift to see whether the discrepancy is repeated before mentioning it to anyone.
Record the actual reading and leave a note for the manager to find when she comes in tomorrow, so that the discrepancy is documented and she can look into it then.
explanation: B: Falsifies a safety record: the dip readings exist to detect leaks from underground fuel tanks, so entering the number you expected rather than the one you measured removes the only signal the system has. That is dishonesty with a safety consequence. C: Delays the decision: the record is right, which matters, but a hundred-litre gap on a fuel tank is exactly the reading somebody qualified should see today rather than after your own retest. D: Fails to escalate a genuine risk: the reading is honest and the urgency is missed. A possible fuel leak waits overnight on a note when a phone call today would have reached the person who can act. The most effective response is to record the actual reading and ring the manager today about the hundred-litre shortfall: the reading goes in as measured, and a discrepancy that size on an underground fuel tank is a possible leak, so she hears about it today rather than tomorrow. It beats taking a second dip yourself at the end of your shift, because retesting before telling anyone delays a safety signal in order to satisfy your own curiosity, when the manager is a phone call away. It beats leaving a note for her to find when she comes in tomorrow, because that leaves a possible leak unattended overnight for no gain. The least effective response is writing down the expected figure because the dipstick is known to be unreliable: it puts a number that was never measured into the record that exists specifically to detect leaks, so a real leak would be invisible, and it does so to avoid creating work. That is worse than the other two, which are too slow but keep the record true. The principle: record what you measured, and get a safety discrepancy to somebody who can act on it on the day you find it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Dùng phương pháp ước lượng chữ số hàng đơn vị hoặc làm tròn đến hàng chục để loại ngay 2 phương án vô lý.

question_text: You pick online grocery orders at a supermarket. A customer’s order includes a specific nut-free chocolate spread, which is out of stock. The system suggests a standard chocolate spread as a substitute. The order notes say it is for a child with a severe nut allergy. Another nut-free spread is available in a different size at a higher price. Your shift manager can authorise price matching. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Reject the substitution and leave the item out of the order, so that nothing unsuitable is sent and the customer can buy her own elsewhere.
Substitute the alternative nut-free spread and ask your shift manager to price match it, so the order arrives with something the child can safely eat.
Substitute the alternative nut-free spread at its higher price, since it is the only safe option and the customer would rather pay more than go without.
Accept the system's suggested standard spread, since it is the recommended substitute and the customer can always refuse it at the door if it does not suit her.
explanation: A: Ignores the customer's actual need: a suitable nut-free spread is on the shelf, so leaving the line unfilled sends her nothing when a workable substitute exists. C: Acts on assumptions without checking: the substitution is right and the price increase is assumed to be acceptable, when a shift manager who could price match it is available and has not been asked. D: Ignores a stated allergy with a health consequence: the notes say the spread is for a child with a severe nut allergy, so accepting the system's suggestion sends the one product that could actually harm him. Following the system over a stated allergy is the worst of the four. The most effective response is to substitute the alternative nut-free spread and ask your shift manager to price match it: the order notes state an allergy, a safe alternative is on the shelf, and the only obstacle is a price difference a manager can authorise away. That gets the child something safe at the price the customer expected. It beats substituting the alternative at its higher price, because that makes the same correct swap while assuming she will accept paying more, when the manager could remove that. It beats rejecting the substitution and leaving the item out of the order, because that sends her nothing when a suitable product exists. The least effective response is accepting the system’s suggested standard spread because she can refuse it at the door: it substitutes an ordinary spread for one flagged for a child with a nut allergy, which is the single product in the aisle that could harm him. That is worse than the other two, which cost her money or an item but send nothing unsafe. The principle: when a customer has stated an allergy, meet it with a safe product and use the authority above you to deal with the price.
tip: Mẹo MT: Nhớ công thức tính nhanh: Tăng trưởng % = (Giá trị mới - Giá trị cũ) / Giá trị cũ × 100%.

question_text: You work in the control room of a taxi firm. Drivers are paid a bonus for completing more than forty jobs a week. You notice a driver has logged three jobs this week that were cancelled by the customer before pickup, which would take him over forty. He says the customers cancelled at the door, so he drove the distance and should be credited. The firm’s rules on cancelled jobs are written and you have not read them. The operations manager is on shift. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Check the written rules on cancelled jobs, and if they do not cover doorstep cancellations put it to the operations manager before the bonus is calculated.
Remove the three cancelled jobs from his total, since the jobs were not completed and the bonus is for completed work.
Leave the three jobs on his total and let the bonus be paid, since he did drive to each address and nobody audits the weekly figures in any detail.
Report the driver to the operations manager for logging cancelled jobs as completed work in order to reach the bonus threshold.
explanation: B: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholder's: the rules may well credit a driver who travelled to a doorstep cancellation, and striking the jobs out decides that without reading them. C: Falsifies a payment record: it lets a bonus be paid on jobs recorded as completed that were not, without checking whether the rules allow it, and relies on the absence of an audit. That is dishonesty, not a judgement call. D: Escalates prematurely: the written rules may entitle him to the credit, so a report of deliberate manipulation is made before the document that settles it has been read. The most effective response is to check the written rules on cancelled jobs, and if they do not cover doorstep cancellations put it to the operations manager before the bonus is calculated: there is a rule that decides whether such a cancellation counts, reading it costs a minute, and he is on shift and can settle it in time. It answers the question without accusing anyone. It beats removing the three cancelled jobs from his total, because that decides the same question in the driver’s disfavour without reading the rule. It beats reporting him for logging cancelled jobs as completed work, because a serious accusation before checking risks condemning him over something the rules may allow. The least effective response is leaving the three on his total because nobody audits the weekly figures: it lets a bonus be paid on incomplete jobs without any check. That is worse than the other two, which act hastily but keep the payment honest. The principle: read the rule that governs it, and take the decision to whoever owns it rather than resolving it quietly either way.
tip: Mẹo MT: Trong đề thi SHL, quản lý thời gian tối đa 60-75 giây cho mỗi câu tính toán số học.

question_text: You work in the accounts office of a small manufacturer. A supplier’s representative drops in with a Christmas hamper addressed to you personally, saying it is a thank you for prompt payment. The company’s policy requires gifts over a nominal value to be declared to a manager, and you are involved in approving that supplier’s invoices. Your finance manager is in the office. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Take the hamper home without mentioning it, since it was addressed to you personally, it is only a seasonal gesture and it will not change how you handle the supplier's invoices.
Accept it provisionally, declare it to your finance manager today given that you approve this supplier's invoices, and follow whatever she decides.
Refuse the hamper on the spot and tell the representative that the company does not allow suppliers to give gifts to staff.
Put the hamper in the staff room for everyone to share, so that no individual benefits from it and nothing needs declaring.
explanation: A: Breaches confidentiality or process: the declaration rule exists precisely because the recipient cannot vouch for their own impartiality, and taking a supplier's gift home unrecorded while approving their invoices is the conflict the policy is written to catch. C: Applies the rule without using it: the policy provides for declaration, not blanket refusal, and turning it away at the door resolves it without the record that the policy exists to create. D: Acts on assumptions without checking: sharing it changes who eats it, not whether a supplier gave a gift to someone who approves their invoices. The declaration is still owed and is now less likely to happen. The most effective response is to accept it provisionally and declare it to your finance manager today, given that you approve this supplier’s invoices: that is exactly the situation the declaration rule exists for, and she is in the office and can decide whether it is kept, returned or shared. Declaring it puts the decision where the policy intends. It beats putting the hamper in the staff room for everyone to share, because that changes who benefits without removing the conflict or creating the record. It beats refusing it on the spot and telling the representative gifts are not allowed, because that is well meant but skips the declaration, so nothing is recorded about a supplier offering gifts to the people who approve their invoices. The least effective response is taking it home without mentioning it because it will not change how you handle the invoices: that assurance is precisely the one the policy exists because nobody can give about themselves. That is worse than the other two, which handle it imperfectly but do not conceal. The principle: declare the thing the policy asks you to declare, and let the person it names decide what happens to it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Nhớ công thức tính nhanh: Tăng trưởng % = (Giá trị mới - Giá trị cũ) / Giá trị cũ × 100%.

question_text: You are an administrator in a pension scheme’s benefits team. Checking a routine calculation you notice that the formula used for a group of about thirty members appears to apply the wrong revaluation rate, which would mean they have been underpaid for several years. You are relatively new and the calculation is complex. The scheme actuary reports quarterly. Your benefits manager is in the office. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Work through the whole group's calculations yourself over the coming weeks so that you can present a fully evidenced case rather than a suspicion.
Take your workings to the benefits manager today, explain which rate appears to have been applied and that the calculation is complex and you may have it wrong.
Raise it with the scheme actuary at the next quarterly report, since the revaluation rate is a technical question that falls squarely within the actuary's remit.
Leave it, since the formula has presumably been reviewed and audited over the years and you are new enough to be misreading a calculation you do not fully understand.
explanation: A: Delays the decision: weeks of solo checking on a complex calculation postpones a possible underpayment to thirty pensioners, when the benefits manager could confirm the principle in an afternoon. C: Delays the decision by choosing the wrong route: the actuary is the right technical authority and the wrong clock, and the benefits manager is the person who can involve them now rather than in three months. D: Fails to escalate a genuine risk: thirty pensioners may have been underpaid for years, and the reason for silence is that others must have checked, which is the assumption the error itself disproves. Being unsure is a reason to ask, not to say nothing. The most effective response is to take your workings to the benefits manager today, explain which rate appears to have been applied and that you may have it wrong: you may have found a long-running underpayment to thirty pensioners, you cannot confirm it, and she can either dismiss it or escalate it to the actuary within the day. Saying plainly that you may be mistaken is honest and costs nothing. It beats working through the whole group’s calculations yourself over the coming weeks, because that postpones a possible underpayment while you build certainty someone else could reach far faster. It beats raising it with the scheme actuary at the next quarterly report, because that is the right expertise on a three- month delay. The least effective response is leaving it because the formula has presumably been reviewed and audited over the years: it lets a possible multi-year underpayment stand on exactly the assumption your own check calls into question. That is worse than the other two, which are too slow but do act. The principle: take an uncertain but serious finding to whoever can confirm it, promptly, and be open about your own uncertainty.
tip: Mẹo MT: Nhớ công thức tính nhanh: Tăng trưởng % = (Giá trị mới - Giá trị cũ) / Giá trị cũ × 100%.

question_text: You are an administrator in a college admissions office. It is results week, your colleague who shares the enquiry inbox is off sick, and incoming enquiries have roughly doubled since Monday. You have also promised the finance office an enrolment reconciliation they need before they can start invoicing tuition fees. This morning the queue of unanswered enquiries is growing visibly, and your team leader asks how you plan to manage the day. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Assure your team leader you will cover the doubled enquiries and still deliver the reconciliation today, so nobody needs to worry about the absence.
Set the reconciliation aside for the week and put all your time into the enquiry queue, assuming the finance office can start invoicing a little later.
Take a few minutes to assess the workload, tell your team leader realistically what you can cover today and where support is needed, then work through the enquiries steadily.
Tell your team leader, in front of the rest of the team, that the situation is unmanageable and management should have arranged cover, and continue only with your normal workload.
explanation: A: Over-promises: committing to absorb a doubled enquiry load and still deliver the reconciliation today gambles on a pace one person is unlikely to sustain, and sets up a late failure that is harder to manage than an honest assessment now. B: Abandons own committed work: dropping the reconciliation on an assumption leaves the finance office unable to start invoicing, without checking what they actually need, a promise quietly shelved rather than pressure honestly managed. D: Blames others publicly: announcing in front of the team that the situation is unmanageable, while refusing to adapt, turns pressure into complaint; it does nothing to reduce the queue and undermines the team leader and colleagues who still have to cope. The most effective response is to assess the workload, tell your team leader realistically what you can cover and where support is needed, then work the queue steadily: it meets the spike calmly and gives an honest picture of what one person can and cannot do, which keeps output up without pretending the pressure away. It beats assuring your team leader you will cover everything, because that promises a pace one person is unlikely to sustain, and the resulting failure would surface late in the day when it is hardest to fix. It beats setting the reconciliation aside for the week, because that quietly shelves a commitment the finance office is relying on, based on an assumption about their timetable rather than a conversation. The least effective response is declaring the situation unmanageable in front of the rest of the team and doing only your normal workload: unlike over-promising, which at least throws effort at the problem, and unlike shelving the reconciliation, which at least keeps the enquiry queue moving, it converts pressure into public blame and refusal, helping nobody and souring the team on a difficult day. The principle: under a workload spike, stay composed. Assess honestly, tell people what is realistic, and keep working, rather than over-promising, quietly dropping commitments, or blaming.
tip: Mẹo MT: Luôn kiểm tra kỹ đơn vị tính (Triệu VNĐ vs Tỷ VNĐ, Tháng vs Năm) trước khi tính toán.

question_text: You are a finance assistant at a charity. Reconciling the restricted funds you notice that a grant given specifically for a youth project appears to have been spent on general running costs over several months. You are new and may be misreading the fund codes. The trustees meet in a fortnight and the grant’s annual report to the funder is due next month. Your finance manager is in the office. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Take your workings to the finance manager this week, explain what the codes appear to show and that you may have misread them, and ask her to check before the trustees meet.
Spend the next fortnight tracing every transaction yourself so that you can present a complete and certain picture rather than a half- formed concern.
Leave it, since you are new, the fund codes are complicated and the finance manager and the auditors will have reviewed the restricted funds already.
Raise it directly with the trustees at their meeting in a fortnight, since restricted funds are their responsibility and the finance manager may have been involved in the spending.
explanation: B: Delays the decision: certainty is worth having and a fortnight of solo work takes you past the trustees' meeting, when the finance manager could confirm or dismiss it in an hour. C: Fails to escalate a genuine risk: a restricted grant may have been misapplied with a report to the funder due next month, and the reason for silence is an assumption that others have checked, which is what your own reconciliation calls into question. D: Escalates prematurely: you are new, you may have misread the fund codes, and going to the trustees first implies wrongdoing by the finance manager on the strength of a reading nobody has checked. The most effective response is to take your workings to the finance manager this week, explain what the codes appear to show and that you may have misread them, and ask her to check before the trustees meet: you may be right or you may have misread, and she can establish which in an hour, well before the meeting and the funder’s report. Saying plainly that you may be wrong is honest and costs nothing. It beats spending the next fortnight tracing every transaction yourself, because reaching certainty that way takes you past the meeting where it would have mattered. It beats raising it directly with the trustees at their meeting, because going there first, as a new member of staff working from an unchecked reading, implies misconduct by your manager before anyone has confirmed there is even an error. The least effective response is leaving it because the fund codes are complicated and others will have reviewed them: it leaves a possible misuse of restricted funds unexamined with a report to the funder due next month. That is worse than the other two, which act too slowly or in the wrong order but do act. The principle: take an unconfirmed but serious finding to the person who can confirm it, promptly, and be honest that you may have it wrong.

question_text: You work as a graduate coordinator in an Accenture operations team. Last week a colleague you share a work queue with told your manager that your handover notes were poor, and your manager agreed with him. He left yesterday for two weeks of leave. This morning you find an unactioned client request sitting in his queue, and the agreed response time on it runs out at noon tomorrow. Your manager is at her desk. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Stop covering that colleague's queue while he is away, because he complained to your manager about you, and leave the client request exactly where he left it.
Tell your manager now that the request in his queue breaches the response time at noon tomorrow, and offer to action it yourself today so the client is not affected.
Send a message to the colleague on leave asking whether he wants the request actioned, and hold off doing anything with it until his answer comes back.
Action the client request quietly yourself and keep the miss out of the queue report, so that nobody has to hear about a colleague's oversight while he is on leave.
explanation: A: Withdraws help after a disagreement: it answers a complaint about your notes by letting a client commitment run out at noon, which puts a private grievance ahead of the client and of the team's word. C: Delays the decision: he is away for two weeks and the response time runs out at noon tomorrow, so waiting on his reply spends the only working hours the request has left. D: Hides the problem: the client is protected this once, but the manager never learns that a queue can hold an unactioned client request for a week without anything noticing. The most effective response is to tell your manager now that the request breaches the response time at noon tomorrow, and to offer to action it yourself today. Your manager is at her desk, the deadline is real, and the fastest route to protecting the client also puts the queue gap in front of the person who can fix it. It beats a message to the colleague on leave, because his answer cannot arrive before the deadline does, and the request needs a decision today rather than a permission. It also beats quietly actioning it and keeping the miss out of the report, because that protects the client this once and leaves the same gap open for the next fortnight. The least effective response is to stop covering the colleague’s queue because he complained about you: the other two responses at least keep the client in view, while this one uses a client commitment as the currency of a disagreement with a colleague. This is what Accenture’s ‘Stewardship’ value points to. The principle: a grievance with a colleague never changes what you owe the client, and the escalation decision is made on the deadline, not on who left the work.
tip: Mẹo MT: Trong đề thi SHL, quản lý thời gian tối đa 60-75 giây cho mỗi câu tính toán số học.

question_text: You are a graduate software engineer in an Accenture team of five, each of you responsible for one component of a release. The whole release hands over to another team on Thursday and can only go if all five components have passed the shared integration suite. At this morning’s stand-up the delivery lead asks the team for a straight yes or no. Yours has passed. You have not looked at the other four, and two of their owners are away today. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Confirm to the delivery lead that all five components have passed, without checking the other four, on the grounds that everything was built from the same code this week.
Ask the delivery lead to put the answer off until Friday, when both absent owners are back and each of them can check their own component properly.
Say that your own component has passed, ask the two owners present to check theirs during the stand-up, and offer to run the suite for the two who are away.
Run the integration suite yourself for all five components before answering, which takes the rest of your day and repeats work each owner could do in minutes.
explanation: A: Gives an assurance you have not checked: Thursday's handover to another team goes ahead on the strength of that yes, and four of the five components standing behind it are unverified. B: Delays the decision: the handover is on Thursday, and the two owners who are present could each check their component in the ten minutes the stand-up is already using. D: Absorbs work that belongs to the team: it reaches a true answer, but it spends a day of your own release work doing what four people could each finish before lunch. The most effective response is to say that your own component has passed, ask the two owners present to check theirs, and offer to run the suite for the two who are away. It answers only for what you know, and it closes the gap inside the meeting rather than after it. It beats putting the answer off until Friday, because the handover is on Thursday and two of the four unknowns could be settled in the room. It also beats running the whole suite single-handed, which buys a true answer at the price of a day you owe the release. The least effective response is to confirm that all five components have passed without checking the other four: the other two responses are slow or expensive but honest about what is known, while this one puts a statement in front of the delivery lead that you are in no position to make, and another team plans three days of work around it. The principle: answer for your own part, and get the rest checked rather than assumed.

question_text: You work as a graduate service analyst on an Accenture managed services account. The client’s operations manager phones, angry that a monthly report reached him late three times this quarter. He wants a named colleague of yours taken off the account, saying your colleague clearly does not care. Two of the delays followed the client’s own data arriving late; the third was your colleague’s own slip. Your service lead is in a meeting until four o’clock. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell the operations manager that two of the three delays came from his own team sending data late, so there is nothing on your side that needs changing at all.
Tell the operations manager you will put his request to your service lead at four o'clock, and end the call once you have taken his name and his number.
Ask the operations manager what the late reports cost his team, say the staffing question sits with your service lead, and send him the cause of each delay and a fix by five.
Agree with the operations manager, blaming your colleague for all three late reports, and add that you have wondered about his attitude to the account for a while yourself.
explanation: A: Answers a complaint by pushing it back at the customer: one of the three delays really was your team's, so a flat defence is untrue as well as being the last thing a customer wants after a bad quarter. B: Passes the customer on without touching what he asked for: the reports arriving late is the thing he actually needs fixed, and nobody has said a word about it by the time the call ends. D: Blames a colleague to keep a customer comfortable: it buys agreement with a judgement about somebody who is not on the call, and it teaches the customer that attacking one of your people is how his reports get fixed. The most effective response is to ask the operations manager what the late reports cost his team, and to send him the cause of each delay and a fix by five. It treats the reports as the problem, keeps the staffing question with the person who owns it, and gives the client something concrete before the day ends. It beats telling him the delays came from his own team sending data late, because one of the three was genuinely yours and a defence that is partly false ends the conversation without fixing anything. It also beats taking his details and waiting for four o’clock, which is polite and leaves the client exactly where he started. The least effective response is to agree with the operations manager and blame your colleague for all three late reports: the other two responses handle the complaint badly, while this one hands a customer a verdict on an absent colleague and still leaves the reporting unfixed. This is what Accenture’s ‘Respect for the Individual’ value points to. The principle: answer the customer’s actual need, and never buy their goodwill with a colleague’s reputation.
tip: Mẹo MT: Dùng phương pháp ước lượng chữ số hàng đơn vị hoặc làm tròn đến hàng chục để loại ngay 2 phương án vô lý.

question_text: You are a graduate analyst on an Accenture consulting engagement for a grocery retailer, with read access to the client’s sales data for the pricing study you work on. The engagement agreement limits that data to this study. A colleague on a different engagement, for another retailer, asks you for last year’s regional sales figures as a sanity check, and says nothing will leave his laptop. No audit trail records who opens the folder. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Decline, and explain that the sales data is limited to your own engagement, then offer to ask your engagement manager whether published market figures would answer the colleague's question.
Extract national totals rather than regional figures for the colleague, on the view that a coarser cut of the numbers is no longer really the client's own data.
Pull the regional figures and let the colleague have them on the understanding that nothing leaves his laptop, since he works for the same firm and no client will ever see it.
Refuse the request and report it to the client's data owner the same day, without speaking to your engagement manager or telling the colleague what you have done about it.
explanation: B: Draws the line yourself instead of where the agreement draws it: the agreement limits the data, not the level of aggregation, so a national cut is the same breach with a rounder number attached to it. C: Breaches a client confidence because it is convenient: the engagement agreement is the only reason the client let anybody see these numbers, and a colleague's promise about his laptop is not a term the client ever agreed to. D: Escalates past everybody who should hear it first: the colleague asked a question rather than took anything, and telling the client ahead of your own manager turns a conversation into an incident nobody can take back. The most effective response is to decline and explain that the sales data is limited to your own engagement, then offer to ask your engagement manager about published market figures. It holds the line the client was given, and it still tries to get the colleague a usable answer from a source that is nobody’s confidence. It beats extracting national totals rather than regional figures, because the agreement restricts the data itself and aggregating it is a judgement you have no standing to make on the client’s behalf. It also beats reporting the colleague straight to the client’s data owner, which treats a request as an incident and does it without the manager who would have to live with the consequences. The least effective response is to pull the regional figures and let the colleague have them on the understanding that nothing leaves his laptop: the other two responses misjudge where a line sits or who to tell, while this one moves a client’s data outside the agreement that was the condition of your seeing it, on the strength of a private assurance and the absence of a trail. This is what Accenture’s ‘Stewardship’ value points to. The principle: a confidence holds because it was given, not because somebody is watching.

question_text: The table shows Rowsley Handling’s charges last month. Next month Ryedale Airways expects 540 sectors at Quenby. At Quenby’s cost per sector last month, what will the Quenby charge be?
explanation: Build Quenby’s own rate, then scale it to next month’s sectors. 122,400 divided by 480 = £255 per sector. 255 x 540 = £137,700. A common error here is averaging the three stations’ rates, which gives £163,800 and answers a question about the network rather than about Quenby. The passengers column is not needed: the charge is asked per sector, not per passenger.

question_text: Based only on the Marbrook Foods data shown, is the following statement True, False, or Cannot say? Statement: “Average sales per store in 2025 were the same in North and South.”
options: True
False
Cannot say
explanation: The statement is True. North had 2025 sales of 49.5 GBP m across 30 stores, which is 1.65 GBP m per store, and South had 66.0 GBP m across 40 stores, which is also 1.65 GBP m per store. The rule: a per-store average is a ratio, so the bigger region is not automatically the bigger average. South’s larger sales are spread over proportionally more stores, and the two ratios come out equal.

question_text: The chart shows training hours delivered by quarter. Trainers are paid €54 an hour and the rate is €1.20 to £1. What did Q3 and Q4 cost in pounds?
explanation: Add the Q3 and Q4 bars, apply the hourly rate, then convert. 460 + 505 = 965 hours. 965 x €54 = €52,110. There are €1.20 to £1, so divide by 1.20: €52,110 divided by 1.20 = £43,425. A common error here is taking 20% off instead of dividing by 1.20, which gives £41,688. Those are different operations: 1 divided by 1.2 is 0.833, not 0.8.

question_text: An agency prices an £8,800 project across design, build and testing in the ratio 3:5:3. The build overruns and is charged at 20% above its allocation. What is the new project total?
explanation: Total parts = 3 + 5 + 3 = 11, so one part = £8,800 ÷ 11 = £800. The build is 5 parts = £4,000, and it is charged 20% above that: £4,000 × 1.2 = £4,800. New total = £8,800 − £4,000 + £4,800 = £9,600. A common error here is applying the 20% to the whole project rather than to the build alone, giving £10,560 (option d).
tip: Mẹo MT: Nhớ công thức tính nhanh: Tăng trưởng % = (Giá trị mới - Giá trị cũ) / Giá trị cũ × 100%.

question_text: You are a cabin crew member. Your flight has landed forty minutes late and is taxiing to the stand. A passenger in row 6 tells you he has fifty minutes to reach his onward flight and asks to be let off first. You know from the crew briefing that several other passengers are also connecting, and you do not know how tight their connections are. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell him to speak to the ground staff waiting in the airbridge, as they have the connection details and can decide who needs to be moved through the terminal quickly.
Ask over the cabin address whether anyone with a connection under an hour will make themselves known, and arrange for those passengers to leave the aircraft ahead of everyone else.
Walk him up to the front of the cabin before the doors open and hold the other passengers back in the aisle until he has stepped off the aircraft.
Tell him that everybody on board is in the same position after a delay of this length and that there is nothing the crew are able to do about the order people leave in.
explanation: A: Passes responsibility to others: the minutes that matter are the ones spent getting off the aircraft, and by the airbridge the chance to help him leave first has already gone. C: Rewards the passenger who asked: someone in row 24 with thirty minutes is left behind a full aisle, and the only thing separating them is who spoke to crew first. D: Dismisses a request without checking: it is not true that nothing can be done, and the passenger is discouraged from asking anyone else while there is still time to act. The most effective response is to ask over the cabin address whether anyone with a connection under an hour will make themselves known, and let those passengers leave ahead of everyone else: the crew can influence the order people leave in, the thing you do not know is who else is tight, and one announcement gets that information and helps everyone it applies to. It beats walking him to the front and holding the other passengers back in the aisle, because that helps the person who asked rather than the person with least time, and others may be tighter still. It beats sending him to the ground staff waiting in the airbridge, because the useful minutes are on board, and by then the aircraft has already emptied in its usual order. The least effective response is telling him everybody is in the same position and nothing can be done about the order people leave in: that is untrue, and it stops him asking anyone else while there is still time. That is worse than pointing him at ground staff, which at least names somebody, and worse than walking him forward, which at least acts. The principle: when the fair answer depends on facts you do not have, go and get them rather than choosing between guessing and refusing.

question_text: You are an operations coordinator. Some of tomorrow’s duties will change because of an aircraft swap, but you will not know which crew are affected for about an hour. Nobody reports for duty before the morning, so nothing is decided by crew tonight. A vague warning to everyone would reach around eighty people, most of whom are unaffected. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Send a note to all crew now saying that duties may change tomorrow, so that nobody can say later that they were not warned before the changes were published.
Wait the hour until you know which crew are affected, then send one message naming them and what has changed, since nobody reports before the morning.
Tell the cabin crew managers now so they are aware, and leave it to them to pass word to whichever of their crew they think will be affected.
Send nothing at all, since the roster system will show the new duties once they are published and crew are expected to check it before they report.
explanation: A: Warns everybody about nothing in particular: eighty people spend the evening wondering, seventy of them for no reason, and none of them can do anything with the message. C: Passes an unfinished message down a chain: each manager guesses at a different list, so some crew hear a rumour, some hear nothing and nobody has the actual answer. D: Leaves people to discover a change in their own duty: an amended report time found by chance in the morning is exactly the message this hour existed to prevent. The most effective response is to wait the hour until you know which crew are affected, then send one message naming them and what has changed: nobody reports before the morning, an hour turns a rumour into a list of names, and one accurate message is worth more than an early vague one. It beats sending a note to all crew now saying duties may change tomorrow, because a warning that says only that gives eighty people nothing to do and seventy of them a wasted evening. It beats telling the cabin crew managers now and leaving them to pass word on, because a chain of managers each guessing at who is affected produces several different versions. The least effective response is sending nothing at all and relying on the roster system: crew find changed duties by chance in the morning, which is the one outcome the hour was there to avoid. That is worse than the other two, which both get a message out, however poorly aimed. The principle: when nobody can act yet, spend the short wait on precision, and then tell the people actually affected.

question_text: You are a production planner at a manufacturer. You and the works manager, Dan, disagree about a schedule change he has made that puts a large export order behind a smaller domestic one. You believe the export order will miss its shipping slot, which is fixed and costly to rebook. Dan is senior to you and has already told the shop floor. The operations director is available today. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Accept Dan's schedule since he is senior and has already briefed the shop floor, and put your concern about the shipping slot in an email so it is on record.
Show Dan the shipping slot dates and what missing them would cost, and if he will not change the schedule take it to the operations director today.
Quietly move the export order back up the schedule, since the shipping slot is fixed and Dan is unlikely to notice the change before the order ships.
Say nothing further and let the export order miss its slot, since Dan owns the schedule and it will be clear soon enough whose decision caused the problem.
explanation: A: Prioritises the record over the outcome: an email protects you while a fixed shipping slot is missed, which is a cost to the business rather than a question about who was right. C: Personalises the conflict: it reverses a senior colleague's decision behind his back on a schedule he has already briefed, which leaves the shop floor working to two different plans. D: Fails to escalate a genuine risk: it allows a known and costly failure to happen in order to demonstrate who was right, which puts being proved correct ahead of the order. Choosing the loss is a different order of wrong from acting badly. The most effective response is to show Dan the shipping slot dates and what missing them would cost, and if he will not change the schedule take it to the operations director today: whether the export order misses a fixed slot is a factual question with a cost attached, he owns the schedule so he gets the information first, and the director is available if he will not move. That is proportionate and fast enough to matter. It beats quietly moving the export order back up the schedule, because reversing a briefed plan behind his back leaves the shop floor working to two versions and destroys the working relationship. It beats accepting his schedule and putting your concern in an email, because a record protects you and does nothing for the slot. The least effective response is saying nothing further and letting the export order miss its slot: it allows a costly failure so that responsibility for it will be visible afterwards, which puts being proved right ahead of the business. That is worse than the other two, which are flawed but aimed at preventing the loss. The principle: put the facts to the person who owns the decision, and escalate the same day if the risk is real and they will not move.
tip: Mẹo MT: Trong đề thi SHL, quản lý thời gian tối đa 60-75 giây cho mỗi câu tính toán số học.

question_text: You pick online grocery orders at a supermarket. A customer’s order includes a specific nut-free chocolate spread, which is out of stock. The system suggests a standard chocolate spread as a substitute. The order notes say it is for a child with a severe nut allergy. Another nut-free spread is available in a different size at a higher price. Your shift manager can authorise price matching. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Reject the substitution and leave the item out of the order, so that nothing unsuitable is sent and the customer can buy her own elsewhere.
Substitute the alternative nut-free spread and ask your shift manager to price match it, so the order arrives with something the child can safely eat.
Substitute the alternative nut-free spread at its higher price, since it is the only safe option and the customer would rather pay more than go without.
Accept the system's suggested standard spread, since it is the recommended substitute and the customer can always refuse it at the door if it does not suit her.
explanation: A: Ignores the customer's actual need: a suitable nut-free spread is on the shelf, so leaving the line unfilled sends her nothing when a workable substitute exists. C: Acts on assumptions without checking: the substitution is right and the price increase is assumed to be acceptable, when a shift manager who could price match it is available and has not been asked. D: Ignores a stated allergy with a health consequence: the notes say the spread is for a child with a severe nut allergy, so accepting the system's suggestion sends the one product that could actually harm him. Following the system over a stated allergy is the worst of the four. The most effective response is to substitute the alternative nut-free spread and ask your shift manager to price match it: the order notes state an allergy, a safe alternative is on the shelf, and the only obstacle is a price difference a manager can authorise away. That gets the child something safe at the price the customer expected. It beats substituting the alternative at its higher price, because that makes the same correct swap while assuming she will accept paying more, when the manager could remove that. It beats rejecting the substitution and leaving the item out of the order, because that sends her nothing when a suitable product exists. The least effective response is accepting the system’s suggested standard spread because she can refuse it at the door: it substitutes an ordinary spread for one flagged for a child with a nut allergy, which is the single product in the aisle that could harm him. That is worse than the other two, which cost her money or an item but send nothing unsafe. The principle: when a customer has stated an allergy, meet it with a safe product and use the authority above you to deal with the price.

question_text: You volunteer as an assistant manager in a charity shop. Sorting donations you notice that a batch of electrical items has been put straight onto the shop floor without the safety testing the charity requires. Nobody has asked you to check this. The shop manager is on holiday for a week and the area manager covers by phone. The shop is open and the items are priced and on display now. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Ring the area manager to report that untested electrical items are on sale and ask whether she wants them removed before you touch anything.
Take the untested electrical items off the shop floor now and ring the area manager to tell her what you have found and ask how testing should be arranged.
Leave the items on display but attach a note to each saying it has not been safety tested, so that customers can decide for themselves whether to buy them.
Leave them as they are, since a volunteer putting stock out is not your responsibility and the manager will sort out the testing when she is back next week.
explanation: A: Delays the decision: the phone call is right and the items stay on sale while it happens. Removing them first costs nothing and is reversible if she disagrees. C: Passes responsibility to the customer: the charity's testing rule exists because a buyer cannot assess an appliance's safety from a label. Disclosing the gap does not close it. D: Fails to escalate a genuine risk: untested electrical goods stay on sale to the public for a week because the person who noticed decided it was not her job. The reason for silence is precisely why nobody else will catch it. The most effective response is to take the untested electrical items off the shop floor now and ring the area manager to tell her what you found: untested electrical goods on sale are a risk to whoever buys them, removing them is immediate, reversible and within your reach, and she needs to know so testing can be arranged properly. It beats ringing her first to ask whether she wants them removed, because that leaves the items on sale during the call and afterwards, when removing them costs nothing and can be undone if she disagrees. It beats attaching a note to each saying it has not been safety tested, because a label does not make an appliance safe, and it moves the judgement onto customers who cannot make it. The least effective response is leaving them as they are until the manager is back next week: it leaves untested electrical items on public sale for a week on the basis that someone else put them there. That is worse than ringing first, which reports it, and worse than labelling them, which at least warns buyers. The principle: when you find a live risk, remove it first if removing it is cheap and reversible, then tell whoever owns the process.
tip: Mẹo MT: Dùng phương pháp ước lượng chữ số hàng đơn vị hoặc làm tròn đến hàng chục để loại ngay 2 phương án vô lý.

question_text: You work for a bespoke furniture maker. A customer commissioned a dining table for delivery before a family celebration in three weeks. Today the workshop tells you the timber has moved during drying and the top must be remade, which takes five weeks. A simpler design in a different timber could be made in three. The customer is contactable. Your workshop manager is available today. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Ring the customer today, explain the timber has moved and the original top now takes five weeks, and set out the simpler alternative so she can choose which she wants.
Start the simpler design straight away so that something is ready for the celebration, and tell the customer what has been done once it is under way.
Tell the customer there has been a problem with the timber and that you will come back to her once the workshop has worked out the options.
Say nothing yet and press on with remaking the original top, since the workshop may make up time and telling her now would spoil the celebration she is planning.
explanation: B: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholder's: she commissioned a specific table, and choosing a different design and timber for her removes the decision that the commission was about. C: Delays the decision: the options are already known, five weeks for the original or three for a simpler design, so withholding them leaves her unable to decide anything and shortens the time she has to. D: Hides the problem / silent deadline slip: she is planning a family celebration around a table that will arrive two weeks late, and the plan is to let her find out. Withholding it to protect her mood removes every option she has. The most effective response is to ring the customer today, explain the timber has moved and the original top now takes five weeks, and set out the simpler alternative so she can choose: she commissioned this table for a specific date, the original now misses it by two weeks, and there is a genuine alternative. Only she can decide whether the date or the design matters more, and today is when that choice is still open. It beats starting the simpler design straight away and telling her once it is under way, because that decides the substance of her commission without asking. It beats telling her there has been a problem and that you will come back once the workshop has worked out the options, because both options are already known, so withholding them runs her time down for nothing. The least effective response is pressing on with remaking the original top and saying nothing: it leaves her planning a celebration around a table that will not arrive, in order to avoid spoiling her mood, which removes every choice she had. That is worse than the other two, which act or communicate imperfectly but do not conceal. The principle: when a commission cannot be met as agreed, put the real alternatives to the customer at once and let the choice be theirs.
tip: Mẹo MT: Nhớ công thức tính nhanh: Tăng trưởng % = (Giá trị mới - Giá trị cũ) / Giá trị cũ × 100%.

question_text:
【Ngữ cảnh】：The review body reported on the training grant scheme in June. It found that the scheme reached fewer people each year than when it started and that the cost of running it had risen. It recommended that the scheme be kept and simplified, and that the eligibility rules be reduced from eleven conditions to four. It said closing the scheme had been considered and rejected, because no other route reached the same group. The report runs to sixty pages.

【Câu hỏi】：Based only on the information in the passage, is the following statement True, False, or Cannot say? Statement: “The review body recommended that the scheme be closed.”
options: True
False
Cannot say
explanation: The statement is False. The passage says the review body “recommended that the scheme be kept and simplified”, and that “closing the scheme had been considered and rejected”. Either sentence contradicts the statement. The rule: False needs a stated contradiction rather than a silence, and here there are two. The most tempting wrong judgement is True, because the findings that come first are all unfavourable, and a reader who reasons from the evidence to the conclusion will not expect the scheme to survive.

The most effective response is to send the figures as usual and then ask her for ten minutes on how they are built and what her decision needed: it keeps the work flowing, it treats the remark as information about a gap rather than as an insult, and it puts the conversation where it belongs, which is between the two of you. It beats adding a public line to the team about how the figures are built, because that answers her in front of an audience and makes the disagreement everybody’s. It beats saying nothing at all, because the complaint stands and the next set of orders is set on the same misunderstanding. The least effective response is stopping the weekly figures after the meeting and making her ask: the work she depends on is withdrawn because of how she spoke to you, which is a different kind of wrong from being defensive in public or being silent. The principle: criticism of your work is answered by improving what the other person needed, never by taking the work away.

question_text: You are a delivery coordinator. A customer’s staff were being logged out at random all last week. Nothing has been changed, but the logouts stopped on Friday and nobody knows why. The customer’s operations manager rings to ask whether the problem is fixed, because she must decide today whether to train forty new staff on the system next week. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell her the logouts have stopped but nobody has found the cause, so you cannot call it fixed, and offer to have somebody watching the system while she trains.
Tell her it has stopped, and advise her to put the training back a fortnight so there is time to be certain before forty people depend on the system.
Explain that you cannot comment until the engineers have finished looking, and offer to ring her back as soon as there is something definite to report.
Tell her it is sorted and the training can go ahead, since nothing has gone wrong for four days and she is asking you for an answer today.
explanation: B: Substitutes your own judgement for the customer's: the delay may cost her more than the risk does, and she is the only person here who knows which. C: Delays a decision she has to make today: it is accurate and it is useless to her, because the deadline she is working to does not move to suit yours. D: Gives an assurance you cannot support: four quiet days with an unknown cause is not a fix, and she will commit forty people on the strength of your word. The most effective response is to tell her the logouts have stopped but nobody has found the cause, so you cannot call it fixed, and offer to have somebody watching while she trains. It gives her the two things she has to weigh and adds cover so her decision is cheaper to get wrong. It beats telling her it has stopped and advising a fortnight’s delay, because the cost of that delay sits with her business, so the choice is hers on full information. It beats explaining that you cannot comment until the engineers have finished, because she cannot wait for certainty and refusing to characterise what you do know leaves her deciding on less. The least effective response is telling her it is sorted and the training can go ahead: it is worse than either of the other two, because each leaves her with a true picture, however unwelcome, while this hands her a false certainty and forty people are trained on it. The principle: tell a customer what is known and what is not, and let the person carrying the risk decide.

question_text: You are a sales assistant at a garden centre. Your manager asked you this morning to price and shelve a delivery of spring bulbs before you finish at 5pm; the bulbs are not on promotion and no customer is waiting for them. At 2pm the till supervisor tells you the card terminal on the main till has failed, a queue is building at the single working till, and you are the only other member of staff trained to open the second one. Your manager is running a planting workshop outside for the next hour. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Open the second till straight away to clear the queue, then go back to the bulbs and let your manager know afterwards that the pricing may run past 5pm.
Carry on pricing the bulbs because your manager asked for them personally, and leave the till supervisor to manage the queue without mentioning that you are trained on the second till.
Serve at the second till between trips to the stockroom, pricing a few trays of bulbs each time the queue drops, so that both jobs keep moving through the afternoon.
Interrupt your manager's planting workshop to ask whether the bulbs or the till queue should come first, and wait for her decision before doing anything else.
explanation: B: Hides the problem: you hold the one fact that would fix the queue and you withhold it, so the supervisor cannot solve a problem she does not know is solvable. That is concealment, not a priority call. C: Splits effort so nothing finishes: customers are waiting now and the queue only clears if someone stays on the till, so stepping away repeatedly leaves the queue growing and the bulbs still unpriced. D: Escalates prematurely: a queue at the only working till against unpriced stock nobody is waiting for is a call you can make yourself, and interrupting a customer workshop costs more than it settles. The most effective response is to open the second till straight away and tell your manager afterwards: customers are waiting now, the bulbs are waiting for nobody, and the pricing deadline is internal and movable while the queue is neither. Telling her afterwards keeps her informed without pulling her out of a workshop. It beats serving at the second till between trips to the stockroom, because serving in bursts never clears a queue; the till needs someone sitting at it, and dividing yourself leaves both jobs half done. It beats interrupting her planting workshop to ask which comes first, because this is a straightforward call between a waiting customer and a task nobody is waiting on, and it does not need a manager pulled away from a customer event to make it. The least effective response is carrying on with the bulbs without mentioning that you are trained on the second till: you are the only other trained operator and you keep that to yourself, so the supervisor is left unable to fix something you could have fixed in seconds. That is worse than serving in bursts, which at least serves some customers, and worse than asking your manager, which at least surfaces the clash to someone. The principle: when one task has people waiting on it and the other does not, serve the people, then tell the person whose deadline slipped.
tip: Mẹo MT: Dùng phương pháp ước lượng chữ số hàng đơn vị hoặc làm tròn đến hàng chục để loại ngay 2 phương án vô lý.

question_text: You are an office assistant at a plumbing and heating firm. This morning the operations manager emailed asking you to compile last quarter’s supplier invoices for a cost review he is running later this week. As you begin, an engineer phones: he is at a customer’s home and cannot start a boiler repair until you email him the parts authorisation, which means finding the customer’s warranty record, about twenty minutes’ work. He and the customer are waiting. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Decide the operations manager's request should come first because it came from senior management, finish compiling the invoices, and tell the engineer to expect the authorisation this afternoon.
Alternate between the two tasks, looking up the warranty record in between batches of invoices, so that both the engineer and the operations manager see steady progress.
Tell the engineer the authorisation is already on its way so he stops chasing, then carry on with the invoices and actually send it once they are finished.
Send the engineer's authorisation first, since he and the customer are blocked until it arrives, then return to the invoices, which are not needed until later in the week.
explanation: A: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholder's: it ranks the manager's request first because of seniority, when his own email says the review is later this week, inventing an urgency he never expressed while two people stand waiting. B: Splits effort so nothing finishes: the authorisation is a single twenty-minute job, and breaking it into fragments between invoice batches stretches the engineer's and customer's wait far beyond what doing it in one go would take. C: Is dishonest to the engineer's face: claiming the authorisation is already on its way buys quiet at the cost of the truth, leaving him and the customer waiting on something that is not coming. That is deception, not a defensible ordering of tasks. The most effective response is to send the engineer’s authorisation first and then return to the invoices: he and the customer are blocked right now, the authorisation takes about twenty minutes, and the invoices are not needed until the review later in the week, so urgency and importance both point the same way. It beats finishing the invoices because the request came from senior management, since that invents an urgency the operations manager never expressed and ranks his request first on seniority while two people stand waiting. It beats alternating between the two tasks, because that chops a single short job into fragments and stretches the engineer’s and customer’s wait well beyond the twenty minutes it needs. The least effective response is telling the engineer the authorisation is already on its way when it is not: unlike putting the invoices first, which at least gives him an honest timeline, and unlike alternating, which at least makes real progress on the authorisation, it tells him a straightforward lie and leaves him and the customer waiting on something that is not coming. The principle: order work by real urgency and stated need, since a person blocked now outranks a task wanted later in the week, and never manage the gap with a lie.
tip: Mẹo MT: Nhớ công thức tính nhanh: Tăng trưởng % = (Giá trị mới - Giá trị cũ) / Giá trị cũ × 100%.

Send the figures as usual, then ask her for ten minutes to go through how they are built and what the decision needed that they did not give her.
Send the figures as usual and say nothing about Monday, on the basis that raising it now would only make the next meeting more uncomfortable for both of you.
Stop sending her the weekly figures after that meeting and let her ask for them if she still wants them, since she made her view of their value clear enough.

question_text:
【Ngữ cảnh】：Eilanreach Trust renews the licence for its rostering software each April. The supplier must give three months’ notice of any change to the price, and it gave that notice in January this year. The trust’s finance team put the renewal to its board in March and the board agreed it. Eilanreach has used the same supplier since 2018 and holds 180 licences. The notice period is set out in the contract signed that year.

【Câu hỏi】：Based only on the information in the passage, is the following statement True, False, or Cannot say? Statement: “The price Eilanreach pays for its rostering software rose this year.”
options: True
False
Cannot say
explanation: The statement is Cannot say. The passage states that the supplier “must give three months’ notice of any change to the price, and it gave that notice in January this year”, and that the board agreed the renewal in March. It never says what the change was. The rule: a claim that matches how the world usually works, but that the passage does not settle, is Cannot say. The most tempting wrong answer is True, because a price notice reads as a price rise to anyone who has received one.
tip: Mẹo MT: Nhớ công thức tính nhanh: Tăng trưởng % = (Giá trị mới - Giá trị cũ) / Giá trị cũ × 100%.

question_text: The table shows Kirkbourne Handling’s baggage record, with mishandling quoted as bags mishandled per 1,000 passengers. By what percentage did the mishandling rate rise from Q1 to Q3?
explanation: Build the per-1,000 rate for each quarter before comparing anything. Q1: 3,600 divided by 600 thousand passengers = 6.0 bags per 1,000. Q3: 3,900 divided by 500 thousand passengers = 7.8 bags per 1,000. Rise: 1.8 divided by 6.0 x 100 = 30.0%. A common error here is comparing the bag counts directly, which gives 8.3% and hides the fact that Q3 handled 100,000 fewer passengers. Dividing the gap by the Q3 rate rather than the Q1 rate gives 23.1%.

question_text: You are a commercial finance assistant at Adidas. A business customer disputes the amount on his account and does not accept your explanation of how it was worked out. You have an internal pricing sheet in front of you that shows the calculation clearly. It is marked internal and includes what other customers pay. He is threatening to take his business elsewhere and wants an answer today. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell him the calculation is confidential and that the amount on the account stands as it is, and suggest he takes the whole question up with his account manager if he remains unhappy.
Write out the calculation for his own account in your own words, show him each step and what it is based on, and check that it now makes sense to him.
Offer him a credit to settle the dispute without going through the calculation, since the argument is costing more time than the amount in question is worth.
Send him the internal pricing sheet so he can see the calculation for himself and check that nothing has been left out of the explanation you gave him.
explanation: A: Answers a reasonable question with a closed door: he is told the sum is right and given nothing that would let him see why. C: Buys off a question instead of answering it: he still does not understand his bill, and the next one will produce the same call. D: Breaches a confidence to win an argument: the sheet carries what other customers pay, and settling one dispute with it exposes every one of them. The most effective response is to write out the calculation for his own account in your own words, show each step and check that it makes sense: he gets the transparency he is asking for, about his own account, and the dispute is settled by explanation rather than by concession. It beats telling him the calculation is confidential, because that answers a fair question with a closed door. It beats offering a credit to end the argument, because he still does not understand the bill and will ring again next month. The least effective response is sending him the internal pricing sheet: it contains what other customers pay, so one dispute is settled by exposing everybody else’s terms, which is a different kind of wrong from being unhelpful or from paying to make a question go away. The principle: give a customer everything about their own position, and never anything about anybody else’s.

question_text: You are a commercial finance assistant at Adidas. Two colleagues you work with, one in trading and one in supply, have fallen out over a promotion whose cost came in well above plan. Each has told you separately that the other changed a number without saying so. Both have asked you what the other said. The figure has to be explained in Monday’s review, and you are the person who holds both versions of the file. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Ask each of them separately to walk you through their version of the change, then decide yourself which account the file supports and take that to Monday's review.
Write up what the file shows and send it straight to the reviewer before Monday, leaving the two of them to sort out between themselves how the change happened and who made it.
Tell each of them what the other has been saying about the change, so that both know where they stand before the review on Monday.
Put both versions of the file in front of the two of them together and say what changed and when, so that they agree between them what Monday's review is told about the cost.
explanation: A: Substitutes your own judgement for theirs: you arbitrate between two colleagues in private, and whichever way it lands, the loser hears the verdict at the review. B: Avoids the difficult conversation: the number is explained and the working relationship the next promotion depends on is left exactly as it is. C: Personalises the disagreement: it turns a question about a figure into a question about two people's accounts of each other, and does it in the way least likely to survive either of them repeating it. The most effective response is to put both versions of the file in front of the two of them together and ask them to agree what the review is told: the disagreement is about what the file shows, the file is in front of everybody, and the people who have to work together next month settle it themselves. It beats writing it up and sending it to the reviewer, because Monday is covered and nothing between the two colleagues is. It beats hearing each version separately and deciding which the file supports, because a private arbitration by the most junior person present leaves one of them told they were wrong by you. The least effective response is telling each of them what the other has been saying: the argument stops being about the promotion cost and becomes about what each said behind the other’s back, which is a different kind of wrong from ducking the conversation or over-reaching in it. The principle: put the evidence in front of both parties at once, and let the disagreement be about the thing rather than about each other.
