question_text: You are an audit associate. A colleague is meeting the client’s financial controller tomorrow to ask for a schedule. Last week the same controller told you sharply that she had already sent it and would not be sending it twice. Your colleague does not know this and has not asked. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Send him a message tomorrow morning just before he goes into the meeting, so that the warning is at least fresh in his mind when he walks in there.
Go and ask the controller yourself whether she ever sent the schedule, without telling your colleague that you are doing it.
Tell your colleague today what the controller said last week, and check together whether the schedule did arrive before he goes and asks for it again.
Let him go into the meeting without mentioning what she said, since he has not asked and she may well be in a better mood about it tomorrow.
explanation: A: Times it too late to act on: checking whether the schedule arrived takes longer than the walk to the meeting room. B: Duplicates the approach: she now hears from two of you about the same schedule, which is precisely what annoyed her. D: Lets a colleague walk into it: a two-minute warning would have changed how he opens the meeting, and the client's goodwill is spent for nothing. The most effective response is to tell your colleague today what the controller said last week, and check together whether the schedule did arrive: it gives him the warning while there is still time to check, and checking is what prevents the second ask altogether. It beats messaging him tomorrow morning just before he goes into the meeting, because that leaves no time to look. It beats going to ask the controller yourself whether she ever sent it, because a second approach from a different person is the thing she objected to. The least effective response is letting him go into the meeting without mentioning what she said: he walks in without a fact you hold that would have changed how he ran it. That is withholding it rather than giving it late or acting on it clumsily. The principle: warn the person early enough that the warning is still useful.
tip: Mẹo MT: Trong đề thi SHL, quản lý thời gian tối đa 60-75 giây cho mỗi câu tính toán số học.

question_text: You are a financial crime analyst. A colleague asks you to take twelve of her cases this week because she has “a lot on”. She asked the same last month and you agreed. Your own queue is full but manageable. Your team leader allocates cases and does not know about either request. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell her you cannot take any of them this week, and leave it there without suggesting anything about the allocation.
Tell her you can take a few but that this is the second time, and that the two of you should put the allocation to your team leader rather than rearranging it privately.
Take a few of them without saying anything, since you managed last month and she would not ask twice without a reason for it.
Send the twelve cases straight over to your team leader to reallocate, without telling your colleague that you have done so or that you were asked.
explanation: A: Refuses without a route: she still has a queue she cannot manage and nothing has been raised with anybody who could change it. C: Prioritises harmony over honesty: a few cases move, the allocation stays hidden from the person who owns it, and the pattern is set for a third time. D: Hands the request to a manager behind the colleague's back: she asked you directly, and the first she hears is a reallocation she did not expect. The most effective response is to tell her you can take a few but that this is the second time, and that the two of you should put the allocation to your team leader: it helps a little, names the pattern honestly to her face, and takes the question to the person whose job it is. It beats taking a few without saying anything because you managed last month, since absorbing it twice hides a real allocation problem. It beats telling her you cannot take any this week and leaving it there, because a flat refusal leaves her exactly where she was. The least effective response is sending the twelve cases to your team leader to reallocate without telling her: the request is escalated over her head, so she is blindsided and the conversation you could have had is now a management one. That is going around a colleague rather than being too soft or too hard. The principle: say it to her, then take the allocation where it belongs, together.
tip: Mẹo MT: Trong đề thi SHL, quản lý thời gian tối đa 60-75 giây cho mỗi câu tính toán số học.

question_text: The tables show the assets and the liabilities of five competitor firms at the financial year end, in pounds. Firm E’s fixed assets are what percentage of firm E’s total assets?
explanation: Read firm E’s fixed assets from the assets table: 90,999. Read firm E’s total assets from the same column: 438,238. Divide and convert to a percentage: 90,999 ÷ 438,238 = 0.20765, so 20.8%. The most tempting wrong method is to divide by the total at the foot of the liabilities column, 453,429, which gives 20.1%. That base settles a different question: it measures fixed assets against what the firm owes, not against what it owns. The loans made, borrowings and other liabilities rows are not needed here.

question_text: The tables show the assets and the liabilities of five competitor firms at the financial year end, in pounds. Firm A’s liquid assets are what percentage of the combined liquid assets of all five firms?
explanation: Add the liquid assets row across all five firms: 198,050 + 145,050 + 178,500 + 158,425 + 195,999 = 876,024. Firm A’s share of that is 198,050 ÷ 876,024 = 0.22608, so 22.6%. The most tempting wrong method is to widen the base by adding the fixed assets row into it, giving 198,050 ÷ 1,314,048 = 15.1%. The base has to be the same quantity as the numerator, and the numerator here is liquid assets alone. The loans made row and the borrowings row are not needed.

question_text: The tables show the assets and the liabilities of five competitor firms at the financial year end, in pounds. Taking the five firms together, what is the mean value of liquid assets and fixed assets held per firm?
explanation: Total the liquid assets row: 198,050 + 145,050 + 178,500 + 158,425 + 195,999 = 876,024. Total the fixed assets row: 75,050 + 92,050 + 71,500 + 108,425 + 90,999 = 438,024. Combined holding = 876,024 + 438,024 = 1,314,048. Mean per firm = 1,314,048 ÷ 5 = £262,809.60, so £262,810 to the nearest pound. The most tempting wrong method is to round each of the ten figures to the nearest 10,000 before adding, which gives £266,000. Rounding taken before the division carries its error into every term and the sum drifts by more than £3,000. Round at the end, not at the start. The derivatives, loans made and liabilities rows are not needed.

question_text: The tables show units sold and units stored across five grocery chains. Across all four categories combined, Testroe’s units stored are what percentage of its units sold?

The most tempting wrong method is to work out the stored to sold ratio for each of the four categories and average the four, which gives 47.0%. That treats packet goods, where 32,598 units were sold, as counting for as much as tinned goods, where 85,275 were. A combined ratio has to be built from the totals, not from the mean of the category ratios.

question_text: The table shows share prices in pounds for five listed companies. If GEV’s price were to fall from today’s price by the same percentage as Duber’s price fell between yesterday and today, what would GEV’s price become?
explanation: First work out Duber’s percentage fall. Duber went from 1.34 yesterday to 1.31 today, a fall of 0.03. 0.03 ÷ 1.34 = 0.022388, so a fall of 2.2388%. Now apply that same percentage to GEV’s price today, which is 1.64: 1.64 × (1 − 0.022388) = 1.64 × 0.977612 = 1.60328, so £1.60. The most tempting wrong method is to read Duber’s fall of 3p as a fall of 3%, which gives 1.64 × 0.97 = £1.59. A fall in pence and a fall as a percentage are different quantities, and the options are a penny apart. Carry the unrounded rate through and round only the final price. GEV’s own price yesterday is not needed, and neither are the high and low columns.

question_text: The table shows five years of figures for a bicycle manufacturer. In 2022, the price of a bike was how many times the combined production cost and other costs per bike?
options: 1.24 times
1.25 times
1.31 times
1.50 times
explanation: Read the 2022 column. Production cost per bike = £4,010 and other costs per bike = £825. Combined cost per bike = 4,010 + 825 = £4,835. Price per bike = £5,999. 5,999 ÷ 4,835 = 1.2407, so 1.24 times. The most tempting wrong method is to divide by the production cost alone, giving 1.50 times. The question names both cost lines, and the other costs row is the one a reader skips because it is the smaller of the two. The sales line and the bikes sold row are not needed.

question_text: The table shows five years of figures for a bicycle manufacturer. Revenue from bikes alone is the number of bikes sold multiplied by the price per bike. By what percentage did revenue from bikes alone change between 2018 and 2022?
explanation: 2018 revenue from bikes = 13,360 × £6,430 = £85,904,800. 2022 revenue from bikes = 16,100 × £5,999 = £96,583,900. Change = 96,583,900 − 85,904,800 = £10,679,100, a rise. As a percentage of the 2018 figure: 10,679,100 ÷ 85,904,800 = 0.12431, so a rise of 12.4%. The most tempting wrong method is to add the two underlying percentage changes, the 20.5% rise in bikes sold and the 6.7% fall in price, for 13.8%. Percentage changes on two factors of a product compound rather than add: 1.205 × 0.933 = 1.124, which is the 12.4% above. The sales line covers accessories as well as bikes, so it does not give revenue from bikes.
tip: Mẹo MT: Trong đề thi SHL, quản lý thời gian tối đa 60-75 giây cho mỗi câu tính toán số học.

question_text: The table shows five years of figures for a bicycle manufacturer. The sales line covers bikes and accessories together. In 2020, what percentage of sales came from accessories?
explanation: Work out 2020 revenue from bikes: 14,900 × £5,820 = £86,718,000, or £86.718m. Total sales in 2020 were £104.5m, and that line covers accessories as well. Accessories revenue = 104.5 − 86.718 = £17.782m. As a percentage of sales: 17.782 ÷ 104.5 = 0.17016, so 17.0%. The most tempting wrong method is to divide the accessories revenue by the bike revenue instead, giving 20.5%. The question asks for a share of sales, so the base is the whole sales line, not the part of it the accessories figure was derived from. The cost rows are not needed.

question_text: You are a property manager for a block of flats. A leaseholder has been chasing you for three weeks about a leak into her flat from the roof. Today the contractor confirms the roof needs a full repair costing more than the reserve fund holds, which means a consultation with all leaseholders and no repair for at least two months. She has already reported damage to her ceiling. Your director is available. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Ring the leaseholder today, explain the roof needs full repair, that consultation means at least two months, and what will be done about her ceiling and the leak meanwhile.
Wait until the consultation is under way before contacting her, so that you can give her firm dates rather than an open-ended answer she will only chase you about again.
Write to all leaseholders with the consultation notice, so that everyone including her receives the same information about the roof at the same time.
Tell her the roof repair has been approved in principle and that you will confirm timescales once the consultation process has been worked through.
explanation: B: Hides the problem: she has water entering her flat and has chased for three weeks. Waiting for tidier information leaves her with no information at all, and the silence is chosen to avoid being chased rather than to help her. C: Tells the wrong audience first: she has been chasing for three weeks and has water coming into her flat, so receiving a standard notice with everyone else answers none of her particular questions. D: Over-promises: describing it as approved in principle implies more certainty than a consultation that has not started, and it withholds the two-month timescale she needs to plan around. The most effective response is to ring the leaseholder today, explain the roof needs full repair, that consultation means at least two months, and what will be done about her ceiling and the leak meanwhile: she has been chasing for three weeks, has an active leak and ceiling damage, and the news is bad in a specific way she needs to plan around. That treats her as someone with a live problem rather than one of a list. It beats writing to all leaseholders with the consultation notice, because a general notice answers the block’s question and not hers. It beats telling her the repair is approved in principle with timescales to follow, because that overstates where things stand and still leaves out the timescale. The least effective response is waiting until the consultation is under way so you can give her firm dates: it delays telling her anything until the information is neater, while water continues to come into her flat, and the reason is to avoid being chased. That is worse than the other two, which communicate partially but do communicate. The principle: tell the person carrying the consequence directly, give them the timescale even when it is bad, and say what happens in the meantime.
tip: Mẹo MT: Luôn kiểm tra kỹ đơn vị tính (Triệu VNĐ vs Tỷ VNĐ, Tháng vs Năm) trước khi tính toán.

question_text: You are a duty operations assistant at a ferry terminal. At 7am three things need you. A vehicle has broken down on the loading ramp and the 8am sailing cannot load past it. A passenger with a wheelchair booking has arrived and needs assistance arranged. And head office wants yesterday’s loading figures by 9am. Recovery for the ramp takes about thirty minutes to arrange and attend. The assistance booking takes five minutes to arrange. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Arrange the recovery for the ramp first since the whole sailing depends on it, then sort out the passenger assistance and send the figures.
Deal with the passenger's assistance and the loading figures first, since both are quick, then arrange the recovery for the blocked ramp.
Arrange the recovery and the figures, and tell the passenger that assistance cannot be guaranteed this morning because of the disruption on the ramp.
Call the recovery for the ramp and arrange the passenger's assistance in the five minutes while it is on its way, then do the figures before 9am.
explanation: A: Delays the decision on the smallest task: the recovery does need starting first, but the assistance booking takes five minutes and the passenger is standing waiting for a sailing she may otherwise miss. Sequencing by size of problem leaves her unattended. B: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholder's: the figures are due at 9am and affect nobody's morning, while a blocked ramp stops an 8am sailing. Doing the quick jobs first spends the recovery's lead time. C: Ignores the passenger's actual need: booked assistance is what allows her to travel at all, and it takes five minutes. Withdrawing it because the terminal is busy leaves her unable to board a sailing she has booked. The most effective response is to call the recovery for the ramp and arrange the passenger’s assistance in the five minutes while it is on its way, then do the figures before 9am: recovery has the longest lead time so the call goes first, and the waiting time is exactly enough to arrange the assistance she has booked. The figures can follow. It beats arranging the recovery first and then sorting the assistance, because recovery is a phone call followed by waiting, and she should not stand unattended through it. It beats dealing with the assistance and the loading figures first as the quick jobs, because that delays the one task whose lead time blocks an entire sailing. The least effective response is telling the passenger assistance cannot be guaranteed this morning because of the disruption: it withdraws booked assistance from someone who depends on it, so she may be unable to travel at all, to manage a problem that takes five minutes to accommodate. That is worse than the other two, which sequence imperfectly but serve everybody. The principle: start the longest lead time first, then use the waiting time for the short tasks rather than leaving people unattended.

question_text: You are an audit associate. A colleague is meeting the client’s financial controller tomorrow to ask for a schedule. Last week the same controller told you sharply that she had already sent it and would not be sending it twice. Your colleague does not know this and has not asked. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Send him a message tomorrow morning just before he goes into the meeting, so that the warning is at least fresh in his mind when he walks in there.
Go and ask the controller yourself whether she ever sent the schedule, without telling your colleague that you are doing it.
Tell your colleague today what the controller said last week, and check together whether the schedule did arrive before he goes and asks for it again.
Let him go into the meeting without mentioning what she said, since he has not asked and she may well be in a better mood about it tomorrow.
explanation: A: Times it too late to act on: checking whether the schedule arrived takes longer than the walk to the meeting room. B: Duplicates the approach: she now hears from two of you about the same schedule, which is precisely what annoyed her. D: Lets a colleague walk into it: a two-minute warning would have changed how he opens the meeting, and the client's goodwill is spent for nothing. The most effective response is to tell your colleague today what the controller said last week, and check together whether the schedule did arrive: it gives him the warning while there is still time to check, and checking is what prevents the second ask altogether. It beats messaging him tomorrow morning just before he goes into the meeting, because that leaves no time to look. It beats going to ask the controller yourself whether she ever sent it, because a second approach from a different person is the thing she objected to. The least effective response is letting him go into the meeting without mentioning what she said: he walks in without a fact you hold that would have changed how he ran it. That is withholding it rather than giving it late or acting on it clumsily. The principle: warn the person early enough that the warning is still useful.
tip: Mẹo MT: Nhớ công thức tính nhanh: Tăng trưởng % = (Giá trị mới - Giá trị cũ) / Giá trị cũ × 100%.

question_text: You are a financial crime analyst. A colleague asks you to take twelve of her cases this week because she has “a lot on”. She asked the same last month and you agreed. Your own queue is full but manageable. Your team leader allocates cases and does not know about either request. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell her you cannot take any of them this week, and leave it there without suggesting anything about the allocation.
Tell her you can take a few but that this is the second time, and that the two of you should put the allocation to your team leader rather than rearranging it privately.
Take a few of them without saying anything, since you managed last month and she would not ask twice without a reason for it.
Send the twelve cases straight over to your team leader to reallocate, without telling your colleague that you have done so or that you were asked.
explanation: A: Refuses without a route: she still has a queue she cannot manage and nothing has been raised with anybody who could change it. C: Prioritises harmony over honesty: a few cases move, the allocation stays hidden from the person who owns it, and the pattern is set for a third time. D: Hands the request to a manager behind the colleague's back: she asked you directly, and the first she hears is a reallocation she did not expect. The most effective response is to tell her you can take a few but that this is the second time, and that the two of you should put the allocation to your team leader: it helps a little, names the pattern honestly to her face, and takes the question to the person whose job it is. It beats taking a few without saying anything because you managed last month, since absorbing it twice hides a real allocation problem. It beats telling her you cannot take any this week and leaving it there, because a flat refusal leaves her exactly where she was. The least effective response is sending the twelve cases to your team leader to reallocate without telling her: the request is escalated over her head, so she is blindsided and the conversation you could have had is now a management one. That is going around a colleague rather than being too soft or too hard. The principle: say it to her, then take the allocation where it belongs, together.

question_text: You are a junior data engineer. You have been asked to compare two database tools on cost, speed and support, and to recommend one. You have used the more expensive one for years and much prefer working with it. On the three measures you were given, the cheaper one comes out ahead on cost and support and they are level on speed. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Recommend the tool you know, since your familiarity with it is worth real money in delivery time, and weight the three measures so that it comes out ahead.
Recommend the cheaper tool on the three measures, and say nothing about the fact that you have years of experience with the other one.
Decline to make a recommendation and hand over the comparison on the three measures, so that somebody without a history with either tool decides it.
Recommend the cheaper tool on the three measures you were given, and note that you have years of experience with the other and would personally prefer it.
explanation: A: Decides a neutral assessment for your own benefit: the weighting is chosen after the answer is known, and nobody reading the recommendation can see that. B: Reports the measures and hides the relevant fact: your familiarity is a genuine consideration and the decision is made without knowing it exists. C: Steps aside rather than declaring: the team loses the only person who has used one of them, over something a sentence would have handled. The most effective response is to recommend the cheaper tool on the three measures you were given, and note that you have years of experience with the other and would personally prefer it. It answers the question on the criteria you were given, and declaring the preference lets whoever decides weigh it consciously. It beats recommending the cheaper tool and saying nothing about your experience with the other, because that experience is a real consideration and hiding it means the decision is made without a fact that could change it. It beats declining to recommend and handing over the comparison, because standing aside costs the team its only person with hands-on experience. The least effective response is recommending the tool you know and weighting the measures so it comes out ahead: it is worse than either of the other two, because both report the measures accurately, while this chooses the weighting after knowing which answer it produces. The principle: answer on the criteria you were given, declare the preference you hold, and never choose the weighting to reach the conclusion you wanted.

question_text: You are a quality assurance analyst. A release checklist needs one line ticked to say the data migration was rehearsed. The colleague who ran the rehearsal is on a flight and unreachable until tomorrow morning. You believe she ran it, but you did not see it. The people running tonight’s release are waiting on the sheet. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Hold the sheet until she lands and send it complete tomorrow morning, rather than sending something tonight that raises a question nobody in the building can answer.
Mark the line as done, since you are confident she ran the rehearsal, and mention it to her tomorrow morning if it should turn out to matter to anybody.
Send the sheet with that line left open, say plainly that the rehearsal cannot be confirmed until she lands, and let them decide what to do about tonight.
Ring round the team until you find somebody who watched the rehearsal, and send the sheet on the strength of what that person tells you about it.
explanation: A: Delays the decision: the release is tonight, so a complete sheet tomorrow arrives after the only moment at which anyone could have used it. B: Records as done what you did not see done: the sheet exists so that somebody can rely on it tonight, and this makes it say something you cannot support. D: Acts on second-hand word without checking: the sheet ends up carrying the same unverified tick, with one more person between you and the thing you did not see. The most effective response is to send the sheet with that line left open, say plainly that the rehearsal cannot be confirmed until she lands, and let them decide about tonight. The people running the release need to know both what is confirmed and what is not, and an open line with a plain explanation gives them a real choice. It beats holding the sheet until she lands and sending it complete tomorrow, because that arrives after the release it was meant to inform. It beats ringing round until you find somebody who watched the rehearsal, because a colleague’s recollection is not the check the line asks for. The least effective response is marking the line as done because you are confident she ran it: it is worse than either of the other two, because both leave the uncertainty visible, late or diluted, while this removes it from the record altogether and somebody tonight relies on that. The principle: when a record would have to say more than you know, send it with the gap showing and let the people carrying the risk decide.

question_text: You are a security analyst. A project has finished and left eleven unused software licences that nobody has asked about. Two colleagues have already taken one each for personal machines and told you it is normal. The licences cost the company four hundred pounds each per year and renew automatically next month unless somebody cancels them. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Cancel the nine that are left before the renewal and say nothing about the two that have already gone, so that the money is saved without anybody being named.
Take one of the licences for your own use as the others have, and cancel the rest before the renewal date, which still saves the company most of the money.
Tell whoever owns the project budget that eleven licences are renewing next month and that two are already on personal machines, so that they decide what happens to all eleven.
Raise it with the two colleagues and ask them to hand theirs back, then cancel all eleven before the renewal without involving anybody else in it.
explanation: A: Solves the cost and buries the rest: four hundred pounds a year is still walking out on two machines and the practice is left described as normal. B: Takes an advantage the role forbids: you are the person who saw the licences, and the saving does not buy you one of them. D: Settles it privately with the people who took them: it may work, and the budget holder still never learns that eleven licences nearly renewed unnoticed. The most effective response is to tell whoever owns the project budget that eleven licences are renewing next month and that two are already on personal machines. The renewal is a real deadline, the budget holder can act on it, and the two already gone are part of the same fact rather than a separate accusation. It beats cancelling the nine that are left and saying nothing about the two, because two are still being paid for and the practice goes unexamined. It beats asking the two colleagues to hand theirs back and cancelling all eleven yourself, because that may resolve today without anybody learning that eleven licences sat unnoticed. The least effective response is taking one of the licences for your own use as the others have: it is worse than either of the other two, because both end with you holding nothing, while this has the person who spotted the problem taking a share of it. The principle: when you find something valuable that nobody is watching, the finding goes to whoever owns it, and finding it earns you none of it.

question_text: You work in a field sales team and process your colleagues’ expense claims. A colleague submits mileage for a client visit on a day you know he was at the regional office, because you saw him there. The amount is small. He is popular and has just had a difficult quarter. The expenses policy is clear that claims must reflect actual journeys. Your sales manager is available. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Process the claim and mention to your sales manager that the mileage looked unusual, so that she can look into it if she thinks it is worth it.
Go back to the colleague, tell him the claimed journey does not match the day he was at the regional office, and ask him to correct or explain it before you process it.
Reject the claim in the system with a note that the journey could not have taken place, and let him take it up if he disagrees.
Process the claim as submitted, since the amount is small, he has had a hard quarter and querying it would be awkward and probably damage your working relationship.
explanation: A: Passes responsibility to others: it pays the claim first and raises a vague concern afterwards, so the money has gone and the manager is given a hint rather than a fact. C: Escalates prematurely: a formal rejection recorded against a colleague is a serious step taken before he has been asked, when there may be a simple explanation such as a wrong date. D: Breaches process to protect a colleague: it knowingly pays a claim for a journey that did not happen, because the sum is small and the conversation would be uncomfortable. That is dishonesty by omission, not discretion. The most effective response is to go back to the colleague, tell him the claimed journey does not match the day he was at the regional office, and ask him to correct or explain it: the discrepancy is a fact, there may be an innocent explanation such as the wrong date entered, and the person who can settle it in a sentence is the one who made the claim. Asking him first is both fairer and faster than any other route. It beats rejecting the claim in the system with a note that the journey could not have taken place, because a formal rejection on his record is a heavy step before he has had the chance to explain a possible typing error. It beats processing it and mentioning to your sales manager that the mileage looked unusual, because that pays out first and passes her a suspicion instead of a question that could already have been answered. The least effective response is processing the claim as submitted because the amount is small and querying it would be awkward: it knowingly pays for a journey that did not take place, which is precisely the reasoning that makes small false claims routine. That is worse than the other two, which act clumsily but do not knowingly pay. The principle: put the discrepancy to the person who created it before either paying it or recording it against them.
tip: Mẹo MT: Nhớ công thức tính nhanh: Tăng trưởng % = (Giá trị mới - Giá trị cũ) / Giá trị cũ × 100%.

question_text: You are a procurement assistant. A new tool your team wants must be signed off by two named reviewers before it can be bought, which takes about a fortnight. The supplier’s quoted price rises at the end of this month, four days away. Nobody has asked you to do anything about it; you noticed the date on the quote yourself. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Start using the trial version on live work now and put the paperwork through afterwards, so that the price is locked in before the reviewers ever reach it.
Email the two reviewers explaining the price date and ask them to look this week, then wait to see whether either of them gets round to it in time.
Let the price rise and buy the tool at the higher figure once both reviews are finished, on the basis that the process is the process and it is not yours.
Tell your manager today that the quote expires on Friday and ask whether the review can be brought forward, so that somebody who can decide that is deciding it.
explanation: A: Builds a workaround round a control: the fortnight is not an accident, it is the two reviewers, and this puts the tool into real use before either of them has looked. B: Asks once and treats the answer as out of your hands: the reviewers do not know the deadline is real, and nobody who could reorder their week has been told. C: Absorbs a cost nobody chose: the extra spend is real and avoidable, and the people who would have wanted the choice never find out it existed. The deadline is real, the decision about hurrying a review is not yours, and telling the person who can make it costs one message. It beats emailing the two reviewers about the price date and waiting to see whether either gets round to it, because reviewers who do not know a date is at stake have no reason to reorder their week. It beats letting the price rise and buying at the higher figure once both reviews are done, because a rise you saw coming and mentioned to nobody is a choice made by default. The least effective response is starting to use the trial version on live work and putting the paperwork through afterwards: it is worse than either of the other two, because both leave the reviewers in front of the decision, late or expensive, while this puts the tool into live use with neither having seen it. The principle: when a control is in the way of a real deadline, take the deadline to whoever owns the control, not round it.

question_text: You are a costs assistant. A fee earner asks you whether a client’s payment on account has cleared, because he wants to instruct counsel today. The bank feed shows a payment received but the accounts team has not yet confirmed it as cleared, and they are not back until tomorrow. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?

Tell him it has cleared, and assure him of it, since the money is showing on the feed and payments of that kind have always cleared by the following morning.

He needs the fact rather than the paperwork, and the bank can supply it today even though accounts cannot. It beats telling him it is showing but unconfirmed and that accounts are back tomorrow, because the uncertainty is removable. It beats telling him he will have to wait for accounts, because an absent team is not the only route to the answer. The least effective response is assuring him the money has cleared because payments of that kind always do by the following morning: clearance you have not established is confirmed, and counsel will be instructed on it. That is a different kind of wrong from the other two, both of which are honest about what is confirmed. The principle: when the usual confirmer is away, find the other source rather than filling the gap or accepting the delay.
tip: Mẹo MT: Nhớ công thức tính nhanh: Tăng trưởng % = (Giá trị mới - Giá trị cũ) / Giá trị cũ × 100%.

question_text: You are a scheduler for a solar panel installer. A customer’s installation is booked for Monday and he has arranged scaffolding at his own cost for that day. On Friday you learn the inverter for his system is out of stock for two weeks. The panels themselves could be fitted on Monday, with the inverter added later, but that would need the scaffolding twice. He is contactable. Your installations manager is available. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Ring the customer today, explain the inverter delay and that fitting the panels on Monday would mean paying for scaffolding twice, and let him choose what to do.
Postpone the whole installation until the inverter arrives, and tell the customer so he can cancel his scaffolding before Monday.
Leave Monday's booking in place and say nothing, since the panels can go up as planned and the inverter question can be dealt with once the installation has started.
Send the team on Monday to fit the panels as planned, and tell the customer on the day that the inverter will follow in two weeks.
explanation: B: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholder's: the scaffolding is his cost and his arrangement, so whether to use Monday's booking for the panels alone is his call, not a scheduling decision to be announced. C: Hides the problem: he is paying for scaffolding on the strength of a complete installation, and the plan is to let him find out mid-job. Withholding a known two-week gap from someone spending his own money is concealment. D: Commits the customer to a second cost: it commits him to a second scaffolding hire without asking, and he learns of the two-week gap only once the team is on his roof. The most effective response is to ring the customer today, explain the inverter delay and that fitting on Monday would mean paying for scaffolding twice, and let him choose: the scaffolding is his cost, the choice between one visit later and two visits with double hire is financial and belongs to him, and Friday leaves him time to cancel or keep the booking. Giving him the facts and both options is the whole job. It beats postponing the whole installation until the inverter arrives, because cancelling on his behalf decides how his own money is spent without asking. It beats sending the team on Monday and telling him on the day that the inverter follows in two weeks, because that commits him to a second hire and tells him afterwards. The least effective response is leaving Monday’s booking in place and saying nothing: it lets him pay for scaffolding believing the system will be complete, and plans to explain mid-installation. That is worse than the other two, which decide for him but at least tell him. The principle: when the trade-off costs the customer money, put the facts and the options to them while they can still change the arrangements.
tip: Mẹo MT: Dùng phương pháp ước lượng chữ số hàng đơn vị hoặc làm tròn đến hàng chục để loại ngay 2 phương án vô lý.

question_text: You are a property manager for a block of flats. A leaseholder has been chasing you for three weeks about a leak into her flat from the roof. Today the contractor confirms the roof needs a full repair costing more than the reserve fund holds, which means a consultation with all leaseholders and no repair for at least two months. She has already reported damage to her ceiling. Your director is available. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Ring the leaseholder today, explain the roof needs full repair, that consultation means at least two months, and what will be done about her ceiling and the leak meanwhile.
Wait until the consultation is under way before contacting her, so that you can give her firm dates rather than an open-ended answer she will only chase you about again.
Write to all leaseholders with the consultation notice, so that everyone including her receives the same information about the roof at the same time.
Tell her the roof repair has been approved in principle and that you will confirm timescales once the consultation process has been worked through.
explanation: B: Hides the problem: she has water entering her flat and has chased for three weeks. Waiting for tidier information leaves her with no information at all, and the silence is chosen to avoid being chased rather than to help her. C: Tells the wrong audience first: she has been chasing for three weeks and has water coming into her flat, so receiving a standard notice with everyone else answers none of her particular questions. D: Over-promises: describing it as approved in principle implies more certainty than a consultation that has not started, and it withholds the two-month timescale she needs to plan around. The most effective response is to ring the leaseholder today, explain the roof needs full repair, that consultation means at least two months, and what will be done about her ceiling and the leak meanwhile: she has been chasing for three weeks, has an active leak and ceiling damage, and the news is bad in a specific way she needs to plan around. That treats her as someone with a live problem rather than one of a list. It beats writing to all leaseholders with the consultation notice, because a general notice answers the block’s question and not hers. It beats telling her the repair is approved in principle with timescales to follow, because that overstates where things stand and still leaves out the timescale. The least effective response is waiting until the consultation is under way so you can give her firm dates: it delays telling her anything until the information is neater, while water continues to come into her flat, and the reason is to avoid being chased. That is worse than the other two, which communicate partially but do communicate. The principle: tell the person carrying the consequence directly, give them the timescale even when it is bad, and say what happens in the meantime.
tip: Mẹo MT: Nhớ công thức tính nhanh: Tăng trưởng % = (Giá trị mới - Giá trị cũ) / Giá trị cũ × 100%.

question_text: You are a sales assistant at a garden centre. Your manager asked you this morning to price and shelve a delivery of spring bulbs before you finish at 5pm; the bulbs are not on promotion and no customer is waiting for them. At 2pm the till supervisor tells you the card terminal on the main till has failed, a queue is building at the single working till, and you are the only other member of staff trained to open the second one. Your manager is running a planting workshop outside for the next hour. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Open the second till straight away to clear the queue, then go back to the bulbs and let your manager know afterwards that the pricing may run past 5pm.
Carry on pricing the bulbs because your manager asked for them personally, and leave the till supervisor to manage the queue without mentioning that you are trained on the second till.
Serve at the second till between trips to the stockroom, pricing a few trays of bulbs each time the queue drops, so that both jobs keep moving through the afternoon.
Interrupt your manager's planting workshop to ask whether the bulbs or the till queue should come first, and wait for her decision before doing anything else.
explanation: B: Hides the problem: you hold the one fact that would fix the queue and you withhold it, so the supervisor cannot solve a problem she does not know is solvable. That is concealment, not a priority call. C: Splits effort so nothing finishes: customers are waiting now and the queue only clears if someone stays on the till, so stepping away repeatedly leaves the queue growing and the bulbs still unpriced. D: Escalates prematurely: a queue at the only working till against unpriced stock nobody is waiting for is a call you can make yourself, and interrupting a customer workshop costs more than it settles. The most effective response is to open the second till straight away and tell your manager afterwards: customers are waiting now, the bulbs are waiting for nobody, and the pricing deadline is internal and movable while the queue is neither. Telling her afterwards keeps her informed without pulling her out of a workshop. It beats serving at the second till between trips to the stockroom, because serving in bursts never clears a queue; the till needs someone sitting at it, and dividing yourself leaves both jobs half done. It beats interrupting her planting workshop to ask which comes first, because this is a straightforward call between a waiting customer and a task nobody is waiting on, and it does not need a manager pulled away from a customer event to make it. The least effective response is carrying on with the bulbs without mentioning that you are trained on the second till: you are the only other trained operator and you keep that to yourself, so the supervisor is left unable to fix something you could have fixed in seconds. That is worse than serving in bursts, which at least serves some customers, and worse than asking your manager, which at least surfaces the clash to someone. The principle: when one task has people waiting on it and the other does not, serve the people, then tell the person whose deadline slipped.
tip: Mẹo MT: Dùng phương pháp ước lượng chữ số hàng đơn vị hoặc làm tròn đến hàng chục để loại ngay 2 phương án vô lý.

question_text: You work for a tour operator. A group of twenty-four is flying out on Saturday on a walking holiday. On Wednesday the mountain hut booked for two nights closes after a water supply failure. An alternative hut is available but is four hours’ walk further on, which changes two days of the itinerary. The group leader is contactable. Your operations manager is available today. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Rebook the alternative hut and send the group leader a revised itinerary, so the holiday is secured and everyone knows the new plan before they fly.
Wait until the water supply position is clearer later in the week, since the hut may reopen before Saturday and a change of itinerary would unsettle the group unnecessarily.
Let the group travel as booked and have the guide explain the change of route when they reach the mountain, since the alternative hut will be arranged by then anyway.
Ring the group leader today, explain the hut closure and what the alternative would mean for two days of walking, and agree the plan before anything is rebooked.
explanation: A: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholder's: adding four hours' walking to two days changes what the group signed up for, and some members may not be able to do it. That is the group leader's call, not a booking amendment. B: Delays the decision: the alternative hut may be taken by another group while you wait, and the leader loses the days in which walkers could have prepared or withdrawn. C: Hides the problem: twenty-four people are told on the mountain that two days now involve four hours' more walking, when some may be unable to manage it and none of them can do anything about it there. That is concealment with a safety dimension. The most effective response is to ring the group leader today, explain the hut closure and what the alternative would mean for two days of walking, and agree the plan before anything is rebooked: four extra hours on two days is a material change, some of twenty-four people may not manage it, and only he can judge that for his group. Wednesday leaves time to prepare, adjust or withdraw. It beats rebooking the alternative hut and sending a revised itinerary, because that presents the change as settled when its acceptability depends on the group. It beats waiting until the water supply position is clearer later in the week, because that risks losing the alternative hut and burns the days the group needs. The least effective response is letting them travel as booked and having the guide explain the change of route on the mountain: it tells twenty-four walkers the route has lengthened substantially at the one point where nobody can opt out. That is worse than the other two, which decide or delay but do not spring it on people in the field. The principle: when a change affects what people are physically committing to, tell whoever speaks for them while they can still choose.
tip: Mẹo MT: Nhớ công thức tính nhanh: Tăng trưởng % = (Giá trị mới - Giá trị cũ) / Giá trị cũ × 100%.

question_text: You are a project coordinator at a web design agency. A client’s new site is due to go live on Friday for a product launch. On Wednesday your developer tells you the payment integration will not be ready and the site can only go live taking enquiries rather than orders. The client’s marketing manager has booked advertising for Friday. She is contactable. Your account director is available today. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Go live on Friday with the enquiry form in place of the payment pages, and explain the change to the client after the launch when the position is clearer.
Email the client's marketing manager to say there is a technical issue with Friday's launch and that the agency will confirm the position as soon as it can.
Ring the client's marketing manager today with your account director, explain that payments will not be ready and what going live without them means, and agree what happens to Friday.
Postpone the launch to the following week so the site goes live complete, and tell the client the new date.
explanation: A: Hides the problem: she has bought advertising to drive people to a shop that will not take orders, and is told after the money has been spent. Launching a different site than the one agreed and explaining afterwards is concealment. B: Delays the message: it reaches her on Wednesday and withholds the specific fact she needs, that the site cannot take orders, so she cannot decide about advertising she has already booked. D: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholder's: her advertising is booked for Friday, so whether to launch without payments or move the whole campaign is a commercial decision that belongs to her. The most effective response is to ring the client’s marketing manager today with your account director, explain that payments will not be ready and what going live without them means, and agree what happens to Friday: she has paid for advertising pointing at a shop that cannot take orders, only she can decide whether to launch for enquiries or move the campaign, and Wednesday still leaves time to change either. Involving the account director means the options offered are ones the agency can stand behind. It beats postponing the launch to the following week and telling her the new date, because that decides the fate of her booked advertising without asking. It beats emailing that there is a technical issue and the agency will confirm the position, because a vague notice withholds the one fact she needs. The least effective response is going live on Friday with the enquiry form in place of the payment pages and explaining afterwards: it launches a site that cannot do what was agreed, against advertising she has already paid for. That is worse than the other two, which communicate or decide imperfectly but do not spend her money on a silent substitution. The principle: when a failure will cost the client money they have already committed, tell them at once and let them decide what happens.
tip: Mẹo MT: Trong đề thi SHL, quản lý thời gian tối đa 60-75 giây cho mỗi câu tính toán số học.

question_text: You are an office administrator at a commercial printing company. While filing paperwork you notice that the shared template the sales team uses for customer quotes still contains last year’s paper prices, which rose noticeably in January. Nobody has been asked to look at the template, and two salespeople are preparing quotes with it this week. The current prices are held in the purchasing system, which you can access. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Update the template now with the January price rises you remember, marking the new figures as provisional to be checked later, so the salespeople are at least closer to the current rates.
Mention to this month's new starter that the template could do with tidying up when they get a chance, without explaining that the prices are wrong, and return to your filing.
Email the sales manager to explain the template still shows last year's prices and that quotes are being prepared this week, leaving the correction with them as owner of the quoting process.
Check the current prices in the purchasing system, update the template to match, and tell the two salespeople and the sales manager what you found and changed.
explanation: A: Acts on assumptions without checking: even flagged as provisional, remembered figures are still guesses in a live quoting template, and the purchasing system could give you the accurate prices in roughly the time the guesswork takes. B: Dumps the problem on the least able person: a vague request to tidy up the template, with no mention that its prices are wrong or that live quotes depend on it, buries the risk you spotted with the one person who cannot recognise it. That is abandonment, not a handover. C: Passes responsibility to others: the sales manager does own the quoting process, but leaving the whole correction in their inbox lets this week's quotes go out on old prices, when you could fix the figures accurately now and simply tell them. The most effective response is to check the current prices in the purchasing system, update the template to match, and tell the salespeople and their manager what you found: you spotted the problem, the accurate figures are within your reach, and quoting is live this week, so fixing it and informing the owners removes the risk. It beats updating the template from the prices you remember and marking them provisional, because the purchasing system could supply the real figures just as quickly, and the salespeople would otherwise be quoting from flagged guesses. It beats emailing the sales manager and leaving the correction with them, because that gives the owner the full picture but leaves the fix waiting in an inbox while this week’s quotes are prepared, when you could complete it accurately straight away. The least effective response is asking the new starter to tidy the template up sometime: unlike using remembered figures, which at least moves them closer to reality and flags the doubt, and unlike emailing the manager, which tells the responsible person exactly what is wrong, it hands a vague job to the one person who cannot know the prices are wrong, so the risk you spotted disappears with nobody equipped to act on it. The principle: when you spot an unowned problem you can fix, verify the facts, fix it, and tell the people it affects. Never bury it with someone who cannot recognise it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Trong đề thi SHL, quản lý thời gian tối đa 60-75 giây cho mỗi câu tính toán số học.

question_text: You are working on a cost improvement case. The deck the partner presents to the client in two days recommends consolidating two distribution sites. Checking a data extract this morning, you find a lease commitment in the client’s own schedule that runs four years longer than the deck assumes, which would materially change the saving. You are confident about the figure but you have not yet traced why the schedule and the deck disagree. Your manager is in the office. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Take the lease schedule straight to the partner this afternoon, since he is the one presenting and there is little time left for the finding to work its way up the team.
Show your manager the lease schedule today, with the specific figure and what it would do to the saving, and say plainly that you have not yet traced why the two disagree.
Keep tracing the difference until you understand it fully, then raise it with your manager once you can explain exactly where the deck's assumption came from and why it is wrong.
Assure your manager the underlying lease assumptions have been checked and hold, so the deck can go to the client as drafted, and look into the schedule difference afterwards.
explanation: A: Escalates prematurely: the manager built the saving and can tell in minutes whether the schedule is the same lease, and going over her removes the one check that would have made the escalation worth the partner's time. C: Delays the decision: the deck goes in two days, and holding a material finding until it is fully explained spends the time the team would need to act on it. D: Assures something you have not established: the manager will take the saving to the client on the strength of that sentence, and it says the opposite of what you actually found this morning. The most effective response is to show your manager the lease schedule today with the figure, what it would do to the saving, and the fact that you have not yet traced the difference. She owns the recommendation and has two days to act, and she can settle in minutes whether the schedule refers to the same lease. It beats taking it straight to the partner, because the manager is the fastest check on whether the finding is real and skipping her spends the partner’s time on something unverified. It beats tracing the difference to the end first, because the deck goes in two days and a material figure held back is a figure the team cannot act on. The least effective response is to assure your manager the lease assumptions have been checked and hold: both weaker responses still put the finding in front of somebody, late or at the wrong level, whereas an assurance closes the question in the mind of the person who would otherwise look, and the client hears a saving you already have reason to doubt. The principle: raise a finding that changes a recommendation as soon as you have it, at the level that can check it, and never describe work you have not done as done.
tip: Mẹo MT: Dùng phương pháp ước lượng chữ số hàng đơn vị hoặc làm tròn đến hàng chục để loại ngay 2 phương án vô lý.

question_text: A client’s finance team has asked for the pricing model behind an analysis you presented last week, so they can run their own scenarios before a board meeting in four days. Your firm’s rule is that models go to clients only after a review by someone independent of the case team, which takes about two working days and has not started. The client contact has said several times that she needs something she can use this week. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell the client the model cannot be shared for at least a week, since the review has not started and there is no realistic way to compress a two day check into the time she is asking for.

Start the review today, and meanwhile send her the scenario outputs she needs in the form your firm does release, explaining what she has now and what follows, since her board meeting is in four days.
Promise her a full walkthrough of the model tomorrow with the case team, so she can see the workings and put her scenarios to you live rather than waiting for a file to clear review.
Send her the working model file from your own account this afternoon so she has it within the hour, and put it into the independent review afterwards as a formality.
explanation: A: Ignores the customer's actual need: she has a board meeting in four days and wants to run scenarios, and a flat refusal answers a question about the model rather than the one she is asking. C: Over-promises: the case team is not free tomorrow and a walkthrough of a model she cannot then use does not get her scenarios run before the board meeting. D: Breaches a stated release control: the review exists because an unchecked model in a client's hands gets used, and sending it first makes the review a record of something that has already happened. The most effective response is to start the review today and meanwhile send her the scenario outputs in the form the firm does release, saying what she has now and what follows. It gets her something she can put in front of the board, it starts the clock on the thing she actually asked for, and it keeps the control intact. It beats a flat refusal, because she needs scenarios rather than the file itself and a refusal answers the wrong question. It beats promising a walkthrough tomorrow, because the case team is not free and a demonstration does not get her scenarios run. The least effective response is to send the working model from your own account: the weaker responses leave her under served or waiting for something that will not arrive, which is recoverable, whereas an unreviewed model in a client’s hands is used, quoted and built on before anybody checks it, and the review afterwards can only record what already happened. The principle: meet the need behind the request in the form you are allowed to release, and never treat a control as paperwork that can follow the thing it controls.
tip: Mẹo MT: Nhớ công thức tính nhanh: Tăng trưởng % = (Giá trị mới - Giá trị cũ) / Giá trị cũ × 100%.

question_text: You are three weeks into an engagement at a retail client, working from their head office. The operations director you work with most closely has been pleased with the team’s work. This morning she hands you a set of staff discount vouchers, one for each member of the team, and says to use them as much as you like while you are on site. Your firm’s rules do not allow you to accept benefits from a client during an engagement. She has offered them warmly and without being asked. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Take the vouchers and shop with them for your own benefit for the rest of the engagement, on the grounds that they are a small courtesy the operations director offered without any prompting.
Thank her, explain that the firm does not let the team accept benefits from a client during an engagement, hand the vouchers back, and tell your manager the offer was made.
Accept the vouchers so as not to embarrass her in front of her own team, put them in a drawer unused for the rest of the engagement, and mention it to nobody.
Tell her the firm has rules about this sort of thing and that she should raise it with your compliance team if she wants to know whether the team can accept them.
explanation: A: Takes a benefit the role forbids: the rule does not turn on the size of the courtesy or on who raised it, and a team on a live engagement spending a client's money on itself is the thing the rule exists to prevent. C: Avoids the difficult conversation: the vouchers are still accepted whether or not they are spent, and nobody at your firm knows an offer was made or that it was handled. D: Passes responsibility to others: it makes a client chase your own firm's rule on your behalf, and leaves the vouchers sitting with you while she waits for an answer. The most effective response is to thank her, explain the firm’s rule, hand the vouchers back, and tell your manager the offer was made. It settles the vouchers, it treats a warm gesture warmly, and it puts the offer on the record with the person at your firm who would want to know. It beats putting them in a drawer, because accepting is what the rule is about and an unspent voucher is still an accepted one. It beats sending her to your compliance team, because it makes the client work out your firm’s rule while the vouchers stay with you. The least effective response is to take the vouchers and shop with them: the weaker responses leave the situation untidy or slow, but nobody has gained anything, whereas a team on a live engagement putting a client’s money into its own shopping is exactly what the rule forbids, and no explanation of it afterwards recovers the position. The principle: decline a benefit your role forbids at the moment it is offered, kindly and in person, and tell your own side that it happened.
tip: Mẹo MT: Nhớ công thức tính nhanh: Tăng trưởng % = (Giá trị mới - Giá trị cũ) / Giá trị cũ × 100%.

question_text: You are a reconciliations clerk. You have been covering two roles for six weeks. Tonight’s break report needs a count of unresolved items and you have lost track of four of them. A careful recount would take ninety minutes you do not have. The report goes to the operations committee. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Report the number you can stand behind, state that four items are uncounted and why, and say plainly that six weeks of double-running is the cause.
Enter a count that you estimate from last week's figure, since it will be close enough and the committee only looks at the direction of travel anyway.
Stay late and do the ninety-minute recount, and say nothing about how long the double-running has gone on.
Submit the report without the count at all, and add it once the recount has been done properly later in the week.
explanation: B: Records an estimate as a count: the committee reads a measured figure, and the one thing that would tell them the reporting has become unreliable is the thing removed. C: Absorbs it again: the number is right this week and the sixth week of covering two roles remains invisible to everybody who could end it. D: Removes the number without the reason: the committee sees a gap and has no idea that a six-week resourcing problem sits behind it. The most effective response is to report the number you can stand behind, state that four items are uncounted and why, and say plainly that six weeks of double-running is the cause: the committee gets a figure it can trust, an honest statement of what is missing, and the only route to the problem being fixed. It beats submitting the report without the count and adding it later in the week, because a gap with no explanation tells them nothing. It beats staying late for the ninety-minute recount and saying nothing about the double-running, because a seventh week of that being invisible is how this happens again. The least effective response is entering a count estimated from last week’s figure: an estimate is presented as a count, so the report looks exactly as reliable as it did before it stopped being reliable. That is falsifying the measure rather than reporting it incompletely or absorbing the strain. The principle: report what you can stand behind, name what you cannot, and name the cause.
tip: Mẹo MT: Dùng phương pháp ước lượng chữ số hàng đơn vị hoặc làm tròn đến hàng chục để loại ngay 2 phương án vô lý.

question_text: You are an audit associate. A colleague is meeting the client’s financial controller tomorrow to ask for a schedule. Last week the same controller told you sharply that she had already sent it and would not be sending it twice. Your colleague does not know this and has not asked. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Send him a message tomorrow morning just before he goes into the meeting, so that the warning is at least fresh in his mind when he walks in there.
Go and ask the controller yourself whether she ever sent the schedule, without telling your colleague that you are doing it.
Tell your colleague today what the controller said last week, and check together whether the schedule did arrive before he goes and asks for it again.
Let him go into the meeting without mentioning what she said, since he has not asked and she may well be in a better mood about it tomorrow.
explanation: A: Times it too late to act on: checking whether the schedule arrived takes longer than the walk to the meeting room. B: Duplicates the approach: she now hears from two of you about the same schedule, which is precisely what annoyed her. D: Lets a colleague walk into it: a two-minute warning would have changed how he opens the meeting, and the client's goodwill is spent for nothing. The most effective response is to tell your colleague today what the controller said last week, and check together whether the schedule did arrive: it gives him the warning while there is still time to check, and checking is what prevents the second ask altogether. It beats messaging him tomorrow morning just before he goes into the meeting, because that leaves no time to look. It beats going to ask the controller yourself whether she ever sent it, because a second approach from a different person is the thing she objected to. The least effective response is letting him go into the meeting without mentioning what she said: he walks in without a fact you hold that would have changed how he ran it. That is withholding it rather than giving it late or acting on it clumsily. The principle: warn the person early enough that the warning is still useful.
tip: Mẹo MT: Nhớ công thức tính nhanh: Tăng trưởng % = (Giá trị mới - Giá trị cũ) / Giá trị cũ × 100%.

question_text: You are an onboarding analyst. A client’s review was due last month and you missed it. Because of the delay the client has been on a higher fee tier for four weeks, costing them about £300. Nobody has queried it, and moving them now would put the fee right from today without anybody asking why. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell the client directly that the review was late and that you will look into the fees, before working out internally what can actually be done about the four weeks.
Move the client to the right tier today, tell your manager the review was missed and the client has overpaid, and ask how the four weeks should be refunded.
Move the client to the right tier today and raise the missed review at your next one-to-one with your manager, when there will be time to talk through how it happened.
Move the client to the right tier today and keep the missed review to yourself, since the fee is correct from now on and nobody has asked about the four weeks.
explanation: A: Opens with the client before the firm: a client told about a refund nobody has agreed yet may be promised something that cannot be delivered. C: Delays the decision that has money in it: the refund is the client's, and it waits on a diary slot that exists for your development. question_text: You are a client services associate. A client emails asking why a charge on her statement is £45 rather than the £30 she expected. Charges are calculated by another team, but the tariff is on a page you can see, and it takes two minutes to read. She has asked twice already. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Read the tariff, reply today explaining exactly how the £45 is made up, and offer to raise it with the charges team if the breakdown still looks wrong to her.
Reply asking her to send you last month's statement as well, so that you can compare the two before saying anything about how the charge was calculated.
Send her email over to the charges team without reading the tariff yourself, and close the query on your side so that it no longer shows on your own list.
Reply with a general explanation of how monthly charges can vary, and offer to look up the exact breakdown for her if she still wants it after that.
explanation: B: Asks the customer for work you do not need: the tariff explains this month's figure on its own, and she is given a task instead of an answer. C: Passes the question on for a second time: she has asked twice, the answer is two minutes away on a page in front of you, and she is handed to a team she has no relationship with. D: Answers a specific question with a general one: she asked how £45 was arrived at, and she has to ask a third time to get it. The most effective response is to read the tariff, reply today explaining exactly how the £45 is made up, and offer to raise it with the charges team if the breakdown still looks wrong: the answer is two minutes away, she has asked twice, and the offer keeps the door open without promising an outcome. It beats replying with a general explanation of how monthly charges can vary, because that does not explain £45. It beats asking her to send last month’s statement for comparison, because nothing in it is needed to read this month’s tariff. The least effective response is sending her email to the charges team unread and closing the query on your side: the question she has now asked three times moves to another team, and she waits again for something you could have answered today. That is handing it on rather than answering it poorly. The principle: if the answer is within reach, reach for it.

question_text: You are a settlements assistant. A change next month means one client’s trades will settle a day later than they do now, which will cost them a small amount of interest each time. The change is decided and cannot be altered. Nobody has told the client. Their relationship manager is on leave for two weeks. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell the client that nothing about their settlement arrangements is changing, since the difference is small and the relationship manager can explain it properly when she is back.
Telephone the client yourself today and explain the change, since somebody should tell them and you are the person who understands the detail.
Wait for the relationship manager to come back and give her the details then, so the client hears it from the person who deals with them.
Write up what changes, what it costs the client and when it starts, and send it to the relationship manager's cover today so the client can be told before it happens.
explanation: A: Denies a change you know is coming: the client plans on it, and when the first trade settles late they will have been told the opposite by name. B: Bypasses the relationship: a cover exists, and a client hearing a cost increase from an unfamiliar voice will ask questions you cannot answer. C: Delays past the event: two weeks is most of the notice available, and the change may land before she returns. The most effective response is to write up what changes, what it costs the client and when it starts, and send it to the relationship manager’s cover today: the cover can act now, the client gets notice before the first late settlement, and the person with the relationship still delivers it. It beats waiting for the relationship manager to come back and giving her the details then, because two weeks of the notice period is spent waiting. It beats telephoning the client yourself today, because a cold call about a cost increase raises questions you are not placed to handle. The least effective response is telling the client nothing about their settlement arrangements is changing: they are told the opposite of what is about to happen, and plan around a fact you know to be false. That is a false statement rather than a poorly routed message. The principle: get the news to somebody who can deliver it, in time for it to be notice.

question_text: You are an onboarding analyst. A colleague in sales asks you to confirm to his prospect that their account can be live by the end of the month, which would win the deal. Accounts like this usually take six weeks and the checks are not yours. It is the eighteenth. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?

Promise him the account will be live by month end, since he needs it to win the deal and there is a reasonable chance the checks come back quickly this time.
Tell him the timing is nothing to do with you at all, and that he will have to ask the checks team himself if he wants a firm date for the prospect.
Tell him you will find out and come back to him, without saying anything now about how long these accounts normally take.
explanation: B: Gives a promise about somebody else's process: the prospect signs on it, and when six weeks turns out to be six weeks the firm has broken a commitment it never made. C: Passes a colleague away from help you could give: you know the typical timescale and could ask, and he is left starting from nothing. D: Withholds the useful part: he is talking to the prospect today, and the six-week norm is the thing that would stop him promising anything. The most effective response is to tell him six weeks is typical, that you cannot commit to month end, and offer to ask the checks team today whether this one could be prioritised: it gives him the fact that matters now, refuses the commitment that is not yours, and offers the one action that might help. It beats telling him the timing is nothing to do with you and he must ask the checks team himself, because you hold information he needs and can ask a question he cannot. It beats saying you will find out and come back without giving him the usual timescale, because he may promise month end today while waiting. The least effective response is promising the account will be live by month end: a firm date is given for a process run by another team, and a prospect signs a deal on it. That is a commitment you cannot back rather than an unhelpful answer. The principle: give the norm, refuse the promise, and offer the ask.

question_text: You are a financial crime analyst. A colleague asks you to take twelve of her cases this week because she has “a lot on”. She asked the same last month and you agreed. Send the twelve cases straight over to your team leader to reallocate, without telling your colleague that you have done so or that you were asked.
