question_text: You work in the control room of a taxi firm. Drivers are paid a bonus for completing more than forty jobs a week. You notice a driver has logged three jobs this week that were cancelled by the customer before pickup, which would take him over forty. He says the customers cancelled at the door, so he drove the distance and should be credited. The firm’s rules on cancelled jobs are written and you have not read them. The operations manager is on shift. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Check the written rules on cancelled jobs, and if they do not cover doorstep cancellations put it to the operations manager before the bonus is calculated.
Remove the three cancelled jobs from his total, since the jobs were not completed and the bonus is for completed work.
Leave the three jobs on his total and let the bonus be paid, since he did drive to each address and nobody audits the weekly figures in any detail.
Report the driver to the operations manager for logging cancelled jobs as completed work in order to reach the bonus threshold.
explanation: B: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholder's: the rules may well credit a driver who travelled to a doorstep cancellation, and striking the jobs out decides that without reading them. C: Falsifies a payment record: it lets a bonus be paid on jobs recorded as completed that were not, without checking whether the rules allow it, and relies on the absence of an audit. That is dishonesty, not a judgement call. D: Escalates prematurely: the written rules may entitle him to the credit, so a report of deliberate manipulation is made before the document that settles it has been read. The most effective response is to check the written rules on cancelled jobs, and if they do not cover doorstep cancellations put it to the operations manager before the bonus is calculated: there is a rule that decides whether such a cancellation counts, reading it costs a minute, and he is on shift and can settle it in time. It answers the question without accusing anyone. It beats removing the three cancelled jobs from his total, because that decides the same question in the driver’s disfavour without reading the rule. It beats reporting him for logging cancelled jobs as completed work, because a serious accusation before checking risks condemning him over something the rules may allow. The least effective response is leaving the three on his total because nobody audits the weekly figures: it lets a bonus be paid on incomplete jobs without any check. That is worse than the other two, which act hastily but keep the payment honest. The principle: read the rule that governs it, and take the decision to whoever owns it rather than resolving it quietly either way.

question_text: You are an audit associate testing a client’s stock records. Four of the thirty items in your sample have no paperwork behind them. Your senior told the client’s finance team yesterday that the testing was going well. The file is reviewed on Friday, and the four items would change what it concludes. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Ask the client's finance team to find the missing paperwork, and decide what the working paper should say once you have seen whether they can produce it.
Write the four items up in the working paper today and take them to your senior straight away, so the conclusion can be revisited well before the file is reviewed on Friday.
Write the four items up in the working paper without telling your senior, so the file records the position and nobody has to reopen what the client has already been told about the testing.
Finish the remaining testing first and put all of the sample's problems to your senior together on Friday morning, so the discussion happens once rather than in pieces.
explanation: A: Lets the client settle a file point: the gap is evidence in its own right, and whether it is recorded stops being your judgement or your senior's. C: Stays silent on a point the reviewer needs: the paper is technically complete, but the one person who could act on it before Friday learns nothing, and the client keeps a picture that is now wrong. D: Delays the decision: Friday morning is the review itself, which leaves no time to do anything about four items that change the conclusion. The most effective response is to write the four items up in the working paper today and take them to your senior straight away: four unsupported items in a sample of thirty is a finding, your senior owns the conclusion, and there are days left to act on it. It beats finishing the remaining testing and putting all the sample’s problems to them together on Friday morning, because Friday is the review, so raising it then is raising it too late to change anything. It beats asking the client’s finance team to find the missing paperwork first, because missing paperwork is itself the evidence, and waiting hands them the decision about what your file says. The least effective response is writing the four items up without telling your senior: the paper is complete and the one person who could act is not told, so the error survives review and the client keeps an assurance that is no longer true. That is silence about something somebody needed, which is a different kind of wrong from raising it late, or from keeping the question open with the client. The principle: put evidence in front of the person who owns the conclusion while they can still use it.

question_text: You are an audit junior. Your manager asked you on Monday to finish the revenue testing by Wednesday. On Tuesday she mentions in passing that it would be “really useful” to have a summary of the client’s new contracts. The summary would take a day. The revenue testing is half done. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Finish the revenue testing by Wednesday as agreed, and say nothing at all about the contracts summary unless and until she raises it with you again.
Ask her which she wants first, saying plainly that the contracts summary would take a day and would put Wednesday's revenue testing at risk.
Start the contracts summary straight away without saying anything about Wednesday, since it was the most recent thing she asked for and it is plainly what is on her mind.
Work on the contracts summary in the evenings so that both the testing and the summary are delivered by Wednesday without anything having to change.
explanation: A: Ignores the second request: an offhand remark from your manager is still a request, and leaving it unanswered means she does not know it is not happening. C: Drops a committed deadline in silence: she is expecting revenue testing on Wednesday and has no idea it has stopped, so she cannot re-plan anything. D: Solves a scheduling problem with your own time: it works once, and it hides from your manager that she asked for two days of work in one. The most effective response is to ask her which she wants first, saying plainly that the contracts summary would take a day and would put Wednesday’s revenue testing at risk: only she can rank her own two requests, and she cannot do it without the fact that one costs a day. It beats finishing the revenue testing as agreed and saying nothing about the summary unless she raises it, because a manager’s passing request still needs an answer. It beats working on the summary in the evenings so both are delivered, because absorbing it privately conceals that the ask was not possible. question_text: You are a reconciliations clerk. You have been covering two roles for six weeks. Tonight’s break report needs a count of unresolved items and you have lost track of four of them. A careful recount would take ninety minutes you do not have. The report goes to the operations committee. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Report the number you can stand behind, state that four items are uncounted and why, and say plainly that six weeks of double-running is the cause.
Enter a count that you estimate from last week's figure, since it will be close enough and the committee only looks at the direction of travel anyway.
Stay late and do the ninety-minute recount, and say nothing about how long the double-running has gone on.
Submit the report without the count at all, and add it once the recount has been done properly later in the week.
explanation: B: Records an estimate as a count: the committee reads a measured figure, and the one thing that would tell them the reporting has become unreliable is the thing removed. C: Absorbs it again: the number is right this week and the sixth week of covering two roles remains invisible to everybody who could end it. D: Removes the number without the reason: the committee sees a gap and has no idea that a six-week resourcing problem sits behind it. The most effective response is to report the number you can stand behind, state that four items are uncounted and why, and say plainly that six weeks of double-running is the cause: the committee gets a figure it can trust, an honest statement of what is missing, and the only route to the problem being fixed. It beats submitting the report without the count and adding it later in the week, because a gap with no explanation tells them nothing. It beats staying late for the ninety-minute recount and saying nothing about the double-running, because a seventh week of that being invisible is how this happens again. The least effective response is entering a count estimated from last week’s figure: an estimate is presented as a count, so the report looks exactly as reliable as it did before it stopped being reliable. That is falsifying the measure rather than reporting it incompletely or absorbing the strain. The principle: report what you can stand behind, name what you cannot, and name the cause.

question_text: You are a financial crime analyst. A colleague on your team has forty alerts outstanding against a five-day limit, and some are now eight days old. They have said twice that they are on top of it. Your own queue is clear. The weekly figures your team leader sees do not show individual backlogs. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Offer to take a share of the older alerts today, and say that if the backlog is still there at the end of the week you will both need to raise it with your team leader.
Send a note over to your team leader asking them to look at your colleague's queue, and offer none of your own spare capacity while somebody senior decides what to do.
Work through a few of the oldest alerts yourself and mention it to your colleague afterwards, so the backlog comes down without an awkward conversation about it now.
Take them at their word that they are on top of it and leave the alerts with them, since it is their own queue to manage and they have now said twice that it is under control.
explanation: B: Hands the colleague to their manager instead of helping: your queue is clear, the alerts are eight days old today, and the first they know of it is a conversation with their team leader. C: Helps quietly and leaves the cause: the queue comes down this week, the reason it built up is never discussed, and it builds up again next month. D: Accepts a reassurance the facts contradict: forty alerts against a five-day limit, some eight days old, is not a queue under control. The most effective response is to offer to take a share of the older alerts today, and say that if the backlog is still there at the end of the week you will both need to raise it: the alerts have a limit already breached, you have capacity, and naming the escalation point makes the offer honest rather than a favour. It beats working through a few of the oldest yourself and mentioning it afterwards, because silently clearing somebody’s queue fixes this week and nothing else. It beats taking them at their word and leaving the alerts with them, because the numbers contradict the reassurance. The least effective response is asking your team leader to look at your colleague’s queue while offering none of your own capacity: help that costs you nothing is withheld, the alerts are no closer to being worked, and a colleague who has twice said they are managing hears about it from above. That is passing a colleague on rather than a slower way of helping. The principle: offer the help you can actually give, and be open about when it stops being enough.

question_text: You are a management accounts assistant. The board pack goes at 9am tomorrow and one department has not sent its cost figures. Their manager is uncontactable until the morning. Last month’s figure for that department was £84,000 and the trend has been flat. Everything else in the pack is finished. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Send the pack without that department's page at all, so that everything in it is a figure somebody has actually supplied.
Enter a figure that you work out from last month's £84,000, since the trend has been flat, and finish the pack as complete without saying where the number came from.
Hold the pack until the department's manager can be reached in the morning, and send it out as soon as the real figure has arrived.
Put the pack together with that department's line marked as not yet received, and tell the finance director tonight which line is missing and why.
explanation: A: Removes the gap from view: a missing page reads as an oversight, and the board cannot ask about a line they cannot see is absent. B: Invents a figure and records it as reported: the board reads a number nobody in that department has given, and nothing on the page says it was estimated. C: Puts a fixed 9am deadline at the mercy of one telephone call: the board gets nothing at all if the manager is late. The most effective response is to put the pack together with that department’s line marked as not yet received, and tell the finance director tonight which line is missing and why: the pack lands at 9am, every figure in it is one somebody supplied, the gap is visible, and the director knows before the room does. It beats holding the pack until the department’s manager can be reached in the morning, because a 9am board pack cannot wait on one manager’s morning. It beats sending it without that department’s page at all, because a silently absent page hides the very thing the board should be asking about. The least effective response is entering a figure worked out from last month’s £84,000 and finishing the pack as complete: an invented number is presented to a board as a reported one, and every decision on that page rests on it. That is a false record rather than a poor way of handling a gap. The principle: ship on time with the hole visible, never with the hole filled in.

question_text: You are a financial crime analyst. A colleague has closed eleven alerts in one afternoon with the same one-line reason. Some of those alerts look to you as though they needed more work. He is well regarded and closed them within policy. Your team leader reviews a sample of closures monthly. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Reopen the eleven alerts yourself and work them properly, without raising it with him or your team leader at all.
Say nothing and let the monthly sample review pick it up, since that is exactly what the sampling process exists to catch.
Ask him first what the one-line reason covers, and if the answer does not satisfy you, put the eleven closures to your team leader as something to look at.
Tell your team leader the eleven closures were properly reasoned and consistent with policy, so that nothing has to be reopened and your colleague is not put under suspicion.
explanation: A: Redoes a colleague's work in silence: he learns nothing, the duplication is invisible, and nobody decides whether the closures were wrong. B: Leaves it to a sample: eleven closures in an afternoon may well not be sampled at all, and the specific thing you noticed is not what sampling looks for. D: Vouches for work you have not verified: your team leader relies on it when choosing the monthly sample, and the one signal that something needed another look is removed by the person who saw it. The most effective response is to ask him first what the one-line reason covers, and if the answer does not satisfy you, put the eleven closures to your team leader: he may have a perfectly good answer, asking costs nothing and is recoverable, and the route onward is clear if the answer is thin. It beats saying nothing and letting the monthly sample review pick it up, because a monthly sample is unlikely to land on these eleven. It beats reopening the alerts yourself and working them properly, because quietly redoing them decides nothing and duplicates everything. The least effective response is telling your team leader the closures were properly reasoned and consistent with policy: she is told they were sound by the one person who thought otherwise, so the sample is chosen on a false picture. question_text: You are an audit associate. A colleague is meeting the client’s financial controller tomorrow to ask for a schedule. Last week the same controller told you sharply that she had already sent it and would not be sending it twice. Your colleague does not know this and has not asked. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Send him a message tomorrow morning just before he goes into the meeting, so that the warning is at least fresh in his mind when he walks in there.
Go and ask the controller yourself whether she ever sent the schedule, without telling your colleague that you are doing it.
Tell your colleague today what the controller said last week, and check together whether the schedule did arrive before he goes and asks for it again.
Let him go into the meeting without mentioning what she said, since he has not asked and she may well be in a better mood about it tomorrow.
explanation: A: Times it too late to act on: checking whether the schedule arrived takes longer than the walk to the meeting room. B: Duplicates the approach: she now hears from two of you about the same schedule, which is precisely what annoyed her. D: Lets a colleague walk into it: a two-minute warning would have changed how he opens the meeting, and the client's goodwill is spent for nothing. The most effective response is to tell your colleague today what the controller said last week, and check together whether the schedule did arrive: it gives him the warning while there is still time to check, and checking is what prevents the second ask altogether. It beats messaging him tomorrow morning just before he goes into the meeting, because that leaves no time to look. It beats going to ask the controller yourself whether she ever sent it, because a second approach from a different person is the thing she objected to. The least effective response is letting him go into the meeting without mentioning what she said: he walks in without a fact you hold that would have changed how he ran it. That is withholding it rather than giving it late or acting on it clumsily. The principle: warn the person early enough that the warning is still useful.

question_text: You are a financial crime analyst. A colleague asks you to take twelve of her cases this week because she has “a lot on”. She asked the same last month and you agreed. Your own queue is full but manageable. Your team leader allocates cases and does not know about either request. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell her you cannot take any of them this week, and leave it there without suggesting anything about the allocation.
Tell her you can take a few but that this is the second time, and that the two of you should put the allocation to your team leader rather than rearranging it privately.
Take a few of them without saying anything, since you managed last month and she would not ask twice without a reason for it.
Send the twelve cases straight over to your team leader to reallocate, without telling your colleague that you have done so or that you were asked.

D: Hands the request to a manager behind the colleague's back: she asked you directly, and the first she hears is a reallocation she did not expect. The most effective response is to tell her you can take a few but that this is the second time, and that the two of you should put the allocation to your team leader: it helps a little, names the pattern honestly to her face, and takes the question to the person whose job it is. It beats taking a few without saying anything because you managed last month, since absorbing it twice hides a real allocation problem. The least effective response is sending the twelve cases to your team leader to reallocate without telling her: the request is escalated over her head, so she is blindsided and the conversation you could have had is now a management one. That is going around a colleague rather than being too soft or too hard. The principle: say it to her, then take the allocation where it belongs, together.

question_text: You are an audit associate testing a client’s stock records. Four of the thirty items in your sample have no paperwork behind them. Your senior told the client’s finance team yesterday that the testing was going well. The file is reviewed on Friday, and the four items would change what it concludes. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Ask the client's finance team to find the missing paperwork, and decide what the working paper should say once you have seen whether they can produce it.
Write the four items up in the working paper today and take them to your senior straight away, so the conclusion can be revisited well before the file is reviewed on Friday.
Write the four items up in the working paper without telling your senior, so the file records the position and nobody has to reopen what the client has already been told about the testing.
Finish the remaining testing first and put all of the sample's problems to your senior together on Friday morning, so the discussion happens once rather than in pieces.
explanation: A: Lets the client settle a file point: the gap is evidence in its own right, and whether it is recorded stops being your judgement or your senior's. C: Stays silent on a point the reviewer needs: the paper is technically complete, but the one person who could act on it before Friday learns nothing, and the client keeps a picture that is now wrong. D: Delays the decision: Friday morning is the review itself, which leaves no time to do anything about four items that change the conclusion. The most effective response is to write the four items up in the working paper today and take them to your senior straight away: four unsupported items in a sample of thirty is a finding, your senior owns the conclusion, and there are days left to act on it. question_text: You are an events coordinator at a conference centre. A client’s two-day conference starts on Thursday. On Tuesday you learn the main auditorium’s air-conditioning has failed and cannot be repaired before Friday. A smaller room could hold the delegates but only seated theatre- style, losing the exhibition space the client has sold to sponsors. The client’s events manager is contactable. Your operations director is on leave until Thursday. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Ring the client's events manager today, explain the failure, set out the smaller room and what it would cost her in exhibition space, and agree the plan with her before anything is moved.
Move the conference to the smaller room and email the client to confirm the change, explaining that the auditorium is unusable and this was the only workable alternative.
Wait until Thursday when your operations director is back, so that the client is given a decision with the authority of the centre behind it rather than an incomplete picture.
Leave the conference in the auditorium and say nothing, since the room may be tolerable in October and telling the client now would cause alarm about something that might not be a problem.

D: Hides the problem / silent deadline slip: it gambles a client's two- day conference and her sponsors on the weather, with the one person who could plan around it deliberately left uninformed. That is concealment, not judgement. The most effective response is to ring the client’s events manager today, explain the failure, and set out the smaller room and what it would cost her in exhibition space: she sold that space to sponsors, so only she can weigh a working room against losing it, and on Tuesday she still has two days to tell them or make other arrangements. Giving her the failure, the option and the cost lets her decide while deciding is still possible. It beats moving the conference to the smaller room and emailing to confirm the change, because that takes a commercial decision about her sponsors out of her hands. It beats waiting until Thursday when your operations director is back, because that consumes the client’s entire remaining planning time for the sake of internal authority. The least effective response is leaving the conference in the auditorium and saying nothing: it leaves a two-day conference in a room with no air-conditioning, tells nobody, and relies on the weather. That is worse than moving the room, which at least secures a usable one, and worse than waiting for the director, which at least intends to tell her. The principle: when a failure forces a trade-off that belongs to the client, give them the facts and the options while they still have time to choose.

question_text: You are a technician at a food-testing laboratory. Today you are preparing a batch of samples from a food manufacturer whose production run is on hold until your results are reported. If the calibration is wrong the results are invalid and the manufacturer would have to courier fresh samples, extending the hold by days. Ask the senior technician to check your calibration before you run the batch, so the manufacturer's samples are analysed right first time.

Skip the unfamiliar calibration step, reasoning that the instrument was set up recently enough for the readings to be close, and report the results in the usual way.

D: Gambles recklessly with the client's batch: skipping a required calibration and reporting the results anyway stakes the validity of the analysis, and days of the manufacturer's held production, on a guess, a reckless disregard of the required method rather than a defensible way of working. The most effective response is to ask the senior technician to check your calibration before you run the batch: the expertise you need is at the next bench, a check takes minutes, and it protects the one thing the manufacturer’s held production depends on, valid results first time, while you keep ownership of your own batch. It beats working through the calibration alone with the manual, because that gambles days of the client’s hold on one unsupervised attempt; taking care is not the same as knowing the procedure, and the risk could be removed by simply asking. The least effective response is skipping the unfamiliar calibration step and reporting the results anyway: unlike attempting it alone, which at least performs the required step carefully, and unlike reassigning the batch, which puts it in experienced hands, it omits the calibration entirely and gambles the client’s held production on guesswork. The principle: when a colleague’s expertise is at hand and the cost of error is high, ask early; do not gamble alone or hand the work away.

question_text: You are a procurement assistant. A new tool your team wants must be signed off by two named reviewers before it can be bought, which takes about a fortnight. The supplier’s quoted price rises at the end of this month, four days away. Nobody has asked you to do anything about it; you noticed the date on the quote yourself. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Start using the trial version on live work now and put the paperwork through afterwards, so that the price is locked in before the reviewers ever reach it.
Email the two reviewers explaining the price date and ask them to look this week, then wait to see whether either of them gets round to it in time.
Let the price rise and buy the tool at the higher figure once both reviews are finished, on the basis that the process is the process and it is not yours.
Tell your manager today that the quote expires on Friday and ask whether the review can be brought forward, so that somebody who can decide that is deciding it.
explanation: A: Builds a workaround round a control: the fortnight is not an accident, it is the two reviewers, and this puts the tool into real use before either of them has looked. B: Asks once and treats the answer as out of your hands: the reviewers do not know the deadline is real, and nobody who could reorder their week has been told. C: Absorbs a cost nobody chose: the extra spend is real and avoidable, and the people who would have wanted the choice never find out it existed. The most effective response is to tell your manager today that the quote expires on Friday and ask whether the review can be brought forward. The deadline is real, the decision about hurrying a review is not yours, and telling the person who can make it costs one message. It beats emailing the two reviewers about the price date and waiting to see whether either gets round to it, because reviewers who do not know a date is at stake have no reason to reorder their week. It beats letting the price rise and buying at the higher figure once both reviews are done, because a rise you saw coming and mentioned to nobody is a choice made by default. The least effective response is starting to use the trial version on live work and putting the paperwork through afterwards: it is worse than either of the other two, because both leave the reviewers in front of the decision, late or expensive, while this puts the tool into live use with neither having seen it. The principle: when a control is in the way of a real deadline, take the deadline to whoever owns the control, not round it.

question_text: You are an operations analyst. A customer has rung three times today about an outage and has been passed between two teams. You have just read the engineering note: the service returns in about four hours and his overnight run will need repeating tomorrow. He is on the phone to you now, angry at being moved around. You are not the person who normally speaks to customers. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Apologise for the three calls, take his number, and promise that somebody from the customer contact team will ring him back within the hour with the detail.
Tell him what the note says, that it is about four hours and his overnight run will need repeating tomorrow, then arrange with him who will confirm it later.
Transfer him to the customer contact team, who own this conversation, since giving a customer timings on an open incident is not really your job to do.
Tell him the outage is being worked on and that you cannot give him timings yourself, and ask him to wait for the official update coming out this evening.
explanation: A: Over-promises on somebody else's behalf: you cannot make that team ring within the hour, and if they do not, he has now been let down four times instead of three. C: Passes the problem on without owning it: it makes his fourth transfer of the day the answer to his complaint about being transferred three times. D: Withholds a timing you are holding: it is cautious rather than dishonest, but the two facts he needs to plan tonight are sitting on your screen unsaid. He has two decisions to make tonight and you are holding both answers, and agreeing who confirms keeps the ownership somewhere rather than nowhere. It beats apologising, taking his number and promising a call within the hour from the customer contact team, because you cannot commit another team to that, and a fourth broken promise costs more than the delay. It beats telling him the outage is being worked on and asking him to wait for the evening update, because the timings exist and are in front of you. The least effective response is transferring him on because giving a customer timings is not really your job: it is worse than either of the other two, because both engage with the man on the phone, while this answers a complaint about being passed around by passing him around again. question_text: You are an office assistant at a plumbing and heating firm. This morning the operations manager emailed asking you to compile last quarter’s supplier invoices for a cost review he is running later this week. As you begin, an engineer phones: he is at a customer’s home and cannot start a boiler repair until you email him the parts authorisation, which means finding the customer’s warranty record, about twenty minutes’ work. He and the customer are waiting. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Decide the operations manager's request should come first because it came from senior management, finish compiling the invoices, and tell the engineer to expect the authorisation this afternoon.
Alternate between the two tasks, looking up the warranty record in between batches of invoices, so that both the engineer and the operations manager see steady progress.
Tell the engineer the authorisation is already on its way so he stops chasing, then carry on with the invoices and actually send it once they are finished.
Send the engineer's authorisation first, since he and the customer are blocked until it arrives, then return to the invoices, which are not needed until later in the week.
explanation: A: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholder's: it ranks the manager's request first because of seniority, when his own email says the review is later this week, inventing an urgency he never expressed while two people stand waiting. B: Splits effort so nothing finishes: the authorisation is a single twenty-minute job, and breaking it into fragments between invoice batches stretches the engineer's and customer's wait far beyond what doing it in one go would take. C: Is dishonest to the engineer's face: claiming the authorisation is already on its way buys quiet at the cost of the truth, leaving him and the customer waiting on something that is not coming. That is deception, not a defensible ordering of tasks. The most effective response is to send the engineer’s authorisation first and then return to the invoices: he and the customer are blocked right now, the authorisation takes about twenty minutes, and the invoices are not needed until the review later in the week, so urgency and importance both point the same way. It beats finishing the invoices because the request came from senior management, since that invents an urgency the operations manager never expressed and ranks his request first on seniority while two people stand waiting. It beats alternating between the two tasks, because that chops a single short job into fragments and stretches the engineer’s and customer’s wait well beyond the twenty minutes it needs. The least effective response is telling the engineer the authorisation is already on its way when it is not: unlike putting the invoices first, which at least gives him an honest timeline, and unlike alternating, which at least makes real progress on the authorisation, it tells him a straightforward lie and leaves him and the customer waiting on something that is not coming. The principle: order work by real urgency and stated need, since a person blocked now outranks a task wanted later in the week, and never manage the gap with a lie.

question_text: You work at a farm shop. At 9am a delivery of fresh fish arrives that must go into the chiller within twenty minutes. A customer is waiting at the counter to collect a pre-ordered meat box, which takes five minutes to fetch and check. Your manager has asked you to price up the new season’s preserves before lunchtime, a job of about an hour. You are alone on the shop floor. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Get the fish into the chiller first, then fetch and check the waiting customer's pre-ordered meat box, and price up the preserves before lunchtime.
Leave the fish on the delivery bay while you serve the customer and price the preserves, and put it into the chiller once the shop floor is quieter.
Serve the waiting customer's meat box first since she is standing at the counter, then put the fish away and price the preserves.
Start pricing the preserves since your manager asked for them this morning, and deal with the fish and the customer as you work through the shelves.
explanation: B: Acts recklessly with a food safety risk: fresh fish left out beyond its chiller window is unsafe to sell, so the whole delivery is put at risk to make the morning run more smoothly. C: Delays the decision: five minutes at the counter takes a quarter of the chiller window on a fresh fish delivery that cannot be recovered if it warms. D: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholder's: an hour of pricing with a whole morning available is put ahead of a twenty-minute chiller window and a customer already waiting. The most effective response is to get the fish into the chiller first, then fetch and check the waiting customer’s pre-ordered meat box, and price the preserves before lunchtime: the fish has a twenty-minute window after which it cannot be sold at all, the meat box takes five minutes, and the preserves have hours. Only one of the three is irreversible. It beats serving the waiting customer’s meat box first because she is at the counter, since five minutes there spends a quarter of a window that cannot be extended. It beats starting on the preserves because your manager asked for them this morning, because an hour of pricing with a whole morning available should not precede either a chiller window or a waiting customer. The least effective response is leaving the fish on the delivery bay until the shop floor is quieter: it leaves fresh fish out well beyond its window, risking the entire delivery becoming unsafe to sell. That is worse than the other two, which sequence badly but get the fish away in time. The principle: protect what spoils first, then serve the person waiting, then do the job with hours of room.

question_text: You are an office administrator at a commercial printing company. While filing paperwork you notice that the shared template the sales team uses for customer quotes still contains last year’s paper prices, which rose noticeably in January. Nobody has been asked to look at the template, and two salespeople are preparing quotes with it this week. The current prices are held in the purchasing system, which you can access. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Update the template now with the January price rises you remember, marking the new figures as provisional to be checked later, so the salespeople are at least closer to the current rates.
Mention to this month's new starter that the template could do with tidying up when they get a chance, without explaining that the prices are wrong, and return to your filing.
Email the sales manager to explain the template still shows last year's prices and that quotes are being prepared this week, leaving the correction with them as owner of the quoting process.
Check the current prices in the purchasing system, update the template to match, and tell the two salespeople and the sales manager what you found and changed.
explanation: A: Acts on assumptions without checking: even flagged as provisional, remembered figures are still guesses in a live quoting template, and the purchasing system could give you the accurate prices in roughly the time the guesswork takes. That is abandonment, not a handover. C: Passes responsibility to others: the sales manager does own the quoting process, but leaving the whole correction in their inbox lets this week's quotes go out on old prices, when you could fix the figures accurately now and simply tell them. The most effective response is to check the current prices in the purchasing system, update the template to match, and tell the salespeople and their manager what you found: you spotted the problem, the accurate figures are within your reach, and quoting is live this week, so fixing it and informing the owners removes the risk. It beats updating the template from the prices you remember and marking them provisional, because the purchasing system could supply the real figures just as quickly, and the salespeople would otherwise be quoting from flagged guesses. It beats emailing the sales manager and leaving the correction with them, because that gives the owner the full picture but leaves the fix waiting in an inbox while this week’s quotes are prepared, when you could complete it accurately straight away. The least effective response is asking the new starter to tidy the template up sometime: unlike using remembered figures, which at least moves them closer to reality and flags the doubt, and unlike emailing the manager, which tells the responsible person exactly what is wrong, it hands a vague job to the one person who cannot know the prices are wrong, so the risk you spotted disappears with nobody equipped to act on it. The principle: when you spot an unowned problem you can fix, verify the facts, fix it, and tell the people it affects. Never bury it with someone who cannot recognise it.

question_text: You are a graduate in a Barclays payments operations team. A corporate customer’s payment file has been loaded three times this morning, so the same twelve payments now sit in the system three times over. Two of the duplicates have already been released to the receiving banks. The team’s usual view is that duplicates wash out by the end of the day, and the checklist says to raise duplicates with the team that sent the file before any of them are released. Your supervisor is at her desk. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell your supervisor now that two duplicate payments have already left, with the references and the customer's name, and start holding the ten that have not gone yet.
Message the sending team with the duplicate references and ask them to confirm which payments they meant to make, then decide what to raise once they have replied.
Start the recall process on the two released payments yourself, and tell your supervisor about the file once you know whether the recalls have actually worked.
Pass the whole file back to the team that sent it and ask them to work out which of the twelve payments have already been released to the receiving banks.
explanation: B: Waits for somebody else before deciding: the two released payments are already outside the bank, and the reply that would tell you to act may arrive after the working day has closed them. C: Substitutes your own remedy for the escalation: the recall may be the right step, but attempting it alone means the customer's exposure is known only to you while it is happening. D: Passes the problem on without owning it: the duplicates started with the sending team, but the checklist stops at duplicates that have not been released, and the two that have are in your queue. The most effective response is to tell your supervisor now that two duplicate payments have already left, with the references and the customer’s name attached, and to hold the ten that have not gone. Something has left the bank that should not have, the person who can decide what happens next is at her desk, and the ten still inside are recoverable while you talk. It beats messaging the sending team and deciding what to raise once they reply, because that puts a live exposure behind somebody else’s inbox. It beats starting the recall yourself and telling your supervisor once you know whether it worked, because the customer’s money is outside the bank for as long as only you know about it. The least effective response is to pass the whole file back to the team that sent it. Waiting and self-help are both slow, but they keep the exception with somebody who can see it, whereas handing it back gives the problem to a team that cannot see your queue and leaves nobody watching the released payments. The checklist route it invokes stops at duplicates that have not been released, and two of these have. The principle: an exception the team treats as routine is still an exception once part of it has left the building, and it goes to somebody who can act, not back to where it came from. Empower, one of the three behaviours in Barclays’ Mindset, asks you to escalate issues appropriately rather than work an exception alone.

question_text: You are a graduate in a client support team in corporate banking at Barclays. A client’s finance manager has emailed you, copying your director, to say your weekly cash summary is always late and half of it is wrong. The summary is built from a balances file her own team sends, which has arrived after the cut-off five weeks running. You have a scheduled call with her tomorrow, and your director has asked for nothing beyond a reply. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Reply to her and your director together, setting out when the balances file arrives against when the summary is due, and offer to agree a workable timetable on tomorrow's call.
Stop copying her into the weekly summary after that email, and send it to the client's other contacts instead, so that she has nothing further to complain about.
Reply to the finance manager alone, apologise for the summary being late, and leave her team's file out of it so that the complaint is not made any worse than it is.
Reply to your director first with the dates her team's file arrived, and ask him to take the accuracy point up with the finance manager on your behalf.
explanation: B: Withdraws from a client after a complaint: the person who raised the problem is removed from the thing she was complaining about, which ends the emails and ends the relationship with them. C: Buys peace with an incomplete account: the lateness has a cause you both need on the table, and an apology that hides it guarantees a sixth late summary next week. D: Routes a reply upwards that you could make yourself: the client wrote to you, and an answer arriving from your director turns a working problem into a matter between senior people. The most effective response is to reply to her and your director together, setting out when the balances file arrives against when the summary is due, and offering to agree a workable timetable on tomorrow’s call. Everyone who read the complaint reads the answer, the facts go out without anybody being called careless, and the call is used for the fix. It beats replying to the finance manager alone and leaving her team’s file out of it, because the apology then stands as the whole explanation and next week’s summary is late for the same reason. It beats replying to your director first and asking him to take the accuracy point up on your behalf, because a message you could send yourself becomes a conversation between senior people. The least effective response is to stop copying her into the weekly summary and send it to the client’s other contacts. A soft apology and an escalation are both answers of a kind, whereas quietly dropping her from the distribution answers a complaint by removing the complainant, and she will find out. The principle: answer a complaint to everyone who saw it, with the facts and without a culprit. Respect, one of Barclays’ values, asks you to trust those you work with and value everyone’s contribution, the person who complained included.

question_text: You are an insight analyst at Boston Consulting Group, building a customer analysis for a client. You asked for their sales extract three weeks ago, chased it twice, and it arrived yesterday. This morning their marketing lead emailed your manager saying the analysis is a week late and asking what has gone wrong. You have sent the client a short note on progress every week throughout. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Stop sending the client the weekly progress note, because they complained about the delay instead of asking you first, and leave them to notice that it has gone.
Reply saying the analysis will be finished by Friday, and leave the reasons for the delay out of it so that the exchange does not turn into an argument.
Reply to the marketing lead today with the dates you asked for the extract and the date it arrived, and give them a finish date, since the extract is now in your hands.
Ask your manager to answer the email, since it was sent to them, and carry on with the analysis without contacting the marketing lead yourself.
explanation: A: Withdraws a courtesy after being criticised: the one thing that was showing the client where the work stood is removed at the moment it would have answered them. B: Buys peace at the cost of the record: the marketing lead keeps a belief that your team is a week slow, and the extract that arrived yesterday goes unmentioned. D: Hands the account to somebody who was not there: the dates are yours, and the client's view of the delay is corrected at second hand or not at all. The most effective response is to reply today with the dates you asked, the date it arrived, and a finish date. It answers today, it replaces an impression with dates that can be checked, and it gives the marketing lead the thing they actually want, which is when the analysis will land. It beats asking your manager to answer the email and carrying on with the analysis, because the dates are in your hands and a second-hand account of them is weaker and slower. It beats replying with a Friday finish date and leaving the reasons out of it, because a Friday date with no explanation leaves the client believing your team lost a week, and that belief will be repeated. The least effective response is stopping the weekly progress note and leaving them to notice: the other three all leave the client better informed than they were this morning, whereas this one answers a complaint by taking away the weekly note, so the client is punished for having complained and loses the one thing that showed them where the work stood. The principle: answer an unfair complaint with the record, and never by withdrawing something the client relies on.

question_text: You are a systems analyst at Boston Consulting Group, setting up a client’s new booking system. Your testing shows that a report the client’s finance team uses every month will not be ready at go-live, and will be missing for about six weeks. The client’s project sponsor presents the go-live plan to their board on Thursday. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Raise it at the weekly project meeting next Tuesday, so that the whole team hears about it at the same time and can work out together what ought to be done about it before go-live.
Put the gap in writing to the manager running the engagement today, setting out what finance loses and for how long, so that the sponsor has it before Thursday.
Tell the client's finance team directly, since they are the people who will be without the report, and let them take it up before the board meeting.
Say nothing until after Thursday, on the basis that the report may still be ready by go-live and there is no point worrying the sponsor before the board has approved the plan.
explanation: A: Delays the decision: Tuesday is after Thursday, so the sponsor has already taken the plan to their board by the time the team first discusses it. C: Substitutes your own judgement for the sponsor's: the right people learn it in the wrong order, and the sponsor can be contradicted at their own board by their own colleagues. D: Withholds something the sponsor needed: they commit to a plan in front of their board without the one fact that changes it, and they find out afterwards that you already knew. The most effective response is to put the gap in writing to the manager today, with what finance loses and for how long. It is in writing, it is today, it says what the loss actually is, and it reaches the sponsor through the person who owns the relationship with them, while Thursday can still be changed. It beats raising it at the weekly project meeting next Tuesday, because Tuesday is after Thursday, so the sponsor stands in front of their board without a fact you were already holding. It beats telling the client’s finance team directly and leaving them to take it up, because finance hearing it first can put the sponsor in the position of being corrected at their own board by their own people. The least effective response is saying nothing until after Thursday in case the report is ready anyway: the other three all get the fact to somebody before Thursday, and this one keeps it back on a hope, so the sponsor commits publicly to a plan you know to be wrong and later learns you knew. The principle: get a fact to the person who is about to rely on it, through the route that does not undercut them.

question_text: You are a client services associate at Boston Consulting Group. A client, Penrose Timber, emails asking when the revised proposal document will reach them. The two people writing it are running a workshop for another client until Thursday and have not said how much is left to do. The client’s finance director wants a date this morning to put into a board pack that goes out this afternoon. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Reply that no date can be given until Thursday, and leave it there, so that nothing is promised that the two writing it have not agreed to.
Ring into the workshop and interrupt the two writing it for a date now, so that the client has an answer in time for the board pack that goes out to them this afternoon.
Tell the client the document will be ready on Friday for the board pack, and ask the two writing it to work to that date.
Reply now that you cannot give a date until you have spoken to the two writing it, since only they know what is left, and say what time today you will come back.
explanation: A: Leaves the client with nothing to plan with: a refusal with no time attached reads to them exactly like silence until Thursday. B: Buys a date by breaking into a workshop: the question is small, and the interruption lands in front of the people they are with. C: States a date as fact when nobody has checked it: the board pack carries Friday, and the two writing the document first hear of the commitment when they come back. The most effective response is to reply that you cannot give a date until you have spoken to the two writing it, and say what time today you will come back. It answers the client inside their morning, it commits you to a time rather than to a guess, and the date they eventually put in the board pack comes from the people doing the work. It beats replying that no date can be given until Thursday, because a refusal with no time attached leaves the finance director exactly where they started. It beats interrupting the workshop for a date now, because the question is small enough to hold for a few hours and the interruption lands in front of other people. The least effective response is telling the client the document will be ready on Friday: the other three all leave the date resting on somebody who knows how much work is left, whereas this one puts a figure you invented into a document the client’s board will act on. The principle: give the client a time for the answer rather than an answer you have not got.

question_text: You are a data analyst at Boston Consulting Group. On Tuesday you sent a client’s operations team an extract of their order data, and you have found this morning that it left out every order placed at the weekend. The client’s operations manager has already used the extract to work out where to move staff next month, and says those numbers go to their own team this afternoon. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Amend the entry in the shared log so it shows the corrected extract as the one sent on Tuesday, and let the client carry on with the figures they have.
Send a corrected extract straight away with a note of what was missing, and leave the operations manager to work out for themselves what it changes.
Tell the manager running the engagement what happened and ask them to decide who speaks to the client and when, doing nothing more about the extract yourself until they come back to you.
Ring the operations manager now, tell them the extract missed every weekend order and should not be shared today, and send a corrected extract explaining what has changed.
explanation: A: Alters a record so a mistake never happened: the log then says the client received a clean extract on Tuesday, and the wrong figures going out this afternoon have nothing behind them to explain where they came from. B: Leaves the reader to size the damage: the manager is hours from sharing conclusions, and a replacement file does not tell them which of those conclusions moves. C: Hands on a clock you are holding: the numbers reach the client's team this afternoon, and the correction now waits on somebody else's diary. The most effective response is to ring the operations manager now and tell them the extract missed every weekend order. The client is hours from acting on figures you know are wrong, a phone call reaches them before that happens, and the corrected extract arrives with the one thing they need, which is what changed. It beats sending a corrected extract straight away with a note of what was missing, because a replacement file leaves the manager to work out on their own which of today’s conclusions has moved. It beats asking the manager running the engagement to decide who speaks to the client, because the deadline is this afternoon and the decision about who rings is smaller than the delay it buys. The least effective response is amending the entry in the shared log so it shows the corrected extract as sent on Tuesday: the other three all leave the client holding something true, whereas this one makes the record say they were sent a clean extract on Tuesday, so a mistake that is still live in their staffing plan is written out of existence rather than corrected. The principle: correct the person who is about to act, and never repair a mistake by repairing the record of it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Dùng phương pháp ước lượng chữ số hàng đơn vị hoặc làm tròn đến hàng chục để loại ngay 2 phương án vô lý.

question_text: You are a programme support officer at Brantwood Services. Purchase orders over five thousand pounds need a second approver before they are raised, and the second approver for your programme is on annual leave until Monday. A supplier will hold a six thousand four hundred pound order at today’s price only until 5pm. Your manager is contactable, and a named deputy approver is listed for exactly this situation, though nobody in your team has used them before. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Contact the named deputy approver now, explain the price deadline and the amount, and ask them to give the second approval today, telling your manager you have done so.
Raise the order and sign the second approval off in your manager's name, then mention it to them when they are next free, keeping the price you were quoted.
Ask your manager to approve it themselves as a one-off, noting on the order that the usual second approver is away and that the price expires at 5pm.
Let the price expire and raise the order on Monday when the second approver is back, telling the supplier the order is coming and asking what the new price will be.
explanation: B: Puts your name to somebody else's approval: the second approver exists so that two people have actually looked at a large commitment, and an approval signed in an absent manager's name means one person looked. C: Escalates prematurely: a named deputy exists for exactly this situation, and asking a manager to step outside the control is a bigger ask than using the route designed for it. D: Gives up before the options are used: the deputy approver is listed for this case and has not been asked, so the price is lost to an assumption that the control cannot be satisfied today. The most effective response is to contact the named deputy approver now, explain the price deadline and the amount, and ask for the second approval today: the control exists to put a second pair of eyes on a large commitment, a deputy is listed for precisely this case, and using them satisfies the control and the 5pm price at once. It beats asking your manager to approve it themselves as a one-off, because it does not need an exception when a designed route is available. It beats letting the price expire and raising the order on Monday, because that loses money to an assumption nobody has tested. The least effective response is signing the second approval off in your manager’s name: only one person has looked at a large order, and the record now says two did. That makes it worse than the one-off exception, which keeps a real second person in the decision, and worse than waiting for Monday, which costs money but leaves the control intact. The principle: when a control blocks the work, use the route the control provides before asking for an exception, and never satisfy it on paper only.
tip: Mẹo MT: Dùng phương pháp ước lượng chữ số hàng đơn vị hoặc làm tròn đến hàng chục để loại ngay 2 phương án vô lý.

question_text: You are a shared services administrator at Brantwood Services. Two things are due at 4pm today. Finance closes its supplier payment run at 4pm and needs your check on eleven invoices before it can go. The training team needs its twenty course confirmations sent by 4pm or the venue releases the rooms. Each job takes about two hours and you have two hours left. Your team leader is at another office and answers messages within ten minutes. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Message your team leader now with both deadlines, the two hours you have and what each job needs, and ask which one to run first while you start on the invoices.
Assure both teams that their work will be done by 4pm, then start on the invoices and get as far through the course confirmations as the remaining time allows.
Split the remaining two hours evenly between the invoices and the course confirmations, leaving both jobs part done when 4pm arrives rather than choosing one of the two teams over the other.
Work through the eleven invoices first, and send the course confirmations tomorrow morning with a note to the training team explaining why they missed the venue deadline.
explanation: B: Gives an assurance you cannot deliver: two hours of work cannot cover four hours of jobs, so the promise is untrue at the moment it is made, and it uses up the ten minutes in which your team leader could have chosen. C: Splits effort so nothing finishes: at 4pm the payment run has no completed check and the venue has no confirmations, so both fixed deadlines fail instead of one. D: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholder's: it decides on your team leader's behalf that the payment run outranks twenty room bookings, when a message answered in ten minutes could have settled it. The most effective response is to message your team leader now with both deadlines, the two hours you have and what each job needs, and start on the invoices while you wait: both deadlines are fixed and external, only one is reachable in the time, and she can answer in ten minutes, so the choice belongs to the person who owns both commitments. It beats splitting the remaining two hours evenly between them, because that misses both deadlines instead of one. It beats working through the eleven invoices and sending the confirmations tomorrow with an explanation, because that makes the same call without asking, and the ten minutes it would have cost were available. The least effective response is assuring both teams their work will be done by 4pm: it tells them something that is not true when it is said, so neither can arrange cover, and the venue and the payment run both discover the problem with no time left. That makes it worse than splitting the time, which at least leaves real work done on both jobs, and worse than doing the invoices, which delivers one deadline in full and tells the other team what happened. The principle: when two fixed commitments collide, surface the clash to whoever owns both rather than choosing on their behalf or promising both.

question_text: You are a support analyst. You are the only person who knows the reporting tool will be unavailable all of next Wednesday, because you took the call from the vendor. The finance team meets this afternoon and is about to fix Wednesday as the day they run their month-end reports. You have a backlog of thirty tickets and your manager has asked you to clear it today. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Clear the backlog first as instructed, then send the outage note this evening, since thirty waiting customers plainly outrank one internal planning meeting.
Work through the backlog without telling anybody about Wednesday. The outage is a week away, and the vendor will very likely have told finance as well.
Spend five minutes now sending the finance team the outage date before their meeting, then return to the backlog and tell your manager why you paused for it.
Put a note about Wednesday into the shared channel and carry on with the backlog, so that the information is at least somewhere people are able to find it.
explanation: A: Ranks the instruction above the deadline that cannot move: the note is worth far less after the meeting has fixed the date it was meant to influence. B: Withholds a dependency only you hold: the meeting will fix a date on a day the tool does not run, and nobody in the room has any way of knowing that. D: Publishes to nobody in particular: the note exists, the finance team has no reason to look for it this afternoon, and the meeting goes ahead unaware. The most effective response is to spend five minutes now sending the finance team the outage date before their meeting, then return to the backlog and tell your manager why you paused. Five minutes before the meeting is worth more than an hour after it, and telling your manager keeps the backlog instruction honest rather than quietly disobeyed. It beats clearing the backlog first and sending the outage note this evening, because the value of the note collapses the moment the date is fixed. It beats putting a note about Wednesday into the shared channel and carrying on, because a channel post is not the same as telling the people about to decide. The least effective response is working through the backlog without telling anybody about Wednesday: it is worse than either of the other two, because both get the fact out eventually or somewhere, while this leaves a room fixing a date on a day the tool will not run. The principle: when a five-minute message is the difference between a team planning correctly and planning wrongly, it outranks the queue.

question_text: You are a security analyst. A customer’s account has been locked for four days while a review runs. Your manager has told the team to say it will be unlocked within twenty-four hours, which has now been said three times. The customer’s operations lead rings you and asks, plainly, when she will have her account back. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell her you cannot give a date at all and that she should take it up with her account manager, who has a better line into the review than you do.
Promise her it will be unlocked within twenty-four hours. That is the line the team has been given, and it is not your place to depart from it.
Tell her the twenty-four hours has been said three times and you cannot promise a fourth, find out today where the review actually is, and ring her back with it.
Tell her the review is complex and that you understand her frustration, and avoid giving any date at all until somebody senior has authorised one.
explanation: A: Refuses her and moves her on: she has rung three times, and being sent elsewhere is what a fourth day of nothing looks like from her side. B: Repeats an assurance you know has failed: the same twenty-four hours has been given three times, so she is being told something the evidence contradicts. D: Substitutes sympathy for information: she is four days in, and understanding without a fact leaves her with nothing new to act on. The most effective response is to tell her the twenty-four hours has been said three times and you cannot promise a fourth, find out today where the review actually is, and ring her back. Three failed promises is itself the most honest thing you can tell her, and finding out turns the call into something that changes her position. It beats telling her you cannot give a date and that she should take it up with her account manager, because she has rung three times and being redirected is indistinguishable from being ignored. It beats saying the review is complex and that you understand her frustration, because sympathy without a fact is the fourth day of nothing. The least effective response is promising it will be unlocked within twenty-four hours: it is worse than either of the other two, because both stop short of telling her something the evidence has disproved, while this repeats a promise that has failed three times. The principle: when the line you have been given has already failed, say that it has and go and find something true, rather than passing it on a fourth time.

question_text: You are a financial crime analyst. A colleague has closed eleven alerts in one afternoon with the same one-line reason. Some of those alerts look to you as though they needed more work. He is well regarded and closed them within policy. Your team leader reviews a sample of closures monthly. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Reopen the eleven alerts yourself and work them properly, without raising it with him or your team leader at all.
Say nothing and let the monthly sample review pick it up, since that is exactly what the sampling process exists to catch.
Ask him first what the one-line reason covers, and if the answer does not satisfy you, put the eleven closures to your team leader as something to look at.
Tell your team leader the eleven closures were properly reasoned and consistent with policy, so that nothing has to be reopened and your colleague is not put under suspicion.
explanation: A: Redoes a colleague's work in silence: he learns nothing, the duplication is invisible, and nobody decides whether the closures were wrong. B: Leaves it to a sample: eleven closures in an afternoon may well not be sampled at all, and the specific thing you noticed is not what sampling looks for. D: Vouches for work you have not verified: your team leader relies on it when choosing the monthly sample, and the one signal that something needed another look is removed by the person who saw it. The most effective response is to ask him first what the one-line reason covers, and if the answer does not satisfy you, put the eleven closures to your team leader: he may have a perfectly good answer, asking costs nothing and is recoverable, and the route onward is clear if the answer is thin. It beats saying nothing and letting the monthly sample review pick it up, because a monthly sample is unlikely to land on these eleven. It beats reopening the alerts yourself and working them properly, because quietly redoing them decides nothing and duplicates everything. The least effective response is telling your team leader the closures were properly reasoned and consistent with policy: she is told they were sound by the one person who thought otherwise, so the sample is chosen on a false picture. That is asserting something you have not checked rather than under-reacting. The principle: ask the person, then take a real doubt to the person who samples.

question_text: You are a sales assistant in a furniture showroom. A customer ordered a sofa eight weeks ago with a promised delivery this week. The warehouse has just told you the fabric is delayed and it will now be a further four weeks. The customer is in the showroom this morning to arrange a delivery slot and does not yet know. Your showroom manager is on the floor. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Book the delivery slot she asks for and let the warehouse contact her about the delay, since they will have the accurate dates and the delay is their fault rather than the showroom's.
Book a provisional delivery slot for four weeks' time and explain that the warehouse has had to move the date, so that she leaves with a new arrangement in place.
Tell her straight away that the fabric is delayed and delivery is now four weeks out, apologise, and go through what she can do about it including speaking to the manager.
Take her delivery preferences as she expects, then ring her this afternoon once you have found out from the warehouse exactly what has caused the delay and how firm the new date is.
explanation: A: Hides the problem: it knowingly books a delivery that cannot happen and leaves someone else to break the news. Sending a customer away believing a false date is concealment, not a handover. B: Delays the decision: it hands her a new date before she has been given the choice of cancelling, waiting or taking something else, and after eight weeks that choice is hers to make. D: Delays the message: she is standing in front of you arranging a delivery that is not going to happen. Letting her make those plans and correcting them later wastes her morning and her trust. The most effective response is to tell her straight away that the fabric is delayed and delivery is now four weeks out, apologise, and go through her options including speaking to the manager: she is in the showroom to arrange something that is no longer possible, so she needs the fact immediately, and after eight weeks of waiting the decision about what happens next belongs to her. It beats booking a provisional slot for four weeks’ time, because that presents her with a decision already taken, when cancelling or changing the order may be what she wants. It beats taking her preferences now and ringing this afternoon once the warehouse has explained, because letting her plan a delivery you know will not happen wastes her time and makes the correction worse. The least effective response is booking the slot she asks for and letting the warehouse contact her: it books a date that cannot be met, so she leaves holding a false promise made knowingly. That is worse than the other two, which mishandle the timing but do not create a false commitment. The principle: when a promise has broken, tell the customer while they are in front of you and let them choose what happens next.
