question_text: You are a property manager for a block of flats. A leaseholder has been chasing you for three weeks about a leak into her flat from the roof. Today the contractor confirms the roof needs a full repair costing more than the reserve fund holds, which means a consultation with all leaseholders and no repair for at least two months. She has already reported damage to her ceiling. Your director is available. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Ring the leaseholder today, explain the roof needs full repair, that consultation means at least two months, and what will be done about her ceiling and the leak meanwhile.
Wait until the consultation is under way before contacting her, so that you can give her firm dates rather than an open-ended answer she will only chase you about again.
Write to all leaseholders with the consultation notice, so that everyone including her receives the same information about the roof at the same time.
Tell her the roof repair has been approved in principle and that you will confirm timescales once the consultation process has been worked through.
explanation: B: Hides the problem: she has water entering her flat and has chased for three weeks. Waiting for tidier information leaves her with no information at all, and the silence is chosen to avoid being chased rather than to help her. C: Tells the wrong audience first: she has been chasing for three weeks and has water coming into her flat, so receiving a standard notice with everyone else answers none of her particular questions. D: Over-promises: describing it as approved in principle implies more certainty than a consultation that has not started, and it withholds the two-month timescale she needs to plan around. The most effective response is to ring the leaseholder today, explain the roof needs full repair, that consultation means at least two months, and what will be done about her ceiling and the leak meanwhile: she has been chasing for three weeks, has an active leak and ceiling damage, and the news is bad in a specific way she needs to plan around. That treats her as someone with a live problem rather than one of a list. It beats writing to all leaseholders with the consultation notice, because a general notice answers the block’s question and not hers. It beats telling her the repair is approved in principle with timescales to follow, because that overstates where things stand and still leaves out the timescale. The least effective response is waiting until the consultation is under way so you can give her firm dates: it delays telling her anything until the information is neater, while water continues to come into her flat, and the reason is to avoid being chased. That is worse than the other two, which communicate partially but do communicate. The principle: tell the person carrying the consequence directly, give them the timescale even when it is bad, and say what happens in the meantime.
tip: Mẹo MT: Dùng phương pháp ước lượng chữ số hàng đơn vị hoặc làm tròn đến hàng chục để loại ngay 2 phương án vô lý.

question_text: You are an operations coordinator working the night shift alone. The handling agent’s supervisor mentions to you, as a favour, that she will not have enough staff for the six o’clock departures and asks you not to put it on the record while she tries to fix it. Your duty manager comes on at five, an hour before the first flight. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Write what she told you into the shift handover so that the duty manager reads it on arrival at five, and leave the decision about what to do with the morning to him.
Agree to keep it between the two of you as she asked, on the basis that she knows her own staffing best and has told you she is dealing with it.
Ring round the standby list yourself tonight to find cover for her shifts, and tell the duty manager in the morning once you know whether it has worked.
Tell her plainly that you cannot keep this off the record, then call the duty manager tonight so that cover can be looked for while there are still hours in which to find it.
explanation: A: Delays the decision: a handover read at five leaves an hour before the first departure, which is too late to bring anyone in, so the warning arrives after it could have been used. B: Trades a warning for a favour: the one person who could have called in cover overnight is deliberately kept from knowing, and the promise not to tell him is what makes it a concealment rather than a delay. C: Substitutes your own fix for his decision: staffing another company's shift is not yours to arrange, and he still arrives at five to find out whether somebody else's improvisation held. The most effective response is to tell her plainly that you cannot keep this off the record, then call the duty manager tonight: the value of the warning is entirely in the hours before five, and being straight with her means she is not misled about what you are going to do. It beats writing what she told you into the shift handover for him to read on arrival, because that surfaces at five with one hour left, when calling anyone in is no longer realistic. It beats ringing round the standby list yourself to find cover for her shifts, because arranging another company’s cover is not yours to do, and he still learns at five whether it worked. The least effective response is agreeing to keep it between the two of you as she asked: it is an agreement to keep the only person who could act in the dark, which is a different thing from judging when to raise it. That is what separates it from the handover note, which gets the information to him too late to use, and from ringing the standby list, which acts on his behalf without telling him. The principle: escalate while the escalation can still change something, and never promise silence you would have to break.
tip: Mẹo MT: Trong đề thi SHL, quản lý thời gian tối đa 60-75 giây cho mỗi câu tính toán số học.

question_text: You are a ticket desk agent. A student has missed her flight because she went to the wrong terminal. On her fare, a missed departure means the ticket has no value and a new one has to be bought at the price of the day. She has very little money and is close to tears. There are two later flights with seats. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Explain that a missed departure means the ticket is no longer valid and that a new one has to be bought, and leave her to decide what she wants to do about it.
Put her name on the standby list for the next departure so that she has a chance of getting away this evening while she works out how to pay for a new ticket.
Tell her that if she writes to the airline explaining what happened they will very probably refund the ticket, so that she leaves the desk with something to hold on to.
Tell her plainly what the fare rules mean, then check what her booking does still allow and what the cheapest way onto a later flight would be, and give her the real figures.
explanation: A: Stops at the rule: the position is stated correctly and no further look is taken at fares, later services or anything her booking might still allow. B: Acts before checking what her booking allows: a place on the standby list may not be open to her fare at all, and she waits at the airport on a hope nobody has verified. C: Sends her away with a false hope: nothing you know supports that promise, and she will make her plans around a refund that is unlikely to come. The most effective response is to tell her plainly what the fare rules mean, then check what her booking does still allow and what the cheapest way onto a later flight would be: the rule is not negotiable and saying so is honest, but what her booking still permits and what the cheapest onward fare is are both things she cannot look up and you can. It beats explaining that a missed departure voids the ticket and leaving her to decide, because stating the rule and stopping leaves her with no idea what is actually possible. It beats putting her name on the standby list for the next departure, because a standby place her fare may not allow leaves her waiting on something nobody has checked. The least effective response is telling her the airline will very probably refund if she writes in: it invents a likely refund to soften the moment, and she will plan around money that is not coming. That is worse than stating the rule, which is unhelpful but true, and worse than the standby list, which is at least trying something. The principle: be straight about what cannot be done, then spend your effort finding what can.
tip: Mẹo MT: Trong đề thi SHL, quản lý thời gian tối đa 60-75 giây cho mỗi câu tính toán số học.

question_text: You are an onboarding analyst. A colleague in sales asks you to confirm to his prospect that their account can be live by the end of the month, which would win the deal. Accounts like this usually take six weeks and the checks are not yours. It is the eighteenth. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell him six weeks is typical, that you cannot commit to month end, and offer to ask the checks team today whether this one could be prioritised.
Promise him the account will be live by month end, since he needs it to win the deal and there is a reasonable chance the checks come back quickly this time.
Tell him the timing is nothing to do with you at all, and that he will have to ask the checks team himself if he wants a firm date for the prospect.
Tell him you will find out and come back to him, without saying anything now about how long these accounts normally take.
explanation: B: Gives a promise about somebody else's process: the prospect signs on it, and when six weeks turns out to be six weeks the firm has broken a commitment it never made. C: Passes a colleague away from help you could give: you know the typical timescale and could ask, and he is left starting from nothing. D: Withholds the useful part: he is talking to the prospect today, and the six-week norm is the thing that would stop him promising anything. The most effective response is to tell him six weeks is typical, that you cannot commit to month end, and offer to ask the checks team today whether this one could be prioritised: it gives him the fact that matters now, refuses the commitment that is not yours, and offers the one action that might help. It beats telling him the timing is nothing to do with you and he must ask the checks team himself, because you hold information he needs and can ask a question he cannot. It beats saying you will find out and come back without giving him the usual timescale, because he may promise month end today while waiting. The least effective response is promising the account will be live by month end: a firm date is given for a process run by another team, and a prospect signs a deal on it. That is a commitment you cannot back rather than an unhelpful answer. The principle: give the norm, refuse the promise, and offer the ask.
tip: Mẹo MT: Luôn kiểm tra kỹ đơn vị tính (Triệu VNĐ vs Tỷ VNĐ, Tháng vs Năm) trước khi tính toán.

question_text: You are an audit junior. The client’s financial controller has asked you for a summary of the queries raised so far, which will take an hour. Your manager has asked for a section of testing by tonight, which will take the rest of the day. The controller is going on leave tomorrow for two weeks. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Do the summary first because the controller is leaving, and tell your manager tonight if the testing has not been finished as a result of it.
Ask the controller to send her questions by email so you can answer them from wherever you are while she is away on leave for the fortnight.
Get on with the testing and leave the controller's summary until she is back in a fortnight, since your manager's work is the priority and nobody has said otherwise about the summary.
Tell your manager that the controller leaves tomorrow and ask whether to spend the hour on her summary before she goes, since the testing can absorb an hour and the controller cannot.
explanation: A: Reorders your manager's work without asking: she may have a reason the testing cannot move that you do not know about. B: Solves the wrong problem: she asked for a summary of queries raised, not for a channel, and she wants it before she goes. C: Declines to raise a two-week window: the controller's leave is the fact your manager does not have, and the choice is made by not making it. The most effective response is to tell your manager that the controller leaves tomorrow and ask whether to spend the hour on her summary before she goes: your manager owns the ordering, the leave is the fact that makes the hour urgent, and asking takes a minute. It beats doing the summary first and telling your manager tonight if the testing slipped, because reordering her work without asking is her call to make. It beats asking the controller to send her questions by email while she is away, because a mailbox is not the summary she asked for. The least effective response is getting on with the testing and leaving the summary until she is back in a fortnight: a two-week window closes tomorrow and the person who could decide is never told it exists. That is avoiding the question rather than answering it wrongly. The principle: when a window is about to close, the person who owns the priorities needs to know today.
tip: Mẹo MT: Trong đề thi SHL, quản lý thời gian tối đa 60-75 giây cho mỗi câu tính toán số học.

question_text: You are an internal helpdesk adviser at Calder Group. Two colleagues in the same team, Tom and Priya, have fallen out over who owns the shared inbox rota. Since Friday neither has picked the rota up, and the inbox now holds forty unanswered staff requests, some of them four days old. You need the rota running to close your own tickets. Both are at their desks. Your team leader is back tomorrow. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Work round the problem by answering the forty requests yourself today and leaving the rota question for your team leader to settle when they are back tomorrow.
Email both of them and your team leader setting out how many requests are waiting and how old the oldest is, and ask for the rota to be decided.
Ask Tom and Priya together for fifteen minutes and agree who covers the inbox today and tomorrow, since the forty waiting requests need an owner before the rota question is settled.
Tell each of them separately what the other has been saying about the rota, in the hope that hearing it will embarrass them both into picking the inbox back up.
explanation: A: Absorbs the failure quietly: doing both people's inbox shift hides the fact that the rota has stopped working, and the same forty requests build again tomorrow. B: Escalates prematurely: the two people who can restart the rota are at their desks and have not yet been asked, and a message to their team leader answers on Wednesday a question that could be settled this morning. D: Personalises the conflict: it makes the dispute about what each has said rather than about forty waiting requests, and a colleague who hears their words repeated back is less likely to cover the inbox, not more. The most effective response is to ask Tom and Priya together for fifteen minutes and agree who covers the inbox today and tomorrow: forty staff requests are waiting on a rota nobody is running, both people who can restart it are available, and getting them together separates the cover from the argument. It beats answering the forty requests yourself and leaving the rota to your team leader tomorrow, because covering the inbox yourself leaves the rota broken. It beats emailing both of them and your team leader with the numbers and asking for a decision, because it does not need somebody who is away until tomorrow. The least effective response is telling each of them separately what the other has been saying: it adds a second grievance to the one already stopping the work, and gives neither of them a reason to pick the inbox up. That makes it worse than covering it yourself, which at least clears today’s requests, and worse than the email, which is slow but puts the real problem in front of somebody who can settle it. The principle: separate the immediate work from the dispute, and deal with the dispute on the facts rather than on what people have said about each other.
tip: Mẹo MT: Trong đề thi SHL, quản lý thời gian tối đa 60-75 giây cho mỗi câu tính toán số học.

question_text: You are a contracts assistant at Redhill Directorate. The contracts database has been down since yesterday. Orders normally go through it so that spend is checked against each budget before it is committed. Three budget holders are asking you to raise urgent orders today. You can raise orders directly with suppliers by email, which the system was brought in to stop, and there is no other way to check the spend. Your manager is available. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell the three budget holders that nothing can be raised until the database is back, and leave it to them to decide how urgent their orders really are.
Tell your manager the database is down and ask which of the three orders genuinely cannot wait, and what check should stand in for the budget check today.
Raise all three orders by email to the suppliers this afternoon, since the budget check can be done retrospectively once the database comes back up again.
Raise the one order from the budget holder who shouts loudest and hold the other two, and mention it to your manager at the end of the day.
explanation: A: Declines without escalating: three budget holders calling something urgent is exactly the situation a manager exists to rank, and an outage is not a decision you have to take alone. C: Breaches the control the system exists to enforce: three orders are committed with no budget check at all, and a check made after the money is committed cannot stop anything. D: Substitutes volume for priority: which order is genuinely urgent is decided by who complained hardest, and the manager who could have decided hears about it after the order has gone. The most effective response is to tell your manager the database is down and ask which of the three orders genuinely cannot wait, and what check should stand in for the budget check today: the outage removes the only check that exists, three people are calling their orders urgent, and both the ranking and the substitute check belong to her. It beats telling the three budget holders nothing can be raised until the database is back, because an outage does not settle which of three orders is genuinely urgent. It beats raising the one from the budget holder who shouts loudest, because volume is not urgency. The least effective response is raising all three by email this afternoon on the basis that the budget check can be done retrospectively: three orders are committed with no check, and one performed afterwards cannot stop money already promised to a supplier. That makes it worse than refusing all three, which keeps the control, and worse than raising one, which exposes a single order rather than three. The principle: when a system failure removes a control, ask what replaces the control, rather than treating the failure as permission to go without it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Nhớ công thức tính nhanh: Tăng trưởng % = (Giá trị mới - Giá trị cũ) / Giá trị cũ × 100%.

question_text: You are a data quality administrator at Calder Group. Your colleague who runs the monthly regulatory data return is off sick and you have been asked to cover. You have watched the process once. Six of the twenty checks in the sign-off sheet require judgements you do not know how to make. The return is due on Friday, it is Tuesday, and the person who signs it off relies entirely on the sheet. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Complete the fourteen checks you can, list the six you cannot make and why, and give the sheet to the person signing with those six clearly left open.
Wait for your colleague to come back and tell the person signing that the return will be late, because six of the twenty checks need judgements you cannot make.
Complete the fourteen checks you can and leave the other six blank on the sheet, and let whoever signs it notice the gaps for themselves.
Complete all twenty checks, marking the six you are unsure about as checked, and leave a note in your own diary to look at them again next month.
explanation: B: Answers a knowledge gap by missing the deadline: fourteen of the twenty checks are within reach, and a regulatory return that is simply late spends a certainty to avoid an uncertainty. C: Leaves the gap without naming it: a blank box and a box nobody could complete look identical, so the signer cannot tell what was not done or why. D: Marks judgements as checked that were never made: the signer relies entirely on the sheet, so six unknowns are converted into six confirmations and the return goes out on them. The most effective response is to complete the fourteen checks you can, list the six you cannot make and why, and give the sheet to the signer with those six left open: you can do fourteen, the six are a fact the signer needs rather than a reason to stop, and a sheet that says exactly what was and was not checked lets them decide about the rest. It beats waiting for your colleague and telling the signer the return will be late, because fourteen checks are within reach and a regulatory deadline is a poor thing to spend. It beats completing the fourteen and leaving the other six blank, because a blank box and an unmakeable judgement look the same to the signer. The least effective response is marking the six you are unsure about as checked: six unknowns become six confirmations on a sheet the signer relies on entirely. That makes it worse than being late, which is honest, and worse than the blank boxes, which claim nothing. The principle: when you are covering work you have not been trained for, do what you can and name what you cannot, rather than filling the gap with a confirmation.
tip: Mẹo MT: Trong đề thi SHL, quản lý thời gian tối đa 60-75 giây cho mỗi câu tính toán số học.

question_text: You are an application assessor at Calder Group. An applicant’s case turns on whether a qualification she holds is recognised. Only the standards team can say, and they answer in five working days. She is due in front of a panel on Thursday, in three days, and the panel will refuse the application if recognition is unresolved. You have seen similar qualifications accepted before. The standards team have a same- day route for panel cases. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Send the question to the standards team by the normal route and tell the applicant the answer will not arrive before Thursday's panel.
Give her the recognition as settled on the strength of similar cases, and put it to the standards team afterwards as a formality.
Put the qualification to the standards team today using their same-day panel route, and tell the applicant it is being checked and when you expect an answer.
Put your own view that the qualification is equivalent into the panel pack, and note that the standards team have not been asked to confirm it.
explanation: A: Uses the slow route when a fast one exists: a same-day panel route is available, and the normal five days is what turns an open question into a refusal on Thursday. B: Gives a recognition as settled that nobody has decided: she prepares for Thursday believing the question is closed, and the panel refuses the application if it is not. D: Substitutes your own judgement for the qualified answer: a panel reading an assessor's view that a qualification is equivalent has been given something that looks like a finding and is not. The most effective response is to put the qualification to the standards team today using their same-day panel route, and tell the applicant it is being checked and when you expect an answer: only they can answer, they have a route built for exactly this deadline, and she can prepare properly once she knows the question is live. It beats sending it by the normal route and telling her the answer will not arrive before Thursday, because the same-day route exists and the normal one guarantees a refusal. It beats putting your own view of equivalence into the panel pack with a note that standards have not been asked, because that looks like a finding and is not one. The least effective response is giving her the recognition as settled on the strength of similar cases: she prepares for Thursday on a certainty that does not exist and the panel refuses her. That makes it worse than the slow route, which is honest about timing, and worse than your own view in the pack, which at least tells the panel what it is looking at. The principle: when only another team can answer, use the fastest route they have and tell the person waiting what has actually been done.

question_text: You are an internal helpdesk adviser at Calder Group. The colleague who handles payroll queries is on leave for two weeks and you have been asked to cover the queue. You have no payroll training. Callers are asking questions about tax codes and pension deductions where a wrong answer changes what somebody is paid. There is a payroll specialist in another office who answers emails within a day. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Take the details, tell callers you will get a payroll answer rather than give one, and send the questions to the specialist each day for a reply.
Answer the tax code and pension questions from what you can find on the intranet, and reassure callers that the figures you give them are right.
Tell callers that payroll queries cannot be dealt with for two weeks, and ask them to ring back when your colleague is home again.
Log every query and hold the whole queue until your colleague returns, without telling callers that anything is being held at all.
explanation: B: Gives an assurance you are not qualified to give: a wrong tax code answer changes what somebody is paid, and the reassurance is what stops them checking it with anybody else. C: Closes a service that is available: a payroll specialist answers within a day, so two weeks of nobody being helped is a choice rather than a constraint. D: Holds a queue silently: the callers are waiting for answers they think are coming, and the specialist who could have provided them is never asked. The most effective response is to take the details, tell callers you will get a payroll answer rather than give one, and send the questions to the specialist each day: you cannot answer payroll questions and should not, but the specialist can and replies within a day, so routing keeps the service running without you giving a single figure. It beats telling callers payroll queries cannot be dealt with for two weeks, because the service is available and two weeks of refusal is a choice. It beats logging every query and holding the queue until your colleague returns, because a silent queue leaves callers waiting for answers nobody is preparing. The least effective response is answering the tax code and pension questions from the intranet and reassuring callers the figures are right: untrained answers are given where being wrong changes what somebody is paid, with a reassurance that stops them checking. That makes it worse than the two-week refusal, which is harmless, and worse than the silent queue, which gives no wrong figures. The principle: when you are covering work you are not trained for, become the route to somebody who is, and never dress a guess as an answer.
tip: Mẹo MT: Trong đề thi SHL, quản lý thời gian tối đa 60-75 giây cho mỗi câu tính toán số học.

question_text: You are a contracts assistant at Calder Group. You have committed today to producing a tender evaluation summary that a panel meets to discuss on Monday. At eleven a supplier’s insurance certificate expires at midnight and the replacement has not arrived; without it a team of six cannot work on site from tomorrow. Chasing the certificate will take most of the afternoon. Your team leader is available. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell your team leader at once that the certificate expires tonight and that chasing it will cost the afternoon, and agree between you which of the two gets your day.
Chase the certificate all afternoon and carry on with the evaluation summary tomorrow, without telling anybody that Monday's panel paper is now at risk.
Finish the evaluation summary as committed and leave the certificate to expire, telling the site team tomorrow morning that they cannot start.
Ask a colleague who has never chased a certificate to do it while you carry on with the summary, and check on them at the end of the day.
explanation: B: Withholds a risk somebody is relying on: the panel meets on Monday to discuss a paper that may not exist, and the only person who knows that has decided not to say so today. C: Ranks a movable commitment above an immovable one: a summary due for Monday has the weekend behind it, and six people cannot be on site tomorrow if the certificate lapses tonight. D: Delegates the urgent task to the least prepared person: an untrained colleague chasing a certificate that expires at midnight is the arrangement most likely to end with it expiring. The most effective response is to tell your team leader at once that the certificate expires tonight and that chasing it will cost the afternoon, and agree which of the two gets your day: one thing expires tonight and cannot be recovered, the other has a weekend behind it, and the call should be made with both facts in front of him. It beats finishing the evaluation summary and letting the certificate expire, because a summary due Monday has a weekend behind it and six people on site do not. It beats asking a colleague who has never chased a certificate to do it, because they are the least likely to catch one expiring at midnight. The least effective response is chasing the certificate all afternoon without telling anybody that Monday’s panel paper is now at risk: the right work is done and the panel expects a paper nobody has flagged, so the weekend passes with the problem invisible. That makes it worse than letting it expire, which chooses badly but openly, and worse than the poor delegation, which keeps both jobs alive. The principle: when a late arrival displaces committed work, the displacement is the thing to tell people about, not just the work.
tip: Mẹo MT: Dùng phương pháp ước lượng chữ số hàng đơn vị hoặc làm tròn đến hàng chục để loại ngay 2 phương án vô lý.

question_text: You are a contracts assistant at Ashmere Trust. You run the desk where budget holders bring purchase requests for checking. One request in front of you has a complicated funding split and will take about forty minutes. Seven people are now waiting, and five of their requests look like two-minute checks. Two of the seven say their orders must be placed today. The desk closes at 4pm and it is half past two. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Work through the queue strictly in the order people arrived and let the desk overrun past four until everybody waiting has been seen.
Ask the two people whose orders must be placed today to leave their requests with you, and check those two for them after the desk has closed at four this afternoon.
Set the forty-minute request aside, tell its owner you will come back to it at three, and work through the five quick checks and the two urgent ones first.
Assure everyone waiting that they will all be seen before four, and carry on with the complicated request in the order people arrived.
explanation: A: Treats order of arrival as the only fairness: forty minutes on the first request leaves five two-minute checks and two same-day orders standing behind it, and an overrun is a cost paid by everybody. B: Defers the urgent work past its own deadline: an order that must be placed today cannot wait for a check made after the desk closes, and the two people leave without knowing whether it will happen. D: Gives an assurance the clock does not support: ninety minutes cannot cover forty minutes of one request plus seven others, so the promise is untrue when it is made and those who could have returned tomorrow stay in the queue. The most effective response is to set the forty-minute request aside, tell its owner you will come back to it at three, and work through the five quick checks and the two urgent ones: seven people are waiting behind one request, five need two minutes, and moving the long one costs its owner half an hour while clearing everybody else. It beats working strictly in arrival order and letting the desk overrun past four, because forty minutes at the front leaves the same-day orders unplaced. It beats asking the two with same-day orders to leave their requests and checking after the desk closes, because a check made after four is too late for an order that must go today. The least effective response is assuring everyone they will be seen before four and carrying on in arrival order: ninety minutes will not cover it, some are not seen, and the ones who could have come back tomorrow have waited instead. That makes it worse than arrival order with an overrun, which at least sees everybody eventually, and worse than checking after four, which mishandles the urgency but is honest about timing. The principle: when a long case is blocking a queue, move the case rather than the queue, and never buy calm with a promise the clock cannot keep.
tip: Mẹo MT: Nhớ công thức tính nhanh: Tăng trưởng % = (Giá trị mới - Giá trị cũ) / Giá trị cũ × 100%.

question_text: You are a contracts assistant at Brantwood Services. You manage twelve live contracts, which your team agrees is a full load. Your manager asks you to take four more from a colleague on long-term sick leave, starting today. Two of your twelve are at renewal and need a fortnight of work each in the next month. Nobody else in the team is under twelve, and your manager has asked for an answer this morning. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Refuse the four, pointing out that twelve is what the whole team agrees is a full load, and leave your manager to find somewhere else for them before the end of today.
Tell your manager you can take the four, and set out that the two renewals need a fortnight each next month so they can decide what moves or slips.
Take the four and hand two of your existing contracts over to a colleague without telling your manager which ones you have moved.
Take the four and say nothing about the two renewals, and work through the month at whatever pace it turns out to need.
explanation: A: Answers the number and not the problem: nobody else in the team is under twelve, so a refusal leaves four contracts with nowhere to go and gives your manager nothing new to work with. C: Passes work on without owning it: two contracts move to a colleague who is also at twelve, your manager does not know which ones, and nobody can tell who is responsible for them. D: Accepts the load and hides its shape: sixteen contracts including two renewals needing a fortnight each is not a month that can be worked at whatever pace it needs, and nobody has been told. The most effective response is to tell your manager you can take the four, and set out that the two renewals need a fortnight each next month: the four have to go somewhere and nobody is under twelve, so refusing solves nothing, and the renewals are the fact that actually changes the decision. It beats refusing the four and pointing to twelve as a full load, because that leaves them with no home and your manager with no new information. It beats taking them and saying nothing about the renewals, because sixteen contracts with two renewals in them is not a load that can be absorbed silently. The least effective response is taking the four and handing two existing contracts to a colleague without saying which: they go to somebody also at twelve, your manager is not told, and responsibility is unclear to everybody. That makes it worse than refusing, which leaves ownership clear, and worse than silent absorption, which keeps the work with the person who knows it. The principle: when you are asked to go past a full load, accept or decline on the record and give the decision-maker the fact that changes their options.
tip: Mẹo MT: Nhớ công thức tính nhanh: Tăng trưởng % = (Giá trị mới - Giá trị cũ) / Giá trị cũ × 100%.

question_text: You are a shared services administrator at Ashmere Trust. Your team runs the central line that customers ring about refunds. A customer has been waiting eleven weeks for a refund of two hundred pounds and is angry on the phone. The delay is entirely with the operations division, which holds the authorisation, and your team cannot release money. You can see that nobody in operations has opened her case for three weeks. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell her the operations division is hopeless, that your team has been complaining about them for months, and suggest she puts in a formal complaint naming that division.
Explain that refunds are authorised by another division entirely and that your team has no way at all of releasing money, and give her the number for the operations enquiry line to ring instead.
Log her call as a chase on the case, tell her it has gone to operations again, and let their normal timescales take their course.
Apologise for the eleven weeks, tell her plainly that the authorisation sits with operations and has not been opened for three weeks, and say you will escalate it today and call her back.
explanation: A: Recruits the customer into a complaint about a colleague: her two hundred pounds is no closer, and she now has a grievance about the organisation's internal relations on top of an eleven- week wait. B: Ignores the customer's actual need: a number for another line asks somebody who has waited eleven weeks to start again with a division that has not opened her case for three. C: Records a chase in place of doing one: normal timescales are what produced eleven weeks, and a logged call reaches nobody who can authorise the money. The most effective response is to apologise for the eleven weeks, tell her plainly that the authorisation sits with operations and has not been opened for three weeks, and say you will escalate it today and call her back: she has waited eleven weeks, the fault is visible to you, and the truth plus an escalation and a call back are the only things you can actually give her. It beats explaining that refunds are authorised elsewhere and giving her the operations enquiry number, because that makes her start again. It beats logging her call as a chase and letting normal timescales run, because a logged chase reaches nobody who can authorise the money. The least effective response is telling her the operations division is hopeless and suggesting a formal complaint naming them: she gets an internal grievance instead of her refund. That makes it worse than the enquiry number, which is unhelpful but points somewhere real, and worse than the logged chase, which at least records the call. The principle: when the fault is somebody else’s, own the customer’s problem to the limit of what you can do, and do not hand them your view of a colleague.
tip: Mẹo MT: Trong đề thi SHL, quản lý thời gian tối đa 60-75 giây cho mỗi câu tính toán số học.

question_text: You are a programme support officer at Redhill Directorate. Two weeks ago you told a board that a supplier survey would be ready for their meeting on the twelfth. You have since realised you never sent the survey out, and it needs ten working days in the field. Today is the fourth and the board papers deadline is the tenth. Nobody has asked you about it. Your programme manager is in the office today. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Send the survey out this afternoon and keep it to yourself that it was never issued, and hope the responses come back fast enough to cover the gap.
Send the survey out today and tell the board on the twelfth that responses are still coming in and that the full analysis will follow at their next meeting in six weeks.
Email the board secretary to withdraw the survey item from the twelfth's agenda, and say nothing about why it is being withdrawn.
Tell your programme manager today that the survey was never issued and that it cannot be ready for the twelfth, and ask what the board should be given instead.
explanation: A: Keeps your own failure quiet and hopes: ten working days of fieldwork cannot fit into six, so the board still gets nothing on the twelfth, and by then nobody has had a chance to arrange anything else. B: Reports a delay and not its cause: the board hears about response rates rather than about a survey that was never issued, so the next report they commission is planned on a false picture. C: Removes the item without the explanation: the board loses the paper and never learns why, and the programme manager who could have offered them something else is not asked. The most effective response is to tell your programme manager today that the survey was never issued and cannot be ready for the twelfth, and ask what the board should be given instead: it cannot exist by then on any arithmetic, the failure is yours, and the six days before the papers deadline are exactly when she could put something else in front of the board. It beats sending the survey today and telling the board responses are still coming in, because that describes a different problem from the one that happened. It beats emailing the secretary to withdraw the item without saying why, because that leaves nobody able to replace it. The least effective response is sending the survey and keeping it to yourself that it was never issued: the cause is hidden on a bet that ten days of fieldwork fits into six, so the board gets nothing anyway and the usable days are gone. That makes it worse than misdescribing the delay, which gives notice, and worse than the silent withdrawal, which frees the agenda. The principle: when a commitment cannot be met and the cause is your own, the cause goes in first, while there is still time to do something else.
tip: Mẹo MT: Nhớ công thức tính nhanh: Tăng trưởng % = (Giá trị mới - Giá trị cũ) / Giá trị cũ × 100%.

question_text: You are a payments assistant. A large client payment has failed and the client’s finance director needs to know within the hour. The approved route is through their relationship manager, who is on a flight. You have the finance director’s mobile number on a file you are not supposed to use for contact details. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Call the relationship manager's team now for another contact route, and tell your manager the clock so somebody with authority can decide how to reach the client.
Take the finance director's mobile number from the file and telephone him directly, since he needs to know within the hour and the number is right there in front of you.
Ask a colleague to telephone the client's main switchboard and try to reach the finance director without saying what it is about.
Email the relationship manager and wait for her to land, since she is the approved route and the client is hers to contact.
explanation: B: Uses a record for a purpose it is not permitted for: the restriction exists whatever the reason, and urgency is exactly the circumstance it was written to cover. C: Sends somebody to make a call they cannot explain: a vague approach from an unnamed colleague will not reach him inside an hour. D: Follows the route past the deadline: an hour is the whole window and a flight is longer than that. The most effective response is to call the relationship manager’s team now for another contact route, and tell your manager the clock so somebody with authority can decide how to reach the client: her team almost certainly has another route, and your manager can authorise whatever is needed if it does not. It beats emailing the relationship manager and waiting for her to land, because the flight is longer than the hour. It beats asking a colleague to ring the client’s switchboard without saying what it is about, because a call nobody can explain will not get through. The least effective response is taking the finance director’s mobile number from the file and telephoning him directly: contact details are used from a source you are specifically not permitted to use for that, on your own judgement that the circumstances justify it. That is breaching a stated restriction rather than being too slow or too indirect. The principle: when the approved route will not make the deadline, get authority for another one.
tip: Mẹo MT: Luôn kiểm tra kỹ đơn vị tính (Triệu VNĐ vs Tỷ VNĐ, Tháng vs Năm) trước khi tính toán.

question_text: You are an onboarding analyst. A client’s go-live has slipped by three weeks. The client’s project manager is relaxed about dates; your own sales colleague has a bonus tied to this quarter and has been telling people it will land. Both need to know today. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Send both of them the same written note at the same time, without speaking to your sales colleague first about what it is going to say.
Tell your sales colleague first so he is not blindsided, then send both him and the client the same written note setting out the new date and why.
Tell the client first and blame your sales colleague for the dates, explaining that he has been giving out timings he was never in a position to commit the firm to.
Tell your sales colleague today and leave him to decide when and how the client should be told about the three-week slip.
explanation: A: Treats two very different stakes identically: he reads about his quarter in a group email, which is the part that could have been handled. C: Criticises a colleague to the client: the slip is real, and what the client now knows is that your own firm's people contradict each other. D: Hands the client message to the person most likely to delay it: the client needs the date today. The most effective response is to tell your sales colleague first so he is not blindsided, then send him and the client the same written note setting out the new date and why: both get the same facts in writing, and the person with most at stake hears it from you first rather than in a group email. It beats sending both the same note at the same time without speaking to him first, because a two-minute warning costs nothing and matters a lot to him. It beats telling him today and leaving him to decide when the client hears, because the client’s date should not wait on his convenience. The least effective response is telling the client that your colleague has been giving out timings he could not commit the firm to: a delivery slip reaches the client as a criticism of your own side, so the firm looks divided and he is undermined in front of the account. That is personalising it rather than sequencing it badly. The principle: same facts to both, and warn the one who will take it hardest.
tip: Mẹo MT: Nhớ công thức tính nhanh: Tăng trưởng % = (Giá trị mới - Giá trị cũ) / Giá trị cũ × 100%.

question_text: You work in the office of a removals company. A customer’s move is booked for Friday. On Wednesday the crew supervisor tells you the larger van has broken down and only a smaller one is available, which will mean two trips and finishing about three hours later than planned. The customer has to hand her keys over at 4pm on Friday. She is contactable. Your operations manager is in today. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Say nothing and hope the crew make up the time on the day, since telling her now would worry her about something that may not turn out to be a problem at all.
Email the customer to say the schedule for Friday has been revised slightly and that the crew will do everything possible to finish as early as they can.
Ring the customer and promise that the move will still be finished by 4pm, then work out with the crew how the two trips can be compressed to make that happen.
Ring the customer today, explain the van problem and the likely three-hour overrun against her 4pm handover, and go through the options with your operations manager's input.
explanation: A: Hides the problem / silent deadline slip: she has a 4pm key handover that cannot move, and the plan is to let her discover the overrun on the day. Betting her completion on the crew catching up is concealment, not optimism. B: Delays the message: it reaches her in time and hides the fact that matters, a three-hour overrun against a 4pm key handover she cannot move. C: Over-promises: it commits to a time before anyone has established that two trips can be done in the original window, which risks breaking the same promise on the day her keys change hands. The most effective response is to ring the customer today, explain the van problem and the likely three-hour overrun against her 4pm handover, and go through the options with your operations manager’s input: the handover is fixed and legal, a three-hour overrun puts it in jeopardy, and on Wednesday she still has two days to arrange a later handover or extra help. Involving the operations manager means the options offered are real ones. It beats emailing that the schedule has been revised slightly and the crew will finish as early as they can, because that withholds the number she needs to plan around. It beats ringing to promise the move will still finish by 4pm, because committing to that before knowing whether two trips fit risks breaking the promise on the day it matters most. The least effective response is saying nothing and hoping the crew make up the time: it leaves her to discover a three-hour overrun on the day her keys change hands, while two days of alternatives were available. That is worse than the other two, which communicate badly but in time. The principle: when a fixed external deadline is threatened, tell the person while they can still move something.
tip: Mẹo MT: Dùng phương pháp ước lượng chữ số hàng đơn vị hoặc làm tròn đến hàng chục để loại ngay 2 phương án vô lý.

question_text: You are a commercial finance assistant at Cargill. A business customer has been charged twice for the same delivery and has rung to ask when the money will be back. The credit has to be raised by the billing team, who usually clear requests within two days but have a backlog this week. You can raise the request now. The customer is on the line and has already waited a week. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Explain that credits are raised by the billing team and give the customer their contact details, so that he can ask them directly how long the backlog is likely to take this week.
Raise the credit request now with the duplicate reference attached, tell the customer it is with the billing team and that you will confirm the date once it is scheduled.
Promise the customer the credit will be on tomorrow's statement, since requests like this usually clear overnight and it saves him ringing back a third time about the same delivery.
Raise the credit request now and say nothing about timing, since any date you gave would be a guess while the billing backlog is as long as it is.
explanation: A: Sends the customer to do your chasing: he rang the business once and is asked to ring it again, and the request still has not been raised by anybody. C: Gives a date nobody has agreed: the billing backlog makes tomorrow unlikely, and the customer plans his own week on a certainty that was offered to end the call. D: Withholds what little you do know: he has waited a week and puts the phone down knowing only that somebody, at some point, will do something. The most effective response is to raise the credit request now with the duplicate reference attached and tell the customer it is with the billing team and that you will confirm the date: the request finally exists, he knows where it is, and the one thing you cannot promise is the one thing you have not promised. It beats giving him the billing team’s details, because he rang once and is being asked to ring again. It beats raising it and saying nothing about timing, because he has waited a week and deserves to know what happens next. The least effective response is promising the credit will be on tomorrow’s statement: the backlog makes that unlikely, he plans on it, and manufacturing a date to end a call is a different kind of wrong from deflecting him or from telling him too little. The principle: give the customer the true state of their case and a commitment you control, never a date somebody else would have to deliver.
