question_text: You are a trading assistant at Cargill. In Monday’s meeting a colleague said, in front of the team, that your weekly figures were guesswork and had cost her a decision. You were annoyed and said nothing. You send her those figures every Wednesday and she uses them to set her orders. It is Wednesday morning and the figures are ready. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Send the figures as usual and add a line to the whole team explaining how they are built, so that everybody can see the remark on Monday was unfair.
Send the figures as usual, then ask her for ten minutes to go through how they are built and what the decision needed that they did not give her.
Send the figures as usual and say nothing about Monday, on the basis that raising it now would only make the next meeting more uncomfortable for both of you.
Stop sending her the weekly figures after that meeting and let her ask for them if she still wants them, since she made her view of their value clear enough.
explanation: A: Answers a private grievance in public: the correction is aimed at an audience rather than at her, and the person it is really about reads it alongside everyone else. C: Prioritises harmony over honesty: the working relationship stays polite, the complaint about your work stands unexamined, and it will be repeated. D: Withdraws your work from a colleague after a disagreement: her orders go out on nothing, and a complaint about quality is answered by removing the thing entirely. The most effective response is to send the figures as usual and then ask her for ten minutes on how they are built and what her decision needed: it keeps the work flowing, it treats the remark as information about a gap rather than as an insult, and it puts the conversation where it belongs, which is between the two of you. It beats adding a public line to the team about how the figures are built, because that answers her in front of an audience and makes the disagreement everybody’s. It beats saying nothing at all, because the complaint stands and the next set of orders is set on the same misunderstanding. The least effective response is stopping the weekly figures after the meeting and making her ask: the work she depends on is withdrawn because of how she spoke to you, which is a different kind of wrong from being defensive in public or being silent. The principle: criticism of your work is answered by improving what the other person needed, never by taking the work away.
tip: Mẹo MT: Nhớ công thức tính nhanh: Tăng trưởng % = (Giá trị mới - Giá trị cũ) / Giá trị cũ × 100%.

question_text: You work in the control room of a taxi firm. Drivers are paid a bonus for completing more than forty jobs a week. You notice a driver has logged three jobs this week that were cancelled by the customer before pickup, which would take him over forty. He says the customers cancelled at the door, so he drove the distance and should be credited. The firm’s rules on cancelled jobs are written and you have not read them. The operations manager is on shift. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Check the written rules on cancelled jobs, and if they do not cover doorstep cancellations put it to the operations manager before the bonus is calculated.
Remove the three cancelled jobs from his total, since the jobs were not completed and the bonus is for completed work.
Leave the three jobs on his total and let the bonus be paid, since he did drive to each address and nobody audits the weekly figures in any detail.
Report the driver to the operations manager for logging cancelled jobs as completed work in order to reach the bonus threshold.
explanation: B: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholder's: the rules may well credit a driver who travelled to a doorstep cancellation, and striking the jobs out decides that without reading them. C: Falsifies a payment record: it lets a bonus be paid on jobs recorded as completed that were not, without checking whether the rules allow it, and relies on the absence of an audit. That is dishonesty, not a judgement call. D: Escalates prematurely: the written rules may entitle him to the credit, so a report of deliberate manipulation is made before the document that settles it has been read. The most effective response is to check the written rules on cancelled jobs, and if they do not cover doorstep cancellations put it to the operations manager before the bonus is calculated: there is a rule that decides whether such a cancellation counts, reading it costs a minute, and he is on shift and can settle it in time. It answers the question without accusing anyone. It beats removing the three cancelled jobs from his total, because that decides the same question in the driver’s disfavour without reading the rule. It beats reporting him for logging cancelled jobs as completed work, because a serious accusation before checking risks condemning him over something the rules may allow. The least effective response is leaving the three on his total because nobody audits the weekly figures: it lets a bonus be paid on incomplete jobs without any check. That is worse than the other two, which act hastily but keep the payment honest. The principle: read the rule that governs it, and take the decision to whoever owns it rather than resolving it quietly either way.
tip: Mẹo MT: Nhớ công thức tính nhanh: Tăng trưởng % = (Giá trị mới - Giá trị cũ) / Giá trị cũ × 100%.

question_text: You volunteer as an assistant manager in a charity shop. Sorting donations you notice that a batch of electrical items has been put straight onto the shop floor without the safety testing the charity requires. Nobody has asked you to check this. The shop manager is on holiday for a week and the area manager covers by phone. The shop is open and the items are priced and on display now. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Ring the area manager to report that untested electrical items are on sale and ask whether she wants them removed before you touch anything.
Take the untested electrical items off the shop floor now and ring the area manager to tell her what you have found and ask how testing should be arranged.
Leave the items on display but attach a note to each saying it has not been safety tested, so that customers can decide for themselves whether to buy them.
Leave them as they are, since a volunteer putting stock out is not your responsibility and the manager will sort out the testing when she is back next week.
explanation: A: Delays the decision: the phone call is right and the items stay on sale while it happens. Removing them first costs nothing and is reversible if she disagrees. C: Passes responsibility to the customer: the charity's testing rule exists because a buyer cannot assess an appliance's safety from a label. Disclosing the gap does not close it. D: Fails to escalate a genuine risk: untested electrical goods stay on sale to the public for a week because the person who noticed decided it was not her job. The reason for silence is precisely why nobody else will catch it. The most effective response is to take the untested electrical items off the shop floor now and ring the area manager to tell her what you found: untested electrical goods on sale are a risk to whoever buys them, removing them is immediate, reversible and within your reach, and she needs to know so testing can be arranged properly. It beats ringing her first to ask whether she wants them removed, because that leaves the items on sale during the call and afterwards, when removing them costs nothing and can be undone if she disagrees. It beats attaching a note to each saying it has not been safety tested, because a label does not make an appliance safe, and it moves the judgement onto customers who cannot make it. The least effective response is leaving them as they are until the manager is back next week: it leaves untested electrical items on public sale for a week on the basis that someone else put them there. That is worse than ringing first, which reports it, and worse than labelling them, which at least warns buyers. The principle: when you find a live risk, remove it first if removing it is cheap and reversible, then tell whoever owns the process.
tip: Mẹo MT: Luôn kiểm tra kỹ đơn vị tính (Triệu VNĐ vs Tỷ VNĐ, Tháng vs Năm) trước khi tính toán.

question_text: All members of the choir can read music. James cannot read music. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
options: James is not a member of the choir.
James is a member of the choir.
Everyone who can read music is a member of the choir.
James does not enjoy music.
explanation: This is modus tollens: if every choir member can read music, then anyone who cannot read music cannot be in the choir, so James is not a member. Claiming that he is a member flatly contradicts this. Concluding that everyone who can read music is in the choir reverses the premise, an illicit conversion. Concluding that he does not enjoy music imports a fact the premises never mention.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân biệt rõ giữa 'Đúng' (True) và 'Có thể xảy ra' (Possible). Chỉ chọn kết luận chắc chắn 100%.

question_text: If a parcel is marked “fragile”, it is placed on the top shelf. The parcel labelled 7 is marked “fragile”. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
options: Every parcel on the top shelf is marked "fragile".
If a parcel is on the top shelf, it is marked "fragile".
Parcel 7 is placed on the top shelf.
Parcel 7 is the only fragile parcel.
explanation: This is modus ponens: parcel 7 is fragile, and fragile parcels go on the top shelf, so parcel 7 is placed there. Claiming that every top-shelf parcel is fragile, or that being on the top shelf implies being fragile, both reverse the rule; that is affirming the consequent, since parcels could sit on that shelf for other reasons. Claiming that parcel 7 is the only fragile parcel invents an exclusivity nothing in the premises supports.
tip: Mẹo MT: Áp dụng sơ đồ Venn hoặc bảng chân trị logic để biểu diễn mối quan hệ giữa các đối tượng.

question_text: All auditors in the firm are qualified accountants. All qualified accountants must complete annual training. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
options: All qualified accountants are auditors in the firm.
All auditors in the firm must complete annual training.
Anyone who completes annual training is an auditor.
Some qualified accountants are not auditors.
explanation: Chaining the two “all” statements gives the conclusion by transitivity: auditors are accountants, and accountants complete training, so auditors complete training. Claiming that all accountants are auditors reverses the first premise, and claiming that anyone who trains is an auditor reverses the second, both illicit conversions. Claiming that some accountants are not auditors may be true but is not forced, since the premises allow every accountant to be an auditor.
tip: Mẹo MT: Áp dụng sơ đồ Venn hoặc bảng chân trị logic để biểu diễn mối quan hệ giữa các đối tượng.

question_text: No delivery driver works in the accounts team. Priya works in the accounts team. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
options: Some delivery drivers work in the accounts team.
Priya manages the delivery drivers.
Everyone in the accounts team was once a delivery driver.
Priya is not a delivery driver.
explanation: Because no delivery driver is in the accounts team, anyone in that team cannot be a delivery driver, so Priya is not one. Claiming that some delivery drivers work in accounts directly contradicts the first premise. Claiming that Priya manages the drivers imports a relationship never stated. Claiming that everyone in accounts was once a driver makes an unsupported historical claim that also cuts against the stated separation of the two roles.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: The shipment left either on Monday or on Tuesday, but not both. It did not leave on Monday. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
options: The shipment left on Tuesday.
The shipment left on both days.
The shipment did not leave that week at all.
The shipment left on Monday.
explanation: This is a disjunctive syllogism: with exactly one of the two days true, ruling out Monday leaves Tuesday. Claiming that it left on both days contradicts the explicit “but not both”. Claiming that it did not leave at all ignores that the premise guarantees the shipment left on one of the two days. Claiming that it left on Monday contradicts the given fact that it did not.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: All technicians carry an access card. Some people who carry an access card work night shifts. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
options: Some technicians work night shifts.
All night-shift workers are technicians.
Some people who work night shifts carry an access card.
No technician works a night shift.
explanation: A “some” statement can be turned around: “some card-carriers work nights” means “some night workers carry a card”. Concluding that some technicians work nights is the undistributed-middle fallacy, because the card-carrying night workers need not be technicians. Concluding that all night workers are technicians over-generalises a “some” into an “all”. Concluding that no technician works nights denies an overlap the premises neither state nor rule out.
tip: Mẹo MT: Áp dụng sơ đồ Venn hoặc bảng chân trị logic để biểu diễn mối quan hệ giữa các đối tượng.

question_text: If the invoice is approved, the payment is scheduled. If the payment is scheduled, the supplier is notified. The supplier was not notified. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
options: The payment was scheduled.
The invoice was not approved.
The invoice was approved but the payment was not scheduled.
The supplier was notified after a delay.
explanation: Work backwards by contrapositive: no notification means no scheduled payment, and no scheduled payment means no approval, so the invoice was not approved. Claiming that the payment was scheduled contradicts that backward chain. Claiming that the invoice was approved but not scheduled is impossible, because approval would have forced scheduling. Claiming that the supplier was notified after a delay contradicts the given fact that no notification happened.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: If a candidate scores above 80, they progress to interview. Dana did not score above 80. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
options: Dana does not progress to interview.
Dana progresses to interview.
Everyone who progresses to interview scored above 80.
It cannot be determined whether Dana progresses to interview.
explanation: Scoring above 80 is stated as sufficient for progressing, not as the only route, so a lower score leaves the outcome open. Concluding that she does not progress is the denying-the-antecedent error: ruling out the sufficient condition does not rule out the result. Concluding that she does progress is the mirror mistake, assuming some alternative route definitely applied when none is stated. Concluding that everyone who progresses scored above 80 reverses the rule into a necessary condition the premise never claims.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: All the graduates on the scheme completed an internship. None of those who completed an internship were hired directly from school. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
options: Everyone hired directly from school completed an internship.
All interns are graduates on the scheme.
None of the graduates on the scheme were hired directly from school.
Some graduates on the scheme were hired directly from school.
explanation: The graduates are all interns, and no intern was hired from school, so no graduate was hired from school. Claiming that everyone hired from school completed an internship reverses the second premise, an illicit conversion. Claiming that all interns are scheme graduates reverses the first premise the same way. Claiming that some graduates were hired from school directly contradicts the valid conclusion.
tip: Mẹo MT: Áp dụng sơ đồ Venn hoặc bảng chân trị logic để biểu diễn mối quan hệ giữa các đối tượng.

question_text: A book is restocked only if it has sold out. The atlas has not sold out. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
options: The atlas is not restocked.
The atlas is restocked.
Every book that has sold out is restocked.
The atlas will sell out shortly.
explanation: “Restocked only if sold out” means restocking requires a sell-out, so with no sell-out there is no restock; the atlas is not restocked. Claiming that it is restocked contradicts this. Claiming that every sold-out book is restocked misreads “only if” as “if”, treating a necessary condition as a sufficient one. Claiming that the atlas will sell out shortly predicts a future event the premises give no basis for.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân biệt rõ giữa 'Đúng' (True) và 'Có thể xảy ra' (Possible). Chỉ chọn kết luận chắc chắn 100%.

question_text: You are a science technician at a secondary school. Preparing for a practical lesson you find a bottle of concentrated acid in the general chemicals cupboard rather than the locked cabinet, with a loose cap. The lesson starts in twenty minutes and thirty pupils will be in the room. The head of science is teaching but the department office is next door and the site manager is available. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Move the bottle to the locked cabinet, tighten the cap, and tell the head of science about it after the lesson when she is free.
Secure the bottle in the locked cabinet now, and interrupt the head of science briefly to tell her before thirty pupils come into the room.
Leave the bottle where it is and mention it to the head of science at break, since the cupboard is at the back of the room and pupils are not allowed to open it.
Cancel the practical and tell the class teacher the lesson cannot go ahead until the chemical storage has been checked properly.
explanation: A: Delays the decision: securing the bottle is right and it leaves unanswered how concentrated acid came to be in an unlocked cupboard, which the head of science needs to know before the next lesson, not after this one. C: Stays silent about a known safety risk: concentrated acid with a loose cap is left in an unlocked cupboard while thirty pupils work in the room, on the assumption that a rule about not opening cupboards will hold. That is a safety failure of a different order from the others. D: Escalates beyond the problem: one misplaced bottle can be secured in two minutes, and cancelling a lesson for thirty pupils is a decision for the head of science rather than a technician. The most effective response is to secure the bottle in the locked cabinet now and interrupt the head of science briefly before thirty pupils come in: putting it away takes two minutes, and she needs to know before the room fills because a misplaced bottle implies something wrong with how chemicals are being stored. Both fit in twenty minutes. It beats moving the bottle and telling her after the lesson when she is free, because that leaves the storage question unexamined through a lesson with thirty pupils in the room. It beats cancelling the practical until chemical storage has been checked, because that is a bigger decision than the problem needs, and is not a technician’s to take when securing the bottle solves the hazard. The least effective response is leaving the bottle where it is and mentioning it at break: it leaves concentrated acid with a loose cap in an unlocked cupboard during a practical, relying on pupils following a rule. That is worse than securing it and telling her later, which at least secures it, and worse than cancelling, which at least stops the lesson. The principle: remove the hazard immediately, then tell the responsible person before the risk period starts.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You are an instructor at an outdoor activity centre. Checking equipment before a climbing session for a school group you find a harness with a frayed stitch on a load-bearing strap. There are enough harnesses without it. The group arrives in fifteen minutes. Centre procedure requires damaged equipment to be quarantined and logged by the technical manager, who is on site. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Put the harness back at the end of the rack so it is not used today, and tell the technical manager after the session when he has more time.
Set the harness aside and log it in the equipment book yourself, so the record exists and the technical manager can review it at the next equipment check.
Use the harness for the session but give it to one of the lighter pupils, since the stitching is only frayed and there is no sign it is close to failing.
Take the harness out of use, put it aside where it cannot be picked up, and tell the technical manager before the group arrives.
explanation: A: Acts on assumptions without checking: a damaged harness left on the rack can be picked up by anybody, and the placement relies on everyone knowing what you know. B: Acts outside own authority: the procedure names the technical manager because he decides whether a fault is repairable or the batch needs checking, and a self-made log entry replaces that judgement with a record. C: Uses equipment known to be damaged: a frayed load-bearing strap on a climbing harness is the failure the inspection exists to catch, and putting a child in it on a judgement about weight is a safety decision nobody is qualified to take that way. The most effective response is to take the harness out of use, put it aside where it cannot be picked up, and tell the technical manager before the group arrives: a frayed load-bearing strap makes it unusable, spares exist so nothing is lost by removing it, and he is on site and is the person the procedure names. Both steps fit inside fifteen minutes. It beats putting it back at the end of the rack and telling him after the session, because a damaged harness left on the rack can be picked up by anyone who does not know, so its position is not a control. It beats setting it aside and logging it in the equipment book yourself, because that substitutes a record for his judgement about whether other harnesses in the batch need checking. The least effective response is using it for one of the lighter pupils because the stitching is only frayed: it puts a child into a harness with a damaged load-bearing strap on a personal judgement about weight. That is worse than the other two, which handle the procedure imperfectly but take the harness out of use. The principle: remove damaged safety equipment from use immediately, then tell the person the procedure names, before the activity starts.
tip: Mẹo MT: Áp dụng sơ đồ Venn hoặc bảng chân trị logic để biểu diễn mối quan hệ giữa các đối tượng.

question_text: You are a junior designer at a graphic design studio. You and a colleague, Ines, are producing a brand pack due to the client on Friday. It is Wednesday. Ines has been given a second urgent project and tells you she can now only do about half her share of the brand pack. You have capacity for some but not all of the rest. Your studio manager assigns work and is in the office. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Take on all of Ines's remaining share and work late Wednesday and Thursday so the brand pack is delivered on Friday as promised.
Work out with Ines exactly what is left, then tell the studio manager today what the two of you can cover and what still needs someone, before Friday.
Tell Ines the brand pack has to come first since it has a client deadline on Friday, and ask her to push back on the second project herself.
Carry on with your own share and let Ines deliver what she can, and raise it on Friday if the brand pack turns out to be incomplete.
explanation: A: Hides the strain until failure: it absorbs a shortfall the studio manager created and never learns about, so she keeps assigning on the assumption that both projects fit. C: Passes responsibility to others: the studio manager assigns the work, so asking Ines to argue about her own workload leaves the person who made the clash out of the conversation. D: Hides the problem / silent deadline slip: it is known on Wednesday that the pack will be short, and the plan is to mention it on the day it is due, when nothing can be done. Waiting to report a certainty is concealment. The most effective response is to work out with Ines exactly what is left, then tell the studio manager today what the two of you can cover and what still needs someone: the shortfall is known on Wednesday, its size can be worked out in ten minutes, and she both created the clash and is the only person who can resolve it. Bringing her the specifics rather than the problem lets her act. It beats taking on all of Ines’s remaining share and working late, because quietly absorbing the gap hides from the manager that two projects were assigned into one person’s week, so she does it again. It beats telling Ines to push back on the second project herself, because that leaves the person who assigns the work out of a conversation about her own assignment. The least effective response is letting Ines deliver what she can and raising it only if the pack turns out incomplete: it knows on Wednesday that Friday will fall short and plans to mention it when no resource can be added. That is worse than absorbing the work, which delivers, and worse than asking her to push back, which at least raises it. The principle: size the gap, then take it to whoever controls the resource while there is still time to fill it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You work in a pet shop. Your colleague Ryan is cleaning out the small animal enclosures, a job that takes two people to do safely because the animals must be held in a carrier while the enclosure is moved. He has started alone and is struggling to manage both. You have finished restocking the shelves and the shop is quiet. The manager is in the stockroom. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell the manager that Ryan is doing the enclosures single-handed so that she can decide whether someone should be helping him.
Ask Ryan whether he wants help, and get on with something else if he says he is managing, since he knows the animals better than you do.
Go over and tell Ryan you have finished the shelves and will hold the carrier, and work through the enclosures with him.
Leave him to it, since he chose to start the job on his own and stepping in might suggest you do not think he can manage the animals.
explanation: A: Escalates prematurely: you are standing free in a quiet shop and the task simply needs a second person. Referring it to the manager adds a step to something you can solve immediately. B: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholder's: someone already committed to a job and coping badly will usually say he is managing, so the question predictably leaves him doing a two-person task alone. D: Leaves a two-person job to one person: a two-person job is being done by one person with live animals involved, and the reason for not helping is a worry about how it might look. That leaves both Ryan and the animals at risk. The most effective response is to go over and tell Ryan you have finished the shelves and will hold the carrier, then work through the enclosures with him: the enclosures need two people to be done safely, you are free, and the shop is quiet, so joining him is both the obvious and the safest answer. Saying your own work is done removes any need for him to ask. It beats asking him whether he wants help and getting on with something else if he says he is managing, because a colleague mid-task will usually say he is coping, and the animals are still being handled by one person afterwards. It beats telling the manager he is doing the enclosures single-handed, because she would only send you, and asking her first delays the help for no gain. The least effective response is leaving him to it because he chose to start on his own: it leaves a two-person job with live animals being done alone, and the reason given is a concern about how offering might be taken. That is worse than telling the manager, which at least raises it, and worse than asking him, which at least offers. The principle: when a task needs two people and you are free, join in rather than asking or referring it upwards.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân biệt rõ giữa 'Đúng' (True) và 'Có thể xảy ra' (Possible). Chỉ chọn kết luận chắc chắn 100%.

question_text: You are a warehouse administrator at a medical devices distributor. Reconciling stock you notice that a batch of single-use surgical instruments recorded as quarantined has been picked and despatched to two hospitals. The quarantine was applied last month and you do not know why. The person who applied it has left. Your quality manager is on site. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Take the records to your quality manager immediately, showing that quarantined stock has gone to two hospitals, and let her decide what happens next.
Find out first why the quarantine was applied, since the reason may be administrative, and take it to the quality manager once you know what you are reporting.
Contact the two hospitals to ask them to hold the batch until its status has been confirmed, then report it to the quality manager.
Correct the stock record to show the batch as despatched and let the quarantine flag lapse, since the goods have already gone and the person who applied it is no longer here.
explanation: B: Delays the decision: quarantined stock is already in two hospitals, and establishing the reason yourself postpones a decision the quality manager is qualified to make today. C: Acts outside own authority: contacting customers about potentially unsafe medical devices is a regulated communication, and a warehouse administrator making it first commits the company before anyone qualified has assessed the batch. D: Conceals a potential safety failure: it tidies away the only evidence that quarantined medical devices reached two hospitals, so nobody can assess whether patients are at risk. That is a different order of wrong from acting too slowly. The most effective response is to take the records to your quality manager immediately, showing that quarantined stock has gone to two hospitals, and let her decide what happens next: the reason for the quarantine is unknown and may be a safety matter, and she is on site and decides about recall and about telling the customers. Speed matters because the devices may be used. It beats finding out first why the quarantine was applied, because researching it yourself delays a decision she can take now, on stock already in clinical settings. It beats contacting the two hospitals to ask them to hold the batch, because a communication about potentially unsafe devices is regulated and must come from the company’s quality function. The least effective response is correcting the stock record to show the batch as despatched and letting the flag lapse: it removes the quarantine and the evidence, so nobody can establish whether patients are at risk. That is worse than the other two, which act slowly or beyond their authority but keep the problem visible. The principle: when a control has failed on something already with customers, go straight to the person who owns the control, and change nothing yourself.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You work behind the counter of a bakery. A customer ordered a birthday cake for collection at noon today with ‘Happy Birthday Amelie’ piped on it. It is 11am and you notice the cake in the fridge reads ‘Happy Birthday Amelia’. The decorator is in until 1pm and could re-pipe the inscription in twenty minutes. The customer’s phone number is on the order. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Hand the cake over at noon as it is, since the difference is one letter, the customer may not notice and it is too late to change it now.
Ring the customer, explain the spelling error, and ask whether she would like it corrected or would rather collect the cake as it is.
Have the decorator re-pipe the inscription and say nothing about the error, since the cake will be correct by the time the customer collects it at noon.
Ask the decorator to re-pipe the inscription now, and ring the customer to let her know it is being corrected and will be ready at noon as arranged.
explanation: A: Ignores the customer's actual need: a misspelled name on a child's birthday cake is the whole point of the order, and it is not too late, since the decorator is in and there is an hour. Relying on her not noticing is concealment of a known defect. B: Delays the decision: it hands her a choice she does not need to make. The name is simply wrong, the decorator is in, and twenty minutes is available before noon. C: Hides the problem: the outcome is right and the customer is never told that a cake with her daughter's name misspelled nearly went out, so she cannot check the spelling on the order for next time. The most effective response is to ask the decorator to re-pipe the inscription now and ring the customer to say it is being corrected and will be ready at noon: the name is wrong, there is an hour and a decorator on site, so it can be put right and still be ready. Telling her means she is not surprised and can confirm the spelling. It beats ringing to ask whether she would like it corrected or would rather collect it as it is, because that puts a decision to her that does not need making, when the fix is already possible. It beats having it re-piped and saying nothing about the error, because that gets the cake right but leaves her unaware of a mistake that came from the order itself. The least effective response is handing it over as it is on the grounds that the difference is one letter she may not notice: it claims the change is too late when an hour and a decorator are available, and relies on a misspelled name on a child’s birthday cake going unremarked. That is worse than the other two, which both produce a correct cake. The principle: when there is time to put a mistake right, put it right and tell the customer you have.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You are an exercise support assistant and you keep the site register of completed pre-use checks. Yesterday you entered all twelve stands as checked, signed off by the safety officer. Overnight a storm brought branches down across four of them. The safety officer has already ruled that those four must be rechecked and has booked to do it on Friday. Groups use the stands on Monday. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Record all twelve as checked on Monday's register, since the entries were properly made yesterday and the officer is rechecking four of them on Friday anyway.
Ask the safety officer to bring the recheck forward from Friday to today, and leave the register untouched until you know which day it happens on.
Add a note to the four entries saying that a storm passed overnight, and leave the entries themselves standing until the officer has been out on Friday.
Mark the four entries as superseded today and note the officer's Friday recheck against them, so the register shows which stands have actually been checked as they now stand.
explanation: A: Records a check that no longer describes the stands: the register is what anybody reads to know what has been inspected, and it will say twelve when four have not been looked at since the storm. B: Waits on a date before recording anything: the officer may well come today, and until then the register says twelve stands are checked and nobody has flagged the four. C: Annotates rather than corrects: a note beside an entry that still reads checked is not what somebody scanning the register for Monday's stands actually sees. The most effective response is marking the four entries as superseded today and noting the officer’s Friday recheck against them, so the register shows which stands have actually been checked as they now stand. The officer has already ruled on the four, Friday is booked, and the register’s job between now and then is to say which stands that ruling covers. It beats adding a note that a storm passed overnight while leaving the entries themselves standing, because an entry that still reads checked is what a reader takes from it. It beats asking the safety officer to bring the recheck forward and leaving the register untouched until you know which day it happens on, because the register stays wrong while the date is settled. The least effective response is recording all twelve as checked on Monday’s register: it is made to say twelve stands are checked when four have not been seen since the storm, which is a different kind of wrong from recording it awkwardly. The principle: when events undo finished work, the record is corrected first and the rest follows.
tip: Mẹo MT: Với bài toán quy luật chuỗi số, hãy xét hiệu số bậc 1, hiệu số bậc 2 hoặc tích lũy tiến.

question_text: You are an exercise support assistant. Putting together next week’s stand timings, you need the vehicle plan from one colleague and the ground allocation from another. The two fell out a fortnight ago and now send everything through you. Each is waiting for the other’s part before finalising their own. The timings are due on Thursday. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Put the two of them in a room together on Wednesday morning to settle the vehicle plan and the ground allocation between them at the same time.
Ask each of them separately for the one piece you need from them by Wednesday, and make it clear that you are not asking either to deal with the other.
Draft both parts yourself from last month's plan and ask each of them only to confirm their own section, so that nothing has to pass between them at all.
Tell each of them what the other has been saying about the delay, in front of the rest of the office, so that neither can go on blaming the other for Thursday.
explanation: A: Forces a reconciliation the task does not need: neither part actually depends on the other, and a meeting risks Thursday on whether two people can be civil. C: Does their work to avoid the friction: last month's plan is not this week's, and a confirmation of somebody else's draft is not the same as their own allocation. D: Personalises the conflict in public: the timings are no closer, the falling out now has an audience, and two people who were merely not speaking have been given something new to be angry about. The most effective response is asking each of them separately for the one piece you need by Wednesday, making clear that you are not asking either to deal with the other. Neither part actually needs the other, so the deadlock is a belief rather than a dependency, and saying so directly to each of them dissolves it. It beats putting the two of them in a room together on Wednesday morning to settle the vehicle plan and the ground allocation between them, because it stakes Thursday on a reconciliation nobody has asked for. It beats drafting both parts yourself from last month’s plan and asking each only to confirm their own section, because a confirmed draft is not their plan. The least effective response is telling each of them what the other has been saying, in front of the rest of the office: the deadlock is untouched and a private falling out has been made a public one. The principle: separate what the work needs from what the argument is about, and never take the argument to an audience.
tip: Mẹo MT: Áp dụng sơ đồ Venn hoặc bảng chân trị logic để biểu diễn mối quan hệ giữa các đối tượng.

question_text: You are a candidate liaison assistant. An applicant rings and asks you to tell him how he scored on last week’s reasoning tests. Scores are not released to applicants, and you can see them on your screen. He says he wants to know whether to keep applying elsewhere. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell him scores are not released and leave it there, since the rule is clear and there is nothing else about it that you are able to discuss with him.
Assure him that his scores were fine and that he has nothing to worry about, so that he stops asking for a number you are not allowed to give him.
Tell him plainly that scores are never released, explain what he will be told and when, and say that applying elsewhere in the meantime costs him nothing here.
Offer to ask whether his scores can be released to him this once, given that he is trying to make a decision about other applications.
explanation: A: Answers the rule and not the question: what he actually asked is whether to keep applying elsewhere, and that has an answer you are allowed to give. B: Gives an assurance the role forbids: it is a score in all but the digits, and he may stop applying elsewhere on the strength of a reassurance nobody authorised. D: Raises a hope the rule will not meet: scores are never released, so the question is asked only to come back refused a week later. The most effective response is telling him plainly that scores are never released, explaining what he will be told and when, and saying that applying elsewhere in the meantime costs him nothing here. The score is genuinely not his to have, and the decision he is trying to make can be helped by two facts you are free to give. It beats telling him scores are not released and leaving it there as the end of what you can discuss, because that stops at the rule and ignores the question. It beats offering to ask whether his scores can be released to him this once, because it raises a hope that has no chance. The least effective response is assuring him his scores were fine and he has nothing to worry about: he is given a reassurance about the very thing that may not be given, and he may act on it by stopping his other applications. The principle: when you cannot give the thing asked for, give the truth and whatever else actually helps.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân biệt rõ giữa 'Đúng' (True) và 'Có thể xảy ra' (Possible). Chỉ chọn kết luận chắc chắn 100%.

question_text: You are a families office assistant. A parent rings about the childcare grant and says she will apply after her course starts in October. The stated rule is that applications must be in before the course begins, and late ones are not considered until the following year. She is planning around October. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Assure her that applying in October will be fine: plenty of people apply once their course is under way, and the office is not usually strict about the order of things.
Send her the guidance notes so that she can read the timing rule for herself and see that it has to be in before the course starts.
Make a note to ring her back in September to check she has applied, and leave her to carry on with her own plan in the meantime.
Tell her on this call that the application has to be in before the course starts, so she has the weeks between now and October to get it in rather than losing a year.
explanation: A: Gives an assurance the rule contradicts: she plans around October on the strength of it, and the consequence of being wrong is that she waits a full year. B: Sends the document instead of the message: she has already told you her plan, and a set of notes may not be read before October arrives. C: Sets a reminder in place of a correction: September is close to the deadline, and she spends the summer believing October is available to her. The most effective response is telling her on this call that the application has to be in before the course starts, so she has the weeks between now and October to get it in rather than losing a year. She is on the telephone, she has told you her plan, and the plan costs her a year, so the correction belongs in this call. It beats sending her the guidance notes so she can read the timing rule for herself, because guidance notes may not be read in time. It beats making a note to ring her back in September to check she has applied, because she spends the summer planning around a date that does not work. The least effective response is assuring her that applying in October will be fine because the office is not usually strict: she is told a rule does not apply when it does, and the price of believing it is a year. The principle: correct a misreading in the conversation where you found it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You are a recruitment office assistant. An applicant has emailed to say he is bringing his passport to Thursday’s document check. The stated requirement is a passport and a birth certificate, and people without both are turned away and rebooked six weeks out. He has misread it. He lives four hours away. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Send him the standard requirements page again without comment, since it contains both documents and he will see the difference when he reads it properly.
Reply today setting out both documents, so that he has three days to find the birth certificate rather than four hours of travelling for nothing.
Leave it, on the ground that the requirement was set out plainly in what he was sent and that reading it is not yours to do for every applicant.
Ring him on Thursday morning before he sets off, to check that he has everything he needs for the document check that afternoon.
explanation: A: Resends what has already been misread: nothing in the page has changed, and the reason he got it wrong the first time is untouched. C: Declines to act on something you have already noticed: the requirement was indeed clear, and the one person who has spotted that he has misread it lets him travel four hours to be turned away. D: Leaves it to the morning: a birth certificate cannot be found in the hour before a four hour drive, and the three days that would have been useful are gone. The most effective response is replying today setting out both documents, so he has three days to find the birth certificate rather than four hours of travelling for nothing. He has misread it, you have seen that he has, and three days is enough to find a document that an hour is not. It beats sending him the standard requirements page again without comment on the basis that he will see the difference, because resending an unread page changes nothing. It beats ringing him on Thursday morning before he sets off to check he has everything, because Thursday morning is too late to find a certificate. The least effective response is leaving it because the requirement was set out plainly in what he was sent: that is true and irrelevant, and a man drives four hours to be turned away by the one office that could have stopped it. The principle: whether somebody should have understood has nothing to do with whether you can still help.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You are a selection centre assistant and you keep the waiting list for cancelled interview slots. It runs strictly in the order people joined it. An applicant twelfth on the list emails to say he is being posted abroad for work in three weeks and asks to be moved up. Two slots have come free for next week. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Offer him the first slot that comes free after these two, and tell the eleven ahead of him that a posting case has been raised so that nobody is surprised.
Leave the list as it is and assume he will raise it again if the posting really does make next week his only chance at an interview this year.
Ask him for the dates of the posting and put the case to whoever owns the list, so a decision about jumping eleven people is made by somebody who can make it.
Reply that the list runs strictly in order and cannot be changed, so that everybody on it is treated the same way whatever their circumstances.
explanation: A: Invents a middle answer: it is open and it still changes the order on one applicant's unverified account, which is the decision the list's owner exists to take. B: Assumes the applicant will come back: he has already asked once, two slots are free next week, and nothing about his request reaches anybody who could decide it. D: Applies the rule and stops there: whether the list can flex for a posting is a real question, and it is answered without being put to anybody who could answer it. The most effective response is asking him for the dates of the posting and putting the case to whoever owns the list, so a decision about jumping eleven people is made by somebody who can make it. A posting abroad may well be a good reason to move somebody up, and it is not your decision, so the useful act is to get it in front of the person it belongs to. It beats replying that the list runs strictly in order and cannot be changed whatever the circumstances, because that refuses without asking. It beats offering him the first slot that comes free after these two and telling the eleven ahead of him a posting case has been raised, because it changes the order on an account nobody has checked. The least effective response is leaving the list as it is and assuming he will raise it again: two slots go to the ordinary order while a request that might have changed it sits unanswered on your desk. The principle: when a rule might reasonably bend, the person who owns the rule decides, and your job is to ask them.
tip: Mẹo MT: Với bài toán quy luật chuỗi số, hãy xét hiệu số bậc 1, hiệu số bậc 2 hoặc tích lũy tiến.

question_text: You are a recruit. Your section has to hand in a written exercise by four o’clock, and you have also promised to help another recruit prepare for the fitness reassessment he has to pass tomorrow. Both need the rest of the afternoon. He cannot practise without somebody timing him and the exercise is marked for the whole section. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Ask him to find somebody else to time him this afternoon, and offer to go through the reassessment with him after five if he still wants it.
Pass the timing on to somebody else in the section, so that he turns up this afternoon and finds a recruit he never asked for waiting instead of you.
Time him for twenty minutes now and finish the section's exercise afterwards, so that he gets something and four o'clock is still met.
Finish the section's exercise first because four o'clock is fixed and the whole section is marked on it, and tell him now that you can time him at five.
explanation: A: Puts the finding on him: he has to arrange his own timer at short notice, when you already know you are free at five. B: Passes a promise on to a third party: somebody does time him, and the person the promise was made to finds out you are not coming by arriving and meeting a stranger. C: Splits the promise rather than moving it: twenty minutes is not a reassessment session, and five o'clock was available and would have given him a whole one. The most effective response is finishing the section’s exercise first because four o’clock is fixed and the whole section is marked on it, and telling him now that you can time him at five. Four o’clock cannot move and the reassessment can, so protecting the deadline and moving the timing to five costs him nothing at all. It beats timing him for twenty minutes now and finishing the exercise afterwards, because twenty minutes is not the session he needs and five o’clock was free. It beats asking him to find somebody else to time him this afternoon and offering to go through it after five, because it makes him do the arranging. The least effective response is passing the timing on to somebody else in the section: the promise is handed over and the person it was made to finds out by turning up. The principle: reschedule the thing that can move, and tell the person waiting before they are waiting.

question_text: You are an expedition support assistant. A group of twelve leaves at six tomorrow morning. Packing the stores this afternoon in a hurry, you realise the food you loaded is for four days and the itinerary is five. There is a resupply point on day three that would have to be arranged tonight. The person who arranges it goes home at six and it is now half past five. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Load the four days as they are and hope it will not be noticed: the group can spread the food out, and the mistake is yours to fix quietly.
Ring the person who arranges resupply in the next half hour and say plainly that you loaded four days instead of five, so that there is time to get day five covered.
Buy a day's food from the town shop first thing in the morning and put it on the vehicle, telling the leader at six exactly what happened and what you have done.
Tell the expedition leader now that the food is a day short, and leave the leader to decide whether to raise it with the resupply desk before six o'clock.
explanation: A: Conceals your own error: the resupply that would fix it has to be arranged tonight by somebody who leaves in half an hour, so the quiet fix does not exist after six o'clock. C: Solves it out of your own pocket: the group is fed and the unit's own resupply arrangement, which exists for precisely this, is never used or told. D: Passes responsibility to others: it is honest, and it spends the half hour that is left routing the problem through somebody who then has to make the same call you could make now. The most effective response is ringing the person who arranges resupply in the next half hour and saying plainly that you loaded four days instead of five. There are thirty minutes before the only person who can cover the missing day goes home, and the shortest route to him is your own account of what happened. It beats telling the expedition leader now and leaving him to decide whether to raise it with the resupply desk, because that spends the last half hour passing the problem through somebody who cannot arrange resupply either. It beats buying a day’s food from the town shop first thing in the morning and putting it on the vehicle, because the arrangement that exists for exactly this is bypassed and paid for privately. The least effective response is loading the four days as they are and hoping it will not be noticed: twelve people leave at six a day’s food short, and the reason nobody can fix it is that nobody has been told. The principle: a mistake found while there is still time is a message you make immediately, and owning it costs less than the hour it buys.

question_text: You work in the membership office of a golf club. Members’ subscriptions are due, and a discounted rate applies to anyone who joined before 2015. A member who joined in 2018 asks you to record him as a pre-2015 member, saying he has been coming as a guest since 2012 and that nobody would ever check. He is friendly and well known at the club. The club secretary is in her office. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell him you cannot change the joining date and suggest he takes it up with the club secretary himself if he believes his guest years should count.
Record him at the pre-2015 rate, since he has genuinely been coming to the club since 2012 and the discount is meant to reward long- standing members.
Apply the standard rate but note on his file that he has attended since 2012, so that the club can consider a discretionary discount at some point in the future.
Tell him the joining date is a matter of record and you cannot change it, and offer to ask the secretary whether guest years have ever been counted towards the discount.
explanation: A: Passes responsibility to others: the refusal is right and the handoff is thin. He has raised a question about how guest years are treated, and sending him to make his own case leaves you having merely declined. B: Falsifies a membership record: his joining date is a fact, and rewriting it to produce a discount he is not entitled to is dishonesty dressed as fairness. It also charges every other member for the shortfall. C: Delays the decision: it charges him correctly, which is right, and parks his actual question on a file note that nobody is due to read. The secretary is in her office today. The most effective response is to tell him the joining date is a matter of record and offer to ask the secretary whether guest years have ever counted: the date is a fact and not yours to alter, but the question underneath it is legitimate and the secretary can answer it. Refusing clearly and taking the question forward does both jobs. It beats telling him to take it up with the club secretary himself, because that refuses in the same way but leaves him to make his own case, when you are standing beside the person who decides. It beats applying the standard rate and noting on his file that he has attended since 2012, because a note for future consideration answers nobody today, and the secretary is available now. The least effective response is recording him at the pre-2015 rate: it rewrites a factual record to create an entitlement that does not exist, and the reasoning offered, that he has been around a long time, is exactly the reasoning that makes small falsifications feel reasonable. That is worse than the other two, which charge him correctly. The principle: refuse to alter a record, then take the fair question underneath it to the person who can actually decide it.

question_text: You work as a machine operative at a joinery workshop. Changing over the crosscut saw, you notice its blade guard is cracked and no longer locks into position. Workshop rules say a defective guard must be reported to the supervisor, who takes the machine out of use until it is repaired. It is the only crosscut saw in the workshop, several colleagues rely on it every day, and losing it would slow the whole team’s work; the last repair took most of a week. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Say nothing about the guard and plan your own jobs around the other machines, leaving the crosscut saw available for the colleagues who rely on it.
Carry on using the saw with extra care yourself, warning colleagues to do the same, and raise the guard at the team meeting later in the week.
Report the cracked guard to your supervisor straight away, so the saw comes out of use until it has been repaired.
Email the company's health and safety officer asking for an urgent inspection of every machine in the workshop, assuming other guards are probably wearing out as well.
explanation: A: Stays silent about a known safety risk: keeping quiet while steering only yourself away from the saw protects you and nobody else; colleagues keep using a machine you know is unsafe, which is self-protective silence rather than a defensible reading of the risk. B: Fails to escalate a genuine risk: care and warnings do not fix a guard that no longer locks, and waiting days for a meeting keeps a known hazard in daily use when the rules give you a route that acts today. D: Escalates on assumptions without checking: widening one observed fault into a workshop-wide inspection request is built on a guess, bypasses the supervisor the rules name, and leaves the one saw you know is unsafe in use while the bigger process gets arranged. The most effective response is to report the cracked guard to your supervisor straight away so the saw comes out of use: a guard that is cracked and no longer locks is a genuine injury risk, the rules name exactly who to tell, and the supervisor can act today. The disruption to the team is real, but it is the trade the workshop’s own rules have already made. It beats carrying on with extra care and raising it at the team meeting, because care and warnings do not make a broken guard safe, and waiting days keeps the hazard in daily use for the sake of avoiding a difficult report. It beats emailing the health and safety officer for a workshop-wide inspection, because that inflates one observed fault into an assumed general problem, bypasses the supervisor who can act now, and leaves the one saw you know is unsafe running while a bigger inspection is arranged. The least effective response is saying nothing and working around the saw yourself: unlike carrying on with warnings, which at least alerts the people at risk, and unlike the inspection request, which at least tells someone with authority, it tells nobody and quietly protects only you, leaving colleagues to use a machine you know is unsafe. The principle: a genuine safety risk is raised at once through the stated route, whatever the disruption, and never managed silently around yourself.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You are an administrator in a secondary school office. You and your colleague Marek share responsibility for the trips inbox. He believes parents’ consent queries should be answered only by the trip lead teacher; you have always answered the routine ones yourself. Yesterday he forwarded three of your answers to the trip lead with a note saying they should not have been sent. A parent deadline falls on Friday and forty replies are outstanding. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Ask Marek to sit down with you today, work out which queries each of you will answer before Friday, and agree to take the underlying disagreement to the trip lead afterwards.
Carry on answering the queries as you always have and, since Marek went over your head to the trip lead, copy the trip lead into your replies so she can see the standard of them for herself.
Answer all forty replies yourself before Friday so the parents' deadline is met, and leave the question of who should be answering them until the trips have gone out.
Email the trip lead teacher setting out why routine consent queries have always been answered in the office, and ask her to confirm the position before any more replies go out.
explanation: B: Personalises the conflict: it answers a professional disagreement by scoring a point through a third party. Forty parent replies become the ground on which two colleagues argue, which is a different order of wrong from the other options. C: Avoids the difficult conversation: it hits Friday and guarantees the same clash next term, with Marek now watching for replies he thinks you should not be sending. D: Delays the decision: it seeks a ruling that may not arrive before Friday, and pauses forty parent replies while waiting for it. The boundary question is real; the parents' deadline will not wait for it. The most effective response is to ask Marek to sit down with you today, work out which queries each of you answers before Friday, and take the underlying disagreement to the trip lead afterwards: there are two problems here, a deadline on Friday and a genuine disagreement about who answers what, and only the first is urgent. It beats answering all forty replies yourself before Friday, because that meets the deadline and leaves the disagreement exactly where it was, with the same clash guaranteed next term. It beats emailing the trip lead to confirm the position before any more replies go out, because that puts forty parent replies behind a decision that may not come before Friday. The least effective response is copying the trip lead into your replies so she can see the standard of them: it uses the parents’ replies as a way of answering Marek, copying her in to make a point rather than to solve anything, which turns a workable disagreement into a contest. That is worse than the other two, which handle the conflict badly but do not weaponise the work. The principle: separate the deadline from the disagreement, meet the deadline together, and settle the disagreement with the person who owns the rule afterwards.

question_text: You work in credit control at a builders’ merchant. A long-standing customer is two months overdue and his account should be put on stop, which would block a delivery he needs tomorrow. He rings you personally, explains his cash flow problem, and asks you to delay the stop by a week as a favour, mentioning that he has always paid eventually. Your credit manager is in the office. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Apply the stop as the process requires and tell him the decision is automatic once an account reaches two months, so there is nothing you can do about it.
Apply the stop, but tell him informally which day the account is reviewed so that he can time a part payment to get the delivery released.
Hold off applying the stop for a week as he asks, since he has always paid eventually and applying it now would cost him a delivery he needs tomorrow.
Tell him you cannot delay the stop yourself, take the details of his cash flow position, and put the request to your credit manager today so she can decide before tomorrow's delivery.
explanation: A: Passes responsibility to others: it hides behind the process to avoid a difficult conversation, when a genuine request from a long- standing customer is exactly the kind that the credit manager exists to consider. B: Coaches the customer around the control: it applies the rule and then coaches the customer on how to work around it, which achieves the same favour as delaying the stop while leaving no record that anyone decided anything. C: Breaches confidentiality or process: the credit limit is the merchant's control on its own exposure, and quietly suspending it as a personal favour is a decision taken outside the process by someone without the authority to take it. The most effective response is to tell him you cannot delay the stop yourself, take the details of his cash flow position, and put the request to your credit manager today: you have no authority to suspend a credit stop, the request is a reasonable one for a long-standing customer, and she is in the office with a day in hand to decide. Taking the facts to her keeps the decision with the person who owns the exposure. It beats telling him the decision is automatic and there is nothing you can do, because that is untrue: something can be done, it is simply not yours to do, and the process has a person in it. It beats telling him informally which day the account is reviewed so he can time a part payment, because that achieves the favour without a record that any decision was taken. The least effective response is holding off applying the stop for a week as he asks: it suspends a control on the merchant’s own credit exposure as a personal favour, with no authority and no record. That is worse than the flat refusal, which is unhelpful but correct, and worse than the informal tip, which at least applies the stop. The principle: when a request is reasonable but outside your authority, take it to the person whose authority it is, in time for them to use it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You are a call handler for a housing repairs line. A storm overnight has produced four times the usual call volume and you have taken complaints for three hours. A tenant tells you that you sound like you do not care and that she has been let down repeatedly. She has a genuinely urgent repair, a leaking roof over her child’s bedroom. Your team leader is available. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Explain that the team is dealing with four times the normal call volume because of the storm and that everyone is being helped as quickly as possible.
Acknowledge that she has been let down, confirm the leak over the child's bedroom as an urgent repair, and tell her exactly what happens next and when.
Tell her that comments about whether you care are not helping and ask her to let you take the details so the repair can be logged.
Apologise and offer to pass her to your team leader, since she is unhappy with how the call is going and may get further with someone more senior.
explanation: A: Answers the accusation and not the leak: it answers her accusation with the team's workload, which is true and irrelevant to a leak over a child's bed, and invites her to argue about whose day is harder. C: Personalises the conflict: it corrects a distressed tenant's manner before addressing a leak over her child's bed, which puts your own treatment ahead of her emergency. D: Passes responsibility to others: it hands over a repair you can raise yourself and makes a tenant with a leaking roof wait through another handover. The most effective response is to acknowledge that she has been let down, confirm the leak over the child’s bedroom as an urgent repair, and tell her exactly what happens next and when: with water coming in over a child’s bed, the fastest route through the call is to accept the part that is true and move straight to classifying the repair and saying what follows. It beats explaining that the team is dealing with four times the normal call volume, because that answers her accusation rather than her leak, and invites a comparison of whose day is worse. It beats offering to pass her to your team leader, because that delays a repair you can raise now and makes her start again. The least effective response is telling her that comments about whether you care are not helping: it corrects her manner before dealing with the water, which puts your own treatment ahead of her emergency. That is worse than explaining the volumes, which at least explains, and worse than passing her on, which at least routes her onward. The principle: when someone is angry and their problem is urgent, acknowledge the grievance briefly and spend the call on the emergency.

question_text: You work at a print bureau. Loading a job you notice that the artwork for a customer’s 5,000 leaflets carries a phone number that does not match the one on their letterhead in the same file. Nobody has asked you to proofread; your job is to run the press. The print run starts in an hour. The customer’s contact details are on the job sheet and your production manager is on site. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Run the job exactly as supplied, since proofreading is not your role and the customer signed off the artwork before it came to the press.
Ring the customer directly to check which phone number is correct before running the job, since it is their leaflet and only they can say.
Print the leaflets using the number from the letterhead, since that is plainly the customer's real number and the one on the artwork must be a mistake.
Take it to your production manager now, show her the two different numbers, and let her decide whether to hold the run and check with the customer.
explanation: A: Fails to escalate a genuine risk: you are the only person who has noticed, and 5,000 leaflets carrying a wrong phone number are worthless once printed. Sign-off does not make an error you can see disappear. B: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholder's: contacting a customer about their artwork is the production manager's call, and going straight to them may cut across a conversation the bureau has already had. C: Acts on assumptions without checking: the artwork number may be a new line or a campaign number. Choosing between them yourself risks printing 5,000 leaflets with the wrong one and no record of who decided. The most effective response is to take it to your production manager now, show her the two different numbers, and let her decide whether to hold the run: you have spotted something nobody else has, the run starts in an hour, and she can decide in minutes. It costs almost nothing and prevents a scrapped run. It beats printing the leaflets using the number from the letterhead, because choosing between the two yourself is a guess about the customer’s business, and being wrong wastes the whole job. It beats ringing the customer directly to check which number is correct, because that relationship is the bureau’s to manage, and the manager may already know the answer. The least effective response is running the job exactly as supplied because proofreading is not your role: it prints 5,000 leaflets with a discrepancy you have seen, on the grounds that the artwork was signed off. That is worse than the other two, which act on it imperfectly but do act. The principle: when you see something wrong that is about to become expensive, raise it with whoever can stop the job, before it starts.

question_text: You work at the ticket desk of a cinema. A family arrives with tickets for a film that started twenty minutes ago; they misread the start time on their booking. The screening is nearly full and there is another showing of the same film in ninety minutes with plenty of seats. Cinema policy allows the desk to transfer tickets to a later showing at your discretion. The duty manager is in the foyer. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Explain that the film started twenty minutes ago and let them into the screen now so they see as much of it as possible.
Explain that the tickets were for a showing that has begun, that the mistake was theirs, and that new tickets would have to be bought for the later screening.
Explain that the tickets cannot be used now and refer them to the duty manager in the foyer, who can decide whether anything can be done.
Apologise for the mix-up, explain the film has already started, and offer to transfer their tickets to the showing in ninety minutes.
explanation: A: Seats them into a spoiled showing: it seats a family twenty minutes into a film in a nearly full screen, which gives them a poor showing and disturbs everyone already watching, when a full one is available later. B: Ignores the customer's actual need: it charges a family twice for a misread start time when policy allows you to transfer the tickets at no cost. Applying the strictest reading available is a service failure, not a rule. C: Passes responsibility to others: transferring tickets is explicitly within your discretion, so sending them to find a manager adds a step to something you are authorised to settle. The most effective response is to apologise for the mix-up, explain the film has already started, and offer to transfer their tickets to the showing in ninety minutes: a later screening has plenty of seats and the policy explicitly lets you transfer. That costs the cinema a seat it would have had empty anyway and saves the family’s evening. It beats letting them into the screen now so they see as much as possible, because seating them twenty minutes late in a nearly full auditorium gives them a poor experience and disturbs the audience, when a complete showing is available. It beats referring them to the duty manager in the foyer, because the transfer is within your discretion, so referring only delays what you can do now. The least effective response is telling them the mistake was theirs and that new tickets must be bought: it makes the family pay twice for a misread time when a free transfer was available to you. That is worse than seating them late, which at least lets them see something, and worse than the referral, which at least keeps a route open. The principle: when you hold the discretion to fix a customer’s problem at no real cost, use it rather than referring it or applying the harshest reading.

question_text: You work in a hospital outpatient booking office. At 11am three things need you. A consultant’s clinic next Tuesday has been cancelled and forty patients need contacting before letters go out tomorrow. A patient is on hold asking to move an appointment scheduled for tomorrow. And your manager wants the weekly waiting-time return by 2pm, which takes an hour. Contacting forty patients takes most of the day. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Start ringing the forty patients immediately since that is the largest task and the letters go out tomorrow, and deal with the waiting patient and the return when you can.
Take the patient off hold and move tomorrow's appointment, do the waiting-time return before 2pm, then spend the rest of the day on the forty cancellations.
Let the cancellation letters go out as they are and contact the forty patients afterwards, so that today's shorter tasks can all be completed properly.
Do the waiting-time return first since it has the earliest deadline, then the patient on hold, then start the cancellation calls.
explanation: A: Splits effort so nothing finishes: it starts the long job while leaving a patient on hold and an hour-long return due at 2pm, so the waiting-time deadline is put at risk by a task that has until tomorrow. C: Hides the problem: it lets forty patients receive letters for a clinic that has been cancelled, which generates forty wasted journeys and forty calls back. Knowingly sending wrong information is worse than mis-sequencing it. D: Ignores the customer's actual need: an hour of reporting is put ahead of a patient already holding on the line about an appointment tomorrow, when her call takes a few minutes. The most effective response is to take the patient off hold and move tomorrow’s appointment, do the waiting-time return before 2pm, then spend the rest of the day on the forty cancellations: the patient takes a few minutes and concerns tomorrow, the return takes an hour against a fixed deadline, and the calls have until the letters go out. Doing the two short fixed items first leaves the whole afternoon for the long one. It beats starting the forty calls immediately as the largest task, because that puts an hour-long 2pm deadline at risk for work that has until tomorrow. It beats doing the waiting-time return first because it has the earliest deadline, because that leaves a patient holding on the line while an internal report is prepared. The least effective response is letting the cancellation letters go out as they are and contacting the forty afterwards: it sends letters for a clinic that will not happen, producing wasted journeys and forty return calls. That is worse than the other two, which order the day badly but do not knowingly send wrong information. The principle: clear the short items with fixed deadlines, then give the long task the time it needs, and never let known wrong information go out.
