question_text: You are a ward administrator at a veterinary hospital. At 4pm three things need you. A dog is due to be collected at 4.30 and its discharge notes are not written, which takes fifteen minutes. A referring vet has rung twice for an update on a case and is waiting for a call back. And the practice manager wants the month-end invoicing reconciled tonight, which takes two hours. You finish at 7pm. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Ring the referring vet first since he has already rung twice, then write the discharge notes and start the invoicing.
Start the month-end invoicing since it is the longest job and is wanted tonight, and fit the discharge notes and the call around it as the evening goes on.
Send the dog home at 4.30 without written discharge notes and telephone the owner with the aftercare instructions later in the evening once the invoicing is done.
Write the discharge notes for the 4.30 collection, ring the referring vet back, then spend the rest of the evening on the invoicing.
explanation: A: Delays the decision: the call has no fixed time and the collection is at 4.30. Answering by who has waited longest rather than by when something is needed risks the owner arriving to notes that are not written. B: Splits effort so nothing finishes: two hours of invoicing has three hours of room, and starting it first leaves a fifteen-minute task with a 4.30 deadline to be squeezed. C: Acts recklessly with a clinical handover: discharge notes are how an owner knows about medication and aftercare, and sending an animal home without them, on a promise to ring later, risks the dog's recovery. The most effective response is to write the discharge notes for the 4.30 collection, ring the referring vet back, then spend the rest of the evening on the invoicing: the collection is fixed and only fifteen minutes away, the vet’s call has no fixed time but has already waited twice, and two hours of invoicing fits comfortably in the three hours left. Sequencing by deadline gets all three done. It beats ringing the referring vet first because he has already rung twice, since that risks an owner arriving to notes that do not exist. It beats starting the month-end invoicing as the longest job wanted tonight, because that squeezes the one task with a hard time on it. The least effective response is sending the dog home without written discharge notes and telephoning the aftercare later: it discharges an animal without written instructions to protect a paperwork deadline. That is worse than the other two, which order the work badly but complete it properly. The principle: do the short task with the fixed clinical deadline first, then the waiting person, then the long job that fits the remaining time.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You are a facilities coordinator for an office building. At 9am you learn that the lift has failed with nobody inside, that a meeting room booked for a client presentation at 10am has no working projector, and that the quarterly fire alarm test is scheduled for 11am. A wheelchair user works on the third floor and is due in at 9.30am. The lift engineer can attend within two hours if called now. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Call the lift engineer immediately, tell the third-floor colleague and her manager before she travels in, then deal with the projector and confirm the alarm test.
Deal with the projector and the alarm test as planned and wait to see whether the lift resets itself, since calling an engineer out is expensive and it may come back on its own.
Sort the projector first since the client presentation is at 10am and is the nearest deadline, then call the lift engineer and confirm the alarm test.
Call the lift engineer, then postpone the fire alarm test since a failed lift makes evacuation arrangements unreliable, and deal with the projector afterwards.
explanation: B: Fails to escalate a genuine risk: it leaves a wheelchair user arriving at a building she cannot move around in, and gambles the two-hour repair window on the lift fixing itself, to save a call-out fee. C: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholder's: the projector is the nearest deadline and the smallest consequence. A colleague who cannot use the stairs is due in at 9.30 and the engineer's two-hour window starts only when he is called. D: Escalates prematurely: postponing a scheduled alarm test is a decision with its own consequences, taken before anyone has checked whether the test is affected, while a colleague is still travelling in to a building she cannot get around. The most effective response is to call the lift engineer immediately, tell the third-floor colleague and her manager before she travels in, then deal with the projector and the alarm test: the lift is the only item with both a closing window, the engineer’s two hours, and a person affected who is already travelling. Calling starts the clock, and warning her before she sets off is the part that cannot wait. The projector and the alarm test both still fit afterwards. It beats sorting the projector first for the 10am presentation, because that puts the smallest consequence first and leaves a colleague to discover on arrival that she cannot reach her desk. It beats calling the engineer and then postponing the fire alarm test, because postponing it is a further decision with its own effects, taken before checking whether it is even affected. The least effective response is waiting to see whether the lift resets itself to avoid a call-out charge: that spends the repair window and leaves a wheelchair user stranded on arrival. That is worse than the other two, which misorder the work but call the engineer. The principle: start the longest lead time first, warn the person affected before they are committed, and fit the rest around it.

question_text: You are a junior designer at a graphic design studio. You and a colleague, Ines, are producing a brand pack due to the client on Friday. It is Wednesday. Ines has been given a second urgent project and tells you she can now only do about half her share of the brand pack. You have capacity for some but not all of the rest. Your studio manager assigns work and is in the office. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Take on all of Ines's remaining share and work late Wednesday and Thursday so the brand pack is delivered on Friday as promised.
Work out with Ines exactly what is left, then tell the studio manager today what the two of you can cover and what still needs someone, before Friday.
Tell Ines the brand pack has to come first since it has a client deadline on Friday, and ask her to push back on the second project herself.
Carry on with your own share and let Ines deliver what she can, and raise it on Friday if the brand pack turns out to be incomplete.
explanation: A: Hides the strain until failure: it absorbs a shortfall the studio manager created and never learns about, so she keeps assigning on the assumption that both projects fit. C: Passes responsibility to others: the studio manager assigns the work, so asking Ines to argue about her own workload leaves the person who made the clash out of the conversation. D: Hides the problem / silent deadline slip: it is known on Wednesday that the pack will be short, and the plan is to mention it on the day it is due, when nothing can be done. Waiting to report a certainty is concealment. The most effective response is to work out with Ines exactly what is left, then tell the studio manager today what the two of you can cover and what still needs someone: the shortfall is known on Wednesday, its size can be worked out in ten minutes, and she both created the clash and is the only person who can resolve it. Bringing her the specifics rather than the problem lets her act. It beats taking on all of Ines’s remaining share and working late, because quietly absorbing the gap hides from the manager that two projects were assigned into one person’s week, so she does it again. It beats telling Ines to push back on the second project herself, because that leaves the person who assigns the work out of a conversation about her own assignment. The least effective response is letting Ines deliver what she can and raising it only if the pack turns out incomplete: it knows on Wednesday that Friday will fall short and plans to mention it when no resource can be added. That is worse than absorbing the work, which delivers, and worse than asking her to push back, which at least raises it. The principle: size the gap, then take it to whoever controls the resource while there is still time to fill it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân biệt rõ giữa 'Đúng' (True) và 'Có thể xảy ra' (Possible). Chỉ chọn kết luận chắc chắn 100%.

question_text: You are a receptionist at a serviced office building. At 9am a courier arrives needing a signature for a package marked urgent for one of the tenant companies. A visitor is waiting to be signed in for a 9am meeting. Your building manager has asked you to update the tenant contact list this morning, a job of about an hour with no fixed time. You are alone on the desk. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Take the courier's package first since he is waiting to get on with his round, then sign the visitor in and update the contact list during the morning.
Sign for the courier's package and tell the visitor to take a seat and wait until you have finished the contact list, since she can be signed in at any point.
Start the contact list update since your building manager asked for it this morning, and deal with the courier and the visitor as you work through it.
Sign the visitor in first since her meeting starts now, take the courier's signature next, and update the contact list once the desk is clear.
explanation: A: Acts on assumptions without checking: the courier's round is his schedule, not yours, while the visitor's meeting is at 9am. Serving whoever seems most impatient is not the same as judging what is time-critical. B: Ignores the visitor's actual need: it makes someone who is due in a 9am meeting wait an hour for a task with no deadline, so the tenant's meeting is delayed to suit the reception desk. C: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholder's: an hour of internal admin with a whole morning available is put ahead of two people standing at the desk, one of them late for a meeting. The most effective response is to sign the visitor in first since her meeting starts now, take the courier’s signature next, and update the contact list once the desk is clear: hers is the only fixed time on the desk, the signature takes seconds and the list has the whole morning. It beats taking the courier’s package first because he is waiting to get on with his round, since his hurry is about his own schedule while she is late for a meeting a tenant is holding. It beats starting the contact list because your building manager asked for it this morning, because an hour of internal admin should not precede two people standing at the desk. The least effective response is telling the visitor to take a seat until the contact list is finished: it makes someone due at a 9am meeting wait an hour so that a task with no deadline can be completed. That is worse than the other two, which mis-sequence but do not park someone deliberately. The principle: serve the fixed appointment first, then the quick task, then the work that can be done at any point.

question_text: You are a reporter at a local newspaper. You and a colleague, Suzanne, have both been working on the same council story without realising it, and she has told a contact that the story is hers. The contact has now stopped returning your calls. The story is due to run this week and the editor does not know there has been any overlap. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Speak to Suzanne today, work out what each of you has, agree who takes it forward and how the contact is approached, then tell the editor where the story stands.
Drop your version and let Suzanne run with it, since the contact is talking to her now and arguing about who started first would only damage the newsroom.
Tell the editor that Suzanne has claimed the story with your contact and ask him to decide which of you should take it forward.
Go back to the contact directly, explain that you were working on the story first, and ask him to deal with you rather than with Suzanne.
explanation: B: Avoids the difficult conversation: it abandons work and material the story may need, so the paper runs a weaker piece and the duplication that caused it is never addressed. The editor never learns two reporters duplicated a week. C: Escalates prematurely: Suzanne may not know you were working on it at all, and the editor's first knowledge of the overlap being a complaint makes an argument out of a misunderstanding. D: Personalises the conflict: it asks a source to choose between two reporters from the same paper, which puts an internal muddle in front of a contact and is likely to lose him altogether. The most effective response is to speak to Suzanne today, work out what each of you has, agree who takes it forward and how the contact is approached, then tell the editor where the story stands: two reporters have duplicated work on a story running this week, the fastest way to a good piece is to pool what you both have, and the editor needs an accurate picture rather than a complaint. Agreeing how the contact is approached also protects the source. It beats telling the editor she has claimed the story with your contact, because she may not know you were on it, and taking it upward first frames a misunderstanding as a dispute. It beats going back to the contact to say you were working on it first, because asking a source to choose between two reporters from the same paper exposes the muddle and risks losing him. The least effective response is dropping your version and letting her run with it: it discards material the story may need and leaves the duplication unexamined, so the paper runs a weaker piece and it happens again. That is worse than the other two, which handle it badly but keep both reporters’ work in play. The principle: sort out the overlap with your colleague first, protect the source, then give the editor the true position.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân biệt rõ giữa 'Đúng' (True) và 'Có thể xảy ra' (Possible). Chỉ chọn kết luận chắc chắn 100%.

question_text: You are a receptionist at a physiotherapy practice. At 11am the practice’s online booking system goes down; patients are ringing and cannot book. A patient in the waiting room needs her follow-up appointments arranged before she leaves, which takes ten minutes. Your practice manager wants the insurance paperwork for three patients completed today, taking an hour. The IT contractor answers within minutes when called. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Take patients' details by phone and tell them the practice will call back to book when the system returns, without reporting the outage to the IT contractor.
Book the waiting patient's follow-up appointments first since she is in front of you, then ring the IT contractor and start the insurance paperwork.
Ring the IT contractor about the booking system straight away, book the waiting patient's follow-ups while you wait for them, and do the insurance paperwork afterwards.
Start the insurance paperwork since your manager wants it today, and deal with the booking system and the waiting patient as the morning allows.
explanation: A: Fails to escalate a genuine fault: it builds a manual workaround for an outage nobody has been told about, so the system stays down all day and the backlog grows with it. B: Delays the decision: the contractor answers in minutes and then works in the background, so calling first costs almost nothing and starts a repair that every ringing patient is waiting on. D: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholder's: an hour of paperwork due at some point today is put ahead of a system outage affecting every patient trying to book and a patient waiting at the desk. The most effective response is to ring the IT contractor about the booking system straight away, book the waiting patient’s follow-ups while you wait for them, and do the insurance paperwork afterwards: the contractor answers within minutes and then works in the background, so that call sets the longest-running fix going at almost no cost, and the ten minutes with the patient fits neatly into the wait. The paperwork has the rest of the day. It beats booking her follow-up appointments first because she is in front of you, since the call is the thing that unblocks everyone else and takes moments. It beats starting the insurance paperwork because your manager wants it today, because an hour of paperwork with a whole day available should not precede an outage affecting every patient trying to book. The least effective response is taking details by phone for a callback without reporting the outage at all: it manages the symptoms of a fault nobody has been told about, so it persists all day and the callback list grows. That is worse than the other two, which sequence badly but do not leave the fault unreported. The principle: start the fix with the longest lead time first, then use the waiting time for the people in front of you.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You are an invigilator at a training centre running a professional certification exam. Ten minutes before the end, you see a candidate glance repeatedly at a phone in his lap. He is a colleague from your own department and you know he needs this qualification for a promotion. The exam rules require any suspected use of a device to be reported to the exam supervisor, who is in the next room. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Note what you saw and report it to the exam supervisor as the rules require, letting her decide what happens.
Say nothing at all, since he is a colleague, you cannot be certain what he was looking at, and reporting him could cost him a promotion.
Walk over and stand near his desk so he puts the phone away, and say nothing afterwards since the exam ends in ten minutes and no harm will have been done.
Quietly ask him after the exam whether he was using his phone, and report it to the supervisor only if he admits that he was.
explanation: B: Breaches process to protect a colleague: the rule requires suspected device use to be reported, and certainty is the supervisor's job to establish, not yours. Staying silent because of who he is undermines every other candidate in the room. C: Prioritises harmony over honesty: it stops the behaviour and leaves the ten minutes already elapsed unexamined, so a candidate who may have gained an advantage keeps it and every other candidate is scored against him. D: Acts on assumptions without checking the right thing: it makes the report depend on the candidate's own admission, which is the one account least able to settle it, and it happens after the exam has been collected. The most effective response is to note what you saw and report it to the exam supervisor as the rules require: the rule asks you to report what you suspect, not to prove it, and she is next door and is the person who decides what it means. Reporting protects the other candidates and, if there is an innocent explanation, gives him a proper hearing rather than a rumour. It beats walking over and standing near his desk so he puts the phone away, because that stops the behaviour without addressing the ten minutes already passed, and leaves the result unsafe. It beats asking him afterwards whether he was using his phone and reporting only if he admits it, because making the report conditional on his own admission puts the decision in the hands of the person with most to lose. The least effective response is saying nothing at all because he is a colleague who could lose a promotion: it suppresses a suspected breach for exactly the interest the rule exists to remove. That is worse than the other two, which handle it badly but do not choose silence. The principle: report what the rule asks you to report, and let the person who owns the process establish what actually happened.

question_text: You work behind the counter of a bakery. A customer ordered a birthday cake for collection at noon today with ‘Happy Birthday Amelie’ piped on it. It is 11am and you notice the cake in the fridge reads ‘Happy Birthday Amelia’. The decorator is in until 1pm and could re-pipe the inscription in twenty minutes. The customer’s phone number is on the order. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Hand the cake over at noon as it is, since the difference is one letter, the customer may not notice and it is too late to change it now.
Ring the customer, explain the spelling error, and ask whether she would like it corrected or would rather collect the cake as it is.
Have the decorator re-pipe the inscription and say nothing about the error, since the cake will be correct by the time the customer collects it at noon.
Ask the decorator to re-pipe the inscription now, and ring the customer to let her know it is being corrected and will be ready at noon as arranged.
explanation: A: Ignores the customer's actual need: a misspelled name on a child's birthday cake is the whole point of the order, and it is not too late, since the decorator is in and there is an hour. Relying on her not noticing is concealment of a known defect. B: Delays the decision: it hands her a choice she does not need to make. The name is simply wrong, the decorator is in, and twenty minutes is available before noon. C: Hides the problem: the outcome is right and the customer is never told that a cake with her daughter's name misspelled nearly went out, so she cannot check the spelling on the order for next time. The most effective response is to ask the decorator to re-pipe the inscription now and ring the customer to say it is being corrected and will be ready at noon: the name is wrong, there is an hour and a decorator on site, so it can be put right and still be ready. Telling her means she is not surprised and can confirm the spelling. It beats ringing to ask whether she would like it corrected or would rather collect it as it is, because that puts a decision to her that does not need making, when the fix is already possible. It beats having it re-piped and saying nothing about the error, because that gets the cake right but leaves her unaware of a mistake that came from the order itself. The least effective response is handing it over as it is on the grounds that the difference is one letter she may not notice: it claims the change is too late when an hour and a decorator are available, and relies on a misspelled name on a child’s birthday cake going unremarked. That is worse than the other two, which both produce a correct cake. The principle: when there is time to put a mistake right, put it right and tell the customer you have.

question_text: You are a gate agent. A passenger tells you that the agent who checked him in promised him one of the extra legroom seats at no charge because of the earlier delay. Those seats carry a fee, none of them is free on this flight, and there is no note of any such promise on his booking. He is not angry, but he is expecting it. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Explain that the agent at check-in was mistaken, since those seats are always chargeable, and confirm that the seat he already has is the one he will be travelling in.
Apologise for the mixed message, tell him plainly that those seats cannot be given free today, and look at whether any seat with more room around it is open to him.
Tell him you will sort something out for him at the aircraft door, then board the flight in the usual order without raising it with anybody else.
Charge him the standard fee for the extra legroom seat he was expecting and log a complaint on his booking so the airline can consider a refund later on.
explanation: A: Corrects the record without answering the passenger: it may be accurate and it leaves a man who was told one thing by the airline and another thing an hour later with nothing at all. C: Buys quiet with a promise you will not keep: he boards expecting something, finds nothing has been arranged, and the crew meet a passenger who has now been let down twice. D: Turns a service failure into a transaction: he pays today for something he was told was free, on the chance that a complaint is upheld weeks from now. The most effective response is to apologise for the mixed message, tell him plainly that those seats cannot be given free today, and look at whether any seat with more room is open to him: the promise cannot be honoured and saying so is the only honest position, but apologising and looking for what is available treats him as somebody the airline let down rather than somebody trying it on. It beats explaining that the check-in agent was mistaken because those seats are always chargeable, because being right about the fee does nothing for a passenger told otherwise by the same airline an hour ago. It beats charging him the standard fee and logging a complaint for a possible refund, because that makes him pay for the airline’s confusion. The least effective response is telling him you will sort something out at the aircraft door and then boarding as usual: he goes down the airbridge expecting something nobody has arranged, so the crew inherit a passenger who has been let down twice. That is worse than the other two, which are both truthful about where he stands. The principle: never repeat a promise you cannot keep, and spend the effort on what you can actually offer.

question_text: You are a contact centre advisor. A caller says he is the brother of a passenger travelling today and asks you to confirm which flight she is on, explaining that the family cannot reach her and are worried. He is calm and plausible, and gives her full name correctly. You are not permitted to confirm a passenger’s booking to anybody but the passenger. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Explain that you cannot confirm anyone else's travel, whatever the circumstances, and tell him how his sister can reach the airline herself if she needs help while she is travelling.
Confirm only that she is travelling today, without saying which flight she is on, so that the family have some reassurance without the booking itself being disclosed.
Tell him which flight she is booked on, since he clearly knows her well, sounds genuinely worried and has given her name correctly at the start of the call.
Put him through the security questions you would ask the passenger, and confirm the flight if he can answer enough of them correctly about her booking.
explanation: B: Discloses part of what is protected: whether a named person is travelling today is exactly the kind of fact the rule exists to keep private, and a partial answer is still an answer. C: Gives a stranger a passenger's movements: a full name is easy to come by and a plausible voice proves nothing, so you have released where a woman will be tonight to somebody unverified. D: Applies a check designed for someone else: those questions establish that the caller is the passenger, and passing them proves only that he knows things about her, not that she wants him told. The most effective response is to explain that you cannot confirm anyone else’s travel, and tell him how his sister can reach the airline herself: the rule protects the passenger rather than the airline, it does not bend for a sympathetic story, and pointing her to a route gives the family something useful without disclosing anything. It beats confirming only that she is travelling today without naming the flight, because that is itself the protected fact, and half an answer still locates her. It beats putting him through the security questions you would ask the passenger, because those are built to identify her, so a brother passing them shows only that he knows her details. The least effective response is telling him which flight she is booked on because he sounds genuinely worried: it hands a stranger a named woman’s movements on the strength of a calm voice. That is worse than the partial confirmation, which leaks less, and worse than the security questions, which at least attempt a check. The principle: a confidentiality rule is for the person it protects, so it holds even when the story is convincing and the caller is sympathetic.

question_text: You are a check-in agent. An hour ago a passenger asked you to let him know if a window seat came free, and gave you his mobile number before going through to the departure lounge. One has just opened up. Boarding starts in forty minutes and he is somewhere on the far side of security. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Leave it, since he will be boarding shortly anyway and a seat change this close to departure is more trouble than the window seat is probably worth to him.
Put him into the window seat and tell him about it when he arrives at the gate, so that the change is already made by the time he gets there.
Send him a message now saying a window seat has come free, and offer to move him to it if he still wants it before the gate opens.
Leave a note on his booking so that the gate agent can offer him the window seat when he presents his boarding pass at the gate.
explanation: A: Quietly drops a promise: he asked, gave you a number and is waiting to hear, and the decision that it is not worth it has been taken on his behalf without him knowing. B: Acts without asking: an hour has passed, he may have swapped with a travelling companion or stopped wanting it, and the first he hears is that his seat has been changed. D: Relies on the note being seen at the busiest moment: the gate agent is boarding a flight, and by then the seat may have gone to somebody else anyway. The most effective response is to send him a message now saying a window seat has come free and offer to move him if he still wants it: he asked to be told, he gave you the means to tell him, and a message costs nothing while leaving the choice with him. It beats putting him into the window seat and telling him when he arrives at the gate, because an hour has passed and moving him without asking assumes his plans have not changed. It beats leaving a note on his booking for the gate agent to offer it, because a note read during boarding is read too late, if it is read at all. The least effective response is leaving it because a change this close to departure is more trouble than it is worth: it drops a promise he is waiting on, and decides for him that he would not want it. That is worse than the other two, which both act on the request even if clumsily. The principle: when somebody has asked to be told and given you a way to do it, tell them, and leave the decision where it belongs.

question_text: You are a crewing assistant. Two cabin crew are arguing in front of you about a roster swap you processed last week: one says the other agreed to take her Saturday duty, the other denies ever agreeing to it. Both are due to report in an hour, both are angry, and each is asking you to confirm their version in front of the other. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Take them away from the crew room, show them the swap request and the approval you actually hold on the system, and work out from there who is covering Saturday.
Reverse the swap on the system there and then, so that the roster goes back to how it was and the pair have nothing left to argue about before they report.
Tell them plainly that this is between the two of them, and leave the crew room so that they can settle the argument themselves before they report for their duty.
Ask the duty manager to come down and rule on which of the two is telling the truth about the conversation they had when the swap was first agreed.
explanation: B: Removes the friction rather than the disagreement: it changes somebody's Saturday without asking either of them, and the two crew still believe different things about what was agreed. C: Walks away from a dispute you can settle: you hold the record that answers it, and withholding it leaves two crew going on duty together believing the other has lied. D: Escalates prematurely: the system record settles what was requested and approved without anyone judging who is honest, and calling a manager in makes the fall-out larger than the dispute. The most effective response is to take them away from the crew room, show them the swap request and the approval you hold on the system, and work out from there who is covering Saturday: the record is evidence neither of them has seen, it answers the question without either being called a liar, and moving away keeps the audience out of it. It beats reversing the swap on the system there and then, because that silences the argument by changing somebody’s weekend without asking, leaving both still convinced of their own version. It beats asking the duty manager to come down and rule on which of them is telling the truth, because the facts are already in your hands and involving a manager turns a settleable disagreement into a formal one. The least effective response is telling them it is between the two of them and leaving the crew room: you hold the only thing that could resolve it and you walk away, so two people about to work together stay convinced the other lied. That is worse than the other two, which both act on the problem even if they act clumsily. The principle: settle a dispute with the record where one exists, away from an audience, before anyone has to take a side.

question_text: You are the only agent at the gate. Boarding must start now or the flight will miss its departure time and a hundred and eighty passengers will be delayed by an hour. At the same moment a passenger reaches the desk with a booking error that has to be corrected in the next two minutes or he cannot travel at all. The next gate is staffed. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Correct the booking first, since two minutes is all it needs and the passenger loses his journey entirely if it is not done, then open boarding as soon as it is sorted.
Open boarding and call the next gate for a spare pair of hands, then work on the booking error between scans while the queue keeps moving down the airbridge.
Open boarding and send the passenger to the transfer desk in the terminal, since the flight has to go and his booking cannot be fixed while you are scanning boarding passes.
Open boarding and deal with the passenger once the queue has gone through, without telling him that the correction has to be made in the next two minutes to be any use.
explanation: A: Spends the departure on one passenger: two minutes at the desk is the window boarding needed, so a hundred and eighty people lose an hour to save one man his flight. C: Sends him away from the only person who can help in time: the transfer desk is minutes away and he has two, so the flight leaves without him when it need not have. D: Lets him wait without the one fact he needs: he stands at the desk believing he is being helped, when the window in which anything could be done has already closed. The most effective response is to open boarding and call the next gate for a spare pair of hands, then work on the booking error between scans: boarding cannot wait, the booking cannot wait either, and the only way to have both is another person, which the next gate can supply in far less than two minutes. It beats correcting the booking first and opening boarding once it is sorted, because holding boarding for one correction costs a hundred and eighty people an hour. It beats sending the passenger to the transfer desk in the terminal, because that desk is further away than the time he has, so sending him is the same as refusing him. The least effective response is dealing with him once the queue has gone through, without telling him the correction has to be made in two minutes: he stands there believing he is being helped while the window quietly closes. That is worse than the other two, which both give him an honest answer about where he stands. The principle: when two things must happen at once, find the extra hands, and never let somebody wait on a chance that has already gone.

question_text: You are a contact centre advisor. A caller says she chose her seats when booking because the website showed seat selection as free, and she has now been charged. Free seat selection was a promotion that ended, and you cannot tell from her file whether it was running on the day she booked. She is polite and quite certain. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Explain the current position, that seat selection carries a charge, and take her through what she has been billed for so that the charge on her card makes sense to her.
Check what the offer was on the date she booked, honour it if the promotion was running then, and if it was not, explain the position and what her options are now.
Refund the seat charge without looking into it, since she is certain about what she saw and the sum involved is small next to the time it would take to establish.
Tell her the promotion never applied to the fare she booked, so the charge is correct and there is nothing on the booking that needs looking at.
explanation: A: Applies today's rule to a booking made earlier: the question is what was on offer on the day she booked, and explaining the present terms does not answer it. C: Settles it by giving in: it costs the airline something it may not owe, and the next caller with the same story reaches a colleague who does not refund it. D: States as fact something you have not checked: you cannot see what was running on the day, and telling her flatly that it never applied closes the question with an assertion. The most effective response is to check what the offer was on the date she booked, honour it if the promotion was running, and explain her options if it was not: what was on offer that day is a question with an answer, finding it is quick, and it settles the matter either way without anybody being taken on trust. It beats explaining the current position and taking her through what she has been billed for, because the current terms are not what she is asking about. It beats refunding the seat charge without looking into it, because that spends money the airline may not owe and leaves the next caller to be told something different. The least effective response is telling her the promotion never applied to the fare she booked: you have no way of knowing that, so a checkable question is closed with an assertion. That is worse than explaining the current terms, which is unhelpful but accurate, and worse than the refund, which is generous rather than wrong. The principle: when the disagreement turns on a fact you can look up, look it up rather than asserting or conceding.

question_text: You are a check-in agent. A passenger tells you that a colleague of yours was rude and dismissive to her at the desk earlier and that she wants something done about it. You know the colleague well and find the account hard to believe. The passenger is calm, specific about what was said, and has a flight to catch in an hour. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Reassure her that there has probably been a misunderstanding, since you know the colleague and it does not sound like him, and leave it there so she can get to her flight.
Find the colleague and ask him what happened before doing anything else, so that you have both accounts before the matter goes any further.
Take down what she says happened and her contact details, tell her it will be passed to the duty manager today, and pass it on before the end of your shift.
Give her the address for written complaints and explain that a complaint about a member of staff has to come in through that channel to be dealt with properly.
explanation: A: Decides the complaint on personal loyalty: a specific account is dismissed by somebody who was not there, and the passenger leaves knowing nothing will be looked at. B: Investigates it yourself first: it is not your complaint to weigh, and warning him in advance compromises the account somebody impartial will later need. D: Sends her to the process rather than into it: she is here now with a specific account, and requiring her to write it again is the easiest way to make sure it is never made. The most effective response is to take down what she says happened and her contact details, tell her it goes to the duty manager today, and pass it on before the end of your shift: an allegation about a colleague’s conduct is not yours to judge, taking the account while she is in front of you preserves it, and the duty manager deals with it. It beats finding the colleague and asking him what happened first, because that puts you in the middle of something you should not be weighing and warns him before anyone impartial has heard her. It beats giving her the address for written complaints, because she is here now, and making her write it later loses most complaints. The least effective response is reassuring her there has probably been a misunderstanding because you know the colleague: it decides against a specific account on the strength of liking the person it is about, so nothing is recorded and nothing is looked at. That is worse than the other two, which both leave the complaint alive. The principle: a complaint about conduct is captured accurately and passed to whoever owns it, not tested by a colleague of the person complained about.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You are a cabin crew member finishing the drinks service before landing. A colleague in the rear galley is struggling to finish the bar count on her own and it has to be done before the aircraft is on the ground. You have one row left to serve and then nothing until the cabin check. She has not asked anybody for help. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Serve the last row, then go back to the galley and count with her, so that the bar is finished before the aircraft begins its descent.
Suggest she completes the count from the loading paperwork rather than the trolley, so that it is finished before landing even though it is not what is actually on board.
Finish your row and carry on with the rest of your own duties, since she has not asked for any help and the bar count is her responsibility on this flight.
Let the senior crew member know that the bar count is running behind so that she can decide whether somebody should be sent back to help in the galley.
explanation: B: Trades the accuracy for the deadline: the count is what tells the airline what was sold, and one taken from the loading sheet records what should be there rather than what is. C: Withholds help that costs nothing: you are free, she is not, and waiting to be asked is what turns a two-minute job into a count that does not get finished. D: Escalates a two-minute job: you are the person standing free with the time to do it, and routing the question through the senior spends more of the descent than the counting would. The most effective response is to serve the last row, then go back to the galley and count with her: the count has to be finished before landing, you are a row away from having nothing to do, and two people finish it comfortably. It beats suggesting she completes the count from the loading paperwork, because that meets the deadline by recording what should be on board rather than what is. It beats letting the senior crew member decide whether somebody should be sent back to help, because that spends time when the somebody is obviously you. The least effective response is finishing your row and carrying on with your own duties because she has not asked: it leaves a colleague to miss a deadline you were free to help her meet. That is worse than the other two, which both try to get the count done, even if by the wrong route. The principle: when you are free and a colleague is not, offer rather than wait to be asked.

question_text: A Thornleigh Air aircraft is scheduled to fly three sectors to Jervaulx on Tuesday, each lasting 2 h 45 min. What is the total flying time in hours?
options: 7.35 hours
8.25 hours
9.00 hours
12.25 hours
explanation: Turn the sector length into decimal hours first, then multiply. 45 minutes is 45 divided by 60 = 0.75 hours, so each sector is 2.75 hours. 3 x 2.75 = 8.25 hours. A common error here is writing 2 h 45 min as 2.45 hours, which gives 7.35 hours. Minutes run to 60, not to 100, so 45 minutes is three quarters of an hour.

question_text: The table shows Thornleigh Air’s turnarounds last month. Taking every turnaround at Ilkeston as a single group, what was the mean ground time per turnaround?
options: 45.0 minutes
49.0 minutes
53.4 minutes
58.8 minutes
explanation: Keep only the routes that start at Ilkeston, pool both columns, then divide once. Turnarounds: 20 + 150 + 30 = 200. Ground time: 900 + 9,750 + 1,110 = 11,760 minutes. 11,760 divided by 200 = 58.8 minutes. A common error here is averaging the three routes’ own figures, which gives 49.0 minutes. The Longmoor route carries three quarters of the turnarounds and the slowest ground time, so an unweighted average sits well below the true figure.

question_text: You are a purchase ledger clerk. Two hundred invoices must be coded before the ledger closes at 6pm and you are ninety behind at 5pm. The coding sheet requires each invoice to be marked as checked against its purchase order. Nobody reviews the sheet. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell your manager at 5pm that ninety will not be coded properly by 6pm, and ask whether to hold the close or code them without the purchase order check.
Code as many as you properly can by 6pm and leave the rest for tomorrow, without telling anybody that the ledger has closed with invoices outstanding.
Stay until eight to code all ninety properly, and say nothing about how close the deadline came to being missed this month.
Code the ninety quickly and mark them all as checked against their purchase orders, since the coding itself is right and nobody ever reviews the sheet afterwards.
explanation: B: Lets a close happen incomplete in silence: whoever relies on the closed ledger has no idea part of it is missing. C: Absorbs the shortfall: the ledger closes right and nobody learns that two hundred invoices does not fit in the day. D: Marks ninety invoices as checked when they were not: the sheet is the only evidence the check happened, and everybody downstream reads it as meaning exactly that. The most effective response is to tell your manager at 5pm that ninety will not be coded properly by 6pm, and ask whether to hold the close or code them without the purchase order check: an hour before the close she can still choose, and only she can make that trade. It beats coding as many as you properly can and leaving the rest without telling anybody the ledger closed with invoices outstanding, because an incomplete close nobody knows about is the worst version of it. It beats staying until eight to code all ninety properly and saying nothing, because three hours of your own time hides a capacity problem. The least effective response is coding the ninety quickly and marking them all as checked against their purchase orders: ninety invoices are recorded as checked against documents nobody opened. That is falsifying the record rather than under-delivering or absorbing it. The principle: the sheet says what you did, and a deadline is not a reason to change that.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân biệt rõ giữa 'Đúng' (True) và 'Có thể xảy ra' (Possible). Chỉ chọn kết luận chắc chắn 100%.

question_text: You are a cargo assistant. A colleague who is late for a meeting asks you to sign the document check on a consignment, saying he looked through the paperwork earlier and it was all in order. Your signature means you personally checked it. He has always been reliable, the consignment is waiting to move, and checking it yourself would take about ten minutes. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell him you will take the ten minutes to go through the paperwork yourself, and sign the check afterwards once you have seen the documents with your own eyes.
Decline to sign and suggest he finds somebody else on the shift to put their name to the check before he leaves for his meeting.
Sign the check on the strength of what he has told you, since he has never been wrong about paperwork before and the consignment is holding up the bay.
Ask him to confirm by email that he went through the documents himself, then sign the check citing his confirmation as the basis for it.
explanation: B: Passes the problem along: the same signature is still being sought without anyone reading the documents, and the next colleague meets the request with less reason to doubt it. C: Signs for work that was not done: the record now says the documents were checked by you, and anyone relying on it later has no way of knowing that nobody read them. D: Substitutes a colleague's word for the check itself: an email makes the shortcut traceable rather than undoing it, and the signature still asserts something you did not do. The most effective response is to tell him you will take the ten minutes to go through the paperwork yourself, and sign afterwards once you have seen the documents: your signature is a statement that you checked, ten minutes is a small price for making that statement true, and it costs the consignment very little. It beats asking him to confirm by email that he went through the documents and signing on that basis, because an email records who to blame rather than getting the documents read, and the signature still says something untrue. It beats declining and suggesting he finds somebody else to put their name to it, because that leaves the same unchecked paperwork looking for a signature, from someone with less reason to question it. The least effective response is signing on the strength of what he has told you: it puts your name to a check nobody performed, so the record is false and everything downstream is decided on it. That is worse than declining, which refuses, and worse than the email, which at least leaves a trail. The principle: sign only for what you did, and where that is inconvenient, do the work rather than redefining the signature.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You are a ticket desk agent. A passenger has just sworn at you across the desk about a fare rule and walked off before you could answer. You are shaken. The next passenger in the queue has stepped up and is waiting, and there are six people behind her. Nobody else saw exactly what was said. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Take a few seconds to collect yourself, serve the next passenger as you normally would, and report what was said to your team leader at the end of the queue.
Close the desk for ten minutes and step away, since being sworn at is not something anybody should be expected to carry straight into the next conversation.
Tell the next passenger what has just happened and how you were spoken to, then work through the queue without mentioning the incident to anybody else at all.
Carry on serving the queue and leave it there, since the passenger has gone, nothing came of it and reporting it would take longer than the incident lasted.
explanation: B: Takes ten minutes where seconds would do: a queue of seven waits and the row is a desk down, for an incident that was over as quickly as it started. C: Hands the incident to a customer and still leaves no record: she is asked to absorb the last passenger's behaviour, which is not hers to carry, and the abuse reaches nobody who could act on it. D: Leaves the abuse unrecorded: it is the record that lets anybody see whether this is happening often, at which desks, and to whom, and without it every instance is the first. The most effective response is to take a few seconds to collect yourself, serve the next passenger as you normally would, and report what was said to your team leader at the end of the queue: a few seconds is what you actually need, the queue is served by somebody composed, and reporting afterwards is what makes it visible rather than absorbed. It beats carrying on and leaving it there because the passenger has gone, since an unreported incident cannot show a pattern, and every one after it looks like the first. It beats closing the desk for ten minutes and stepping away, because that is a large response to something that was over in a moment. The least effective response is telling the next passenger what has just happened and how you were spoken to: it asks her to carry the last customer’s behaviour, which is not hers to carry. That is worse than the other two, which each carry one of those failings rather than both at once. The principle: take the seconds you need, serve the next person as though it had not happened, and report it so it is on the record.

question_text: You are the only agent at the gate. Boarding must start now or the flight will miss its departure time and a hundred and eighty passengers will be delayed by an hour. At the same moment a passenger reaches the desk with a booking error that has to be corrected in the next two minutes or he cannot travel at all. The next gate is staffed. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Correct the booking first, since two minutes is all it needs and the passenger loses his journey entirely if it is not done, then open boarding as soon as it is sorted.
Open boarding and call the next gate for a spare pair of hands, then work on the booking error between scans while the queue keeps moving down the airbridge.
Open boarding and send the passenger to the transfer desk in the terminal, since the flight has to go and his booking cannot be fixed while you are scanning boarding passes.
Open boarding and deal with the passenger once the queue has gone through, without telling him that the correction has to be made in the next two minutes to be any use.
explanation: A: Spends the departure on one passenger: two minutes at the desk is the window boarding needed, so a hundred and eighty people lose an hour to save one man his flight. C: Sends him away from the only person who can help in time: the transfer desk is minutes away and he has two, so the flight leaves without him when it need not have. D: Lets him wait without the one fact he needs: he stands at the desk believing he is being helped, when the window in which anything could be done has already closed. The most effective response is to open boarding and call the next gate for a spare pair of hands, then work on the booking error between scans: boarding cannot wait, the booking cannot wait either, and the only way to have both is another person, which the next gate can supply in far less than two minutes. It beats correcting the booking first and opening boarding once it is sorted, because holding boarding for one correction costs a hundred and eighty people an hour. It beats sending the passenger to the transfer desk in the terminal, because that desk is further away than the time he has, so sending him is the same as refusing him. The least effective response is dealing with him once the queue has gone through, without telling him the correction has to be made in two minutes: he stands there believing he is being helped while the window quietly closes. That is worse than the other two, which both give him an honest answer about where he stands. The principle: when two things must happen at once, find the extra hands, and never let somebody wait on a chance that has already gone.

question_text: You are a turnaround coordinator. A loader from the handling company says sharply, in front of your whole team, that your paperwork is always late and that his crew are sick of standing around waiting for it. Today’s paperwork went across on time and you can show that. The two teams have to work the next four turnarounds together. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Catch him away from the group, ask which mornings he has in mind, and agree between you how and when the paperwork should reach his crew from now on.
Answer him there and then with the times the paperwork went across this morning, so that the accusation is not left standing in front of your own team.
Let it go without replying, and tell your own team afterwards that he is difficult to deal with and that they should come to you rather than speak to him directly.
Report the way he spoke to you to his own supervisor, so that the handling company can deal with how their loaders address people from other teams on the ramp.
explanation: B: Wins the exchange in public: today's timings may be unanswerable, but the two teams have four more turnarounds together and he now has to back down in front of his crew. C: Talks about him instead of to him: the complaint is never tested, and the two teams are pushed further apart by a version of him that he never gets to answer. D: Escalates before speaking to him: it turns a bad-tempered remark into a complaint between two companies, and the question of whether the paperwork really has been late is never answered. The most effective response is to catch him away from the group, ask which mornings he has in mind, and agree how and when the paperwork should reach his crew: there may well be something real behind the complaint, asking is how you find out, and away from the audience he can say so without either of you losing face. It beats answering there and then with the times the paperwork went across this morning, because being right in front of both crews costs you the working relationship you need for the next four turnarounds. It beats reporting the way he spoke to you to his own supervisor, because that makes a formal matter of it while leaving the underlying question untouched. The least effective response is letting it go and telling your own team afterwards that he is difficult to deal with: it leaves the accusation unexamined and then briefs your team against him, so the two sides work four more turnarounds further apart than they started. That is worse than the other two, which both engage with the substance, however clumsily. The principle: take the disagreement to the person, in private, and find out whether the complaint is true before deciding how to answer it.

question_text: You are a turnaround coordinator. The cleaning team have told you they will finish about fifteen minutes later than planned, which means boarding cannot start on time. The gate agent is due to open the gate in five minutes and does not know. The cabin crew are already on board, and a colleague from another stand has just asked you out of interest how the turnaround is going. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Say nothing for now and let the gate open on time, since the passengers will be walking down the airbridge while the cleaners are finishing and the two may well overlap.
Wait until the cleaning supervisor gives you an exact finishing time, so that when you do tell the gate agent she can be given a firm minute to work to.
Tell the gate agent now that boarding will be about fifteen minutes late, so that she can hold the gate and make an announcement before anybody queues.
Tell the cabin crew first, since they are already on board and will want to know that the cleaners are running behind and boarding will be later than planned.
explanation: A: Lets a queue build on a known problem: passengers end up standing in the airbridge because the one person who could have held the gate was not told by the one person who knew. B: Delays the decision: she opens the gate in five minutes, and an exact time that arrives after she has started boarding is worth less than a rough one that arrives before. D: Tells the people who are not about to act: the crew can do nothing with fifteen minutes' notice, while the gate agent is five minutes from opening a gate she should be holding. The most effective response is to tell the gate agent now that boarding will be about fifteen minutes late, so she can hold the gate and announce it before anybody queues: she is the only person in the scenario about to do something the delay changes, and she has five minutes in which knowing is still useful. It beats waiting until the cleaning supervisor gives you an exact finishing time, because an approximate figure now is worth more than an exact one after boarding has started. It beats telling the cabin crew first because they are already on board, since they cannot act on the news, so that spends the window on the wrong audience. The least effective response is saying nothing and letting the gate open on time: it lets a queue form in the airbridge over a problem you already knew about, and the people who could have prevented it were not told. That is worse than the other two, which pass the information on imperfectly rather than withholding it. The principle: tell the person who is about to act first, and tell them in time to act differently.

question_text: You are a check-in agent four hours into a day of heavy disruption. Passengers have been angry with you since the morning, none of it your doing, and you have two hours of your shift left. You can hear yourself becoming short with people at the desk, and the last passenger noticed it. There are three other agents working the row. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell your team leader that you need ten minutes away from the desk, take the break, and come back to the queue for the last part of your shift.
Keep working the queue without a break, since the row is short-handed and stopping now would push more disrupted passengers onto the colleagues either side of you.
Stay at the desk and let the sharpness show, on the basis that passengers who have spent the day shouting at staff can hardly complain about a short answer.
Ask to be moved off the desk to back-office work for the rest of the shift, so that you are not dealing with disrupted passengers face to face again today.
explanation: B: Absorbs the strain until it shows: the queue keeps moving, but it is moving through somebody who has already started snapping, and the last two hours are the worst of the day. C: Passes the day's treatment on to the next passenger: the person in front of you has done nothing, and a member of staff deciding they have earned the right to be curt is the one version of this the airline cannot defend. D: Solves two hours by removing yourself for all of them: the row loses an agent at its busiest, when what the situation actually calls for is a short break. The most effective response is to tell your team leader you need ten minutes away from the desk, take the break, and come back for the last part of your shift: ten minutes is the smallest thing that fixes it, the row can absorb that far more easily than two hours, and saying so plainly is what makes it possible. It beats working the queue without a break because the row is short-handed, since that means the queue is served by somebody who has already started to snap, for the two hardest hours. It beats asking to be moved to back-office work for the rest of the shift, because that takes an agent out of a short-handed row when a break would have done. The least effective response is staying at the desk and letting the sharpness show: it decides that passengers have earned short treatment, so the day gets passed on to people who had no part in it. That is worse than the other two, which are poor answers to the pressure rather than an answer aimed at the customer. The principle: name what you need, take the smallest break that restores you, and never let the day come out on the next person in the queue.

question_text: You are a cargo assistant. A regular customer whose shipment is booked on tomorrow’s flight quietly offers you twenty pounds to move it onto this afternoon’s, which has space. Shipments are flown in the order they were booked, and three other customers are waiting on that space. The customer is friendly and treats the offer as a thank you. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Take the note, move his shipment onto the afternoon flight, and treat the money as a customer thanking you for good service rather than as a payment for jumping the order.
Refuse the money politely, explain that shipments fly in booking order, and leave it there without mentioning the offer to your supervisor afterwards.
Decline the money, explain that the booking order decides which shipment flies, and tell your supervisor afterwards that the offer was made so it is on record.
Turn down the money but tell him you will see what you can do about the afternoon flight, then leave the booking as it is when the space is allocated later on.
explanation: A: Sells a place in the queue: three customers who booked earlier lose space they were entitled to, and the reason they lost it is one that cannot be written on any record. B: Handles it privately: the right answer is given to this customer, but nobody else learns that cash is being offered at the counter, so the next colleague meets it unprepared. D: Over-promises to avoid the awkwardness: it lets the customer leave believing he may have bought something, and the refusal he was owed is never actually given. The most effective response is to decline the money, explain that the booking order decides which shipment flies, and tell your supervisor afterwards that the offer was made: the offer is refused, the reason is a rule the customer can hear without embarrassment, and the record means the airline knows cash was offered at its counter. It beats refusing politely and leaving it there without mentioning it, because a refusal that stops with you leaves the next colleague to meet the same offer cold, with no record that it is happening. It beats turning down the money but saying you will see what you can do about the afternoon flight, because that vague assurance leaves him thinking the money may still work, which is a refusal in name only. The least effective response is taking the note and moving his shipment onto the afternoon flight: it accepts the payment and reorders the queue for it, so three earlier bookings lose out for a reason that appears nowhere. That is dishonesty rather than an awkward conversation handled badly, which is what separates it from the other two. The principle: decline plainly, and tell somebody, because the second half is what protects everyone else.

question_text: You are a cabin crew member. At the end of the last sector a colleague hands you one of the unsold sandwiches, saying the whole tray is about to be thrown away and that everybody takes one. The airline’s rule is that unsold stock is disposed of and not taken by crew. Nobody else is in the galley and the tray really is going in the bin. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Say no thank you and put it back on the tray, and leave the question of what other people do out of it, since it is not your business what the rest of the crew take.
Take the sandwich, since the tray is going in the bin either way and a rule about disposing of food nobody is going to eat is not one that really matters.
Accept it and note it in the galley record as stock taken by crew, so that at least what happened is written down and the count still adds up.
Decline the sandwich, and ask the senior crew member whether the disposal rule could be looked at, since the tray is wasted on every sector and the crew clearly think it is silly.
explanation: A: Declines quietly and stops there: the rule and the practice remain a long way apart, and nobody who could close that gap ever learns it exists. B: Decides which rules count: the reasoning would excuse taking anything due for disposal, and the fact that everybody does it is what keeps anybody from looking at it. C: Records a breach as though recording made it allowed: the rule says disposed of, so the entry is a note of the rule being broken rather than an authorisation. The most effective response is to decline the sandwich and ask the senior crew member whether the disposal rule could be looked at: declining keeps you the right side of a rule that exists whatever the crew think of it, and raising it is the only route by which a rule everybody quietly ignores gets either enforced or changed. It beats saying no thank you and leaving the question of what other people do out of it, because a private refusal leaves the gap between the rule and the practice exactly where it was. It beats accepting it and noting it in the galley record as stock taken by crew, because writing it down does not make it permitted, it just records the breach. The least effective response is taking the sandwich because the tray is going in the bin either way: it decides the rule does not really count, and the reason it feels safe is that everybody does it. That is worse than the other two, which both stay inside the rule or at least declare the departure. The principle: do not quietly break a rule you think is wrong; decline it and ask for it to be changed.

question_text: You are one of four in a baggage hall team. Every shift, one colleague gets to the tracing desk first and spends the day there in the warm, leaving the hall work to the other three. Nobody has said anything to him and the other two grumble about it to each other. There is no rota: the desk has always been whoever sits down at it. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Get to the tracing desk before him at the start of the next few shifts, so that he finds out what the hall is like when somebody else has taken the comfortable job.
Suggest at the next team briefing that the tracing desk should run on a rota, without mentioning him, so that the arrangement changes without anybody being singled out.
Say to him directly that the desk has fallen to him every shift and ask whether the four of you should take it in turns, treating it as a question rather than a complaint.
Ask the team leader to put a rota in place for the tracing desk, since the way the work is shared out is properly a matter for whoever runs the shift.
explanation: A: Answers the problem by copying it: it settles nothing about how the desk is shared, and turns an unspoken irritation into something the whole team can see being done deliberately. B: Raises it around the person: the change may well happen, but he hears it as a rule aimed at somebody unnamed and never learns that the team has been unhappy for months. D: Escalates before asking: four colleagues can agree a rota between them in a minute, and going to the team leader makes a supervised arrangement out of an ordinary conversation. The most effective response is to say to him directly that the desk has fallen to him every shift and ask whether the four of you should take it in turns: nobody has actually told him, the habit may be nothing more than habit, and putting it as a question gives him an easy way to agree. It beats suggesting at the next briefing that the desk should run on a rota without mentioning him, because a rota proposed to the room leaves him unaware the team has been unhappy, so the same thing recurs in the next arrangement nobody has spelt out. It beats asking the team leader to put a rota in place, because four people can settle this between them without a supervisor writing it down. The least effective response is getting to the tracing desk before him at the start of the next few shifts: it takes the desk to make a point, so the team watches a silent contest and the question of how the work is shared is never asked. That is worse than the other two, which both aim at an arrangement everyone can see. The principle: say the unsaid thing to the person, plainly and without accusation, before reaching for a rule or a manager.

question_text: You are a risk assistant. Over three months you have noticed the same team submitting expense claims just under the £250 receipt threshold: nineteen of them, all between £240 and £249. Leave it, since every claim is inside the policy and nineteen individually compliant expense claims are not what your manager meant by a real issue.

Approach the team's manager informally to ask why the claims cluster just under the threshold, before mentioning it to anybody in your own team.

D: Tips off the subject before the record exists: whatever the answer, the pattern is now known to be watched and nothing has been logged. The most effective response is to put the nineteen claims and the pattern on one page for your manager, say that each is within policy, and ask whether she wants it looked at further: one page makes visible what no individual claim shows, it is honest that nothing breaches policy, and the decision goes to the person who owns it. It beats approaching the team’s manager informally to ask about the clustering, because approaching the subject first is the one order that cannot be undone. The least effective response is leaving it because every claim is inside the policy: the pattern dies with the person who spotted it, on a reading of what counts as a real issue that nobody has confirmed. That is avoidance rather than a misjudged route. The principle: escalate the shape, not the instances, and let the decision sit where it belongs.

question_text: You are a risk assistant. Three weeks ago your team leader ruled that a colleague’s risk rating should be overridden by yours. Since then he has declined to attend the weekly session you both run, sending apologies each time. The session is thinner without him and nobody has said anything. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Stop inviting him to the session altogether so that you do not have to deal with him each week, and leave your team leader to notice the change herself.
Carry on sending the invitation and never mention the absences, on the basis that he will come back when he is ready to.
Ask him directly for ten minutes, say the session needs him and that you would rather clear the air about the rating than keep working around it.
Tell your team leader that he has missed three sessions since the ruling, and ask her to require him to attend.
explanation: A: Answers a withdrawal with a withdrawal: the invitation is removed so the awkwardness goes away, and a working relationship the team needs is quietly ended. B: Waits out a pattern three weeks old: nothing about the situation is changing on its own and the session keeps degrading. D: Escalates before speaking to him: he has not been asked, and being ordered back by the person who ruled against him makes it worse. The most effective response is to ask him directly for ten minutes, say the session needs him and that you would rather clear the air about the rating: it is direct, it separates the ruling from the working relationship, and it is the only response that gives him a way back without losing face. It beats carrying on sending the invitation and never mentioning the absences, because three weeks of apologies is a pattern, not a mood. It beats telling your team leader he has missed three sessions and asking her to require attendance, because an instruction from the person who ruled against him hardens it. The least effective response is dropping him from the session so you do not have to deal with him each week: it ends the working relationship to avoid the discomfort and hides the whole thing from the person who could help. That is answering payback with payback rather than under-reacting or over-escalating. The principle: ask him directly, and keep the door you control wide open.

question_text: You are a personal banking assistant. A customer’s son has power of attorney and has moved £30,000 out of her account this month. She has come in confused about her balance. You must not discuss your suspicions, and a review has already been raised. She trusts her son completely. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Go through the transactions with her plainly so she can see what has left and when, and ask whether she is happy with each of them.
Assure her that everything on the account is perfectly in order, so that she is not upset, and leave the review to reach whatever conclusion it reaches in its own time.
Suggest to her directly that her son may well be taking money that he should not be taking, so that she understands what the pattern of payments on the account actually looks like.
Tell her there is a review under way and that you cannot discuss the transactions with her until it has been completed and somebody contacts her.
explanation: B: Tells her the account is in order when a review says otherwise: she leaves reassured, and the one person who could question the payments has been told there is nothing to question. C: States a suspicion as a conclusion: it is not yours to reach, and it may wreck a family relationship over payments she authorised. D: Withholds her own account information: she is entitled to see her transactions, and refusing them makes the visit useless to her. The most effective response is to go through the transactions with her plainly so she can see what has left and when, and ask whether she is happy with each: she is entitled to her own transactions, seeing them is what lets her form her own view, and the question opens the door without accusing anybody. It beats telling her a review is under way and that you cannot discuss the transactions until it finishes, because a review does not remove her right to see her account. It beats suggesting to her that her son may be taking money he should not, because the conclusion is not yours to draw. The least effective response is assuring her everything on the account is perfectly in order: she is told it is fine when it is under review, so the one person who could question the payments is actively reassured. That is a false statement rather than an unhelpfully narrow or overreaching one. The principle: show her the facts and let her ask the question.
