question_text: You are a research assistant. A chart you produced last month has a scale error that makes a decline look like growth. It was used in a pitch to a client three weeks ago, which the firm won. Nobody has questioned it. The same chart is in the pack for a second client next week. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Raise it directly with the colleague who presented the pitch, and leave it to him to decide whether your manager needs to be told about the chart.
Correct the chart quietly in next week's pack, without telling anybody that the version used in the pitch three weeks ago showed a decline as though it were growth.
Correct next week's pack and mention the earlier pitch to your manager at your next scheduled catch-up in a fortnight's time.
Tell your manager today about the error, both where it has already been used and where it is about to be used again, and correct next week's pack now.
explanation: A: Gives the decision to the person with most reason to bury it: he presented the wrong chart to a client he won. B: Withholds where the error has already been: a client made a decision on a chart that pointed the wrong way, and the only person who knows has fixed the future and left the past. C: Delays the half that matters most: the client who has already acted is the exposure, and a fortnight is a long time on that. The most effective response is to tell your manager today about the error, both where it has already been used and where it is about to be used again, and correct next week’s pack now: both exposures go to her together, and the fixable one is fixed the same day. It beats correcting next week’s pack and mentioning the earlier pitch at your catch-up in a fortnight, because that delay on a client who has already acted is the real risk. It beats raising it with the colleague who presented the pitch and leaving him to decide whether your manager hears, because the presenter is the last person who should make that call. The least effective response is correcting the chart quietly in next week’s pack and telling nobody about the pitch: the future is repaired and a client who decided on a reversed chart is left where they are, with only one person knowing. That is silence about the part that matters rather than slowness or misrouting. The principle: fix forwards and disclose backwards, on the same day.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You are a purchase ledger clerk. A supplier will stop a delivery unless a £12,000 invoice is paid today. It needs your manager’s approval and she is in hospital appointments all day. Her deputy is not set up in the system. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Process the £12,000 invoice today without waiting for any approval at all, since the delivery stops otherwise and your manager would certainly have approved it if she had been reachable.
Let the delivery be stopped and process the invoice tomorrow when your manager is back, since the approval genuinely cannot be given today at all.
Ask the deputy to approve it verbally and process it on her say-so, then have your manager confirm the approval in the system when she returns tomorrow.
Telephone your manager between her appointments to ask how she wants it handled, and tell the supplier what is happening and when you will be coming back to them with an answer.
explanation: A: Releases a payment the control says must be approved: £12,000 moves on one person's confidence about what somebody else would have said, which is the exact judgement an approval exists to take out of your hands. B: Accepts the consequence without testing it: nobody has asked your manager whether she can take two minutes between appointments. C: Records an approval that has not been given: the deputy is not set up precisely so that her say-so is not an approval. The most effective response is to telephone your manager between her appointments to ask how she wants it handled, and tell the supplier what is happening and when you will come back: two minutes of her time settles it, hospital appointments have gaps, and the supplier can be managed meanwhile. It beats letting the delivery be stopped and processing it tomorrow when she is back, because nobody has tried to reach her. It beats asking the deputy to approve it verbally and having your manager confirm it in the system tomorrow, because a verbal say-so from somebody without system access is not an approval. The least effective response is processing the £12,000 invoice today with no approval at all: money leaves without the approval the control requires, on one person’s confidence about what somebody else would have said. That is setting the control aside rather than working around its edges. The principle: when the approver cannot be reached, the deadline is what gives way, never the control.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You are an audit associate. Two schedules are due to your manager by Friday and each takes a day. It is Wednesday morning. A colleague uses the first one on Thursday to start his own testing; the second is only read at the Friday review. Nobody has told you which order to do them in. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Do the schedule your colleague needs first so that his Thursday is not lost, then finish the second one on Thursday in good time for the Friday review.
Ask your manager on Thursday morning which of the two she would rather have first, and work on neither of them until she has come back to you.
Start with the schedule for the Friday review and leave the other until Thursday afternoon, without telling your colleague that his testing will not be able to start.
Split Wednesday and Thursday between the two schedules so that both of them are partly done by the time the Friday review comes round.
explanation: B: Spends a day of a two-day budget on a question with an evident answer: one schedule has somebody waiting on it and the other does not. C: Costs a colleague a day without warning him: he plans Thursday around a schedule that will not arrive, and the person who knew that on Wednesday says nothing. D: Splits effort so nothing finishes: two half-schedules on Friday morning are worth less than one complete one, and his Thursday is lost either way. The most effective response is to do the schedule your colleague needs first so his Thursday is not lost, then finish the second on Thursday for the Friday review: only one of the two has a person waiting behind it, both still land by Friday, and nothing is lost. It beats asking your manager on Thursday morning which she would rather have first, because a whole day goes on a question whose answer is on the page. It beats splitting Wednesday and Thursday between the two, because two unfinished schedules help nobody. The least effective response is starting with the Friday review schedule and not telling your colleague his testing cannot start: he loses a day he has planned around, and the one person who could have told him on Wednesday says nothing. That is silence about something he needed rather than a defensible ordering. The principle: when your order costs somebody else a day, they hear about it before the day starts.

question_text: You are an accounts assistant. A supplier payment run has to be approved by 3pm or the supplier will not be paid until Monday, and they have said they will hold a delivery until they are. It is 2:15pm. A colleague asks you to reformat last month’s expenses spreadsheet, which is wanted for a meeting next week. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Start on the expenses spreadsheet and leave the payment run alone until it is done, on the grounds that somebody more senior would have said something if the 3pm deadline really mattered today.
Ask a colleague to take the payment run so that you can make a proper start on the expenses spreadsheet while the request is still fresh in your mind.
Get the payment run approved before 3pm, then tell your colleague you will reformat the expenses spreadsheet afterwards and give them a time when it will be with them.

Work on the expenses spreadsheet and the payment run in turn through the afternoon, giving each of them a few minutes at a time, so that your colleague sees progress and the payment is not left untouched.
explanation: A: Assumes the deadline away: nobody has been asked and nothing has been checked, so a delivery is put at risk on the strength of a silence that means nothing at all. B: Hands off the urgent job: the deadline stays yours, and the harder task goes to somebody who has not been following it, to protect work that is not wanted until next week. D: Splits effort so nothing finishes: the payment run needs a clear run at it before 3pm, and alternating is the one approach that risks missing a deadline nothing else in the day competes with. The most effective response is to get the payment run approved before 3pm, then tell your colleague you will reformat the expenses spreadsheet afterwards and give them a time: 3pm is the only fixed point in the day, the spreadsheet is wanted next week, and a word means they are not left wondering. It beats working on both in turn through the afternoon, because dividing the next forty-five minutes is exactly how the payment run misses 3pm. It beats asking a colleague to take the payment run so you can start the spreadsheet, because moving the urgent work to somebody unfamiliar with it buys time on a task nothing is waiting for. The least effective response is starting on the expenses spreadsheet and leaving the payment run on the assumption that somebody would have said if 3pm mattered: it puts a delivery at risk on a premise nobody was asked to confirm. That is avoidance rather than a defensible ordering of work. The principle: protect the deadline the outside world is holding you to, and tell the person whose work waits.

question_text: Four runners finish a race with no ties. X finished ahead of Y. Z finished last. W did not finish first. Who finished first?
options: Y
W
X
It cannot be determined.
explanation: Z is last, so first place goes to W, X or Y. W did not finish first, leaving X or Y, and since X finished ahead of Y, Y cannot be first, so X finished first. Placing Y first ignores that X is ahead of Y. Placing W first ignores that W did not finish first. Concluding it cannot be determined overlooks that the three clues together fix first place exactly.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: Five colleagues, F, G, H, J and K, sit in a row of five seats numbered 1 to 5 from left to right. G sits in seat 3. F sits immediately to the left of G. K sits in seat 5. J sits somewhere to the left of F. Who sits in seat 1?
options: J
F
H
It cannot be determined.
explanation: G is in seat 3, and F is immediately to its left, so F is in seat 2. J must be left of F, and the only seat left of seat 2 is seat 1, so J is in seat 1, leaving H in seat 4. Placing F in seat 1 ignores that F is pinned to seat 2. Placing H in seat 1 ignores that J must sit to the left of F. Concluding it cannot be determined overlooks that the clues fix every seat.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân biệt rõ giữa 'Đúng' (True) và 'Có thể xảy ra' (Possible). Chỉ chọn kết luận chắc chắn 100%.

question_text: Six trainees, P, Q, R, S, T and U, are split into two project groups of three. P and Q are in the same group. R and S are in different groups. T is not in the same group as P. Which trainee must be in the same group as T?
options: P
Q
It cannot be determined.
U
explanation: P and Q share a group, and T is barred from it, so T is in the other group. R and S are split, so exactly one of them joins P and Q, filling that group of three. That leaves T, the other of R and S, and U together, so U must be with T. Placing T with P is barred directly; placing T with Q is barred too, because Q sits with P, so joining Q would put T with P. Concluding it cannot be determined misses that U is forced, even though which of R or S joins T is not.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: Four warehouses are compared by floor area. The Northgate site is larger than the Riverside site. The Eastfield site is smaller than the Riverside site. The Westbank site is the largest of the four. Which site is the smallest?
options: Riverside
Eastfield
Northgate
It cannot be determined.
explanation: The clues chain into Eastfield smaller than Riverside smaller than Northgate, with Westbank largest above them all, so Eastfield is smallest. Choosing Riverside stops at it being below Northgate but ignores that Eastfield is smaller still. Choosing Northgate reverses the comparison, since Northgate is second largest. Concluding it cannot be determined overlooks that the chain orders all four sites.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân biệt rõ giữa 'Đúng' (True) và 'Có thể xảy ra' (Possible). Chỉ chọn kết luận chắc chắn 100%.

question_text: A shop runs one training session on each of Monday to Thursday, covering one topic per day: Safety, Systems, Service and Stock, in some order. Safety is not on Monday. Systems is scheduled on the day immediately before Service. Stock is on Thursday. On which day is Safety?
options: Wednesday
Monday
Tuesday
Thursday
explanation: Stock takes Thursday, so Safety, Systems and Service fill Monday to Wednesday. Systems immediately before Service means the pair is either Monday and Tuesday or Tuesday and Wednesday; the second leaves Safety on Monday, which is barred, so Systems is Monday, Service Tuesday and Safety Wednesday. Monday breaks the “not Monday” clue; Tuesday is Service’s day; Thursday is Stock’s day.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: Three boxes are labelled A, B and C. Exactly one contains a manual. The manual is not in box A. If the manual is in box C, then box B is empty. Box B is not empty. Which box holds the manual?
options: Box C
Box A
It cannot be determined.
Box B
explanation: If the manual were in C, box B would be empty; but box B is not empty, so by the contrapositive the manual is not in C. It is not in A either, so it must be in B. Choosing box C ignores that a full box B rules C out. Choosing box A breaks the “not in A” clue. Concluding it cannot be determined misses that eliminating A and C leaves B as the only possibility.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân biệt rõ giữa 'Đúng' (True) và 'Có thể xảy ra' (Possible). Chỉ chọn kết luận chắc chắn 100%.

question_text: Five books are stacked in a single pile. The dictionary sits directly on top of the thesaurus. The atlas is somewhere above the dictionary. The novel is at the very bottom. The guide sits directly above the atlas. Which book is on top?
options: The atlas
The guide
The dictionary
The thesaurus
explanation: The novel is at the bottom. The dictionary sits on the thesaurus, and the atlas is above the dictionary with the guide directly above the atlas, giving from the top: guide, atlas, dictionary, thesaurus, novel. So the guide is on top. Choosing the atlas forgets the guide sits above it. Choosing the dictionary starts the pile there, ignoring the atlas and guide above it. Choosing the thesaurus inverts the “directly on top of” relation.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân biệt rõ giữa 'Đúng' (True) và 'Có thể xảy ra' (Possible). Chỉ chọn kết luận chắc chắn 100%.

question_text: Four staff, Ade, Bea, Cai and Dot, each take exactly one of four roles: chair, notes, timing and welcome. Bea takes timing. Ade takes neither notes nor the chair. Dot will not take the chair. Cai takes welcome only if Ade takes the chair. Which role does Cai take?
options: Welcome
Notes
Chair
Timing
explanation: Bea has timing. Ade cannot take notes, the chair or timing, so Ade takes welcome. Cai takes welcome only if Ade takes the chair; Ade does not, and welcome is gone, so Cai cannot take welcome. Chair and notes remain for Cai and Dot, and since Dot will not take the chair, Dot takes notes and Cai takes the chair. Choosing welcome ignores the “only if” condition; choosing notes would force Dot into the chair, which is barred; timing is Bea’s role.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: Every item on a shelf is either a mug or a plate, and is either blue or green. All mugs are blue. An item is chosen and it is green. Which of these must be true of it?

It is blue.

It is a plate.
explanation: Every mug is blue, so a green item cannot be a mug, and as each item is only a mug or a plate, the green item must be a plate. Claiming it is a mug contradicts “all mugs are blue”. question_text: You are a service desk assistant at a border protection agency. Looking something up this morning, you notice that the standard reply the desk sends to anybody asking about the application process gives a closing date that passed three weeks ago. The reply goes out automatically to everyone who writes in. The person who owns that wording sits in another team and is busy this week. Nobody at the desk has mentioned it, nothing you are working on depends on it, and no one has complained. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Leave it as it is and get on with your own work, on the basis that the wording belongs to another team and nobody has complained about it in three weeks.
Raise it at the desk meeting next week so that the team can agree together whether the wrong date is worth taking to the other team at all.
Note exactly what the wrong date says, send it to the person who owns the wording today with corrected words attached, so that they need only approve it this week.
Answer the enquiries yourself with the right date whenever one reaches your desk, so that anybody who writes in this week is told correctly, and leave the standard reply alone.
explanation: A: Assumes the error is somebody else's to notice: an automatic reply keeps sending a dead date to every person who writes in, and the fact that nobody has complained is what makes you the only person who can raise it. B: Downgrades a plain error to an agenda item: a date that has demonstrably passed needs no group view, and the reply goes out every day between now and the meeting. D: Treats the symptom and not the source: the automatic reply still reaches everybody who does not happen to land on your desk, and it goes on doing so after this week. The most effective response is writing down what the wrong date says and sending it to the person who owns the wording today with corrected words attached: the wording is theirs to change, they are busy, and the fastest way to get a change made is to hand them something ready to approve rather than something they have to work out for themselves. It is stronger than raising it at the desk meeting next week, because the reply goes out automatically every day in between and there is nothing for a team to decide about a date that has plainly passed. It is also stronger than answering enquiries yourself with the right date, since the automatic reply keeps reaching everybody who does not come through you. The least effective response is leaving the wording as it is on the basis that it belongs to another team: an error nobody has noticed is still an error, and the people writing in are the ones who pay for it. The principle: something wrong that nobody has claimed is still somebody’s to raise, and the person who noticed it is that somebody.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân biệt rõ giữa 'Đúng' (True) và 'Có thể xảy ra' (Possible). Chỉ chọn kết luận chắc chắn 100%.

question_text: You are an enquiry desk assistant at a border protection agency. Last week you and a colleague argued in front of the desk about which of you should have taken a long queue, and neither of you has mentioned it since. Today the person who builds the desk rota asks you, in confidence, how the two of you work together, because they are deciding who is paired with whom for the next three months and will act on what you say. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Describe the disagreement honestly, say it has not been talked about since, and tell the rota person that you would rather sort it out with the colleague directly before the pairs are set.
Say the two of you work well enough together and leave last week out of it, since the argument was a one off and the rota person only needs to know whether you can share a desk.
Say you would rather not answer, and suggest the rota person asks the colleague the same question, since it seems unfair to describe a disagreement only one of you is being asked about.
Say there is a problem you would rather not describe, and hand it straight to the desk manager to deal with, since sorting out staff disagreements is their job.
explanation: B: Prioritises harmony over honesty: the rota person has said they will act on what you say, so a reassuring answer sets three months of pairings on a picture you know is incomplete. C: Steps back from a question only you were asked: fairness is met by saying what happened rather than by saying nothing, and the rota is set either way, with or without your account. D: Passes the problem on without owning it: a disagreement you have never raised with the colleague becomes something the manager has to take up formally, and the rota person is left with a flag and no account of it. The most effective response is describing the disagreement honestly and telling the rota person you would rather sort it out with the colleague directly. The rota person has said they will act on what you say, the argument happened in front of the desk and has never been talked about, and the only version of this that ends well is one the colleague hears from you first. It beats saying the two of you work well enough together and leaving last week out of it, because three months of pairings would then rest on a picture you know is incomplete. It beats declining to answer and suggesting they ask the colleague the same question, because the rota is set either way and your silence simply removes what you know from it. The least effective response is saying there is a problem you would rather not describe and handing it straight to the desk manager: it turns a disagreement the colleague has never heard raised into somebody else’s case to look into, and gives the rota person a flag without an account, which is a different kind of wrong from being too kind or too quiet. It is worse than the reassuring answer and worse than the refusal because both of those leave the disagreement where it can still be fixed between the two of you, while this one moves it to a manager who now has to act on something nobody has described. The principle: feedback that will be acted on is for describing what happened, not for handing an unraised disagreement to somebody else.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You are a selection centre assistant at a border protection agency. The room booked for Thursday’s selection day is no longer available and the whole day has to start two hours later in a different building. Fourteen candidates have already been given the original time and several are travelling the night before. The rule is that a change to a selection date or time goes to candidates in one standard message, sent by the person who runs the selection centre, so that every candidate is told the same thing. That person is in the office this afternoon. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Hold the news until the new building is confirmed in writing, so that the fourteen candidates are not given a second time that changes again before Thursday.
Take the change to the person who runs the selection centre this afternoon, with the fourteen names and the time given, so the standard message can go out today.
Ring the fourteen candidates yourself this evening from the numbers on their forms and tell each of them the new time in your own words, so that nobody travels early.
Email the person who runs the selection centre about the new building and the new time, and let them pick it up whenever they next work through their inbox.
explanation: A: Delays the decision: several candidates travel the night before, so a confirmation that lands on Thursday morning reaches them after they have already set off on the old time. C: Breaches the stated way changes are sent: fourteen candidates get fourteen versions of one change, none of it written down, and the rule exists so that no candidate can be told less than another. D: Passes responsibility without the urgency: the right person is in the office now, and an email that waits its turn spends the afternoon in which the message could still reach everybody. The most effective response is taking the change to the person who runs the selection centre this afternoon with the fourteen names: they are in the building, the rule puts the message in their hands, and one message today reaches every candidate before anybody sets off. It is stronger than holding the news until the new building is confirmed in writing, because several candidates travel the night before and certainty on Thursday morning is a day too late for them. It is also stronger than emailing the problem and letting it be picked up in turn, since the person who can send the message is in the office and an email leaves the timing to chance. The least effective response is ringing the fourteen candidates yourself in your own words: fourteen separate accounts of one change go out with no record of what each candidate was told, which is exactly what the single standard message prevents. The principle: when one change has to reach several people, use the route that reaches all of them identically.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You are a candidate liaison assistant at a border protection agency. A colleague told an applicant yesterday that their selection day is the 14th. You have just seen the note moving it to the 21st. The stated rule is that date changes go to applicants only from the person who runs the selection centre, and only in writing. The applicant has already booked time off for the 14th and rings tomorrow morning to run through what to bring. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Wait for the weekly update that goes out to all applicants on Friday to carry the new date, since it will reach them in writing from the right person anyway.
Ask the applicant, when they ring, to check the date with the selection centre themselves, without saying that you already know it has moved.
Tell the colleague what you have seen today, and ask the person who runs the selection centre to write to the applicant with the new date before tomorrow's call.
Message the applicant yourself this evening with the new date, even though the stated rule is that only the person who runs the selection centre puts a date change in writing.
explanation: A: Leaves the applicant holding a wrong date: they ring tomorrow and have booked time off for the 14th, so Friday is several days after the point at which the error costs them something. B: Passes the correction to the applicant: you are holding the answer, and making them go and find it treats a mistake made inside the organisation as their errand. D: Breaches a stated rule on date changes: an applicant who has booked time off now holds two dates from two sources, and the person the rule makes responsible does not know either has been sent. The most effective response is telling the colleague what you have seen and asking the person who runs the selection centre to write to the applicant. It gets the correct date to the applicant through the route the rule names, and it gets there before tomorrow’s call, which is the moment the wrong date starts costing them. That is better than waiting for Friday’s weekly update, because the applicant has booked time off for the 14th and rings tomorrow. It is also better than asking them to check with the selection centre themselves, since you already hold the answer and sending them to look for it makes the organisation’s mistake their job. The least effective response is messaging the applicant yourself with the new date: the rule exists so that one person owns what applicants are told, and now two dates are in the open from two sources with nobody responsible for either, which is worse than being slow and worse than being unhelpful. The principle: get the right information to the person who needs it, by the route that keeps one owner for what they are told.
tip: Mẹo MT: Áp dụng sơ đồ Venn hoặc bảng chân trị logic để biểu diễn mối quan hệ giữa các đối tượng.

question_text: You are a trainee at a border protection agency, three weeks into your course. The person who runs the course asks you to tell the rest of the group that Thursday’s session has moved to Monday. You think this is wrong: the timetable you were all given puts the written assessment on Monday, and two weeks look as though they have been mixed up. The group will book travel and swap shifts tonight on what you tell them. The person who runs the course is still in the building. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Pass the message on exactly as you were given it, since it is not your place to question the person who runs the course, and email them afterwards to ask about the assessment date.
Go to the person who runs the course before telling anybody, since the group books travel tonight, show them the timetable and ask which day, then pass that on.
Tell the group the session may have moved but that you are not certain, and suggest they hold off booking travel until somebody confirms which day it is.
Pass the message on and say in front of the group that you think the person who runs the course has muddled two weeks, so that nobody blames you if the date is wrong.
explanation: A: Passes on a message you already doubt: repeating it faithfully does not make it right, and the group books travel tonight on something you believe is a mistake. C: Hands on your own uncertainty: the whole group is left holding a doubt that one question would have settled, and the shifts they need to swap have to be swapped tonight. D: Undermines the person who gave you the message: it makes somebody who is not in the room the problem, and the group is still no clearer about which day to book for. The most effective response is going back to the person who runs the course with the timetable and asking which day they mean before telling anybody: they are still in the building, the group commits money and shifts tonight, and one question settles it either way. It is stronger than passing the message on exactly as given on the grounds that it is not your place to question it, since a message you believe is wrong does not become right by being repeated faithfully. It is also stronger than telling the group the session may have moved and asking them to hold off, because that leaves the whole group managing your doubt when one person could have resolved it. The least effective response is passing the message on while telling the group the person who runs the course has muddled the weeks: it puts the blame somewhere before the facts are known, in front of people who cannot check it, and nobody is any clearer about the date. The principle: take a doubt to the person who can resolve it, not to the people who cannot.
tip: Mẹo MT: Với bài toán quy luật chuỗi số, hãy xét hiệu số bậc 1, hiệu số bậc 2 hoặc tích lũy tiến.

question_text: You are a training school assistant at a border protection agency, and you hold the bookings for a course that runs three times a year. The stated rule is that a place moves to a later run only if the request arrives before the list closes. The list closed on Monday. Two people asked to move afterwards and you told both of them no. A third person now asks, points out that the next run has spaces, and says that the list is still open on your screen and nobody else would ever know. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Move them onto the next run and agree with them to keep it between the two of you, since that run has spaces, the move costs nobody anything and the two earlier refusals need never come into it.
Tell them no for the same reason you gave the other two, explain when the list opens for the following run, and offer to flag their request to the person who runs the course the moment it does.
Move them onto the next run and go back to the two you refused to offer them the same move, so that everybody who asked after Monday is treated the same way in the end.
Ask the person who runs the course whether the rule can be set aside for this run, and tell the person asking that you will come back to them once you have an answer.
explanation: A: Agrees to an exception that depends on nobody knowing: two people were told no under the same rule this week, and an arrangement you could not repeat to either of them is one you cannot defend at all. C: Widens a breach in order to make it even: the rule was applied correctly on Monday, the two refusals were right when they were made, and nothing in this request is a reason to reopen a closed list. D: Escalates a question the rule has already answered: the list closed on Monday, two people have been refused on that basis, and any relaxation granted now would have to be offered back to them. The most effective response is telling them no for the same reason you gave the other two, explaining when the list opens for the following run, and offering to flag their request to the person who runs the course as soon as it does. Consistency is the whole of the judgement here, and the offer gives the person something real without touching the rule. That is better than moving them and going back to the two you refused, because it treats a rule that was applied correctly on Monday as the thing that needs fixing. It is better than asking whether the rule can be set aside for this run, because the list has already closed and any relaxation would owe the two refused people the same offer. The least effective response is moving them and agreeing to keep it between the two of you: reopening it for everybody at least applies one standard to all three, and asking for the rule to be relaxed at least puts the question where people can see it, whereas a private exception is one you could not repeat to the two people you turned down. The principle: an exception you would have to keep quiet is the test that tells you it is not an exception you can make.
tip: Mẹo MT: Áp dụng sơ đồ Venn hoặc bảng chân trị logic để biểu diễn mối quan hệ giữa các đối tượng.

question_text: You are a shift team member at a border protection agency. Ten minutes before the end of your shift, the person who opens the building in the morning rings to ask whether the room booked for tomorrow’s course has been set up. You do not know: the colleague who was doing it has gone home, and the answer is in the shift notes you have not read. If the room has not been done, somebody has to do it this evening. The caller says they need to know now, and sounds irritated. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell the caller you do not know yet but will find out, read the shift notes straight away, and ring back within ten minutes, since tonight is the only window.
Say nothing about the room not being checked, write the caller's question into the shift notes, and leave it for the morning team to pick up when they come in.
Tell the caller you cannot find out before you leave, explaining that your shift ends in ten minutes, and suggest they try the colleague who was setting the room up at home this evening.

Read the whole shift handover from the beginning before saying anything, so nothing else from the day is missed, and ring the caller back once you have been through all of it, however long that takes.
explanation: B: Withholds what the caller needs tonight: they are told neither the answer nor that there is a doubt, so the one evening in which the room could still be set up passes without anybody acting. C: Passes responsibility to others: the answer is in notes on your own desk, and the caller ends up chasing somebody who has finished for the day to get it. D: Delays a one-line answer: the caller is waiting on a single fact and has an evening's work riding on it, so a full read of the handover spends time neither of you has. The most effective response is telling the caller you do not know yet, reading the shift notes and ringing back within ten minutes: the answer exists, it is a few lines away, and the caller can still get the room done tonight. It is stronger than suggesting they try the colleague who set the room up at home, because that colleague has finished for the day and the notes in front of you hold the answer. It is also stronger than reading the whole handover from the beginning before saying anything, since one fact is wanted and the rest of your shift is not. The least effective response is writing the question into the notes and leaving it for the morning team: the caller is told nothing at all, and if the room was missed, the evening in which somebody could have put it right goes by. The principle: pressure is a reason to say when you will answer, never a reason to answer badly or not at all.

question_text: You are an enquiry desk assistant at a border protection agency. A member of the public has waited twenty minutes at the desk for an answer that only another team holds. You have rung them four times and emailed twice with no reply. The desk closes at four o’clock, half an hour from now, and the enquirer has said twice that they cannot come back. The rule at the desk is that internal contact details and staff names are not given out. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Keep ringing that team until four o'clock and ask the enquirer to stay where they are, since somebody may pick up at any moment and the answer is one call away.
Tell the enquirer to come back tomorrow when that team is easier to reach, and start on the next person waiting so the desk closes on time.

Tell the enquirer plainly what you have tried and what happens next, take their contact details, and leave that team a written note before the desk closes, since the enquirer cannot come back tomorrow.
Tell the enquirer you cannot give out internal contacts but that it is sorted and the team will ring them tomorrow, then send them away expecting a call that nobody has promised.
explanation: A: Spends the last half hour on a line nobody is answering: six attempts have already failed, and at four o'clock the enquirer leaves with nothing written down anywhere. B: Ignores what the enquirer has already told you: they have said twice that they cannot come back, so tomorrow is not a route they have. D: Assures the enquirer it is sorted without checking: nobody in that team has answered you, nothing is written down, and the enquirer stops chasing an answer that now exists only in what you said. The most effective response is to tell the enquirer plainly what you have tried and what happens next, take their contact details and leave that team a written note before the desk closes. The enquirer cannot come back, the desk closes in half an hour, and a written note carrying their details is the only thing that survives four o’clock. Ringing that team until four and asking the enquirer to keep waiting is weaker, because six attempts have already failed and the last half hour buys nothing. Telling the enquirer to come back tomorrow is weaker too, because they have twice said they cannot. The least effective response is to tell the enquirer it is sorted and that the team will ring them tomorrow: six attempts have gone unanswered, so nothing has been sorted and nobody in that team has agreed to ring, and the enquirer goes away relying on it and stops chasing. Both of the weaker responses at least leave the enquirer in no doubt about where the request stands, which is what an assurance nobody can honour takes away. Pressure is a reason to make sure a request outlives you, never a reason to say something you have not checked or to send somebody away with nothing.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: A team of 6 people completes a task in 8 days. Working at the same rate, how many days would 4 people take to complete the same task?
explanation: The work is 6 multiplied by 8, which is 48 person-days; shared among 4 people that is 48 divided by 4, or 12 days. Fewer people means more days, so 8 times 4 divided by 6 (about 5.3) scales the wrong way. The value 6 subtracts the two lost workers from the 8 days. The value 48 leaves the answer as the total person-days without dividing.
tip: Mẹo MT: Với bài toán quy luật chuỗi số, hãy xét hiệu số bậc 1, hiệu số bậc 2 hoặc tích lũy tiến.

question_text: Cautious is to reckless as frugal is to which word?
options: Thrifty
Careful
Wealthy
Extravagant
explanation: Cautious and reckless are opposites, so the answer must be the opposite of frugal, which is extravagant. Thrifty is a synonym of frugal rather than its opposite. Careful belongs to the cautious side of the first pair, not the frugal one. Wealthy describes having money rather than being the opposite of frugal.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: The average of five numbers is 20. Four of the numbers are 12, 18, 25 and 15. What is the fifth number?
explanation: Five numbers averaging 20 have a total of 5 times 20, or 100. The four given numbers sum to 70, so the fifth is 100 minus 70, which is 30. The value 17.5 averages only the four given numbers (70 divided by 4). The value 10 multiplies the mean by four instead of five before subtracting. The value 20 simply repeats the mean.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân biệt rõ giữa 'Đúng' (True) và 'Có thể xảy ra' (Possible). Chỉ chọn kết luận chắc chắn 100%.

question_text: Which word is closest in meaning to “concise”?
options: Brief
Detailed
Vague
Complex
explanation: Concise means expressed in few words, so it is closest to brief. Detailed is its opposite. Vague concerns a lack of clarity rather than length, and a concise statement can be perfectly clear. Complex describes difficulty rather than brevity.
tip: Mẹo MT: Với bài toán quy luật chuỗi số, hãy xét hiệu số bậc 1, hiệu số bậc 2 hoặc tích lũy tiến.

question_text: In an office of 30 people, 18 drink tea and 14 drink coffee. Every person drinks at least one of the two. How many drink both?
explanation: Because everyone drinks at least one, adding the two groups counts the both-drinkers twice: 18 plus 14 is 32, which is 2 more than the 30 people, so 2 drink both. The value 32 stops at 18 plus 14 without removing the overlap. The value 12 is 30 minus 18, the tea-only complement, not the overlap. The value 16 is 30 minus 14 in the same mistaken way.
tip: Mẹo MT: Với bài toán quy luật chuỗi số, hãy xét hiệu số bậc 1, hiệu số bậc 2 hoặc tích lũy tiến.

question_text: Four of these five numbers share a property that the fifth does not: 64, 27, 100, 8, 125. Which is the odd one out?
explanation: The numbers 27, 8, 125 and 64 are perfect cubes (3 cubed, 2 cubed, 5 cubed and 4 cubed); 100 is a square but not a cube, so it is the odd one out. Singling out 64 as a perfect square still leaves it 4 cubed, fitting the cube rule the others share. Picking 8 or 125 selects by size only, though both are cubes.
tip: Mẹo MT: Với bài toán quy luật chuỗi số, hãy xét hiệu số bậc 1, hiệu số bậc 2 hoặc tích lũy tiến.

question_text: You are an assurance trainee. A meeting note you wrote three weeks ago records that the client “would consider” a change. Your senior says the client has since told him they “agreed” it at that meeting, and asks you to amend the note to say agreed. You remember it as considered. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Refuse and tell him the note cannot be touched, without offering any way to capture what the client has now said.
Amend the original note to say the client agreed, since your senior was in the meeting too and the client has now confirmed that is what happened.
Take it straight to the engagement partner as a request to falsify a record, without first putting the alternative to your senior.
Offer to add a dated line recording what the client has now said, and explain that you would rather not change what the original note recorded at the time.
explanation: A: Defends the record and drops the substance: the client's later position is real and needs recording somewhere. B: Alters a contemporaneous record: the note's whole value is that it says what was recorded on the day, and rewriting it removes the only evidence of the difference. C: Names it as falsification before asking: your senior may simply not have thought about it, and this is very hard to walk back. The most effective response is to offer to add a dated line recording what the client has now said, and explain that you would rather not change what the original note recorded at the time: it protects what the note is for, captures the new information properly, and gives your senior an easy way to accept. It beats refusing outright and offering no way to capture what the client has now said, because that later position still needs to be on file. It beats taking it straight to the engagement partner as a request to falsify a record, because an unheralded partner conversation is a large response to a request he may withdraw at once. The least effective response is amending the original note to say the client agreed: the record of what was said on the day is overwritten to match what people now believe, which destroys the one thing a contemporaneous note provides. That is altering a record rather than handling the request rigidly or dramatically. The principle: never rewrite the old record; add a new one with today’s date on it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân biệt rõ giữa 'Đúng' (True) và 'Có thể xảy ra' (Possible). Chỉ chọn kết luận chắc chắn 100%.

question_text: You are a purchase ledger clerk. Your manager asked you this morning to file last year’s invoices, which will take the day. At 10am you notice a supplier’s bank details were changed yesterday by someone outside the team, and nobody has confirmed with the supplier that the change is genuine. Your manager is at her desk. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Finish the filing exactly as she asked and tell your manager about the changed bank details at the end of the day, when the job she gave you this morning is actually complete.
Send a note about the bank details over to the payments team, mark it as theirs now, and carry on with the filing without checking that anybody has picked it up.
Ask the supplier directly whether they changed their own bank details, then carry on with the filing and mention it to your manager when there is a moment.
Stop and tell your manager about the changed bank details now, and ask whether the filing should wait while somebody looks at where the change came from.
explanation: A: Ranks the instruction above the information: a day is a long time for a change of this kind to sit unexamined. B: Hands off the urgent item and keeps the routine one: the payments team has no context, nobody has confirmed they picked it up, and the filing was never the thing that mattered today. C: Acts before anybody senior has looked: contacting the supplier on the number in the record is exactly what somebody would want to control first. The most effective response is to stop and tell your manager about the changed bank details now, and ask whether the filing should wait while somebody looks at where the change came from: a bank detail change from outside the team is exactly the thing worth interrupting for, she is two steps away, and the filing has no deadline at all. It beats finishing the filing as asked and telling her at the end of the day, because a day is a long time to leave it. It beats asking the supplier directly whether they changed their own details, because that destroys the evidence before anybody has looked. The least effective response is sending a note to the payments team and carrying on with the filing without checking anybody picked it up: the urgent item is pushed to a team with no context and no confirmation. That is offloading it rather than sequencing it badly. The principle: an instruction from this morning does not outrank what you have found since.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You are an accounts assistant. A supplier’s credit insurer emails asking you to confirm that your firm has “no disputed invoices” with them. There are two disputed invoices, both small, and your manager is on leave for a week. The insurer says a reply is needed within two days or cover will be withdrawn. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Leave the email until your manager returns, since a request of this kind is plainly above your level to answer either way.
Assure the insurer that there are no disputed invoices, since the two in question are small and will almost certainly be resolved within the week anyway.
Reply that the request has to be answered by somebody with authority, tell the insurer when that will be, and put it to your manager's cover today.
Reply setting out the two disputed invoices and the amounts, so that the insurer has an accurate answer inside their two-day deadline.
explanation: A: Lets a deadline run out: cover is withdrawn in two days, and a cover exists precisely so that a week's absence does not do that. B: Asserts something you know is untrue to a third party: an insurer withdraws or maintains cover on it, and the two disputes exist today whatever happens next week. D: Answers on the firm's behalf without authority: an accurate disclosure to a credit insurer is still a disclosure somebody senior should make. The most effective response is to reply that the request has to be answered by somebody with authority, tell the insurer when that will be, and put it to your manager’s cover today: it declines to answer without authority, protects the two-day deadline by saying what is happening, and puts it in front of the person standing in. It beats replying with the two disputed invoices and the amounts, because the disclosure itself needs authority even when it is true. It beats leaving the email until your manager returns, because a week’s silence loses the cover. The least effective response is confirming there are none on the grounds that the two are small and will be resolved within the week: a false confirmation goes to somebody who will act on it, from a person with no authority to send it at all. That is a false statement rather than an over-reach or a delay. The principle: when you cannot answer, say who can and by when, and start that today.
tip: Mẹo MT: Áp dụng sơ đồ Venn hoặc bảng chân trị logic để biểu diễn mối quan hệ giữa các đối tượng.

question_text: You are a compliance analyst. A department head asks you whether his team’s new process “has been approved”. Your review is half done and the parts you have seen are fine, but two sections are untouched. He wants to start using the process on Monday and is pressing for an answer today. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell him exactly which parts you have reviewed and which you have not, say when the remaining two will be done, and be clear that it is not approved yet.
Tell him to raise it with your manager, since a question about whether something is approved should come from somebody more senior than you.
Tell him the review is not finished and that you cannot say anything further about it until it is, without giving him any sort of date for the remaining two sections.
Tell him it is fine to go ahead on Monday, since everything you have looked at so far has been perfectly in order and the rest is very unlikely to differ.
explanation: B: Passes a question you can answer: you know exactly what has and has not been reviewed, and he now waits for a diary slot. C: Withholds the timing: he is planning a Monday start and a date is the one thing that would let him plan around it. D: Gives an approval you have not reached: he starts a process on Monday believing it is signed off, and two unreviewed sections carry his name and yours. The most effective response is to tell him exactly which parts you have reviewed and which you have not, say when the remaining two will be done, and be clear it is not approved yet: it is precise about what is done, honest about the status, and gives him a date he can plan against. It beats telling him the review is not finished and that you cannot say more, because a refusal without a date leaves him no better off. It beats telling him to raise it with your manager, because you hold the facts and she would only repeat them. The least effective response is telling him it is fine to go ahead on Monday: an approval is given for two sections nobody has read, and a department starts using the process on the strength of it. That is asserting something untrue rather than being unhelpfully vague. The principle: report the status precisely and give a date, never round it up to yes.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You are an audit junior. Your manager needs the cash section closed by 6pm. Two of the twelve bank confirmations have not arrived and the banks will not answer until tomorrow. The file template requires each confirmation to be marked received before the section can be signed. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Mark the two outstanding confirmations as received so the section can be closed at 6pm, and update the file properly tomorrow when they actually arrive.
Close the section at 6pm leaving the two confirmations blank, so that nothing untrue is recorded and the gap is visible to whoever looks at it next.
Tell your manager at once that two confirmations are outstanding until tomorrow, and ask whether to close the section with those two flagged or hold it.
Keep telephoning the two banks past 6pm until somebody answers, and tell your manager the section is on track in the meantime.
explanation: A: Records evidence as received that has not been received: the file says twelve confirmations are in hand, and the reviewer, the manager and the client all read it that way. B: Signs a section that is not complete: nothing false is written down, and the section is still declared closed with two items outstanding. D: Reports a position you cannot support: the banks will not answer until tomorrow, so "on track" is a hope offered as a status. The most effective response is to tell your manager at once that two confirmations are outstanding until tomorrow, and ask whether to close the section with those flagged or hold it: the constraint is real and external, she owns whether to close or hold, and both options are still open at 6pm. It beats closing the section at 6pm leaving the two blank, because closing with known gaps is a decision above your level even when nothing false is written. It beats telephoning the two banks past 6pm while reporting the section on track, because that is a status nobody can rely on. The least effective response is marking the two outstanding confirmations as received: the file asserts evidence was received when it was not, and everybody downstream reads that as fact. That is a false record rather than a badly judged close or an optimistic update. The principle: never let the record say something the work does not.
tip: Mẹo MT: Áp dụng sơ đồ Venn hoặc bảng chân trị logic để biểu diễn mối quan hệ giữa các đối tượng.

question_text: You are a reconciliations clerk. Four breaks need clearing before the 2pm cut-off and each takes about an hour. It is 10am. Three desks have each told you theirs is the priority. Your supervisor is uncontactable this morning. One of the four affects a client payment; the other three affect internal reporting only. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Work the four breaks in the order the desks contacted you, and tell all three desks plainly that arrival order is the rule you are applying today.
Clear the client payment break first, then wait for your supervisor to become contactable before deciding the order of the remaining three breaks.
Clear the client payment break first, tell all three desks the order you are working in and why, and say which break will not make the cut-off.
Send the three internal breaks over to another team without telling them which one is urgent, and treat all four as no longer yours to worry about.
explanation: A: Treats order of arrival as priority: it is at least transparent, and a client payment is not more or less urgent for having been raised second. B: Stops after the easy call: the hard part is the other three, and waiting spends the morning that could have cleared two of them. D: Moves the work rather than the decision: another team has no context on three breaks, the ordering problem is untouched, and three desks still do not know where they stand. The most effective response is to clear the client payment break first, tell all three desks the order you are working in and why, and say which break will not make the cut-off: the client payment is the only one with an outside party behind it, and telling the desks the order and the casualty makes it a decision rather than a queue. It beats working the four in the order the desks contacted you and telling them arrival order is the rule, because arrival order has nothing to do with consequence. It beats clearing the client payment and waiting for your supervisor before deciding the rest, because waiting burns the hours that would have cleared two more. The least effective response is sending the three internal breaks to another team without saying which is urgent: they go to people who cannot judge them, nobody is told anything, and the decision that had to be made is simply not made. That is passing it on rather than sequencing it wrongly. The principle: rank by consequence, then tell the people who lose.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân biệt rõ giữa 'Đúng' (True) và 'Có thể xảy ra' (Possible). Chỉ chọn kết luận chắc chắn 100%.

question_text: You are a settlements assistant. At the end of your shift one trade is unmatched because the counterparty’s reference does not match yours. You have worked out what is wrong but not fixed it. The night team will pick up the queue and does not usually see this counterparty. Your shift ends in five minutes. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Write two lines on the handover saying what the mismatch is and what you think the fix is, and flag it to the night team lead before you leave.
Email the counterparty explaining the reference problem, and leave the trade in the queue for the night team to pick up when the reply comes.
Stay late and fix the mismatch yourself, since you understand it and the night team would take much longer to get to the same point.
Put the unmatched trade over to the night team in the queue with the others, since it is their shift now and they will work through it the same way they work through everything else.
explanation: B: Starts something the next shift cannot finish: a reply arrives to an inbox nobody on tonight is watching. C: Absorbs a handover problem: it works tonight, and the night team is no better placed the next time this counterparty appears. D: Hands over the problem without the part only you know: the night team has never seen this counterparty, and the diagnosis you already have leaves the building with you. The most effective response is to write two lines on the handover saying what the mismatch is and what you think the fix is, and flag it to the night team lead: two lines transfer the diagnosis, the flag makes sure it is read, and they can act immediately. It beats staying late and fixing the mismatch yourself, because that fixes tonight and teaches nobody. It beats emailing the counterparty about the reference problem and leaving the trade in the queue, because a reply landing in your inbox overnight helps nobody on shift. The least effective response is putting the unmatched trade into the queue with the others: it is passed on stripped of the only thing that would let the next person solve it. That is offloading rather than handing over imperfectly. The principle: what you hand on is the problem plus what you learned about it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Áp dụng sơ đồ Venn hoặc bảng chân trị logic để biểu diễn mối quan hệ giữa các đối tượng.

question_text: You are a duty assistant at a gym. A member tells you the emergency stop cord on one of the treadmills does not seem to work. You test it and the belt does not stop. The gym is busy, six other treadmills are working, and the maintenance contractor is not on site. Your duty manager is in the building and reachable on the radio. There is no out-of-order signage kept on the gym floor. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Note the fault in the maintenance logbook so it is picked up at the contractor's next scheduled visit, and mention it to your duty manager at the end of your shift.
Ring the maintenance contractor yourself to ask how soon someone can attend and what should be done with the treadmill until then.
Take the treadmill out of use immediately, make it obvious it must not be used, and radio your duty manager straight away so she can arrange the repair and proper signage.
Leave the treadmill in use, since the belt can still be stopped with the console button and six other treadmills are available if a member would rather not use that one.
explanation: A: Delays the decision: the logbook is the right record and the wrong speed. It leaves a treadmill with no working emergency stop available to members for the rest of the day. B: Acts on assumptions without checking: the contractor's answer is useful and the decision about whether members may use a machine with no emergency stop belongs to your duty manager, who is in the building now. D: Stays silent about a known safety risk: you have confirmed the emergency stop does not work and leave the machine open to members anyway, with nobody told. That is a safety failure, not a judgement about priorities. The most effective response is to take the treadmill out of use immediately and radio your duty manager: an emergency stop that does not work on a moving belt is a safety fault, so the machine comes out of use first, and she is in the building and is the person who can arrange both signage and the contractor. It beats noting the fault in the maintenance logbook for the contractor’s next scheduled visit, because that records it for a future visit while members carry on using the machine today. It beats ringing the maintenance contractor yourself, because they can say when they will come but cannot decide whether the gym may keep a machine with no emergency stop in service; that is the duty manager’s call and she is thirty seconds away on the radio. The least effective response is leaving the treadmill in use because the belt can still be stopped with the console button: it is the only response that leaves a confirmed safety fault in service and tells nobody, on the reasoning that members have alternatives. That is worse than the other two, which are too slow but do report it. The principle: make a safety fault safe first, then tell the person on site who can decide what happens next.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân biệt rõ giữa 'Đúng' (True) và 'Có thể xảy ra' (Possible). Chỉ chọn kết luận chắc chắn 100%.

question_text: You are an events assistant at a wedding venue. A couple’s wedding is on Saturday. On Thursday the marquee supplier tells you the marquee ordered is no longer available and only a smaller one can be delivered, which will not seat the full guest list of a hundred and twenty. The couple are contactable. Your venue manager is off until Saturday morning. The couple have already sent seating plans. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Ring the couple today, explain the marquee is unavailable and what the smaller one would mean for their guest list, and go through the options with them before anything is confirmed.
Work out a revised seating arrangement that fits the smaller marquee, then send it to the couple so they can see the problem and the solution together.
Accept the smaller marquee and tell the couple on Saturday morning when the venue manager is back, since there is nothing they can usefully do about it beforehand.
Spend Thursday and Friday ringing round other marquee suppliers, and contact the couple only if you cannot find one that fits the full guest list.
explanation: B: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholder's: how a hundred and twenty guests are seated at their own wedding is the couple's decision, and presenting a finished plan removes it from them. C: Hides the problem / silent deadline slip: it is untrue that nothing can be done on Thursday and Friday, and telling them on the morning of the wedding removes every remaining option. That is concealment at the worst possible moment. D: Delays the message: the search is worth doing and it is being done instead of telling them. If it fails, the couple learn on Friday night with no time left at all. The most effective response is to ring the couple today, explain the marquee is unavailable and what the smaller one would mean for their guest list, and go through the options before anything is confirmed: it is their wedding and their guest list, they have two days in which real alternatives exist, and only they can weigh a smaller marquee against the rest. Telling them first keeps the decision theirs. It beats working out a revised seating arrangement and sending it so they see the problem and the solution together, because that decides for them how their guests are arranged, which is not a logistics question. It beats spending Thursday and Friday ringing round other suppliers, because that search, however sensible, uses up both remaining days before they are told anything. The least effective response is accepting the smaller marquee and telling them on Saturday morning: it leaves them to discover on the morning of their wedding that a hundred and twenty guests will not fit, when two days of alternatives were available. That is worse than the other two, which act on their behalf but at least act. The principle: when a failure affects someone’s own event, tell them at once and let them choose, rather than solving it for them or waiting until you have solved it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Với bài toán quy luật chuỗi số, hãy xét hiệu số bậc 1, hiệu số bậc 2 hoặc tích lũy tiến.

question_text: You work on a university student services helpdesk during enrolment week. The queue is long and the online system has been down all morning. A student who has queued twice tells you loudly that the university is a shambles and that you have wasted two hours of his day. He has a genuine problem: his enrolment is not complete and his accommodation depends on it. Your team leader is nearby. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Explain that the system outage has affected everyone this morning and that the helpdesk staff have no control over it, and ask him to bear with you.
Apologise and ask your team leader to take over, since the student is angry and a more senior person may be able to resolve his enrolment faster.
Acknowledge the two hours he has lost, tell him exactly what you can do for his enrolment now and what it means for his accommodation, and start on it.
Tell him the system is down so nothing can be done today, and ask him to come back tomorrow when it has been restored.
explanation: A: Personalises the conflict: the explanation is true and it answers his anger rather than his enrolment, in front of a queue that is listening and equally frustrated. B: Passes responsibility to others: it hands over a case you can start on, makes him repeat his story a third time, and takes a team leader off the floor during the busiest week. D: Ignores the customer's actual need: it sends away a student whose accommodation depends on enrolment, on the claim that nothing can be done, without establishing whether anything can be done manually. That is a dismissal, not an answer. The most effective response is to acknowledge the two hours he has lost, tell him exactly what you can do for his enrolment now and what it means for his accommodation, and start on it: he has a real problem with a real consequence, so acknowledging the wasted time and moving straight to what can be done answers the complaint properly. It beats explaining that the outage has affected everyone and asking him to bear with you, because defending the helpdesk, however fairly, engages his anger instead of his enrolment while the queue watches. It beats asking your team leader to take over, because that makes him tell the story a third time and removes a supervisor from the floor when you can begin now. The least effective response is telling him nothing can be done today and asking him to come back tomorrow: it says that to a student whose accommodation depends on enrolment, without checking whether anything can be done manually, and sends him away for a third visit. That is worse than the other two, which respond badly but keep him in the process. The principle: acknowledge the cost to the person, then move immediately to the most concrete thing you can actually do.
