question_text: You are a shop floor assistant in a supermarket. You have finished facing up your aisle. Your colleague Dev is alone on the fresh produce aisle with three cages of stock to put out before the evening rush in an hour, and is clearly not going to finish. He has not asked for help. Your section manager is on a break for another twenty minutes. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Ask Dev whether he would like a hand, and find something else to do if he says he is fine, since he may have a system for working through the cages.
Go over to produce, tell Dev your aisle is done and you will take one of the cages, and work alongside him until the stock is out.
Wait for the section manager to come back from her break in twenty minutes and suggest that someone is moved onto produce to help Dev clear the cages.
Find another job in your own section, since produce is Dev's aisle tonight and stepping in without being asked might look as though you are checking up on him.
explanation: A: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholder's: a colleague halfway through three cages with an hour to go will usually say he is managing, so the question is polite and predictably leaves him alone with them. C: Delays the decision: it spends a third of the remaining hour waiting to ask someone else to do what you could start now, and the cages are no smaller when she returns. D: Invents a reason not to help: it invents a reason not to help while three cages of fresh produce miss the evening rush. Manufacturing a concern about appearances to justify standing by is the failure here. The most effective response is to go over to produce, tell Dev your aisle is done and you will take one of the cages, and work alongside him: your aisle is finished, he has an hour and more stock than he can move, and the fastest fix is a second pair of hands. Saying your aisle is done removes any need for him to admit he is behind. It beats asking whether he would like a hand and finding something else if he says he is fine, because putting that question to a colleague mid-task invites the polite refusal, and the cages remain. It beats waiting for the section manager to come back from her break, because that spends a third of the available time arranging what you could simply do. The least effective response is finding another job in your own section: it leaves a colleague to miss the evening rush while you look for other work, and the justification is a worry about how helping might look. That is worse than offering, which at least asks, and worse than waiting for the manager, which at least seeks help. The principle: when your own work is done and a colleague plainly cannot finish, start helping rather than asking or waiting.
tip: Mẹo MT: Áp dụng sơ đồ Venn hoặc bảng chân trị logic để biểu diễn mối quan hệ giữa các đối tượng.

question_text: You are an administrator at a driving instructor training company. A candidate is booked for an assessment on Thursday. On Tuesday the examiner tells you he cannot attend and the next available date is in three weeks. The candidate has already paid and has told you he has a job offer conditional on passing this month. He is contactable. Your centre manager is available today. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Ring the candidate today, explain the examiner cannot attend and the next date is three weeks away, and ask your centre manager what else can be offered given his job offer.
Leave the booking in place and tell him on Thursday when he arrives, since another examiner may become available before then and there is no point worrying him early.
Rebook him into the next available assessment in three weeks and email him the new date, apologising for the change and confirming that his fee carries over.
Email him today to say Thursday's assessment has to be moved and that you will confirm a new date once the examiner's availability has been finalised.
explanation: B: Hides the problem / silent deadline slip: he travels to an assessment you know is not happening, and loses two days in which he could have sought an alternative. Betting his job offer on an examiner appearing is concealment. C: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholder's: it fixes the diary and ignores the fact he told you about, a job offer conditional on passing this month, which the new date defeats. D: Delays the message: it reaches him in time and withholds the three week gap, which is the fact that collides with his job offer and the only one he can act on. The most effective response is to ring the candidate today, explain the examiner cannot attend and the next date is three weeks away, and ask your centre manager what else can be offered: he has a job offer conditional on passing this month, a three-week delay defeats it, and she may have options, another examiner or another centre, that you do not. Telling him today while that is being explored is the only response that engages with what is actually at stake. It beats rebooking him into the next available assessment and emailing the new date, because that treats a problem about his job offer as a diary entry. It beats emailing to say Thursday has to move with a date to follow, because withholding the three-week gap keeps from him the one fact he needs to act on. The least effective response is leaving the booking in place and telling him when he arrives on Thursday: it lets him travel to an assessment that is not happening and burns two days of a deadline he told you about. That is worse than the other two, which respond inadequately but in time. The principle: when someone has told you what is riding on a date, give them the bad news at once and take the problem to whoever might have another route.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân biệt rõ giữa 'Đúng' (True) và 'Có thể xảy ra' (Possible). Chỉ chọn kết luận chắc chắn 100%.

question_text: You work in the post room of a large office. At 3pm the courier arrives for the daily collection, which leaves at 3.15. A colleague has just brought down a contract that must reach a client tomorrow, and it needs an envelope and a label, taking five minutes. Your supervisor has also asked you to reorganise the shelving before you finish, a job with no deadline. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Put the contract in the collection unlabelled so it makes the 3.15 courier, and sort out the paperwork with the courier company afterwards.
Start the shelving as your supervisor asked, and put the contract in tomorrow's collection since it will still reach the client the following day.
Prepare and label the contract straight away so it goes with the 3.15 collection, and start the shelving afterwards.
Ask the courier to wait while you check with your supervisor whether the contract or the shelving should come first.
explanation: A: Acts recklessly with the client's document: an unlabelled contract in a courier bag is a document with no destination, so the one item that had to arrive tomorrow is the one most likely to be lost entirely. B: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholder's: it decides the client's deadline can slip a day in order to start a job with no deadline at all, when five minutes would have caught the courier. D: Escalates prematurely: a five-minute job against a job with no deadline is a call you can make yourself, and holding the courier to ask it risks the whole collection. The most effective response is to prepare and label the contract straight away so it goes with the 3.15 collection, then start the shelving: the courier leaves at 3.15, the contract takes five minutes and has a client deadline tomorrow, and the shelving has no deadline at all. Doing the short, time-critical job first costs the shelving nothing. It beats starting the shelving and putting the contract in tomorrow’s collection, because that treats a task with no deadline as outranking a client contract that would have made today’s courier with ten minutes to spare. It beats asking the courier to wait while you check with your supervisor, because choosing between a five-minute job and an open-ended one does not need a supervisor, and asking risks holding the courier. The least effective response is putting the contract in the collection unlabelled: an unlabelled contract in a courier bag has no destination, so the attempt to save it is the thing most likely to lose it. That is worse than sending it tomorrow, which is a day late but safe, and worse than holding the courier, which at least keeps it intact. The principle: when a short task has a closing window and a long one has none, do the short one properly, then the long one.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân biệt rõ giữa 'Đúng' (True) và 'Có thể xảy ra' (Possible). Chỉ chọn kết luận chắc chắn 100%.

question_text: You work in a council customer services team. You and your colleague Nadia job-share the housing repairs inbox. She believes tenants should be told realistic timescales even when they are long; you have been giving the target timescales the service publishes. A tenant has complained that he was told two different things by the two of you. Your team leader has asked you both to sort it out. Forty repair emails are waiting. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Agree to use Nadia's realistic timescales from now on, since the complaint came from a tenant being given the published target and then finding it was not met.
Ask your team leader to rule on which timescales should be quoted, and hold the forty repair emails until she has decided so that no more tenants get conflicting answers.
Carry on quoting the published targets, since they are the service's official position, and let Nadia answer her share however she prefers until somebody tells one of you otherwise.
Sit down with Nadia today, agree a single form of words that gives the published target and what is realistic, use it on the forty waiting emails, and take it to your team leader to confirm.
explanation: A: Prioritises harmony over honesty: it settles the disagreement by conceding rather than resolving it, and commits the team to quoting timescales that differ from the ones the service publishes. B: Delays the decision: it seeks the right ruling at the cost of forty tenants waiting longer for any answer at all, when a shared form of words could go out today and be confirmed afterwards. C: Avoids the difficult conversation: it accepts that tenants will keep getting two different answers from the same inbox, which is the exact complaint, and waits for someone else to fix it. Choosing to continue a known defect is worse than choosing the wrong fix. The most effective response is to sit down with Nadia today, agree a single form of words giving both the published target and what is realistic, use it on the forty waiting emails, and take it to your team leader to confirm: there are two problems, forty tenants waiting and a genuine disagreement about what to tell them, and a shared form of words solves both at once. Giving the target and the realistic expectation together is not a compromise between the two positions, it is the answer a tenant actually needs. It beats agreeing to use her realistic timescales from now on, because conceding to one view commits the team to quoting something other than the published target without anyone senior agreeing. It beats asking your team leader to rule and holding the emails until she has decided, because that makes tenants pay for an internal disagreement. The least effective response is carrying on quoting the published targets and letting Nadia answer her share however she prefers: it knowingly continues the practice that generated the complaint, with tenants still receiving two different answers from one inbox, and waits to be told to stop. That is worse than the other two, which pick a direction. The principle: agree a shared answer with your colleague, use it now, and have it confirmed afterwards rather than pausing the work.
tip: Mẹo MT: Áp dụng sơ đồ Venn hoặc bảng chân trị logic để biểu diễn mối quan hệ giữa các đối tượng.

question_text: You are a ward clerk at a hospital. Your colleague Anita, who covers discharges, has been off sick for two days and returns tomorrow. Discharge summaries have piled up, and the ward sister asks you to work through them today on top of your own admissions work. You have done the task before but are slower at it. You cannot complete both by the end of the shift. The ward sister is on the ward. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Say nothing about the clash, do what you can of both, and leave the rest for Anita to pick up when she is back tomorrow since discharges are her responsibility.
Tell the ward sister you can clear either the admissions or most of the discharge summaries today but not both, and ask which she wants prioritised before you start.
Work on the discharge summaries first since the sister has asked for them, and leave any admissions paperwork you cannot finish for whoever is on the ward tomorrow morning.
Start the discharge summaries and work through as many as you can alongside admissions, switching between the two so that both piles go down over the course of the shift.
explanation: A: Hides the problem: the sister believes the summaries are being handled, and a colleague returning from sick leave walks into a backlog nobody has flagged. The silence is the failure, not the workload. C: Abandons own committed work: admissions paperwork left undone lands on tomorrow's ward with nobody told it is coming, so the pile simply moves rather than shrinking. D: Splits effort so nothing finishes: alternating between two unfamiliar and familiar tasks leaves both partly done at the end of the shift, and a half-processed discharge is of no use to anyone. The most effective response is to tell the ward sister you can clear either the admissions or most of the discharge summaries but not both, and ask which she wants prioritised: she does not know that taking on the summaries means the admissions work will not be finished, and she is the person who can weigh those against each other. Asking before you start costs a minute and makes the rest of the shift deliberate. It beats working on the discharge summaries first and leaving unfinished admissions paperwork for tomorrow, because silently dropping admissions leaves tomorrow’s ward with a backlog nobody warned them about. It beats switching between the two so both piles go down, because that leaves both half done, and a partly completed discharge summary releases nobody. The least effective response is saying nothing about the clash and leaving the rest for Anita tomorrow: it leaves the sister believing both are in hand, and a colleague back from sick leave to discover the pile, with nobody having said anything to either of them. That is worse than the other two, which mismanage the work but do not conceal it. The principle: when you cannot do everything asked, say so before you start and let the person who owns the priorities choose.
tip: Mẹo MT: Áp dụng sơ đồ Venn hoặc bảng chân trị logic để biểu diễn mối quan hệ giữa các đối tượng.

question_text: You are a knowledge assistant. You raised with a colleague that the case summaries she writes for the bulletin are arriving too long to use, and she took it as criticism of her work. She has since stopped attending the weekly planning call that the two of you and two others use to divide the month. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Divide the month between the three of you who still attend, and send her whatever is left over, since the call cannot wait for somebody who has decided not to come.
Stop sending her the bulletin plan because she said you were being pedantic, since somebody who will not come to the call has no particular claim on knowing what the rest of you decide.
Ask her for a few minutes, say the point was about length rather than about her writing, and ask what would make the planning call worth coming back to.
Raise it with the person who owns the bulletin, since a contributor refusing to attend the planning call is affecting the output and is not really yours to sort out.
explanation: A: Works around the absence: it keeps the call going and makes her permanently peripheral, so the summaries get worse and the reason she stopped attending is never touched. B: Withdraws information after the disagreement: the person writing several summaries stops knowing what the month contains, so the bulletin is worse because two people fell out. D: Escalates before asking: she has never been told that the comment was about length rather than quality, so the first thing that happens is somebody senior asking her why she stopped coming. The most effective response is to ask her for a few minutes, say the point was about length rather than about her writing, and ask what would make the planning call worth coming back to. She has drawn a conclusion the feedback did not carry, only you can correct that, and the call is what the shared work runs on. It beats dividing the month between the three of you who still attend and sending her the remainder, because making her peripheral guarantees the summaries stay unusable. It beats raising it with the person who owns the bulletin, because nobody has yet told her what was actually meant. The least effective response is stopping sending her the bulletin plan: it answers her withdrawal with yours and cuts the person writing the summaries out of the plan, which is a different kind of wrong from the other two because both of those try to keep the output intact. The principle: correct what the feedback was taken to mean, and protect the meeting the work depends on.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân biệt rõ giữa 'Đúng' (True) và 'Có thể xảy ra' (Possible). Chỉ chọn kết luận chắc chắn 100%.

question_text: You are a client services adviser. The firm’s booking system will not let you hold a meeting room for more than two hours, and three times this month a longer meeting has had to move rooms halfway through. You have found that the limit can be got round by making two bookings back to back under different names. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Write up the three occasions and what the two-hour limit did to each, and take it to the office manager with the suggestion that the limit be changed.
Tell the fee earners who book long meetings about the two-booking method, so that they can use it themselves whenever they need a room for longer.
Raise the two-hour limit with the office manager when you next see her, and carry on moving meetings halfway through in the meantime as everybody has been doing.
Use the two-booking method whenever a longer meeting comes up, since it solves the problem today and nobody is harmed by a room being held under two names.
explanation: B: Spreads the workaround: it turns one person's trick into the way the firm books rooms, and it puts the diary further from the truth every time it is used. C: Raises it without the evidence: three occasions with what each cost is an argument, and mentioning a limit in passing is a remark that will be lost among everything else she has. D: Builds a workaround around a control: bookings under names that are not the people meeting make the room diary describe something that is not happening, and the limit itself is never looked at. The most effective response is to write up the three occasions and what the two-hour limit did to each, and take it to the office manager with the suggestion that the limit be changed. Three occasions with their consequences is what turns an irritation into a case, and she is the person who can change it. It beats raising the limit with her when you next see her while carrying on moving meetings halfway through, because the same point made without the evidence goes nowhere. It beats telling the fee earners who book long meetings about the two-booking method, because teaching a trick to more people is not a fix. The least effective response is using the two-booking method whenever a longer meeting comes up: it puts bookings in the diary under names that are not meeting there, so the record stops describing the building. That is a different kind of wrong from the other two, because it is you rather than the system that makes the diary wrong. The principle: take the evidence to whoever owns the rule rather than routing around it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Với bài toán quy luật chuỗi số, hãy xét hiệu số bậc 1, hiệu số bậc 2 hoặc tích lũy tiến.

question_text: You are a reception coordinator. Three times this month a client has arrived for a meeting that was not in the room diary, and each time you have found a room at the last minute. Nobody has complained. You have noticed that all three bookings came from the same team and were made by email rather than through the system. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Reply to the next email booking asking the sender to use the system instead, and do the same each time until that team gets used to booking the way everybody else does.
Carry on finding rooms as you have been, since no client has been kept waiting and raising it would make trouble for a team that is plainly under pressure.
Set out the three occasions, what happened each time and where the bookings came from, and take it to the office manager with a suggestion for closing the gap.
Block out two rooms every morning so there is always somewhere to put an unbooked meeting, which removes the risk without anybody needing to change how they work.
explanation: A: Corrects one message at a time: it works only when somebody happens to email you, and it puts the fix in the hands of the team that has been getting it wrong for a month. B: Passes the risk quietly forward: three saves in a month is luck rather than a system, and the first time there is no free room a client will be standing in reception with nowhere to go. D: Builds a workaround: it takes two rooms out of use every day to cover an occasional fault, and it makes the underlying booking problem permanently invisible. The most effective response is to set out the three occasions, what happened each time and where the bookings came from, and take it to the office manager with a suggestion. Three occasions with a common source is a pattern rather than three accidents, and she is the person who can change how that team books. It beats replying to each email booking asking the sender to use the system, because correcting them one at a time leaves the next to chance. It beats blocking out two rooms every morning, because holding rooms empty pays for the fault every day and hides it. The least effective response is carrying on finding rooms as you have been: it keeps a run of luck going and leaves nobody able to act, so the first failure lands on a client. That is a different kind of wrong from the other two, both of which at least change something. The principle: when you have absorbed the same fault three times, the absorbing is the problem.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You are a records assistant in a week when half the team is off. A fee earner has twice raised with your team leader that files are taking too long to retrieve, and this morning said in the corridor, where others could hear, that the records team has stopped bothering. You know the delays are the staffing. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell him in the corridor that half the team is off this week, and that his files would come back faster if he stopped complaining and started planning ahead.
Say nothing to him and raise the staffing with your team leader, since she is the one he has complained to twice and the one who can explain it to him.
Prioritise his requests above everybody else's for the rest of the week, so that the complaints stop and he sees for himself that the team has not stopped bothering.
Tell him quietly that the team is at half strength this week, give him a realistic time for his current request, and say you will flag the staffing to your team leader.
explanation: A: Answers a complaint with a criticism of the complainer: it turns a question about retrieval times into an exchange between two people in a corridor with an audience. B: Leaves the wrong account standing: he will carry on believing the team has stopped bothering until somebody tells him otherwise, and nothing says she will. C: Rewards the loudest voice: it fixes one person's experience by making everyone else's worse, and it leaves the staffing problem unreported because the symptom has gone quiet. The most effective response is to tell him quietly that the team is at half strength this week, give him a realistic time for his current request, and say you will flag the staffing to your team leader. He is missing one fact, he needs a time he can work with, and the staffing belongs in front of the person who can act on it. It beats saying nothing to him and raising the staffing with your team leader, because he will otherwise keep the wrong account. It beats prioritising his requests above everybody else’s for the rest of the week, because moving him to the front hides the cause. The least effective response is telling him in the corridor that his files would come back faster if he stopped complaining: it answers his complaint by criticising him, in front of whoever is there. That is a different kind of wrong from the other two, neither of which makes it about him. The principle: give the missing fact quietly, give a real time, and send the cause upward.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You are a knowledge assistant. You notice that a precedent letter on the firm’s system still names a fee arrangement the firm stopped offering last year. Three teams use that letter. The person who owns the precedent library is at a conference until Monday. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Message the three teams today to say the letter is out of date and should not go out until it is corrected, and email the library owner so it is dealt with on Monday.
Say nothing until Monday, when the person who owns the library is back and can decide what to do about a precedent that has been wrong for the better part of a year already.
Correct the letter yourself so that nobody sends the old fee arrangement out, and tell the library owner what you changed when she is back on Monday.
Email the library owner setting out the problem so that it is at the top of her messages on Monday, and carry on with your own work in the meantime.
explanation: B: Withholds a warning people needed: three teams can send that letter to a client at any point before Monday, and the only person who knows it is wrong has decided to wait. C: Changes a controlled document without authority: the correction may well be right and it is made by somebody who does not own the precedent, in a library whose whole value is that its contents are approved. D: Fails to warn the people at risk: the email reaches the right person and reaches her after the weekend, while the three teams who might send the letter hear nothing at all. The most effective response is to message the three teams today to say the letter is out of date and should not go out, and email the library owner for Monday. The urgent part is that three teams could send a wrong letter before Monday, and that is fixed by telling them; the correction itself belongs to the owner. It beats correcting the letter yourself and telling her what you changed on Monday, because amending an approved precedent is not yours to do. It beats emailing her so it is at the top of her messages, because that protects Monday and not the next four days. The least effective response is saying nothing until Monday: the only person who knows sits on it while three teams carry on, which is a different kind of wrong from the other two because both of those at least act on somebody. The principle: warn the people exposed today, and route the fix to whoever owns it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Áp dụng sơ đồ Venn hoặc bảng chân trị logic để biểu diễn mối quan hệ giữa các đối tượng.

question_text: You are a billing assistant. A fee earner asks whether a client has paid an invoice from last month. The accounts system shows a payment of the right amount but not which invoice it was for, and the person who allocates payments is off today. He wants to open a further piece of work on the strength of it. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell him the payment is showing and that it has not yet been matched to an invoice, and offer to get the bank reference checked this morning so he has something definite.
Tell him you cannot confirm it until the person who allocates payments is back tomorrow, since matching a payment to an invoice is her job rather than yours.
Tell him it has been paid and state it as confirmed, since the amount matches exactly and no other invoice on the account is anywhere near that figure.
Tell him a payment is showing, and note on the account that he asked, so there is a record of the query for whoever picks up the allocation tomorrow.
explanation: B: Answers with the obstacle: it is accurate about who does what and it leaves him a day behind, when the bank reference could settle it in half an hour. C: Asserts a fact the record does not carry: the system shows money in and not what it was for, and he is going to open new work on the strength of your answer. D: Records the question instead of answering it: the note helps tomorrow and he is making a decision today with half a fact. The most effective response is to tell him the payment is showing but not yet matched to an invoice, and offer to get the bank reference checked this morning. He needs to know what the record does and does not show, and the reference can turn that into a definite answer within the morning. It beats telling him you cannot confirm it until the person who allocates payments is back tomorrow, because a day’s wait is not necessary. It beats telling him a payment is showing and noting the query on the account, because a note does not reach the decision he is about to make. The least effective response is telling him it has been paid and stating it as confirmed: he is given something the system does not support, and he will commit the firm to further work on it. That is a different kind of wrong from the other two, both of which are clear about what is unmatched. The principle: say exactly what the record shows, and go and get the rest.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân biệt rõ giữa 'Đúng' (True) và 'Có thể xảy ra' (Possible). Chỉ chọn kết luận chắc chắn 100%.

question_text: You are a candidate liaison assistant at a correctional service. An applicant telephones to ask why she was not put through to the next stage and how she was scored. The stated rule is that scores are released only in the written feedback the selection team sends, which takes ten working days. She says she has another application closing on Friday and needs to know what to work on. Her scores are on the screen in front of you. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Take her number and offer to ring her back once the written feedback has been sent in ten working days, which is the point at which you will be able to talk her through the scores line by line.
Tell her there is nothing on file beyond the written feedback she will be sent, and that everybody at her stage receives the same, so that she stops asking about the scores.

Explain the ten working day rule and that it applies to every applicant, say you cannot help further, and end the call politely, since the rule is clear and the selection team is the only route to her scores.
Explain that the scores come only in the written feedback and when it is due, ask the selection team today whether anything can be given sooner given her Friday date, and ring her back either way.
explanation: A: Ignores the deadline she has told you about: ten working days lands well after Friday, so the call she is offered arrives when it can no longer help her. B: Denies information you are holding: her scores are on the screen as you speak, and she is being told they do not exist in order to end an awkward call. C: Stops at the rule: it is true and it is not the whole answer, because nobody has asked the selection team whether her Friday date changes anything. The most effective response is to explain when the written feedback is due, ask the selection team today whether anything can be given sooner in light of her Friday date, and ring her back either way: it keeps the release rule where it belongs, with the team that owns it, and still puts her actual deadline in front of somebody who could act on it. It is stronger than taking her number and offering a call after the feedback is sent, because ten working days lands after Friday and the offer is worth nothing to her. It is stronger than explaining the rule and ending the call, because that is accurate and incurious: nobody has been asked whether her date makes any difference. The least effective response is to tell her there is nothing on file beyond the written feedback and that everybody at her stage receives the same: the delayed callback at least keeps the door open, and the polite refusal at least tells her the truth about the rule, whereas denying that the scores exist while looking at them is untrue and leaves her working on the wrong thing before Friday. The principle: a rule you cannot bend is still explained honestly, and somebody else’s deadline is worth one question to the people who own the decision.
tip: Mẹo MT: Áp dụng sơ đồ Venn hoặc bảng chân trị logic để biểu diễn mối quan hệ giữa các đối tượng.

question_text: You are a selection centre assistant at a correctional service. Eleven candidates are waiting to have their identity documents checked before the day starts, and the stated cut-off is nine o’clock: anybody not checked in by then cannot take part and has to be offered another date. It is twenty to nine and each check takes about three minutes. Two of the eleven have already told you they cannot come back on another day. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Hand the queue to a colleague from the room next door and go and set up the first exercise, since the checks are somebody's job for the day and the room has to be ready.

Work through the eleven in the order they are standing, starting at the front of the line and working straight back along it, at three minutes each, and see how far you get before nine rather than making anybody feel singled out.

Ask the person running the day to move the nine o'clock cut-off back by fifteen minutes, explaining that eleven checks at three minutes each will not fit into the twenty left, so that everybody can be checked before anything begins.
Check the two who cannot come back first, then work through the rest in order, and tell the person running the day now how many will not be checked by nine, so that another date can be offered.
explanation: A: Passes responsibility to others: the colleague inherits a queue they cannot clear either, and nobody has told the person running the day that eleven will not be checked by nine. B: Treats order of arrival as fairness: it spends the last checks on people who can be offered another date, and the two who cannot come back are at the mercy of where they happened to stand. C: Reopens a fixed constraint before working inside it: the cut-off was stated to every candidate and the whole day is built on it, and you have not yet tried the one ordering that saves the people who cannot return. The most effective response is to check the two who cannot come back first, then work through the rest in order, and tell the person running the day at once how many will not be checked by nine: the cut-off is fixed and cannot be met for eleven people, so the thing left to protect is the two for whom another date is no use, and the person running the day needs the number while a second date can still be arranged. It is better than working through the eleven in the order they are standing, because order of arrival is not a reason and it spends the last checks on people who can come back. It is better than asking for the nine o’clock cut-off to be moved, because the cut-off was stated to every candidate and the day is built on it. The least effective response is to hand the queue to a colleague from the room next door and go and set up the first exercise: the checks were yours, the colleague inherits a queue they cannot clear either, and nobody has told the person running the day what is about to happen. The principle: when a stated cut-off will pass, work the queue by who has most to lose and tell the person who can still act.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân biệt rõ giữa 'Đúng' (True) và 'Có thể xảy ra' (Possible). Chỉ chọn kết luận chắc chắn 100%.

question_text: You are a service desk assistant at a correctional service. A member of the public arrives for an appointment that a different team booked, and it turns out the appointment was cancelled last week without anybody telling them. They are angry with you, they have taken a day off work to come in, and they say this is the second time it has happened to them. You can see the cancellation on your screen but not the reason for it, and the team that made the booking can be reached this morning. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Apologise, explain that the appointment was booked by a different team and that you cannot see why it was cancelled, and give the person the number for the team who can tell them, along with the booking reference from your screen.
Apologise for the wasted day, ring the team who made the booking while the person waits with you, and come back with either a new appointment or a time today when they will hear from somebody.
Blame the team who made the booking, telling the person that this happens every time their bookings come through this desk and that they ought to be complaining about them rather than about you.

Offer the person the next available appointment on the spot, checking the date is one they can take without another day off, and suggest they raise the cancellation with the team who booked it if they want to know why nobody told them.
explanation: A: Sends the person on with the problem: they have already lost a day and been let down twice, and a phone number puts the next piece of effort back onto them. C: Personalises the complaint: the person wants an appointment and an explanation, and turning a wasted day into an argument about which team is at fault leaves them holding neither. D: Fixes the diary and leaves the grievance: a second cancellation with no warning is the thing they came in angry about, and nobody has taken responsibility for finding out why. The most effective response is apologising for the wasted day, ringing the team who made the booking while the person waits with you, and coming back with either a new appointment or a time today when they will hear from somebody. The team is reachable this morning, so the person can leave with something instead of another errand. That is better than explaining that a different team booked it and giving them the number, because somebody who has lost a day and been let down twice should not have to make the next call themselves. It is better than offering the next appointment and suggesting they chase the cancellation, because that answers the diary and not the reason they are angry. The least effective response is blaming the team who made the booking and telling the person that they ought to be complaining about them: handing over the number at least points somewhere useful, and offering an appointment at least gives them a date, whereas an argument about whose fault it is puts your own position ahead of the person standing in front of you and gets them no closer to either. The principle: anger about something another team did is still your problem to resolve while the person is in front of you.
tip: Mẹo MT: Áp dụng sơ đồ Venn hoặc bảng chân trị logic để biểu diễn mối quan hệ giữa các đối tượng.

question_text: You are a candidate liaison assistant at a correctional service. An applicant rings, angry, having been told he was unsuccessful at the selection stage he sat last week. You had no part in that decision and cannot change it. The stated rule is that written reasons are sent by the team that runs the selection centre within five working days, and three days have passed. You have not seen his reasons and do not know how he scored. He wants somebody to tell him what went wrong. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell him the decision was close and that he will very likely succeed if he applies again, even though you cannot see how he scored or what the reasons say.
Read the stated five working days back to him, repeat that his reasons are not due for another two days, and end the call politely once you have said it a second time.

Offer to raise a formal complaint on his behalf about the selection stage today, and take down what he wants it to say, so that somebody senior looks at the decision again before his written reasons arrive.
Let him finish, tell him only what you can confirm when his reasons are due, and check today with the team that runs the selection centre that the date holds.
explanation: A: Gives an assurance you cannot stand behind: you have not seen his reasons, so a comfort offered now becomes a second contradiction when the written reasons arrive inside the five days. B: Ignores the applicant's actual need: the process is quoted correctly and the man is left with nothing he did not already have, three days into a five-day wait he is already struggling with. C: Escalates prematurely: the reasons he is entitled to are still two days away, and starting a complaint before he has read them commits him to a route he has not asked for. The most effective response is letting him finish, telling him only what you can confirm when his reasons are due, and checking today with the team that runs the selection centre that the date holds. He is angry about something you cannot change, so the only things you own are hearing him out and making sure the one commitment the organisation has made to him is kept. It beats reading the five working days back to him and ending the call, because quoting a rule at somebody who has already understood it answers nothing and leaves the five-day date unchecked. It is also better than offering to raise a complaint on his behalf, which starts a process he has not asked for before he has read the reasons he is waiting for. The least effective response is telling him the decision was close and that he will very likely succeed if he applies again: unlike the quoted process, which is at least true, and unlike the offered complaint, which he could decline, this is a statement you have no basis for, and it will be contradicted in writing within two days by the very document he is waiting on. The principle: when you cannot change a decision, give the person the facts you can stand behind and make sure the promises already made to them are kept.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân biệt rõ giữa 'Đúng' (True) và 'Có thể xảy ra' (Possible). Chỉ chọn kết luận chắc chắn 100%.

question_text: You are an information handling assistant at a correctional service. Over lunch a colleague tells you, asking you to keep it to yourself, that a letter about a member of the public went to the wrong address last week. Back at your desk you find that another team is due to post a second letter to that same address on Thursday. The stated rule is that a letter sent to a wrong address is reported the same day to the person who owns the record. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Assume the colleague has already reported it themselves, since the rule is well known, and leave Thursday's letter to the team that is sending it.
Warn the other team to hold Thursday's letter without saying why, so that the confidence is kept and the second letter does not go to the same wrong address.
Tell the colleague you must report the wrong address today, because a second letter goes there on Thursday, and report it to the person who owns the record.
Raise it at the team meeting next week, where the people who own the record will all be present and the pattern can be looked at properly.
explanation: A: Assumes the report has been made rather than checking: the colleague asked you to keep it quiet, which is a poor sign that they have declared it, and Thursday posts a second letter to the same wrong address. B: Hides the reason from the people acting on it: Thursday is covered, but the person who owns the record still does not know, and a team asked to stop without a reason will send it next time. D: Delays past Thursday: the second letter is posted before the meeting happens, so the one action that could have prevented a repeat arrives after the repeat. The most effective response is telling the colleague you must report the wrong address today and reporting it to the person who owns the record. A confidence cannot cover something that is about to happen again on Thursday, and telling the colleague first is what keeps it straight with them while still meeting the rule’s same day deadline. That is better than warning the other team without saying why, since Thursday is saved but the owner of the record is still unaware and the team has no reason to check next time. It is also better than raising it at next week’s meeting, because the second letter goes out first and the meeting can then only discuss what has already happened twice. The least effective response is assuming the colleague has reported it and leaving Thursday’s letter alone: somebody who asks you to keep a thing quiet is unlikely to have declared it, so nobody checks, nobody reports, and the same address receives a second letter, which is worse than a partial warning or a late discussion. The principle: a confidence stops being yours to keep the moment it bears on work somebody else is about to do.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân biệt rõ giữa 'Đúng' (True) và 'Có thể xảy ra' (Possible). Chỉ chọn kết luận chắc chắn 100%.

question_text: You are a candidate liaison assistant at a correctional service. A colleague you share the applicant enquiry inbox with did not come in yesterday and did not tell anybody. Six applicants who were promised calls got none. This morning they ask you, quite forcefully, to write in the shared log that they were working from home and to tell the person who runs the inbox the same if asked. You have already said you are not comfortable with it, and they are now annoyed with you. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Refuse again and tell the person who runs the inbox this morning what your colleague asked you to write, without speaking to your colleague again first.
Tell your colleague directly that you will not write anything untrue, that the six missed calls need fixing today, and that they should explain their own absence, since you were not there yourself.
Assure the person who runs the inbox that your colleague was working from home yesterday, which is what they asked, so that the disagreement ends and you can both get on with the day.
Agree to say nothing either way and simply ring the six applicants yourself today, leaving your colleague to explain their absence or not as they choose.
explanation: A: Escalates prematurely: your colleague has not yet been given a clear chance to put their own absence right, and going straight past them hardens a disagreement that could still be settled between you. C: Denies a fact you are holding: the absence is stated as unexplained, so this is not a version of events you are unsure about, and the person relying on the inbox is given a false account to keep a colleague comfortable. D: Prioritises harmony over honesty: the six applicants are looked after, but you have accepted a share in covering an absence, and the person who runs the inbox still has no idea why the calls were missed. The most effective response is to tell your colleague directly that you will not write anything untrue and that they should explain their own absence themselves: it settles the demand at its source, leaves the explaining with the person whose absence it was, and keeps the six missed calls on today rather than tomorrow. That is better than refusing again and reporting the request without speaking to your colleague first, because a disagreement that could still be resolved between two people is turned into a formal matter before either of them has tried. It is also better than saying nothing either way and quietly ringing the six applicants yourself, since that buys peace by taking on a share of the cover while the missed calls stay unexplained. The least effective response is to assure the person who runs the inbox that your colleague was working from home: the absence was unexplained and you know it, so a person relying on that inbox is handed something untrue, which is a different order of wrong from an awkward or premature conversation. The principle: settle the conflict with the person in front of you, and never settle it with a statement you know to be false.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân biệt rõ giữa 'Đúng' (True) và 'Có thể xảy ra' (Possible). Chỉ chọn kết luận chắc chắn 100%.

question_text: You are a contact handling assistant at a correctional service. You have spent a fortnight clearing a backlog of written enquiries. This morning you find that eleven of them have been reassigned overnight to a colleague, with no message to you, and six are ones you had already drafted replies for. The desk rule is that only the person an enquiry is assigned to may answer it, and the stated service standard is a reply within ten working days. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Answer the six you had already drafted that afternoon and close them off, although the desk rule is that only the person an enquiry is assigned to may answer it.
Say nothing and start on the next set of enquiries, telling yourself the fortnight of work still got done and that arguing about who answers what would only look petty.
Ask the person who moved the enquiries, today, why they were reassigned and what should happen to the six replies you have drafted, then agree with them how the ten day standard is met.
Raise it straight away with the person your supervisor reports to, as a fortnight of your work taken without a word, before speaking to anybody who moved the enquiries.
explanation: A: Breaches a stated rule to take the work back: two people are now answering the same eleven enquiries with no record of who said what, and the ten day standard is put at risk to settle a point about ownership. B: Swallows it in silence: the six drafted replies exist and nobody knows it, so the colleague starts them again and the ten day clock runs while the work is done twice. D: Escalates before asking: nobody has yet given a reason for the move, so the complaint is made about a decision whose purpose you have not heard, and the six drafts still go nowhere. The most effective response is asking the person who moved the enquiries why they were reassigned and what should happen to the six replies you have drafted. Eleven enquiries are running against a ten day standard, six of them already have replies that only you know about, and one conversation today settles both the reason and the plan. It beats saying nothing and starting on the next set, because the drafts are then wasted and the colleague repeats a fortnight of work under the same clock. It beats going straight to the person your supervisor reports to, because you would be complaining about a decision before hearing why it was made. The least effective response is answering the six yourself in spite of the desk rule that only the assigned person may reply: it breaks the rule the stem states, and it risks two replies going out on the same enquiry, which is a worse outcome for the public than either the silence or the early escalation. It is worse than saying nothing, which only wastes your own effort, and worse than the early escalation, which at least leaves the enquiries in one pair of hands. The principle: when work you own is taken, find out why before you react, and never take it back by breaking the rule that says who answers.
tip: Mẹo MT: Với bài toán quy luật chuỗi số, hãy xét hiệu số bậc 1, hiệu số bậc 2 hoặc tích lũy tiến.

question_text: You are a volunteer coordination assistant at a correctional service. A volunteer who has helped at events for two years asks whether they can bring a friend to Saturday’s event. The stated process is that anybody helping as a volunteer is registered a week beforehand, and Saturday is three days away. Two volunteers have dropped out and the event is short of people. The volunteer says the friend has done this at other events. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell the volunteer the friend can probably come and that you will sort the registration out afterwards, then spend the next two days asking colleagues whether anybody has the authority to approve it before Saturday.

Reply that registration needs a week's notice and leave it there, without asking the person running the event whether an exception is possible or telling the volunteer anything more, since the process is set by others.
Tell the volunteer today that the friend cannot be registered in time, explain what the week's notice is there for, and ask the person running the event how the shortfall can be covered.
Put the friend on Saturday's list yourself and let them turn up on the day, since the event is short of people and nobody checks the list once everybody is on site.
explanation: A: Over-promises: a probably that turns into a no on Saturday morning costs the volunteer more than a clear answer today, and the registration cannot be done afterwards. B: Ignores the volunteer's actual need: they are given a rule with no reason and no alternative, and the event is still two pairs of hands short on Saturday. D: Breaches the stated process quietly: the registration week exists for a reason, and doing it privately means nobody who could have found a proper answer is ever asked. The most effective response is telling the volunteer today that the friend cannot be registered in time, explaining what the week’s notice is there for, and asking the person running the event how the shortfall can be covered: the volunteer needs an answer they can act on, and the shortage belongs to somebody who can actually solve it. It beats telling the volunteer the friend can probably come while you look for somebody to approve it, because a probably that turns into a no on Saturday morning is worse for them than a clear answer today. It beats replying that the process is a week’s notice and leaving it there without asking whether an exception is possible, since the volunteer is left with a rule and no reason and the event is still short. The least effective response is putting the friend on the list yourself and letting them turn up on the day: it sets aside a registration process the organisation runs for a reason, and it does so quietly, so nobody who could have found another answer is ever asked. The principle: a good reason to break a process is a good reason to take it to the people who own it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You are a correspondence assistant at a correctional service. A member of the public wrote in three weeks ago, and a colleague replied promising a full written answer by Friday. You now know the answer cannot be prepared before the middle of next month, and the colleague who made that reply has left for two weeks. The person has already rearranged a meeting of their own so that they can act on the answer on Friday. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Wait until Friday morning and then telephone the person with the news, so that there is a chance the answer is further along by the time you have to explain the delay.
Write to the person today, say the answer cannot come before the middle of next month, apologise, and offer what Friday allows, since they can still put their own meeting back.
Let Friday pass without telling the person anything, since the answer is genuinely not ready, and wait until the middle of next month when there is something real to send.
Send the person a short note today saying their enquiry is still being worked on, and leave the date alone so that nobody has to explain a promise somebody else made.
explanation: A: Delays the difficult message: the meeting they moved is on Friday, so news that arrives that morning reaches them too late to be worth anything to them. C: Silent deadline slip: they rearranged a meeting on the strength of a date this organisation gave them, and the first thing they will learn is that Friday came and nothing arrived. D: Answers without correcting the expectation: a note that does not touch Friday leaves them still planning around it, which is the one thing they needed changing. The most effective response is to write to the person today, say the answer cannot come before the middle of next month, apologise for the reply they were given and offer what can be provided by Friday: they rearranged a meeting around a date that will not hold, and today is the last point at which they can rearrange it back. It is stronger than telephoning on Friday morning, because by then the meeting they moved is upon them and the information has lost the only value it had. It is stronger than sending a note that says the enquiry is still being worked on, because that leaves the wrong date standing and the wrong date is the whole problem. The least effective response is to let Friday pass without telling them anything and wait until there is something real to send: a late call at least reaches them, and a holding note at least shows somebody is there, whereas silence means the first thing they learn is that a date they were given passed unremarked. The principle: when a commitment made to somebody outside the organisation cannot be kept, tell them while they can still act on the news.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân biệt rõ giữa 'Đúng' (True) và 'Có thể xảy ra' (Possible). Chỉ chọn kết luận chắc chắn 100%.

question_text: You are a duty supervisor at a large consumer business. A weekly walk round the area you cover has to be recorded every week. On two of the last eight weeks it was not done, both times during unusually busy periods, and the sheet simply has gaps. A reviewer is going through the records with you this afternoon and has asked whether the walk has been completed every week. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Say that the walk is done every week as a matter of routine, and offer to send the reviewer the sheet afterwards so that she can look through the detail in her own time.
Tell the reviewer the walk was missed twice in eight weeks, show her the sheet, and say what was happening in the area on both of those weeks.
Tell her the sheet has gaps and that you will look into what happened on those two weeks, without saying that you already know both were busy periods.
Assure the reviewer that the walk was completed in every one of the eight weeks, since it nearly always is and the two gaps were the result of unusually busy periods.
explanation: A: Answers with the routine rather than the record: the gaps are still there and the reviewer finds them later, having been told something different to her face. C: Holds back the half you already know: the gaps are disclosed, and the explanation that would let her judge them properly is kept in reserve. D: Gives an assurance you know to be untrue: the reviewer's whole purpose is to find out what happened, and she is told the opposite by the one person who knows. The most effective response is to tell the reviewer the walk was missed twice in eight weeks, show her the sheet and say what was happening on those weeks: the record and your account of it agree, the context that makes the gaps understandable is offered rather than withheld, and she can do the job she is here to do. It beats answering with what happens as a matter of routine, because she will find the gaps afterwards having heard otherwise from you. It beats disclosing the gaps while keeping back what you know about them, because the explanation is the part that lets her judge them. The least effective response is assuring her that the walk was completed in every one of the eight weeks: the person with the facts tells the person checking them something untrue, which is a different kind of wrong from deflecting or from being incomplete. The principle: when somebody is checking a record, the record and what you say about it must be the same thing.

question_text: You are a scheduling coordinator at a large consumer business. A team member has asked for a weekend off in three weeks’ time and needs to know soon because she wants to book something. The manager who approves these is away until Thursday and has not seen the request. Requests like hers are usually agreed, but two other people have already been given that weekend. She has asked you today whether she can go ahead and book. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell her the request is as good as approved and that the weekend will be fine, since requests like hers are nearly always agreed once the manager sees them.
Tell her the request is with the manager, that two others already have that weekend, and that you will have an answer for her by Thursday evening.
Tell her you cannot say anything until the manager is back, and leave it there so that nothing you say can be taken as an answer either way.
Tell her to book something refundable and say you will try to sort the rota out afterwards if the manager turns the request down.
explanation: A: Gives a certainty you have not got: two people already have that weekend, so the one thing that might make this request different is the thing she is told not to worry about. C: Withholds what you do know to stay safe: she is planning something, and the fact that two people already have that weekend is exactly what would help her plan. D: Commits somebody else's decision on her behalf: the booking is safer, and a manager who has not been asked is expected to make the rota fit. The most effective response is to tell her the request is with the manager, that two others already have that weekend, and that she will have an answer by Thursday evening: she gets the true state of it, the one complication that might change the answer, and a date, which together are what let her decide about booking. It beats saying you cannot comment until the manager is back, because the two existing bookings are useful to her now. It beats telling her to book something refundable, because it still expects a manager who has not been asked to make the rota fit afterwards. The least effective response is telling her it is as good as approved and the weekend will be fine: the complication that makes her case different is waved away, which is a different kind of wrong from telling her nothing or from over-promising a fix. The principle: tell somebody what is actually known, complications included, and give them a date rather than a comfort.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân biệt rõ giữa 'Đúng' (True) và 'Có thể xảy ra' (Possible). Chỉ chọn kết luận chắc chắn 100%.

question_text: You are a brand assistant at a large consumer business. In a review of a campaign you had worked on for two months, a senior colleague went through your work in front of eight people and said most of it would have to be redone. Some of what she said was fair. You are in the group that has to deliver the reworked campaign in three weeks, and the next working session is tomorrow morning. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Withdraw from the campaign group after that review and ask your manager to put you on something else, since your work on it is evidently not what they want.
Go to tomorrow's session and say nothing about the review, since raising it would look like you cannot take criticism and the work is what matters now.
Ask your manager to raise with her how the review was conducted, since going through somebody's work like that in front of eight people is not how feedback should be given.
Go to tomorrow's session with a plan for the parts you accept and ask her to go through the parts you do not, so that the rework starts from an agreed brief.
explanation: A: Withdraws from a commitment after a hard hour: the group loses the person who knows the work best, three weeks before it is due, because of how the review felt. B: Buries the part you disagree with: the fair criticism and the unfair criticism are accepted together, and you rebuild to a brief you do not believe in. C: Turns the work into a complaint about conduct: it may well be justified, and three weeks before delivery it is the campaign that needs the attention. The most effective response is to go to tomorrow’s session with a plan for the parts you accept and ask her to go through the parts you do not: the three weeks start immediately, the criticism is separated into the half that improves the work and the half that needs testing, and the conversation happens with the person who made it. It beats saying nothing about the review, because you would rebuild against a brief you do not believe. It beats asking your manager to raise how the review was conducted, because that is a separate conversation and the campaign is due in three weeks. The least effective response is withdrawing from the group: a hard hour costs the campaign the person who knows it best, three weeks from delivery, which is a different kind of wrong from over-agreeing or from making it about conduct. The principle: take the part of hard feedback that is right, test the part that is not, and stay in the work.
tip: Mẹo MT: Với bài toán quy luật chuỗi số, hãy xét hiệu số bậc 1, hiệu số bậc 2 hoặc tích lũy tiến.

question_text: You are a shift supervisor at a large consumer business. A delivery the team has been waiting for since eight o’clock has not arrived, and the transport desk cannot say when it will. Six people are standing available and their shift ends at two. The team leader is asking you for a time, and the work that depends on the delivery has to be finished today or it moves to the weekend. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell the team exactly what transport has said and that you do not have a time yet, since guessing helps nobody, and come back to them by eleven with a time or another plan.
Say nothing to the team until transport gives you a time, so that you are not passing on information that might turn out to be wrong an hour later.
Put the team on other work for the morning and mention the delivery only if somebody asks about it, since there is nothing anybody standing here can do about a vehicle that has not arrived.
Tell the team leader the delivery is on its way and will be with them before the shift ends, which is what a team standing about needs to hear this morning.
explanation: B: Treats uncertainty as a reason for silence: six people spend the morning planning around a delivery nobody can promise, and the person who knows that is the one saying nothing. C: Manages the shift without informing it: the morning is used sensibly and the team leader still cannot plan the afternoon or the weekend around what you know. D: Gives an assurance nothing supports: transport has no time to give, so the comfort lasts until two o'clock and then the weekend plan is made on a promise that was never true. The most effective response is to tell the team exactly what transport has said, that there is no time yet, and that you will come back by eleven: it gives six people the real picture, it puts a decision point in the morning rather than at two o’clock, and it commits you to the follow-up rather than to a fact you do not have. It beats saying nothing until transport gives a time, because the morning is spent planning around something nobody can promise. It beats moving the team to other work and mentioning it only if asked, because the team leader is deciding about the afternoon and the weekend without what you know. The least effective response is telling the team leader the delivery is on its way and will arrive before the shift ends: no such assurance exists, and inventing one is a different kind of wrong from withholding or from managing quietly, because the plans made on it are wrong until two o’clock. The principle: when you do not know, say what you do know and when you will know more.
tip: Mẹo MT: Với bài toán quy luật chuỗi số, hãy xét hiệu số bậc 1, hiệu số bậc 2 hoặc tích lũy tiến.

question_text: You are a brand assistant at a large consumer business. Three things are due before Friday: a customer announcement, a set of images for the team who publish them, and a summary for your manager. The announcement has to go on a shared channel whose owner runs a queue and has given you a slot on Thursday. Your announcement matters most this week, and you can post to the channel yourself. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Do the images and the summary first because they are quick, and take the announcement to the channel owner on Thursday exactly as the queue arranges it.
Ask your manager to tell the channel owner to move your announcement up the queue, since it matters more this week than the items sitting in front of it.
Ask the channel owner today whether the announcement can move up, explain what is riding on it, and do the images and the summary while you wait for his answer.
Post the announcement on the shared channel yourself ahead of the queue, since your item is the most time-critical this week and the slot system is only there to keep things orderly.
explanation: A: Sequences by what is easy: the two small jobs are cleared, and the item with the most riding on it gets whatever attention Thursday leaves. B: Escalates before asking: the person who runs the queue has not been spoken to, and the first thing he hears is a manager rearranging his week. D: Breaches somebody else's control of a shared channel: the queue exists because everybody's item feels urgent, and jumping it decides that question on your own behalf. The most effective response is to ask the channel owner whether the announcement can move up, explain what is riding on it, and do the images and the summary while you wait: the request goes to the person who owns the queue, the case for it is made rather than assumed, and the other two jobs progress meanwhile. It beats doing the quick jobs first and taking Thursday as it comes, because the most important item is then given the least thought. It beats asking your manager to have it moved, because nobody has yet asked the person who runs the queue. The least effective response is posting ahead of the queue yourself: a shared arrangement is set aside by somebody who decided their own item outranked the others, which is a different kind of wrong from sequencing badly or from going over somebody’s head. The principle: where a shared queue decides the order, the way to move up it is to ask its owner, not to step round it.

question_text: You are a supply chain graduate at a large consumer business. A business customer’s order was due yesterday and has not arrived. The tracking shows it left and then nothing. The customer has emailed once, politely, asking where it is. Deliveries occasionally turn up a day or two late without anybody intervening. Chasing it properly means ringing the carrier and waiting on hold. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Reply to the customer that the order has left and that tracking will update when it moves, which is all the information the system currently gives you about it.
Ring the carrier now and say nothing to the customer until you have an answer, since a reply with no news in it will only invite another email.
Wait for the order to arrive in its own time, since deliveries often turn up a day or two late and the customer has only written once so far.
Reply today to say you are chasing the carrier and when you will come back to him, ring the carrier, and update him either way so that he knows a person has it.
explanation: A: Passes on the screen rather than the situation: he can read tracking himself, and nothing about his order has actually been chased. B: Leaves a waiting customer with silence: the chase is right and he does not know it is happening, so his next email arrives anyway. C: Waits out a customer who has asked a direct question: nothing is checked, nothing is answered, and the outcome depends entirely on the order turning up. The most effective response is to reply today saying you are chasing the carrier and when you will come back, ring them, and update him either way: he knows a person has his problem, the chase actually happens, and the commitment is one you control. It beats telling him tracking will update when it moves, because he can see that himself. It beats saying nothing to the customer until the carrier answers, because his second email arrives while you are on hold. The least effective response is waiting for the order to turn up in its own time: a direct question goes unanswered and nothing is checked, so a good outcome depends entirely on luck, which is a different kind of wrong from being unhelpfully literal or from being quiet while you work. The principle: a customer who has asked where something is gets an action and a time, not a probability.

question_text: You are a resourcing assistant at a large consumer business. Two vacancies have to be filled before a busy fortnight starts on Monday, and you have spent two days working through agencies, three of which have already come back with nobody. You also have a routine reporting task due Friday that takes an afternoon. It is Wednesday. Your team leader has asked how the vacancies are going. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell your team leader the vacancies are in hand, finish the reporting task today while it is quiet, and go back to the agencies with the whole of Thursday and Friday.
Give the two vacancies to a colleague on the team without going through which agencies have already been tried, so that you can get the reporting task cleared before Friday.
Tell your team leader today that three agencies have come back with nobody and ask whether the reporting task can move, so that Thursday can go into the vacancies instead.
Split Thursday between the agencies and the reporting task so that both are moving, and decide on Friday morning which of the two needs the remaining time.
explanation: A: Reports comfort rather than position: two days of work have produced nobody, and the person who could widen the search hears that everything is fine. B: Hands the harder job on without its history: the colleague repeats two days of calls from the beginning, with a Monday deadline that is now three days closer. D: Defers the choice by dividing the day: Friday morning is too late to start either job properly, and Monday does not move. The most effective response is to tell your team leader that three agencies have come back with nobody, ask whether the reporting task can move, and put Thursday into the vacancies: the deadline that matters is Monday, the person who can change the other deadline is the one being asked, and the real position is on the table. It beats saying the vacancies are in hand, because two days have produced nobody and that is the fact she needs. It beats splitting Thursday between both, because neither job is finished and Friday morning is too late to start. The least effective response is giving the vacancies to a colleague without the history: two days of calls are repeated from scratch with three days left before Monday, which is a different kind of wrong from reassuring your manager or from dividing your time badly. The principle: when the work will not fit, put the real position in front of the person who owns the deadlines rather than rearranging it yourself.
