question_text: You are a customer care assistant at a large consumer business. A customer has been waiting three weeks for a replacement and has now rung for the fourth time. You can see a manager’s authorisation code in a shared document, left there for a different type of case, which would let you settle the whole thing today. Your team leader is in a meeting until three, and the customer is on the line now. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Settle the case now with the manager's authorisation code from the shared document, since the customer has waited three weeks and the outcome would be the same either way.
Tell the customer that nothing can be done until your team leader is out of her meeting this afternoon, and ask him to ring the team back himself after three o'clock.
Apologise, take the case number, and put a written request to your team leader so that she can look at it when her meeting finishes this afternoon.
Tell the customer what you can do now and what needs approval, put an urgent note to your team leader with the case number, and commit to ringing him back before five.
explanation: A: Breaches an authority that was never given to you: the code was left for another purpose, and a good outcome reached that way is still an approval nobody made. B: Ignores the customer's actual need: a fourth call is answered with a fifth call, and the work that could be done meanwhile is not started. C: Leaves the customer holding the uncertainty: the request is sound, and the person who has rung four times is told nothing about what will happen or when. The most effective response is to tell the customer what you can do now and what needs approval, put an urgent note to your team leader, and commit to ringing back before five: it gives a customer on his fourth call the two things he does not have, which are a picture and a time, and it moves the approval without pretending you hold it. It beats asking him to ring back after three, because the fifth call is his to make and nothing progresses meanwhile. It beats a written request with nothing said to him, because he is left holding the uncertainty for another afternoon. The least effective response is settling it now with a manager’s code found in a shared document: the outcome may be right and the approval is one nobody gave, which is a different kind of wrong from being unhelpful or slow. The principle: an authority you can reach is not an authority you have, and the customer’s wait is not the thing that grants it.

question_text: You are a deployment analyst at a consultancy, two days into setting up a client’s new stock system. You were shown the steps once, and much of what you are doing you do not follow. Nobody has asked how you are getting on, and what you have produced so far has not been looked at by anyone. The client expects the setup to be finished on Friday. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Work through the remaining steps on your own and assume the parts you do not follow will come clear by the time Friday arrives.
Tell your team lead today which parts you do not follow, ask for an hour to go through them, and have what you have built so far checked, so that Friday's setup does not rest on guesswork.
Work through Friday night and the weekend so that the setup is finished, and raise what you did not understand at the review afterwards.
Ask a colleague quietly at lunch to explain the steps you are stuck on, and say nothing to your team lead about how far behind you feel.
explanation: A: Declines to check something you already know you do not understand: Friday arrives with a client's stock system set up by somebody who was guessing, and nobody has looked at any of it. C: Spends effort on the wrong problem: the hours go into work you cannot judge, and the gap in your understanding surfaces after the point where it could have been closed. D: Fixes half of it: you get an explanation, and the one person who could have your work checked before Friday still believes it is going well. The most effective response is to tell your team lead today which parts you do not follow and ask for an hour to go through them. Two days in there is still time to learn the steps and to have the early work looked at, and the person who can arrange both is the one who currently believes you are fine. It beats asking a colleague at lunch to explain the steps and saying nothing to your team lead, because an explanation at lunch still leaves everything you have built unchecked, and the client’s Friday depends on that work being right. It beats working the weekend to finish the setup and raising what you did not understand afterwards, because more hours on steps you do not follow produce more of the same uncertain output, not a system anybody can trust. The least effective response is working through the remaining steps alone and assuming the parts you do not follow will come clear: the other three at least add something, whether understanding or hours or both, whereas this one settles for hoping the difficulty resolves itself, so nobody checks the work and nobody learns there was a problem until the client has the system. The principle: say early that you are out of your depth, while there is still time for it to cost nothing.

question_text: You are a project support officer at a consultancy. Since somebody left three weeks ago, one person on the engagement has covered two people’s actions and has worked every evening, while the rest of you finish at a normal hour. They have asked you not to raise it, because they do not want to look as though they cannot cope. The plan for next month gives them more, not less. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Take some of the actions on quietly yourself over the next few weeks, so that the hours come down without anybody having to be told what has been happening.
Leave next month's plan alone and keep the extra actions where they are, because sharing them out would put two more of them on you every week.
Tell your colleague they should raise it with the team lead themselves, and leave it with them to decide whether they want to do that or not.
Tell your colleague you will raise how the work is spread rather than how they are coping, then put the two people's actions in front of your team lead this week.
explanation: A: Treats a resourcing gap as a personal favour: two people's work is still being done by two people, and whoever writes next month's plan is still working from a team that looks fully staffed. B: Takes the advantage for your own gain: the arrangement lasts another month because it suits the people it does not fall on, and the one person carrying it pays for that quietly. C: Puts the step on the person least able to take it: they have already said why they will not, and next month's plan is written whether they speak or not. The most effective response is to tell your colleague you will raise how the work is spread and put the actions in front of your team lead. It respects what your colleague asked by making the subject the workload rather than their capacity, it reaches the person who writes next month’s plan while it can still change, and it does not leave one person carrying two roles by default. It beats taking some of the actions on quietly yourself, because absorbing the overflow yourself keeps the shortfall invisible to whoever plans the month, so the same gap is planned again. It beats telling your colleague to raise it with the team lead themselves, because they have already explained why they will not raise it, and the plan does not wait for them. The least effective response is leaving next month’s plan alone and keeping the extra actions where they are: the other three all move something, whereas this one leaves an exhausted colleague where they are for another month for the plain reason that the alternative costs you, which turns a judgement about the engagement into a judgement about your own week. The principle: raise a workload that has stopped being sustainable, and separate the work from the person doing it.

question_text: You are a deployment analyst at a consultancy, checking the facts in a bid document that goes to Ashenden Ports on Friday. One paragraph says the team has put the same system into three ports. The team has done two ports and one inland depot. A checklist goes with the document, and you are the person filling it in. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell the manager running the bid today exactly what the team has done, since the third port was an inland depot, and ask for the paragraph to be reworded before the document goes out.
Mark the claim as checked on the checklist and let the document go out with the wording exactly as it stands.
Reword the paragraph yourself to say two ports and one depot, and mark the checklist as checked without telling anybody it was changed.
Note on the checklist that one of the three was an inland depot, and leave the paragraph itself exactly as the bid team wrote it.
explanation: B: Certifies something you know is untrue: the checklist is the only record that the claim was tested, and it now says a third port exists because you were the person who signed it off. C: Changes somebody else's words unannounced: the wording is right afterwards, and the people whose bid it is find a paragraph they did not write. D: Records a correction where nobody will read it: the checklist stays with your team, and the client still receives a document saying three ports. The most effective response is to tell the manager running the bid what the team has done and ask for the paragraph to be reworded. The difference between three ports and two ports and a depot is exactly the kind of thing a reader will test, and there are days left in which to fix the sentence. It beats rewording the paragraph yourself without telling anybody, because the bid team find their own paragraph altered by somebody who never told them. It beats noting on the checklist that one of them was an inland depot and leaving the paragraph, because the checklist stays inside your team while the client reads the paragraph. The least effective response is marking the claim as checked on the checklist and letting the document go out: the other three all leave a true account somewhere, whereas this one puts your name against a check that was never passed, so the only record of the claim being tested says it was sound. The principle: the checklist says what you found, and a wrong sentence is corrected by the people who own it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You are a market research assistant at a consultancy, interviewing people at a client’s sites from a list of names the client drew up themselves. You have realised that one of the six interviews you did was with somebody who does the same job but was not on that list. The client expects the notes tomorrow. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Leave the off-list interview out of the pack altogether and send the client five interviews tomorrow, so that everything in the notes came from the list they drew up.
Send the notes over tomorrow with the off-list interview included and a line saying who it was with, and tell the manager running the study about it afterwards.
Tell the manager running the study today that one of the six interviews was with somebody off the client's list, since they must decide before the notes go over.
Put the write-up in the pack as the sixth interview the client asked for, and keep your own mistake to yourself so that nobody has to redo the work.
explanation: A: Reduces the evidence rather than reporting it: the client gets five interviews where six were agreed, and is never told why the sixth is missing. B: Tells the client before telling your own team: the manager running the study learns from the client's reply that an interview was off the list. D: Hides your own mistake: the client's findings rest on six interviews whose people they chose, and one of them is now somebody they did not choose. The most effective response is to tell the manager today that one of the six interviews was with somebody off the client’s list. It reaches the person who can decide what to do while there is still a day to do it in, and the choice between redoing the interview, keeping it with a note, or dropping it stays with the engagement rather than with you alone. It beats sending the notes tomorrow with a line about the off-list interview and telling the manager afterwards, because your own manager should not learn about it from the client’s reply. It beats leaving the off-list interview out and sending the client five interviews instead, because quietly shipping five interviews where six were agreed leaves the client wondering what happened to the sixth, or worse, not noticing. The least effective response is putting the write-up in the pack as the sixth interview and keeping your own mistake to yourself: the other three all leave the client or the manager able to see what the pack actually contains, whereas this one presents an interview with somebody the client did not pick as one they did, so findings they will act on rest on evidence they never agreed to. The principle: an error in evidence belongs in front of the person who owns the study, on the day you find it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You are a strategy analyst at a consultancy, finishing an options paper for a client’s steering group. The paper was due last Wednesday and was finished yesterday. The manager running the engagement asks you to put last Wednesday’s date on the front of it before it is circulated, so that the steering group reads it as having arrived on time. The client’s project office keeps its own list of what was received and when. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Say you would rather put today's date on it, since the client's project office logs what arrived when, and offer a covering line explaining the delay.
Circulate the paper with today's date on it and say nothing at all about the week it lost, leaving the steering group to notice the gap if they ever look for it.
Ask the manager to put the date on it themselves, and circulate the paper only once somebody else has dated the front page.
Change the date on the report to last Wednesday before circulating it, and let the steering group read the paper as delivered on the day it was due.
explanation: B: Leaves the client to find the slip: the date is honest, and the week the paper lost is left for the steering group to work out for itself. C: Passes an act you are already part of: the paper still goes out under last Wednesday, and the only thing that changes is whose hand typed it. D: Alters a record of when work arrived: the client's own list of what was received stops matching what happened, over a week nobody can get back anyway. The most effective response is to say you would rather put today’s date on it and to offer to explain the delay in the covering email. The date is a fact about when the paper arrived, the manager is entitled to a reason and a remedy rather than a refusal, and a covering line costs the engagement far less than a steering group discovering the paper was late. It beats circulating the paper with today’s date and saying nothing about the week it lost, because the steering group is left to work out for itself that a week went missing. It beats asking the manager to date it themselves and waiting until somebody else has done it, because the paper still goes out under last Wednesday and the only difference is whose hand typed it. The least effective response is changing the date on the report to last Wednesday before circulating it: the other three all leave the client able to see when the paper really arrived, whereas this one makes a record say something that did not happen, and the project office’s list stops being worth reading. The principle: a date records when something arrived, so fix the lateness in the covering words, never in the record.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You are a correspondence assistant at a fire and rescue service. The company that prints and posts your standard letters has put the wrong reference number on 200 letters going out on Thursday, and says it will not reprint them because the run is boxed. Anybody ringing the enquiry line to quote that number will find it matches no record. The person who owns the letter template is away until Friday. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell the people who answer the enquiry line today what the wrong number is and what to do with anybody who quotes it, and ask the print company to confirm in writing what has gone out.
Send the whole matter to the template owner's manager on Thursday morning and ask them to stop the run, before finding out whether 200 boxed letters can be held at all.
Write to all 200 recipients with a correction of your own wording, on the basis that the template owner would want that done, and tell the enquiry line what you have sent them.
Let Thursday's run go out as it is and wait for Friday, without telling the people who answer the enquiry line what the number on those 200 letters is going to look like.
explanation: B: Escalates prematurely: nobody has established whether a boxed run can be stopped, and the calls still land on Thursday while the request works its way up. C: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholder's: a second letter from somebody who does not own the template risks contradicting the first, and the owner returns on Friday to a correction they never agreed. D: Withholds what colleagues need before they need it: the people taking Thursday's calls become the only ones who cannot explain a number that matches nobody's record. The most effective response is telling the people who answer the enquiry line today what the wrong number is and what to do with anybody who quotes it: 200 letters land on Thursday, the template owner is not back until Friday, and the only people who can absorb the calls are the ones who take them. It beats sending the whole matter to the template owner’s manager and asking for the run to be stopped, because nobody has yet established whether boxed letters can be held, and the calls arrive on Thursday either way. It beats writing to the recipients with a correction of your own wording, since a second letter from somebody who does not own the template risks contradicting the first one. The least effective response is letting Thursday’s run go out and waiting for Friday without warning the enquiry line: the people who will take the calls are then the only ones in the organisation who do not know what is coming. The principle: when something is going to land on colleagues, tell them before it lands rather than after.
tip: Mẹo MT: Với bài toán quy luật chuỗi số, hãy xét hiệu số bậc 1, hiệu số bậc 2 hoặc tích lũy tiến.

question_text: You are a service desk assistant at a fire and rescue service. Looking something up this morning, you notice that the standard reply the desk sends to anybody asking about the application process gives a closing date that passed three weeks ago. The reply goes out automatically to everyone who writes in. The person who owns that wording sits in another team and is busy this week. Nobody at the desk has mentioned it, nothing you are working on depends on it, and no one has complained. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Leave it as it is and get on with your own work, on the basis that the wording belongs to another team and nobody has complained about it in three weeks.
Raise it at the desk meeting next week so that the team can agree together whether the wrong date is worth taking to the other team at all.
Note exactly what the wrong date says, send it to the person who owns the wording today with corrected words attached, so that they need only approve it this week.
Answer the enquiries yourself with the right date whenever one reaches your desk, so that anybody who writes in this week is told correctly, and leave the standard reply alone.
explanation: A: Assumes the error is somebody else's to notice: an automatic reply keeps sending a dead date to every person who writes in, and the fact that nobody has complained is what makes you the only person who can raise it. B: Downgrades a plain error to an agenda item: a date that has demonstrably passed needs no group view, and the reply goes out every day between now and the meeting. D: Treats the symptom and not the source: the automatic reply still reaches everybody who does not happen to land on your desk, and it goes on doing so after this week. The most effective response is writing down what the wrong date says and sending it to the person who owns the wording today with corrected words attached: the wording is theirs to change, they are busy, and the fastest way to get a change made is to hand them something ready to approve rather than something they have to work out for themselves. It is stronger than raising it at the desk meeting next week, because the reply goes out automatically every day in between and there is nothing for a team to decide about a date that has plainly passed. It is also stronger than answering enquiries yourself with the right date, since the automatic reply keeps reaching everybody who does not come through you. The least effective response is leaving the wording as it is on the basis that it belongs to another team: an error nobody has noticed is still an error, and the people writing in are the ones who pay for it. The principle: something wrong that nobody has claimed is still somebody’s to raise, and the person who noticed it is that somebody.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân biệt rõ giữa 'Đúng' (True) và 'Có thể xảy ra' (Possible). Chỉ chọn kết luận chắc chắn 100%.

question_text: You are an enquiry desk assistant at a fire and rescue service. You have promised eleven callers a reply before the desk closes at four, and you are halfway through the list. At two, the person who runs the department asks you to type up and circulate the notes from this morning’s briefing instead, saying it will take an hour. When you explain the eleven callers, they answer sharply that the notes matter more and walk off. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Type the notes up straight away and get through as many of the eleven replies as the remaining time allows, leaving whoever you do not reach to ring back tomorrow.
Type the notes up, then stop taking anything beyond your own list after that exchange, and let the eleven callers wait rather than raise the clash with someone who spoke to you like that.
Go back to the person who runs the department, say plainly that the notes will cost you the eleven promised replies, and ask which of the two they want by four.
Carry on with the eleven replies and put the notes off until tomorrow morning, on the basis that a promise to a caller outranks an internal request made at short notice.
explanation: A: Lets a promise lapse without a word: the callers who are not reached were given a time by you, and none of them learns before four that the reply is not coming. B: Withdraws help after a disagreement: the sharp answer is turned into a reason to stop cooperating, so eleven people who were promised a reply pay for a two minute exchange at the desk. D: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholder's: the person who asked may well have a reason for wanting the notes circulated today, and they are never given the chance to weigh the eleven callers against it. The most effective response is to go back to the person who runs the department and ask which of the two they want by four: they made the request without knowing what it displaces, and two hours is still enough time for them to move one or the other. That is better than typing the notes and reaching as many replies as the time allows, because the callers who miss out were given a time by you and would hear nothing at all. It is also better than carrying on with the replies and putting the notes off until tomorrow, since that decides on the requester’s behalf without ever telling them the choice existed. The least effective response is to type the notes and then stop taking anything beyond your own list after that exchange: a sharp remark becomes a reason to withhold ordinary cooperation, and eleven callers who were promised a reply before four are the people who actually pay for it. The principle: when pressure lands badly, answer the work and not the tone, and put the clash back to the person who can settle it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You are a team support assistant at a fire and rescue service. A colleague on your team tells you that she posted a letter to the wrong address last week, and asks you to keep it to yourself because she will be in trouble if it comes out. The person the letter was meant for has been waiting for it and has to act on what it says by Friday. Nobody else knows. The person who runs your team is in this afternoon. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell your colleague you cannot keep it quiet, since somebody must act on that letter by Friday, and ask her to speak to the person who runs your team today, or say that you will.
Keep it to yourself as she asked, but ring the person the letter was meant for yourself to check whether anything has reached them this week.
Bring it up with the rest of the team behind her back, so that everybody knows whose mistake it was before the person waiting for the letter starts asking questions.
Say nothing for now and watch whether the person waiting gets in touch before Friday, on the basis that the letter may still find its way to the right address.
explanation: B: Works round the problem instead of naming it: a quiet check does not get the letter reissued before Friday, and it leaves your colleague carrying a mistake nobody can help her fix. C: Turns a colleague's mistake into team gossip: it reaches everybody except the two people who could act on it, and the person waiting on Friday is no better off for any of it. D: Waits for the problem to solve itself: the letter has gone to the wrong address, so nothing about waiting makes it arrive, and Friday comes with somebody unable to act. The most effective response is telling your colleague you cannot keep it quiet while somebody is waiting to act, and asking her to speak to the person who runs your team today: the mistake is hers to own, the offer to raise it yourself gives her a way through, and Friday is close. It is stronger than keeping it to yourself and ringing the person the letter was meant for, because a quiet check confirms the problem without getting anything reissued. It is also stronger than saying nothing and watching whether they get in touch, since a letter at the wrong address does not arrive at the right one by being left. The least effective response is bringing it up with the rest of the team behind her back: it makes the mistake everybody’s business except that of the two people whose business it is, and the person waiting is still waiting. The principle: a mistake with somebody waiting on it goes to the people who can put it right, and to nobody else.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân biệt rõ giữa 'Đúng' (True) và 'Có thể xảy ra' (Possible). Chỉ chọn kết luận chắc chắn 100%.

question_text: You are a shift team member at a fire and rescue service. At the end of each shift every person is supposed to write and sign their own entry in the handover record, so that the team coming on knows who to ask about what. To get everybody away on time, one of your team has taken to writing and signing all four entries in advance. Everybody knows, nobody has raised it, and the team coming on has twice asked you about an entry you did not write. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Raise it with the colleague first, say that you will be writing and signing your own entry from now on, and tell them why the team coming on needs to know who to ask.
Write and sign your own entry each shift without saying anything to the colleague, and let the team coming on work out for themselves whose entries are whose.
Report the practice to your supervisor without speaking to the colleague first, since the rule is plain and it is not your place to police the habits of your own team.
Bring it up in front of the whole team at the start of the next shift, naming the colleague and reading out the entries, and say they have been signing for work they did not do.
explanation: B: Fixes it only for yourself: three of the four entries stay in one hand, so the people coming on are still asking the wrong person about most of the shift. C: Escalates before speaking to the person: nobody has ever raised it, so the colleague has had no chance to stop, and a report lands as an accusation rather than a correction. D: Blames a colleague in front of the team: it makes a private correction into a public accusation, aimed at the person everybody relies on to get them away on time. The most effective response is to raise it with the colleague first, say that you will be writing and signing your own entry from now on, and tell them why the team coming on needs to know who to ask: the shortcut has a real benefit so it deserves a conversation rather than an ambush, and the team coming on has already been sent to the wrong person twice. It is better than writing and signing your own entry each shift without saying anything, because the other three entries stay in one hand and the people coming on still cannot tell whose is whose. It is better than reporting the practice to your supervisor without speaking to the colleague first, because nobody has ever raised it and the colleague has had no chance to stop. The least effective response is to bring it up in front of the whole team at the start of the next shift and say the colleague has been signing for work they did not do: it makes a private correction into a public accusation, aimed at somebody the whole team relies on. The principle: a shortcut that breaks a stated rule is raised with the person taking it, in private, before it is raised anywhere else.
tip: Mẹo MT: Áp dụng sơ đồ Venn hoặc bảng chân trị logic để biểu diễn mối quan hệ giữa các đối tượng.

question_text: You are an engagement events assistant at a prison service. A community group running Thursday’s joint event needs the final numbers and the room layout from you by noon tomorrow, which you agreed with its organiser a fortnight ago. Yesterday you were also given the write-up of feedback forms from last month’s events, wanted by the end of the week. It became clear this morning that you cannot finish both by noon tomorrow, and the organiser does not know that yet. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Give the morning to the feedback write-up and the afternoon to the numbers and layout, then see tomorrow which of the two is nearer to being finished.
Assume the community group will be relaxed about noon, say nothing to its organiser, and spend today and tomorrow morning on the feedback write-up, leaving the numbers and layout unfinished.
Finish the numbers and the room layout for noon tomorrow, and tell the person who asked for the feedback write-up this morning that it will now come at the end of next week.
Do the feedback write-up first because it was the most recent thing you were asked to do, and start the numbers and layout with whatever time is left tomorrow.
explanation: A: Splits effort so nothing finishes: noon tomorrow is fixed and the feedback is not due until the end of the week, so dividing today between them risks missing the only date somebody outside is waiting on. B: Assumes goodwill instead of checking it: nobody has asked the organiser anything, she is expecting the layout at noon for an event two days later, and she finds out only when it fails to arrive. D: Ranks the work by who asked most recently: recency is not a reason, the feedback has four more days and the layout has until noon, so the two dates are never actually compared. The most effective response is finishing the numbers and the room layout for noon tomorrow and telling the person who asked for the feedback write-up that it will now come at the end of next week. One date is tomorrow with an outside group behind it and the other has the rest of the week, so the order is settled by the dates, and the person whose work slips hears it while they can still do something. It beats giving the morning to the feedback and the afternoon to the numbers, because the fixed noon deadline should not be spending half of today competing with work that is not due yet. It is also better than doing the feedback first because it was asked most recently, which orders the day by nothing at all. The least effective response is assuming the community group will be relaxed about noon: unlike alternating, which at least advances both, and unlike the recency order, which at least decides something, this rests the whole plan on goodwill nobody has tested, and the organiser learns of the slip only when noon passes. The principle: order work by the dates people are relying on, and tell whoever loses out while they still have room to move.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You are a trainee at a prison service. Each morning the group is supposed to check its own equipment against the issue list and initial the sheet, which takes twenty minutes. For the past fortnight one of the group has initialled the sheet for everybody at once, before anyone has checked anything, and nobody has said a word, because it buys the group twenty minutes. The stated rule is that you initial only for equipment you have checked yourself. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Agree with the person doing it to keep it between the group until somebody senior asks, since a fortnight has passed without trouble and raising it now would land everybody in it.

Tell the person that from tomorrow you will initial only for equipment you have checked yourself, and raise the fortnight of unchecked sheets with the person running the course, since people rely on that equipment.

Check your own equipment against the issue list each morning and initial only your own line on the sheet, and say nothing to anybody about the fortnight of sheets that were initialled before anybody had checked anything.

Raise it with the person running the course as something the whole group has been doing for a fortnight, without saying anything first to the person who has been initialling the sheet for everybody before anybody has checked.
explanation: A: Joins an agreement to keep it quiet: a fortnight of sheets says the equipment was checked when it was not, and you are now one of the people keeping that from anybody who relies on it. C: Fixes your own conduct and leaves the sheet wrong: the fortnight of entries still says the equipment was checked, and the group carries on exactly as it was. D: Escalates without speaking to the person first: they have been doing it openly for a fortnight in the belief that nobody minds, and the first they hear of the objection is from above. The most effective response is telling the person that from tomorrow you will initial only for equipment you have checked yourself and raising it with the person running the course. The stated rule is that an initial means you checked it, a fortnight of sheets now says something untrue about the equipment, and both halves are needed: your own conduct from tomorrow, and somebody able to put the sheets right. It beats checking your own equipment and initialling only your own line while saying nothing about the fortnight, because the sheets already signed still assert checks that never happened. It beats raising it with the person running the course without speaking to the person doing it, because they have been doing it openly and deserve to hear the objection from you first. The least effective response is agreeing to keep it between the group until somebody senior asks: it makes you part of an arrangement to hold back something the people relying on that equipment need to know, and unlike the other two it makes the concealment deliberate and shared. It is worse than fixing only your own line, which at least stops adding to it, and worse than going over the person’s head, which at least gets it looked at. The principle: a shortcut that saves everybody time is still a false record, and an agreement to say nothing about it makes it yours as well.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You are a reception desk assistant at a prison service. A member of the public has come to the desk angry about a decision made by a team you have no part in, and that decision cannot be changed by anybody at the desk. He has already been telephoned twice about it and says nobody explains anything. The team that made the decision publishes a written appeal route, and the deadline for using it is a week today. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell him you will look into it yourself and come back to him, then send a message to the team that made the decision asking them to think again about it.
Pass him over to the team that made the decision by giving him their number to ring, since they are the only people who can explain it and the desk cannot change anything.
Apologise for the way he has been treated and promise to note his concerns on the file, then take his details so that somebody can telephone him about it a third time.
Hear him out, say plainly that the desk cannot change the decision, and give him the written appeal route marked with the deadline a week today, since two calls have already failed him.
explanation: A: Over-promises: you cannot look into a decision you had no part in and cannot change, and the days he spends waiting for your answer come out of the appeal week. B: Passes the problem back to where it failed: he has rung twice without getting an explanation, so the same number is not an answer, and nobody has told him about the appeal deadline. C: Repeats what has already failed: a third telephone call is what left him without an explanation twice over, and the written appeal route with its deadline still goes unmentioned. The most effective response is to hear him out, tell him plainly that the desk cannot change the decision, and give him the written appeal route with the deadline of a week today marked on it: he has been telephoned twice without getting an explanation, the appeal is the one thing that can still change the outcome, and the deadline is close enough to matter. It is better than telling him you will look into it yourself and asking the team to think again, because you cannot look into a decision you had no part in and the waiting comes out of his appeal week. It is better than apologising, noting his concerns on the file and taking his details for a third telephone call, because calls are exactly what has already failed him. The least effective response is to pass him over to the team that made the decision by giving him their number to ring: he has rung twice, nobody explained anything, and sending him back to the same number is the desk deciding his problem belongs to somebody else. The principle: when you cannot change the outcome, give the person the honest position and the one route that can.
tip: Mẹo MT: Với bài toán quy luật chuỗi số, hãy xét hiệu số bậc 1, hiệu số bậc 2 hoặc tích lũy tiến.

question_text: You are an information handling assistant at a prison service. Over lunch a colleague tells you, asking you to keep it to yourself, that a letter about a member of the public went to the wrong address last week. Back at your desk you find that another team is due to post a second letter to that same address on Thursday. The stated rule is that a letter sent to a wrong address is reported the same day to the person who owns the record. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Assume the colleague has already reported it themselves, since the rule is well known, and leave Thursday's letter to the team that is sending it.
Warn the other team to hold Thursday's letter without saying why, so that the confidence is kept and the second letter does not go to the same wrong address.
Tell the colleague you must report the wrong address today, because a second letter goes there on Thursday, and report it to the person who owns the record.
Raise it at the team meeting next week, where the people who own the record will all be present and the pattern can be looked at properly.
explanation: A: Assumes the report has been made rather than checking: the colleague asked you to keep it quiet, which is a poor sign that they have declared it, and Thursday posts a second letter to the same wrong address. B: Hides the reason from the people acting on it: Thursday is covered, but the person who owns the record still does not know, and a team asked to stop without a reason will send it next time. D: Delays past Thursday: the second letter is posted before the meeting happens, so the one action that could have prevented a repeat arrives after the repeat. The most effective response is telling the colleague you must report the wrong address today and reporting it to the person who owns the record. A confidence cannot cover something that is about to happen again on Thursday, and telling the colleague first is what keeps it straight with them while still meeting the rule’s same day deadline. That is better than warning the other team without saying why, since Thursday is saved but the owner of the record is still unaware and the team has no reason to check next time. It is also better than raising it at next week’s meeting, because the second letter goes out first and the meeting can then only discuss what has already happened twice. The least effective response is assuming the colleague has reported it and leaving Thursday’s letter alone: somebody who asks you to keep a thing quiet is unlikely to have declared it, so nobody checks, nobody reports, and the same address receives a second letter, which is worse than a partial warning or a late discussion. The principle: a confidence stops being yours to keep the moment it bears on work somebody else is about to do.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You are a candidate liaison assistant at a prison service. An applicant rings, angry, having been told he was unsuccessful at the selection stage he sat last week. You had no part in that decision and cannot change it. The stated rule is that written reasons are sent by the team that runs the selection centre within five working days, and three days have passed. You have not seen his reasons and do not know how he scored. He wants somebody to tell him what went wrong. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell him the decision was close and that he will very likely succeed if he applies again, even though you cannot see how he scored or what the reasons say.
Read the stated five working days back to him, repeat that his reasons are not due for another two days, and end the call politely once you have said it a second time.

Offer to raise a formal complaint on his behalf about the selection stage today, and take down what he wants it to say, so that somebody senior looks at the decision again before his written reasons arrive.
Let him finish, tell him only what you can confirm when his reasons are due, and check today with the team that runs the selection centre that the date holds.
explanation: A: Gives an assurance you cannot stand behind: you have not seen his reasons, so a comfort offered now becomes a second contradiction when the written reasons arrive inside the five days. B: Ignores the applicant's actual need: the process is quoted correctly and the man is left with nothing he did not already have, three days into a five-day wait he is already struggling with. C: Escalates prematurely: the reasons he is entitled to are still two days away, and starting a complaint before he has read them commits him to a route he has not asked for. The most effective response is letting him finish, telling him only what you can confirm when his reasons are due, and checking today with the team that runs the selection centre that the date holds. He is angry about something you cannot change, so the only things you own are hearing him out and making sure the one commitment the organisation has made to him is kept. It beats reading the five working days back to him and ending the call, because quoting a rule at somebody who has already understood it answers nothing and leaves the five-day date unchecked. It is also better than offering to raise a complaint on his behalf, which starts a process he has not asked for before he has read the reasons he is waiting for. The least effective response is telling him the decision was close and that he will very likely succeed if he applies again: unlike the quoted process, which is at least true, and unlike the offered complaint, which he could decline, this is a statement you have no basis for, and it will be contradicted in writing within two days by the very document he is waiting on. The principle: when you cannot change a decision, give the person the facts you can stand behind and make sure the promises already made to them are kept.
tip: Mẹo MT: Áp dụng sơ đồ Venn hoặc bảng chân trị logic để biểu diễn mối quan hệ giữa các đối tượng.

question_text: You are a records assistant at a prison service. Every batch of letters is read against the address list by a second person before it goes out, and the stated reason is that a letter reaching the wrong address has to be reported the same day it is found. Yesterday’s batch of ninety went out without that second read, because the person who does it was away and nobody said. You notice this on Tuesday morning. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Check yesterday's ninety against the address list yourself before saying anything, so that you can report a number rather than raise an alarm over a batch that may turn out to be fine.

Tell your supervisor this morning that ninety letters went out unread, start the address check now so that any wrong ones can be reported today, and ask who covers the read while the second person is away.
Write a note for the person who does the second read to check yesterday's batch on their return next week, and hold today's batch until somebody can read it against the list.
Do the second read yourself this morning and, if it turns up nothing, treat the batch as checked and let today's batch go out the same way while the second person is still away.
explanation: A: Delays the report to be certain of it: the reporting duty runs from the day a wrong address is found, and the checking takes hours the same day does not have. C: Leaves a same-day duty to next week: anything wrong in yesterday's ninety stays unfound for seven days, and nobody who could arrange cover for the read has been told at all. D: Acts recklessly with the batch still to come: one clean result is used as grounds for skipping the read again, so a gap that happened by accident becomes the way the work is done. The most effective response is to tell your supervisor this morning that ninety letters went out unread, start the address check now, and ask who covers the read while the second person is away: the reporting duty runs the same day, and the reason the check was missed will repeat tomorrow unless somebody fixes the cover. It is stronger than checking the ninety before saying anything, because the person who has to act on a wrong address hears hours later than they needed to, and the batch may not be clean. It is stronger than leaving a note for the colleague who returns next week and holding today’s batch, because a duty measured in a day cannot wait seven of them and nobody able to arrange cover has heard. The least effective response is to do the read yourself and then treat the batch as checked and let today’s go out the same way: checking first at least finds the errors, and holding today’s batch at least keeps the control intact, whereas turning one clean result into permission to skip the read again converts an accident into a practice. The principle: an accidental gap in a control is reported and closed, never used as evidence that the control was never needed.
tip: Mẹo MT: Áp dụng sơ đồ Venn hoặc bảng chân trị logic để biểu diễn mối quan hệ giữa các đối tượng.

question_text: You are a duty team member at a prison service, working the desk that keeps the team’s duty diary. The stated rule is that a change to the diary is made only after the person who runs the team has approved it. That person is out of the office until four but can be reached by phone. A colleague asks you to move her name to tomorrow morning so that she can keep a family appointment, and says the person who runs the team will not mind. The diary is circulated at three. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell your colleague it is arranged and put the change into the diary before three, without checking with the person who runs the team, whose view you are sure of.
Ring the person who runs the team with the one request before three, explain the appointment and the timing, and tell your colleague you will confirm once you have an answer.
Leave the diary as it stands, put the request to the person who runs the team when they are back at four, and reissue the diary tomorrow with the change in it.
Tell your colleague the rule does not allow the change and leave it there, so that she can take the appointment up with the person who runs the team herself.
explanation: A: Gives an assurance you have not got: the rule names one approver, that approver is a phone call away, and the diary that goes out at three then carries a change nobody agreed to. C: Delays the decision: the diary people work from goes out at three, so a change made after four reaches everybody on the morning it was supposed to cover. D: Treats the rule as the whole answer: the rule says who decides, not that the answer is no, and your colleague has no way of reaching that person before three while you have. The most effective response is ringing the person who runs the team with the one request before three: they are reachable, the rule puts the decision with them, and asking costs a single phone call. It is stronger than leaving the diary as it stands and reissuing it tomorrow, because the diary people work from goes out at three and a later correction arrives on the morning it was meant to cover. It is also stronger than telling your colleague the rule does not allow it and leaving her to raise it herself, since she cannot reach the approver before the diary is circulated and you can. The least effective response is telling your colleague the change is arranged and entering it in the diary without checking: it puts a statement you have not verified in front of a colleague and an unapproved change in front of the whole team, and both are harder to unpick than the question you skipped. The principle: when the rule points at somebody else’s decision and that person can still be reached, get the decision rather than supply one.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân biệt rõ giữa 'Đúng' (True) và 'Có thể xảy ra' (Possible). Chỉ chọn kết luận chắc chắn 100%.

question_text: You are a reception desk assistant at a prison service. Every enquiry at the desk goes into the desk log with the name of the person who made it, and the team works from that log the next morning. This afternoon a neighbour you have known for years comes to the desk with an enquiry about a matter your team is dealing with. They ask you to leave their name out of the log, because they would rather nobody knew they had been in. The person who runs your team is in the office. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Remove your neighbour's name from the log entry after they leave, and record the visit as a general question, leaving the entry nameless in the log the team works from.
Put the enquiry in the log in full but keep to yourself that you know the person, since the connection makes no difference to what the team does with it tomorrow.
Ask the person who runs your team whether an enquiry can ever go in the log without a name, without saying who has asked, and hold the entry until they answer.
Write the enquiry into the log with your neighbour's name, as you would for anybody else, and tell the person who runs your team today that you know the person who came in.
explanation: A: Alters a record to suit somebody you know: the log then describes a visit that did not happen, and everybody who works from it in the morning is working from something you made untrue. B: Leaves your own connection undeclared: whoever picks the enquiry up cannot weigh your part in it if nobody has told them there is one, and they will hear about it eventually from somebody else. C: Asks the question without the facts: the answer to a general question cannot settle this one, and the log stays incomplete overnight while the team is meant to work from it. The most effective response is writing the enquiry into the log with your neighbour’s name and telling the person who runs your team that you know them: the log is what the team works from tomorrow, and a connection declared today costs nothing while one discovered later costs a great deal. It is stronger than logging it in full and keeping the connection to yourself, because whoever picks the enquiry up cannot weigh your involvement if nobody has told them there is any. It is also stronger than asking whether an entry can ever go in without a name while holding the entry back, since the question you would be asking is not the question in front of you and the log is wrong overnight either way. The least effective response is removing your neighbour’s name and recording the visit as a general question: the log then says something that did not happen, and every later reader is misled by it. The principle: declare a personal connection early and keep the record straight, because the two protect each other.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You are a shift team member at a police force. You keep the swap list for your team, and the stated rule is that a swap has to be requested three days ahead so the person who runs the rota can check the cover. You have turned two people down this week for asking late. Now a colleague you get on with well asks for a swap tomorrow, says nobody will notice, and points out that the cover is obviously fine. The two you refused are on shift with you tonight. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Put the swap through, and if the two you refused ask, assure them that this request came in within the three days, which is not what happened.
Put the swap through quietly and say nothing to anybody, on the basis that the cover really is fine tomorrow and no harm is done by one late request.
Refuse the swap and tell the colleague that you will report the request to the person who runs the rota, since they asked you to break a rule you have just enforced twice.
Tell the colleague the same as the other two, that a swap tomorrow is outside the three days, and offer to put it to whoever runs the rota, since they check the cover.
explanation: A: Gives an assurance you know is untrue: the favour is bad enough on its own, but defending it with a false account of the timing means the two people you turned down are lied to by the person who applied the rule to them. B: Breaches a stated rule for a quiet life: the rule exists so the cover is checked by the person who runs the rota, and two colleagues who accepted the same answer this week are now on a different footing from this one. C: Escalates prematurely: a late request from a colleague who has been told no is an ordinary exchange, and turning it into a report makes an incident out of something that ended the moment you said no. The most effective response is to tell the colleague the same as the other two and offer to put the request to the person who runs the rota to decide: the rule is applied consistently, the colleague is not simply shut down, and the person whose job it is to check the cover gets to make any exception rather than you. That is better than putting the swap through quietly on the basis that the cover is fine, because whether the cover holds is exactly the judgement the rule reserves for somebody else, and two colleagues have already been held to it this week. It is also better than refusing and telling the colleague you will report the request, since a late ask is an ordinary thing to try and reporting it makes an incident out of a conversation that ended with your answer. The least effective response is to put the swap through and then assure the two you refused that it came in within the three days: on top of an inconsistent decision, the people who accepted your answer are told something untrue by the person who gave it. The principle: apply the rule the same way to everybody, and push any exception to the person who owns it rather than inventing cover for your own.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân biệt rõ giữa 'Đúng' (True) và 'Có thể xảy ra' (Possible). Chỉ chọn kết luận chắc chắn 100%.

question_text: You are a data quality assistant at a police force. A colleague has sent a letter containing another person’s details to the wrong address. The written rule is that a letter sent to the wrong person is logged the same day with the person who keeps the correspondence log, who then writes to the person whose details went out. The colleague asks you to leave it, because they will get the letter back themselves. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Give the colleague until the end of the week to log it themselves, and check on Friday whether they have, so that they get the chance to put their own mistake right.
Tell the colleague you will log it with them today, because the rule exists so that the person whose details went out gets written to, and offer to write the entry together.
Ring the address that received the letter yourself, ask them to destroy it, and treat the matter as closed once they agree, since getting the letter back is what the rule is for.
Report the colleague to their supervisor before saying anything to them, and describe it as a mistake they tried to bury, so that the letter is dealt with quickly.
explanation: A: Delays the decision: the rule says the same day, and the person whose details went to a stranger gains nothing from four more days of not being told. C: Breaches the stated rule with a private arrangement: nothing is logged, the promise of a stranger stands in for the process, and the person whose details went out is never written to. D: Goes straight past the colleague: they can still do the right thing today and have been given no chance to, and the account you give of them is harsher than what happened. The most effective response is telling the colleague you will log it with them today so that the person whose details went out is written to: the rule fixes the day, and the person affected is the one who does not yet know where their details went. It beats giving the colleague until the end of the week to log it themselves, because the rule says the same day and the person waiting to be written to gains nothing from the delay. It beats reporting the colleague to their supervisor before saying anything to them, since the colleague can still put it right today and has been given no chance to. The least effective response is ringing the address that received the letter and asking them to destroy it: it swaps a written rule for a private arrangement, leaves nothing logged, and leaves the person whose details went out with no letter and no idea. The principle: a mistake with consequences for somebody outside the team goes through the process that exists to tell them.
tip: Mẹo MT: Áp dụng sơ đồ Venn hoặc bảng chân trị logic để biểu diễn mối quan hệ giữa các đối tượng.

question_text: You are a trainee at a police force, six weeks into your course. Over the weekend another trainee, Sam, talked at length in a pub about a matter your team is dealing with, and afterwards told you it was harmless because no names were used. You were told at the start of the course that anything to do with your team’s work stays inside it, and that the person who runs your training course must be told about any breach. Sam says he will not do it again. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Hand the whole thing over to a colleague on the course who knows Sam better and ask them to raise it with the person who runs the course, then leave it with them from there.
Accept Sam's word for now and raise it with the person who runs the course first thing tomorrow, once this evening's assessment is over and you have slept on what you heard.
Tell Sam you will report it and why, then tell the person who runs the course today what was said, including that Sam believes no names were used, since that duty is yours.
Tell Sam to report himself to the person who runs the course by the end of the day and check with him afterwards that he has, without raising it yourself if he says he did.
explanation: A: Hands a judgement to somebody with no standing in it: you are the one who heard it, the rule puts the telling on you, and a second-hand account arrives days later if it arrives at all. B: Delays a report the rule wanted promptly: the duty is yours and it is not conditional on being certain, so a night's wait buys nothing the report needed and the course hears about it a day after it could have. D: Makes the breach the other person's to declare: the obligation the course gave you does not transfer, and his account of whether he went is the only evidence you would have. The most effective response is to tell Sam you are going to report it and why the rule exists, then tell the person who runs the course today what was said: the course put the telling on you, and saying it to Sam first is what separates reporting from going behind him. It is stronger than accepting his word and waiting until tomorrow morning, because the duty is not conditional on being sure of every word, and a night’s wait buys the report nothing it needed. It is stronger than telling him to report himself, because the duty does not move with the instruction and his word is all you would ever have that he went. The least effective response is to hand the whole thing over to a colleague who knows Sam better and ask them to raise it: reporting it a day late at least gets a first-hand account to the right person, and sending him to declare it at least gets the right facts there if he goes, whereas a relayed account spreads the matter to a third trainee and reaches the course second hand, from somebody who was not there. The principle: a duty to tell somebody sits with the person who saw it, and telling the person concerned first is part of doing it well.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You are an enquiry desk assistant at a police force. The person who runs the enquiry line has asked you to sit in on a briefing at ten on Wednesday to explain how the desk logs calls. The person who runs the training timetable has asked you to help run a session at the same hour, and says the trainees have no other date. Each of them has told you that their own is the one that matters. A decision has to be made by Monday. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Decide yourself that the briefing matters more because the enquiry line asked you first, and let the training timetable know on Monday that you will not be at the session after all.
Agree to both and plan to slip out of the briefing after twenty minutes to join the session late, telling neither of them that you will be splitting the hour between the two.
Write to both together on Monday setting out the clash and what each would lose, and ask them to settle which one you attend, since neither has yet heard the other.
Reply to the person who runs the training timetable and criticise the enquiry line for booking over trainees at the last minute, copying in the people who were asked to the briefing.
explanation: A: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholders': who asked first is not a reason, and the trainees have no other date while the briefing has not been tested against one. B: Splits effort so nothing finishes: half of each leaves both people short of what they asked for, and neither of them knows in time to bring somebody else in. D: Personalises the conflict: the clash is a diary problem with a Monday decision on it, and this turns it into a standing dispute between two teams, with an audience. The most effective response is to write to both of them together on Monday setting out the clash and what each would lose, and ask them to settle which one you attend: neither has heard the other’s case, the decision belongs to the two people whose work is affected, and Monday is when it has to be made. It is better than deciding yourself that the briefing matters more because the enquiry line asked you first, because who asked first is not a reason and the trainees have no other date. It is better than agreeing to both and slipping out of the briefing after twenty minutes, because half of each leaves both people short of what they asked for and neither of them knows. The least effective response is to reply to the person who runs the training timetable and criticise the enquiry line for booking over trainees at the last minute, copying in the people who were asked to the briefing: the clash is a diary problem, and this makes it a public dispute between two teams that will outlast Wednesday. The principle: put a clash in front of the people who own the priorities, in the same words to each of them, and let them choose.

question_text: You are a contact handling assistant at a police force. A colleague on your desk has found that they were left off the list for the weekly handover meeting for the past two months, and has just told the person who keeps that list, in a raised voice, that it was done deliberately. The person who keeps the list says the name was lost when the list was rebuilt. Both have now asked you separately what you think, and the next handover is tomorrow. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Put the name back on the list for tomorrow, check that nobody else was lost when the list was rebuilt, and leave the argument alone, on the basis that once the meeting invitation arrives the complaint goes away by itself.
Say the same thing to each of them, since they asked separately: that you do not know how the name came off, that it can be put back before tomorrow, and offer both ten minutes with you today.

Take it to your supervisor this afternoon and ask them to decide who is right, setting out what each of them has told you separately, since two people on the desk are now not speaking and the handover is tomorrow morning.
Agree with your colleague that they were pushed out on purpose, and say so at the desk in front of the other colleagues, so that the person who keeps the list hears how it looked.
explanation: A: Fixes the diary and leaves the grievance: the invitation settles nothing about whether it was deliberate, and the two of them still have to work the same desk tomorrow. C: Escalates before the two people have spoken: there is nothing yet for a supervisor to weigh, and a ruling handed down will not make either of them trust the other. D: Personalises the conflict: you do not know that it was deliberate, and saying it publicly turns an oversight one conversation could settle into a charge the other person now has to defend. The most effective response is to say the same thing to each of them, that you do not know how the name came off, that it can be put back before tomorrow, and offer to sit with both of them for ten minutes today: you were asked separately, saying the same thing to each is what stops a second version forming, and ten minutes with the two of them is the only route to an account they share before the handover. It is better than putting the name back on the list and leaving the argument alone, because the invitation fixes the diary and not the accusation. It is better than taking it to your supervisor to decide who is right, because nothing has yet been said between the two people involved for anybody to rule on. The least effective response is to agree with your colleague that they were pushed out on purpose and say so at the desk in front of the other colleagues: you do not know that, and saying it publicly hardens an oversight into an accusation with witnesses. The principle: in a dispute you did not see, hold to what you actually know and get the two people into the same conversation.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You are a reception desk assistant at a police force. Every enquiry at the desk goes into the desk log with the name of the person who made it, and the team works from that log the next morning. This afternoon a neighbour you have known for years comes to the desk with an enquiry about a matter your team is dealing with. They ask you to leave their name out of the log, because they would rather nobody knew they had been in. The person who runs your team is in the office. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Remove your neighbour's name from the log entry after they leave, and record the visit as a general question, leaving the entry nameless in the log the team works from.
Put the enquiry in the log in full but keep to yourself that you know the person, since the connection makes no difference to what the team does with it tomorrow.
Ask the person who runs your team whether an enquiry can ever go in the log without a name, without saying who has asked, and hold the entry until they answer.
Write the enquiry into the log with your neighbour's name, as you would for anybody else, and tell the person who runs your team today that you know the person who came in.
explanation: A: Alters a record to suit somebody you know: the log then describes a visit that did not happen, and everybody who works from it in the morning is working from something you made untrue. B: Leaves your own connection undeclared: whoever picks the enquiry up cannot weigh your part in it if nobody has told them there is one, and they will hear about it eventually from somebody else. C: Asks the question without the facts: the answer to a general question cannot settle this one, and the log stays incomplete overnight while the team is meant to work from it. The most effective response is writing the enquiry into the log with your neighbour’s name and telling the person who runs your team that you know them: the log is what the team works from tomorrow, and a connection declared today costs nothing while one discovered later costs a great deal. It is stronger than logging it in full and keeping the connection to yourself, because whoever picks the enquiry up cannot weigh your involvement if nobody has told them there is any. It is also stronger than asking whether an entry can ever go in without a name while holding the entry back, since the question you would be asking is not the question in front of you and the log is wrong overnight either way. The least effective response is removing your neighbour’s name and recording the visit as a general question: the log then says something that did not happen, and every later reader is misled by it. The principle: declare a personal connection early and keep the record straight, because the two protect each other.

question_text: You are a duty team member at a police force. Your supervisor has asked you to rewrite the whole of last week’s handover notes by tomorrow morning and has given no reason for it. The notes looked fine to you, the work will take most of a day, and you already have a report due on Friday that she is expecting. A colleague on the same shift asks why you look so fed up. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Ask the supervisor what the rewritten notes are needed for and by when, and tell her that Friday's report will slip if the notes take a full day.
Criticise the request to the rest of the shift, saying the supervisor never explains herself and hands out pointless work, rather than asking her what the notes are for.
Rewrite all of last week's notes tonight and hand Friday's report in late, on the basis that the supervisor asked for the notes and she can sort the report out afterwards.
Rewrite the parts of the notes you think were weak, leave the rest as they are, and hand them in tomorrow without saying which parts you changed.
explanation: B: Personalises the frustration: the shift ends up with a view of the supervisor instead of an answer, the notes are still due tomorrow, and the one person who knows what they are for has not been asked. C: Abandons your own committed work: the report is due on Friday and is expected, so a second deadline is quietly broken to protect the first without anybody being told. D: Substitutes your own judgement for the supervisor's: you do not know what the rewrite is for, so guessing at which parts matter risks handing back exactly the pages she needed done. The most effective response is asking the supervisor what the rewritten notes are needed for and telling her that Friday’s report will slip. One question turns an unexplained task into a job you can size, and the person who set both deadlines is the only one who can choose between them. That is better than rewriting everything tonight and handing the report in late, because that quietly breaks a deadline she is expecting you to meet and she never gets the chance to move it. It is also better than rewriting only the parts you think were weak, since without knowing the purpose you may leave undone the very pages the rewrite exists for. The least effective response is criticising the request to the rest of the shift: it turns a question about the work into a verdict on a colleague, spreads it through the team, and leaves both the notes and Friday’s report exactly where they were, which is worse than doing too much or doing the wrong half. The principle: when a task arrives without a reason, ask the person who set it before you judge either the task or them.
