question_text: You are a contracts assistant at Calder Group. You and a colleague, Priti, jointly check supplier insurance certificates before contracts start. Priti has told you she has been passing certificates through on the expiry date shown in the covering email rather than opening the certificate itself. Two suppliers started work last month with expired cover. A contract starts on Monday. Your team leader is in the office and does not know. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Open every certificate for Monday's contract yourself, and tell your team leader that certificates have been passed on covering emails rather than actually checked.
Check Monday's certificates yourself without telling anybody what Priti has been doing, and hope the two expired suppliers are not noticed.
Ask Priti to go back through the last two months of certificates with you, and agree between you not to trouble the team leader with any of it.
Email Priti a reminder of how certificates should be checked, and open Monday's certificate yourself to make sure that one at least is right.
explanation: B: Withholds a failure somebody needs to know about: two suppliers are already working with expired cover, and the only person aware that the check has not been running has decided not to say. C: Prioritises harmony over honesty: two contracts already started uninsured, which is past the point where two colleagues quietly review each other's work between themselves. D: Fixes one certificate and none of the cause: Monday is covered, Priti's method is unchanged, and the two suppliers already working with expired cover are still working. The most effective response is to open every certificate for Monday’s contract yourself, and tell your team leader that certificates have been passed on covering emails rather than checked: Monday’s has to be opened whatever happens, and two suppliers already working with expired cover is a live exposure only somebody with authority over the process can deal with. It beats asking Priti to go back through two months of certificates and agreeing not to trouble the team leader, because two uninsured contracts are past the point where colleagues correct each other quietly. It beats emailing her a reminder and opening Monday’s certificate yourself, because a reminder leaves the method unchanged and the exposures untouched. The least effective response is checking Monday’s certificates without telling anybody what she has been doing: two suppliers go on working with cover the organisation believes it has, and nobody can act on it. That makes it worse than the joint review, which at least revisits the past two months, and worse than the reminder, which tells her something. The principle: when a colleague’s shortcut has already produced a live exposure, the exposure goes to whoever can act on it, not just the next case.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You are a contracts assistant at Calder Group. You have committed today to producing a tender evaluation summary that a panel meets to discuss on Monday. At eleven a supplier’s insurance certificate expires at midnight and the replacement has not arrived; without it a team of six cannot work on site from tomorrow. Chasing the certificate will take most of the afternoon. Your team leader is available. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell your team leader at once that the certificate expires tonight and that chasing it will cost the afternoon, and agree between you which of the two gets your day.
Chase the certificate all afternoon and carry on with the evaluation summary tomorrow, without telling anybody that Monday's panel paper is now at risk.
Finish the evaluation summary as committed and leave the certificate to expire, telling the site team tomorrow morning that they cannot start.
Ask a colleague who has never chased a certificate to do it while you carry on with the summary, and check on them at the end of the day.
explanation: B: Withholds a risk somebody is relying on: the panel meets on Monday to discuss a paper that may not exist, and the only person who knows that has decided not to say so today. C: Ranks a movable commitment above an immovable one: a summary due for Monday has the weekend behind it, and six people cannot be on site tomorrow if the certificate lapses tonight. D: Delegates the urgent task to the least prepared person: an untrained colleague chasing a certificate that expires at midnight is the arrangement most likely to end with it expiring. The most effective response is to tell your team leader at once that the certificate expires tonight and that chasing it will cost the afternoon, and agree which of the two gets your day: one thing expires tonight and cannot be recovered, the other has a weekend behind it, and the call should be made with both facts in front of him. It beats finishing the evaluation summary and letting the certificate expire, because a summary due Monday has a weekend behind it and six people on site do not. It beats asking a colleague who has never chased a certificate to do it, because they are the least likely to catch one expiring at midnight. The least effective response is chasing the certificate all afternoon without telling anybody that Monday’s panel paper is now at risk: the right work is done and the panel expects a paper nobody has flagged, so the weekend passes with the problem invisible. That makes it worse than letting it expire, which chooses badly but openly, and worse than the poor delegation, which keeps both jobs alive. The principle: when a late arrival displaces committed work, the displacement is the thing to tell people about, not just the work.

question_text: You are a contracts assistant at Brantwood Services. A community group that hires a hall from you every Saturday emails asking you to cancel their booking for the next six weeks. In the same email they mention that their usual room has been too cold to use since October and that they have complained twice. Cancelling loses them their Saturday slot permanently, and the heating fault has an open job number. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Reply asking whether the cold room is the reason for cancelling, tell them the heating job is open, and offer to hold their Saturday slot while it is fixed.
Cancel the six bookings straight away as the email asks, release the Saturday slot to the waiting list, and close the enquiry as a customer request.
Reply asking them to confirm the cancellation in writing from their group's secretary, and process it once you have that confirmation in front of you.
Cancel the bookings as asked and separately chase the heating job, letting the group know when the room is warm again in case they want to come back to it.
explanation: B: Closes the request on its face: the email contains a cancellation and a reason for it, and acting on the first while ignoring the second gives away a permanent Saturday slot over a fault that already has a job number. C: Delays the decision: a written confirmation adds a step to a cancellation that may not be wanted at all, and the six weeks run out while the paperwork goes back and forth. D: Ignores the customer's actual need: the group loses its Saturday slot permanently today and is invited back to a slot that will no longer exist, which is not what an offer to return means. The most effective response is to reply asking whether the cold room is the reason for cancelling, tell them the heating job is open, and offer to hold their Saturday slot: the email gives you a request and the reason behind it, the reason has an open job number, and a slot lost permanently cannot be given back. It beats asking them to confirm the cancellation in writing from their secretary, because that delays a cancellation nobody has established is wanted. It beats cancelling as asked and separately chasing the heating, because that offers them a return to a slot that will already have gone. The least effective response is cancelling the six bookings and releasing the Saturday slot to the waiting list: it acts on the words and discards the reason in the same email, and the group loses a permanent slot over a fault the organisation is already fixing. That makes it worse than the written confirmation, which is slow but leaves the slot intact, and worse than cancelling and chasing, which at least chases the fault. The principle: when a request and its reason arrive together, deal with the reason before acting irreversibly on the request.

question_text: You are a shared services administrator at Ashmere Trust. Your team processes staff expense claims in the order they arrive, usually within three weeks. Your sister-in-law works in another division and has asked you to push her four-hundred-pound claim through this week because she is short before a holiday. She has offered to buy you a gift at the weekend. You have the access to move claims, and nobody reviews the order. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Move her claim to the front of the queue this week and accept the gift she has offered at the weekend, treating it as a favour anybody would do for family.
Move her claim forward but decline the weekend gift, on the view that the favour is harmless as long as you take nothing at all for it.
Tell her you would rather not move it and say nothing to anybody, and let her claim run through in its normal place in the queue.
Tell her you cannot move claims for family, explain the three- week timescale and the hardship route if one exists, and mention the request to your team leader.
explanation: A: Accepts a benefit for using your access: everybody else in the queue waits longer so that a relative does not, and the weekend gift makes it a transaction rather than a lapse. B: Grants the favour and keeps the conscience: the queue is still jumped and every other claimant still waits longer, and declining the gift changes nothing for them. C: Withholds a request your team leader should know about: you hold access that can move a queue nobody reviews, and a family member has just asked you to use it. The most effective response is to tell her you cannot move claims for family, explain the three-week timescale and the hardship route, and mention the request to your team leader: the answer has to be no, she is short of money and the hardship route is the useful part of the reply, and a relative asking you to use unreviewed access is exactly what a team leader is told about. It beats moving her claim forward while declining the weekend gift, because that still jumps the queue and only declines the payment for it. It beats telling her you would rather not and saying nothing to anybody, because the request itself is what your team leader needs to know. The least effective response is moving her claim to the front and accepting the gift: unreviewed access puts a relative ahead of everybody else and a gift is taken for it, which turns a lapse into a transaction. That makes it worse than the unpaid favour, which takes nothing, and worse than the quiet refusal, which leaves the queue alone. The principle: refuse the favour, offer the route that genuinely helps, and tell somebody that the access was asked for.

question_text: You are an enquiries officer at Redhill Directorate. In this morning’s team meeting, in front of eight colleagues, another officer said that your replies to enquirers are so slow that people ring back and make more work for everybody. You know your average is in line with the team’s. You and that officer share the duty rota and have to hand over to each other twice a week. The meeting has finished. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Let it go and change nothing, on the view that responding at all would make the disagreement bigger than the remark itself was.
Email your team leader with your reply times and the officer's comment, and ask them to correct the record with the team.
Read the officer's own reply times out at the next team meeting in front of the team, since the comparison ought to be heard by the same people who heard the criticism.
Speak to the officer privately today, say that the comment in front of the team was not welcome, and go through the actual reply times with them.
explanation: A: Avoids the difficult conversation: you hand over to this officer twice a week, and an unaddressed remark made in front of eight people sits underneath every one of those handovers. B: Escalates prematurely: the officer has not yet been spoken to, and a team leader asked to correct the record in front of the team turns a remark into a formal matter. C: Answers a criticism with a criticism: it makes the disagreement about which of you is slower rather than about the figures, in front of the same audience, and the twice-weekly handover gets harder for both of you. The most effective response is to speak to the officer privately today, say the comment in front of the team was not welcome, and go through the actual reply times: the remark was public and wrong, you work with this person twice a week, and a private conversation with the figures deals with both the accuracy and the relationship. It beats letting it go and changing nothing, because the remark then stands underneath every handover. It beats emailing your team leader with your reply times and asking them to correct the record, because the officer has not been spoken to and bringing a manager in first turns a remark into a formal matter. The least effective response is reading the officer’s own reply times out at the next team meeting: it moves the disagreement in front of everybody, makes it about which of you is worse, and leaves you both handing over twice a week afterwards. That makes it worse than letting it go, which adds nothing, and worse than the email, which is heavy-handed but aimed at the facts. The principle: answer a public criticism privately and on the evidence, rather than in kind and in front of the same audience.

question_text: You are a correspondence officer at Calder Group. In this morning’s stand-up a colleague, Nuala, said in front of the team that you never pick up your phone and that she ends up taking your calls. You share the duty line on alternate days. You do miss calls when you are drafting, and so does she. The stand-up has finished and your team leader was not there. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Ask Nuala for ten minutes today, agree what cover each of you actually needs when the other is drafting, and say the stand-up was not the place for it.
Answer in the next stand-up with the number of her calls you have taken this month, since the team heard only one side of it.
Say nothing and make a point of answering every call for the next fortnight, and see whether she raises it again.
Stop picking up Nuala's calls after the way she raised it, and let her find out how many of hers you have been taking.
explanation: B: Answers a public remark in public: the figures may be on your side, and the two of you still share a duty line with a team now watching the score. C: Fixes the symptom for a fortnight: you both miss calls when drafting, and nothing about answering harder for two weeks settles what cover the line actually needs. D: Withdraws cover after a remark: the calls that go unanswered are the public's, not Nuala's, and she learns nothing about how the two of you should be covering the line. The most effective response is to ask Nuala for ten minutes today, agree what cover each of you needs when the other is drafting, and say the stand-up was not the place for it: the remark was public and partly fair, you both miss calls while drafting, and what needs settling is what the duty line requires. It beats answering in the next stand-up with the number of her calls you have taken, because a public rebuttal leaves you both keeping score in front of the team. It beats saying nothing and answering every call for a fortnight, because that does not settle what the line needs. The least effective response is stopping picking up her calls after the way she raised it: the unanswered calls belong to the public rather than to her, and the question of how the line is covered stays exactly where it was. That makes it worse than the public rebuttal, which is escalatory but factual, and worse than answering harder, which costs nobody. The principle: answer a public remark privately, and never let a disagreement about cover be settled by withdrawing it.

question_text: You are a case officer at Redhill Directorate. A decision letter approving a grant of eight thousand pounds went out on Friday to an applicant who does not qualify; a colleague, Ruth, used the wrong eligibility list. The applicant has already emailed to say they have ordered equipment. Your team leader is on leave until Monday and the deputy is running the team. Ruth is at her desk and does not know yet. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Email the applicant straight away telling them the letter was sent in error and that they should not spend the money, and tell the deputy afterwards.
Wait until Monday when your team leader is back, and put the whole thing to them with a recommendation rather than taking it to the deputy.
Raise the error with the deputy behind her back this morning, and leave it to them to decide whether Ruth is told which eligibility list she used.
Tell Ruth what you have found, then take it together to the deputy this morning with the letter, the eligibility list and the applicant's email about the equipment.
explanation: A: Acts alone on a decision that is not yours: withdrawing an approval is the organisation's decision to communicate, and an applicant told by one officer that a formal letter is void has nothing in writing to rely on. B: Fails to escalate a genuine risk: the applicant has already ordered equipment, so three more days of believing they qualify is the part of the problem that is still growing. C: Reports a colleague instead of telling her: it makes the first move about Ruth rather than about the letter and an applicant buying equipment, and Ruth learns of her own error from a manager. The most effective response is to tell Ruth what you have found, then take it together to the deputy this morning with the letter, the eligibility list and the applicant’s email: somebody is spending money on a letter that should not have been sent, it has to reach somebody who can act today, and going with her and the evidence deals with the money and the error at once. It beats emailing the applicant straight away to say the letter was sent in error, because withdrawing a formal approval is not one officer’s message to send. It beats waiting until Monday and putting it to your team leader with a recommendation, because the applicant is buying equipment now. The least effective response is raising it with the deputy behind her back: it makes the first move about who made the mistake, leaves her to hear about her own error from a manager, and does nothing faster for the applicant. That makes it worse than emailing the applicant, which is irregular but stops the spending, and worse than waiting for Monday, which is slow but aimed at the decision rather than at a colleague. The principle: bad news goes to whoever can act on it, with the person who caused it rather than around them.

question_text: You are a management information assistant at Redhill Directorate. A dashboard you presented last week has been well received, and your director has emailed the division praising your work on it. A colleague, Bea, built most of the underlying queries, and you have heard she is telling other people you took the credit. The director’s email is still being forwarded around the division. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Blame Bea to the rest of your team for spreading the story, and add that her queries needed a good deal of correcting before the dashboard worked at all.
Speak to Bea today, agree between you what her contribution actually was, and then email the director correcting the record with Bea copied in.
Reply to the director's email saying the dashboard was a joint effort, and leave it to Bea to raise her own part if she wants to.
Say nothing publicly and thank Bea privately for the queries, on the view that the director's email will be forgotten in a fortnight.
explanation: A: Answers a grievance with an attack on the person: the director's email is still wrong, Bea's account of it becomes more credible, and your team is given a dispute instead of a correction. C: Corrects the credit without naming who earned it: a joint effort leaves the director none the wiser about Bea, and puts the burden of claiming her own work on the person with none of the standing. D: Settles the relationship and leaves the record wrong: a private thank you does nothing about an email still being forwarded round the division under your name alone. The most effective response is to speak to Bea today, agree what her contribution actually was, and then email the director correcting the record with her copied in: the email is wrong and still circulating, she built most of the queries, and a correction agreed with her fixes the record and the relationship at once. It beats replying that the dashboard was a joint effort and leaving her to raise her own part, because that tells the director nothing about who did what. It beats saying nothing publicly and thanking her privately, because a private thank you does not reach an email being forwarded round the division. The least effective response is blaming her to your team for spreading the story and adding that her queries needed correcting: a complaint about credit is answered by attacking the person who earned it, and the director’s email stays as wrong as it was. That makes it worse than the joint-effort reply, which moves the record towards the truth, and worse than the private thanks, which damages nobody. The principle: when credit has landed in the wrong place, correct it with the person who earned it, in writing, to whoever got it wrong.
tip: Mẹo MT: Áp dụng sơ đồ Venn hoặc bảng chân trị logic để biểu diễn mối quan hệ giữa các đối tượng.

question_text: You are a programme support officer at Brantwood Services. Every project closure needs a lessons-learned session recorded on the closure form before the project can be signed off. A project is being closed on Friday and the session has not happened; the team has dispersed and two members have left. Your programme manager wants the form completed today. Nothing stops you filling in the box, and nobody checks whether the session happened. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Complete the form leaving the lessons-learned box blank, and let whoever signs the closure off decide for themselves what they want to do about a session that never took place at all.
Ask your programme manager to sign the closure off without the form, and raise the missing session at the next programme board instead.
Tell your programme manager the session has not happened, and propose a thirty-minute call this week with the three people still here, because the form is the only record.
Complete the lessons-learned box today from the project's own progress reports, and record the session as completed so the closure can be signed off on Friday.
explanation: A: Leaves a gap without naming it: an empty box on a closure form is indistinguishable from an oversight, and the signer has to guess whether the session was missed or forgotten. B: Solves the paperwork and loses the substance: the form can be waived, but the three people still here are the last chance anybody has to capture what the project learned. D: Records a session as completed that never took place: the closure file will say lessons were captured from a meeting nobody attended, and the two people who left took the only account of them. The most effective response is to tell your programme manager the session has not happened, and propose a thirty-minute call this week with the three people still here: the session is the substance and the form is the record of it, and half an hour produces something real for a Friday sign- off. It beats completing the form with the lessons-learned box left blank, because a blank box tells the signer nothing about whether the session was missed or forgotten. It beats asking her to sign the closure off without the form, because waiving it loses the last chance to capture what the project learned. The least effective response is filling the box from the project’s progress reports and recording the session as completed: a meeting that never happened is written into the closure file, so the organisation’s record is an account nobody gave. That makes it worse than the blank box, which claims nothing, and worse than waiving the form, which does not falsify it. The principle: when a record requires a step that has not happened, do the step or say it is missing, and never write it in.
tip: Mẹo MT: Với bài toán quy luật chuỗi số, hãy xét hiệu số bậc 1, hiệu số bậc 2 hoặc tích lũy tiến.

question_text: You work in a hospital pharmacy stores team. Your colleague Amir is checking a large delivery against the order alone, a job normally done by two people so that quantities are double checked. He is halfway through and the fridge lines still need putting away within the hour. You have finished your own tasks. The stores supervisor is at a meeting until midday. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Carry on with your own area and leave Amir to finish, since he started the check and interrupting halfway through might cause him to lose his place.
Put the fridge lines away yourself while Amir finishes the check, so that the cold chain is protected and he is not interrupted.
Tell Amir you are free and join him on the check so it is properly double checked, then put the fridge lines away together.
Ring the stores supervisor out of her meeting to ask whether the delivery check should be paused until two people are available.
explanation: A: Lets a two-person control run with one: a double-check that exists to catch quantity errors in medicines is being done by one person, and the reason for not helping is a worry about interrupting. Standing by a known control failure is the failure here. B: Splits the wrong task: it protects the fridge lines and leaves the single-person check running, so the control designed to catch quantity errors stays broken for the rest of the delivery. D: Escalates prematurely: you are the second person, you are free, and the answer she would give is obvious. Interrupting a meeting to be told to do what you can already do costs time the fridge lines do not have. The most effective response is to tell Amir you are free and join him on the check so it is properly double checked, then put the fridge lines away together: the check is a two-person control precisely because one person miscounts, you are free, and joining him restores the control for the rest of the delivery and still gets the fridge lines away in time. It beats putting the fridge lines away yourself while he finishes the check, because that protects the cold chain and leaves the quantity check still being done by one person, which is the more serious gap. It beats ringing the stores supervisor out of her meeting to ask whether the check should be paused, because you are the second person she would send, so the call only delays it. The least effective response is carrying on with your own area and leaving him to finish alone: it lets a medicines quantity check run without its double-check, and the reason offered is a concern about interrupting him. That is worse than the other two, which act on part of the problem. The principle: when a two-person control is running with one person and you are free, become the second person.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You are an assistant at a children’s after-school activity club. A parent has paid for her son to attend a climbing session on Thursday. This morning the instructor tells you he is unwell and Thursday’s climbing will be replaced by indoor games. The parent chose the club specifically for the climbing. She can be reached by phone or email. The club manager is on leave until Friday. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Email all parents on Wednesday evening with the amended timetable, so that everyone is told at the same time and the message is consistent.
Ring the parent to say Thursday's session is changing, and tell her you will confirm what it is being replaced with once the timetable has been sorted out.
Say nothing and let Thursday go ahead as indoor games, since the children enjoy those too and the parent may not mind once her son has had a good afternoon.
Contact the parent today, explain the instructor is unwell and Thursday will be indoor games instead, and tell her what the alternatives are including a refund or a later climbing session.
explanation: A: Delays the message: a Wednesday evening notice reaches her the night before, when she has already arranged her Thursday around a session that is not happening. B: Delays the decision: it reaches her today, which is right, and withholds the two facts she needs, what is happening instead and what her options are, so she still cannot decide anything. C: Hides the problem: she paid for climbing specifically and is left to discover the change at collection, with no chance to decide whether she still wanted the session. Assuming she will not mind is not her decision to make. The most effective response is to contact the parent today, explain the instructor is unwell and Thursday will be indoor games, and set out the alternatives including a refund or a later climbing session: she chose and paid for climbing specifically, the substitution changes what she bought, and telling her today lets her decide whether her son still attends. It beats ringing to say only that Thursday is changing and you will confirm the replacement later, because that leaves her unable to act when you already know what it changes to. It beats emailing all parents on Wednesday evening with the amended timetable, because a general notice the night before arrives after she has organised her Thursday. The least effective response is saying nothing and letting Thursday go ahead as indoor games: it lets her pay for climbing, send her son to something else, and find out afterwards, on the assumption that she will not mind. That is worse than the other two, which tell her late or partially but do tell her. The principle: when what someone paid for changes, tell them promptly, tell them what it changes to, and give them the choice.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân biệt rõ giữa 'Đúng' (True) và 'Có thể xảy ra' (Possible). Chỉ chọn kết luận chắc chắn 100%.

question_text: You work in a shoe repair and key cutting shop. A customer collects a key cut yesterday and says it does not turn in her front door; she has been locked out once already. Recutting takes ten minutes and there is no queue. She is annoyed and says she has wasted a morning. Your shop manager is in the back and can authorise refunds. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Explain that keys sometimes need easing in older locks, and suggest she try a little lubricant on the lock before assuming the key was cut incorrectly.
Apologise, take the key and the original back, and ask her to return this afternoon once it has been recut and checked properly.
Recut the key straight away and hand it over with an apology, since the fastest fix is the best answer and she plainly wants to get on with her day.
Apologise, recut the key now while she waits since it takes ten minutes, and ask the manager about refunding the original charge for the trouble.
explanation: A: Ignores the customer's actual need: it explains away a key that does not work, puts the remedy back onto a customer who has already been locked out, and never offers the ten-minute recut that would settle it. B: Adds a second journey: the recut takes ten minutes and there is no queue, so asking her to come back a second time adds another journey to a morning she has already lost. C: Ignores part of the customer's actual need: the recut solves the key and not the wasted morning, when a manager who could offer a refund is a few steps away and has not been asked. The most effective response is to apologise, recut the key now while she waits since it takes ten minutes, and ask the manager about refunding the original charge: the key does not work, there is no queue, and she has lost a morning, so both the practical fix and the goodwill question can be dealt with while she is here. It beats recutting the key straight away and handing it over with an apology, because that addresses the key and not the wasted morning, when a manager who could refund the charge is a few steps away. It beats taking the key back and asking her to return this afternoon, because a second journey for a ten-minute job adds to exactly the cost she is complaining about. The least effective response is suggesting she tries a little lubricant because older locks need easing: it offers a theory instead of a working key, and makes the customer responsible for solving a fault the shop created. That is worse than the other two, which both end with a key that turns. The principle: fix the fault on the spot when you can, and use the authority above you for the part that is about the customer’s lost time.
tip: Mẹo MT: Với bài toán quy luật chuỗi số, hãy xét hiệu số bậc 1, hiệu số bậc 2 hoặc tích lũy tiến.

question_text: You work in the admissions office of a private college. Applicants must provide original qualification certificates. An agent who recruits students for the college submits a photocopy for one applicant, saying the original is with the embassy, and asks you to record it as verified so the offer can go out this week. The agent brings the college a lot of business. Your admissions manager is available. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Record the certificate as verified so the offer can go out this week, since the photocopy looks genuine and the agent brings the college a great deal of business.
Tell the agent you cannot record a photocopy as verified, and ask your admissions manager what alternative evidence the college accepts when an original is with an embassy.
Reject the application until the original certificate is produced, and tell the agent that the offer cannot proceed this week whatever the reason for the delay.
Send the offer out marked as conditional on the original certificate being produced later, and record the photocopy as received rather than verified.
explanation: A: Falsifies a verification record: recording a document as verified when you have not seen the original is a false statement in the college's own admissions record, and the reason given is the agent's commercial value. That is dishonesty, not pragmatism. C: Applies the rule without using it: the college may well have a route for certificates held by an embassy, and refusing outright forecloses a legitimate application without asking anyone who would know. D: Acts outside own authority: making an offer conditional is a decision about admissions terms, not a records entry, and issuing one to work around a verification rule commits the college on your own judgement. The most effective response is to tell the agent you cannot record a photocopy as verified, and ask your admissions manager what alternative evidence the college accepts when an original is with an embassy: you cannot record something as verified that you have not verified, but the applicant’s problem is a common one the college may well have a route for. Refusing the false entry and asking the right question does both jobs. It beats rejecting the application until the original is produced, because outright rejection forecloses a legitimate application without asking whether alternative evidence is accepted. It beats sending a conditional offer and recording the photocopy as received, because inventing that condition to work around the rule is an admissions decision you have no authority to take. The least effective response is recording the certificate as verified so the offer can go out this week: it records an unverified document as checked, and the reason offered is how much business the agent brings, which is precisely the pressure the verification rule exists to resist. That is worse than the other two, which act beyond or below their authority but keep the record true. The principle: never record a check you did not perform, and take the underlying problem to whoever can authorise an alternative.
tip: Mẹo MT: Áp dụng sơ đồ Venn hoặc bảng chân trị logic để biểu diễn mối quan hệ giữa các đối tượng.

question_text: You work on the security desk of an office building. A contractor asks to be let into the server room, saying he is booked to replace a faulty switch and is running late. He has no work order and is not on today’s authorised list, but he knows the IT manager’s name and is wearing a company uniform. The IT manager is contactable by phone. Your security supervisor is on site. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Escort him to the server room and stay with him while he works, so that access is supervised even though he is not on the authorised list.
Let him in, since he knows the IT manager by name, is in company uniform and is clearly expected, and note the visit in the log for the record.
Turn him away and tell him to rebook through the proper channel, since he is not on the authorised list and has no work order.
Ask him to wait in reception while you ring the IT manager to confirm the visit, and tell your security supervisor what you are doing.
explanation: A: Breaches confidentiality or process: supervision is not authorisation. An unverified visitor is in the server room either way, and standing beside him does not establish that he should be there. B: Acts on assumptions without checking: a name and a uniform are precisely what someone seeking unauthorised access would present, and the one person who could confirm it is a phone call away. Logging it afterwards records the failure rather than preventing it. C: Applies the rule without using it: the list is a control, not the only source of truth, and a genuine engineer is sent away with a failed switch unfixed when a two-minute call would have settled it. The most effective response is to ask him to wait in reception while you ring the IT manager to confirm the visit, and tell your security supervisor what you are doing: the authorised list is the control and the IT manager can extend it, so a short wait and a phone call resolves the question either way. Telling your supervisor means the decision is not yours alone. It beats turning him away and telling him to rebook through the proper channel, because that applies the rule correctly and wastes a genuine visit when verification takes two minutes. It beats escorting him to the server room and staying with him, because that grants the access first and verifies nothing; being watched is not the same as being authorised. The least effective response is letting him in because he knows the IT manager by name and is in uniform: it grants server room access on the strength of the two things easiest for an unauthorised visitor to produce, and records it afterwards. That is worse than escorting him, which at least supervises, and worse than turning him away, which at least refuses. The principle: when someone falls outside a control, verify with the person who owns it before deciding either way.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân biệt rõ giữa 'Đúng' (True) và 'Có thể xảy ra' (Possible). Chỉ chọn kết luận chắc chắn 100%.

question_text: You are a customer service assistant at a railway station. Severe weather has cancelled three services and the concourse is crowded. You have been answering questions for two hours without a break. A passenger who has already asked you twice returns and tells you, angrily, that you clearly do not know what you are talking about and asks for someone competent. Your supervisor is on the concourse. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Say nothing, look past him and start serving the next passenger in the queue, since he has already been given the information twice and the concourse is full of people who need help.
Tell him you have given him the information you have, that the delays are caused by the weather rather than by staff, and ask him to let you help the passengers waiting behind him.
Apologise and fetch your supervisor to deal with him, then carry on with the queue while she takes over the conversation.
Acknowledge that the information has kept changing, tell him what is confirmed right now and when the next update is due, and offer to take him to your supervisor if he wants more.
explanation: A: Avoids the difficult conversation: ignoring a passenger mid- complaint in a crowded concourse turns one angry man into a scene and tells everyone watching that staff disengage under pressure. B: Personalises the conflict: it is accurate and it answers his tone rather than his problem, which invites him to escalate in front of a crowded concourse. C: Passes responsibility to others: handing him straight over confirms his view that you could not help, and takes a supervisor off the concourse during a disruption when you can answer him yourself. The most effective response is to acknowledge that the information has kept changing, tell him what is confirmed right now and when the next update is due, and offer to take him to your supervisor: what he is actually short of is reliable information, so giving him that, and offering the supervisor as a route rather than a rescue, answers the complaint without conceding the insult. It beats telling him the delays are caused by the weather rather than by staff, because defending yourself, however fairly, engages with his tone instead of his problem, in front of a crowd. It beats fetching your supervisor to deal with him while you carry on with the queue, because that confirms his claim that you could not help and removes a supervisor from the concourse during disruption. The least effective response is looking past him and starting to serve the next passenger: ignoring a passenger who is mid-complaint on a crowded concourse escalates it into a scene and signals to everyone watching that staff stop engaging when it gets hard. That is worse than defending the airline, which engages badly, and worse than fetching the supervisor, which at least routes him. The principle: under personal criticism, answer the need rather than the tone, and give the person the next concrete thing they can rely on.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You are a shop floor assistant in a supermarket. You have finished facing up your aisle. Your colleague Dev is alone on the fresh produce aisle with three cages of stock to put out before the evening rush in an hour, and is clearly not going to finish. He has not asked for help. Your section manager is on a break for another twenty minutes. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Ask Dev whether he would like a hand, and find something else to do if he says he is fine, since he may have a system for working through the cages.
Go over to produce, tell Dev your aisle is done and you will take one of the cages, and work alongside him until the stock is out.
Wait for the section manager to come back from her break in twenty minutes and suggest that someone is moved onto produce to help Dev clear the cages.
Find another job in your own section, since produce is Dev's aisle tonight and stepping in without being asked might look as though you are checking up on him.
explanation: A: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholder's: a colleague halfway through three cages with an hour to go will usually say he is managing, so the question is polite and predictably leaves him alone with them. C: Delays the decision: it spends a third of the remaining hour waiting to ask someone else to do what you could start now, and the cages are no smaller when she returns. D: Invents a reason not to help: it invents a reason not to help while three cages of fresh produce miss the evening rush. Manufacturing a concern about appearances to justify standing by is the failure here. The most effective response is to go over to produce, tell Dev your aisle is done and you will take one of the cages, and work alongside him: your aisle is finished, he has an hour and more stock than he can move, and the fastest fix is a second pair of hands. Saying your aisle is done removes any need for him to admit he is behind. It beats asking whether he would like a hand and finding something else if he says he is fine, because putting that question to a colleague mid-task invites the polite refusal, and the cages remain. It beats waiting for the section manager to come back from her break, because that spends a third of the available time arranging what you could simply do. The least effective response is finding another job in your own section: it leaves a colleague to miss the evening rush while you look for other work, and the justification is a worry about how helping might look. That is worse than offering, which at least asks, and worse than waiting for the manager, which at least seeks help. The principle: when your own work is done and a colleague plainly cannot finish, start helping rather than asking or waiting.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân biệt rõ giữa 'Đúng' (True) và 'Có thể xảy ra' (Possible). Chỉ chọn kết luận chắc chắn 100%.

question_text: You are an enquiry desk assistant at a probation service. The written desk rule is that a caller is read something from their own record only after giving two pieces of information that match it. For the last month everybody on the desk has been accepting one, because the queue is long and the second question adds time to every call. Nobody has raised it. Your supervisor is working on the desk all this week. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Go back to asking for both pieces on your own calls, and say nothing to anybody about what the rest of the desk is doing, so that at least your calls follow the rule.
Send a note to the person who wrote the desk rule asking for it to be rewritten around the queue, and keep taking one piece until a new rule comes back.
Carry on taking one piece of information like everybody else, reading callers what is on their record after a single answer, and say nothing to your supervisor this week.
Ask your supervisor on the desk this week whether the second question stands, and say plainly that the desk has taken one piece for a month, since one answer covers everybody.
explanation: A: Fixes it for yourself only: your own calls were never the problem, and a month-old drift across the whole desk carries on beside you with nobody any the wiser. B: Delays the decision: a rewrite takes weeks, and every caller in the meantime is read their own record on one piece of information while the request sits in somebody's tray. C: Breaches a stated rule because everybody else does: the rule governs who gets told what is on their record, and a month of collective drift is the reason to raise it rather than the reason not to. The most effective response is asking your supervisor this week whether the second question still stands, and saying plainly that the desk has been taking one piece for a month: the rule is written, the whole desk has drifted from it, and one decision covers everybody instead of leaving each person to choose. It beats going back to asking for both pieces on your own calls while saying nothing about the rest of the desk, because your own calls were never the problem and the drift carries on beside you. It beats sending a note asking for the rule to be rewritten around the queue, since that leaves a month of callers being read their records on one piece while a rewrite is considered. The least effective response is carrying on taking one piece like everybody else: it is a written rule about who is told what is on their record, and the fact that everybody has been ignoring it is what makes raising it necessary. The principle: a rule everybody is quietly ignoring is exactly the rule somebody has to name out loud.

question_text: You are a correspondence assistant at a probation service. A member of the public wrote in three weeks ago, and a colleague replied promising a full written answer by Friday. You now know the answer cannot be prepared before the middle of next month, and the colleague who made that reply has left for two weeks. The person has already rearranged a meeting of their own so that they can act on the answer on Friday. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Wait until Friday morning and then telephone the person with the news, so that there is a chance the answer is further along by the time you have to explain the delay.
Write to the person today, say the answer cannot come before the middle of next month, apologise, and offer what Friday allows, since they can still put their own meeting back.
Let Friday pass without telling the person anything, since the answer is genuinely not ready, and wait until the middle of next month when there is something real to send.
Send the person a short note today saying their enquiry is still being worked on, and leave the date alone so that nobody has to explain a promise somebody else made.
explanation: A: Delays the difficult message: the meeting they moved is on Friday, so news that arrives that morning reaches them too late to be worth anything to them. C: Silent deadline slip: they rearranged a meeting on the strength of a date this organisation gave them, and the first thing they will learn is that Friday came and nothing arrived. D: Answers without correcting the expectation: a note that does not touch Friday leaves them still planning around it, which is the one thing they needed changing. The most effective response is to write to the person today, say the answer cannot come before the middle of next month, apologise for the reply they were given and offer what can be provided by Friday: they rearranged a meeting around a date that will not hold, and today is the last point at which they can rearrange it back. It is stronger than telephoning on Friday morning, because by then the meeting they moved is upon them and the information has lost the only value it had. It is stronger than sending a note that says the enquiry is still being worked on, because that leaves the wrong date standing and the wrong date is the whole problem. The least effective response is to let Friday pass without telling them anything and wait until there is something real to send: a late call at least reaches them, and a holding note at least shows somebody is there, whereas silence means the first thing they learn is that a date they were given passed unremarked. The principle: when a commitment made to somebody outside the organisation cannot be kept, tell them while they can still act on the news.
tip: Mẹo MT: Với bài toán quy luật chuỗi số, hãy xét hiệu số bậc 1, hiệu số bậc 2 hoặc tích lũy tiến.

question_text: You are a service desk assistant at a probation service. A member of the public arrives for an appointment that a different team booked, and it turns out the appointment was cancelled last week without anybody telling them. They are angry with you, they have taken a day off work to come in, and they say this is the second time it has happened to them. You can see the cancellation on your screen but not the reason for it, and the team that made the booking can be reached this morning. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Apologise, explain that the appointment was booked by a different team and that you cannot see why it was cancelled, and give the person the number for the team who can tell them, along with the booking reference from your screen.
Apologise for the wasted day, ring the team who made the booking while the person waits with you, and come back with either a new appointment or a time today when they will hear from somebody.
Blame the team who made the booking, telling the person that this happens every time their bookings come through this desk and that they ought to be complaining about them rather than about you.

Offer the person the next available appointment on the spot, checking the date is one they can take without another day off, and suggest they raise the cancellation with the team who booked it if they want to know why nobody told them.
explanation: A: Sends the person on with the problem: they have already lost a day and been let down twice, and a phone number puts the next piece of effort back onto them. C: Personalises the complaint: the person wants an appointment and an explanation, and turning a wasted day into an argument about which team is at fault leaves them holding neither. D: Fixes the diary and leaves the grievance: a second cancellation with no warning is the thing they came in angry about, and nobody has taken responsibility for finding out why. The most effective response is apologising for the wasted day, ringing the team who made the booking while the person waits with you, and coming back with either a new appointment or a time today when they will hear from somebody. The team is reachable this morning, so the person can leave with something instead of another errand. That is better than explaining that a different team booked it and giving them the number, because somebody who has lost a day and been let down twice should not have to make the next call themselves. It is better than offering the next appointment and suggesting they chase the cancellation, because that answers the diary and not the reason they are angry. The least effective response is blaming the team who made the booking and telling the person that they ought to be complaining about them: handing over the number at least points somewhere useful, and offering an appointment at least gives them a date, whereas an argument about whose fault it is puts your own position ahead of the person standing in front of you and gets them no closer to either. The principle: anger about something another team did is still your problem to resolve while the person is in front of you.
