question_text: You are a contact handling assistant at a probation service. Over lunch a colleague tells you, asking you to keep it to yourself, that they have not managed to reach a person who has been ringing the enquiry line for three weeks. That same person is on the list of callers another team is writing to on Friday, and that team is working on the basis that contact has been made. Your supervisor, who reports to the person running the department, is in the office this afternoon. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell the other team that contact with the caller has been made and that nothing on their Friday list needs changing, so that your colleague's confidence is kept and the letters still go out on time.
Ask your colleague to tell the other team themselves before Friday and leave it with them, since the information is theirs and they are the one who knows what has and has not been tried.

Go to your supervisor this afternoon, say a caller on Friday's list may not have been reached, since that team assumes otherwise, and let them decide who needs telling, without repeating the lunchtime conversation.
Send the other team a note suggesting they check that caller's record before Friday, saying nothing about where your doubt came from, and let them reach their own conclusion.
explanation: A: States as fact what you have not checked: your colleague said only that they had failed to reach the caller, so Friday's letters would go out on an assurance nobody in the organisation can stand behind. B: Leaves the outcome resting on somebody else's nerve: Friday is three days away, and if your colleague says nothing you will have spent the time that could have fixed it. D: Hints instead of raising it: a note with no reason behind it is easy to file, and the team has no way of knowing the doubt is solid enough to hold Friday's letters for. The most effective response is going to your supervisor this afternoon to say a caller on Friday’s list may not have been reached and letting them decide who needs telling. The judgement here is whose problem this is: a confidence does not survive contact with work that somebody else is about to act on, and your supervisor is the person who can weigh both without you retelling the lunchtime conversation. That is better than asking your colleague to tell the other team themselves, because the deadline then depends on somebody who has already chosen to keep it quiet. It is better than sending an unexplained note suggesting a record check, because the team cannot tell a real warning from routine tidying and Friday arrives either way. The least effective response is telling the other team that contact has been made and nothing needs changing: the note at least prompts a check and the request to your colleague at least involves somebody who knows the facts, whereas an assurance you invented removes the last chance anybody had of catching it. The principle: a confidence binds you to discretion about how you raise something, never to silence about work that other people are relying on.
tip: Mẹo MT: Áp dụng sơ đồ Venn hoặc bảng chân trị logic để biểu diễn mối quan hệ giữa các đối tượng.

question_text: You are a contact handling assistant at a probation service. A colleague on your team has twice described calls the two of you took, including what the callers said and where they live, to friends in a pub where other people could hear. They say it is harmless because no names were used. The rule you both signed says nothing about a call leaves the team. Your supervisor asks the team every Friday whether anything needs raising. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell the colleague directly that what they described could identify a caller, say that you will raise it on Friday if it happens again, and then do exactly that.
Repeat it around the team and spread the story of the pub, so that everybody knows who talks about callers and the colleague hears about it from somebody other than you.
Raise it with the whole team on Friday without speaking to the colleague first, and restate the rule about calls without mentioning the pub or naming anybody at all.
Leave it alone and take your breaks away from the colleague, on the basis that what they do in a pub is between them and the rule they signed.
explanation: B: Turns it into gossip about a person: the confidentiality problem is left exactly where it was, the colleague learns it secondhand, and nobody who could act has been told anything. C: Chooses the group over the person: a general restatement lets the one person it is aimed at conclude it was aimed at somebody else, and the retelling carries on. D: Avoids the difficult conversation: the calls being described are ones you took as well, the colleague thinks it is harmless, and nobody has told them otherwise. The most effective response is telling the colleague directly that what they described could identify a caller, and saying you will raise it on Friday if it happens again: they believe it is harmless, nobody has told them otherwise, and the rule they signed is what settles it. It beats raising it with the whole team on Friday without speaking to the colleague first, because a general restatement lets the person it is about decide it was meant for somebody else. It beats leaving it alone and taking your breaks elsewhere, since the calls being described are ones the two of you took and the next retelling is days away. The least effective response is repeating it around the team and spreading the story of the pub: it makes a confidentiality problem into entertainment about a colleague, and still nobody who could act on the rule has heard a word. The principle: deal with a colleague’s conduct with the colleague, and take it to the person who can act if it does not stop.
tip: Mẹo MT: Với bài toán quy luật chuỗi số, hãy xét hiệu số bậc 1, hiệu số bậc 2 hoặc tích lũy tiến.

question_text: You are a new entrant at a probation service. You are helping with the paperwork for the next intake. Yesterday you heard a colleague tell an applicant on the phone that the intake starts on the ninth. This morning the course timetable you were given shows it starting on the sixteenth, and the applicant has to give a month’s notice to leave their current job. The colleague is away until next week, and the person running the course is at their desk today. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Ring the applicant yourself and say the timetable you were given this morning shows the sixteenth, without first finding out from anybody at the course which of the two dates the intake is actually running to.
Say nothing to anybody and carry on with the paperwork, since the colleague knows the intake better than you do and will be back next week to put it right.
Check the intake date with the person running the course today, and tell them what the applicant was told, since the applicant must give a month's notice against that date.
Leave a note on the colleague's desk setting out both dates for their return next week, so that the person who gave the applicant the date is the one who corrects it with them.
explanation: A: Acts on an assumption without checking: you hold one timetable and a colleague told them something else, so a second date from a second person may leave the applicant no better informed. B: Withholds a fact somebody needs now: the applicant is about to give a month's notice on a date that may be wrong, and next week is after the point at which that becomes hard to undo. D: Waits for the person who made the mistake: the correction then arrives a week later than it could have, and the applicant may already have handed in notice against the wrong date. The most effective response is checking the intake date with the person running the course today and telling them what the applicant was told yesterday. One of the two dates is wrong, the person running the course can settle which in a minute, and the applicant is about to act on it by giving notice. It beats ringing the applicant yourself with the sixteenth, because you would be the second person to give them an unverified date. It beats leaving a note for the colleague to deal with next week, because notice given in the meantime cannot easily be taken back. The least effective response is saying nothing to anybody and carrying on with the paperwork, leaving it for the colleague to put right next week: the one person who needs the fact is the applicant, and the whole cost of the delay falls on them. It is worse than ringing the applicant, which at least gets the timetable date to them, and worse than the note, which at least starts a correction moving. The principle: when you hold a fact that contradicts what somebody outside has been told, raise it with whoever can confirm it while there is still time for the correction to matter.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân biệt rõ giữa 'Đúng' (True) và 'Có thể xảy ra' (Possible). Chỉ chọn kết luận chắc chắn 100%.

question_text: You are a shift team member at a probation service. At the end of each shift every person is supposed to write and sign their own entry in the handover record, so that the team coming on knows who to ask about what. To get everybody away on time, one of your team has taken to writing and signing all four entries in advance. Everybody knows, nobody has raised it, and the team coming on has twice asked you about an entry you did not write. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Raise it with the colleague first, say that you will be writing and signing your own entry from now on, and tell them why the team coming on needs to know who to ask.
Write and sign your own entry each shift without saying anything to the colleague, and let the team coming on work out for themselves whose entries are whose.
Report the practice to your supervisor without speaking to the colleague first, since the rule is plain and it is not your place to police the habits of your own team.
Bring it up in front of the whole team at the start of the next shift, naming the colleague and reading out the entries, and say they have been signing for work they did not do.
explanation: B: Fixes it only for yourself: three of the four entries stay in one hand, so the people coming on are still asking the wrong person about most of the shift. C: Escalates before speaking to the person: nobody has ever raised it, so the colleague has had no chance to stop, and a report lands as an accusation rather than a correction. D: Blames a colleague in front of the team: it makes a private correction into a public accusation, aimed at the person everybody relies on to get them away on time. The most effective response is to raise it with the colleague first, say that you will be writing and signing your own entry from now on, and tell them why the team coming on needs to know who to ask: the shortcut has a real benefit so it deserves a conversation rather than an ambush, and the team coming on has already been sent to the wrong person twice. It is better than writing and signing your own entry each shift without saying anything, because the other three entries stay in one hand and the people coming on still cannot tell whose is whose. It is better than reporting the practice to your supervisor without speaking to the colleague first, because nobody has ever raised it and the colleague has had no chance to stop. The least effective response is to bring it up in front of the whole team at the start of the next shift and say the colleague has been signing for work they did not do: it makes a private correction into a public accusation, aimed at somebody the whole team relies on. The principle: a shortcut that breaks a stated rule is raised with the person taking it, in private, before it is raised anywhere else.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You are an engagement events assistant at a probation service. A community group running Thursday’s joint event needs the final numbers and the room layout from you by noon tomorrow, which you agreed with its organiser a fortnight ago. Yesterday you were also given the write-up of feedback forms from last month’s events, wanted by the end of the week. It became clear this morning that you cannot finish both by noon tomorrow, and the organiser does not know that yet. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Give the morning to the feedback write-up and the afternoon to the numbers and layout, then see tomorrow which of the two is nearer to being finished.
Assume the community group will be relaxed about noon, say nothing to its organiser, and spend today and tomorrow morning on the feedback write-up, leaving the numbers and layout unfinished.
Finish the numbers and the room layout for noon tomorrow, and tell the person who asked for the feedback write-up this morning that it will now come at the end of next week.
Do the feedback write-up first because it was the most recent thing you were asked to do, and start the numbers and layout with whatever time is left tomorrow.
explanation: A: Splits effort so nothing finishes: noon tomorrow is fixed and the feedback is not due until the end of the week, so dividing today between them risks missing the only date somebody outside is waiting on. B: Assumes goodwill instead of checking it: nobody has asked the organiser anything, she is expecting the layout at noon for an event two days later, and she finds out only when it fails to arrive. D: Ranks the work by who asked most recently: recency is not a reason, the feedback has four more days and the layout has until noon, so the two dates are never actually compared. The most effective response is finishing the numbers and the room layout for noon tomorrow and telling the person who asked for the feedback write-up that it will now come at the end of next week. One date is tomorrow with an outside group behind it and the other has the rest of the week, so the order is settled by the dates, and the person whose work slips hears it while they can still do something. It beats giving the morning to the feedback and the afternoon to the numbers, because the fixed noon deadline should not be spending half of today competing with work that is not due yet. It is also better than doing the feedback first because it was asked most recently, which orders the day by nothing at all. The least effective response is assuming the community group will be relaxed about noon: unlike alternating, which at least advances both, and unlike the recency order, which at least decides something, this rests the whole plan on goodwill nobody has tested, and the organiser learns of the slip only when noon passes. The principle: order work by the dates people are relying on, and tell whoever loses out while they still have room to move.
tip: Mẹo MT: Với bài toán quy luật chuỗi số, hãy xét hiệu số bậc 1, hiệu số bậc 2 hoặc tích lũy tiến.

question_text: You are an incident coordinator. You promised the on-call handover pack by Friday and it will now be Tuesday. The person who runs the weekend rota is building this weekend’s cover around it and is on annual leave until Thursday. Her deputy is at his desk today and has the rota open in front of him. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Email her now so that she reads it on Thursday when she is back, and carry on with the pack in the meantime without troubling anybody else.
Say nothing until she is back on Thursday. She owns the rota, and one working day either way will not change very much about what she decides.
Tell her deputy today that the pack will be Tuesday rather than Friday, so that this weekend's cover is built on the real date, and email her as well.
Tell the deputy the pack may be a little late without giving him the new date, so that he is warned and she is not alarmed while she is away.
explanation: A: Sends the warning to the one person who cannot act on it: she is on leave until Thursday and the cover is being built this week. B: Stays silent while the plan is built: the weekend cover is assembled around a Friday pack that is not coming, and only you know that. D: Warns without the number he needs: he cannot rebuild a weekend rota around might be late, and Tuesday is the only fact that would let him. The most effective response is to tell her deputy today that the pack will be Tuesday rather than Friday, and email her as well. He is at his desk with the rota open, the weekend is being planned now, and emailing her means nothing is done behind her back. It beats emailing her now so she reads it on Thursday, because she cannot act until then and the cover is assembled this week. It beats telling the deputy the pack may be a little late without giving him the new date, because a vague warning cannot be planned around. The least effective response is saying nothing until she is back on Thursday: it is worse than either of the other two, because both reach somebody with something, while this leaves a weekend rota being built around a pack that is not coming. The principle: when your slip lands inside somebody else’s plan, tell whoever is holding it today, with the date.
tip: Mẹo MT: Áp dụng sơ đồ Venn hoặc bảng chân trị logic để biểu diễn mối quan hệ giữa các đối tượng.

question_text: You are a release coordinator. A customer emails you directly because yesterday’s release changed a screen her staff use all day and she cannot find a setting they rely on. She has written to you because your name was on the release note. You know where the setting has moved to. The support queue is running at three days. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Reply to her today telling her where the setting has moved, and raise a ticket yourself so that the change gets documented for everybody else who will hit it.
Reply asking her to raise it through the support portal, where her question will be picked up by whoever is on the queue that day.
Reply with where the setting has moved to and leave it there, since her question is answered and the release note is somebody else's document to maintain.
Forward her email to the team who wrote the screen and ask them to reply to her directly, as they will explain the change far better than you could.
explanation: B: Passes the problem on without owning it: she wrote to the one person who knows the answer, and is sent to a three-day queue to be told what you could say now. C: Answers her and stops: the next twenty customers hit the same wall, and the note that caused it stays exactly as wrong as it was this morning. D: Adds a hop she did not ask for: they may well explain it better, and she is now waiting on people who have not agreed to write to her. The most effective response is to reply to her today telling her where the setting has moved, and raise a ticket so the change gets documented. She needs one sentence you already have, and the fact that she had to ask is evidence the release note is missing something others will need. It beats replying with where the setting has moved and leaving it there, because that leaves the same gap for everyone behind her, and the note carries your name. It beats forwarding her email to the team who wrote the screen, because they have not agreed to write to customers and she gets no faster answer. The least effective response is asking her to raise it through the support portal: it is worse than either of the other two, because both end with her being told something, while this sends the person who reached the only individual holding the answer into a three-day queue. The principle: when a customer reaches the person who knows, answer, and fix the thing that made her have to ask.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân biệt rõ giữa 'Đúng' (True) và 'Có thể xảy ra' (Possible). Chỉ chọn kết luận chắc chắn 100%.

question_text: You are an incident coordinator. You and a colleague disagree about whether last week’s outage should be recorded as a supplier failure or as one of the team’s own. The disagreement has been going on for days. A customer who was affected rings you today and asks, in passing, what caused it. Your colleague is not on the call. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell her the cause is still being agreed internally and that she will have the finished account this week, so that she has a date, and settle it with your colleague after.
Give her both accounts and let her make up her own mind, since she was the one affected and has as much right to the facts as anybody inside the team.
Tell her you cannot discuss the cause at all and end the conversation there, so that nothing is said which might contradict the final write-up.
Give her your version of the cause and mention that a colleague sees it differently, so that a customer's view carries some weight in settling it.
explanation: B: Hands a customer an unfinished argument: she now has two conflicting causes from one supplier and no way at all of choosing between them. C: Refuses a question you can partly answer: that the account is being finalised is itself true, useful and safe to say. D: Recruits the customer into an internal argument: it puts a person outside the company into a dispute between two colleagues in order to win it. The most effective response is to tell her the cause is still being agreed internally and that she will have the finished account this week, and settle it with your colleague afterwards. She asked a fair question and the honest answer is both true and useful, while the disagreement belongs with him. It beats giving her both accounts and letting her make up her own mind, because two conflicting causes from one supplier is worse than none. It beats telling her you cannot discuss the cause at all, because that withholds something you can safely tell her. The least effective response is giving her your version and mentioning that a colleague sees it differently: it is worse than either of the other two, because both leave the disagreement inside the company, while this uses a customer as leverage against a colleague who is not on the call. The principle: tell the customer honestly where the account stands, and never reach outside the team for weight in an argument inside it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Với bài toán quy luật chuỗi số, hãy xét hiệu số bậc 1, hiệu số bậc 2 hoặc tích lũy tiến.

question_text: You are a build engineer. You and a colleague have argued twice this week about whose checks run first in the release, and neither of you has given ground. The releases are now going out later each day because of it. This morning the person who owns the release schedule asks you, casually, how the two of you are getting along. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Say the two of you disagree about the order of the checks and that it is costing time, and ask him to settle it, so that it stops being decided by whoever pushes hardest.
Raise his judgement with the schedule owner behind his back, so that the order gets decided by somebody who has heard only one side of the argument.
Say the two of you are getting along fine and sort the order out with him yourself, without involving the person who owns the schedule in something small.
Describe it as a process problem without saying who is on which side, and leave him to work out for himself who he ought to be asking about it.
explanation: B: Personalises the conflict: it converts a disagreement about sequencing into a verdict on him, delivered to the one person with power over both your weeks. C: Reports a problem as solved while it is still costing time: two failed attempts is evidence you cannot settle it, and the releases keep slipping meanwhile. D: Names the problem but not the people: he cannot resolve a dispute whose parties are hidden, so the disclosure buys nothing and costs another day. The most effective response is to say the two of you disagree about the order of the checks and that it is costing time, and ask him to settle it. The disagreement is about sequencing, which is what the schedule owner owns, and it has already failed twice to settle itself. It beats saying the two of you are getting along fine and sorting the order out yourselves, because two attempts have proved you cannot, and the daily slippage keeps running. It beats describing it as a process problem without saying who is on which side, because a dispute with its parties removed cannot be arbitrated. The least effective response is raising his judgement with the schedule owner behind his back: it is worse than either of the other two, because both keep the conversation about the checks, while this puts his judgement in front of the person who decides his work, in a conversation he is not in. The principle: take a sequencing dispute to whoever owns the sequence, describe both sides, and never make the argument about the other person while they are absent.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You are a product assistant. Five weeks ago a customer asked for a change to how a report is filtered. You logged it and never went back to her. She has not chased. Today you are choosing which four requests go into next month’s work, and hers is one of eleven candidates with no recent activity against it. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Email her today asking whether the request still matters and how much, and use the answer when you choose the four rather than guessing from the silence.
Put her request into next month's four on the basis that five weeks is too long to have waited, whether or not she still needs it now.
Leave hers out of the four, since five weeks without a chase almost certainly means she found another way round it or it was never that important.
Ask the support team whether she has raised it again through any other route, and decide about next month once you hear back from them.
explanation: B: Buys back the delay with the wrong currency: a place in next month's four may go to something she no longer wants, and three other customers lose it. C: Assumes the silence away: she stopped chasing because nobody replied, and the request is now dropped on the strength of your own failure to answer. D: Checks the wrong side of the silence: she can tell you today whether it still matters, and the support team can only tell you whether she asked twice. The most effective response is to email her today asking whether the request still matters and how much, and use the answer when you choose the four. Only she can say whether it is still live, one email settles it, and next month’s four should be chosen on what customers currently need. It beats putting her request into next month’s four because five weeks is too long to have waited, since a slot given out of guilt may go to something she has stopped wanting while three others lose their place. It beats asking the support team whether she has raised it again elsewhere, because they can only report whether she asked, and she can tell you whether she needs it. The least effective response is leaving hers out because five weeks without a chase means she found another way round it: it is worse than either of the other two, because both act on the request, while this reads her silence as her having stopped needing it, when the likelier cause is that nobody answered her. The principle: five weeks of silence after you failed to reply is evidence about you, not about how much the customer wants it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You are a service desk analyst. Every Friday you send a note confirming that all sixty open tickets have been reviewed and updated. This week you have got through forty-five; the last fifteen belong to a colleague who is off sick and whose notes you cannot see. Three managers use that note to decide where to put people next week. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Record all sixty as checked and updated. The fifteen have not changed hands this week, and nobody reading a Friday note is going to open them one by one.
Send the note saying forty-five were reviewed and fifteen could not be, name why, and say when you expect to reach the last fifteen.
Hold the note until Monday when your colleague is back, and tell the three managers that this week's version is going to arrive late.
Send the note covering only the forty-five you did review, without mentioning anywhere that another fifteen tickets exist behind it.
explanation: A: Certifies work that was not done: the note's only value is that somebody looked, and three managers will place people next week on fifteen tickets nobody read. C: Delays a note that is used before Monday: the placement decisions are made on Friday, so a complete note on Monday informs nothing at all. D: Omits the part that matters: a clean note about forty-five reads as a clean note about everything, and the gap is invisible to the people relying on it. The most effective response is to send the note saying forty-five were reviewed and fifteen could not be, name why, and say when you expect to reach the last fifteen. The managers need to know what was checked and what was not, on Friday, and the reason turns your problem into one somebody can cover. It beats holding the note until Monday when your colleague is back, because the decisions are taken on Friday. It beats sending a note covering only the forty-five you did review, because a note listing forty-five reads as a note about the whole queue. The least effective response is recording all sixty as checked and updated: it is worse than either of the other two, because both leave a reader able to work out what was covered, late or incomplete, while this states that all sixty were reviewed when fifteen were not. The principle: a status note earns its value from being accurate about its own gaps, so report the part you did and name the part you could not.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You are an access administrator. You and a colleague check each other’s access requests before they are granted. Last month he wrote on one of yours that you had clearly not looked at the job titles. He was right and it was fairly put, but you have thought about it since. Three of his requests are now sitting in your queue. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Check the three requests today as you always would, and mention to him when you next speak that the comment landed harder than he probably intended it to.
Stop checking his requests after that comment, and leave the three of them in the queue for whichever of the other checkers gets to them first.
Check the three and go through them far more slowly than usual, so that nothing at all could be said about the care you have taken over them.
Ask to be paired with a different checker in future, so that the two of you are not marking each other's work and last month cannot happen again.
explanation: B: Withdraws help after a fair correction: three people are waiting on access, and the reason their requests stopped moving exists nowhere they could find it. C: Turns a correction into over-caution: the queue slows for everybody, and the extra time buys accuracy nobody needed on requests that were fine. D: Rearranges the team around one remark: it is a real fix for a problem that may not exist, and it costs the pairing that caught your mistake. The most effective response is to check the three requests today as you always would, and mention when you next speak that the comment landed harder than he probably intended. The correction was right and fairly made, three people are waiting, and saying it stung is a smaller thing than rearranging your work around it. It beats checking the three and going through them far more slowly than usual, because that buys no accuracy on requests that were already sound and the queue pays. It beats asking to be paired with a different checker in future, because the pairing worked exactly as intended. The least effective response is stopping checking his requests and leaving the three in the queue: it is worse than either of the other two, because both keep them moving, while this simply stops and the three people waiting have no way of knowing why. The principle: a correction you agree with is worth saying out loud, and it is never worth paying for out of other people’s queue.
tip: Mẹo MT: Áp dụng sơ đồ Venn hoặc bảng chân trị logic để biểu diễn mối quan hệ giữa các đối tượng.

question_text: In the sequence B, D, G, K, P, … each step follows a fixed rule. Which letter comes next?
options: U
V
T
W
explanation: Using each letter’s position (B=2, D=4, G=7, K=11, P=16), the gaps grow 2, 3, 4, 5, so the next gap is 6. Adding 6 to P’s position of 16 gives 22, which is V. The letter U (21) keeps the gap at 5; T (20) keeps it at 4; W (23) jumps the gap to 7. Only a gap of 6 continues the pattern.

question_text: In a certain code, FISH is written as GJTI. Using the same rule, how is BIRD written?
options: CJSE
AHQC
CJSD
DKTF
explanation: Each letter moves one place forward in the alphabet: F to G, I to J, S to T, H to I. Applying the same shift to BIRD gives C, J, S, E, so CJSE. AHQC moves each letter one place backward instead of forward. CJSD leaves the final D unshifted. DKTF moves every letter two places forward rather than one.

question_text: Author is to book as composer is to which of the following?
options: Orchestra
Instrument
Symphony
Concert
explanation: An author is the creator of a book, so by the same creator-to-creation relationship a composer is the creator of a musical work, and a symphony is the only created work among the options. A concert is the event where a work is performed, not the work itself.

question_text: Four of these five numbers share a property that the fifth does not: 12, 16, 20, 25, 28. Which is the odd one out?
explanation: The numbers 12, 16, 20 and 28 are all multiples of four; 25 is not (it is also the only odd number), so 25 is the odd one out. Singling out 16 as the only power of two still leaves it a multiple of four, the property the other three share. Singling out 12 or 28 picks them by size or by an unrelated factor, yet both remain multiples of four.

question_text: A sequence begins 4, 9, 19, 39, 79, … Each term follows the same fixed rule. What is the next term?
explanation: Each term is double the one before plus one: 4, then 9, 19, 39, 79, so the next is 79 times 2 plus 1, which is 159. Equivalently the gaps double (5, 10, 20, 40, then 80), giving 79 plus 80 = 159. The value 158 doubles 79 but forgets the plus one. The value 119 keeps the gap fixed at 40 (79 + 40). The value 99 uses the earlier gap of 20 (79 + 20).
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: A parcel routing rule states that parcels heavier than 2 kg go by courier and lighter parcels go by post. Courier parcels are insured; postal parcels are not. A parcel weighs 3 kg. Which of these is certain?
options: It goes by post.
It is not insured.
It is insured.
It could go either way.
explanation: At 3 kg the parcel is heavier than 2 kg, so it goes by courier, and courier parcels are insured; therefore it is insured. Concluding it goes by post misreads the weight rule, since 3 kg is above the 2 kg threshold, not below it. Concluding it is not insured applies the postal branch, which does not apply here. Concluding it could go either way ignores that the two rules together fix the outcome exactly.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You are a shop floor assistant in a supermarket. You have finished facing up your aisle. Your colleague Dev is alone on the fresh produce aisle with three cages of stock to put out before the evening rush in an hour, and is clearly not going to finish. He has not asked for help. Your section manager is on a break for another twenty minutes. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Ask Dev whether he would like a hand, and find something else to do if he says he is fine, since he may have a system for working through the cages.
Go over to produce, tell Dev your aisle is done and you will take one of the cages, and work alongside him until the stock is out.
Wait for the section manager to come back from her break in twenty minutes and suggest that someone is moved onto produce to help Dev clear the cages.
Find another job in your own section, since produce is Dev's aisle tonight and stepping in without being asked might look as though you are checking up on him.
explanation: A: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholder's: a colleague halfway through three cages with an hour to go will usually say he is managing, so the question is polite and predictably leaves him alone with them. C: Delays the decision: it spends a third of the remaining hour waiting to ask someone else to do what you could start now, and the cages are no smaller when she returns. D: Invents a reason not to help: it invents a reason not to help while three cages of fresh produce miss the evening rush. Manufacturing a concern about appearances to justify standing by is the failure here. The most effective response is to go over to produce, tell Dev your aisle is done and you will take one of the cages, and work alongside him: your aisle is finished, he has an hour and more stock than he can move, and the fastest fix is a second pair of hands. Saying your aisle is done removes any need for him to admit he is behind. It beats asking whether he would like a hand and finding something else if he says he is fine, because putting that question to a colleague mid-task invites the polite refusal, and the cages remain. It beats waiting for the section manager to come back from her break, because that spends a third of the available time arranging what you could simply do. The least effective response is finding another job in your own section: it leaves a colleague to miss the evening rush while you look for other work, and the justification is a worry about how helping might look. That is worse than offering, which at least asks, and worse than waiting for the manager, which at least seeks help. The principle: when your own work is done and a colleague plainly cannot finish, start helping rather than asking or waiting.

question_text: You work in a freight forwarding office. Your colleague Ben handles customs paperwork and is off sick today. A shipment he was preparing must be lodged with customs by 4pm or it misses its vessel and waits a week. You have done the paperwork before but not for this commodity. It is 1pm. Your office manager is on site and there is a customs broker the company uses. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Leave the shipment for Ben to lodge when he is back, since the paperwork is his responsibility and it would be worse to submit a customs entry that turns out to be wrong.
Start the paperwork yourself and work through it carefully, asking the office manager only if you reach something you genuinely cannot resolve before 4pm.
Ring the customs broker and ask them to lodge the entry, since they handle this commodity routinely and the deadline leaves no room for a mistake.
Tell the office manager now that Ben is off and the 4pm customs deadline is at risk, say what you can do, and agree whether you proceed or the broker is used.
explanation: A: Hides the problem / silent deadline slip: the shipment misses its vessel and waits a week, and nobody with the power to prevent it is told. Caution about accuracy does not explain the silence. B: Acts on assumptions without checking: three hours is enough only if nothing goes wrong on a commodity you have never handled, and the point at which you find out is likely to be too late to change course. C: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholder's: using the broker incurs a cost the office manager has not agreed, and she is on site and able to decide in a minute. The most effective response is to tell the office manager now that Ben is off and the 4pm customs deadline is at risk, say what you can do, and agree whether you proceed or the broker is used: there are three hours, two possible routes and a cost decision attached to one of them, and she is on site and owns that choice. Telling her what you can and cannot do lets her pick quickly. It beats starting the paperwork yourself and asking only if you reach something you cannot resolve, because pressing on alone with an unfamiliar commodity risks discovering the problem when neither route is available any more. It beats ringing the customs broker to lodge the entry, because that commits the company to a cost that is not yours to authorise, when she is a minute away. The least effective response is leaving the shipment for Ben to lodge when he is back: it lets it miss its vessel and wait a week without telling anyone who could have prevented it, using the absent colleague’s ownership as the reason. That is worse than the other two, which pick a route without permission but keep the shipment moving. The principle: when a deadline is at risk and the choice of route has a cost, raise it with the person who decides while both routes are still open.

question_text: You are a field support technician for a telecoms company. You are on site installing a new phone system for a small business that closes for the weekend at 5pm today. By 2pm it is clear one part is missing and the system cannot be finished today; it can be completed on Monday. The office manager who booked the work is on site. Your own scheduler, who arranges return visits, is at her desk. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Work on until 5pm, leave once the office has closed, and let your scheduler contact the office manager on Monday morning to arrange the return visit for the missing part.
Ring your scheduler to book Monday's return visit, then carry on until 5pm so the office manager sees the work has progressed as far as it possibly could today.
Tell the office manager that you have hit a snag and are doing everything you can, and give her a full picture on Monday once you know exactly what is needed to finish.
Tell the office manager now that a missing part means the system cannot go live today, confirm what still works over the weekend, and agree a Monday return before you leave site.
explanation: A: Hides the problem / silent deadline slip: the business closes believing its phones are live and discovers on Monday that they are not. Leaving site without telling the customer is concealment, and it removes every chance she had to arrange cover. B: Tells the wrong audience first: the person standing on site, whose business runs on the phones this weekend, learns last about a problem you have already reported internally. C: Delays the message: a snag with no detail leaves her unable to plan her weekend cover, when you already know the specific fact she needs, that the system will not go live before Monday. The most effective response is to tell the office manager now that a missing part means the system cannot go live today, confirm what still works, and agree a Monday return before you leave: she is standing there, she runs a business that depends on those phones over the weekend, and she needs those three facts before 5pm. It beats ringing your scheduler to book the return visit first, because that puts internal tidiness ahead of the person whose weekend depends on the answer. It beats telling her you have hit a snag and are doing everything you can, because a vague snag withholds the one hard fact she can plan around, when you already know it. The least effective response is leaving once the office has closed and letting your scheduler arrange it on Monday: it is the only response where she finds out after you have gone, which removes every opportunity she had to arrange cover, and it leaves the news to be broken by someone who was never on site. That is worse than the other two, which communicate imperfectly but in time. The principle: tell the person carrying the consequence first, tell them while they can still act, and tell them what you actually know.

question_text: You are a mechanic in the workshop of a bicycle shop. A customer’s bike is booked in for a gear repair, agreed for collection on Saturday morning. She phones to confirm, mentioning she is riding a charity event on Sunday. Your supplier has just confirmed the replacement part cannot be delivered before the middle of next week, and no other stockist holds it. The shop keeps a small fleet of loan bikes for situations like this. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Explain that repairs depend on parts suppliers and there is nothing anyone can do, and point out that bikes for weekend events really need booking in earlier.
Tell her the part cannot arrive before her event, apologise, and offer a loan bike set up for Sunday, with the repair finished next week.
Promise the repair will be ready for Saturday as agreed, phone the supplier every day to push for an earlier delivery, and keep her updated on progress.
Give her the supplier's phone number so she can chase the part herself, since the supplier can tell her first-hand whether an earlier delivery is possible.
explanation: A: Blames the customer and dismisses her need: the delay is the supplier's, not hers, and telling her nothing can be done while a loan fleet sits available sends her away without a bike for Sunday, a service failure of attitude rather than just of stock. C: Over-promises: the supplier has already confirmed the part cannot arrive before the middle of next week, so promising Saturday commits to an outcome you cannot control and risks her discovering too late that she has no bike for Sunday. D: Passes responsibility to others: sending the customer to chase your supplier hands her the shop's problem, and since delivery before next week has already been ruled out, the calls would change nothing about her real need, which is a bike to ride on Sunday. The most effective response is to tell her the part cannot arrive before her event, apologise, and offer a loan bike set up for Sunday: the supplier has ruled out an earlier delivery, so the honest answer plus the one thing the shop can actually do meets her real need, riding the charity event, while the repair follows next week. It beats promising the repair for Saturday and chasing the supplier daily, because that promises a completion the supplier has already said is impossible, raising her hopes on an outcome you cannot control and risking her finding out too late to arrange anything else. It beats giving her the supplier’s number to chase the part herself, because the delivery date is already settled and that does nothing about Sunday. The least effective response is explaining that nothing can be done and that she should have booked earlier: unlike the Saturday promise, which at least tries to serve her and keeps her informed, and unlike handing her the supplier’s number, which at least engages with the part problem, it blames her for a delay that is not her fault and turns her away with nothing while a loan fleet sits available. The principle: when you cannot deliver what was agreed, say so honestly and meet the customer’s underlying need with what you can deliver.

question_text: You are an adviser in an insurance company’s customer contact centre. Your colleague Marta, who sits beside you and often helps you with tricky cases, has been locked out of the customer-records system; the IT helpdesk resets locked accounts within about half an hour. Company policy says logins must never be shared, because every change to a customer’s record is logged against the account that made it, and sharing one is treated as a disciplinary matter. Marta asks you to give her your login so she can keep working while she waits. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?

Give Marta your username and password so she can keep taking calls, planning to change the password once her own account has been restored.
Sidestep the request by saying you are about to need the system yourself for back-to-back calls, hoping she asks somebody else instead of you.
Keep hold of your own session and enter Marta's record updates yourself as she reads them out, so her customers are still served while she waits.
explanation: B: Breaches confidentiality or process: handing over your login gives untracked access to customer records under your name, in knowing breach of a stated disciplinary rule, to save part of a half-hour wait, a deliberate policy breach rather than a judgement call about helpfulness. The most effective response is to tell Marta you cannot share your login and suggest she asks the team leader to help cover the queue: it declines plainly, keeps the audit trail the policy exists to protect, and deals with the real pressure through a legitimate route, for a lockout the helpdesk will clear within about half an hour. It beats saying you are about to need the system yourself, because that ducks the refusal behind an invented excuse, leaving Marta free to ask someone else and the queue problem unraised. It beats keying her record updates yourself as she reads them out, because that, though well meant, enters her judgements on customer records under your name, which is precisely the accountability the logging rule protects, and it halves your own call handling while doing nothing to restore her access. The least effective response is giving her your username and password: unlike the invented excuse, which shares nothing, and unlike typing her updates yourself, which keeps you in control of your own session, it hands untracked access to customer records in knowing breach of a stated disciplinary rule, all to shave minutes off a half-hour wait. The principle: when loyalty or convenience pulls against a clear protective rule, decline plainly and solve the pressure through a legitimate route.

question_text: You are a duty supervisor at a retail chain. A new process was explained at this morning’s briefing, but only half the team was there because the rest were dealing with a delivery. Your manager has asked whether the briefing covered everybody, as she is reporting on it this afternoon. The remaining half can be briefed tomorrow morning before they start. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell her the briefing covered everybody who was available and leave it there, since the ones who missed it were working and that is hardly a failure of the briefing.
Brief the other half yourself before the end of today's shift and tell her afterwards that everybody has now been covered.
Tell her the briefing has been done, and mention the delivery separately later on today when there is more time to explain.
Tell her half the team was briefed and why, say the rest are booked for tomorrow morning, and ask whether she needs it done before her report goes in.
explanation: A: Answers with a form of words: it is technically defensible and she still reports this afternoon that the team has been briefed. B: Fixes the fact and delays the answer: she is reporting this afternoon and has to write it before she hears from you. C: States a completion that has not happened: she writes this afternoon's report on the strength of it, and the qualification arrives after the report she needed it for. The most effective response is to tell her half the team was briefed and why, say the rest are booked for tomorrow morning, and ask whether she needs it finished before her report: she gets the true position, the plan that fixes it, and the chance to say that this afternoon is the deadline that matters. It beats briefing the rest today and telling her afterwards, because her report goes in before she hears. It beats answering that everybody available was briefed, because that is a form of words designed to pass rather than to inform. The least effective response is telling her the briefing has been done and mentioning the delivery later: an incomplete briefing is reported as complete to somebody who is about to write it down, which is a different kind of wrong from answering slowly or from answering evasively. The principle: when somebody needs a fact for a report, give them the fact and the plan, in that order and at once.

question_text: You are a supply chain graduate at a retail chain. In yesterday’s planning call a colleague from the site team said, sharply, that your volume numbers were “made up in a spreadsheet by somebody who has never seen a delivery”. You run that call every week and he is the person who knows what the sites can actually take. Next week’s call is on Monday and the volumes have to be agreed on it. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Stop inviting him to the planning call after that exchange, and send him the agreed numbers afterwards so that he still has what he needs for the week.
Raise it with his team leader before Monday, since a remark like that in front of the whole call is not something you should have to work around every week.
Say nothing and carry on running the call exactly as before, on the basis that the numbers speak for themselves and the remark will be forgotten by Monday.
Ask him for twenty minutes before Monday to walk through how the volumes are built and what he would change, so that Monday's numbers carry what he knows about the sites.

C: Avoids the conversation the call needs: the numbers are not the point, his confidence in them is, and nothing has changed that by Monday. The least effective response is dropping him from the call and sending the numbers afterwards: the person who knows most about the constraint is removed from the meeting that decides it, which is a different kind of wrong from escalating or from staying quiet. The principle: answer a challenge to your work by involving the challenger in it, never by removing them from the room.

question_text: You are a supplier quality assistant at a retail chain. Documents from a supplier have to be checked against a list of six points before they go to the approver. Three sets have come in at once, the approver leaves at four, and it is half past two. The same supplier’s last three sets were all correct. Checking one set properly takes about forty minutes. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?

Check all three quickly against the two points that usually cause problems, and send them through to the approver before four with the other four points left unchecked.
Send all three sets through to the approver without running the checks at all, and rely on this supplier's record over the last three sets.

It beats checking one and holding the others silently, because the approver plans around three. The least effective response is sending all three sets through without running the checks: he signs believing six points were verified, and a clean record last time is not a check this time, which is a different kind of wrong from going quiet or from cutting the check short. The principle: when there is not enough time, change what you promise, never what the check means.

Reply to the two colleagues who messaged you, agree that it was unfair, and see whether they will say something on today's call if it happens again.

It beats agreeing privately with the two sympathetic colleagues, because that turns a morning call into a matter of sides. It beats cutting the numbers back to what he tolerates, because the lines that disappear are the ones the sites need. The least effective response is leaving the call and sending an email instead: the only forum where shortfalls get discussed loses them, which is a different kind of wrong from seeking allies or from watering the content down. The principle: when your work is attacked in a meeting, keep doing the work and take the criticism to its author.
tip: Mẹo MT: Với bài toán quy luật chuỗi số, hãy xét hiệu số bậc 1, hiệu số bậc 2 hoặc tích lũy tiến.

question_text: You are a junior designer at a graphic design studio. You and a colleague, Ines, are producing a brand pack due to the client on Friday. It is Wednesday. Ines has been given a second urgent project and tells you she can now only do about half her share of the brand pack. You have capacity for some but not all of the rest. Your studio manager assigns work and is in the office. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Take on all of Ines's remaining share and work late Wednesday and Thursday so the brand pack is delivered on Friday as promised.
Work out with Ines exactly what is left, then tell the studio manager today what the two of you can cover and what still needs someone, before Friday.
Tell Ines the brand pack has to come first since it has a client deadline on Friday, and ask her to push back on the second project herself.
Carry on with your own share and let Ines deliver what she can, and raise it on Friday if the brand pack turns out to be incomplete.
explanation: A: Hides the strain until failure: it absorbs a shortfall the studio manager created and never learns about, so she keeps assigning on the assumption that both projects fit. C: Passes responsibility to others: the studio manager assigns the work, so asking Ines to argue about her own workload leaves the person who made the clash out of the conversation. D: Hides the problem / silent deadline slip: it is known on Wednesday that the pack will be short, and the plan is to mention it on the day it is due, when nothing can be done. Waiting to report a certainty is concealment. The most effective response is to work out with Ines exactly what is left, then tell the studio manager today what the two of you can cover and what still needs someone: the shortfall is known on Wednesday, its size can be worked out in ten minutes, and she both created the clash and is the only person who can resolve it. Bringing her the specifics rather than the problem lets her act. It beats taking on all of Ines’s remaining share and working late, because quietly absorbing the gap hides from the manager that two projects were assigned into one person’s week, so she does it again. It beats telling Ines to push back on the second project herself, because that leaves the person who assigns the work out of a conversation about her own assignment. The least effective response is letting Ines deliver what she can and raising it only if the pack turns out incomplete: it knows on Wednesday that Friday will fall short and plans to mention it when no resource can be added. That is worse than absorbing the work, which delivers, and worse than asking her to push back, which at least raises it. The principle: size the gap, then take it to whoever controls the resource while there is still time to fill it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Với bài toán quy luật chuỗi số, hãy xét hiệu số bậc 1, hiệu số bậc 2 hoặc tích lũy tiến.

question_text: You are an apprentice with an electrical contractor, working alone today finishing sockets in an office refurbishment. Opening a wall box you find an older cable that appears to be connected to a live circuit but is not on the drawings and is not what you were sent to work on. You are not qualified to test it. Your supervisor is on another site. The client’s fit-out team are due to board over this wall tomorrow morning. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Stop work at that box, ring your supervisor now to describe what you have found, and tell the client's fit-out team the wall must not be boarded until it has been checked.
Photograph the cable, finish the sockets you were sent to do, and raise the unidentified cable with your supervisor at the end of the day when you report back on the job.
Isolate the circuit at the board yourself so the cable is dead, then carry on with the sockets and mention it to your supervisor later.
Say nothing and board the wall as planned, since the cable is not on the drawings, is not part of your work, and whoever installed it presumably knew what they were doing.
explanation: B: Delays the decision: the record is useful and the wall is boarded over tomorrow morning. An end-of-day report may still be in time, but it leaves no margin and nobody has been asked to act. C: Acts on assumptions without checking: isolating a circuit you cannot identify may kill something the building needs, and you are not qualified to test what the cable feeds. It makes one thing safe by guessing at another. D: Fails to escalate a genuine risk: it seals an unidentified, apparently live cable inside a wall where nobody will find it. The reason given, that someone else must have known, is the assumption the missing drawing already disproves. The most effective response is to stop work at that box, ring your supervisor now, and tell the client’s fit-out team the wall must not be boarded until it has been checked: an unidentified live cable is outside your competence, and the wall is boarded tomorrow morning, so it has to be stopped and reported while both are still possible. Warning the fit-out team is the part that prevents the real damage, because a supervisor informed after boarding cannot undo it. It beats photographing the cable, finishing the sockets, and raising it when you report back at the end of the day, because that leaves no margin against a morning boarding and warns nobody actually holding a sheet of plasterboard. It beats isolating the circuit at the board yourself, because cutting a circuit you cannot identify may kill something the building depends on, and still does not tell you what the cable is. The least effective response is saying nothing and boarding the wall as planned: it seals an apparently live, undocumented cable inside a wall on the assumption that whoever installed it knew what they were doing, which the missing drawing already contradicts. That is worse than the other two, which act imperfectly but do not hide it. The principle: when you find something outside your competence that is about to become inaccessible, stop the work, tell the person who can assess it, and warn whoever would seal it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You are a warehouse administrator at a medical devices distributor. Reconciling stock you notice that a batch of single-use surgical instruments recorded as quarantined has been picked and despatched to two hospitals. The quarantine was applied last month and you do not know why. The person who applied it has left. Your quality manager is on site. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Take the records to your quality manager immediately, showing that quarantined stock has gone to two hospitals, and let her decide what happens next.
Find out first why the quarantine was applied, since the reason may be administrative, and take it to the quality manager once you know what you are reporting.
Contact the two hospitals to ask them to hold the batch until its status has been confirmed, then report it to the quality manager.
Correct the stock record to show the batch as despatched and let the quarantine flag lapse, since the goods have already gone and the person who applied it is no longer here.
explanation: B: Delays the decision: quarantined stock is already in two hospitals, and establishing the reason yourself postpones a decision the quality manager is qualified to make today. C: Acts outside own authority: contacting customers about potentially unsafe medical devices is a regulated communication, and a warehouse administrator making it first commits the company before anyone qualified has assessed the batch. D: Conceals a potential safety failure: it tidies away the only evidence that quarantined medical devices reached two hospitals, so nobody can assess whether patients are at risk. That is a different order of wrong from acting too slowly. The most effective response is to take the records to your quality manager immediately, showing that quarantined stock has gone to two hospitals, and let her decide what happens next: the reason for the quarantine is unknown and may be a safety matter, and she is on site and decides about recall and about telling the customers. Speed matters because the devices may be used. It beats finding out first why the quarantine was applied, because researching it yourself delays a decision she can take now, on stock already in clinical settings. It beats contacting the two hospitals to ask them to hold the batch, because a communication about potentially unsafe devices is regulated and must come from the company’s quality function. The least effective response is correcting the stock record to show the batch as despatched and letting the flag lapse: it removes the quarantine and the evidence, so nobody can establish whether patients are at risk. That is worse than the other two, which act slowly or beyond their authority but keep the problem visible. The principle: when a control has failed on something already with customers, go straight to the person who owns the control, and change nothing yourself.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You are a waiter in a restaurant. Your colleague Tomasz has been given a large party of sixteen on top of his own section and is visibly falling behind; starters have not gone out and the party has been seated twenty minutes. Your own tables are all served and content. The restaurant manager is dealing with a supplier at the door. Tomasz has not asked for help. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Ask Tomasz whether he would like help with the party and stay with your own section if he says he has it, since he knows what the party has ordered.
Go to Tomasz, tell him your tables are settled, and take the drinks and starters for the party of sixteen while he works his own section.
Stay with your own section and let Tomasz manage, since the party was assigned to him and stepping in might confuse who is serving which table.
Interrupt the restaurant manager at the door to tell her that the party of sixteen is not being served and that Tomasz needs someone put on it.
explanation: A: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholder's: a waiter twenty minutes behind on a party of sixteen will usually say he has it, so the offer is courteous and leaves the party waiting. C: Stands available and does nothing: a party of sixteen has waited twenty minutes for starters while a waiter with nothing to do stands by, and the reason given is a worry about table allocation. Standing idle beside a visible failure is the worst of the four. D: Escalates prematurely: you are the person she would send, she is with a supplier, and the walk over costs minutes that the party has already spent waiting. The most effective response is to go to Tomasz, tell him your tables are settled, and take the drinks and starters for the party of sixteen: they have waited twenty minutes, and splitting the work that way is the fastest route back to a normal service. Telling him your section is done removes any need for him to admit he is behind. It beats asking whether he would like help and staying with your own section if he says he has it, because a colleague that far behind will usually decline a general offer, and the party waits regardless. It beats interrupting the restaurant manager at the door to say the party is not being served, because you are the resource she would assign, and fetching her costs minutes. The least effective response is staying with your own section and letting him manage: it leaves sixteen covers unserved while you stand available, justified by a concern about who is assigned to which table. That is worse than offering, which at least asks, and worse than telling the manager, which at least raises it. The principle: when your own section is settled and a colleague is visibly drowning, take a defined part of his work and start.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You are a technician in a dental laboratory. You and a colleague, Rhian, share a batch of crowns due to the practice tomorrow morning. She has been working slowly since returning from leave and tells you she is struggling to get back up to speed. Six crowns remain and you can complete about four by the end of the day. Your laboratory manager is on site. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Send the crowns that are ready in the morning and say nothing about the missing ones, since the practice will probably not use them all on the same day.
Take all six crowns yourself and work late to finish them, so the practice gets the full batch and Rhian is not put under more pressure.
Complete the four you can manage and leave the remaining two for Rhian, since they are her share of the batch and she needs to get back up to speed.
Work out with Rhian how many the two of you can realistically finish, and tell the laboratory manager today so the shortfall can be covered or the practice warned.
explanation: A: Hides the problem / silent deadline slip: an incomplete batch arrives with nobody told, so the practice discovers the shortfall with patients booked. Assuming they will not need them is a guess made on their behalf. B: Hides the strain until failure: it delivers tomorrow and conceals from the manager that the batch needed one person working late, so the same workload is planned again next week. C: Passes responsibility to others: it hands the shortfall to the person who has already said she cannot keep pace, which makes the batch late and teaches her nothing. The most effective response is to work out with Rhian how many the two of you can realistically finish, and tell the laboratory manager today: the shortfall is real and knowable now, and he is the only person who can add capacity or warn the practice in time for tomorrow morning. Working the number out with her first makes it accurate rather than pessimistic. It beats taking all six yourself and working late, because absorbing it delivers tomorrow and hides that the batch was never deliverable in normal hours, so it recurs. It beats completing four and leaving the remaining two for Rhian, because leaving them with a colleague who has said she cannot keep pace guarantees the batch is late and helps nobody. The least effective response is sending the crowns that are ready and saying nothing about the missing ones: it sends an incomplete batch to a practice with patients booked, on an assumption about what they will need. That is worse than the other two, which mishandle the workload but do not conceal the outcome. The principle: size the gap with your colleague, then tell whoever can fix or communicate it while tomorrow can still be changed.
tip: Mẹo MT: Áp dụng sơ đồ Venn hoặc bảng chân trị logic để biểu diễn mối quan hệ giữa các đối tượng.

question_text: You are a physiotherapy assistant at a community clinic. A patient attending for knee rehabilitation mentions in passing that he has had chest tightness when walking uphill for the past fortnight and has not told anyone. He seems well now and is keen to get on with his exercises. You are not clinically qualified to assess this. A physiotherapist is with another patient next door and free in fifteen minutes. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Carry on with the session as planned, since he seems well, the chest tightness is not what he has been referred for, and it is not your place to ask about symptoms outside your remit.
Advise him to see his GP about the chest tightness, then carry on with his knee exercises as planned for today's session.
Hold off starting the exercises, tell the physiotherapist about the chest symptoms as soon as she is free, and let her decide whether today's session should go ahead.
Ask him more about the chest tightness, how long it lasts and what brings it on, so you can judge whether it needs raising with the physiotherapist today.
explanation: A: Stays silent about a known clinical risk: exertional chest tightness is exactly the symptom that matters before exercise, and the reason for saying nothing is that it falls outside your remit, which is why it needs passing to someone whose remit it is. B: Passes responsibility to others: the advice is sound and it leaves a patient about to exercise now, with a symptom nobody qualified has assessed, on his own to arrange a GP appointment. D: Acts outside own training: gathering symptoms is reasonable and deciding what they mean is not. Filtering the information through your own untrained judgement risks it never reaching anyone qualified. The most effective response is to hold off starting the exercises and tell the physiotherapist about the chest symptoms as soon as she is free: exertional chest tightness matters most immediately before exercise, you are not qualified to assess it, and someone who is will be free in fifteen minutes. Holding the session costs a quarter of an hour and removes the risk. It beats asking him more about how long it lasts and what brings it on, because collecting detail is fine but deciding on its significance is not yours to do, and the filtering is where it could be lost. It beats advising him to see his GP and carrying on with the knee exercises, because that leaves him exercising today with the symptom unassessed. The least effective response is carrying on with the session because he seems well and it is outside your remit: it proceeds with exertion despite a symptom that specifically concerns exertion, and tells nobody. That is worse than sending him to his GP, which at least directs him somewhere, and worse than questioning him, which at least explores it. The principle: when something outside your competence could matter now, pause and put it to the qualified person who is minutes away.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You work in a shoe repair and key cutting shop. A customer collects a key cut yesterday and says it does not turn in her front door; she has been locked out once already. Recutting takes ten minutes and there is no queue. She is annoyed and says she has wasted a morning. Your shop manager is in the back and can authorise refunds. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Explain that keys sometimes need easing in older locks, and suggest she try a little lubricant on the lock before assuming the key was cut incorrectly.
Apologise, take the key and the original back, and ask her to return this afternoon once it has been recut and checked properly.
Recut the key straight away and hand it over with an apology, since the fastest fix is the best answer and she plainly wants to get on with her day.
Apologise, recut the key now while she waits since it takes ten minutes, and ask the manager about refunding the original charge for the trouble.
explanation: A: Ignores the customer's actual need: it explains away a key that does not work, puts the remedy back onto a customer who has already been locked out, and never offers the ten-minute recut that would settle it. B: Adds a second journey: the recut takes ten minutes and there is no queue, so asking her to come back a second time adds another journey to a morning she has already lost. C: Ignores part of the customer's actual need: the recut solves the key and not the wasted morning, when a manager who could offer a refund is a few steps away and has not been asked. The most effective response is to apologise, recut the key now while she waits since it takes ten minutes, and ask the manager about refunding the original charge: the key does not work, there is no queue, and she has lost a morning, so both the practical fix and the goodwill question can be dealt with while she is here. It beats recutting the key straight away and handing it over with an apology, because that addresses the key and not the wasted morning, when a manager who could refund the charge is a few steps away. It beats taking the key back and asking her to return this afternoon, because a second journey for a ten-minute job adds to exactly the cost she is complaining about. The least effective response is suggesting she tries a little lubricant because older locks need easing: it offers a theory instead of a working key, and makes the customer responsible for solving a fault the shop created. That is worse than the other two, which both end with a key that turns. The principle: fix the fault on the spot when you can, and use the authority above you for the part that is about the customer’s lost time.
tip: Mẹo MT: Áp dụng sơ đồ Venn hoặc bảng chân trị logic để biểu diễn mối quan hệ giữa các đối tượng.

question_text: You are a dispensing assistant at an opticians. It is 3pm. A customer is waiting for glasses promised for today, and the lenses need twenty minutes of fitting work. At the same time the practice manager asks you to complete the monthly stock return, due to head office by 5pm, which takes about an hour. A third customer is browsing frames and has not been greeted. You are alone in the dispensary. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell the practice manager you cannot do the stock return today and ask her to submit it herself, since two customers are in the practice and you are alone in the dispensary.
Start the stock return first because head office has a fixed 5pm deadline, then fit the lenses and greet the browsing customer once the return has been submitted.
Greet the browsing customer and say you will be with her shortly, fit the waiting customer's lenses, then do the stock return before 5pm.
Fit the lenses, then the stock return, and leave the browsing customer to look at the frames on her own, since she has not asked for help and may prefer to browse undisturbed.
explanation: A: Passes responsibility to others: it hands a manageable task back to the manager before doing the arithmetic. Twenty minutes of fitting and an hour of reporting sit comfortably inside the two hours available, so the refusal is based on a clash that does not exist. B: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholder's: it puts an hour of internal reporting ahead of a customer who was promised her glasses today and is already waiting in the practice. D: Ignores the customer's actual need: a few seconds of greeting costs nothing and is what stops a browsing customer leaving.
