Treating silence as a preference is an assumption made for your own convenience. The most effective response is to greet the browsing customer, fit the waiting customer’s lenses, then do the stock return before 5pm: two hours remain, the fitting takes twenty minutes and the return an hour, so everything fits if it is sequenced properly, and a greeting costs seconds. Doing the promised glasses first honours the commitment already made. It beats starting the stock return first because head office has a fixed deadline, since that treats an internal report as outranking a customer who was promised her glasses today and is sitting there waiting for them. It beats leaving the browsing customer to look at the frames on her own, because a customer who is never greeted is the one most likely to leave, and acknowledging her costs nothing. The least effective response is telling the practice manager you cannot do the stock return today: it hands a manageable task back to her without checking that it fits, when twenty minutes and an hour sit comfortably inside the two hours available. That is worse than the other two, which at least attempt everything. The principle: check whether the work actually fits before declining any of it, then sequence by who is waiting and what was promised.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You are a supervisor at a coffee shop. Your two colleagues have both called in sick, you are running the shop alone through the morning rush, and the queue is out of the door. Your area manager rings to say she is coming in at midday to review the shop’s cleaning records with you, which will take an hour. You have not had a break. The records are up to date. It is 10am. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Say nothing about being short-staffed, serve through the rush, and get through the review at midday as arranged so that your area manager is not given the impression you cannot cope.
Tell your area manager now that you are alone with both colleagues off, ask whether the review can move or whether she can send cover, and carry on serving while she decides.
Close the shop for fifteen minutes to take your break and reset before the review, since you have been alone since opening and cannot keep serving without one.
Ask your area manager to postpone the review, explaining that you are on your own, and leave it to her to find a new date when the shop is properly staffed.
explanation: A: Hides the strain until failure: it conceals the one fact that would change her plan, so she arrives to a shop with a queue and no cover, and the next rota is built as though today worked. C: Abandons own committed work: shutting a trading shop mid-rush with a queue outside is a unilateral decision affecting customers and takings, taken without telling the area manager who is on the phone at that moment. D: Passes responsibility to others: it raises the problem, which is right, then narrows it to one solution. Cover for the shop would suit her visit and you better than a cancelled review, and it is never offered. The most effective response is to tell your area manager now that you are alone with both colleagues off, and ask whether the review can move or whether she can send cover: she set the midday review without knowing, that is the fact that would change her plan, and she is on the phone now. Offering her the choice keeps both options open while you keep serving. It beats asking her to postpone the review and leaving her to find a new date, because that raises the same problem but presents only one solution, when cover would suit the shop and her visit better than a cancellation. It beats serving through the rush in silence so she is not given the impression you cannot cope, because that leaves her arriving to a queue and no cover, and confirms to the business that a single-staffed rush is workable. The least effective response is closing the shop for fifteen minutes to take your break: it shuts a trading shop mid-rush on your own authority, with a queue outside and your area manager on the phone, without telling her. That is worse than the other two, which mishandle the conversation but keep the shop open. The principle: when circumstances have changed under someone else’s plan, give them the fact and the options while they can still act, and keep working meanwhile.
tip: Mẹo MT: Áp dụng sơ đồ Venn hoặc bảng chân trị logic để biểu diễn mối quan hệ giữa các đối tượng.

question_text: You are an application assessor at Redhill Directorate. On Monday you told a college you would have all sixty of its student funding applications assessed by Friday. It is Wednesday afternoon and you have done twenty-two. The remaining thirty-eight need about fourteen hours and you have twelve working hours left, two of which are already booked for training you cannot move. The college holds its enrolment day on Monday. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Ask your team leader whether another assessor can take fifteen of the applications off you, and carry on with the rest of them at the pace you have been working this week.
Work through Thursday's training slot as well as your normal hours, and get as close to all sixty as the remaining hours allow before Friday comes round.
Assume the estimate will come right once you get into a rhythm on Thursday, and leave the college to hear about any shortfall when Friday's batch arrives.
Tell the college this afternoon that you are on track for about fifty by Friday, ask which ten matter least for Monday, and confirm the rest will follow first thing Monday.
explanation: A: Escalates prematurely: a second assessor has to be found, briefed and given the criteria, and the college has not yet been asked which applications it actually needs for enrolment day. B: Spends protected time to chase a number: the training was booked and cannot be moved, and even every remaining hour falls short of sixty, so the college still gets a short batch on Friday. C: Treats an estimate as a reason to do nothing: the shortfall is arithmetic rather than a matter of pace, and the college loses the two days in which it could have told you which applications matter for Monday. The most effective response is to tell the college this afternoon that you are on track for about fifty by Friday, ask which ten matter least for Monday, and confirm the rest follow first thing: the shortfall is arithmetic and it is Wednesday, so they still have two days to say what enrolment day needs. It beats asking your team leader whether another assessor can take fifteen off you, because the college’s own priorities have not been asked for and a second assessor cannot be briefed faster. It beats working through Thursday’s training slot as well, because that protects the original estimate at the cost of training you were told not to move. The least effective response is assuming the estimate will come right once you get into a rhythm: nothing about the arithmetic changes on Thursday, and the college finds out on Friday with the weekend in the way. That makes it worse than seeking a second assessor, which at least tries to close the gap, and worse than working the training slot, which spends every available hour. The principle: when an estimate you gave is going to be missed and there is still time, revise it with the person relying on it while they can still act.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You are an enquiries officer at Ashmere Trust. A man phones about a repayment demand for eleven hundred pounds. He is distressed, says he has just lost his job, and asks you to cancel the demand. Only the debt review team can pause or vary a demand, and they have a hardship form that takes ten minutes and can be started on the phone. He says he cannot face any more forms. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell him you cannot cancel the demand and that the rules are the same for everybody, and suggest he writes in if he wants it looked at.
Note on his record that he says he has lost his job, and let the debt review team pick it up when they next look at the account.
Send him on to the debt review team with their number and tell him to ring them himself about the hardship form, then close the call.
Stay on the line and complete the hardship form with him now, explaining that the debt review team can pause the demand once they have it.
explanation: A: Answers the rule and not the person: a hardship route exists and takes ten minutes, and writing in is the one thing somebody who cannot face another form will not do. B: Records the hardship without starting it: the debt review team cannot pause a demand on a note, and nobody has told him that a route exists at all. C: Passes the caller on without owning it: he has said he cannot face more forms, and the ten-minute form he is being sent away to start is one you could have completed with him on this call. The most effective response is to stay on the line and complete the hardship form with him now, explaining that the debt review team can pause the demand once they have it: only they can vary it, but the thing standing between him and them is a form he has said he cannot face, and that is precisely what you can remove. It beats telling him the rules are the same for everybody and suggesting he writes in, because writing in is what somebody in this state will not do. It beats noting on his record that he says he has lost his job, because a note pauses nothing and tells him no route exists. The least effective response is giving him the debt review team’s number and telling him to ring them himself: a distressed caller is sent away to start the exact form you could have completed with him, which is the likeliest of the four to end with no application at all. That makes it worse than stating the position, which at least states it, and worse than the note, which puts something on the record. The principle: when a rule can only be varied elsewhere, take the person as far down that route as you can rather than pointing at it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Với bài toán quy luật chuỗi số, hãy xét hiệu số bậc 1, hiệu số bậc 2 hoặc tích lũy tiến.

question_text: You are a programme support officer at Redhill Directorate. Two weeks ago you told a board that a supplier survey would be ready for their meeting on the twelfth. You have since realised you never sent the survey out, and it needs ten working days in the field. Today is the fourth and the board papers deadline is the tenth. Nobody has asked you about it. Your programme manager is in the office today. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Send the survey out this afternoon and keep it to yourself that it was never issued, and hope the responses come back fast enough to cover the gap.
Send the survey out today and tell the board on the twelfth that responses are still coming in and that the full analysis will follow at their next meeting in six weeks.
Email the board secretary to withdraw the survey item from the twelfth's agenda, and say nothing about why it is being withdrawn.
Tell your programme manager today that the survey was never issued and that it cannot be ready for the twelfth, and ask what the board should be given instead.
explanation: A: Keeps your own failure quiet and hopes: ten working days of fieldwork cannot fit into six, so the board still gets nothing on the twelfth, and by then nobody has had a chance to arrange anything else. B: Reports a delay and not its cause: the board hears about response rates rather than about a survey that was never issued, so the next report they commission is planned on a false picture. C: Removes the item without the explanation: the board loses the paper and never learns why, and the programme manager who could have offered them something else is not asked. The most effective response is to tell your programme manager today that the survey was never issued and cannot be ready for the twelfth, and ask what the board should be given instead: it cannot exist by then on any arithmetic, the failure is yours, and the six days before the papers deadline are exactly when she could put something else in front of the board. It beats sending the survey today and telling the board responses are still coming in, because that describes a different problem from the one that happened. It beats emailing the secretary to withdraw the item without saying why, because that leaves nobody able to replace it. The least effective response is sending the survey and keeping it to yourself that it was never issued: the cause is hidden on a bet that ten days of fieldwork fits into six, so the board gets nothing anyway and the usable days are gone. That makes it worse than misdescribing the delay, which gives notice, and worse than the silent withdrawal, which frees the agenda. The principle: when a commitment cannot be met and the cause is your own, the cause goes in first, while there is still time to do something else.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân biệt rõ giữa 'Đúng' (True) và 'Có thể xảy ra' (Possible). Chỉ chọn kết luận chắc chắn 100%.

question_text: You are a management information assistant at Redhill Directorate. A dashboard you presented last week has been well received, and your director has emailed the division praising your work on it. A colleague, Bea, built most of the underlying queries, and you have heard she is telling other people you took the credit. The director’s email is still being forwarded around the division. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Blame Bea to the rest of your team for spreading the story, and add that her queries needed a good deal of correcting before the dashboard worked at all.
Speak to Bea today, agree between you what her contribution actually was, and then email the director correcting the record with Bea copied in.
Reply to the director's email saying the dashboard was a joint effort, and leave it to Bea to raise her own part if she wants to.
Say nothing publicly and thank Bea privately for the queries, on the view that the director's email will be forgotten in a fortnight.
explanation: A: Answers a grievance with an attack on the person: the director's email is still wrong, Bea's account of it becomes more credible, and your team is given a dispute instead of a correction. C: Corrects the credit without naming who earned it: a joint effort leaves the director none the wiser about Bea, and puts the burden of claiming her own work on the person with none of the standing. D: Settles the relationship and leaves the record wrong: a private thank you does nothing about an email still being forwarded round the division under your name alone. The most effective response is to speak to Bea today, agree what her contribution actually was, and then email the director correcting the record with her copied in: the email is wrong and still circulating, she built most of the queries, and a correction agreed with her fixes the record and the relationship at once. It beats replying that the dashboard was a joint effort and leaving her to raise her own part, because that tells the director nothing about who did what. It beats saying nothing publicly and thanking her privately, because a private thank you does not reach an email being forwarded round the division. The least effective response is blaming her to your team for spreading the story and adding that her queries needed correcting: a complaint about credit is answered by attacking the person who earned it, and the director’s email stays as wrong as it was. That makes it worse than the joint-effort reply, which moves the record towards the truth, and worse than the private thanks, which damages nobody. The principle: when credit has landed in the wrong place, correct it with the person who earned it, in writing, to whoever got it wrong.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân biệt rõ giữa 'Đúng' (True) và 'Có thể xảy ra' (Possible). Chỉ chọn kết luận chắc chắn 100%.

question_text: You are a programme support officer at Brantwood Services. Every project closure needs a lessons-learned session recorded on the closure form before the project can be signed off. A project is being closed on Friday and the session has not happened; the team has dispersed and two members have left. Your programme manager wants the form completed today. Nothing stops you filling in the box, and nobody checks whether the session happened. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Complete the form leaving the lessons-learned box blank, and let whoever signs the closure off decide for themselves what they want to do about a session that never took place at all.
Ask your programme manager to sign the closure off without the form, and raise the missing session at the next programme board instead.
Tell your programme manager the session has not happened, and propose a thirty-minute call this week with the three people still here, because the form is the only record.
Complete the lessons-learned box today from the project's own progress reports, and record the session as completed so the closure can be signed off on Friday.
explanation: A: Leaves a gap without naming it: an empty box on a closure form is indistinguishable from an oversight, and the signer has to guess whether the session was missed or forgotten. B: Solves the paperwork and loses the substance: the form can be waived, but the three people still here are the last chance anybody has to capture what the project learned. D: Records a session as completed that never took place: the closure file will say lessons were captured from a meeting nobody attended, and the two people who left took the only account of them. The most effective response is to tell your programme manager the session has not happened, and propose a thirty-minute call this week with the three people still here: the session is the substance and the form is the record of it, and half an hour produces something real for a Friday sign- off. It beats completing the form with the lessons-learned box left blank, because a blank box tells the signer nothing about whether the session was missed or forgotten. It beats asking her to sign the closure off without the form, because waiving it loses the last chance to capture what the project learned. The least effective response is filling the box from the project’s progress reports and recording the session as completed: a meeting that never happened is written into the closure file, so the organisation’s record is an account nobody gave. That makes it worse than the blank box, which claims nothing, and worse than waiving the form, which does not falsify it. The principle: when a record requires a step that has not happened, do the step or say it is missing, and never write it in.
tip: Mẹo MT: Áp dụng sơ đồ Venn hoặc bảng chân trị logic để biểu diễn mối quan hệ giữa các đối tượng.

question_text: You are a contracts assistant at Brantwood Services. A community group that hires a hall from you every Saturday emails asking you to cancel their booking for the next six weeks. In the same email they mention that their usual room has been too cold to use since October and that they have complained twice. Cancelling loses them their Saturday slot permanently, and the heating fault has an open job number. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Reply asking whether the cold room is the reason for cancelling, tell them the heating job is open, and offer to hold their Saturday slot while it is fixed.
Cancel the six bookings straight away as the email asks, release the Saturday slot to the waiting list, and close the enquiry as a customer request.
Reply asking them to confirm the cancellation in writing from their group's secretary, and process it once you have that confirmation in front of you.
Cancel the bookings as asked and separately chase the heating job, letting the group know when the room is warm again in case they want to come back to it.
explanation: B: Closes the request on its face: the email contains a cancellation and a reason for it, and acting on the first while ignoring the second gives away a permanent Saturday slot over a fault that already has a job number. C: Delays the decision: a written confirmation adds a step to a cancellation that may not be wanted at all, and the six weeks run out while the paperwork goes back and forth. D: Ignores the customer's actual need: the group loses its Saturday slot permanently today and is invited back to a slot that will no longer exist, which is not what an offer to return means. The most effective response is to reply asking whether the cold room is the reason for cancelling, tell them the heating job is open, and offer to hold their Saturday slot: the email gives you a request and the reason behind it, the reason has an open job number, and a slot lost permanently cannot be given back. It beats asking them to confirm the cancellation in writing from their secretary, because that delays a cancellation nobody has established is wanted. It beats cancelling as asked and separately chasing the heating, because that offers them a return to a slot that will already have gone. The least effective response is cancelling the six bookings and releasing the Saturday slot to the waiting list: it acts on the words and discards the reason in the same email, and the group loses a permanent slot over a fault the organisation is already fixing. That makes it worse than the written confirmation, which is slow but leaves the slot intact, and worse than cancelling and chasing, which at least chases the fault. The principle: when a request and its reason arrive together, deal with the reason before acting irreversibly on the request.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You are a correspondence officer at Redhill Directorate. You handle complaints, so you can read every complaint file. A colleague from another team asks you, quietly, whether a named member of staff has had complaints made about them; she says she is on an interview panel for that person next week. Complaint files are not part of recruitment. Your team leader is available, and file access is logged but rarely reviewed. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Refuse to look and say nothing to anybody about the request, on the view that a conversation that goes no further has done no harm.
Tell her you cannot help with that, and suggest she asks the member of staff's own line manager about their record instead.
Tell her what you remember about that member of staff's complaint history from having read the files, and leave the panel to make of it what it will.
Tell her complaint files cannot be used for recruitment and that you will not look, and mention the request to your team leader today.
explanation: A: Declines and records nothing: file access is logged but rarely reviewed, so an approach asking a complaints officer to inform an interview panel leaves no trace unless you leave one. B: Moves the request rather than refusing it: a manager asked for somebody's record by a panel member is being asked to do the same thing through a different door. C: Judges a colleague to a panel deciding on them: a recollection of complaint files, unchecked and out of context, reaches an interview panel that has no right to it and no way to test it. The most effective response is to tell her complaint files cannot be used for recruitment and that you will not look, and mention the request to your team leader today: the answer has to be explicit, and because file access is logged but rarely reviewed, the only reliable record that the request was made is one you create. It beats refusing to look and saying nothing about the request, because a refusal nobody knows about leaves no trace of the approach. It beats suggesting she asks the member of staff’s own line manager, because that asks for the same thing by another route. The least effective response is telling her what you remember of that person’s complaint history: an interview panel is given your recollection of files it has no right to see, unchecked and without context, about somebody who cannot answer it. That makes it worse than the silent refusal, which discloses nothing, and worse than the redirection, which discloses nothing either. The principle: refuse information asked for outside its purpose, and report the request where nothing else would record it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Với bài toán quy luật chuỗi số, hãy xét hiệu số bậc 1, hiệu số bậc 2 hoặc tích lũy tiến.

question_text: You are a correspondence officer at Calder Group. In this morning’s stand-up a colleague, Nuala, said in front of the team that you never pick up your phone and that she ends up taking your calls. You share the duty line on alternate days. You do miss calls when you are drafting, and so does she. The stand-up has finished and your team leader was not there. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Ask Nuala for ten minutes today, agree what cover each of you actually needs when the other is drafting, and say the stand-up was not the place for it.
Answer in the next stand-up with the number of her calls you have taken this month, since the team heard only one side of it.
Say nothing and make a point of answering every call for the next fortnight, and see whether she raises it again.
Stop picking up Nuala's calls after the way she raised it, and let her find out how many of hers you have been taking.
explanation: B: Answers a public remark in public: the figures may be on your side, and the two of you still share a duty line with a team now watching the score. C: Fixes the symptom for a fortnight: you both miss calls when drafting, and nothing about answering harder for two weeks settles what cover the line actually needs. D: Withdraws cover after a remark: the calls that go unanswered are the public's, not Nuala's, and she learns nothing about how the two of you should be covering the line. The most effective response is to ask Nuala for ten minutes today, agree what cover each of you needs when the other is drafting, and say the stand-up was not the place for it: the remark was public and partly fair, you both miss calls while drafting, and what needs settling is what the duty line requires. It beats answering in the next stand-up with the number of her calls you have taken, because a public rebuttal leaves you both keeping score in front of the team. It beats saying nothing and answering every call for a fortnight, because that does not settle what the line needs. The least effective response is stopping picking up her calls after the way she raised it: the unanswered calls belong to the public rather than to her, and the question of how the line is covered stays exactly where it was. That makes it worse than the public rebuttal, which is escalatory but factual, and worse than answering harder, which costs nobody. The principle: answer a public remark privately, and never let a disagreement about cover be settled by withdrawing it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân biệt rõ giữa 'Đúng' (True) và 'Có thể xảy ra' (Possible). Chỉ chọn kết luận chắc chắn 100%.

question_text: You are a supplier liaison officer at Ashmere Trust. You told a supplier three weeks ago that their new contract paperwork would be signed and returned by the end of this month. Two of the four internal sign-offs are still outstanding and one of the approvers is away for a fortnight. The supplier has told you they are holding two staff on notice for the contract. There are nine working days left. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Reassure the supplier that the paperwork is on track for month end, and chase the two outstanding sign-offs quietly in the meantime.
Ask the absent approver's deputy to sign in their place without telling the supplier anything about the delay until the paperwork is complete.

Email the two outstanding approvers setting a deadline of Friday for their signatures, and decide at the end of the week whether the supplier needs to be told anything at all about it before month end.
Tell the supplier today where the paperwork actually is and that month end is now at risk, because they are holding two people on notice and nine days is long enough for them to plan.
explanation: A: Gives an assurance the sign-offs do not support: two approvals are outstanding and one approver is away for a fortnight, so the supplier keeps two people on notice on the strength of a claim you cannot make. B: Solves the process and not the problem: a deputy signature may or may not be available, and the supplier is still holding two people on notice with no idea that anything is uncertain. C: Delays the decision: what matters to the supplier is that month end is at risk, and waiting until Friday spends four of the nine days they could have used. The most effective response is to tell the supplier today where the paperwork actually is and that month end is now at risk: they are holding two people on notice, the risk is genuine and already known to you, and nine days is enough for them to plan around it. It beats asking the absent approver’s deputy to sign while telling the supplier nothing, because a deputy signature may not be available and they are left uncertain either way. It beats emailing the two approvers a Friday deadline and deciding at the end of the week whether to tell them, because that spends four of the nine days. The least effective response is reassuring the supplier that the paperwork is on track: two approvals are outstanding and an approver is away for a fortnight, so two people stay on notice on the strength of something untrue. That makes it worse than the deputy signature, which is silent but tries to remove the blockage, and worse than the Friday deadline, which is slow but claims nothing. The principle: when an estimate is at risk and the other side is carrying a cost, tell them while the time is still worth something.
tip: Mẹo MT: Với bài toán quy luật chuỗi số, hãy xét hiệu số bậc 1, hiệu số bậc 2 hoặc tích lũy tiến.

question_text: You are a gate agent. A passenger is unhappy about a decision you have made correctly under the airline’s rules and is demanding to speak to a manager. The duty manager is dealing with something at another gate and would take about fifteen minutes to reach you. Boarding is not affected and the passenger is not being abusive, just insistent. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell him there is no manager available at the moment, so that he accepts the decision and the duty manager is not pulled away from what he is dealing with at the other gate.
Call the duty manager over straight away, since the passenger has asked for one and it is not for an agent to decide whether the request is reasonable.
Explain the decision and the reason for it once more, and if he still wants a manager, call the duty manager and tell him honestly that it will be about fifteen minutes.
Tell him that a manager will not change a decision that has been made correctly, so there is nothing to be gained by waiting for one to come to the gate.
explanation: A: Denies him access by inventing an absence: a duty manager exists and could come, and the passenger is told otherwise to save an interruption. B: Escalates without trying: many passengers who ask for a manager want the decision explained, and calling one over before explaining it spends fifteen minutes of somebody else's time. D: Refuses the request on your own authority: you may well be right about the outcome, but deciding that his appeal is pointless is not a judgement for the person he is appealing about. The most effective response is to explain the decision and the reason once more, and if he still wants a manager, call the duty manager and tell him honestly it will be about fifteen minutes: a second explanation settles many of these, the request is his to make if it does not, and the honest wait lets him decide whether it is worth it. It beats calling the duty manager over straight away, because doing that before explaining spends fifteen minutes on something a sentence often resolves. It beats telling him a manager will not change a decision made correctly, because whether an appeal is worth making is not for the person being appealed about to decide. The least effective response is telling him no manager is available at the moment: one is, so a real route is closed with something untrue. That is worse than the other two, which are both honest about what is possible. The principle: try the explanation first, then give people the access they have asked for, with an honest account of the wait.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You are a crewing assistant. A cabin crew member has arrived at the airport for a duty you rostered her for, and it is tomorrow’s duty, not today’s. The mistake is yours: you entered the wrong date. She has driven forty miles to get here and is standing at your desk. Your duty manager will certainly ask how it happened. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell her the rostering system must have shown her the wrong date, sort out her journey home, and leave it there unless the duty manager comes and asks you about it later.
Deal with getting her home and her expenses first, and explain how the wrong date came to be on her roster once the immediate problem has been settled.
Tell her at the desk that you entered the date wrongly, sort out her journey home and her expenses, and tell the duty manager what happened before he hears it from anyone else.
Apologise for the wasted journey and arrange for her travel to be paid back, without going into who put the wrong date on the roster in the first place.
explanation: A: Puts your own error onto the system: she goes home believing a tool she relies on is unreliable, and the duty manager will look for a fault that does not exist. B: Separates the apology from the moment: she spends the drive home not knowing why she was called in, and the explanation arrives when it can no longer change how the day felt. D: Apologises without owning it: the money is refunded and the cause stays vague, so she cannot tell whether it was her misreading or somebody else's mistake. The most effective response is to tell her at the desk that you entered the date wrongly, sort out her journey home and her expenses, and tell the duty manager before he hears it elsewhere: she has driven forty miles and is owed a straight answer, the practical problem still has to be solved, and the correction reaches him from the person who knows what happened. It beats apologising and arranging for her travel to be paid back without going into who put the wrong date on the roster, because that leaves her wondering whether she misread her own roster. It beats sorting the journey and expenses first and explaining the cause afterwards, because the explanation matters most while she is standing in front of you, not after the drive home. The least effective response is telling her the rostering system must have shown the wrong date: it moves your error onto the system, so she distrusts a tool she has to use and the duty manager goes looking for a fault that is not there. That is worse than the other two, which are incomplete rather than untrue. The principle: own the mistake to the person it cost, fix what it cost them, and tell your manager before he asks.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You are a check-in agent. An hour ago a passenger asked you to let him know if a window seat came free, and gave you his mobile number before going through to the departure lounge. One has just opened up. Boarding starts in forty minutes and he is somewhere on the far side of security. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Leave it, since he will be boarding shortly anyway and a seat change this close to departure is more trouble than the window seat is probably worth to him.
Put him into the window seat and tell him about it when he arrives at the gate, so that the change is already made by the time he gets there.
Send him a message now saying a window seat has come free, and offer to move him to it if he still wants it before the gate opens.
Leave a note on his booking so that the gate agent can offer him the window seat when he presents his boarding pass at the gate.
explanation: A: Quietly drops a promise: he asked, gave you a number and is waiting to hear, and the decision that it is not worth it has been taken on his behalf without him knowing. B: Acts without asking: an hour has passed, he may have swapped with a travelling companion or stopped wanting it, and the first he hears is that his seat has been changed. D: Relies on the note being seen at the busiest moment: the gate agent is boarding a flight, and by then the seat may have gone to somebody else anyway. The most effective response is to send him a message now saying a window seat has come free and offer to move him if he still wants it: he asked to be told, he gave you the means to tell him, and a message costs nothing while leaving the choice with him. It beats putting him into the window seat and telling him when he arrives at the gate, because an hour has passed and moving him without asking assumes his plans have not changed. It beats leaving a note on his booking for the gate agent to offer it, because a note read during boarding is read too late, if it is read at all. The least effective response is leaving it because a change this close to departure is more trouble than it is worth: it drops a promise he is waiting on, and decides for him that he would not want it. That is worse than the other two, which both act on the request even if clumsily. The principle: when somebody has asked to be told and given you a way to do it, tell them, and leave the decision where it belongs.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You are a lounge host. The coffee machine has run out and about twenty people can see you noticing it. At the same moment you realise the lounge flight board still shows the old departure time for a flight that has been brought forward, and the passengers on it need to leave for the gate within about five minutes. Refilling the machine takes ten minutes. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Correct the flight board and announce the earlier departure so those passengers can leave for the gate, then refill the coffee machine once they are on their way.
Correct the flight board quietly and then start refilling the coffee machine, without saying anything to the passengers whose flight has been brought forward.
Apologise to the people waiting for coffee, explain that supplies are being fetched, and deal with the flight board once the queue at the machine has settled down.
Ask one of the people waiting at the coffee machine to keep an eye on it while you go and sort out the flight board and speak to the affected passengers.
explanation: B: Fixes the display and not the people: the board is right, and the passengers who read it twenty minutes ago and settled down with a newspaper have no reason to look at it again. C: Buys calm with an announcement about the wrong thing: the passengers who could still make their gate hear nothing at all, and the only person who knew the board was wrong has turned to the coffee queue. D: Hands a job to somebody who does not work here: a passenger cannot refill a machine or answer for the lounge, so the coffee is no nearer and you have delegated your own role to a guest. The most effective response is to correct the flight board and announce the earlier departure so those passengers can leave for the gate, then refill the coffee machine: the board is wrong about something that expires in five minutes, and passengers who miss a gate because they read it cannot get that back, while coffee is an inconvenience that keeps. It beats correcting the board quietly and starting on the coffee machine, because a silent correction helps only the passengers who happen to look again, and the ones who already read it have no reason to. It beats asking someone waiting at the machine to keep an eye on it while you go, because a passenger cannot take over a lounge job, so nothing is actually covered. The least effective response is apologising about the coffee supplies and dealing with the board once that queue settles: it makes an announcement about coffee and none about the flight, so the people with a gate to reach are the only ones left uninformed. That is worse than the quiet correction, which at least intends to fix the board next, and worse than delegating the machine, which is at least heading for the board. The principle: the thing that expires goes first, however few people are watching it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Với bài toán quy luật chuỗi số, hãy xét hiệu số bậc 1, hiệu số bậc 2 hoặc tích lũy tiến.

question_text: You are a crewing assistant. Tomorrow’s roster takes about two hours to build and has to be published tonight. Every ten minutes or so a crew member telephones with a short query, and each interruption means going back over what you were doing. At this rate the roster will not be finished in time, and the queries themselves are all straightforward. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Keep taking the calls as they come and publish the roster at the deadline in whatever state it has reached, without mentioning that it was built between interruptions.
Carry on answering every call as it arrives and accept that the roster will be published late, since crew who telephone deserve an answer when they ring.
Tell the desk you are unavailable for the next hour and will answer queries after that, put the calls to the shared line, and finish the roster.
Stop picking up the telephone for the rest of the evening so you can concentrate, and deal with whatever messages have built up once the roster has been published.
explanation: A: Publishes work you have reason to doubt: crew plan their day around a roster built in ten-minute fragments, and nobody reading it knows to look twice at it. B: Lets the interruptions set the order: a dozen short queries that could wait an hour take priority over the document all of those crew need tonight. D: Goes quiet without telling anybody: crew ring a desk that simply does not answer, and the people covering the shared line have no idea they are covering. The most effective response is to tell the desk you are unavailable for the next hour, put the calls to the shared line, and finish the roster: it is what every one of those crew members actually needs tonight, an hour of clear time finishes it, and announcing the arrangement means the calls still land somewhere. It beats stopping picking up the telephone for the rest of the evening to concentrate, because going silent without telling anyone leaves crew ringing an unanswered desk and colleagues covering without knowing. It beats answering every call as it arrives and accepting a late roster, because a dozen queries that could wait an hour are allowed to delay the document all of them depend on. The least effective response is publishing at the deadline in whatever state it has reached without mentioning how it was built: it hands out a roster the author knows was assembled in fragments, so nobody knows to check it. That is worse than the other two, which both produce a roster somebody concentrated on. The principle: protect a block of time for the work everyone is waiting on, and tell people where their queries should go meanwhile.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You are a gate agent. A colleague you are friendly with has been asked to account for an incident at the gate yesterday, and asks you to confirm her version to the duty manager. You were there. Her account is broadly right, but on one important point, what she said to the passenger, your memory is clearly different. She is anxious and treats your agreement as settled. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Give the duty manager only the parts of the incident you are certain about, and leave out the point where your memory differs from hers, so that you contradict nobody.
Tell her before you speak to anyone that you remember what she said to the passenger differently, and that you will have to give your own account of that part.
Tell her you would rather not be drawn into it, and ask the duty manager to leave you out of the account since there were other people at the gate who also saw it.
Confirm her version as she has described it, since she is a friend, she is right about most of it, and the point where you remember things differently is a detail.
explanation: A: Edits an account to avoid a collision: the duty manager is left with a version shaped by what you chose to omit, and neither he nor she knows that something has been left out. C: Withdraws from something you witnessed: you were there and the point at issue is one you remember clearly, so declining to say so leaves the question to people who saw less. D: Puts loyalty into an account of fact: what she said to the passenger is the part being examined, and it is being confirmed by somebody who remembers it differently. The most effective response is to tell her before you speak to anyone that you remember what she said to the passenger differently and will have to give your own account: your account has to be your own, and telling her first means she is not ambushed and can decide what to say herself. It beats giving the duty manager only the parts you are certain about, because leaving out the disputed point produces a version that is misleading precisely where it matters, and nobody knows it has been edited. It beats asking to be left out of the account because others also saw it, because you saw the thing in question, and standing back leaves it to people who saw less. The least effective response is confirming her version as she has described it: it presents as fact something you remember differently, on the strength of a friendship, and the point confirmed is the one under examination. That is worse than the other two, which are evasive rather than untrue. The principle: give your own account, and warn the person in advance where it will differ from theirs.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You are working the ticket desk alone. Two passengers are waiting. The first to arrive wants to book a trip for next month. The second is trying to reach a flight that closes in fifteen minutes and needs a ticket reissued to do it. No other agent is free, and the booking will take longer than fifteen minutes. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Deal with them in the order they arrived, because queueing in turn is the fairest way to run a desk, and say nothing to either about the flight that is closing.
Ask the passenger who arrived first to come back later, and start on the reissue, without going into why the order is being changed.
Ask both what they need, take the reissue first because that flight closes in fifteen minutes, and tell the other passenger how long he will be waiting.
Deal with the reissue first because it is urgent, and leave the other passenger standing at the desk without saying anything about the change in order or how long he will wait.
explanation: A: Treats order of arrival as the only fairness: a passenger loses a flight that could have been saved, and neither of them is even told that a choice was being made. B: Reorders without explaining: the right passenger is served, but the first is moved aside with no reason given and no idea when to return. D: Gets the order right and the person wrong: he watches somebody who arrived after him being served first, with nothing said, and concludes the desk is simply arbitrary. The most effective response is to ask both what they need, take the reissue first because that flight closes in fifteen minutes, and tell the other passenger how long he will be waiting: one need expires and the other does not, asking is what reveals that, and a sentence to the waiting passenger costs nothing and keeps him with you. It beats dealing with the reissue first and leaving him standing without a word, because getting the order right in silence leaves him watching a queue jump he cannot explain. It beats asking the passenger who arrived first to come back later without explaining why, because sending him away with no reason and no return time is a worse version of the same conversation. The least effective response is dealing with them strictly in arrival order and telling neither about the closing flight: it holds to the queue while a flight closes. That is worse than the other two, which both save the flight even if they handle the other passenger poorly. The principle: order the queue by what expires, and tell the person who waits why they are waiting and for how long.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân biệt rõ giữa 'Đúng' (True) và 'Có thể xảy ra' (Possible). Chỉ chọn kết luận chắc chắn 100%.

question_text: You are a gate agent. A flight has just gone to a three-hour delay and the new departure time is confirmed. Passengers are asking about meal vouchers. The airline usually issues them for a delay of this length, but the decision has not been taken yet and you have been told it will come within the hour. The gate room is full and people are making plans. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell the gate room that you have no information at present and that everyone should watch the screens, so that nothing you say can turn out to be wrong later on.
Announce the new departure time and say nothing at all about vouchers until the airline has made its decision and you can give a definite answer.
Announce the confirmed departure time, say that the decision on vouchers is being taken and is not yours, and tell them the time by which you will come back with the answer.
Announce the new departure time and tell the room that vouchers are normally issued for a delay this long, so they should expect to be given them shortly.
explanation: A: Denies holding information you do hold: the confirmed departure time is the one fact passengers need to plan an evening, and pleading ignorance about all of it is untrue. B: Leaves a question hanging: the room is asking about food, and silence on the point they care about invites them to keep queueing at your desk for an answer you could have framed. D: Over-promises on somebody else's decision: if the answer comes back no, the passengers were told otherwise by the only member of staff in the room, and every one of them heard it from you. The most effective response is to announce the confirmed departure time, say that the decision on vouchers is being taken and is not yours, and give the time by which you will come back: it hands the room the fact that is settled, is honest that the other is not yours to settle, and replaces an open question with a time. It beats announcing the departure time and telling the room vouchers are normally issued for a delay this long, because that commits the airline to a decision it has not made, in front of a full gate room. It beats announcing the departure time and saying nothing about vouchers, because passengers are asking about food, and refusing to acknowledge the question keeps them at the desk instead of settling them. The least effective response is telling the gate room you have no information and that everyone should watch the screens: it claims you know nothing when you have a confirmed departure time in your hand, so people plan an evening around a blank. That is worse than withholding only the uncertain half, and worse than the voucher promise, which is generous rather than untruthful. The principle: say what is certain, be plain about what is not, and give a time for the rest.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You work behind the counter at a community pharmacy. A regular customer collects her repeat prescription and, back at the counter two minutes later, says the box contains 28 tablets but her prescription is for 56 and she has none left at home. The dispensing record on screen shows 56 issued. The pharmacist is with a patient in the consultation room and will be free in about ten minutes. The customer is due at work and is becoming anxious. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Explain that the computer record shows 56 tablets were issued, so the second box must be at home or in her bag, and suggest she checks there before coming back to the pharmacy.
Take a second box of 28 from the shelf and hand it over so she is not late for work, then tell the pharmacist what you have done when she comes out of the consultation room.
Apologise, take her details and the box, tell her the pharmacist will check the dispensing within ten minutes, and ask her to wait or take a call at work so nothing is guessed at.
Tell her the pharmacy cannot look into it while the pharmacist is busy and ask her to come back tomorrow when the counter is quieter and someone can go through the records properly.
explanation: A: Acts on assumptions without checking: the record shows what was meant to be issued, not what went into the bag, and treating the screen as proof sends a customer with no tablets left home to look for a box that may not exist. B: Breaches confidentiality or process: handing out prescription medicine without the pharmacist checking the dispensing is not yours to do, and a ten-minute wait is not a reason to bypass the one control that catches a dispensing error. D: Ignores the customer's actual need: she has no tablets left and a ten-minute wait was available. Sending her away untreated overnight to suit the counter's convenience is a service failure of a different kind from the other options, which at least try to resolve it today. The most effective response is to apologise, take her details, and tell her the pharmacist will check the dispensing within ten minutes: it takes the complaint seriously, puts the one person qualified to check it on the job, and still gives the customer a way to get to work. It beats quoting the computer record and suggesting she looks at home, because the dispensing record shows the intention, not the contents of the bag, so repeating it back to her settles nothing and puts the burden of proof on the customer. It beats handing her a second box of 28 yourself, because the pharmacist’s check is exactly the control that catches a short dispense, and skipping it to save ten minutes risks compounding one error with another. The least effective response is telling her to come back tomorrow when the counter is quieter: it is the only response that leaves a customer with no medication overnight when a qualified check was ten minutes away, and it does so for the pharmacy’s convenience rather than any clinical reason. That is worse than quoting the record, which at least offers her a next step, and worse than handing over a second box, which errs by trying too hard to help. The principle: when a customer has a genuine need and the right check is minutes away, make the check happen rather than deferring or bypassing it.

question_text: You are a junior designer at a graphic design studio. You and a colleague, Ines, are producing a brand pack due to the client on Friday. It is Wednesday. Ines has been given a second urgent project and tells you she can now only do about half her share of the brand pack. You have capacity for some but not all of the rest. Your studio manager assigns work and is in the office. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Take on all of Ines's remaining share and work late Wednesday and Thursday so the brand pack is delivered on Friday as promised.
Work out with Ines exactly what is left, then tell the studio manager today what the two of you can cover and what still needs someone, before Friday.
Tell Ines the brand pack has to come first since it has a client deadline on Friday, and ask her to push back on the second project herself.
Carry on with your own share and let Ines deliver what she can, and raise it on Friday if the brand pack turns out to be incomplete.
explanation: A: Hides the strain until failure: it absorbs a shortfall the studio manager created and never learns about, so she keeps assigning on the assumption that both projects fit. C: Passes responsibility to others: the studio manager assigns the work, so asking Ines to argue about her own workload leaves the person who made the clash out of the conversation. D: Hides the problem / silent deadline slip: it is known on Wednesday that the pack will be short, and the plan is to mention it on the day it is due, when nothing can be done. Waiting to report a certainty is concealment. The most effective response is to work out with Ines exactly what is left, then tell the studio manager today what the two of you can cover and what still needs someone: the shortfall is known on Wednesday, its size can be worked out in ten minutes, and she both created the clash and is the only person who can resolve it. Bringing her the specifics rather than the problem lets her act. It beats taking on all of Ines’s remaining share and working late, because quietly absorbing the gap hides from the manager that two projects were assigned into one person’s week, so she does it again. It beats telling Ines to push back on the second project herself, because that leaves the person who assigns the work out of a conversation about her own assignment. The least effective response is letting Ines deliver what she can and raising it only if the pack turns out incomplete: it knows on Wednesday that Friday will fall short and plans to mention it when no resource can be added. That is worse than absorbing the work, which delivers, and worse than asking her to push back, which at least raises it. The principle: size the gap, then take it to whoever controls the resource while there is still time to fill it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân biệt rõ giữa 'Đúng' (True) và 'Có thể xảy ra' (Possible). Chỉ chọn kết luận chắc chắn 100%.

question_text: You are a teaching assistant. You and another assistant, Bev, support the same class. She regularly changes the seating plan the teacher agreed with you, without telling either of you, and two pupils who work badly together keep ending up side by side. The teacher has noticed the disruption but not the cause. Bev has been at the school much longer than you. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Leave the seating as Bev arranges it, since she has been at the school far longer than you and the teacher will raise it herself if she thinks it is a problem.
Speak to Bev privately, explain why those two pupils were separated in the agreed plan, and agree that changes to the seating go through the teacher first.
Tell the teacher that the seating plan is being changed and that this is why the two pupils keep ending up together and disrupting the class.
Move the two pupils back apart each time you notice they have been seated together, so the agreed plan is restored without any need for a confrontation.
explanation: A: Fails to escalate a genuine problem: two pupils who work badly together are repeatedly seated side by side and the class is being disrupted, and the reason for silence is Bev's length of service. Choosing to let the disruption continue is worse than raising it clumsily. C: Escalates prematurely: Bev has not been told the changes are causing the disruption, and the first she would hear of it is from the teacher, over something a private conversation could settle. D: Avoids the difficult conversation: it corrects the seating and leaves Bev changing it again, so pupils are moved back and forth in class and the cause is never addressed. The most effective response is to speak to Bev privately, explain why those two pupils were separated in the agreed plan, and agree that seating changes go through the teacher first: she almost certainly does not know why they were separated, the fix is one conversation plus an agreement about who changes the plan, and it keeps the teacher’s arrangement intact. It beats telling the teacher the seating plan is being changed and that this is why the two keep disrupting the class, because going to her first makes a complaint out of something Bev has never been told about. It beats moving the two pupils back apart each time you notice, because that leaves them shuttled around the room and Bev still rearranging, so the disruption continues. The least effective response is leaving the seating as she arranges it because she has been at the school far longer: it accepts continuing disruption to pupils’ learning on grounds of seniority and waits for the teacher to work it out. That is worse than the other two, which raise or address it imperfectly. The principle: tell the colleague what the change causes, agree who owns the decision, and only then involve the person above you.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân biệt rõ giữa 'Đúng' (True) và 'Có thể xảy ra' (Possible). Chỉ chọn kết luận chắc chắn 100%.

question_text: You are an administrator at a day nursery. A child has had a minor fall in the garden this morning, was checked by the room leader and is fine, and an accident form has been completed. The room leader is busy with the children and asks you to let the parent know. The parent collects at 5pm. It is 11am and you have the parent’s phone number. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Ring the parent now, tell her what happened, that her child was checked and is fine, and that the accident form will be ready to sign at collection.
Leave it to the room leader to mention at collection if she gets the chance, since the child is fine and the accident form is on file if the parent asks to see it.
Wait until 5pm and tell the parent at collection, handing over the accident form then so she can hear what happened and see her child at the same time.
Send the parent a short text saying there has been a minor accident and that staff will explain everything when she collects her child at 5pm.
explanation: B: Hides the problem: it makes telling the parent optional and depends on a busy colleague remembering. A parent who later learns of a fall nobody mentioned has been kept in the dark by default. C: Delays the message: it is defensible and it means the parent spends six hours not knowing. A child's fall is something most parents would rather hear about at once, and the call costs a minute. D: Alarms without reassuring: it sends the frightening half of the message and holds back the half that settles it, so a parent spends six hours worrying about something already resolved. The most effective response is to ring the parent now, tell her what happened, that her child was checked and is fine, and that the form will be ready to sign at collection: she wants to know, the news is reassuring once she has all of it, and a call carries the fall and the reassurance together. It beats sending a short text saying there has been a minor accident, because announcing an accident without the reassurance is the worst possible half of the message, and leaves her anxious all afternoon for no reason. It beats waiting until 5pm and telling her at collection, because six hours of not knowing is avoidable at the cost of a one-minute call. The least effective response is leaving it to the room leader to mention at collection if she gets the chance: it leaves telling the parent to chance and to a colleague busy with children, so a fall may never be mentioned at all. That is worse than the other two, which tell her late or partially but do tell her. The principle: when something has happened to someone’s child, tell them promptly and tell them the whole of it, including the part that reassures.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You work in the membership office of a golf club. Members’ subscriptions are due, and a discounted rate applies to anyone who joined before 2015. A member who joined in 2018 asks you to record him as a pre-2015 member, saying he has been coming as a guest since 2012 and that nobody would ever check. He is friendly and well known at the club. The club secretary is in her office. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell him you cannot change the joining date and suggest he takes it up with the club secretary himself if he believes his guest years should count.
Record him at the pre-2015 rate, since he has genuinely been coming to the club since 2012 and the discount is meant to reward long- standing members.
Apply the standard rate but note on his file that he has attended since 2012, so that the club can consider a discretionary discount at some point in the future.
Tell him the joining date is a matter of record and you cannot change it, and offer to ask the secretary whether guest years have ever been counted towards the discount.
explanation: A: Passes responsibility to others: the refusal is right and the handoff is thin. He has raised a question about how guest years are treated, and sending him to make his own case leaves you having merely declined. B: Falsifies a membership record: his joining date is a fact, and rewriting it to produce a discount he is not entitled to is dishonesty dressed as fairness. It also charges every other member for the shortfall. C: Delays the decision: it charges him correctly, which is right, and parks his actual question on a file note that nobody is due to read. The secretary is in her office today. The most effective response is to tell him the joining date is a matter of record and offer to ask the secretary whether guest years have ever counted: the date is a fact and not yours to alter, but the question underneath it is legitimate and the secretary can answer it. Refusing clearly and taking the question forward does both jobs. It beats telling him to take it up with the club secretary himself, because that refuses in the same way but leaves him to make his own case, when you are standing beside the person who decides. It beats applying the standard rate and noting on his file that he has attended since 2012, because a note for future consideration answers nobody today, and the secretary is available now. The least effective response is recording him at the pre-2015 rate: it rewrites a factual record to create an entitlement that does not exist, and the reasoning offered, that he has been around a long time, is exactly the reasoning that makes small falsifications feel reasonable. That is worse than the other two, which charge him correctly. The principle: refuse to alter a record, then take the fair question underneath it to the person who can actually decide it.

question_text: You are a warehouse administrator at a medical devices distributor. Reconciling stock you notice that a batch of single-use surgical instruments recorded as quarantined has been picked and despatched to two hospitals. The quarantine was applied last month and you do not know why. The person who applied it has left. Your quality manager is on site. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Take the records to your quality manager immediately, showing that quarantined stock has gone to two hospitals, and let her decide what happens next.
Find out first why the quarantine was applied, since the reason may be administrative, and take it to the quality manager once you know what you are reporting.
Contact the two hospitals to ask them to hold the batch until its status has been confirmed, then report it to the quality manager.
Correct the stock record to show the batch as despatched and let the quarantine flag lapse, since the goods have already gone and the person who applied it is no longer here.
explanation: B: Delays the decision: quarantined stock is already in two hospitals, and establishing the reason yourself postpones a decision the quality manager is qualified to make today. C: Acts outside own authority: contacting customers about potentially unsafe medical devices is a regulated communication, and a warehouse administrator making it first commits the company before anyone qualified has assessed the batch. D: Conceals a potential safety failure: it tidies away the only evidence that quarantined medical devices reached two hospitals, so nobody can assess whether patients are at risk. That is a different order of wrong from acting too slowly. The most effective response is to take the records to your quality manager immediately, showing that quarantined stock has gone to two hospitals, and let her decide what happens next: the reason for the quarantine is unknown and may be a safety matter, and she is on site and decides about recall and about telling the customers. Speed matters because the devices may be used. It beats finding out first why the quarantine was applied, because researching it yourself delays a decision she can take now, on stock already in clinical settings. It beats contacting the two hospitals to ask them to hold the batch, because a communication about potentially unsafe devices is regulated and must come from the company’s quality function. The least effective response is correcting the stock record to show the batch as despatched and letting the flag lapse: it removes the quarantine and the evidence, so nobody can establish whether patients are at risk. That is worse than the other two, which act slowly or beyond their authority but keep the problem visible. The principle: when a control has failed on something already with customers, go straight to the person who owns the control, and change nothing yourself.

question_text: You are a production assistant at a signage workshop. Two jobs are on your bench. A shop fascia must be finished today because the fitters collect it at 4pm for a Saturday installation, and a set of exhibition panels is due to be couriered tomorrow. At 11am the vinyl for the fascia arrives damaged; a replacement roll can be collected from a supplier forty minutes away. Your supervisor is at the supplier’s trade counter this morning and contactable by phone. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Carry on with the fascia using the damaged vinyl, working around the worst of the damage, and say nothing to the fitters since the fault may not be obvious once the fascia is installed.
Start on the exhibition panels while you think about the fascia, so that at least one of the two jobs is definitely progressing rather than both waiting on a roll of vinyl.
Ring your supervisor at the supplier now, ask him to bring back a replacement roll, and prepare everything else on the fascia so it can be finished the moment the vinyl arrives.
Drive to the supplier yourself to collect the replacement roll, so the vinyl is on the bench as quickly as possible and the fascia can still be finished before the fitters arrive.
explanation: A: Hides the problem: it knowingly sends out damaged work on a Saturday shopfront and relies on nobody noticing. That is concealment of a defect, not a scheduling decision like the other options. B: Abandons own committed work: the panels have a day in hand and the fascia has five hours. Turning to the job that is not in trouble uses up the only time in which the fascia could still be saved. D: Acts on assumptions without checking: your supervisor is standing in that supplier's trade counter now. An eighty-minute round trip spends the fascia's remaining time on a journey a phone call could have avoided. The most effective response is to ring your supervisor at the supplier for a replacement roll and prepare everything else on the fascia meanwhile: he is already standing in that shop, so one phone call solves the shortage at no travel cost, and preparing the rest means the vinyl goes straight on when it arrives. It beats driving to the supplier yourself, because that spends eighty minutes of the fascia’s remaining five hours doing something the person already there could do for free. It beats starting on the exhibition panels while you think about it, because the panels have a full day in hand while the fascia has a fixed 4pm collection, so that spends the fascia’s last usable hours on the job that was never at risk. The least effective response is working around the damage and saying nothing to the fitters: it is the only response that lets defective work leave the workshop, on a shopfront the public will see, with the fitters and the customer told nothing. That is worse than the other two, which mismanage the time but produce sound work. The principle: solve the shortage the cheapest way available, prepare everything you can meanwhile, and never let a deadline persuade you to ship a defect quietly.

question_text: You are a compliance assistant. A fee earner asks you to confirm that a client’s source of funds check was completed before a transfer goes this afternoon. The system shows the check requested and not returned, and the provider is usually a day. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell him the check is not back and that the transfer will have to wait until it is, since that is what the rule requires and there is nothing else to be said.
Tell him the check is requested and not returned, and that you will chase the provider now and come back to him before the transfer window closes.
Tell him it is requested and suggest he goes ahead on the basis that the check will land later today, so the transfer is not held up by paperwork.
Tell him the check is complete and guarantee it, since checks of this kind almost always come back clear and the provider has never raised anything on this client.
explanation: A: Answers with the rule and stops: it is right about the position and it accepts a delay before anybody has chased the provider, who may well answer within the hour. C: Advises acting ahead of the check: the timing of the result is not the point, and a transfer made before a source of funds check is exactly the sequence the rule forbids. D: States a result that has not arrived: a transfer will go this afternoon on the strength of a check nobody has seen, which is the one thing the check exists to prevent. The most effective response is to tell him the check is requested and not returned, and that you will chase the provider now and come back before the transfer window closes. He needs the true position and the check needs chasing, and doing both means the transfer either goes properly or waits for a reason. It beats telling him the transfer must wait until the check is back and saying nothing else, because nobody has chased. It beats suggesting he goes ahead on the basis that the check will land later today, because the order of check and transfer is the whole point. The least effective response is telling him the check is complete and guaranteeing it: a result that has not come back is reported, and a transfer goes on it. That is a different kind of wrong from the other two, both of which are honest about the check’s status. The principle: say exactly where the check is, and go and move it.
