question_text: You work as a machine operative at a joinery workshop. Changing over the crosscut saw, you notice its blade guard is cracked and no longer locks into position. Workshop rules say a defective guard must be reported to the supervisor, who takes the machine out of use until it is repaired. It is the only crosscut saw in the workshop, several colleagues rely on it every day, and losing it would slow the whole team’s work; the last repair took most of a week. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Say nothing about the guard and plan your own jobs around the other machines, leaving the crosscut saw available for the colleagues who rely on it.
Carry on using the saw with extra care yourself, warning colleagues to do the same, and raise the guard at the team meeting later in the week.
Report the cracked guard to your supervisor straight away, so the saw comes out of use until it has been repaired.
Email the company's health and safety officer asking for an urgent inspection of every machine in the workshop, assuming other guards are probably wearing out as well.
explanation: A: Stays silent about a known safety risk: keeping quiet while steering only yourself away from the saw protects you and nobody else; colleagues keep using a machine you know is unsafe, which is self-protective silence rather than a defensible reading of the risk. B: Fails to escalate a genuine risk: care and warnings do not fix a guard that no longer locks, and waiting days for a meeting keeps a known hazard in daily use when the rules give you a route that acts today. D: Escalates on assumptions without checking: widening one observed fault into a workshop-wide inspection request is built on a guess, bypasses the supervisor the rules name, and leaves the one saw you know is unsafe in use while the bigger process gets arranged. The most effective response is to report the cracked guard to your supervisor straight away so the saw comes out of use: a guard that is cracked and no longer locks is a genuine injury risk, the rules name exactly who to tell, and the supervisor can act today. The disruption to the team is real, but it is the trade the workshop’s own rules have already made. It beats carrying on with extra care and raising it at the team meeting, because care and warnings do not make a broken guard safe, and waiting days keeps the hazard in daily use for the sake of avoiding a difficult report. It beats emailing the health and safety officer for a workshop-wide inspection, because that inflates one observed fault into an assumed general problem, bypasses the supervisor who can act now, and leaves the one saw you know is unsafe running while a bigger inspection is arranged. The least effective response is saying nothing and working around the saw yourself: unlike carrying on with warnings, which at least alerts the people at risk, and unlike the inspection request, which at least tells someone with authority, it tells nobody and quietly protects only you, leaving colleagues to use a machine you know is unsafe. The principle: a genuine safety risk is raised at once through the stated route, whatever the disruption, and never managed silently around yourself.

question_text: You are a groundworker in a landscaping crew of three. You are laying a patio that must be finished today because the client is holding a party tomorrow. Your colleague Josh has cut the paving slabs to the wrong dimension for one edge and has not noticed; there is enough spare stone to recut them, which takes about an hour. It is 11am and the crew leader is collecting materials and back at noon. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Lay the slabs as cut and leave the edge slightly short, since the client is unlikely to notice under furniture and the party is tomorrow.
Tell Josh what you have spotted, and start recutting the slabs with him now so the edge is right and the patio is still finished today.
Wait until the crew leader is back at noon and let him tell Josh, since he runs the job and it is not your place to correct a colleague's cutting.
Recut the slabs yourself over the next hour without mentioning it, so the edge is right and Josh is not shown up in front of the crew.
explanation: A: Hides the problem: it builds a known defect into a patio for a client holding a party, and relies on furniture hiding it. That is concealment of poor work, not a decision about time. C: Delays the decision: an hour of recutting is lost waiting for somebody else to deliver the message, on a patio that has to be finished today. D: Prioritises harmony over honesty: it fixes today's edge and leaves Josh cutting to the same wrong dimension on the next job, because nobody has told him. The most effective response is to tell Josh what you have spotted and start recutting the slabs with him now: there is an hour of recutting, spare stone and a whole afternoon, so the patio can still be right, and he needs to know what went wrong. Doing it together solves today and the next job. It beats recutting the slabs yourself without mentioning it, because that fixes this edge and leaves him measuring the same way tomorrow. It beats waiting until the crew leader is back at noon to let him tell Josh, because that spends an hour of the day you need, to have someone else say what you can say now. The least effective response is laying the slabs as cut and leaving the edge slightly short: it builds a known defect into a client’s patio and depends on it not being noticed, the one response that leaves bad work in the ground. That is worse than the other two, which manage it awkwardly but produce a proper patio. The principle: tell your colleague, fix it together while there is still time, and never build in a defect because it might not be seen.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân biệt rõ giữa 'Đúng' (True) và 'Có thể xảy ra' (Possible). Chỉ chọn kết luận chắc chắn 100%.

question_text: You are a production coordinator at an events company. It is 2pm on the day of a conference. Three things need you: the client’s keynote speaker has arrived and cannot find the green room, the audio-visual crew report a microphone fault in the main hall where the keynote begins at 3pm, and your manager wants tomorrow’s crew rota confirmed by 4pm. You have one runner available to help. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Deal with the speaker and the rota yourself and leave the microphone to the audio-visual crew, since they are the specialists and it is their equipment to fix.
Take the speaker to the green room yourself since the client will judge the company on how she is looked after, then deal with the microphone and the rota afterwards.
Send the runner to collect the speaker, go to the main hall yourself to get the microphone fault resolved before 3pm, and confirm the rota after the keynote starts.
Confirm the rota first since your manager has set a 4pm deadline, then help with the microphone and ask the runner to find the speaker.
explanation: A: Fails to escalate a genuine risk: the crew have reported the fault rather than fixed it, which is the signal that they need a decision or a replacement. Treating a reported problem as somebody else's job means the keynote starts without a working microphone. B: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholder's: escorting a guest is the one task on the list that anyone can do, and doing it personally spends the coordinator on the job the runner exists for while a keynote microphone stays broken. D: Delays the decision: the rota has two hours and no audience, while the microphone has one hour and a keynote behind it. Doing the administrative task first spends the only hour that matters. The most effective response is to send the runner to collect the speaker, go to the main hall yourself to get the microphone fault resolved before 3pm, and confirm the rota after the keynote starts: the microphone is the only item with a hard deadline and a public failure attached, the speaker needs collecting rather than coordinating, and the rota has until 4pm. That puts each person on the job matching what they can do. It beats taking the speaker to the green room yourself, because escorting a guest is exactly what the runner is there for, and doing it personally leaves the microphone unattended. It beats confirming the rota first to meet your manager’s 4pm deadline, because the rota has two hours and no audience while the keynote has one. The least effective response is leaving the microphone to the audio-visual crew as the specialists: they have reported a fault rather than resolved it, so a decision or a replacement is needed, and treating it as theirs alone risks a keynote starting without sound in front of the client. That is worse than the other two, which misallocate the time but keep the fault in view. The principle: delegate what anyone can do, take personally the thing with the closing window and the visible consequence.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You are a facilities coordinator for an office building. At 9am you learn that the lift has failed with nobody inside, that a meeting room booked for a client presentation at 10am has no working projector, and that the quarterly fire alarm test is scheduled for 11am. A wheelchair user works on the third floor and is due in at 9.30am. The lift engineer can attend within two hours if called now. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Call the lift engineer immediately, tell the third-floor colleague and her manager before she travels in, then deal with the projector and confirm the alarm test.
Deal with the projector and the alarm test as planned and wait to see whether the lift resets itself, since calling an engineer out is expensive and it may come back on its own.
Sort the projector first since the client presentation is at 10am and is the nearest deadline, then call the lift engineer and confirm the alarm test.
Call the lift engineer, then postpone the fire alarm test since a failed lift makes evacuation arrangements unreliable, and deal with the projector afterwards.
explanation: B: Fails to escalate a genuine risk: it leaves a wheelchair user arriving at a building she cannot move around in, and gambles the two-hour repair window on the lift fixing itself, to save a call-out fee. C: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholder's: the projector is the nearest deadline and the smallest consequence. A colleague who cannot use the stairs is due in at 9.30 and the engineer's two-hour window starts only when he is called. D: Escalates prematurely: postponing a scheduled alarm test is a decision with its own consequences, taken before anyone has checked whether the test is affected, while a colleague is still travelling in to a building she cannot get around. The most effective response is to call the lift engineer immediately, tell the third-floor colleague and her manager before she travels in, then deal with the projector and the alarm test: the lift is the only item with both a closing window, the engineer’s two hours, and a person affected who is already travelling. Calling starts the clock, and warning her before she sets off is the part that cannot wait. The projector and the alarm test both still fit afterwards. It beats sorting the projector first for the 10am presentation, because that puts the smallest consequence first and leaves a colleague to discover on arrival that she cannot reach her desk. It beats calling the engineer and then postponing the fire alarm test, because postponing it is a further decision with its own effects, taken before checking whether it is even affected. The least effective response is waiting to see whether the lift resets itself to avoid a call-out charge: that spends the repair window and leaves a wheelchair user stranded on arrival. That is worse than the other two, which misorder the work but call the engineer. The principle: start the longest lead time first, warn the person affected before they are committed, and fit the rest around it.

question_text: You are a patient transport driver taking an elderly patient home from hospital. On arrival she tells you she lives alone, has no food in the house and is not sure she can manage the stairs to her flat. Your job is transport only and you have three more collections booked this afternoon. Your control room is contactable by radio, and the hospital discharge team can still be reached. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Leave her at the door as the job requires, since transport is what you are booked for and the hospital will have assessed her before discharging her.
Help her up the stairs and into the flat, then continue with your remaining collections since she is at least safely inside her home.
Stay with her, radio control to report that she cannot manage at home, and ask them to contact the hospital discharge team before you leave.
Ring her family or a neighbour if she has a number, so that someone local can check on her, then carry on with your remaining collections.
explanation: A: Fails to escalate a genuine risk: she has told you directly that she cannot manage, and the assumption that the discharge assessment covered it is the assumption her own account contradicts. Leaving is the one response that resolves nothing. B: Treats the symptom and leaves the risk: getting her through the door solves this afternoon and leaves an elderly woman alone with no food and stairs she is unsure of, with nobody informed. D: Acts on assumptions without checking: an informal arrangement with whoever answers the phone is not a discharge decision, and it leaves the hospital unaware that the discharge has not worked. The most effective response is to stay with her, radio control to report that she cannot manage at home, and ask them to contact the hospital discharge team before you leave: she has told you she cannot manage, the discharge appears to have missed it, and the people who can reopen that are reachable now. Staying with her while it is raised is what makes the report count. It beats helping her up the stairs and into the flat before continuing your collections, because that solves the stairs for one afternoon and leaves the food, the isolation and the unsafe discharge untouched. It beats ringing her family or a neighbour to check on her, because that is a private arrangement, not a reassessment, and the hospital never learns its discharge did not hold. The least effective response is leaving her at the door because transport is what you are booked for: it assumes the assessment must have covered it, when she has just said it did not. That is worse than the other two, which at least do something for her. The principle: when someone tells you a plan has failed, keep them safe and get the fact to the people who own the plan, before you leave.

question_text: You are a service desk analyst at an IT support provider. A system outage has left the queue at four times its usual length and you have worked through your break. Your team leader now tells you that a call you handled yesterday has been complained about, and asks you to write it up by the end of the day. You believe you handled the call correctly. Three hours of your shift remain and the queue is still growing. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Write the complaint response first while the call is fresh in your mind, so it is done properly, and return to the queue once your team leader has what she asked for.
Work the queue for the rest of your shift and write the complaint response at home this evening, so that neither the customers waiting nor your team leader's deadline is let down.
Get on with both as best you can without raising it, since the outage is everyone's problem today and saying you cannot manage would not look good while the whole team is under pressure.
Tell your team leader the queue has quadrupled, ask whether the write-up can wait until tomorrow or be covered by someone else, and keep working the queue while she decides.
explanation: A: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholder's: it assumes the write-up must come first because she asked for it today, when she does not know the queue has quadrupled. The assumption is never tested with the one person who could rebalance it. B: Hides the strain until failure: it meets both demands by absorbing the overload privately, so your team leader never learns the shift was undeliverable and plans the next one the same way. C: Avoids the difficult conversation: it stays silent about a workload that cannot be delivered, for fear of how it looks. Your team leader is the only person who can rebalance it, and she is the one person not told. The most effective response is to tell your team leader the queue has quadrupled and ask whether the write-up can wait until tomorrow or be covered by someone else, while you keep working the queue: she set that deadline without knowing the queue had quadrupled, so the fact she is missing is the one worth giving her, and she is the only person who can rebalance the two. Continuing to work while she decides means nothing stalls. It beats writing the complaint response first while the call is fresh, because that treats the order of the two tasks as already settled when the person who set it does not have the information, and the queue pays for the assumption. It beats working the queue and writing the response at home this evening, because taking the work home makes the shift look deliverable when it was not, so the same pressure is scheduled again next time. The least effective response is getting on with both as best you can without raising it: it is the only response that neither raises the conflict nor resolves it, and the reason given is how it might look rather than anything about the work. That leaves both jobs half done and your team leader unaware. The principle: when the workload you have been given cannot be delivered, give the person who set it the fact they are missing, and keep working while they decide.

question_text: You are an instructor at an outdoor activity centre. Checking equipment before a climbing session for a school group you find a harness with a frayed stitch on a load-bearing strap. There are enough harnesses without it. The group arrives in fifteen minutes. Centre procedure requires damaged equipment to be quarantined and logged by the technical manager, who is on site. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Put the harness back at the end of the rack so it is not used today, and tell the technical manager after the session when he has more time.
Set the harness aside and log it in the equipment book yourself, so the record exists and the technical manager can review it at the next equipment check.
Use the harness for the session but give it to one of the lighter pupils, since the stitching is only frayed and there is no sign it is close to failing.
Take the harness out of use, put it aside where it cannot be picked up, and tell the technical manager before the group arrives.
explanation: A: Acts on assumptions without checking: a damaged harness left on the rack can be picked up by anybody, and the placement relies on everyone knowing what you know. B: Acts outside own authority: the procedure names the technical manager because he decides whether a fault is repairable or the batch needs checking, and a self-made log entry replaces that judgement with a record. C: Uses equipment known to be damaged: a frayed load-bearing strap on a climbing harness is the failure the inspection exists to catch, and putting a child in it on a judgement about weight is a safety decision nobody is qualified to take that way. The most effective response is to take the harness out of use, put it aside where it cannot be picked up, and tell the technical manager before the group arrives: a frayed load-bearing strap makes it unusable, spares exist so nothing is lost by removing it, and he is on site and is the person the procedure names. Both steps fit inside fifteen minutes. It beats putting it back at the end of the rack and telling him after the session, because a damaged harness left on the rack can be picked up by anyone who does not know, so its position is not a control. It beats setting it aside and logging it in the equipment book yourself, because that substitutes a record for his judgement about whether other harnesses in the batch need checking. The least effective response is using it for one of the lighter pupils because the stitching is only frayed: it puts a child into a harness with a damaged load-bearing strap on a personal judgement about weight. That is worse than the other two, which handle the procedure imperfectly but take the harness out of use. The principle: remove damaged safety equipment from use immediately, then tell the person the procedure names, before the activity starts.

question_text: Rowsley Handling charges Ryedale Airways £150 for each turnaround at Vernham, plus £2.60 for every passenger carried. One turnaround at Vernham carried 180 passengers. The invoice is settled in euros, and £1 buys €1.25. What is that turnaround’s invoice total in euros?
explanation: Build the sterling invoice first, then convert it once. Passenger charge: 180 x 2.60 = £468.00. Sterling total: 150 + 468 = £618.00. 618.00 x 1.25 = €772.50. A common error here is stopping at £618.00 and reading it as euros. Another is dividing by 1.25 rather than multiplying, which gives €494.40; £1 buys €1.25, so a sterling figure is multiplied to reach euros.

question_text: Fees convert at £1 = 1.15 euros, and the court refunds the fee on 5% of the claims it issues. How much did the Vanteuil court collect in fees, after refunds, in pounds?
explanation: Vanteuil charges in euros: 1,500 x 253 = 379,500 euros. The refunds take off 5%, leaving 95%: 379,500 x 0.95 = 360,525 euros. At £1 = 1.15 euros, 360,525 / 1.15 = £313,500. A common error here is stopping at the euro figure and reading it as pounds, which gives £360,525. The two sterling courts and the other euro court are not asked for.

question_text: You work in a payroll bureau. You discover that forty employees of a client company were underpaid in yesterday’s run because a shift allowance was not applied. The client’s HR manager is your contact. The bank file has already gone, so a correction cannot reach staff before next Tuesday. Your team leader is on leave. The client’s staff will notice the shortfall when they check their accounts today. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Prepare the correction run for Tuesday and email the client's HR manager once it is ready, so that she receives the problem and the fix in a single message.
Ring the client's HR manager now, explain what happened, tell her the correction lands Tuesday, and offer the list of affected staff so she can tell them today.
Email the client's HR manager explaining the error, and ask her how she would like the bureau to communicate it to the forty affected employees.
Process the correction quietly for Tuesday and say nothing, since the money will reach everyone within a week and raising it would damage the bureau's standing with the client.
explanation: A: Delays the message: the staff see the shortfall in their accounts today. An HR manager who hears about it first from forty employees cannot do anything but apologise. C: Passes responsibility to others: it tells her in time, which is right, then hands her an open question when what she needs is the facts and a recommendation she can act on this morning. D: Hides the problem: forty people are short of pay today and the client is deliberately left unaware to protect the bureau's reputation. That is concealment for self-interest, not a communication choice. The most effective response is to ring the client’s HR manager now, tell her the correction lands Tuesday, and offer the list of affected staff: forty people will see short pay in their accounts today, so she needs the facts before they reach her, plus the two things she can act on. A phone call is the only channel fast enough. It beats preparing the correction run first and emailing her once it is ready, because waiting means she hears about it from her own staff first. It beats emailing to ask how she would like the bureau to communicate it, because that leaves her holding an open question when what she needs is a recommendation and a list. The least effective response is processing the correction quietly for Tuesday and saying nothing: it leaves forty people short of pay with nobody told, in order to protect the bureau’s standing with the client. That is worse than the other two, which communicate imperfectly but do communicate. The principle: when your error is about to be discovered by the people it affects, reach the person who has to answer for it first, with the facts and what you propose to do.
tip: Mẹo MT: Áp dụng sơ đồ Venn hoặc bảng chân trị logic để biểu diễn mối quan hệ giữa các đối tượng.

question_text: You are a trainee at an accountancy practice, working with a colleague on a client’s year-end file due to the manager on Friday. You have finished your sections. Your colleague, who joined a month ago, has fallen behind on hers and tells you privately that she does not understand the fixed-asset schedule and has been guessing. It is Wednesday afternoon. Your manager is available and approachable. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Take her fixed-asset sections and complete them yourself alongside your own work, so the file is right and she is not exposed as struggling in her first month.
Sit with her now, work through the fixed-asset schedule together so she can do it herself, and agree that she tells the manager today if it still will not be ready for Friday.
Tell her she needs to speak to the manager today, since guessing at a fixed-asset schedule on a client file is not something you can help her with, and get on with your own review work.
Say nothing and let the file go to the manager on Friday as it stands, since the sections are hers and it is the manager's job to review the work and pick up any errors.
explanation: A: Prioritises harmony over honesty: it saves her embarrassment this week and leaves her unable to do the schedule next time, while the manager still believes she can. C: Passes responsibility to others: the advice is right and delivered as a handoff. A month into the job, being told to go and confess alone is the likeliest way to ensure she does not. D: Fails to escalate a genuine risk: you know a client file contains guessed figures and let it reach the manager as finished work. Relying on review to catch what you already know is wrong is silence, not delegation. The most effective response is to sit with her now and work through the fixed-asset schedule together, agreeing that she tells the manager today if it still will not be ready: there are two days left, the gap is a teachable one, and doing it together fixes both the file and the reason it went wrong, with a clear trigger if time runs out. It beats taking her fixed-asset sections and completing them yourself, because that gets Friday’s file right and leaves her exactly as unable to do a fixed-asset schedule as she was on Monday. It beats telling her she needs to speak to the manager today and getting on with your own review, because a month-old trainee told to go and explain herself alone will very often not do it, so the advice is correct and the outcome is unchanged. The least effective response is letting the file go to the manager on Friday as it stands: it is the only response that knowingly lets guessed figures reach a manager as completed client work, and it justifies that by calling it someone else’s job to catch. That is worse than doing her sections, which produces a correct file, and worse than sending her to the manager, which at least points her at help. The principle: help a colleague become able to do the work, and agree who tells the manager if it still will not be ready.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân biệt rõ giữa 'Đúng' (True) và 'Có thể xảy ra' (Possible). Chỉ chọn kết luận chắc chắn 100%.

question_text: You work in the membership office of a golf club. Members’ subscriptions are due, and a discounted rate applies to anyone who joined before 2015. A member who joined in 2018 asks you to record him as a pre-2015 member, saying he has been coming as a guest since 2012 and that nobody would ever check. He is friendly and well known at the club. The club secretary is in her office. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell him you cannot change the joining date and suggest he takes it up with the club secretary himself if he believes his guest years should count.
Record him at the pre-2015 rate, since he has genuinely been coming to the club since 2012 and the discount is meant to reward long- standing members.
Apply the standard rate but note on his file that he has attended since 2012, so that the club can consider a discretionary discount at some point in the future.
Tell him the joining date is a matter of record and you cannot change it, and offer to ask the secretary whether guest years have ever been counted towards the discount.
explanation: A: Passes responsibility to others: the refusal is right and the handoff is thin. He has raised a question about how guest years are treated, and sending him to make his own case leaves you having merely declined. B: Falsifies a membership record: his joining date is a fact, and rewriting it to produce a discount he is not entitled to is dishonesty dressed as fairness. It also charges every other member for the shortfall. C: Delays the decision: it charges him correctly, which is right, and parks his actual question on a file note that nobody is due to read. The secretary is in her office today. The most effective response is to tell him the joining date is a matter of record and offer to ask the secretary whether guest years have ever counted: the date is a fact and not yours to alter, but the question underneath it is legitimate and the secretary can answer it. Refusing clearly and taking the question forward does both jobs. It beats telling him to take it up with the club secretary himself, because that refuses in the same way but leaves him to make his own case, when you are standing beside the person who decides. It beats applying the standard rate and noting on his file that he has attended since 2012, because a note for future consideration answers nobody today, and the secretary is available now. The least effective response is recording him at the pre-2015 rate: it rewrites a factual record to create an entitlement that does not exist, and the reasoning offered, that he has been around a long time, is exactly the reasoning that makes small falsifications feel reasonable. That is worse than the other two, which charge him correctly. The principle: refuse to alter a record, then take the fair question underneath it to the person who can actually decide it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân biệt rõ giữa 'Đúng' (True) và 'Có thể xảy ra' (Possible). Chỉ chọn kết luận chắc chắn 100%.

question_text: You are a field support technician for a telecoms company. You are on site installing a new phone system for a small business that closes for the weekend at 5pm today. By 2pm it is clear one part is missing and the system cannot be finished today; it can be completed on Monday. The office manager who booked the work is on site. Your own scheduler, who arranges return visits, is at her desk. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Work on until 5pm, leave once the office has closed, and let your scheduler contact the office manager on Monday morning to arrange the return visit for the missing part.
Ring your scheduler to book Monday's return visit, then carry on until 5pm so the office manager sees the work has progressed as far as it possibly could today.
Tell the office manager that you have hit a snag and are doing everything you can, and give her a full picture on Monday once you know exactly what is needed to finish.
Tell the office manager now that a missing part means the system cannot go live today, confirm what still works over the weekend, and agree a Monday return before you leave site.
explanation: A: Hides the problem / silent deadline slip: the business closes believing its phones are live and discovers on Monday that they are not. Leaving site without telling the customer is concealment, and it removes every chance she had to arrange cover. B: Tells the wrong audience first: the person standing on site, whose business runs on the phones this weekend, learns last about a problem you have already reported internally. C: Delays the message: a snag with no detail leaves her unable to plan her weekend cover, when you already know the specific fact she needs, that the system will not go live before Monday. The most effective response is to tell the office manager now that a missing part means the system cannot go live today, confirm what still works, and agree a Monday return before you leave: she is standing there, she runs a business that depends on those phones over the weekend, and she needs those three facts before 5pm. It beats ringing your scheduler to book the return visit first, because that puts internal tidiness ahead of the person whose weekend depends on the answer. It beats telling her you have hit a snag and are doing everything you can, because a vague snag withholds the one hard fact she can plan around, when you already know it. The least effective response is leaving once the office has closed and letting your scheduler arrange it on Monday: it is the only response where she finds out after you have gone, which removes every opportunity she had to arrange cover, and it leaves the news to be broken by someone who was never on site. That is worse than the other two, which communicate imperfectly but in time. The principle: tell the person carrying the consequence first, tell them while they can still act, and tell them what you actually know.
tip: Mẹo MT: Với bài toán quy luật chuỗi số, hãy xét hiệu số bậc 1, hiệu số bậc 2 hoặc tích lũy tiến.

question_text: You work in a hospital pharmacy stores team. Your colleague Amir is checking a large delivery against the order alone, a job normally done by two people so that quantities are double checked. He is halfway through and the fridge lines still need putting away within the hour. You have finished your own tasks. The stores supervisor is at a meeting until midday. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Carry on with your own area and leave Amir to finish, since he started the check and interrupting halfway through might cause him to lose his place.
Put the fridge lines away yourself while Amir finishes the check, so that the cold chain is protected and he is not interrupted.
Tell Amir you are free and join him on the check so it is properly double checked, then put the fridge lines away together.
Ring the stores supervisor out of her meeting to ask whether the delivery check should be paused until two people are available.
explanation: A: Lets a two-person control run with one: a double-check that exists to catch quantity errors in medicines is being done by one person, and the reason for not helping is a worry about interrupting. Standing by a known control failure is the failure here. B: Splits the wrong task: it protects the fridge lines and leaves the single-person check running, so the control designed to catch quantity errors stays broken for the rest of the delivery. D: Escalates prematurely: you are the second person, you are free, and the answer she would give is obvious. Interrupting a meeting to be told to do what you can already do costs time the fridge lines do not have. The most effective response is to tell Amir you are free and join him on the check so it is properly double checked, then put the fridge lines away together: the check is a two-person control precisely because one person miscounts, you are free, and joining him restores the control for the rest of the delivery and still gets the fridge lines away in time. It beats putting the fridge lines away yourself while he finishes the check, because that protects the cold chain and leaves the quantity check still being done by one person, which is the more serious gap. It beats ringing the stores supervisor out of her meeting to ask whether the check should be paused, because you are the second person she would send, so the call only delays it. The least effective response is carrying on with your own area and leaving him to finish alone: it lets a medicines quantity check run without its double-check, and the reason offered is a concern about interrupting him. That is worse than the other two, which act on part of the problem. The principle: when a two-person control is running with one person and you are free, become the second person.
tip: Mẹo MT: Áp dụng sơ đồ Venn hoặc bảng chân trị logic để biểu diễn mối quan hệ giữa các đối tượng.

question_text: You are a kitchen assistant in a school canteen. Lunch service starts at 12.15 and it is 11.30. The head cook has asked you to prepare a tray of allergen-free meals for four pupils, which takes twenty minutes, and to restock the salad bar, which takes fifteen. You cannot do both before service and the head cook is in the delivery bay for the next ten minutes. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Restock the salad bar first because it is the quicker job, then start the allergen-free meals and finish them as soon after 12.15 as you can.
Restock the salad bar and serve the four pupils from the standard menu, choosing dishes that look unlikely to contain the allergens they need to avoid.
Prepare the allergen-free meals first so the four pupils can eat at 12.15, and tell the head cook when she returns that the salad bar still needs restocking.
Start both, alternating between the allergen-free tray and the salad bar so that each is as far along as possible when service begins.
explanation: A: Delays the decision: it does the shorter task first and leaves four pupils who cannot eat anything else waiting after service has already started. B: Acts recklessly with a known risk: judging by eye whether a dish contains an allergen puts four pupils at risk of a reaction. That is a safety failure, not a scheduling choice. D: Splits effort so nothing finishes: allergen-free meals prepared alongside general restocking risks both being incomplete at 12.15, and moving between tasks in a kitchen is exactly how cross- contamination happens. The most effective response is to prepare the allergen-free meals first so the four pupils can eat at 12.15, then tell the head cook the salad bar still needs restocking: those four cannot eat anything else, so the meals have to exist by service, and a salad bar restocked slightly late affects nobody’s ability to eat. Telling her means she can put someone on it. It beats doing the quicker job first, because that leaves the four pupils with nothing at the start of service. It beats alternating between the allergen-free tray and the general restocking, because that risks both being unfinished and creates a real contamination risk. The least effective response is serving the four from the standard menu, choosing dishes that look unlikely to contain the allergens they need to avoid: it substitutes a guess about ingredients for the allergen-free meals themselves, which risks a reaction in four children. That is worse than the other two, which order the work badly but keep the pupils safe. The principle: do the task that someone depends on absolutely, and never replace a safety control with a judgement by eye.
tip: Mẹo MT: Áp dụng sơ đồ Venn hoặc bảng chân trị logic để biểu diễn mối quan hệ giữa các đối tượng.

question_text: You have realised that a report you sent to a client last week contains an error. The client has not noticed, and correcting it now would be embarrassing. Rate each response.
options: Say nothing and hope the mistake has no consequences.
Tell your manager about the mistake but wait for their instructions before doing anything, even though the client may rely on the report meanwhile.
Contact the client promptly, explain the error, and send a corrected version with an apology.
Wait to see whether the client spots the error, and act only if they raise it.
explanation: Contacting the client promptly is most effective: a fast, honest correction limits the harm because the client may act on the flawed report at any moment, and owning the error protects the relationship. Saying nothing and hoping is least effective, as it leaves a known error live and risks far greater damage. Telling the manager but passively waiting for instructions is well-intentioned but middling, because it delays a correction that speed makes urgent; waiting to see if the client notices is also middling, monitoring the problem but gambling on their inaction.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân biệt rõ giữa 'Đúng' (True) và 'Có thể xảy ra' (Possible). Chỉ chọn kết luận chắc chắn 100%.

question_text: A colleague on your team is clearly overwhelmed and falling behind on a shared deadline, while you have some spare capacity this week. They have not asked for help and seem reluctant to admit they are struggling. Rate each response.
options: Quietly finish some of their tasks yourself without telling them, to avoid embarrassing them.
Mention to the wider team in a meeting that they seem to be falling behind and need support.
Focus only on your own work, since they have not asked you for any help.
Ask them privately how they are getting on and offer specific help with the shared deadline.
explanation: Asking privately and offering specific help is most effective: it respects the colleague and directly addresses the shared deadline. Raising their struggles publicly in a meeting is least effective, as it embarrasses them and damages trust. Silently doing their tasks is well-meant but middling, since it is unilateral and could confuse who is doing what; focusing only on your own work is also middling, protecting your tasks but leaving a shared goal at avoidable risk.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: You receive critical feedback from your manager on a piece of work you were proud of. Some of the points feel unfair to you, but others may be valid. Rate each response.
options: Defend your work point by point during the conversation to show the criticism is misplaced.
Listen carefully, ask questions to understand the feedback, and reflect before responding.
Dismiss the feedback afterwards and carry on working exactly as you did before.
Accept every point without comment and change everything immediately to avoid further discussion.
explanation: Listening, asking clarifying questions, and reflecting is most effective: it shows openness and lets you act on the valid points. Dismissing the feedback entirely is least effective, as it wastes a chance to improve and signals poor self-awareness. Defending everything immediately is middling, closing off learning in the moment; accepting all of it uncritically is also middling, since it may mean changing things that were actually fine.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân biệt rõ giữa 'Đúng' (True) và 'Có thể xảy ra' (Possible). Chỉ chọn kết luận chắc chắn 100%.

question_text: An urgent request from a senior colleague arrives while you are close to a firm deadline on other important work. You cannot complete both in the time available. Rate each response.
options: Ignore the urgent request until your deadline is met, without telling the senior colleague anything.
Quickly do the most urgent part of the senior request, then flag to your manager that your other deadline is now at risk.
Attempt both at once and hope the quality of each does not suffer.
Explain your current deadline to the senior colleague and agree together which should take priority.
explanation: Explaining your deadline and agreeing priorities together is most effective: the right work is done first with informed consent rather than guesswork. Silently ignoring the senior colleague’s urgent request is least effective, leaving them blind to the delay and damaging trust. Doing the most urgent part and flagging the risk is reasonable but middling, since it commits to an order unilaterally; attempting both at once is also middling, relying on hope and risking two weak outputs.
tip: Mẹo MT: Với bài toán quy luật chuỗi số, hãy xét hiệu số bậc 1, hiệu số bậc 2 hoặc tích lũy tiến.

question_text: A client emails you frustrated because a service they expected has been delayed, and the delay was caused by a genuine issue on your team’s side. The client is an important one and wants an explanation quickly. Rate each response.
options: Delay replying until you have a full solution, leaving the client without any acknowledgement.
Send a brief apology but avoid explaining the cause or committing to any next steps.
Reply promptly, acknowledge the delay honestly, explain what happened, and set out the next steps.
Reply blaming the delay on circumstances outside your control to avoid admitting fault.
explanation: Replying promptly with an honest acknowledgement, explanation, and next steps is most effective: it shows accountability and reassures an important client. Blaming outside circumstances dishonestly is least effective, as it destroys trust when the cause was internal. Delaying any reply is middling, leaving the client anxious in silence; a bare apology with no explanation or next steps is also middling, offering little real reassurance.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc Modus Tollens: Nếu A suy ra B, thì phủ định B chắc chắn suy ra phủ định A.

question_text: Two colleagues disagree sharply during a team discussion, and it is turning tense and personal. You can see valid points on both sides. Rate each response.
options: Announce to the whole team that both colleagues are being unprofessional.
Suggest the team refocus on the shared goal and calmly weigh the merits of each approach.
Suggest the two colleagues continue the discussion privately after the meeting once tempers have cooled.
Stay silent and let the two colleagues resolve the argument between themselves however it ends.
explanation: Refocusing on the shared goal and weighing both approaches calmly is most effective: it defuses the personal heat while still using the valid points on each side. Publicly announcing that both colleagues are unprofessional is least effective, humiliating them and escalating the conflict. Moving the discussion offline is a sensible middle, cooling tempers but deferring the decision; staying silent is also middling, avoiding inflaming things but letting a personal clash run unchecked.
tip: Mẹo MT: Với bài toán quy luật chuỗi số, hãy xét hiệu số bậc 1, hiệu số bậc 2 hoặc tích lũy tiến.

question_text: You are an area support assistant for a restaurant chain, visiting a branch to help with stock counts. In the kitchen you notice the fridge temperature log has identical readings written in for the past two weeks, including for a day the branch was closed. Food safety is not your role and you have no authority here. The branch manager is on site. Your area manager is contactable by phone. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Say nothing, since food safety is not your role, you have no authority at this branch, and the branch manager will have his own reasons for how the log is kept.
Raise it with the branch manager, ask him to check the fridges now, and ring your area manager today because the log for two weeks cannot be relied on.
Mention it to the branch manager and suggest he starts recording the readings properly from now on, then get on with the stock count you came to do.
Photograph the log and include it in your visit report, so that the area manager sees the evidence when the report is circulated next week.
explanation: A: Fails to escalate a genuine risk: identical readings including a closed day mean the log is not a record of anything, so nobody knows whether food has been held safely. Having no authority is a reason to tell someone who has, not to say nothing. C: Treats a safety failure as a paperwork fix: recording properly from now on corrects the form and leaves two weeks in which nobody knows whether the fridges held temperature, with that food still in them. D: Delays the decision: the evidence is captured and the food is still being served. A report next week arrives long after the fortnight it describes. The most effective response is to raise it with the branch manager, ask him to check the fridges now, and ring your area manager today: identical readings across a fortnight including a day the branch was shut mean the log records nothing, so nobody knows whether the fridges have held temperature, and food is being served now. Getting the fridges checked today and telling the area manager addresses both the immediate risk and the recording failure. It beats suggesting he starts recording the readings properly from now on, because that leaves the last two weeks, and the food from them, entirely unexamined. It beats photographing the log for your visit report next week, because that is far too slow for a live food safety question. The least effective response is saying nothing because you have no authority at this branch: it leaves an unreliable food safety record and possibly mishandled food untouched, on grounds that are precisely why it should go to someone who does have authority. That is worse than the other two, which act too slowly but do act. The principle: when a control turns out not to be working, get the immediate check done and tell the person with authority the same day.
tip: Mẹo MT: Nhận diện ý chính của từng đoạn bằng câu chủ đề (thường nằm ở đầu hoặc cuối đoạn).

question_text: You are a process operator at a waste water treatment works. Passing a monitoring screen that is not part of your round, you notice the outflow ammonia reading has been climbing steadily for three days and is close to the permitted limit. Exceeding it is reportable to the environmental regulator. The operator responsible is on leave. Your works manager is on site. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Adjust the aeration settings yourself to bring the ammonia down, since the trend is clear and the limit is close.
Take the three-day trend to your works manager now, show him the readings and how close they are to the limit, and let him decide what to do.
Record the trend in the shift log so the operator responsible picks it up when he returns from leave next week.
Leave it, since the screen is not on your round, the reading is still inside the permitted limit and the plant's alarms would trigger if it went over.
explanation: A: Acts outside own authority: changing process settings on a plant running near a permitted limit can drive the reading the wrong way, and the works manager has not been told the trend exists. C: Delays the decision: the log reaches the right person on the wrong day. The reading is close to a reportable limit now, and next week is after any breach would have happened. D: Fails to escalate a genuine risk: a three-day climb towards a reportable limit is exactly the signal that precedes a breach, and relying on the alarm means acting only once the limit has already been exceeded. The most effective response is to take the three-day trend to your works manager now, show him the readings and how close they are to the limit, and let him decide: a steady climb towards a reportable limit is a developing breach rather than a stable reading, you are the only person who has noticed with the responsible operator away, and he can act today. It beats adjusting the aeration settings yourself to bring the ammonia down, because that is a process decision beyond your authority on a plant running close to a limit, and could make the reading worse. It beats recording the trend in the shift log for the operator returning next week, because that arrives after the breach it should have prevented. The least effective response is leaving it because the reading is still inside the permitted limit and the alarms would trigger: it waits for an alarm that by definition sounds only once the limit has been exceeded and the breach is already reportable. That is worse than the other two, which act wrongly or slowly but do act. The principle: a trend towards a limit is information somebody needs before the limit is reached, so take it to whoever can act while it is still preventable.
tip: Mẹo MT: Cảnh giác với các từ chỉ mức độ tuyệt đối như 'luôn luôn', 'chắc chắn', 'duy nhất', 'tất cả'.

question_text:
【Ngữ cảnh】：Skelwith Group declared a final dividend of 7.4 pence a share, taking the total for the year to 11.2 pence. The results say the dividend is covered twice by earnings and that the board intends to keep cover at about that level. They give free cash flow of £74 million and note that the group bought back no shares during the year. Skelwith has paid a final dividend in each of the last twelve years.

【Câu hỏi】：Based only on the information in the passage, is the following statement True, False, or Cannot say? Statement: “The group’s final dividend is 7.4 pence a share.”
options: True
False
Cannot say
explanation: The statement is True. The passage says Skelwith “declared a final dividend of 7.4 pence a share”, which is the statement. The rule: where the passage states the claim, the answer is True. The most tempting wrong answer is False, from reading the 11.2 pence total for the year as the final dividend.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc vàng True/False/Cannot Say: Chỉ dựa vào thông tin được cung cấp trong bài đọc, không suy đoán từ hiểu biết bên ngoài.

question_text: Four meetings are held from Monday to Thursday, one per day. The budget meeting is before the hiring meeting. The safety meeting is on Wednesday. Which statement must be true?
options: The hiring meeting is on Thursday.
The budget meeting is on Monday.
The training meeting is after the safety meeting.
The budget meeting is not on Thursday.
explanation: The safety meeting takes Wednesday, leaving Monday, Tuesday and Thursday for the other three. Rule 1 puts the hiring meeting after the budget meeting, so the budget meeting cannot take the last day of the week. Nothing else is settled. The budget and hiring meetings take Monday and Tuesday, Monday and Thursday, or Tuesday and Thursday, with training taking whichever day is left, so the hiring meeting on Thursday, the budget meeting on Monday and training after safety each hold in some of those weeks and fail in others. The most tempting trap is the hiring meeting on Thursday, because Thursday is the obvious home for the later of a pair. Tuesday works too.
tip: Mẹo MT: Nhận diện ý chính của từng đoạn bằng câu chủ đề (thường nằm ở đầu hoặc cuối đoạn).

question_text:
【Ngữ cảnh】：Cooper’s Field is a development of eighteen houses on the site of a former dairy. Plot 14 has a garden of 210 square metres, and plot 15, on the corner, has a garden of 260 square metres. Plot 14 is the larger house, with four bedrooms against plot 15’s three. Gardens are turfed and fenced before completion, with a paved path to the rear gate. Both plots face the retained oak at the centre of the development, and both carry the same estate management charge for the shared landscaping.

【Câu hỏi】：Based only on the information in the passage, is the following statement True, False, or Cannot say? Statement: “Plot 14 at Cooper’s Field has a larger garden than plot 15.”
options: True
False
Cannot say
explanation: The statement is False. The passage says “plot 14 has a garden of 210 square metres, and plot 15, on the corner, has a garden of 260 square metres”. On the stated garden areas plot 14’s is smaller, so the claim is contradicted. The rule: comparing two stated figures on the same measure settles the claim either way. The most tempting wrong answer is True, from carrying the house-size comparison onto the gardens.
tip: Mẹo MT: Nhận diện ý chính của từng đoạn bằng câu chủ đề (thường nằm ở đầu hoặc cuối đoạn).

question_text: You are a check-in agent. A colleague applying for a role in another department asks you to write a short statement about how she handles difficult passengers. She is competent but that is the part of the job she finds hardest, and the statement she has drafted for you describes her as outstanding at it. She asks you to sign it as it stands. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell her you cannot sign her draft as it stands, and offer to write something yourself covering what you can honestly say about her work.
Decline to sign it and leave it there, since a statement about somebody else's work is not something you should be drawn into either way.
Sign the draft as she has written it, since statements of this kind are always generous, everybody knows that, and it costs nothing to help a colleague.
Sign it with the wording softened enough that it is not quite untrue, so that she gets her statement without you saying anything you would have to defend.
explanation: B: Refuses without offering the alternative: she has real strengths you could describe, and a flat no leaves her with nothing and no idea why. C: Puts your name to a description you know to be wrong: whoever reads it relies on it precisely because it comes from somebody who has worked beside her. D: Writes to be defensible rather than accurate: the reader still takes it as a recommendation of the part she is weakest at, and the care has gone into wording rather than truth. The most effective response is to tell her you cannot sign her draft as it stands, and offer to write something yourself covering what you can honestly say: the draft says something you do not believe, and writing your own gives her a genuine statement from somebody who has seen her work. It beats declining to sign and leaving it there, because she has real strengths and a refusal with nothing after it helps neither of you. It beats signing it with the wording softened enough not to be quite untrue, because carefully worded ambiguity still leaves the reader believing what the draft claims. The least effective response is signing the draft as she has written it because statements of this kind are always generous: it endorses a description of a colleague you know to be wrong, for a reader relying on your having worked beside her. That is worse than the other two, which stop short of endorsing the claim outright. The principle: write what you can honestly say and offer that, rather than signing somebody else’s version or hiding behind wording.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc vàng True/False/Cannot Say: Chỉ dựa vào thông tin được cung cấp trong bài đọc, không suy đoán từ hiểu biết bên ngoài.

question_text: Which meter reading was transcribed incorrectly?
options: Meter M1
Meter M2
Meter M3
Meter M4
explanation: Meter M2 reads 18.35 but was logged as 183.5: the decimal point has moved one place to the right, multiplying the value by ten. The digits themselves are unchanged, which is what makes the slip easy to miss.
tip: Mẹo MT: Đọc lướt câu hỏi trước khi đọc đoạn văn để định vị từ khóa (Keywords) nhanh hơn.

question_text: Three colleagues each made one statement about who won an internal quiz. Ada said, “I did not win.” Ben said, “Ada won.” Cara said, “I did not win.” Exactly one of the three won, and exactly one of these three statements is true. Who won?
options: Cara
Ada
Ben
It cannot be determined.
explanation: Test each winner against the “exactly one true” rule. If Ada won, Ben’s statement and Cara’s are both true; if Ben won, Ada’s and Cara’s are both true; if Cara won, only Ada’s statement is true and the other two are false, which is exactly one, so Cara won. A winner of Ada or Ben each produces two true statements, breaking the rule. Concluding it cannot be determined misses that only one winner satisfies the count.
tip: Mẹo MT: Đọc lướt câu hỏi trước khi đọc đoạn văn để định vị từ khóa (Keywords) nhanh hơn.

question_text:
【Ngữ cảnh】：A software company decided to trial a four-day working week for six months. Under the trial, staff worked Monday to Thursday instead of the usual Monday to Friday, and the company asked employees to record how they felt at the end of each week so that it could judge the effect the shorter week was having on their wellbeing over time. Throughout the trial, staff were paid the same as before, on the condition that they completed the same amount of work as in a normal five-day week. The company was clear that no one’s salary would be cut simply because the working week was shorter, and that the trial was meant to test whether the same output could be achieved in fewer days without any loss of pay for the people taking part.

【Câu hỏi】：Employees were paid the same during the trial as they had been before it.
options: True
False
Cannot say
explanation: True: the passage states that under the trial staff “were paid the same as before”. False is wrong because nothing in the text says pay changed. Cannot say is wrong because the passage states the pay directly, so the reader can decide the statement from the text rather than being left uncertain about it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Đọc lướt câu hỏi trước khi đọc đoạn văn để định vị từ khóa (Keywords) nhanh hơn.

question_text:
【Ngữ cảnh】：During its trial of a four-day working week, a software company asked most of its staff to work Monday to Thursday and to take Fridays off. Some managers, however, were concerned that customers might struggle to reach the company at the very end of the week, when the offices would be much quieter than usual and most desks would be empty. To deal with this, the company arranged for a small team of its own staff to answer urgent messages on that day. This meant that while the great majority of employees were away on Fridays, the business was not left completely unstaffed. The company explained that keeping a few people available on Fridays was a deliberate part of the trial, so urgent customer needs could still be met each week.

【Câu hỏi】：No staff worked on Fridays during the trial.
options: True
False
Cannot say
explanation: False: the passage says the company “arranged for a small team of its own staff to answer urgent messages on that day”, meaning Friday, so some staff did work on Fridays. True is wrong because it takes the Monday-to-Thursday pattern at face value and overlooks that Friday team. Cannot say is wrong because the passage settles the point rather than leaving it open, so the statement can be judged false against the text.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc vàng True/False/Cannot Say: Chỉ dựa vào thông tin được cung cấp trong bài đọc, không suy đoán từ hiểu biết bên ngoài.

question_text:
【Ngữ cảnh】：When a software company trialled a four-day week, some managers were concerned that customers might find it harder to reach the company on Fridays, when most of the staff were away from the office. The company took the worry seriously and put a small team in place to handle any urgent messages that might arrive while the rest of the workforce was off. At the end of the trial, the company reviewed how the arrangement had worked from its own point of view, but it did not gather or publish any feedback from customers about their experience on Fridays. Whether customers had in fact found it harder to get in touch, or had noticed no difference at all, was not something the report recorded, and the company said such feedback would be considered separately.

【Câu hỏi】：Customers found it harder to reach the company on Fridays during the trial.
options: True
False
Cannot say
explanation: Cannot say: the passage reports only that some managers were “concerned that customers might find it harder” and that a team handled urgent messages; it never records what customers actually experienced. True is wrong because a concern that something might happen is not a statement that it did. False is wrong because the passage does not claim customers had no difficulty either; it simply leaves their experience unreported.

question_text:
【Ngữ cảnh】：A delivery company installed self-service lockers outside shops in several neighbourhoods, so that customers could have parcels delivered to a locker instead of to their home. Each customer collects their parcel using a code that the company sends to their phone once the parcel has arrived and been placed inside the locker ready for them to pick up. The company reported that parcels sent to lockers were, on average, delivered a day faster than parcels sent to homes. This was because a driver could fill a single bank of lockers with many parcels in one stop, rather than driving to many separate home addresses. The time saved on the road, the company said, was passed on to customers as quicker delivery, and was a main reason it planned to expand the network.

【Câu hỏi】：Parcels sent to lockers were delivered faster on average than parcels sent to homes.
options: True
False
Cannot say
explanation: True: the passage states that parcels sent to lockers were “on average, delivered a day faster than parcels sent to homes”. False is wrong because the passage reports the lockers as faster, not slower. Cannot say is wrong because the comparison is stated directly, so the reader can decide it from the text rather than being left unsure.

question_text:
【Ngữ cảnh】：A delivery company’s self-service lockers were designed to make collecting parcels far more convenient for its customers. When a parcel arrives at a locker, the customer is sent a code to their phone, which they then enter at the locker to open the correct compartment and take out their delivery whenever they happen to be passing by that particular location. The lockers were available at any hour, so customers did not need to be at home to receive a delivery, and could pick up a parcel early in the morning or late at night if that suited them. Because collection depends only on the code and not on the customer being at any particular address, someone could have a parcel delivered while they were at work and then collect it whenever it best suited them.

【Câu hỏi】：Customers must be at home to collect a parcel from a locker.
options: True
False
Cannot say
explanation: False: the passage says lockers were “available at any hour, so customers did not need to be at home to receive a delivery”, and parcels are collected using a code sent to the phone. True is wrong because it contradicts the passage’s stated point of a locker. Cannot say is wrong because the text settles the matter rather than leaving it open.

question_text:
【Ngữ cảnh】：A delivery company explained the rules that applied whenever a parcel was left sitting unclaimed in one of its self-service lockers. Customers are sent reminders to collect their items, and because the space inside the lockers is limited, uncollected parcels cannot be allowed to stay in them indefinitely and take up room that other deliveries would otherwise need. The company noted that a parcel left uncollected for more than five days was returned to the sender, but it did not say how often this happened. It gave no figure for the share of parcels that ended up uncollected, and did not indicate whether such returns were a common event or a rare one. The report therefore described what happened to an abandoned parcel without showing how frequently the situation actually arose.

【Câu hỏi】：Parcels left in lockers are returned to the sender frequently.
options: True
False
Cannot say
explanation: Cannot say: the passage states that a parcel uncollected for more than five days “was returned to the sender”, but adds that it “did not say how often this happened”, so the frequency is unknown. True is wrong because “frequently” claims a rate the passage never gives. False is wrong because the passage does not say returns are rare either; it simply does not report how often they occur.

question_text: All the items in the sale are discounted. Some discounted items are electrical goods. Which statement must be true?
options: Some sale items are electrical goods.
Some electrical goods are discounted.
All electrical goods are discounted.
All discounted items are in the sale.
explanation: “Some discounted items are electrical goods” can be turned around to “some electrical goods are discounted”. Concluding that some sale items are electrical goods is the undistributed-middle error, because the discounted electrical goods need not be the sale items. Concluding that all electrical goods are discounted turns a “some” into an “all”. Concluding that all discounted items are in the sale reverses “all sale items are discounted” into a converse that does not follow.

question_text: You are a research analyst at a consultancy, finishing a market study for a drinks producer, Highmoor Brewing. One of your findings says the client’s new range is unlikely to reach the volumes they have planned for it. Their insight manager asks you to soften that sentence before the report goes to their board, and says that if you do, he will ask for you by name on the next study. The report is due with the board on Monday. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Make the change he wants in return for the favour he is offering, and put the softened sentence into the report that goes to the board on Monday.
Tell the insight manager the finding stays as it is, put what he asked for to the manager running the study today, and offer to add the client's own view.
Rewrite the sentence in gentler language while keeping the number in it, and send it back to him for his approval before anybody else in the team sees the finished report.
Leave the wording exactly as it stands and say nothing to anybody about what he offered, so that the finding reaches the board unchanged.
explanation: A: Takes a favour for changing a finding: the board reads a softer conclusion than the evidence supports, and what bought the change was something offered to you personally. C: Negotiates a finding with the person it is about: the wording is settled privately with the reader who wants it softened. D: Leaves an offer unreported: the finding survives, and the person who tried to trade for it is free to try the same thing on whoever comes next. The most effective response is to tell the insight manager the finding stays as it is and to put what he asked for to the manager running the study. The finding is what the client is paying for, the offer is something the manager running the study needs to know about, and adding the client’s own view is the honest way to give them a voice in the report. It beats leaving the wording as it stands and saying nothing about what he offered, because an offer like that needs to reach somebody, or it simply gets made again to whoever comes next. It beats rewriting the sentence in gentler language and sending it to him for approval, because letting the person a finding is about approve its wording quietly puts the evidence in their gift. The least effective response is making the change he wants in return for the favour he is offering: the other three all leave the board reading what the study found, whereas this one trades the wording of the evidence for something offered to you, which is a different kind of wrong from handling it clumsily. The principle: findings are not currency, and an offer attached to one is itself the thing to report.

question_text: You are a technical support adviser. A member of the public rings after reading about a problem at your company and asks whether her details were affected. The security team is still working on it and has published nothing. Nobody has told the support desk what to say, and yours is the first call of this kind. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell her you are not allowed to comment and that she should watch the company's website for an announcement when one is published.
Take her details and promise that somebody from the security team will ring her back today with an answer about her own records specifically.
Tell her an investigation is running and nothing is ruled in or out, take her details, and tell your manager the desk needs a line, since more of these will come.
Tell her that her details are almost certainly fine, since nothing has been confirmed as taken and there is no point worrying somebody over a maybe.
explanation: A: Refuses a caller you could partly help: that an investigation is running is itself true and sayable, and she is left with nothing to do. B: Commits another team to a call they have not agreed to: the security team is mid-investigation and has no capacity to ring individual callers. D: Gives an assurance nobody has authorised: no one has established what was taken, and she will make decisions about her own accounts on your word. The most effective response is to tell her an investigation is running and nothing is ruled in or out, take her details, and tell your manager the desk needs a line. She gets the truthful state of play, her details are captured, and the fact that this is the first such call is something your manager needs because it will not be the last. It beats telling her you are not allowed to comment and that she should watch the website, because the existence of an investigation is safe to say and gives her something real. It beats promising that somebody from the security team will ring her back today, because they have not agreed to that and cannot mid- investigation. The least effective response is telling her that her details are almost certainly fine: it is worse than either of the other two, because both stop short of telling her anything untrue, while this reassures a member of the public about her own data on an investigation that has not concluded. The principle: give the honest state of play, capture the caller, and tell your own manager that a line is needed before the second call arrives.

question_text: You are a junior developer. Reading through tonight’s release you have noticed that a change renames a field that a report your colleague owns depends on. Her report runs every Tuesday morning and she is not working today. The release goes out at eight this evening. You may have misread it, and nobody has asked you to check anything. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Email your colleague so that she sees it tomorrow morning, and leave the release alone, since she is the one who owns the report and should decide about it.
Leave it. You may have misread it, nobody asked you to check the release, and the person who owns the report is the one who should have spotted it.
Change the release yourself to keep the old field name alongside the new one, so that her report carries on working whichever way it turns out to be.
Raise it now with whoever is running tonight's release, say what you think you have seen and that you may have misread it, and let them decide before eight.
explanation: A: Sends a warning that arrives after the event: she reads it on Tuesday, by which time the release went out on Monday evening and her report has already run. B: Stays silent on something only you have seen: the release goes out at eight whether or not you misread it, and nobody else is looking at this at all. C: Acts on a reading you are not sure of: it edits somebody else's change on the evening it ships, on the strength of something you think you saw. The most effective response is to raise it now with whoever is running tonight’s release, say what you think you have seen and that you may have misread it. There are hours left, they can check it in minutes, and saying openly that you may be wrong costs nothing and lets them weigh it. It beats emailing your colleague so she sees it tomorrow morning, because that arrives after Monday evening’s release and after her report has run. It beats changing the release yourself to keep the old field name alongside the new one, because editing somebody else’s change on the evening it ships, on a reading you are unsure of, risks more than it protects. The least effective response is leaving it because you may have misread it and nobody asked you to check: it is worse than either of the other two, because both act on what you saw, while this leaves the only observation anybody has made unspoken until Tuesday. The principle: an uncertain observation with hours to spare goes to whoever can check it, and uncertainty is a thing to say aloud rather than a reason to stay quiet.
