question_text: You are a risk assistant. In a meeting, a manager from another team says your report was late and “not worth reading”, in front of eight people. The report was two days late because their team sent data late, which you can show. The meeting has ten minutes left and the chair is waiting for the next item. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Point out in front of the others that their own team sent the data two days late, and that this is not the first time their delays have been described as somebody else's problem.
Say that you will take the quality point away and look at it, note that the timing depended on data that arrived late, and offer to go through both with them afterwards.
Say nothing in the meeting and send the manager the dates afterwards, so that the correction is made privately and the meeting can move on.
Ask the chair for time now to go through the timeline properly, so that the meeting can see exactly when the data arrived and when the report followed.
explanation: A: Answers a criticism with a criticism in the room: the substance of both points is lost, and eight people watch a dispute between two teams instead of the next item. C: Leaves an unchallenged claim standing: eight people heard the report called not worth reading and none of them will see the private correction. D: Spends a contested ten minutes on your own position: the meeting has other business, and a timeline walk-through reads as defensiveness whatever it shows. The most effective response is to say you will take the quality point away and look at it, note that the timing depended on data that arrived late, and offer to go through both afterwards: it concedes what might be fair, corrects the factual point briefly in front of the same eight people, and moves the argument somewhere it can be had properly. It beats saying nothing in the meeting and sending the manager the dates afterwards, because a private correction never reaches the audience that heard the claim. It beats asking the chair for time now to go through the timeline properly, because taking the meeting’s last ten minutes to litigate it costs more than it recovers. The least effective response is pointing out in front of the others that their own team sent the data two days late and that this is not the first time: it turns a criticism of a report into a public dispute about another team’s reliability, and the room leaves remembering the row. That is personalising it rather than pitching the response badly. The principle: take the point, correct the fact briefly, and move the argument off the floor.

question_text: You are a client services associate. A client emails at 9am insisting that a routine quarterly statement is sent to her today rather than next week, and will not say why. Producing it early takes about forty minutes. Your other work today has no fixed deadline. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Reply that the statement will follow on the usual date next week, and assume that a client who will not explain the urgency does not really have any.
Reply asking her to explain why she needs it today, and produce the statement once she has told you what the underlying deadline actually is.
Produce the statement today and send it without any covering message, so that she has what she asked for and nothing more is made of it.
Produce the statement today, and when you send it ask whether there is a deadline behind the request so the timing can be built in from next quarter.
explanation: A: Declines to find out: forty minutes of uncommitted time is available, and the reason she will not explain is treated as evidence that there is no reason. B: Makes help conditional on an explanation: she has already declined to give one, and forty minutes of your time is not worth the standoff. C: Solves today and not next quarter: the same scramble happens again because nobody ever asked what sits behind the date. The most effective response is to produce the statement today and ask, when you send it, whether there is a deadline behind the request: she gets what she asked for inside a day that has room for it, and the question is asked at the point where it costs nothing. It beats replying to ask why she needs it today before producing anything, because forty spare minutes is not worth a standoff over an explanation. It beats producing it today and sending it without any covering message, because asking once prevents the same request arriving urgently every quarter. The least effective response is replying that the statement will follow on the usual date next week: a client is refused something the day plainly had room for, on an assumption about her motives that nobody tested. That is avoidance rather than an unhelpful way of helping. The principle: do the cheap thing, and ask the question that stops it recurring.

question_text: You are an assurance trainee. Your senior has told you to drop a test she says the client “sorted out verbally”. Firm policy is that evidence goes on the file. She is the person you report to, she reviews your work, and she has been supportive. The file is signed off next Tuesday. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Assure her that the test is complete and the evidence is on the file, and leave it as it is so that nobody has to reopen the question before Tuesday.
Ask her directly to point you at what she was told and by whom, so you can put it on the file, and say you are not comfortable leaving it with nothing recorded.
Do as she asked and drop the test, but write a note in your own records that you were told to drop it, so your own position is documented if it ever comes up.
Take it to the engagement partner this week, since a missing test on a file being signed on Tuesday is exactly what a partner should know about.
explanation: A: Tells your reviewer something untrue: she signs a file believing a test was done, and the fabrication is now hers to defend as well as yours. C: Documents rather than resolves: the file still lacks the evidence, and a private note protects you and nobody else. D: Escalates before asking: she has given a reason, you have not tested it, and going straight past her is hard to walk back if the answer is innocent. The most effective response is to ask her directly to point you at what she was told and by whom so you can put it on the file, and say you are not comfortable leaving it with nothing recorded: it treats her explanation as probably genuine, asks for the thing policy requires, and says where you stand without making it an accusation. It beats taking it to the engagement partner this week, because going over her before asking is unrecoverable if her answer is fine. It beats dropping the test but writing a note in your own records, because a private note leaves the file exactly as wrong as before. The least effective response is assuring her the test is complete and the evidence is on the file: your reviewer is told something untrue and signs on the strength of it. That is a false statement to the person relying on you, a different kind of wrong from the other two, which at least leave the facts intact. The principle: ask the person first, plainly, for the thing the policy needs.

question_text: You work in a delivery-only kitchen. Checking the walk-in fridge you find the temperature gauge reading well above the safe limit and the log shows it was last checked twelve hours ago. There is a large quantity of prepared food inside. Orders start in an hour. Your head chef is on site and the food safety procedure requires temperature failures to be reported to him. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Stop the food being used, tell the head chef now that the fridge is above the safe limit and was last checked twelve hours ago, and let him decide what happens to it.
Use the food for tonight's orders since it is still cold to the touch and the gauge may well be faulty, and report the fridge for repair tomorrow.
Move the prepared food to another fridge so it starts cooling again, and tell the head chef once the transfer is done.
Check the temperature again with a probe thermometer to confirm the gauge is accurate before raising it, so the head chef is not called over a faulty gauge.
explanation: B: Serves food of unknown safety: a fridge above the safe limit for an unknown period is exactly the situation the temperature control exists to catch, and judging it by touch puts customers at risk. That is a safety failure, not a judgement about waste. C: Acts on assumptions without checking: moving the food cools it and tells nobody how long it was warm, which is the fact that decides whether it can be used at all. D: Delays the decision: verifying the gauge is sensible and takes time the head chef could direct in a moment, with service starting in an hour and food that may already be unsafe. The most effective response is to stop the food being used and tell the head chef now that the fridge is above the safe limit and was last checked twelve hours ago: prepared food may have been warm for up to twelve hours, that decision is his under the food safety procedure, and he is on site with an hour before service. Stopping its use first is what makes the decision possible. It beats moving the prepared food to another fridge and telling him once the transfer is done, because cooling it destroys the evidence of how long it was warm, which is the fact the judgement rests on. It beats checking again with a probe thermometer before raising it, because confirming the gauge is work he can direct in seconds, and the clock is running. The least effective response is using the food for tonight’s orders because it is still cold to the touch: it serves food of unknown temperature history to customers on the basis of how it feels. That is worse than the other two, which act imperfectly but do not serve it. The principle: when a safety control has failed, stop the product and get the decision to the person the procedure names, without disturbing the evidence.

question_text: You are an exhibitions assistant at a museum. You and a curator, Helena, disagree about the label text for a display opening in a fortnight. She wants wording you believe overstates what the evidence supports; you have raised it once and she dismissed it. She is far more senior. The head of exhibitions is available. Labels go to print in three days. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Defer to Helena's wording since she is the curator and it is her display, and note your reservation in an email so there is a record of your concern.
Let the label go to print as Helena wants and say nothing further, since you have raised it once, she is far more senior and the distinction is unlikely to be noticed by visitors.
Put your evidence to Helena once more in writing, and if she still disagrees ask the head of exhibitions to look at the wording before it goes to print in three days.
Amend the label text to the wording you believe the evidence supports before it goes to print, since the deadline is close and the change is small.
explanation: A: Prioritises the record over the outcome: an email protects you while the museum publishes a claim you believe the evidence does not support, which is a question about the display rather than about who was right. B: Fails to escalate a genuine concern: it lets the museum publish a claim you believe overstates the evidence, and the reasons given are seniority and the hope that nobody will notice. Choosing silence about accuracy is a different order of wrong from raising it clumsily. D: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholder's: it rewrites a curator's label without resolving the disagreement, so the museum publishes text its curator has not agreed. The most effective response is to put your evidence to Helena once more in writing, and if she still disagrees ask the head of exhibitions to look at the wording before it goes to print: whether the text is supported by the evidence is a question with an answer, she owns the display so she gets the argument in full first, and the head of exhibitions can settle it inside the three days. Putting it in writing makes the evidence reviewable. It beats amending the label text yourself before it goes to print, because that publishes wording she has not agreed and replaces one unresolved judgement with another. It beats deferring to her and noting your reservation in an email, because a record protects you and lets the overstatement be printed anyway. The least effective response is letting the label go to print and saying nothing further: it allows the museum to publish a claim you believe the evidence does not support, because she is senior and visitors probably will not notice. That is worse than the other two, which are flawed but aimed at the accuracy of the label. The principle: make the evidential case to the person who owns the work, then escalate before the point of no return.

question_text: You are a personal banking assistant. A customer’s account will go overdrawn on Friday when a direct debit leaves, and charges will follow. The standard warning is an automated text. She told you last month that she finds texts confusing and misses them, and she is caring for her mother. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Telephone her today to explain the position, and leave the account preference as it is since the automated text is the standard for everybody.
Write to her by post explaining the position, so she has it in a form she can read carefully rather than a message on a telephone.
Send the automated text over to her in the usual way and leave it to the standard process, since that is what it is there for and the warning will have been given.
Telephone her today, explain what will happen on Friday and what she can do about it, and note on the account that she prefers a call to a text.
explanation: A: Fixes this week and not next: the same problem recurs every time, because nothing about how she is contacted has changed. B: Chooses a channel slower than the deadline: Friday is two days away and post may not arrive in time to act on. C: Passes the customer to a process you already know does not reach her: the warning is technically issued, and she told you last month that she misses exactly this. The most effective response is to telephone her today, explain what will happen on Friday and what she can do about it, and note that she prefers a call to a text: a call reaches her before Friday, it explains what she can actually do, and the note means the next warning reaches her too. It beats writing to her by post, because post may miss Friday. It beats telephoning today but leaving the account preference as it is, because that guarantees a repeat. The least effective response is sending the automated text in the usual way: she is handed to a process you have been told does not work for her, so the warning is issued and not received. That is passing her to the process rather than choosing a slower or narrower channel. The principle: reach the customer by the route that actually reaches them, and record it.

question_text: You are a claims assistant at an insurance company. Reviewing a routine file you notice that a customer’s subsidence claim was declined last year on the basis of a policy exclusion that, reading it now, does not appear to apply to her circumstances. The claim is closed and nobody has asked you to look at it. The customer has not appealed. Your claims manager is in the office. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Take the file to your claims manager, show her the exclusion and why it may not apply, and ask whether the decision should be reviewed.
Write to the customer explaining that the decline may have been wrong and inviting her to appeal, so that the case is reopened through the proper route.
Reopen the claim in the system and reassess it against the policy wording yourself, so that the correct decision is on file before anyone needs to be told.
Leave the file closed, since the claim was decided by someone more senior, the customer accepted it and did not appeal, and it is not your case to reopen.
explanation: B: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholder's: telling a customer her claim was wrongly declined commits the company to a position nobody has agreed, on your reading of an exclusion you have not had checked. C: Breaches confidentiality or process: reopening and reassessing a closed claim is not a claims assistant's authority, and doing it before telling anyone means a decision is remade with no oversight. D: Fails to escalate a genuine risk: a customer may have been wrongly refused a subsidence claim, and the reason for saying nothing is that somebody senior decided it and she did not argue. Her not appealing is not evidence the decision was right. The most effective response is to take the file to your claims manager, show her the exclusion and why it may not apply, and ask whether the decision should be reviewed: you may have found a wrongly declined claim, you are not the person who can determine that, and she is in the office and can. Raising it with the file and the reasoning puts it in front of the right authority immediately. It beats writing to the customer to say the decline may have been wrong and inviting her to appeal, because that commits the company to a view on your reading of the policy before anyone has checked it. It beats reopening the claim and reassessing it against the policy wording yourself, because that is beyond your authority and removes the oversight that should sit over a reversal. The least effective response is leaving the file closed because it was decided by someone more senior and she did not appeal: it leaves a customer possibly out of pocket on a claim that may have been wrongly refused, for reasons that are exactly why nobody else will ever find it. That is worse than the other two, which overstep but act. The principle: when you find a possible error in a decision you cannot overturn, take it to whoever can, rather than acting on it or leaving it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Nhận diện ý chính của từng đoạn bằng câu chủ đề (thường nằm ở đầu hoặc cuối đoạn).

question_text: You are a quality assistant at a food manufacturer. Routine testing shows a batch of sauce with a slightly higher salt reading than the declared label value, above the tolerance in your own specification but not a safety issue. The batch is due to leave for a supermarket customer this afternoon. Your quality manager is at another site but reachable by phone. The production supervisor tells you it is within normal variation. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Put the batch on hold, ring the quality manager with the reading and the specification tolerance, and let her decide whether it ships this afternoon.
Accept the production supervisor's view that it is within normal variation, let the batch go, and say nothing further since it is not a safety concern.
Retest the batch yourself to confirm the reading before involving anyone, since a single result outside tolerance may simply be a testing error.
Release the batch and note the reading in the quality log, so that the trend is recorded and can be reviewed at the next specification meeting.
explanation: B: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholder's: the specification tolerance is the customer's and the label is a declaration to consumers, so neither the supervisor nor you can decide it is close enough. Letting it go unrecorded is the one option that leaves nobody aware at all. C: Delays the decision: a retest is sensible and the batch is loading this afternoon. Confirming the number before telling anyone spends the decision window on work the quality manager could have directed in a minute. D: Fails to escalate a genuine risk: it ships a batch that misses the declared label value and records the fact afterwards. A log entry documents the decision without anyone having made one. The most effective response is to put the batch on hold and ring the quality manager with the reading and the tolerance: the result is outside your own specification, the label is a declaration to consumers, and she owns that judgement and is a phone call away with the batch still on site. Holding it costs an afternoon; shipping it wrongly cannot be undone. It beats retesting the batch yourself before involving anyone, because that is reasonable work in the wrong order: she can direct a retest in a minute, and the batch is loading. It beats releasing the batch and noting the reading in the quality log, because that records a decision nobody actually took. The least effective response is accepting the production supervisor’s view that it is within normal variation and letting the batch go: it accepts a production judgement about a quality specification, ships against a declared label value, and leaves no record and no one informed. That is worse than retesting, which delays but checks, and worse than logging it, which at least documents it. The principle: when a result falls outside a specification you do not own, stop the goods and get the decision to whoever owns it, while stopping is still possible.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc vàng True/False/Cannot Say: Chỉ dựa vào thông tin được cung cấp trong bài đọc, không suy đoán từ hiểu biết bên ngoài.

question_text: You are an insight assistant at Diageo. You are finishing a pack of customer survey results for a decision meeting on Thursday. One question in the survey went out to a much smaller group than the rest, so its result rests on about a fifth of the usual number of replies. The result is the most striking number in the pack, and nobody reading it would know how few replies sit behind it. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Leave the striking result out of the pack altogether, since a number resting on a fifth of the usual replies is not solid enough to put in front of a decision meeting.
Include the result in the pack as it stands, without flagging that the sample behind it was a fifth of the size of the others.
Include the result with the number of replies shown next to it and a line saying what that means for how much weight it should carry.
Include the result as it stands and mention the small sample verbally if the question comes up while you are presenting the pack on Thursday.
explanation: A: Removes evidence rather than qualifying it: the meeting loses a real signal because it could not be given a sentence of context. B: Withholds the fact that decides how much weight the number carries: the most striking figure in the pack is the one nobody is told to treat carefully. D: Leaves a caveat to chance: the pack outlives the meeting and is read by people who were never in the room to hear the qualification. The most effective response is to include the result with the number of replies shown next to it and a line on what that means for its weight: the meeting gets the signal and the size of it, which is what lets people decide how far to lean on it. It beats leaving the result out, because a real finding is discarded when a sentence would have made it usable. It beats mentioning the small sample only if somebody asks, because the pack is read later by people who were never in the room. The least effective response is including the striking result without flagging the size of the sample behind it: the most eye-catching number in the pack is presented as though it were as solid as the rest, and the one person who knows otherwise says nothing, which is a different kind of wrong from being over-cautious or from relying on the meeting to ask. The principle: publish the caveat next to the number, in the document, where everybody who reads one reads the other.

question_text: You are a marketing graduate at Compass Online. A page that went live this morning carries a claim about delivery times that changed last month, so it is now wrong. Changes to live pages go through a release that runs each afternoon, requested by eleven o’clock. It is ten past eleven. You have the access to edit the page directly, and customers are reading it now. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Edit the live page yourself now, since you have the access, the claim is plainly wrong, and customers are reading it while a release process takes its course.
Put the correction into tomorrow's release and note the page as a known issue, since the deadline for today's release has already gone by ten minutes.
Ask the release team to take the page down until the correction can go through properly, so that customers see nothing rather than something untrue.
Ask the release team to take the correction into this afternoon's release despite the cut-off, explain what the claim says now, and tell your manager it is live.
explanation: A: Breaches the release process because the cause is good: an unreviewed change goes live outside the route that exists to stop unreviewed changes going live. B: Accepts a day of a wrong claim on a technicality: nobody has asked whether a correction ten minutes late can still make this afternoon. C: Removes more than the error: the whole page disappears for a day because one sentence about delivery times is out of date. The most effective response is to ask the release team to take the correction this afternoon despite the cut-off, explain what the claim currently says, and tell your manager: the fastest legitimate route is tried, the people who own the release decide, and the person accountable knows a wrong claim is live. It beats putting it in tomorrow’s release, because nobody has asked whether ten minutes late can still be accommodated. It beats taking the whole page down, because one sentence does not justify losing all of it. The least effective response is editing the live page yourself: an unreviewed change goes live outside the process whose entire purpose is to stop that, which is a different kind of wrong from being too accepting or from over-correcting. The principle: a good reason is exactly when a control gets tested, and the answer is to ask for an exception rather than take one.

question_text: You are a graduate in Deloitte’s internal learning team. You noticed that new joiners were being sent the wrong pre-reading pack, so you rebuilt the mailing list and told the team what you had changed. In this morning’s stand-up the colleague who owns that list said, in front of everyone, that you should have come to her first and that she is taking it back. Twenty new joiners are due their packs on Friday. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Build your own copy of the mailing list and run a second send on Friday as well, so the twenty new joiners get the right pack whatever state her version of the list is in.
Hand the list back and stop checking the Friday send, because she said in the stand-up that it is hers, and let Friday's packs go out however they go out.
Find her after the stand-up, agree that the list is hers, take her through what you changed and why, and check with her that Friday's twenty packs will go out correctly.
Take it to your own manager instead and ask him to settle who owns the mailing list before Friday, since she has made her view of it clear in front of the whole team.
explanation: A: Answers a disagreement by duplicating a control: two sends from two lists is worse for the new joiners than one, and it tells her plainly that you do not trust her to run her own list. B: Withdraws your help because you were criticised: the twenty new joiners have nothing to do with the argument, and the fault you found on Monday is allowed back for the sake of a point. D: Escalates a conversation you have not yet had: ownership was never really the question, and asking a manager to rule on it turns one sharp remark into a standing dispute. The most effective response is to find her after the stand-up, agree that the list is hers, take her through what you changed and why, and check that Friday’s twenty packs will go out correctly. It gives her the ownership she asked for and still leaves somebody making sure the packs are right. It beats building your own copy and running a second send, because two lists sending to the same twenty people is a worse outcome than the fault you started with. It beats taking it to your own manager to settle who owns the list, because you have not yet had the two-minute conversation that would probably settle it. The least effective response is to hand the list back and stop checking the Friday send: the weaker responses both keep working the problem, clumsily or over somebody’s head, whereas this one answers being criticised by pulling your attention off twenty new joiners who had no part in it, and it lets the original fault run again. The principle: taking something on means seeing it through, and a sharp word about how you did it does not change who is affected on Friday. This is what Deloitte’s ‘Lead the way’ points to.

question_text: You are a quality inspector at a textile manufacturer. Checking a finished batch you notice the same small weaving fault on several rolls from one loom, and looking back at last week’s records you see it on that loom’s output too. Nobody has asked you to review previous batches. Last week’s output has already gone to a customer. Your quality manager is on site. The loom is running now. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Reject the current batch and say nothing about last week's records, since that output has already been accepted by the customer and reopening it would cause unnecessary trouble.
Reject the current batch and have the loom stopped for maintenance, then report it once the immediate production problem has been dealt with.
Reject the current batch as faulty and record it in the quality log, since the fault is caught before dispatch and the log is where recurring issues are reviewed.
Take the current batch and last week's records to your quality manager now, show her the fault is recurring on one loom, and let her decide about the loom and the customer.
explanation: A: Hides the problem: it knowingly withholds that a customer has already received cloth with the same fault, in order to avoid trouble. Choosing silence about goods already delivered is concealment, not discretion. B: Acts outside own authority on the wider issue: stopping the loom is reasonable and it leaves the shipped batch, which is the part with a customer at the other end, unaddressed and unreported. C: Delays the decision: rejecting this batch protects this shipment and the log is reviewed later, so a loom producing faulty cloth keeps running and last week's delivery stays with the customer unmentioned. The most effective response is to take the current batch and last week’s records to your quality manager now, show her the fault is recurring on one loom, and let her decide about the loom and the customer: the machine is running now and last week’s faulty output is already delivered, and only she can decide about both. Bringing the batch and the records together makes the pattern visible. It beats rejecting the batch and recording it in the quality log, because that leaves the loom running and the delivered goods unmentioned. It beats rejecting the batch and having the loom stopped for maintenance, because that addresses production while the customer who already has faulty cloth is still not considered. The least effective response is rejecting the batch and saying nothing about last week’s records: it deliberately withholds that faulty goods have already been delivered, to avoid trouble. That is worse than the other two, which act partially but do not conceal. The principle: when a fault turns out to have a history, take the history as well as the sample to whoever can act on both.

question_text: You are a process operator at a waste water treatment works. Passing a monitoring screen that is not part of your round, you notice the outflow ammonia reading has been climbing steadily for three days and is close to the permitted limit. Exceeding it is reportable to the environmental regulator. The operator responsible is on leave. Your works manager is on site. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Adjust the aeration settings yourself to bring the ammonia down, since the trend is clear and the limit is close.
Take the three-day trend to your works manager now, show him the readings and how close they are to the limit, and let him decide what to do.
Record the trend in the shift log so the operator responsible picks it up when he returns from leave next week.
Leave it, since the screen is not on your round, the reading is still inside the permitted limit and the plant's alarms would trigger if it went over.
explanation: A: Acts outside own authority: changing process settings on a plant running near a permitted limit can drive the reading the wrong way, and the works manager has not been told the trend exists. C: Delays the decision: the log reaches the right person on the wrong day. The reading is close to a reportable limit now, and next week is after any breach would have happened. D: Fails to escalate a genuine risk: a three-day climb towards a reportable limit is exactly the signal that precedes a breach, and relying on the alarm means acting only once the limit has already been exceeded. The most effective response is to take the three-day trend to your works manager now, show him the readings and how close they are to the limit, and let him decide: a steady climb towards a reportable limit is a developing breach rather than a stable reading, you are the only person who has noticed with the responsible operator away, and he can act today. It beats adjusting the aeration settings yourself to bring the ammonia down, because that is a process decision beyond your authority on a plant running close to a limit, and could make the reading worse. It beats recording the trend in the shift log for the operator returning next week, because that arrives after the breach it should have prevented. The least effective response is leaving it because the reading is still inside the permitted limit and the alarms would trigger: it waits for an alarm that by definition sounds only once the limit has been exceeded and the breach is already reportable. That is worse than the other two, which act wrongly or slowly but do act. The principle: a trend towards a limit is information somebody needs before the limit is reached, so take it to whoever can act while it is still preventable.

question_text: You are an exhibitions assistant at a museum. You and a curator, Helena, disagree about the label text for a display opening in a fortnight. She wants wording you believe overstates what the evidence supports; you have raised it once and she dismissed it. She is far more senior. The head of exhibitions is available. Labels go to print in three days. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Defer to Helena's wording since she is the curator and it is her display, and note your reservation in an email so there is a record of your concern.
Let the label go to print as Helena wants and say nothing further, since you have raised it once, she is far more senior and the distinction is unlikely to be noticed by visitors.
Put your evidence to Helena once more in writing, and if she still disagrees ask the head of exhibitions to look at the wording before it goes to print in three days.
Amend the label text to the wording you believe the evidence supports before it goes to print, since the deadline is close and the change is small.
explanation: A: Prioritises the record over the outcome: an email protects you while the museum publishes a claim you believe the evidence does not support, which is a question about the display rather than about who was right. B: Fails to escalate a genuine concern: it lets the museum publish a claim you believe overstates the evidence, and the reasons given are seniority and the hope that nobody will notice. Choosing silence about accuracy is a different order of wrong from raising it clumsily. D: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholder's: it rewrites a curator's label without resolving the disagreement, so the museum publishes text its curator has not agreed. The most effective response is to put your evidence to Helena once more in writing, and if she still disagrees ask the head of exhibitions to look at the wording before it goes to print: whether the text is supported by the evidence is a question with an answer, she owns the display so she gets the argument in full first, and the head of exhibitions can settle it inside the three days. Putting it in writing makes the evidence reviewable. It beats amending the label text yourself before it goes to print, because that publishes wording she has not agreed and replaces one unresolved judgement with another. It beats deferring to her and noting your reservation in an email, because a record protects you and lets the overstatement be printed anyway. The least effective response is letting the label go to print and saying nothing further: it allows the museum to publish a claim you believe the evidence does not support, because she is senior and visitors probably will not notice. That is worse than the other two, which are flawed but aimed at the accuracy of the label. The principle: make the evidential case to the person who owns the work, then escalate before the point of no return.

question_text: You are a graduate on an EY transactions team preparing a due diligence pack. Everyone writes up their own section of the shared model, and the team has a standing rule that nobody edits a section they do not own: corrections go to the owner or to the engagement lead. Reading through, you spot that a colleague’s section carries a supplier figure that does not match the schedule the target sent. He is at his desk this afternoon. The lead combines the sections tomorrow morning. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Open his section of the shared model and correct the figure yourself, since the fix takes a minute and the rule about editing only your own section exists to stop duplicated work.
Raise it with the engagement lead so she can decide whether that section needs changing, and leave it with her rather than going to your colleague directly.
Message your colleague with the figure you think is wrong and the schedule you checked it against, and offer to sit with him for ten minutes so he can change it himself.
Leave a review comment on the shared file against that figure so it is picked up whenever he next opens his section, and carry on with your own part of the pack.
explanation: A: Breaches a team rule to save a minute: the number may well end up right, but the rule is set aside on your own authority and the owner presents a write-up containing work he has never seen. B: Escalates prematurely: the owner is at his desk this afternoon and can fix his own figure, and routing it upwards turns a ten minute correction into an item on the lead's list. D: Relies on a channel nobody is watching: the lead combines the sections tomorrow morning, and a comment your colleague does not open before then leaves the wrong figure in the pack. The most effective response is to message your colleague with the figure you think is wrong and the schedule you checked it against, then offer to sit with him for ten minutes. He owns the section, he is at his desk, and the team’s rule points corrections at the owner precisely so the person answering for the work knows what changed in it. It beats raising it with the engagement lead so she can decide whether the section needs changing, because the owner can fix his own figure this afternoon and the lead gains an item she never needed. It also beats leaving a review comment on the shared file for him to find, because the sections are combined tomorrow morning and a comment he does not open before then leaves the wrong figure in the pack. The least effective response is opening his section of the shared model and correcting the figure yourself: the other responses all work through somebody entitled to make the change, while this one puts your hands inside another person’s work against a rule the team has stated, so he answers for a write-up he did not make. The principle: fix other people’s work through them, never instead of them. Teaming is one of the four qualities EY names in its first published value.

question_text: You are a personal banking assistant. A customer’s account will go overdrawn on Friday when a direct debit leaves, and charges will follow. The standard warning is an automated text. She told you last month that she finds texts confusing and misses them, and she is caring for her mother. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Telephone her today to explain the position, and leave the account preference as it is since the automated text is the standard for everybody.
Write to her by post explaining the position, so she has it in a form she can read carefully rather than a message on a telephone.
Send the automated text over to her in the usual way and leave it to the standard process, since that is what it is there for and the warning will have been given.
Telephone her today, explain what will happen on Friday and what she can do about it, and note on the account that she prefers a call to a text.
explanation: A: Fixes this week and not next: the same problem recurs every time, because nothing about how she is contacted has changed. B: Chooses a channel slower than the deadline: Friday is two days away and post may not arrive in time to act on. C: Passes the customer to a process you already know does not reach her: the warning is technically issued, and she told you last month that she misses exactly this. The most effective response is to telephone her today, explain what will happen on Friday and what she can do about it, and note that she prefers a call to a text: a call reaches her before Friday, it explains what she can actually do, and the note means the next warning reaches her too. It beats writing to her by post, because post may miss Friday. It beats telephoning today but leaving the account preference as it is, because that guarantees a repeat. The least effective response is sending the automated text in the usual way: she is handed to a process you have been told does not work for her, so the warning is issued and not received. That is passing her to the process rather than choosing a slower or narrower channel. The principle: reach the customer by the route that actually reaches them, and record it.

question_text: You are an area support assistant for a restaurant chain, visiting a branch to help with stock counts. In the kitchen you notice the fridge temperature log has identical readings written in for the past two weeks, including for a day the branch was closed. Food safety is not your role and you have no authority here. The branch manager is on site. Your area manager is contactable by phone. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Say nothing, since food safety is not your role, you have no authority at this branch, and the branch manager will have his own reasons for how the log is kept.
Raise it with the branch manager, ask him to check the fridges now, and ring your area manager today because the log for two weeks cannot be relied on.
Mention it to the branch manager and suggest he starts recording the readings properly from now on, then get on with the stock count you came to do.
Photograph the log and include it in your visit report, so that the area manager sees the evidence when the report is circulated next week.
explanation: A: Fails to escalate a genuine risk: identical readings including a closed day mean the log is not a record of anything, so nobody knows whether food has been held safely. Having no authority is a reason to tell someone who has, not to say nothing. C: Treats a safety failure as a paperwork fix: recording properly from now on corrects the form and leaves two weeks in which nobody knows whether the fridges held temperature, with that food still in them. D: Delays the decision: the evidence is captured and the food is still being served. A report next week arrives long after the fortnight it describes. The most effective response is to raise it with the branch manager, ask him to check the fridges now, and ring your area manager today: identical readings across a fortnight including a day the branch was shut mean the log records nothing, so nobody knows whether the fridges have held temperature, and food is being served now. Getting the fridges checked today and telling the area manager addresses both the immediate risk and the recording failure. It beats suggesting he starts recording the readings properly from now on, because that leaves the last two weeks, and the food from them, entirely unexamined. It beats photographing the log for your visit report next week, because that is far too slow for a live food safety question. The least effective response is saying nothing because you have no authority at this branch: it leaves an unreliable food safety record and possibly mishandled food untouched, on grounds that are precisely why it should go to someone who does have authority. That is worse than the other two, which act too slowly but do act. The principle: when a control turns out not to be working, get the immediate check done and tell the person with authority the same day.

question_text: You work in an airline contact centre. Storms have cancelled dozens of flights and you have handled distressed calls for three hours. A passenger tells you that you sound like you are reading from a script and that you clearly do not care that his family are stranded abroad. Rebooking options are limited but some exist. Your team leader is available. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Explain that the cancellations are weather-related, that you have been helping stranded passengers all morning and that you are doing your best for everyone.
Acknowledge that his family being stranded is what matters, tell him the rebooking options that do exist, and start on whichever one he chooses.
Tell him the options are extremely limited because of the weather and that there is very little the airline can do until the backlog clears.
Apologise and offer to pass him to your team leader, since he is unhappy with how the call is going and may prefer to deal with someone senior.
explanation: A: Personalises the conflict: it answers his criticism of you rather than the problem of his family being stranded, which invites him to argue about your manner instead of his booking. C: Ignores the customer's actual need: it presents the situation as hopeless when rebooking options do exist, so a passenger with a stranded family is given despair instead of the seats that are actually available. D: Passes responsibility to others: it hands off a rebooking you can do and makes a passenger with a stranded family queue again for a supervisor during the busiest hours. The most effective response is to acknowledge that his family being stranded is what matters, tell him the rebooking options that do exist, and start on whichever he chooses: some options exist, and moving straight to them answers the substance without engaging the criticism of your manner. It beats explaining that the cancellations are weather-related and that you have been helping stranded passengers all morning, because defending yourself spends the call on your performance rather than on his family. It beats offering to pass him to your team leader, because that makes him wait again for something you can do now. The least effective response is telling him the options are extremely limited and there is very little the airline can do: it says nothing can be done when options do exist, so a passenger who could have been rebooked is left believing he is stuck. That is worse than explaining the weather, which at least explains, and worse than passing him on, which at least routes him to someone. The principle: when someone criticises you under pressure, put the available options in front of them and let the criticism go unanswered.
tip: Mẹo MT: Đọc lướt câu hỏi trước khi đọc đoạn văn để định vị từ khóa (Keywords) nhanh hơn.

question_text: You are a technical support adviser. A member of the public rings after reading about a problem at your company and asks whether her details were affected. The security team is still working on it and has published nothing. Nobody has told the support desk what to say, and yours is the first call of this kind. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell her you are not allowed to comment and that she should watch the company's website for an announcement when one is published.
Take her details and promise that somebody from the security team will ring her back today with an answer about her own records specifically.
Tell her an investigation is running and nothing is ruled in or out, take her details, and tell your manager the desk needs a line, since more of these will come.
Tell her that her details are almost certainly fine, since nothing has been confirmed as taken and there is no point worrying somebody over a maybe.
explanation: A: Refuses a caller you could partly help: that an investigation is running is itself true and sayable, and she is left with nothing to do. B: Commits another team to a call they have not agreed to: the security team is mid-investigation and has no capacity to ring individual callers. D: Gives an assurance nobody has authorised: no one has established what was taken, and she will make decisions about her own accounts on your word. The most effective response is to tell her an investigation is running and nothing is ruled in or out, take her details, and tell your manager the desk needs a line. She gets the truthful state of play, her details are captured, and the fact that this is the first such call is something your manager needs because it will not be the last. It beats telling her you are not allowed to comment and that she should watch the website, because the existence of an investigation is safe to say and gives her something real. It beats promising that somebody from the security team will ring her back today, because they have not agreed to that and cannot mid- investigation. The least effective response is telling her that her details are almost certainly fine: it is worse than either of the other two, because both stop short of telling her anything untrue, while this reassures a member of the public about her own data on an investigation that has not concluded. The principle: give the honest state of play, capture the caller, and tell your own manager that a line is needed before the second call arrives.
tip: Mẹo MT: Đọc lướt câu hỏi trước khi đọc đoạn văn để định vị từ khóa (Keywords) nhanh hơn.

question_text: You are a trainee solicitor. A witness statement must reach the court by four o’clock today or next week’s hearing will be lost. Your supervisor has also asked for a research note on an unrelated matter, which she wants to read before she leaves at five. You cannot finish both. She is in a meeting until half past three. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Start the research note first because your supervisor asked for it directly, and then do as much of the witness statement as the time left allows.
Finish the witness statement so it reaches the court by four, then message your supervisor now to say the research note will follow this evening or first thing tomorrow morning.
Split the afternoon between the two so that each is partly done, and leave a note for your supervisor explaining where you reached on each of them.
Hand the witness statement to your supervisor, who has not seen the file, so that you are free to finish the research note your supervisor asked you for.
explanation: A: Substitutes your own ranking for the one the deadlines set: it puts the person who asked ahead of the deadline that cannot move, and the statement is the only item here with a consequence attached to being late. C: Splits effort so nothing finishes: partly done is worth nothing on a document the court will not accept late, and it also leaves the research note short of what your supervisor needs before five. D: Passes responsibility to others: it moves the harder job, against the tighter deadline, to the person least placed to do it, purely so that the task with no external deadline can start sooner. The most effective response is to finish the witness statement so it reaches the court by four, then message your supervisor that the research note will follow this evening. Four o’clock is the only deadline in the scenario that cannot move, and a message now costs her nothing while she is still in her meeting. It beats starting the research note first because she asked for it directly, since the note has no consequence attached to arriving this evening and the statement does. It beats splitting the afternoon between the two, because a partly finished statement is worth nothing to the court, so that loses the one thing that had to be protected. The least effective response is handing the witness statement to your supervisor, who has not seen the file: it produces the same risk to the statement as doing the note first, but it also puts the work with somebody who has no knowledge of the file, so nobody is left owning the outcome. That is what makes it a different kind of wrong from the other two, which at least keep the work with the person who can do it. The principle: protect the deadline that cannot move, and tell the person waiting on the other thing before they are waiting.
tip: Mẹo MT: Nhận diện ý chính của từng đoạn bằng câu chủ đề (thường nằm ở đầu hoặc cuối đoạn).

question_text: You are an assurance trainee. Your senior has told you to drop a test she says the client “sorted out verbally”. Firm policy is that evidence goes on the file. She is the person you report to, she reviews your work, and she has been supportive. The file is signed off next Tuesday. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Assure her that the test is complete and the evidence is on the file, and leave it as it is so that nobody has to reopen the question before Tuesday.
Ask her directly to point you at what she was told and by whom, so you can put it on the file, and say you are not comfortable leaving it with nothing recorded.
Do as she asked and drop the test, but write a note in your own records that you were told to drop it, so your own position is documented if it ever comes up.
Take it to the engagement partner this week, since a missing test on a file being signed on Tuesday is exactly what a partner should know about.
explanation: A: Tells your reviewer something untrue: she signs a file believing a test was done, and the fabrication is now hers to defend as well as yours. C: Documents rather than resolves: the file still lacks the evidence, and a private note protects you and nobody else. D: Escalates before asking: she has given a reason, you have not tested it, and going straight past her is hard to walk back if the answer is innocent. The most effective response is to ask her directly to point you at what she was told and by whom so you can put it on the file, and say you are not comfortable leaving it with nothing recorded: it treats her explanation as probably genuine, asks for the thing policy requires, and says where you stand without making it an accusation. It beats taking it to the engagement partner this week, because going over her before asking is unrecoverable if her answer is fine. It beats dropping the test but writing a note in your own records, because a private note leaves the file exactly as wrong as before. The least effective response is assuring her the test is complete and the evidence is on the file: your reviewer is told something untrue and signs on the strength of it. That is a false statement to the person relying on you, a different kind of wrong from the other two, which at least leave the facts intact. The principle: ask the person first, plainly, for the thing the policy needs.
tip: Mẹo MT: Nhận diện ý chính của từng đoạn bằng câu chủ đề (thường nằm ở đầu hoặc cuối đoạn).

question_text: You are a site reliability assistant. A customer’s overnight job has failed and the ticket has come to you because your name is on a runbook you wrote a year ago. The job belongs to the data team. You have an incident summary due at four. Reading the ticket and either fixing it or telling the data team what the runbook covers would take twenty minutes. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Reply on the ticket that the runbook is out of date and that the data team owns the job now, then get back to writing the incident summary.
Spend twenty minutes now reading it and either fix it or tell the data team what the runbook actually covers, so that the customer's job runs tonight.
Pass the ticket to the data team without reading it and get back to the summary. The job is theirs, and the runbook was written a year ago.
Read the ticket, add what you know to it, and leave it assigned to yourself until after four so that the summary is not interrupted.
explanation: A: Corrects the record and leaves the job failed: the ownership note is accurate, and the customer's overnight run is exactly where it was. C: Passes the problem on without owning it: they receive a failed job with none of the context that only the runbook's author has. D: Holds a ticket you have already understood: the context is captured and the customer waits until after four for something you could have said at once. The most effective response is to spend twenty minutes now reading it and either fix it or tell the data team what the runbook actually covers. Twenty minutes is affordable against a four o’clock deadline, and you are the only person who knows what that runbook does and does not cover. It beats replying on the ticket that the runbook is out of date and the data team owns the job now, because a note about ownership does not make the overnight job run. It beats reading the ticket, adding what you know and holding it until after four, because once you know the answer, sitting on it costs the customer a night. The least effective response is passing the ticket to the data team without reading it: it is worse than either of the other two, because both add something they could use, while this forwards a failed job with none of the context only you hold. The principle: when you are the person who knows what a document means, twenty minutes of yours is cheaper than anybody else’s hour.
tip: Mẹo MT: Nhận diện ý chính của từng đoạn bằng câu chủ đề (thường nằm ở đầu hoặc cuối đoạn).

question_text: You are a risk assistant. In a meeting, a manager from another team says your report was late and “not worth reading”, in front of eight people. The report was two days late because their team sent data late, which you can show. The meeting has ten minutes left and the chair is waiting for the next item. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Point out in front of the others that their own team sent the data two days late, and that this is not the first time their delays have been described as somebody else's problem.
Say that you will take the quality point away and look at it, note that the timing depended on data that arrived late, and offer to go through both with them afterwards.
Say nothing in the meeting and send the manager the dates afterwards, so that the correction is made privately and the meeting can move on.
Ask the chair for time now to go through the timeline properly, so that the meeting can see exactly when the data arrived and when the report followed.
explanation: A: Answers a criticism with a criticism in the room: the substance of both points is lost, and eight people watch a dispute between two teams instead of the next item. C: Leaves an unchallenged claim standing: eight people heard the report called not worth reading and none of them will see the private correction. D: Spends a contested ten minutes on your own position: the meeting has other business, and a timeline walk-through reads as defensiveness whatever it shows. The most effective response is to say you will take the quality point away and look at it, note that the timing depended on data that arrived late, and offer to go through both afterwards: it concedes what might be fair, corrects the factual point briefly in front of the same eight people, and moves the argument somewhere it can be had properly. It beats saying nothing in the meeting and sending the manager the dates afterwards, because a private correction never reaches the audience that heard the claim. It beats asking the chair for time now to go through the timeline properly, because taking the meeting’s last ten minutes to litigate it costs more than it recovers. The least effective response is pointing out in front of the others that their own team sent the data two days late and that this is not the first time: it turns a criticism of a report into a public dispute about another team’s reliability, and the room leaves remembering the row. That is personalising it rather than pitching the response badly. The principle: take the point, correct the fact briefly, and move the argument off the floor.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc vàng True/False/Cannot Say: Chỉ dựa vào thông tin được cung cấp trong bài đọc, không suy đoán từ hiểu biết bên ngoài.

question_text: You are an area support assistant for a restaurant chain, visiting a branch to help with stock counts. In the kitchen you notice the fridge temperature log has identical readings written in for the past two weeks, including for a day the branch was closed. Food safety is not your role and you have no authority here. The branch manager is on site. Your area manager is contactable by phone. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Say nothing, since food safety is not your role, you have no authority at this branch, and the branch manager will have his own reasons for how the log is kept.
Raise it with the branch manager, ask him to check the fridges now, and ring your area manager today because the log for two weeks cannot be relied on.
Mention it to the branch manager and suggest he starts recording the readings properly from now on, then get on with the stock count you came to do.
Photograph the log and include it in your visit report, so that the area manager sees the evidence when the report is circulated next week.
explanation: A: Fails to escalate a genuine risk: identical readings including a closed day mean the log is not a record of anything, so nobody knows whether food has been held safely. Having no authority is a reason to tell someone who has, not to say nothing. C: Treats a safety failure as a paperwork fix: recording properly from now on corrects the form and leaves two weeks in which nobody knows whether the fridges held temperature, with that food still in them. D: Delays the decision: the evidence is captured and the food is still being served. A report next week arrives long after the fortnight it describes. The most effective response is to raise it with the branch manager, ask him to check the fridges now, and ring your area manager today: identical readings across a fortnight including a day the branch was shut mean the log records nothing, so nobody knows whether the fridges have held temperature, and food is being served now. Getting the fridges checked today and telling the area manager addresses both the immediate risk and the recording failure. It beats suggesting he starts recording the readings properly from now on, because that leaves the last two weeks, and the food from them, entirely unexamined. It beats photographing the log for your visit report next week, because that is far too slow for a live food safety question. The least effective response is saying nothing because you have no authority at this branch: it leaves an unreliable food safety record and possibly mishandled food untouched, on grounds that are precisely why it should go to someone who does have authority. That is worse than the other two, which act too slowly but do act. The principle: when a control turns out not to be working, get the immediate check done and tell the person with authority the same day.
tip: Mẹo MT: Nhận diện ý chính của từng đoạn bằng câu chủ đề (thường nằm ở đầu hoặc cuối đoạn).

question_text: You are a marketing graduate at Hilton. A launch pack cannot go out until the legal team’s sign-off is recorded in the tracker. The lawyer who reviewed it told you verbally on Friday that she was happy with it, but she is away this week and has not sent the written confirmation. The pack has to go to the printers this afternoon, and your manager is chasing you for the tracker to be updated. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Record the sign-off as received in the tracker so the pack can go this afternoon, and chase the written confirmation from her when she is back next week.
Hold the pack until she is back next week and can send the confirmation herself, and tell the printers that this afternoon's slot will not be used after all.
Ask your manager to make the call on whether her verbal agreement is enough, and update the tracker to whatever he decides this afternoon.
Tell your manager the written sign-off has not arrived, ask the legal team whether a colleague can confirm it today, and leave the tracker as it is until one of them does.
explanation: A: Enters something in a record that has not happened: the tracker is the only evidence anybody downstream has, and it is being made to say the opposite of the truth. B: Treats the deadline as the only thing that can move: a week is lost without anybody asking whether another lawyer could confirm what she said on Friday. C: Passes a recording decision upwards to have it made quickly: he can decide about the pack, and the tracker still has to say what actually happened. The most effective response is to tell your manager the written sign-off has not arrived, ask the legal team whether a colleague can confirm it today, and leave the tracker until one of them does: the deadline is attacked in the only way that keeps the record honest, and everybody making decisions this afternoon knows exactly where things stand. It beats holding the pack until next week, because nobody has asked whether another lawyer can confirm what was said on Friday. It beats asking your manager to rule on whether a verbal agreement is enough, because the tracker still has to record what happened rather than what was decided about it. The least effective response is recording the sign-off as received: the tracker is the only evidence anybody downstream has, and making it say something that has not happened is a different kind of wrong from losing a week or from escalating a decision. The principle: a record says what happened, and a deadline is a reason to find another route, never to write one in.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc vàng True/False/Cannot Say: Chỉ dựa vào thông tin được cung cấp trong bài đọc, không suy đoán từ hiểu biết bên ngoài.
