question_text: You are a marketing graduate at Woolworths. A page that went live this morning carries a claim about delivery times that changed last month, so it is now wrong. Changes to live pages go through a release that runs each afternoon, requested by eleven o’clock. It is ten past eleven. You have the access to edit the page directly, and customers are reading it now. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Edit the live page yourself now, since you have the access, the claim is plainly wrong, and customers are reading it while a release process takes its course.
Put the correction into tomorrow's release and note the page as a known issue, since the deadline for today's release has already gone by ten minutes.
Ask the release team to take the page down until the correction can go through properly, so that customers see nothing rather than something untrue.
Ask the release team to take the correction into this afternoon's release despite the cut-off, explain what the claim says now, and tell your manager it is live.
explanation: A: Breaches the release process because the cause is good: an unreviewed change goes live outside the route that exists to stop unreviewed changes going live. B: Accepts a day of a wrong claim on a technicality: nobody has asked whether a correction ten minutes late can still make this afternoon. C: Removes more than the error: the whole page disappears for a day because one sentence about delivery times is out of date. The most effective response is to ask the release team to take the correction this afternoon despite the cut-off, explain what the claim currently says, and tell your manager: the fastest legitimate route is tried, the people who own the release decide, and the person accountable knows a wrong claim is live. It beats putting it in tomorrow’s release, because nobody has asked whether ten minutes late can still be accommodated. It beats taking the whole page down, because one sentence does not justify losing all of it. The least effective response is editing the live page yourself: an unreviewed change goes live outside the process whose entire purpose is to stop that, which is a different kind of wrong from being too accepting or from over-correcting. The principle: a good reason is exactly when a control gets tested, and the answer is to ask for an exception rather than take one.

explanation: False: the passage states the outer-district stations “were used less frequently than those in the centre”, which is the opposite of the statement. Cannot say is wrong because the passage gives a direct comparison of the two areas, so the statement can be decided against rather than left open.
tip: Mẹo MT: Cảnh giác với các từ chỉ mức độ tuyệt đối như 'luôn luôn', 'chắc chắn', 'duy nhất', 'tất cả'.

question_text:
【Ngữ cảnh】：After a successful first year, the operator of a city bicycle-hire scheme announced plans to expand it with additional docking stations. It said any expansion would depend on securing further funding, and that no work would begin until a full review of the first year had been completed and formally published for the council to consider. At the time of the announcement the operator has not confirmed where the new stations will be placed. Local groups in several districts, both central and outer, have asked for stations of their own, but the operator said it would decide the locations only after studying where demand across the city was strongest. No shortlist of possible sites has been published, and residents were told to expect further details later in the year.

【Câu hỏi】：The new docking stations added during the expansion will be placed in the outer districts.
options: True
False
Cannot say
explanation: Cannot say: the passage states the operator “has not confirmed where the new stations will be placed”, so their location is unknown. True is wrong because no location is asserted. False is wrong because the passage does not rule the outer districts out either; it leaves the placement undecided, which is the definition of cannot say.
tip: Mẹo MT: Nhận diện ý chính của từng đoạn bằng câu chủ đề (thường nằm ở đầu hoặc cuối đoạn).

question_text:
【Ngữ cảnh】：A publishing house studied the borrowing habits of subscribers to its digital library, drawing on records of every title borrowed over the course of a full year. It then grouped the results by category to see which kinds of book were the most popular among the many thousands of readers who used the service each month. The house found that among all subscribers, fiction was borrowed more often than non-fiction, a gap that held in every single month of the year studied. Within fiction, crime and romance titles were borrowed most, while among non-fiction, biographies and popular science led the way. The house said the findings would help it decide which categories to expand in the year ahead, while still offering a broad range of both.

【Câu hỏi】：Non-fiction was borrowed more often than fiction among the library’s subscribers.
options: True
False
Cannot say
explanation: False: the passage states that “among all subscribers, fiction was borrowed more often than non-fiction”, which is the reverse of the statement. True is wrong because it asserts the opposite of the text. Cannot say is wrong because the passage gives the direct comparison between fiction and non-fiction, so the reader can decide the statement rather than being left uncertain.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc vàng True/False/Cannot Say: Chỉ dựa vào thông tin được cung cấp trong bài đọc, không suy đoán từ hiểu biết bên ngoài.

question_text:
【Ngữ cảnh】：A publishing house examined how the device a subscriber used related to how much that person read on its digital library. It compared subscribers who mainly read on large tablets with those who mainly read on small-screen phones, looking closely at how many books each of the two groups managed to finish in a typical month. Subscribers who read on tablets finished, on average, more books each month than those who read on small-screen phones. The analysts suggested that the larger screen made longer reading sessions more comfortable, though they noted they had not tested that explanation directly. The house offers the same catalogue to every subscriber, so the difference could not be put down to some titles being unavailable on one type of device.

【Câu hỏi】：Subscribers who read on tablets finished more books per month, on average, than those who read on small-screen phones.
options: True
False
Cannot say
explanation: True: the passage states subscribers reading on tablets “finished, on average, more books each month than those who read on small-screen phones”. False is wrong because it denies a directly stated comparison. Cannot say is wrong because the averages are explicitly compared in the text, so the reader can decide it rather than treating it as unresolved.
tip: Mẹo MT: Đọc lướt câu hỏi trước khi đọc đoạn văn để định vị từ khóa (Keywords) nhanh hơn.

question_text:
【Ngữ cảnh】：A publishing house looked at whether a goal-setting feature in its reading app was linked to how much its subscribers used the library. Subscribers could choose to set themselves a monthly reading goal, and the house compared the borrowing of those who chose to set a goal with the borrowing of those who did not set one at all. Subscribers who set a monthly reading goal borrowed more titles than those who did not. However, the study did not measure whether borrowing more titles meant reading more of them, nor whether those who set goals actually met the targets they had chosen. The analysts cautioned that a borrowed title is not necessarily a finished one, and said a separate study would be needed to see how much of each book was actually read.

【Câu hỏi】：Subscribers who set a monthly reading goal read more books than those who did not set one.
options: True
False
Cannot say
explanation: Cannot say: the passage says goal-setters “borrowed more titles”, but adds the study “did not measure whether borrowing more titles meant reading more of them”, so reading more cannot be inferred. True is wrong because borrowing is not the same as reading, and the text blocks that leap. False is wrong because the passage does not state goal-setters read fewer or the same; reading was simply not measured.
tip: Mẹo MT: Cảnh giác với các từ chỉ mức độ tuyệt đối như 'luôn luôn', 'chắc chắn', 'duy nhất', 'tất cả'.

question_text: You are a site reliability assistant. A customer’s overnight job has failed and the ticket has come to you because your name is on a runbook you wrote a year ago. The job belongs to the data team. You have an incident summary due at four. Reading the ticket and either fixing it or telling the data team what the runbook covers would take twenty minutes. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Reply on the ticket that the runbook is out of date and that the data team owns the job now, then get back to writing the incident summary.
Spend twenty minutes now reading it and either fix it or tell the data team what the runbook actually covers, so that the customer's job runs tonight.
Pass the ticket to the data team without reading it and get back to the summary. The job is theirs, and the runbook was written a year ago.
Read the ticket, add what you know to it, and leave it assigned to yourself until after four so that the summary is not interrupted.
explanation: A: Corrects the record and leaves the job failed: the ownership note is accurate, and the customer's overnight run is exactly where it was. C: Passes the problem on without owning it: they receive a failed job with none of the context that only the runbook's author has. D: Holds a ticket you have already understood: the context is captured and the customer waits until after four for something you could have said at once. The most effective response is to spend twenty minutes now reading it and either fix it or tell the data team what the runbook actually covers. Twenty minutes is affordable against a four o’clock deadline, and you are the only person who knows what that runbook does and does not cover. It beats replying on the ticket that the runbook is out of date and the data team owns the job now, because a note about ownership does not make the overnight job run. It beats reading the ticket, adding what you know and holding it until after four, because once you know the answer, sitting on it costs the customer a night. The least effective response is passing the ticket to the data team without reading it: it is worse than either of the other two, because both add something they could use, while this forwards a failed job with none of the context only you hold. The principle: when you are the person who knows what a document means, twenty minutes of yours is cheaper than anybody else’s hour.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc vàng True/False/Cannot Say: Chỉ dựa vào thông tin được cung cấp trong bài đọc, không suy đoán từ hiểu biết bên ngoài.

question_text: You are an area support assistant for a restaurant chain, visiting a branch to help with stock counts. In the kitchen you notice the fridge temperature log has identical readings written in for the past two weeks, including for a day the branch was closed. Food safety is not your role and you have no authority here. The branch manager is on site. Your area manager is contactable by phone. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective? (Biến thể ôn tập #1)
options: Say nothing, since food safety is not your role, you have no authority at this branch, and the branch manager will have his own reasons for how the log is kept.
Raise it with the branch manager, ask him to check the fridges now, and ring your area manager today because the log for two weeks cannot be relied on.
Mention it to the branch manager and suggest he starts recording the readings properly from now on, then get on with the stock count you came to do.
Photograph the log and include it in your visit report, so that the area manager sees the evidence when the report is circulated next week.
explanation: A: Fails to escalate a genuine risk: identical readings including a closed day mean the log is not a record of anything, so nobody knows whether food has been held safely. Having no authority is a reason to tell someone who has, not to say nothing. C: Treats a safety failure as a paperwork fix: recording properly from now on corrects the form and leaves two weeks in which nobody knows whether the fridges held temperature, with that food still in them. D: Delays the decision: the evidence is captured and the food is still being served. A report next week arrives long after the fortnight it describes. The most effective response is to raise it with the branch manager, ask him to check the fridges now, and ring your area manager today: identical readings across a fortnight including a day the branch was shut mean the log records nothing, so nobody knows whether the fridges have held temperature, and food is being served now. Getting the fridges checked today and telling the area manager addresses both the immediate risk and the recording failure. It beats suggesting he starts recording the readings properly from now on, because that leaves the last two weeks, and the food from them, entirely unexamined. It beats photographing the log for your visit report next week, because that is far too slow for a live food safety question. The least effective response is saying nothing because you have no authority at this branch: it leaves an unreliable food safety record and possibly mishandled food untouched, on grounds that are precisely why it should go to someone who does have authority. That is worse than the other two, which act too slowly but do act. The principle: when a control turns out not to be working, get the immediate check done and tell the person with authority the same day.
tip: Mẹo MT: Nhận diện ý chính của từng đoạn bằng câu chủ đề (thường nằm ở đầu hoặc cuối đoạn).

question_text: You are a process operator at a waste water treatment works. Passing a monitoring screen that is not part of your round, you notice the outflow ammonia reading has been climbing steadily for three days and is close to the permitted limit. Exceeding it is reportable to the environmental regulator. The operator responsible is on leave. Your works manager is on site. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective? (Biến thể ôn tập #2)
options: Adjust the aeration settings yourself to bring the ammonia down, since the trend is clear and the limit is close.
Take the three-day trend to your works manager now, show him the readings and how close they are to the limit, and let him decide what to do.
Record the trend in the shift log so the operator responsible picks it up when he returns from leave next week.
Leave it, since the screen is not on your round, the reading is still inside the permitted limit and the plant's alarms would trigger if it went over.
explanation: A: Acts outside own authority: changing process settings on a plant running near a permitted limit can drive the reading the wrong way, and the works manager has not been told the trend exists. C: Delays the decision: the log reaches the right person on the wrong day. The reading is close to a reportable limit now, and next week is after any breach would have happened. D: Fails to escalate a genuine risk: a three-day climb towards a reportable limit is exactly the signal that precedes a breach, and relying on the alarm means acting only once the limit has already been exceeded. The most effective response is to take the three-day trend to your works manager now, show him the readings and how close they are to the limit, and let him decide: a steady climb towards a reportable limit is a developing breach rather than a stable reading, you are the only person who has noticed with the responsible operator away, and he can act today. It beats adjusting the aeration settings yourself to bring the ammonia down, because that is a process decision beyond your authority on a plant running close to a limit, and could make the reading worse. It beats recording the trend in the shift log for the operator returning next week, because that arrives after the breach it should have prevented. The least effective response is leaving it because the reading is still inside the permitted limit and the alarms would trigger: it waits for an alarm that by definition sounds only once the limit has been exceeded and the breach is already reportable. That is worse than the other two, which act wrongly or slowly but do act. The principle: a trend towards a limit is information somebody needs before the limit is reached, so take it to whoever can act while it is still preventable.
tip: Mẹo MT: Cảnh giác với các từ chỉ mức độ tuyệt đối như 'luôn luôn', 'chắc chắn', 'duy nhất', 'tất cả'.

question_text:
【Ngữ cảnh】：Skelwith Group declared a final dividend of 7.4 pence a share, taking the total for the year to 11.2 pence. The results say the dividend is covered twice by earnings and that the board intends to keep cover at about that level. They give free cash flow of £74 million and note that the group bought back no shares during the year. Skelwith has paid a final dividend in each of the last twelve years.

【Câu hỏi】：Based only on the information in the passage, is the following statement True, False, or Cannot say? Statement: “The group’s final dividend is 7.4 pence a share.” (Biến thể ôn tập #3)
options: True
False
Cannot say
explanation: The statement is True. The passage says Skelwith “declared a final dividend of 7.4 pence a share”, which is the statement. The rule: where the passage states the claim, the answer is True. The most tempting wrong answer is False, from reading the 11.2 pence total for the year as the final dividend.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc vàng True/False/Cannot Say: Chỉ dựa vào thông tin được cung cấp trong bài đọc, không suy đoán từ hiểu biết bên ngoài.

question_text: Four meetings are held from Monday to Thursday, one per day. The budget meeting is before the hiring meeting. The safety meeting is on Wednesday. Which statement must be true? (Biến thể ôn tập #4)
options: The hiring meeting is on Thursday.
The budget meeting is on Monday.
The training meeting is after the safety meeting.
The budget meeting is not on Thursday.
explanation: The safety meeting takes Wednesday, leaving Monday, Tuesday and Thursday for the other three. Rule 1 puts the hiring meeting after the budget meeting, so the budget meeting cannot take the last day of the week. Nothing else is settled. The budget and hiring meetings take Monday and Tuesday, Monday and Thursday, or Tuesday and Thursday, with training taking whichever day is left, so the hiring meeting on Thursday, the budget meeting on Monday and training after safety each hold in some of those weeks and fail in others. The most tempting trap is the hiring meeting on Thursday, because Thursday is the obvious home for the later of a pair. Tuesday works too.
tip: Mẹo MT: Nhận diện ý chính của từng đoạn bằng câu chủ đề (thường nằm ở đầu hoặc cuối đoạn).

question_text:
【Ngữ cảnh】：Cooper’s Field is a development of eighteen houses on the site of a former dairy. Plot 14 has a garden of 210 square metres, and plot 15, on the corner, has a garden of 260 square metres. Plot 14 is the larger house, with four bedrooms against plot 15’s three. Gardens are turfed and fenced before completion, with a paved path to the rear gate. Both plots face the retained oak at the centre of the development, and both carry the same estate management charge for the shared landscaping.

【Câu hỏi】：Based only on the information in the passage, is the following statement True, False, or Cannot say? Statement: “Plot 14 at Cooper’s Field has a larger garden than plot 15.” (Biến thể ôn tập #5)
options: True
False
Cannot say
explanation: The statement is False. The passage says “plot 14 has a garden of 210 square metres, and plot 15, on the corner, has a garden of 260 square metres”. On the stated garden areas plot 14’s is smaller, so the claim is contradicted. The rule: comparing two stated figures on the same measure settles the claim either way. The most tempting wrong answer is True, from carrying the house-size comparison onto the gardens.
tip: Mẹo MT: Nhận diện ý chính của từng đoạn bằng câu chủ đề (thường nằm ở đầu hoặc cuối đoạn).

question_text: You are a check-in agent. A colleague applying for a role in another department asks you to write a short statement about how she handles difficult passengers. She is competent but that is the part of the job she finds hardest, and the statement she has drafted for you describes her as outstanding at it. She asks you to sign it as it stands. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective? (Biến thể ôn tập #6)
options: Tell her you cannot sign her draft as it stands, and offer to write something yourself covering what you can honestly say about her work.
Decline to sign it and leave it there, since a statement about somebody else's work is not something you should be drawn into either way.
Sign the draft as she has written it, since statements of this kind are always generous, everybody knows that, and it costs nothing to help a colleague.
Sign it with the wording softened enough that it is not quite untrue, so that she gets her statement without you saying anything you would have to defend.
explanation: B: Refuses without offering the alternative: she has real strengths you could describe, and a flat no leaves her with nothing and no idea why. C: Puts your name to a description you know to be wrong: whoever reads it relies on it precisely because it comes from somebody who has worked beside her. D: Writes to be defensible rather than accurate: the reader still takes it as a recommendation of the part she is weakest at, and the care has gone into wording rather than truth. The most effective response is to tell her you cannot sign her draft as it stands, and offer to write something yourself covering what you can honestly say: the draft says something you do not believe, and writing your own gives her a genuine statement from somebody who has seen her work. It beats declining to sign and leaving it there, because she has real strengths and a refusal with nothing after it helps neither of you. It beats signing it with the wording softened enough not to be quite untrue, because carefully worded ambiguity still leaves the reader believing what the draft claims. The least effective response is signing the draft as she has written it because statements of this kind are always generous: it endorses a description of a colleague you know to be wrong, for a reader relying on your having worked beside her. That is worse than the other two, which stop short of endorsing the claim outright. The principle: write what you can honestly say and offer that, rather than signing somebody else’s version or hiding behind wording.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc vàng True/False/Cannot Say: Chỉ dựa vào thông tin được cung cấp trong bài đọc, không suy đoán từ hiểu biết bên ngoài.

question_text: Which meter reading was transcribed incorrectly? (Biến thể ôn tập #7)
options: Meter M1
Meter M2
Meter M3
Meter M4
explanation: Meter M2 reads 18.35 but was logged as 183.5: the decimal point has moved one place to the right, multiplying the value by ten. The digits themselves are unchanged, which is what makes the slip easy to miss.
tip: Mẹo MT: Đọc lướt câu hỏi trước khi đọc đoạn văn để định vị từ khóa (Keywords) nhanh hơn.

question_text: Three colleagues each made one statement about who won an internal quiz. Ada said, “I did not win.” Ben said, “Ada won.” Cara said, “I did not win.” Exactly one of the three won, and exactly one of these three statements is true. Who won? (Biến thể ôn tập #8)
options: Cara
Ada
Ben
It cannot be determined.
explanation: Test each winner against the “exactly one true” rule. If Ada won, Ben’s statement and Cara’s are both true; if Ben won, Ada’s and Cara’s are both true; if Cara won, only Ada’s statement is true and the other two are false, which is exactly one, so Cara won. A winner of Ada or Ben each produces two true statements, breaking the rule. Concluding it cannot be determined misses that only one winner satisfies the count.
tip: Mẹo MT: Đọc lướt câu hỏi trước khi đọc đoạn văn để định vị từ khóa (Keywords) nhanh hơn.

question_text:
【Ngữ cảnh】：A software company decided to trial a four-day working week for six months. Under the trial, staff worked Monday to Thursday instead of the usual Monday to Friday, and the company asked employees to record how they felt at the end of each week so that it could judge the effect the shorter week was having on their wellbeing over time. Throughout the trial, staff were paid the same as before, on the condition that they completed the same amount of work as in a normal five-day week. The company was clear that no one’s salary would be cut simply because the working week was shorter, and that the trial was meant to test whether the same output could be achieved in fewer days without any loss of pay for the people taking part.

【Câu hỏi】：Employees were paid the same during the trial as they had been before it. (Biến thể ôn tập #9)
options: True
False
Cannot say
explanation: True: the passage states that under the trial staff “were paid the same as before”. False is wrong because nothing in the text says pay changed. Cannot say is wrong because the passage states the pay directly, so the reader can decide the statement from the text rather than being left uncertain about it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Đọc lướt câu hỏi trước khi đọc đoạn văn để định vị từ khóa (Keywords) nhanh hơn.

question_text:
【Ngữ cảnh】：During its trial of a four-day working week, a software company asked most of its staff to work Monday to Thursday and to take Fridays off. Some managers, however, were concerned that customers might struggle to reach the company at the very end of the week, when the offices would be much quieter than usual and most desks would be empty. To deal with this, the company arranged for a small team of its own staff to answer urgent messages on that day. This meant that while the great majority of employees were away on Fridays, the business was not left completely unstaffed. The company explained that keeping a few people available on Fridays was a deliberate part of the trial, so urgent customer needs could still be met each week.

【Câu hỏi】：No staff worked on Fridays during the trial. (Biến thể ôn tập #10)
options: True
False
Cannot say
explanation: False: the passage says the company “arranged for a small team of its own staff to answer urgent messages on that day”, meaning Friday, so some staff did work on Fridays. True is wrong because it takes the Monday-to-Thursday pattern at face value and overlooks that Friday team. Cannot say is wrong because the passage settles the point rather than leaving it open, so the statement can be judged false against the text.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc vàng True/False/Cannot Say: Chỉ dựa vào thông tin được cung cấp trong bài đọc, không suy đoán từ hiểu biết bên ngoài.

question_text:
【Ngữ cảnh】：When a software company trialled a four-day week, some managers were concerned that customers might find it harder to reach the company on Fridays, when most of the staff were away from the office. The company took the worry seriously and put a small team in place to handle any urgent messages that might arrive while the rest of the workforce was off. At the end of the trial, the company reviewed how the arrangement had worked from its own point of view, but it did not gather or publish any feedback from customers about their experience on Fridays. Whether customers had in fact found it harder to get in touch, or had noticed no difference at all, was not something the report recorded, and the company said such feedback would be considered separately.

【Câu hỏi】：Customers found it harder to reach the company on Fridays during the trial. (Biến thể ôn tập #11)
options: True
False
Cannot say
explanation: Cannot say: the passage reports only that some managers were “concerned that customers might find it harder” and that a team handled urgent messages; it never records what customers actually experienced. True is wrong because a concern that something might happen is not a statement that it did. False is wrong because the passage does not claim customers had no difficulty either; it simply leaves their experience unreported.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc vàng True/False/Cannot Say: Chỉ dựa vào thông tin được cung cấp trong bài đọc, không suy đoán từ hiểu biết bên ngoài.

question_text:
【Ngữ cảnh】：A delivery company installed self-service lockers outside shops in several neighbourhoods, so that customers could have parcels delivered to a locker instead of to their home. Each customer collects their parcel using a code that the company sends to their phone once the parcel has arrived and been placed inside the locker ready for them to pick up. The company reported that parcels sent to lockers were, on average, delivered a day faster than parcels sent to homes. This was because a driver could fill a single bank of lockers with many parcels in one stop, rather than driving to many separate home addresses. The time saved on the road, the company said, was passed on to customers as quicker delivery, and was a main reason it planned to expand the network.

【Câu hỏi】：Parcels sent to lockers were delivered faster on average than parcels sent to homes. (Biến thể ôn tập #12)
options: True
False
Cannot say
explanation: True: the passage states that parcels sent to lockers were “on average, delivered a day faster than parcels sent to homes”. False is wrong because the passage reports the lockers as faster, not slower. Cannot say is wrong because the comparison is stated directly, so the reader can decide it from the text rather than being left unsure.
tip: Mẹo MT: Cảnh giác với các từ chỉ mức độ tuyệt đối như 'luôn luôn', 'chắc chắn', 'duy nhất', 'tất cả'.

question_text:
【Ngữ cảnh】：A delivery company’s self-service lockers were designed to make collecting parcels far more convenient for its customers. When a parcel arrives at a locker, the customer is sent a code to their phone, which they then enter at the locker to open the correct compartment and take out their delivery whenever they happen to be passing by that particular location. The lockers were available at any hour, so customers did not need to be at home to receive a delivery, and could pick up a parcel early in the morning or late at night if that suited them. Because collection depends only on the code and not on the customer being at any particular address, someone could have a parcel delivered while they were at work and then collect it whenever it best suited them.

【Câu hỏi】：Customers must be at home to collect a parcel from a locker. (Biến thể ôn tập #13)
options: True
False
Cannot say
explanation: False: the passage says lockers were “available at any hour, so customers did not need to be at home to receive a delivery”, and parcels are collected using a code sent to the phone. True is wrong because it contradicts the passage’s stated point of a locker. Cannot say is wrong because the text settles the matter rather than leaving it open.
tip: Mẹo MT: Nhận diện ý chính của từng đoạn bằng câu chủ đề (thường nằm ở đầu hoặc cuối đoạn).

question_text:
【Ngữ cảnh】：A delivery company explained the rules that applied whenever a parcel was left sitting unclaimed in one of its self-service lockers. Customers are sent reminders to collect their items, and because the space inside the lockers is limited, uncollected parcels cannot be allowed to stay in them indefinitely and take up room that other deliveries would otherwise need. The company noted that a parcel left uncollected for more than five days was returned to the sender, but it did not say how often this happened. It gave no figure for the share of parcels that ended up uncollected, and did not indicate whether such returns were a common event or a rare one. The report therefore described what happened to an abandoned parcel without showing how frequently the situation actually arose.

【Câu hỏi】：Parcels left in lockers are returned to the sender frequently. (Biến thể ôn tập #14)
options: True
False
Cannot say
explanation: Cannot say: the passage states that a parcel uncollected for more than five days “was returned to the sender”, but adds that it “did not say how often this happened”, so the frequency is unknown. True is wrong because “frequently” claims a rate the passage never gives. False is wrong because the passage does not say returns are rare either; it simply does not report how often they occur.

question_text: All the items in the sale are discounted. Some discounted items are electrical goods. Which statement must be true? (Biến thể ôn tập #15)
options: Some sale items are electrical goods.
Some electrical goods are discounted.
All electrical goods are discounted.
All discounted items are in the sale.
explanation: “Some discounted items are electrical goods” can be turned around to “some electrical goods are discounted”. Concluding that some sale items are electrical goods is the undistributed-middle error, because the discounted electrical goods need not be the sale items. Concluding that all electrical goods are discounted turns a “some” into an “all”. Concluding that all discounted items are in the sale reverses “all sale items are discounted” into a converse that does not follow.

question_text: You are a research analyst at a consultancy, finishing a market study for a drinks producer, Highmoor Brewing. One of your findings says the client’s new range is unlikely to reach the volumes they have planned for it. Their insight manager asks you to soften that sentence before the report goes to their board, and says that if you do, he will ask for you by name on the next study. The report is due with the board on Monday. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective? (Biến thể ôn tập #16)
options: Make the change he wants in return for the favour he is offering, and put the softened sentence into the report that goes to the board on Monday.
Tell the insight manager the finding stays as it is, put what he asked for to the manager running the study today, and offer to add the client's own view.
Rewrite the sentence in gentler language while keeping the number in it, and send it back to him for his approval before anybody else in the team sees the finished report.
Leave the wording exactly as it stands and say nothing to anybody about what he offered, so that the finding reaches the board unchanged.
explanation: A: Takes a favour for changing a finding: the board reads a softer conclusion than the evidence supports, and what bought the change was something offered to you personally. C: Negotiates a finding with the person it is about: the wording is settled privately with the reader who wants it softened. D: Leaves an offer unreported: the finding survives, and the person who tried to trade for it is free to try the same thing on whoever comes next. The most effective response is to tell the insight manager the finding stays as it is and to put what he asked for to the manager running the study. The finding is what the client is paying for, the offer is something the manager running the study needs to know about, and adding the client’s own view is the honest way to give them a voice in the report. It beats leaving the wording as it stands and saying nothing about what he offered, because an offer like that needs to reach somebody, or it simply gets made again to whoever comes next. It beats rewriting the sentence in gentler language and sending it to him for approval, because letting the person a finding is about approve its wording quietly puts the evidence in their gift. The least effective response is making the change he wants in return for the favour he is offering: the other three all leave the board reading what the study found, whereas this one trades the wording of the evidence for something offered to you, which is a different kind of wrong from handling it clumsily. The principle: findings are not currency, and an offer attached to one is itself the thing to report.

question_text: You are a technical support adviser. A member of the public rings after reading about a problem at your company and asks whether her details were affected. The security team is still working on it and has published nothing. Nobody has told the support desk what to say, and yours is the first call of this kind. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective? (Biến thể ôn tập #17)
options: Tell her you are not allowed to comment and that she should watch the company's website for an announcement when one is published.
Take her details and promise that somebody from the security team will ring her back today with an answer about her own records specifically.
Tell her an investigation is running and nothing is ruled in or out, take her details, and tell your manager the desk needs a line, since more of these will come.
Tell her that her details are almost certainly fine, since nothing has been confirmed as taken and there is no point worrying somebody over a maybe.
explanation: A: Refuses a caller you could partly help: that an investigation is running is itself true and sayable, and she is left with nothing to do. B: Commits another team to a call they have not agreed to: the security team is mid-investigation and has no capacity to ring individual callers. D: Gives an assurance nobody has authorised: no one has established what was taken, and she will make decisions about her own accounts on your word. The most effective response is to tell her an investigation is running and nothing is ruled in or out, take her details, and tell your manager the desk needs a line. She gets the truthful state of play, her details are captured, and the fact that this is the first such call is something your manager needs because it will not be the last. It beats telling her you are not allowed to comment and that she should watch the website, because the existence of an investigation is safe to say and gives her something real. It beats promising that somebody from the security team will ring her back today, because they have not agreed to that and cannot mid- investigation. The least effective response is telling her that her details are almost certainly fine: it is worse than either of the other two, because both stop short of telling her anything untrue, while this reassures a member of the public about her own data on an investigation that has not concluded. The principle: give the honest state of play, capture the caller, and tell your own manager that a line is needed before the second call arrives.

question_text: You are a junior developer. Reading through tonight’s release you have noticed that a change renames a field that a report your colleague owns depends on. Her report runs every Tuesday morning and she is not working today. The release goes out at eight this evening. You may have misread it, and nobody has asked you to check anything. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective? (Biến thể ôn tập #18)
options: Email your colleague so that she sees it tomorrow morning, and leave the release alone, since she is the one who owns the report and should decide about it.
Leave it. You may have misread it, nobody asked you to check the release, and the person who owns the report is the one who should have spotted it.
Change the release yourself to keep the old field name alongside the new one, so that her report carries on working whichever way it turns out to be.
Raise it now with whoever is running tonight's release, say what you think you have seen and that you may have misread it, and let them decide before eight.
explanation: A: Sends a warning that arrives after the event: she reads it on Tuesday, by which time the release went out on Monday evening and her report has already run. B: Stays silent on something only you have seen: the release goes out at eight whether or not you misread it, and nobody else is looking at this at all. C: Acts on a reading you are not sure of: it edits somebody else's change on the evening it ships, on the strength of something you think you saw. The most effective response is to raise it now with whoever is running tonight’s release, say what you think you have seen and that you may have misread it. There are hours left, they can check it in minutes, and saying openly that you may be wrong costs nothing and lets them weigh it. It beats emailing your colleague so she sees it tomorrow morning, because that arrives after Monday evening’s release and after her report has run. It beats changing the release yourself to keep the old field name alongside the new one, because editing somebody else’s change on the evening it ships, on a reading you are unsure of, risks more than it protects. The least effective response is leaving it because you may have misread it and nobody asked you to check: it is worse than either of the other two, because both act on what you saw, while this leaves the only observation anybody has made unspoken until Tuesday. The principle: an uncertain observation with hours to spare goes to whoever can check it, and uncertainty is a thing to say aloud rather than a reason to stay quiet.

question_text: You are a process operator at a waste water treatment works. Passing a monitoring screen that is not part of your round, you notice the outflow ammonia reading has been climbing steadily for three days and is close to the permitted limit. Exceeding it is reportable to the environmental regulator. The operator responsible is on leave. Your works manager is on site. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective? (Biến thể ôn tập #19)
options: Adjust the aeration settings yourself to bring the ammonia down, since the trend is clear and the limit is close.
Take the three-day trend to your works manager now, show him the readings and how close they are to the limit, and let him decide what to do.
Record the trend in the shift log so the operator responsible picks it up when he returns from leave next week.
Leave it, since the screen is not on your round, the reading is still inside the permitted limit and the plant's alarms would trigger if it went over.
explanation: A: Acts outside own authority: changing process settings on a plant running near a permitted limit can drive the reading the wrong way, and the works manager has not been told the trend exists. C: Delays the decision: the log reaches the right person on the wrong day. The reading is close to a reportable limit now, and next week is after any breach would have happened. D: Fails to escalate a genuine risk: a three-day climb towards a reportable limit is exactly the signal that precedes a breach, and relying on the alarm means acting only once the limit has already been exceeded. The most effective response is to take the three-day trend to your works manager now, show him the readings and how close they are to the limit, and let him decide: a steady climb towards a reportable limit is a developing breach rather than a stable reading, you are the only person who has noticed with the responsible operator away, and he can act today. It beats adjusting the aeration settings yourself to bring the ammonia down, because that is a process decision beyond your authority on a plant running close to a limit, and could make the reading worse. It beats recording the trend in the shift log for the operator returning next week, because that arrives after the breach it should have prevented. The least effective response is leaving it because the reading is still inside the permitted limit and the alarms would trigger: it waits for an alarm that by definition sounds only once the limit has been exceeded and the breach is already reportable. That is worse than the other two, which act wrongly or slowly but do act. The principle: a trend towards a limit is information somebody needs before the limit is reached, so take it to whoever can act while it is still preventable.

question_text: You are an insight assistant at a retail chain. You are finishing a pack of customer survey results for a decision meeting on Thursday. One question in the survey went out to a much smaller group than the rest, so its result rests on about a fifth of the usual number of replies. The result is the most striking number in the pack, and nobody reading it would know how few replies sit behind it. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective? (Biến thể ôn tập #30)
options: Leave the striking result out of the pack altogether, since a number resting on a fifth of the usual replies is not solid enough to put in front of a decision meeting.
Include the result in the pack as it stands, without flagging that the sample behind it was a fifth of the size of the others.
Include the result with the number of replies shown next to it and a line saying what that means for how much weight it should carry.
Include the result as it stands and mention the small sample verbally if the question comes up while you are presenting the pack on Thursday.
explanation: A: Removes evidence rather than qualifying it: the meeting loses a real signal because it could not be given a sentence of context. B: Withholds the fact that decides how much weight the number carries: the most striking figure in the pack is the one nobody is told to treat carefully. D: Leaves a caveat to chance: the pack outlives the meeting and is read by people who were never in the room to hear the qualification. The most effective response is to include the result with the number of replies shown next to it and a line on what that means for its weight: the meeting gets the signal and the size of it, which is what lets people decide how far to lean on it. It beats leaving the result out, because a real finding is discarded when a sentence would have made it usable. It beats mentioning the small sample only if somebody asks, because the pack is read later by people who were never in the room. The least effective response is including the striking result without flagging the size of the sample behind it: the most eye-catching number in the pack is presented as though it were as solid as the rest, and the one person who knows otherwise says nothing, which is a different kind of wrong from being over-cautious or from relying on the meeting to ask. The principle: publish the caveat next to the number, in the document, where everybody who reads one reads the other.

question_text: You are a marketing graduate at a retail chain. A launch pack cannot go out until the legal team’s sign-off is recorded in the tracker. The lawyer who reviewed it told you verbally on Friday that she was happy with it, but she is away this week and has not sent the written confirmation. The pack has to go to the printers this afternoon, and your manager is chasing you for the tracker to be updated. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective? (Biến thể ôn tập #31)
options: Record the sign-off as received in the tracker so the pack can go this afternoon, and chase the written confirmation from her when she is back next week.
Hold the pack until she is back next week and can send the confirmation herself, and tell the printers that this afternoon's slot will not be used after all.
Ask your manager to make the call on whether her verbal agreement is enough, and update the tracker to whatever he decides this afternoon.
Tell your manager the written sign-off has not arrived, ask the legal team whether a colleague can confirm it today, and leave the tracker as it is until one of them does.
explanation: A: Enters something in a record that has not happened: the tracker is the only evidence anybody downstream has, and it is being made to say the opposite of the truth. B: Treats the deadline as the only thing that can move: a week is lost without anybody asking whether another lawyer could confirm what she said on Friday. C: Passes a recording decision upwards to have it made quickly: he can decide about the pack, and the tracker still has to say what actually happened. The most effective response is to tell your manager the written sign-off has not arrived, ask the legal team whether a colleague can confirm it today, and leave the tracker until one of them does: the deadline is attacked in the only way that keeps the record honest, and everybody making decisions this afternoon knows exactly where things stand. It beats holding the pack until next week, because nobody has asked whether another lawyer can confirm what was said on Friday. It beats asking your manager to rule on whether a verbal agreement is enough, because the tracker still has to record what happened rather than what was decided about it. The least effective response is recording the sign-off as received: the tracker is the only evidence anybody downstream has, and making it say something that has not happened is a different kind of wrong from losing a week or from escalating a decision. The principle: a record says what happened, and a deadline is a reason to find another route, never to write one in.

question_text: Four handovers run from Monday to Friday, one per day. Wednesday is left free. The handovers are Peebles, Roslin, Selkirk and Traquair. Traquair is on the calendar day immediately after Selkirk. Peebles is not on Tuesday. Which statement must be true? (Biến thể ôn tập #32)
options: Peebles is on Monday or on Friday.
Selkirk is on Monday or on Thursday.
Roslin is on Tuesday.
Peebles is earlier in the week than Roslin.
explanation: Wednesday is free, so the handovers use Monday, Tuesday, Thursday and Friday. Rule 1 needs Selkirk and Traquair on consecutive days, and the only consecutive pairs left are Monday with Tuesday and Thursday with Friday. Selkirk takes the earlier day of whichever pair is used, so Selkirk is on Monday or on Thursday. Everything else stays open. With the pair on Monday and Tuesday, Peebles and Roslin split Thursday and Friday either way; with the pair on Thursday and Friday, rule 2 keeps Peebles off Tuesday, so Peebles takes Monday and Roslin Tuesday. That is three permitted weeks, and Peebles on Monday or on Friday, Roslin on Tuesday, and Peebles earlier in the week than Roslin each fail in at least one. The move that matters is that a free Wednesday breaks the week into two blocks of two.

question_text: You work in an airline contact centre. Storms have cancelled dozens of flights and you have handled distressed calls for three hours. A passenger tells you that you sound like you are reading from a script and that you clearly do not care that his family are stranded abroad. Rebooking options are limited but some exist. Your team leader is available. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective? (Biến thể ôn tập #33)
options: Explain that the cancellations are weather-related, that you have been helping stranded passengers all morning and that you are doing your best for everyone.
Acknowledge that his family being stranded is what matters, tell him the rebooking options that do exist, and start on whichever one he chooses.
Tell him the options are extremely limited because of the weather and that there is very little the airline can do until the backlog clears.
Apologise and offer to pass him to your team leader, since he is unhappy with how the call is going and may prefer to deal with someone senior.
explanation: A: Personalises the conflict: it answers his criticism of you rather than the problem of his family being stranded, which invites him to argue about your manner instead of his booking. C: Ignores the customer's actual need: it presents the situation as hopeless when rebooking options do exist, so a passenger with a stranded family is given despair instead of the seats that are actually available. D: Passes responsibility to others: it hands off a rebooking you can do and makes a passenger with a stranded family queue again for a supervisor during the busiest hours. The most effective response is to acknowledge that his family being stranded is what matters, tell him the rebooking options that do exist, and start on whichever he chooses: some options exist, and moving straight to them answers the substance without engaging the criticism of your manner. It beats explaining that the cancellations are weather-related and that you have been helping stranded passengers all morning, because defending yourself spends the call on your performance rather than on his family. It beats offering to pass him to your team leader, because that makes him wait again for something you can do now. The least effective response is telling him the options are extremely limited and there is very little the airline can do: it says nothing can be done when options do exist, so a passenger who could have been rebooked is left believing he is stuck. That is worse than explaining the weather, which at least explains, and worse than passing him on, which at least routes him to someone. The principle: when someone criticises you under pressure, put the available options in front of them and let the criticism go unanswered.

question_text: You work in a delivery-only kitchen. Checking the walk-in fridge you find the temperature gauge reading well above the safe limit and the log shows it was last checked twelve hours ago. There is a large quantity of prepared food inside. Orders start in an hour. Your head chef is on site and the food safety procedure requires temperature failures to be reported to him. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective? (Biến thể ôn tập #34)
options: Stop the food being used, tell the head chef now that the fridge is above the safe limit and was last checked twelve hours ago, and let him decide what happens to it.
Use the food for tonight's orders since it is still cold to the touch and the gauge may well be faulty, and report the fridge for repair tomorrow.
Move the prepared food to another fridge so it starts cooling again, and tell the head chef once the transfer is done.
Check the temperature again with a probe thermometer to confirm the gauge is accurate before raising it, so the head chef is not called over a faulty gauge.
explanation: B: Serves food of unknown safety: a fridge above the safe limit for an unknown period is exactly the situation the temperature control exists to catch, and judging it by touch puts customers at risk. That is a safety failure, not a judgement about waste. C: Acts on assumptions without checking: moving the food cools it and tells nobody how long it was warm, which is the fact that decides whether it can be used at all. D: Delays the decision: verifying the gauge is sensible and takes time the head chef could direct in a moment, with service starting in an hour and food that may already be unsafe. The most effective response is to stop the food being used and tell the head chef now that the fridge is above the safe limit and was last checked twelve hours ago: prepared food may have been warm for up to twelve hours, that decision is his under the food safety procedure, and he is on site with an hour before service. Stopping its use first is what makes the decision possible. It beats moving the prepared food to another fridge and telling him once the transfer is done, because cooling it destroys the evidence of how long it was warm, which is the fact the judgement rests on. It beats checking again with a probe thermometer before raising it, because confirming the gauge is work he can direct in seconds, and the clock is running. The least effective response is using the food for tonight’s orders because it is still cold to the touch: it serves food of unknown temperature history to customers on the basis of how it feels. That is worse than the other two, which act imperfectly but do not serve it. The principle: when a safety control has failed, stop the product and get the decision to the person the procedure names, without disturbing the evidence.
tip: Mẹo MT: Quy tắc vàng True/False/Cannot Say: Chỉ dựa vào thông tin được cung cấp trong bài đọc, không suy đoán từ hiểu biết bên ngoài.

question_text: You are a quality assistant at a food manufacturer. Routine testing shows a batch of sauce with a slightly higher salt reading than the declared label value, above the tolerance in your own specification but not a safety issue. The batch is due to leave for a supermarket customer this afternoon. Your quality manager is at another site but reachable by phone. The production supervisor tells you it is within normal variation. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective? (Biến thể ôn tập #35)
options: Put the batch on hold, ring the quality manager with the reading and the specification tolerance, and let her decide whether it ships this afternoon.
Accept the production supervisor's view that it is within normal variation, let the batch go, and say nothing further since it is not a safety concern.
Retest the batch yourself to confirm the reading before involving anyone, since a single result outside tolerance may simply be a testing error.
Release the batch and note the reading in the quality log, so that the trend is recorded and can be reviewed at the next specification meeting.
explanation: B: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholder's: the specification tolerance is the customer's and the label is a declaration to consumers, so neither the supervisor nor you can decide it is close enough. Letting it go unrecorded is the one option that leaves nobody aware at all. C: Delays the decision: a retest is sensible and the batch is loading this afternoon. Confirming the number before telling anyone spends the decision window on work the quality manager could have directed in a minute. D: Fails to escalate a genuine risk: it ships a batch that misses the declared label value and records the fact afterwards. A log entry documents the decision without anyone having made one. The most effective response is to put the batch on hold and ring the quality manager with the reading and the tolerance: the result is outside your own specification, the label is a declaration to consumers, and she owns that judgement and is a phone call away with the batch still on site. Holding it costs an afternoon; shipping it wrongly cannot be undone. It beats retesting the batch yourself before involving anyone, because that is reasonable work in the wrong order: she can direct a retest in a minute, and the batch is loading. It beats releasing the batch and noting the reading in the quality log, because that records a decision nobody actually took. The least effective response is accepting the production supervisor’s view that it is within normal variation and letting the batch go: it accepts a production judgement about a quality specification, ships against a declared label value, and leaves no record and no one informed. That is worse than retesting, which delays but checks, and worse than logging it, which at least documents it. The principle: when a result falls outside a specification you do not own, stop the goods and get the decision to whoever owns it, while stopping is still possible.
tip: Mẹo MT: Nhận diện ý chính của từng đoạn bằng câu chủ đề (thường nằm ở đầu hoặc cuối đoạn).

question_text: Based only on the Kestrel Logistics data shown, is the following statement True, False, or Cannot say? Statement: “Kestrel Logistics averaged 100,000 deliveries per depot in 2022.” (Biến thể ôn tập #47)

question_text: You are an administrator at an occupational health clinic. At 2pm three things need you. A manager is waiting on a fitness-for-work report needed for a return-to-work meeting at 3pm, which takes twenty minutes to prepare. A nurse has asked you to book six routine health surveillance appointments this week. And your manager wants the quarterly activity figures by 5pm, taking an hour. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Send the manager the previous fitness-for-work report on file so the 3pm meeting has something to work from, and prepare the current one afterwards.
Book the six surveillance appointments first since they are quick and the nurse is waiting on them, then do the report and the quarterly figures.
Prepare the fitness-for-work report for the 3pm meeting, then do the quarterly figures before 5pm, and book the surveillance appointments afterwards or tomorrow.
Start the quarterly figures since they are the longest job and are due at 5pm, and fit the report and the bookings around them during the afternoon.
explanation: A: Supplies a document known to be out of date: a return-to-work meeting decided on a superseded fitness assessment risks an employee being put back to work on the wrong basis, which is a clinical harm rather than a scheduling error. B: Splits effort so nothing finishes: six bookings ahead of a twenty- minute report leaves a return-to-work meeting at 3pm relying on whatever time is left, for appointments that have all week. D: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholder's: an hour of internal reporting with three hours of room is put ahead of a report an employee's return-to-work meeting depends on in one hour. The most effective response is to prepare the fitness-for-work report for the 3pm meeting, then do the quarterly figures before 5pm, and book the surveillance appointments afterwards: the meeting is fixed and depends on a twenty-minute report, the figures have three hours for an hour of work, and the bookings have the week. Everything fits if the fixed appointment goes first. It beats booking the six surveillance appointments first because they are quick and the nurse is waiting, since six bookings with a week of slack should not precede a report a meeting depends on in an hour. It beats starting the quarterly figures as the longest job due at 5pm, because that leaves the one immovable deadline dependent on what is left over. The least effective response is sending the previous fitness-for- work report from the file so the meeting has something: it supplies a superseded assessment for a live return-to-work decision, risking an employee being returned on the wrong medical basis. That is worse than the other two, which sequence badly but produce the correct document. The principle: do the short task the fixed meeting depends on first, and never substitute an out-of-date document for a current one.
tip: Mẹo MT: Loại trừ nhanh các phương án vi phạm quy tắc xoay góc chiều kim đồng hồ.

question_text: You work in an HR shared service team. It is Wednesday. Three things are outstanding: a new starter’s contract must go out today or she cannot begin on Monday, a manager wants a report on absence figures by Friday, and a colleague has asked you to review her draft policy whenever you have time. The contract takes an hour, the report three hours. You have five hours left today. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Work through all three in the order they were asked for, and let your manager know at the end of the day if anything has not been finished.
Start the absence report because it is the longest job, then do the contract at the end of the day once the bulk of the report is behind you.
Do the contract and the policy review first because they are the two shorter jobs, then start the absence report and continue it tomorrow morning.
Send the new starter's contract first, then work on the absence report, and tell your colleague you will review her policy tomorrow.
explanation: A: Hides the problem / silent deadline slip: the contract is the one item that cannot slip, and reporting at the end of the day is after the point at which anyone could rescue it. Reporting a missed deadline once it is missed is not communication. B: Delays the decision: it leaves an hour-long task with a today-or- never deadline to the end of a five-hour day, so any overrun on the report costs the new starter her start date. C: Splits effort so nothing finishes: it fits the favour in ahead of a report with a named Friday deadline, and pushes three hours of work into a day that already has other demands. The most effective response is to send the new starter’s contract first, then work on the absence report, and tell your colleague the policy review waits until tomorrow: only the contract has a deadline of today with a consequence attached, a start date, and it takes one of the five hours available. That leaves four hours for a three-hour report due Friday, and the policy review has no deadline at all. It beats starting the absence report first because it is the longest job, since that puts a fixed, unrecoverable deadline behind an open-ended one. It beats doing the contract and the policy review first as the two shorter jobs, because that fits an unscheduled favour ahead of a report with a stated deadline. The least effective response is working through all three in the order they were asked for and reporting at the end of the day: it works to the order things were asked in rather than to their deadlines, and reports the failure only once the new starter’s Monday cannot be saved. That is worse than the other two, which sequence badly but at least do the contract today. The principle: identify the task that cannot slip, do it first, and say early which of the others will move.
tip: Mẹo MT: Đếm số lượng đỉnh hoặc số lượng góc nhọn khi các hình có hình dạng biến thiên phức tạp.

question_text: You are a resourcing coordinator at a recruitment agency. A candidate you placed in a temporary warehouse role two weeks ago rings to say his shifts have been changed to nights without notice and he cannot do them because of childcare. Your agency’s contract with the client says shift patterns are agreed in advance. Your account manager, who owns the client relationship, is in a pitch until 4pm. The candidate is due on a night shift this evening. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Get the details from the candidate, check the agreed pattern on the contract file, and put the facts to your account manager before 4pm so she can raise it with the client before tonight's shift.
Tell the candidate that shift changes are between him and the site supervisor and that he should raise it there, since the agency only placed him and does not run the client's rotas.
Ring the client's site supervisor yourself, point out that the contract requires shift patterns to be agreed in advance, and ask for the candidate to be put back on days from tonight.
Tell the candidate not to attend tonight's night shift, since the change breaches the agreed pattern, and confirm to him that the agency will sort it out with the client afterwards.
explanation: B: Passes responsibility to others: the agreed pattern is in your agency's own contract, so this is exactly the agency's business. Sending a temporary worker to argue it alone with the site abandons the person you placed. C: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholder's: your account manager owns this relationship and a contractual challenge to the client is hers to frame. Making it yourself commits the agency to a position she has not seen. D: Acts on assumptions without checking: it tells a worker to miss a shift before anyone has confirmed the pattern or spoken to the client, which risks his placement on a reading of the contract nobody senior has looked at. The most effective response is to get the details, check the agreed pattern on the contract file, and put the facts to your account manager before 4pm: this is a contractual point the agency owns, it needs the person who owns the client relationship, and there is time to reach her before the shift. Gathering the facts first means she can act rather than investigate. It beats ringing the client’s site supervisor yourself, because a challenge to a client about their contract is the account manager’s to make, and pre-empting it commits the agency to a position she has not agreed. It beats telling the candidate not to attend tonight, because that risks his placement on your reading of a contract, before anyone has checked the agreed pattern or spoken to the client. The least effective response is telling him shift changes are between him and the site supervisor: it is the only response that denies the agency has any part in this, when the agreed pattern sits in the agency’s own contract, and it leaves a temporary worker to argue his own case against the site. That is worse than the other two, which are both wrong about who acts, but at least act. The principle: when something is genuinely yours to own, take it to the person who owns the relationship, with the facts, in time for them to use them.
tip: Mẹo MT: Đếm số lượng đỉnh hoặc số lượng góc nhọn khi các hình có hình dạng biến thiên phức tạp.

question_text: You are a management accounts assistant. Every month you rekey the same figures between two systems, which takes half a day and causes errors. You could write a small spreadsheet tool that does it automatically. Tools that move data between these systems have to be registered and reviewed by the systems team first. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Build a prototype, show your manager the half-day saving, and ask them to put it to the systems team for registration before anybody uses it for real.
Ask the systems team to build the tool themselves, since they own the registration process and will know how it should be done.
Carry on rekeying each month and raise the idea at the next systems team forum in three months, when there is a proper slot for suggestions like this one.
Build the tool and start using it for this month's close, and register it with the systems team afterwards once it has proved that it works properly.
explanation: B: Hands away the part you are best placed to do: you know the process and the failure modes, and their queue is long. C: Delays the decision for a quarter: three more months of half-days and known errors, to wait for a meeting. The most effective response is to build a prototype, show your manager the half-day saving, and ask him to put it to the systems team for registration before anybody uses it for real: the prototype makes the case concrete, he owns the priority, and registration happens before anything real depends on it. question_text: You are a compliance assistant. Your team reports each month how many new files had their checks completed before work started. One of this month’s files had its check completed the day after work began, because the fee earner was told the wrong thing by somebody else. Your team leader asks for the figures. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Record the check as completed before work started, since the check was done and the reason it was a day late had nothing to do with the fee earner or with the compliance team.
Give her the figure with the exception shown, and leave the explanation to whoever asks about it, since the numbers are what the report is for.
Give her the figure with the exception shown and a line explaining that the fee earner was given wrong information, so the report carries the cause as well as the count.
Ask her whether the one late file needs to be in the figures at all, given that it was caused by something outside the process the report is meant to measure.
explanation: A: Marks a file as compliant when it was not: the whole point of the figure is that it counts checks done before work began, and a file recorded as fine removes the only trace of what went wrong. B: Reports the number without its cause: the exception will be read as a fee earner ignoring a check, and the thing that actually needs fixing is somebody giving out wrong information. D: Invites the data to be trimmed: the report measures whether checks were done before work started, and this one was not, whatever the reason. The most effective response is to give her the figure with the exception shown and a line explaining that the fee earner was given wrong information. The figure is what it is, and the one line is what turns an apparent breach into something the firm can act on. It beats giving her the figure with the exception shown and leaving the explanation to whoever asks, because an unexplained exception will be read as the wrong kind of failure. It beats asking whether the one late file needs to be in the figures at all, because the measure is about what happened, not about whose fault it was. The least effective response is recording the check as completed before work started: it records the file as compliant when it was not, which is a different kind of wrong from the other two because both of those leave the exception visible. The principle: report the exception and its cause together, and never make the record say the exception did not happen.

question_text: You are a new enquiries adviser. A colleague on the same desk has twice taken enquiries that were passed to you while you were on another call, and both became instructions credited to him. He says he was only keeping the callers from waiting. The team’s figures are reviewed monthly. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Speak to him directly, say what you have noticed on both occasions, and agree between you what should happen to a transferred enquiry when the person it was passed to is busy.
Ask two others on the desk, behind his back, whether he has done the same to them, so that you know whether this is a pattern before you decide what to do about it.
Let it go on the basis that his explanation is reasonable, and make a point of getting to transferred calls faster yourself so that the situation does not come up again.
Raise it with your team leader before the monthly review and ask her to look at how the two enquiries were credited, given what was happening when each of them came in.
explanation: B: Canvasses colleagues behind his back: it collects a view of a person from people who were not involved, so by the time he is asked anything the desk has already made up its mind about him. C: Prioritises harmony over honesty: it accepts an explanation without testing it and puts the whole remedy on you, so the same thing happens the next time you are on a long call. D: Escalates before speaking to him: it turns a two-person question into a management one without him ever being asked, and does so shortly before the figures that make it worth something to you. The most effective response is to speak to him directly, say what you noticed on both occasions, and agree what should happen to a transferred enquiry when the person it went to is busy. There is a real question about transferred enquiries and a real question about credit, and both are answerable in one conversation. It beats letting it go and getting to transferred calls faster yourself, because his explanation has not been tested and the remedy it accepts is entirely yours. It beats raising it with your team leader before the monthly review, because a manager is the right destination only once he has been asked. The least effective response is asking two others on the desk whether he has done the same to them: it gathers opinion about him from people with no part in it, so the desk forms a view before he has said a word. That is a different kind of wrong from the other two, neither of which involves anybody who was not already in the situation. The principle: ask the person first, and never build a case about them among people who were not there.

question_text: You are a paralegal. You have been asked to complete two schedules by five today. At two you realise the second one needs a figure from the client, who does not usually reply the same day. The fee earner who asked for them is in the building. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Finish both schedules using an estimate for the missing figure, and mark that figure clearly as provisional until the client confirms it.
Email the client asking for the figure, finish the first schedule, and let the fee earner find out at five which of the two is ready and which is not.
Ring the client repeatedly through the afternoon until you get the figure, leaving the first schedule until you have it so that both can be finished together.
Email the client, finish the first schedule, and tell the fee earner now that the second depends on a reply that may not come today.
explanation: A: Fills a gap with a number nobody gave you: a schedule containing an estimate is not the schedule that was asked for, and a provisional marking is easy to lose once it is passed on. B: Leaves somebody to discover it at the deadline: he is in the building all afternoon, and at five the options he had at two, including asking the client himself, have all gone. C: Stakes everything on the uncertain half: the schedule you could certainly deliver is put at risk for one that depends on somebody who may not answer today. The most effective response is to email the client, finish the first schedule, and tell the fee earner now that the second depends on a reply that may not come today. Everything you can do is done, the client is asked, and he learns at two rather than five, when he can still chase them himself. It beats finishing both schedules using an estimate for the missing figure, because an estimated figure is not the figure. It beats ringing the client repeatedly and leaving the first schedule until you have the number, because that risks the one that was certain. The least effective response is emailing the client, finishing the first schedule, and letting him find out at five: it produces the same work as the best answer and tells him nothing, so he discovers it when nothing can be done. That is a different kind of wrong from the other two, both of which at least leave him with something at five. The principle: when a commitment starts to depend on somebody else, say so while there is still afternoon left.
