question_text: You are a trading assistant at a large consumer business. A figure you produced for a weekly pack rests on an assumption about supplier lead times that changed on Friday. With the new lead times the figure would be materially different. The pack goes to a manager this afternoon and the meeting that uses it is tomorrow. Reworking the figure properly takes half a day, which you do not have. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Rework the figure quickly this afternoon with an estimate of the new lead times, and put the estimated version in the pack instead of the one you can support.
Put the figure in the pack as it stands, without flagging that the lead times behind it changed on Friday, since the rework cannot be done before this afternoon in any case.
Put the figure in with a clear note that the lead times changed on Friday and what that does to it, and tell the manager before the pack goes out so nothing surprises him.
Leave the figure out of the pack altogether and explain in its place that the number is being reworked after a change to supplier lead times.
explanation: A: Substitutes a guess for a stale fact: neither number has been checked, and the estimate carries none of the working the original at least had. B: Withholds the fact that decides what the number is worth: tomorrow's meeting uses a figure whose basis is known to be out of date by the only person who knows it. D: Removes the evidence rather than qualifying it: tomorrow's meeting loses a usable number and gains nothing it can decide with. The most effective response is to put the figure in with a clear note on the lead time change and what it is likely to do, and tell the manager before the pack goes out: the meeting keeps a number it can use, everybody knows what it rests on, and the manager can decide whether tomorrow needs the rework. It beats reworking it quickly on an estimate, because an unchecked guess replaces a number whose working at least exists. It beats leaving the figure out, because the meeting is then deciding with nothing. The least effective response is putting the figure in without flagging the lead time change: the only person who knows the basis has changed says nothing, and the meeting treats a stale figure as current, which is a different kind of wrong from guessing or from withdrawing the number. The principle: when you cannot fix a number in time, publish what is wrong with it to the person who is about to rely on it.

question_text: You are a trading assistant at a large consumer business. You and a colleague have built a set of figures for a business customer, she on the volumes and you on the pricing. Checking them this morning you found two of her assumptions were out of date and corrected them, which changes her volumes slightly. The figures go to the customer at noon and she is at a site until the afternoon. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Message her now with the two assumptions you changed and why, send the figures at noon, and go through it with her afterwards so that she is not asked about volumes blind.
Hold the figures until she is back and can look at the changes herself, and tell the customer they will arrive later this afternoon instead of at noon.
Send the figures at noon with her original assumptions left in, and tell the customer the volumes may be revised once she is back.
Send the corrected figures at noon without telling her that two of her assumptions were changed, since the correction is right and she will see the final version anyway.
explanation: B: Moves an external commitment for an internal check: the customer's deadline slips for two assumptions she can review just as well afterwards. C: Sends numbers you know are wrong with a caveat attached: the customer gets a figure the sender does not believe, and a promise of a possible revision. D: Withholds a change to a colleague's own work: she may be asked about volumes she did not produce, and the first she knows of it is when somebody queries them. The most effective response is to message her now with the two assumptions you changed and why, send at noon, and go through it when she is back: the customer gets accurate figures on time, and the person whose work was changed knows before anybody asks her about it. It beats holding the figures until the afternoon, because an external commitment is moved for a check that can happen afterwards. It beats sending her original assumptions untouched, because the customer then gets numbers you know to be out of date. The least effective response is sending the corrected figures without telling her: she may be questioned about volumes she did not produce and finds out from the query, which is a different kind of wrong from being over-cautious or from being too deferential. The principle: correct the work when it is wrong, and tell the person whose name is on it before anybody else does.

question_text: You are a data quality assistant at a fire and rescue service. A colleague, Aled, has spent two days preparing a set of figures for a meeting on Thursday. This afternoon you learn that the meeting has been switched to a different set of records, so the figures Aled has prepared are no longer the ones anybody will look at. Aled is away until Wednesday and does not know. You have his mobile number, and the person organising the meeting sits near you. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Leave a note on Aled's desk explaining the switch and which records the meeting now wants, ready for his return on Wednesday, and get on with the new figures yourself meanwhile.
Ask the organiser to switch the meeting back to the original records so that Aled's two days are not wasted, and say nothing to Aled until you know whether that worked.
Ring Aled this afternoon so he knows before he spends more time on it, then check with the organiser which records the meeting now needs and start pulling those together.
Hand the problem straight to the person organising the meeting and ask them to break the news to Aled, since the change was theirs to make, then carry on with your own work.
explanation: A: Chooses the slowest channel: he is reachable this afternoon and the meeting is on Thursday, so a note found on Wednesday costs him a day he did not have to lose. B: Substitutes your own judgement for the organiser's: they changed the records for a reason you have not asked about, and Aled stays in the dark while you try to undo it. D: Hands the problem on: you are the one who knows, Aled is reachable now, and the organiser has no idea he spent two days on figures that Thursday no longer wants. The most effective response is to ring Aled this afternoon so he knows before he spends more time on it, then check with the organiser which records the meeting now needs: he is the person losing the work, and Thursday is close enough that the replacement figures have to be started today. It is stronger than leaving a note on his desk, because he does not come back until Wednesday and a day of preparation for the wrong records goes on in the meantime. It is stronger than asking the organiser to switch back, because the change was made for a reason nobody has asked about, and Aled learns nothing while that is tried. The least effective response is to hand the problem straight to the organiser and ask them to break the news: a note at least reaches Aled eventually, and trying to reverse the change at least aims at his two days, whereas passing it on leaves the person who knows doing nothing and the person who does not know explaining it. The principle: when you hold news that makes somebody’s work pointless, tell them yourself and tell them now.

question_text: You are a shared services administrator at Brantwood Services. Each quarter you certify on a one-page return how many staff completed mandatory training. This quarter’s figure comes from a system report that you know double-counts anyone who restarted a module. You cannot tell how many that is without a manual check taking two days. The return is due tomorrow and is used to report externally. The person who signs it is available this afternoon. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Submit the return with the system figure as it stands and add a line to it saying that the number may include some people who restarted a module more than once, which nobody has counted.
Start the two-day manual check now and tell the signer that the return will be a day late this quarter.
Take the figure and the double-counting problem to the person who signs the return this afternoon, and set out what a two-day manual check would cost against submitting with a caveat.
Certify the system figure as correct on the return and note in your own file that a manual check is needed at some point next quarter.
explanation: A: Decides the disclosure alone: the caveat may be exactly right, but the person whose name goes on an externally reported figure has not been asked whether they will sign it with one. B: Spends a deadline to buy certainty nobody asked for: the return is due tomorrow and is reported externally, and lateness is a cost the signer should get to weigh. D: Certifies a figure you know is wrong: the return goes out externally as accurate, the double-count stays in it, and the only record of the problem is a note in your own file. The most effective response is to take the figure and the double-counting problem to the person who signs the return this afternoon, setting out what a two-day manual check would cost against submitting with a caveat: the figure is knowably wrong in a known direction, and both the caveat and the lateness are their calls because it is their name on an externally reported number. It beats submitting with a line saying the number may include people who restarted a module, because that decides on their behalf what they are willing to certify. It beats starting the manual check and telling them the return will be a day late, because that spends a deadline they have not agreed to spend. The least effective response is certifying the system figure as correct and noting privately that a check is needed next quarter: a number you know double-counts is certified and sent outside the organisation. That makes it worse than the caveat, which does disclose, and worse than the manual check, which is late but true. The principle: when the figure is doubtful and the certificate is somebody else’s, put the doubt and the cost of resolving it in front of them before the deadline.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân tích theo từng thuộc tính độc lập: Hướng xoay góc (90°/45°), số lượng nét, màu sắc (Đen/Trắng), và vị trí.

question_text: You are a records assistant at a probation service. On Monday your supervisor told you to clear a backlog of two hundred record corrections by Thursday, because the team that uses those records cannot work from them until it is done. This morning the person who runs the department, to whom your supervisor reports, tells you to put everything else down and prepare a set of figures for a meeting on Wednesday. You cannot do both by Thursday, and neither of them knows what the other has asked you for. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Start the figures this morning and keep chipping at the corrections in the evenings, so that both land on time, and raise the clash with both of them only if it becomes clear you cannot finish.
Do the figures first because the request came from the person your supervisor reports to, and tell your supervisor on Thursday that the corrections have slipped and will need another few days.
Hand the corrections to a colleague on the team and ask them to carry them until Thursday while you do the figures, leaving them to explain where it has got to if anybody asks about it.
Tell both of them today that the requests clash, since neither knows of the other, set out what you can finish by each date, and ask which should give way and what happens to it.
explanation: A: Splits the effort so neither finishes: two hundred corrections and a set of figures cannot both be done properly in three days, and by the time you can see that, the dates the two of them could have moved have gone. B: Settles a clash by seniority and reports it too late: the team waiting on the records finds out on Thursday, when nobody can move the date or find anybody else to do the work. C: Passes the problem on without owning it: your colleague never accepted Thursday, does not know which of the two hundred matter most, and neither of the people who set the dates learns that they clash. The most effective response is telling both of them today that the two requests clash, setting out what you can finish by each date, and asking which of the two should give way. Only the two people who set the dates can decide which matters more, and today is the last point at which either of them can act on the answer. That is better than starting the figures and chipping at the corrections in the evenings, because three days will not stretch to cover both and the clash stays invisible until it is too late. It is better than doing the figures first and reporting the slip on Thursday, because seniority is not a reason and Thursday is after the day the records were needed. The least effective response is handing the corrections to a colleague and leaving them to explain where it has got to: working evenings at least keeps the job with the person who was given it, and doing the figures first at least reflects a real decision, whereas a colleague who never took on the deadline cannot judge which corrections matter and the two people who could resolve it are still unaware. The principle: when two instructions cannot both be met, the clash belongs with the people who set them, while they can still change one.
tip: Mẹo MT: Kiểm tra quy luật cộng/trừ hình (XOR pattern) theo hàng ngang trước, nếu không thỏa mãn thì xét theo cột dọc.

question_text: Gear A turns clockwise. Which way does gear B turn?
options: Clockwise
Anticlockwise
It stays still
It turns clockwise, then reverses
explanation: The answer is B. When two gears mesh, their teeth push directly against each other, so meshed gears always turn in opposite directions. Gear A turns clockwise, so gear B must turn anticlockwise. Option A is the direction you would get if the gears were joined by an open belt or chain rather than meshing teeth. A driven gear does not stay still while A turns it, and a steady drive never makes a meshed gear reverse, so C and D are wrong.
tip: Mẹo MT: Kiểm tra quy luật cộng/trừ hình (XOR pattern) theo hàng ngang trước, nếu không thỏa mãn thì xét theo cột dọc.

question_text: Gear A turns clockwise. Which way does gear C turn?
options: Anticlockwise
Clockwise
It cannot turn, it is locked
It turns clockwise, then anticlockwise
explanation: The answer is B. Meshed gears alternate direction along a train: A clockwise makes B anticlockwise, and B anticlockwise makes C clockwise. With an odd number of gears the last one always matches the first, so C turns the same way as A. Option A is the direction of the middle gear B, a common slip. A three-gear train turns freely rather than locking, and a constant drive gives a constant direction, so C and D are wrong.

question_text: The small driver gear has 8 teeth and turns at 60 rpm. The large gear has 16 teeth. How fast does the large gear turn?
options: 120 rpm
30 rpm
60 rpm
15 rpm
explanation: The answer is B. For meshed gears the number of teeth times the turning speed is the same for both, because every tooth of one gear moves exactly one tooth of the other. So 8 times 60 equals 16 times the unknown speed, giving 30 rpm. The larger gear has twice the teeth, so it turns at half the speed. Option A doubles the speed instead of halving it, C leaves it unchanged, and D halves it twice over. Only 30 rpm fits 8 x 60 = 16 x 30.

question_text: Pulley A drives an open belt and turns clockwise. Which way does pulley B turn?
options: Clockwise
Anticlockwise
It stays still
It turns anticlockwise, then clockwise
explanation: The answer is A. An open, uncrossed belt keeps the same edge of the belt on top across both pulleys, so the two pulleys turn the same way. Driver A turns clockwise, therefore B also turns clockwise. Opposite directions would need the belt crossed into a figure of eight, which is not shown, so B is wrong. A taut belt drives B steadily, so it neither stays still nor flips direction, which rules out C and D.
tip: Mẹo MT: Loại trừ nhanh các phương án vi phạm quy tắc xoay góc chiều kim đồng hồ.

question_text: Pulley A drives a crossed belt and turns clockwise. Which way does pulley B turn?
options: Clockwise
It stays still
Anticlockwise
It changes direction each turn
explanation: The answer is C. A crossed belt swaps which edge of the belt sits on top between the two pulleys, so the driven pulley turns the opposite way to the driver. A turns clockwise, so B turns anticlockwise. The same direction would need an open, uncrossed belt, which rules out A. The crossing does not stop the belt or make it flip on every turn, so B and D are wrong; it simply reverses the sense once.

question_text: The two pulleys are joined by a belt. Which pulley completes more turns each minute?
options: The small pulley
The large pulley
They complete the same number
Neither pulley turns
explanation: The answer is A. A belt moves at the same speed all along its length, so both pulleys pass the same length of rim in a given time. The small pulley has a shorter circumference, so it needs more turns to move that length and therefore spins faster. The large pulley covers more rim per turn and so turns fewer times, making B wrong. Equal turns would need equal-sized pulleys, ruling out C, and the belt clearly drives both, ruling out D.
tip: Mẹo MT: Kiểm tra quy luật cộng/trừ hình (XOR pattern) theo hàng ngang trước, nếu không thỏa mãn thì xét theo cột dọc.

question_text: The load weighs 200 N. Ignoring friction, what effort is needed to hold it using this single movable pulley?
explanation: The answer is B. A single movable pulley hangs from two sections of rope, and together they share the load so each section carries half. The effort on the free end equals the tension in one section, which is half of 200 N, or 100 N, once friction is ignored. Option A forgets that the pulley helps at all. Option C doubles the force the wrong way, and D would need four supporting ropes rather than two. Two supporting ropes give a mechanical advantage of two, so 100 N is correct.
tip: Mẹo MT: Đếm số lượng đỉnh hoặc số lượng góc nhọn khi các hình có hình dạng biến thiên phức tạp.

question_text: The beam is released from level. Which way does it tip?
options: The left-hand side goes down
The right-hand side goes down
It stays balanced
It tips right, then left
explanation: The answer is A. A beam turns towards the side with the larger turning effect, found by multiplying each weight by its distance from the pivot. The left side gives 5 kg x 4 m = 20, the right gives 8 kg x 2 m = 16. Because 20 is greater than 16, the left-hand side drops. Option B is tempting because the right-hand weight is heavier, but distance from the pivot counts just as much as weight. The turning effects are unequal, so it neither balances nor rocks to and fro, ruling out C and D.
tip: Mẹo MT: Kiểm tra quy luật cộng/trừ hình (XOR pattern) theo hàng ngang trước, nếu không thỏa mãn thì xét theo cột dọc.

question_text: Pressing down at which point raises the load with the least effort?
options: Point A
Point B
Point C
Point D
explanation: The answer is D. The further the effort acts from the fulcrum, the longer its lever arm, and the less force is needed to raise the same load, because turning effect is force multiplied by distance. Point D is furthest from the fulcrum, so pressing there needs the least effort. Point A is nearest the pivot and would need the most force, while B and C sit in between. Choosing the longest available lever arm always minimises the effort, so D is correct.
tip: Mẹo MT: Kiểm tra quy luật cộng/trừ hình (XOR pattern) theo hàng ngang trước, nếu không thỏa mãn thì xét theo cột dọc.

question_text: Which support carries more of the load’s weight?
options: Support P
Support Q
They carry equal weight
The plank carries it, not the supports
explanation: The answer is A. When a load rests between two supports, each support carries more of the weight the closer the load sits to it. Here the load is much nearer P than Q, so P bears the greater share. Support Q still carries some of the weight, but less, which makes B wrong. The shares would only be equal if the load sat midway between the supports, ruling out C. The supports are what hold the plank up, so D is wrong.

question_text: You are a stock control assistant at a retail chain. A recount you asked for turned up a mistake in your own figures, and the colleague who did it said, in front of two others, that he had wasted an afternoon on your arithmetic. It stung and he was largely right. The next count is due on Thursday and it needs two people, one of whom is normally him. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Ask your supervisor to put somebody else on Thursday's count, since working alongside him this week would be uncomfortable for both of you after what was said.
Refuse to work with him on Thursday's count after the way he spoke to you, and say you would rather do it on your own or not at all.
Acknowledge to him that the figures were wrong and say what you have changed, and do Thursday's count with him as planned since the count needs two people.
Say nothing about it, do Thursday's count as planned, and let the remark fade rather than reopening something that was fair comment anyway.
explanation: A: Redesigns the rota around one awkward afternoon: the count is harder to staff, and the two of you have to work together again the week after in any case. B: Withdraws from a job that needs two people after a disagreement: Thursday's count is put at risk to answer a remark made about an afternoon. D: Lets an unrepaired working relationship stand: the count happens and he has no reason to think the mistake will not simply repeat. The most effective response is to acknowledge that the figures were wrong, say what you have changed, and do Thursday’s count with him: the criticism was largely fair, saying so is what restores the working relationship, and the count that needs two people gets them. It beats asking for somebody else on Thursday, because the rota is rearranged around one bad afternoon and you will work together next week anyway. It beats letting the remark fade, because he has no reason to expect anything different next time. The least effective response is refusing to work with him on Thursday: a count that needs two people is put at risk to answer a remark, which is a different kind of wrong from avoiding him or from staying silent. The principle: when the criticism is fair, own it and stay in the work with the person who made it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Loại trừ nhanh các phương án vi phạm quy tắc xoay góc chiều kim đồng hồ.

question_text: You are a correspondence officer at Redhill Directorate. A briefing note you are about to send to a director was drafted by a colleague, Nia, who left the team last month; you updated two figures. Nia’s name is on the front of the document. The director has already praised the note in an email to your team leader, naming you. Nia is still employed elsewhere in the organisation. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Take Nia's name off the front of the document before sending it, and keep it to yourself that the note was drafted by somebody who has left.
Send the note with Nia's name still on it, and reply to the director's email saying that Nia drafted it and you updated two figures.
Send the note as it is with Nia's name on it, and say nothing to the director about who drafted what.
Reply to the director saying the note was a team effort, without naming Nia or saying which parts were hers.
explanation: A: Conceals the author to keep the credit: Nia is still employed here, her name was on the document, and taking it off is an act rather than an omission. C: Leaves the document right and the record wrong: the director's email names you, your team leader has read it, and the front of the note is not something either of them will look at. D: Blurs the credit rather than correcting it: a team effort leaves your name attached and Nia's absent, which is the part that matters to somebody still working here. The most effective response is to send the note with Nia’s name still on it, and reply to the director’s email saying she drafted it and you updated two figures: she wrote it, you changed two numbers, she still works here, and one reply corrects the record while it is fresh. It beats sending it as it is with her name on and saying nothing to the director, because the email naming you has already been read by your team leader. It beats replying that the note was a team effort, because that tells the director nothing about who did what. The least effective response is taking her name off the front before sending it: that is an act rather than an oversight, and it removes the only remaining evidence of who wrote it. That makes it worse than the silent send, which destroys nothing, and worse than the team-effort reply, which does not conceal. The principle: correct a wrong attribution in writing to whoever made it, and never remove the author’s name to make the credit fit.
tip: Mẹo MT: Kiểm tra quy luật cộng/trừ hình (XOR pattern) theo hàng ngang trước, nếu không thỏa mãn thì xét theo cột dọc.

question_text: You are a resourcing coordinator at a recruitment agency. A candidate you placed in a temporary warehouse role two weeks ago rings to say his shifts have been changed to nights without notice and he cannot do them because of childcare. Your agency’s contract with the client says shift patterns are agreed in advance. Your account manager, who owns the client relationship, is in a pitch until 4pm. The candidate is due on a night shift this evening. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Get the details from the candidate, check the agreed pattern on the contract file, and put the facts to your account manager before 4pm so she can raise it with the client before tonight's shift.
Tell the candidate that shift changes are between him and the site supervisor and that he should raise it there, since the agency only placed him and does not run the client's rotas.
Ring the client's site supervisor yourself, point out that the contract requires shift patterns to be agreed in advance, and ask for the candidate to be put back on days from tonight.
Tell the candidate not to attend tonight's night shift, since the change breaches the agreed pattern, and confirm to him that the agency will sort it out with the client afterwards.
explanation: B: Passes responsibility to others: the agreed pattern is in your agency's own contract, so this is exactly the agency's business. Sending a temporary worker to argue it alone with the site abandons the person you placed. C: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholder's: your account manager owns this relationship and a contractual challenge to the client is hers to frame. Making it yourself commits the agency to a position she has not seen. D: Acts on assumptions without checking: it tells a worker to miss a shift before anyone has confirmed the pattern or spoken to the client, which risks his placement on a reading of the contract nobody senior has looked at. The most effective response is to get the details, check the agreed pattern on the contract file, and put the facts to your account manager before 4pm: this is a contractual point the agency owns, it needs the person who owns the client relationship, and there is time to reach her before the shift. Gathering the facts first means she can act rather than investigate. It beats ringing the client’s site supervisor yourself, because a challenge to a client about their contract is the account manager’s to make, and pre-empting it commits the agency to a position she has not agreed. It beats telling the candidate not to attend tonight, because that risks his placement on your reading of a contract, before anyone has checked the agreed pattern or spoken to the client. The least effective response is telling him shift changes are between him and the site supervisor: it is the only response that denies the agency has any part in this, when the agreed pattern sits in the agency’s own contract, and it leaves a temporary worker to argue his own case against the site. That is worse than the other two, which are both wrong about who acts, but at least act. The principle: when something is genuinely yours to own, take it to the person who owns the relationship, with the facts, in time for them to use them.

question_text: You are an administrator at an occupational health clinic. At 2pm three things need you. A manager is waiting on a fitness-for-work report needed for a return-to-work meeting at 3pm, which takes twenty minutes to prepare. A nurse has asked you to book six routine health surveillance appointments this week. And your manager wants the quarterly activity figures by 5pm, taking an hour. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Send the manager the previous fitness-for-work report on file so the 3pm meeting has something to work from, and prepare the current one afterwards.
Book the six surveillance appointments first since they are quick and the nurse is waiting on them, then do the report and the quarterly figures.
Prepare the fitness-for-work report for the 3pm meeting, then do the quarterly figures before 5pm, and book the surveillance appointments afterwards or tomorrow.
Start the quarterly figures since they are the longest job and are due at 5pm, and fit the report and the bookings around them during the afternoon.
explanation: A: Supplies a document known to be out of date: a return-to-work meeting decided on a superseded fitness assessment risks an employee being put back to work on the wrong basis, which is a clinical harm rather than a scheduling error. B: Splits effort so nothing finishes: six bookings ahead of a twenty- minute report leaves a return-to-work meeting at 3pm relying on whatever time is left, for appointments that have all week. D: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholder's: an hour of internal reporting with three hours of room is put ahead of a report an employee's return-to-work meeting depends on in one hour. The most effective response is to prepare the fitness-for-work report for the 3pm meeting, then do the quarterly figures before 5pm, and book the surveillance appointments afterwards: the meeting is fixed and depends on a twenty-minute report, the figures have three hours for an hour of work, and the bookings have the week. Everything fits if the fixed appointment goes first. It beats booking the six surveillance appointments first because they are quick and the nurse is waiting, since six bookings with a week of slack should not precede a report a meeting depends on in an hour. It beats starting the quarterly figures as the longest job due at 5pm, because that leaves the one immovable deadline dependent on what is left over. The least effective response is sending the previous fitness-for- work report from the file so the meeting has something: it supplies a superseded assessment for a live return-to-work decision, risking an employee being returned on the wrong medical basis. That is worse than the other two, which sequence badly but produce the correct document. The principle: do the short task the fixed meeting depends on first, and never substitute an out-of-date document for a current one.
tip: Mẹo MT: Đếm số lượng đỉnh hoặc số lượng góc nhọn khi các hình có hình dạng biến thiên phức tạp.

question_text: Which option is the same shape as the one shown, only rotated?

Figure B
Figure C
Figure D

Give the shape a quarter turn clockwise and the column lies flat, the middle square points up and the end square points down, which is A. B is the shape flipped over and then turned, so no amount of turning reaches it. C is the shape flipped left to right, and D is the shape flipped top to bottom: both are mirror images.

options: Figure A
Figure B
Figure C
Figure D

A is the shape turned upside down (a half turn). B is a reflection in a horizontal line, which swaps top and bottom instead. D is the shape unchanged.

question_text: This solid is built from identical cubes joined face to face. What is the smallest number of cubes it could contain?
explanation: The answer is 10. A cube can only rest on the floor or on another cube, and these are joined, so every top you can see stands on a full column, even where the lower cubes are hidden. Count the columns by their tops: one column is 3 cubes high, two are 2 high and three are 1 high, so 3 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 10. 7 is the number of cubes you can see at least part of; it leaves out the 3 cubes hidden at the back, under the taller columns. 6 counts only the tops, one cube per column. 12 adds cubes that nothing in the picture needs.

question_text: The net is folded into a cube with the markings on the outside. Which cube could it make?
options: Figure A
Figure B
Figure C
Figure D
explanation: The answer is D. In the row of four, squares two apart end up opposite each other, so the dot is opposite the ring and the cross is opposite the blank square at the end of the row. The shaded square is opposite the blank square below the cross. Stand the cube with the shaded face on top and the cross facing you on the left: the ring folds round to meet it on the right, which is D. A and C both show the dot and the ring side by side, but those two are opposite, so they are never seen together. B has the right three faces with the cross and the ring swapped: that is the mirror image of the real cube, and no amount of turning produces it.

question_text: Three of the options are the shape shown, rotated. Which one is not?

Figure B

Figure D
explanation: The answer is B. A quick way to check each option: start at the single square on the end of the short arm, walk along the shape to the other end, and note which way you turn at each corner. In the shape shown the walk turns right, then left, then left. Turning a shape never changes its turns, so A, C and D all give right, left, left: they are the shape given a quarter turn clockwise, a half turn and a quarter turn anticlockwise. In B the same walk turns left, right, right, which only flipping the shape over can do. B is a mirror image.

question_text: A square of paper is folded twice as shown, then a hole is punched through every layer. Which option shows the paper when it is unfolded?
options: Figure A
Figure B
Figure C
Figure D
explanation: The answer is A. The paper is four layers thick when it is punched, so there are four holes. Undo the folds one at a time. Unfolding the top half reflects the hole in the horizontal fold line, so a second hole appears above it, the same distance from the line. Unfolding the left half reflects both holes in the vertical fold line. Every hole mirrors its neighbour across a fold, so all four sit close to the vertical centre line and close to the top and bottom edges. B copies the hole into the same spot in every quarter, which slides the paper instead of unfolding it. C reflects across the vertical fold but slides across the horizontal one. D undoes only one fold, so it has two holes.

question_text: Which of these nets can be folded to make a cube?
options: Figure A
Figure B
Figure C
Figure D
explanation: The answer is D. Fold the top row of three into a U. The bottom row of three wraps round the open sides from the other direction, and the step between the rows lets its last two squares close the cube without overlapping. A is a row of four with both end squares on the same side. The row wraps into a loop that brings its two ends together, so both flaps try to cover the same face and the opposite face stays open. B is five squares in a row, but a loop round a cube has only four sides, so the fifth square lands on top of the first. In C, the square at the left end of the row and the square at the bottom of the column fold onto the same face, which leaves another face open.

question_text: This solid is built from identical cubes joined face to face, using the smallest number that could make it. How many of those cubes cannot be seen?
explanation: The answer is 8. First find the smallest number of cubes. A cube can only rest on the floor or on another cube, and the cubes are joined, so each top you can see stands on a full column. Three columns are 3 cubes high, three are 2 high and five are 1 high: 9 + 6 + 5 = 20 cubes. Now count the cubes you can see at least part of: 12. The rest, 20 - 12 = 8, are buried behind and beneath others. 20 is the total, not the hidden number, and 12 is the number you can see. 9 counts every cube that is not a top as hidden, but many of those show their sides at the front of the solid.

question_text: The net is folded into a cube with the markings on the outside. Which cube could it make?
options: Figure A
Figure B
Figure C
Figure D
explanation: The answer is B. Fold the net round the ring. With the ring facing you, the cross above it folds back to become the top, the shaded square beside it folds back to become the right side, and the dot, joined to the cross, folds down to become the left side. The two blank squares close the bottom and the back, so the dot is opposite the shaded face. Now look at the corner where the cross, the shaded face and the ring meet: going clockwise round it, seen from outside, the order is cross, shaded, ring. B reads ring, cross, shaded clockwise from the top, which is the same cycle, so it is that corner turned round. A puts the dot, cross and ring in the wrong order: on the real cube they run dot, cross, ring clockwise, and A runs dot, ring, cross, the mirror image. C shows the dot beside the shaded face, but they are opposite. D runs shaded, blank, cross clockwise, where the real cube runs shaded, cross, blank: another mirror image.

question_text: Which option is the solid shown, turned to a new position?
options: Figure A
Figure B
Figure C
Figure D
explanation: The answer is D. The solid is a chain of three straight arms, each at right angles to the last: a short arm of two cubes, then an arm of three, then another arm of three. Every option is built the same way, so what decides it is the direction of the last arm. Picture the short arm pointing straight up and walk from it along the middle arm: on the solid shown, the last arm turns off to your right. Stand D with its short arm up in the same way and its last arm turns right too. In A, B and C the last arm turns to the left, so they are mirror images of the solid: each looks convincing, but no amount of turning makes it match.

question_text: You are an equipment store assistant at a traffic enforcement agency. The yearly count of the store has to be finished by Friday, because the figure it produces is what the people who order replacements work from for the next twelve months. It was given three weeks ago to a colleague who has since moved to another team. This morning you find that nothing has been counted at all, and nobody else has noticed. Your supervisor is in meetings all day but answers messages. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Start counting the store yourself today, working through the shelves in the order they are numbered, and keep going until Wednesday, then decide whether to raise it once you can see how much you have managed.
Message your supervisor this morning that the count has not been started and that Friday is at risk, saying what you can cover today, so they can put people on it.
Reassure the people who order replacements that the count is in hand and will reach them on Friday, then work out afterwards whether three days is enough.
Ask the colleague who moved teams to come back for the rest of the week and finish the count, since it was handed to them three weeks ago and they know what was intended.
explanation: A: Absorbs it quietly while the days run out: the hours in which somebody could have been put alongside you are the hours you spend counting on your own. C: Gives an assurance nobody has checked: the people who depend on the figure stop watching for the one thing that may not arrive, and they stop watching on your word. D: Chases somebody who no longer owns the work: they have another team's work in front of them, nothing obliges them to drop it, and Friday arrives whatever they answer. The most effective response is to message your supervisor this morning that the count has not been started and that Friday is at risk. You are the only person who knows, Friday feeds a figure the people who order replacements use for a year, and your supervisor can put others alongside you while three days are left. Starting the count alone and deciding on Wednesday whether to raise it is weaker, because the days in which help could have been arranged are the days you spend counting. Asking the colleague who moved teams to come back and finish it is weaker too, because the work is no longer theirs and nothing obliges them to drop what they now do. The least effective response is to reassure the people who order replacements that the count is in hand and will reach them on Friday: it asserts as settled something nobody has checked, and the people the figure is for stop watching the one thing that may not come. Being the only person who knows is the reason to escalate, not a reason to try to absorb it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Đếm số lượng đỉnh hoặc số lượng góc nhọn khi các hình có hình dạng biến thiên phức tạp.

question_text: You are an analyst at a market-research agency. A client’s marketing director is building a product-launch presentation for Thursday around survey results you are producing. Today, Tuesday, you find your fieldwork supplier has so far delivered only half the promised responses; the remainder arrive tomorrow night, and the headline figures may shift once they are in. The marketing director has just emailed asking for the figures today so she can start building her presentation. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Send the preliminary figures now, stating clearly they are based on half the sample and flagging which headline numbers may move when the remaining responses arrive tomorrow night.
Hold the figures back until the full sample has arrived and been checked tomorrow night, so the marketing director only ever sees numbers that will not change.
Reply that the results are in good shape, and send the figures today without mentioning the missing half of the sample, since the final numbers will probably be close.
Raise the problem with your own account manager first and leave it to them to decide what, if anything, the client should be told about the sample.
explanation: B: Delays the message: the marketing director has asked for the figures today to start building a Thursday presentation, and withholding everything until tomorrow night costs her a full day of preparation when a clearly-caveated interim answer would serve her now. C: Falsely reassures the stakeholder: telling the client her results are in good shape while knowingly omitting that half the sample is missing is dishonesty about reliability. She may lock claims you know are unstable into a launch presentation, a different kind of wrong from being slow or indirect. D: Tells the wrong audience first: briefing the account manager is sensible, but leaving the whole decision with them delays a straightforward factual caveat the marketing director needs today, while her request for the figures sits unanswered. The most effective response is to send the preliminary figures now, stating clearly that they rest on half the sample and flagging which headline numbers may move: the marketing director asked for figures today, and a plainly caveated interim answer lets her start building the presentation without locking in claims that could change tomorrow night. It beats holding everything back until the full sample is checked, because that costs her a full day of preparation against a Thursday deadline when a clearly caveated answer meets her stated need now. It beats routing the issue through your account manager first, because that delays a simple factual caveat the client needs today, and her request goes unanswered in the meantime. The least effective response is telling her the results are in good shape and sending the figures without mentioning the missing half: unlike holding them back, which is slow but honest, and unlike escalating internally, which at least surfaces the problem to someone, it assures the client of a reliability you know the numbers do not have. If the headline figures shift tomorrow night, she has built her launch on numbers you knew were unstable. The principle: give stakeholders what they need on time, with an honest statement of how reliable it is, never certainty you do not have.
tip: Mẹo MT: Loại trừ nhanh các phương án vi phạm quy tắc xoay góc chiều kim đồng hồ.

question_text: You are a baggage services agent. Five delayed bags have to be booked onto courier deliveries before the courier’s five o’clock cut-off, or their owners wait another day. At half past three your manager asks you to pull together some figures she wants for a meeting tomorrow morning, adding “whenever you get a chance”. The bookings take about an hour. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell your manager she will have the figures within the hour, then work on them, and book what bags you can once they are finished and sent across to her.
Start on the figures now, since a request from your manager takes priority over routine work, and turn to the courier bookings once she has what she asked for.
Book the five deliveries before the five o'clock cut-off, then start on the figures, and tell your manager she will have them first thing tomorrow morning.
Ask your manager whether she would rather have the figures this afternoon or the bags booked onto today's courier round, and act on whichever she says.
explanation: A: Promises a manager a deadline she never asked for: five passengers go another day without their luggage so that a set of figures for tomorrow arrives this afternoon. B: Reads seniority as urgency: the words used were "whenever you get a chance", and the meeting is tomorrow while the courier stops taking bookings at five. D: Hands back a question already answered: "whenever you get a chance" tells you where it sits, and asking spends her time on a decision you are in a better position to make. The most effective response is to book the five deliveries before the five o’clock cut-off, then start on the figures and tell your manager she will have them first thing tomorrow: the cut-off is fixed and passes at five, the meeting is tomorrow morning, and a line telling her when the figures arrive costs nothing. It beats starting on the figures now because a request from your manager takes priority, since the request was explicitly not urgent, and treating seniority as urgency costs five people their luggage. It beats asking her which she would rather have, because she has already answered that with whenever you get a chance. The least effective response is promising her the figures within the hour and booking the bags afterwards: it invents a deadline nobody set, and five passengers lose another day to it. That is worse than doing the figures first, which at least promises nothing, and worse than asking her, which loses minutes rather than the cut-off. The principle: listen to how urgent a request actually is, protect the deadline that expires, and say when the rest will land.

Working the chain from left to right: ⊘ exchanges the first and last symbols, leaving the middle pair in place, so ○■▽◆ becomes ◆■▽○; ⊛ inverts the fill of every symbol, leaving all positions unchanged, so ◆■▽○ becomes ◇□▼●. question_text: You are a support analyst. The monthly figure for tickets resolved first time looks about twenty points too high, and the only way it could be that high is if a colleague has been closing and reopening tickets. The figure goes into a board pack tomorrow. You have a full queue and a difficult history with that colleague. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Rebuild the whole month's figure from the raw ticket data yourself tonight, and take a finished alternative number to whoever compiles the pack tomorrow.
Leave it alone and get on with the queue. The figure is not yours to police, and raising it would mean an awkward conversation about somebody else's numbers.
Send a note to whoever compiles the pack saying the figure looks high and that they may want to check it before tomorrow, without saying why you think so.
Ask your colleague today how the figure got so high, and if the answer does not explain it, tell whoever compiles the pack what you have found before tomorrow.
explanation: A: Spends a night proving what a question would settle: the pack goes tomorrow either way, and one conversation this afternoon would have resolved it. B: Avoids the difficult conversation: a board reads a first-time-fix rate tomorrow that only you have any reason to doubt, and the queue was never the reason. C: Flags a doubt without its reason: they cannot check a number without knowing what to check, so the warning arrives too vague to act on. The most effective response is to ask your colleague today how the figure got so high, and if the answer does not explain it, tell whoever compiles the pack before tomorrow. The one thing that settles this is a question only he can answer, it takes minutes, and there is still time to warn the compiler. It beats rebuilding the whole month’s figure from the raw ticket data tonight, because a night of that produces a rival number without establishing whether the first was wrong. It beats sending the compiler a note saying the figure looks high without saying why, because they have no way to check it. The least effective response is leaving it alone and getting on with the queue: it is worse than either of the other two, because both put something in front of somebody before the pack goes, while this lets a board read a figure only you have reason to doubt. The principle: when the fastest route to the truth is a conversation you would rather avoid, the discomfort is the cost of the check, not a reason to skip it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Kiểm tra quy luật cộng/trừ hình (XOR pattern) theo hàng ngang trước, nếu không thỏa mãn thì xét theo cột dọc.

question_text: You are a receptionist at a dental practice. Part of your job is logging each patient’s arrival time, which the practice uses to report waiting times to the health board. A patient arrives forty minutes late for a check-up and is seen straight away. Your colleague on the desk, who joined the practice last month, says the waiting figures are already poor and suggests offhand that you log the arrival as on-time, since the patient was not kept waiting. She has never suggested anything like it before. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Log the correct arrival time and tell the practice manager that your colleague asked you to record it falsely so that she can deal with it as she sees fit.
Log the arrival as on-time as your colleague suggests, since the patient was seen immediately and an accurate entry would make the practice's figures look worse than the service it actually gave.
Leave the arrival time blank rather than enter either figure, so that the record is not falsified and the practice's monthly waiting figures are not dragged down by one late patient.
Log the actual arrival time, and tell your colleague you are not willing to record something you know is untrue, whatever it does to this month's figures.
explanation: A: Escalates prematurely: the entry is right and the point is made by making it. Turning a colleague's bad suggestion into a report before telling her what you think skips the conversation that would probably settle it. B: Falsifies a business record: the log is the practice's evidence to the health board, and entering a time you know is wrong is a deliberate misstatement. That is dishonesty, not a judgement call about presentation. C: Hides the problem: a blank is a quieter way of removing an inconvenient fact. The health board's figures still end up wrong, and nobody can see that a decision was taken. The most effective response is to log the actual arrival time and tell your colleague you are not willing to record something untrue: the log is a record the health board relies on, so it gets the true time, and saying so plainly settles the matter where it arose. It beats logging it correctly and telling the practice manager your colleague asked you to falsify it, because the record is already correct and the disagreement is one sentence away from being resolved; going straight to the manager makes a formal matter of something a direct answer handles. It beats leaving the arrival time blank, because an empty field achieves the same distortion your colleague asked for, only without leaving fingerprints, so the figures are still wrong and nobody can tell why. The least effective response is recording the arrival as on-time because the patient was seen immediately: it is the only response that puts a figure you know to be false into a record the practice reports externally, and the reasoning offered for it, that the service was fine, is exactly the reasoning that makes small falsifications easy. That is worse than the blank field, which at least refuses to write the lie, and worse than going to the manager, which is clumsy rather than dishonest. The principle: record what happened, and say plainly that you will not record what did not.
tip: Mẹo MT: Loại trừ nhanh các phương án vi phạm quy tắc xoay góc chiều kim đồng hồ.

question_text: You are a production coordinator at a print and mail house. At 11am three things need you. A mailing of 20,000 renewal notices must reach the Royal Mail collection at 2pm or the legal notice period is missed. A colleague needs help fixing a jammed inserter on a different job. And your manager wants headcount figures for a meeting at noon. The renewal job needs ninety minutes of your attention. The headcount figures take fifteen minutes. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Help your colleague with the jammed inserter first, since a stopped machine is costing time on the floor, then do the renewals and the headcount figures.
Work on the renewals and the inserter together, moving between them, and do the headcount figures if the mailing is finished before the 2pm collection.
Do the fifteen minutes of headcount figures for the noon meeting, then give the renewal mailing your full attention until the 2pm collection, and pass the inserter to another operator.
Start the renewal mailing immediately and tell your manager the headcount figures will have to wait until after the 2pm collection.
explanation: A: Abandons own committed work: an unquantified machine fix is taken on ahead of a ninety-minute job with a 2pm legal deadline, which leaves no margin if the jam takes longer than expected. B: Splits effort so nothing finishes: a mailing with a legal notice period is left to compete for attention with a machine fault, which risks missing a deadline that cannot be recovered and is the most costly of the four outcomes. D: Splits the wrong thing: it protects the deadline that matters and sacrifices a fifteen-minute task that fits inside the margin anyway, so the manager goes into a noon meeting without figures for no gain. The most effective response is to do the fifteen minutes of headcount figures for the noon meeting, then give the renewal mailing your full attention until the 2pm collection, and pass the inserter to another operator: there are three hours, the mailing needs ninety minutes of them and has a legal deadline, and the figures are needed at noon. Both fit if the short one goes first, and the machine fault is work someone else can take. It beats starting the mailing immediately and telling your manager the figures must wait, because that protects the same deadline while needlessly sacrificing a fifteen-minute task that comfortably fits. It beats helping your colleague with the jammed inserter first, because taking on a machine fault of unknown length ahead of a legally timed mailing risks the one deadline that cannot be moved. The least effective response is moving between the renewals and the inserter and fitting the figures in afterwards: it lets a mailing with a legal notice period compete for attention with a machine jam, which is the most likely way to miss the collection entirely. That is worse than the other two, which mis- sequence but keep the mailing whole. The principle: check what actually fits in the time, protect the deadline that cannot move, and hand off what someone else can do.
tip: Mẹo MT: Đếm số lượng đỉnh hoặc số lượng góc nhọn khi các hình có hình dạng biến thiên phức tạp.

question_text: You are a trading assistant at Asda. A figure you produced for a weekly pack rests on an assumption about supplier lead times that changed on Friday. With the new lead times the figure would be materially different. The pack goes to a manager this afternoon and the meeting that uses it is tomorrow. Reworking the figure properly takes half a day, which you do not have. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Rework the figure quickly this afternoon with an estimate of the new lead times, and put the estimated version in the pack instead of the one you can support.
Put the figure in the pack as it stands, without flagging that the lead times behind it changed on Friday, since the rework cannot be done before this afternoon in any case.
Put the figure in with a clear note that the lead times changed on Friday and what that does to it, and tell the manager before the pack goes out so nothing surprises him.
Leave the figure out of the pack altogether and explain in its place that the number is being reworked after a change to supplier lead times.
explanation: A: Substitutes a guess for a stale fact: neither number has been checked, and the estimate carries none of the working the original at least had. B: Withholds the fact that decides what the number is worth: tomorrow's meeting uses a figure whose basis is known to be out of date by the only person who knows it. D: Removes the evidence rather than qualifying it: tomorrow's meeting loses a usable number and gains nothing it can decide with. The most effective response is to put the figure in with a clear note on the lead time change and what it is likely to do, and tell the manager before the pack goes out: the meeting keeps a number it can use, everybody knows what it rests on, and the manager can decide whether tomorrow needs the rework. It beats reworking it quickly on an estimate, because an unchecked guess replaces a number whose working at least exists. It beats leaving the figure out, because the meeting is then deciding with nothing. The least effective response is putting the figure in without flagging the lead time change: the only person who knows the basis has changed says nothing, and the meeting treats a stale figure as current, which is a different kind of wrong from guessing or from withdrawing the number. The principle: when you cannot fix a number in time, publish what is wrong with it to the person who is about to rely on it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân tích theo từng thuộc tính độc lập: Hướng xoay góc (90°/45°), số lượng nét, màu sắc (Đen/Trắng), và vị trí.

question_text: You are a stock control assistant at Adidas. The same line has shown a discrepancy at count on four occasions in six weeks, always in the same direction and always in the same area. Each time it has been written off as a counting error. You have now checked and the counts were done correctly. Discrepancies of this size and pattern are supposed to be reported to the loss prevention team. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Hand the four counts to the colleague who covers that area on Thursdays, since he knows the line better than you do, and consider your part in it finished.
Keep watching the line for another two counts to be sure the pattern is real, since four occasions could still turn out to be an unfortunate run of coincidences.
Raise it with your supervisor and let her decide whether it goes any further, without mentioning that the counts themselves have now been checked and are sound.
Report the four counts to the loss prevention team today with the checking you have done, since a pattern like that is what the reporting route exists for, and tell your supervisor.
explanation: A: Passes a reportable pattern on without owning it: the colleague has no idea it is four occurrences or that it should be reported, so the one person who knew both facts has stepped out of it. B: Waits for certainty that a report does not require: two more counts is three more weeks, and the threshold for reporting was passed some time ago. C: Escalates without the fact that changes the decision: she is asked to judge a pattern while the one thing that rules out a counting error is left out. The most effective response is to report the four counts to the loss prevention team today with your checking attached, and tell your supervisor you have done it: the pattern is exactly what the reporting route exists for, your checking is what makes it more than a suspicion, and nobody is surprised later. It beats waiting for two more counts, because the threshold was passed weeks ago and waiting adds three weeks. It beats raising it with your supervisor while leaving out that the counts were checked, because that is the fact the decision turns on. The least effective response is handing the four counts to the Thursday colleague and treating your part as finished: he does not know it is four occurrences or that it is reportable, so the only person holding both facts has stepped out, which is a different kind of wrong from waiting too long or from telling somebody too little. The principle: when something crosses a reporting line, take it there yourself, with what you know attached.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân tích theo từng thuộc tính độc lập: Hướng xoay góc (90°/45°), số lượng nét, màu sắc (Đen/Trắng), và vị trí.

question_text: You are a junior data engineer. A supplier who provides a daily data feed has told you their file will be late every day for the next fortnight while they move systems. The team that publishes the morning figures depends on that feed and has committed to a customer deadline of nine o’clock each day. Nobody outside your inbox knows. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Keep pressing the supplier every day to deliver on time. It is their commitment to meet, and chasing them is the fastest route back to a nine o'clock file.
Tell the publishing team that the feed may be late occasionally over the next two weeks, without going into the supplier's system move or the full fortnight.
Tell the publishing team today that the feed will be late every day for a fortnight, and ask what they need from you to protect their nine o'clock commitment.
Put a note in the shared channel about the supplier's system move, so that anybody depending on the feed can see it and plan around it themselves.
explanation: A: Passes the problem on without owning it: the supplier has already said a fortnight, and the team promising nine o'clock still does not know it is at risk. B: Softens a warning until it cannot be planned with: occasionally and a fortnight every day are different problems and only one of them can be prepared for. D: Publishes to nobody in particular: the team with the nine o'clock commitment has no reason to be reading that channel this morning. The most effective response is to tell the publishing team today that the feed will be late every day for a fortnight, and ask what they need to protect their nine o’clock commitment. A fortnight of late files against a daily deadline is their problem to solve, and they can only solve it knowing the shape of it. It beats telling them the feed may be late occasionally over the next two weeks, because that produces no plan and every day for two weeks is a different problem. It beats putting a note in the shared channel about the supplier’s system move, because that is not the same as telling the people with a customer commitment. The least effective response is pressing the supplier every day to deliver on time: it is worse than either of the other two, because both put something in front of the affected team, while this spends a fortnight chasing a supplier who has already given their answer. The principle: when a supplier’s problem lands on somebody else’s promise, tell the people who made the promise first.

question_text: You are a build engineer. Last week you told the programme office that the average build takes nine minutes. Since a change on Monday it takes twenty-six. The programme office is publishing a paper this afternoon that uses the nine-minute figure to argue against buying more capacity. Your team lead is in interviews all day and has asked not to be disturbed. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Say nothing to anybody until your team lead is out of interviews, and raise the corrected figure with her then rather than going round her to the programme office.
Send the corrected figure to the programme office now and copy your team lead, so that the paper is written on twenty-six minutes rather than on nine.
Interrupt the interviews to tell your team lead, since a paper going to the programme board on a wrong figure is more urgent than an hour of an interview.
Send the programme office a note saying the figure may have moved and that they should check it before publishing anything this afternoon.
explanation: A: Stays silent while waiting for a route: the paper publishes this afternoon and the interviews run until the end of the day. C: Escalates past a stated instruction when a direct route exists: the programme office can be told without disturbing anybody. D: Hedges a fact you are certain of: you know it is twenty-six, and may have moved leaves them deciding whether to believe their own paper. The most effective response is to send the corrected figure to the programme office now and copy your team lead. They own the paper, they can be reached directly, and the copy means nothing is done behind her back while she is unavailable. It beats interrupting the interviews to tell her, because that is unnecessary when the people publishing the paper can be told in one email. It beats sending the programme office a note saying the figure may have moved, because you are certain it is twenty-six, and that passes your certainty on as doubt. The least effective response is saying nothing until she is out of interviews: it is worse than either of the other two, because both reach somebody before the paper publishes, while this waits for a route that will not open until after the argument has been made on a figure you know is wrong. The principle: when a decision is being taken this afternoon on a number you know has changed, go to whoever holds the document and copy the people who should know.

question_text: You are a delivery coordinator. You compile the weekly figures showing how the team’s hours split across three projects. This week roughly a third went on unplanned support, which has no project to sit against and makes the delivery figure look poor. Your manager has said she would rather the report did not raise questions from the programme board this month. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Show the support hours as their own line and add a note saying they were unavoidable, so that the delivery figure is read with that caveat attached.
Show the support hours as their own line and say nothing about them unless somebody asks, since the figures speak for themselves either way.
Show the support hours as their own line, and tell your manager the figure will raise questions, so that she has the answer ready before the board asks it.
Record the support hours as covered by the nearest project. The delivery figure then holds up properly, and the board is not distracted by an odd line item this month.
explanation: A: Softens the number with a label: unavoidable is your judgement rather than a fact, and it invites the board to discount a third of the week. B: Reports accurately and abandons the explanation: a third of the week appears without a cause, which is exactly what will generate the questions. D: Records effort against work it was not spent on: a third of the week now appears as project delivery in a report the board uses to allocate people. The most effective response is to show the support hours as their own line, and tell your manager the figure will raise questions. The figures should say what happened, and the honest way to handle her concern is to warn her what the question will be and hand her the answer. It beats showing them as their own line with a note saying they were unavoidable, because that is an opinion added to a fact and it encourages the board to set the week aside. It beats showing the line and saying nothing unless somebody asks, because a large unexplained line is precisely what produces the questions she is worried about. The least effective response is recording the support hours as covered by the nearest project: it is worse than either of the other two, because both leave the hours visible, spun or bare, while this moves a third of the week into project delivery in a report used to allocate people. The principle: report the number as it is and prepare the person who will be asked about it, rather than changing the number so the question is never asked.
tip: Mẹo MT: Kiểm tra quy luật cộng/trừ hình (XOR pattern) theo hàng ngang trước, nếu không thỏa mãn thì xét theo cột dọc.

question_text: You are a disclosure assistant. Your team records the number of documents each person reviews per day and reports the totals to the client each Friday. You have been slower this week because a batch you were given is unusually complex. Your team leader asks you for your figures before she sends the report. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Give her the number and tell her why it is lower this week, so that whatever she sends the client carries the reason along with the figure.
Record a higher figure for the last two days than you actually reviewed, since you will make the difference up next week and the client only ever sees the weekly total.
Give her the number without comment, on the basis that she has the same view of the batches as you do and can see for herself why the week looks like this.
Ask her to leave your figures out of this week's report until the complex batch is finished, so that the client sees a fair picture rather than an unusual week.
explanation: B: Alters a record: it puts a number into the client's report that describes work nobody has done, and it does so in the one system anybody would later use to check. C: Assumes the context is obvious: she is about to send the figure onwards and may not have looked at what was in your batch, so the reason travels only if you send it with the number. D: Removes the awkward data: a report with a person missing invites exactly the question it was meant to avoid, and it treats an unusual week as something to be hidden rather than explained. The most effective response is to give her the number and tell her why it is lower this week, so whatever she sends the client carries the reason along with the figure. It beats giving her the number without comment because she can see the batches herself, since she is the person sending it on and cannot supply a context she has not been given. It beats asking her to leave your figures out of this week’s report, because leaving a name out is more conspicuous than a low number with an explanation. The least effective response is recording a higher figure for the last two days than you actually reviewed: it changes what the record says happened, which is a different kind of wrong from the other two because both of those report a true number badly and this one reports a false one. The principle: send the number with its reason, and never make the number say something else.

question_text: You are a reporting analyst. You and a colleague disagreed sharply last week about whose figures were wrong; yours turned out to be right. He now needs the data extract you produce as a favour each Friday, which nobody has ever asked you to do. His deadline is Monday. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Send him the extract on Friday as usual, and separately say that the disagreement is finished as far as you are concerned so it does not sit between you.
Tell him you will send the extract but only if he acknowledges that his figures were the ones that were wrong last week.
Stop producing the Friday extract now that he has been shown to be wrong, so that you do not have to deal with him every week about a job nobody asked you to do.
Send him the extract on Friday exactly as usual and say nothing at all about last week, on the basis that being proved right is enough and the whole thing will fade by itself soon enough.
explanation: B: Makes the work conditional on an apology: it turns a settled factual question into a price, and he will pay it resentfully or not at all. C: Withdraws a favour after winning an argument: his Monday deadline fails, and the timing makes the reason unmistakable to everybody who sees it. D: Avoids the difficult conversation: the work continues and he is left guessing whether you are still aggrieved about it. The most effective response is to send him the extract on Friday as usual, and separately say the disagreement is finished as far as you are concerned: it protects his deadline, separates the work from the argument, and says the thing that lets both of you drop it. It beats sending the extract exactly as usual and saying nothing at all about last week, because silence leaves the grievance alive on both sides. It beats telling him you will send it only if he acknowledges his figures were wrong, because trading work for an admission poisons the next six months. The least effective response is stopping the Friday extract now that he has been shown to be wrong: a favour is withdrawn in the week he lost the argument, so his Monday fails and the reason is obvious. That is retaliation rather than an awkward or graceless way of moving on. The principle: winning the argument does not license withdrawing the help.

question_text: You work in an HR shared service team. It is Wednesday. Three things are outstanding: a new starter’s contract must go out today or she cannot begin on Monday, a manager wants a report on absence figures by Friday, and a colleague has asked you to review her draft policy whenever you have time. The contract takes an hour, the report three hours. You have five hours left today. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Work through all three in the order they were asked for, and let your manager know at the end of the day if anything has not been finished.
Start the absence report because it is the longest job, then do the contract at the end of the day once the bulk of the report is behind you.
Do the contract and the policy review first because they are the two shorter jobs, then start the absence report and continue it tomorrow morning.
Send the new starter's contract first, then work on the absence report, and tell your colleague you will review her policy tomorrow.
explanation: A: Hides the problem / silent deadline slip: the contract is the one item that cannot slip, and reporting at the end of the day is after the point at which anyone could rescue it. Reporting a missed deadline once it is missed is not communication. B: Delays the decision: it leaves an hour-long task with a today-or- never deadline to the end of a five-hour day, so any overrun on the report costs the new starter her start date. C: Splits effort so nothing finishes: it fits the favour in ahead of a report with a named Friday deadline, and pushes three hours of work into a day that already has other demands. The most effective response is to send the new starter’s contract first, then work on the absence report, and tell your colleague the policy review waits until tomorrow: only the contract has a deadline of today with a consequence attached, a start date, and it takes one of the five hours available. That leaves four hours for a three-hour report due Friday, and the policy review has no deadline at all. It beats starting the absence report first because it is the longest job, since that puts a fixed, unrecoverable deadline behind an open-ended one. It beats doing the contract and the policy review first as the two shorter jobs, because that fits an unscheduled favour ahead of a report with a stated deadline. The least effective response is working through all three in the order they were asked for and reporting at the end of the day: it works to the order things were asked in rather than to their deadlines, and reports the failure only once the new starter’s Monday cannot be saved. That is worse than the other two, which sequence badly but at least do the contract today. The principle: identify the task that cannot slip, do it first, and say early which of the others will move.

question_text: You are a customer service adviser. A colleague tells you she gave a customer the wrong charges figure last week, that the customer accepted it, and that she has decided not to raise it because “it worked out fine”. She asks you not to mention it. The team logs pricing errors weekly. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
