question_text: You are a reporting analyst. You and a colleague disagreed sharply last week about whose figures were wrong; yours turned out to be right. He now needs the data extract you produce as a favour each Friday, which nobody has ever asked you to do. His deadline is Monday. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Send him the extract on Friday as usual, and separately say that the disagreement is finished as far as you are concerned so it does not sit between you.
Tell him you will send the extract but only if he acknowledges that his figures were the ones that were wrong last week.
Stop producing the Friday extract now that he has been shown to be wrong, so that you do not have to deal with him every week about a job nobody asked you to do.
Send him the extract on Friday exactly as usual and say nothing at all about last week, on the basis that being proved right is enough and the whole thing will fade by itself soon enough.

It beats sending the extract exactly as usual and saying nothing at all about last week, because silence leaves the grievance alive on both sides. It beats telling him you will send it only if he acknowledges his figures were wrong, because trading work for an admission poisons the next six months. The least effective response is stopping the Friday extract now that he has been shown to be wrong: a favour is withdrawn in the week he lost the argument, so his Monday fails and the reason is obvious. That is retaliation rather than an awkward or graceless way of moving on. The principle: winning the argument does not license withdrawing the help.

question_text: You are a billing assistant. Two fee earners have each told you the other is responsible for a bill that has not gone out, and each has asked you to say so if the month-end figures are queried. The bill is now three weeks late and the client has asked about it. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell the month-end review, if it comes up, that neither of them has taken responsibility, so that the record shows what actually happened rather than either account.
Ask them both for ten minutes, put the client's question and the three weeks in front of them, and ask which of them will get the bill out this week.
Draft the bill yourself and send it to both of them for approval, since the client is waiting and somebody has to break the stalemate before month end.
Blame each of them to the other in front of the billing team, so that they both understand the position and can settle who is responsible between themselves.
explanation: A: Answers a question nobody has asked yet: it prepares a position for a meeting instead of getting the bill out, and the client is still waiting either way. C: Works around the stalemate: the bill may go out and the question of who owns it is left exactly as it was, so the next one stalls the same way. D: Carries private remarks between colleagues: it makes the argument about the two of them rather than about a bill the client is waiting on, and neither can unhear what the other said. The most effective response is to ask them both for ten minutes, put the client’s question and the three weeks in front of them, and ask which of them will get the bill out this week. Those are facts neither disputes, and putting both in front of them together turns a blame exchange into a decision. It beats drafting the bill yourself and sending it to both for approval, because drafting round them leaves ownership unresolved. It beats telling the month-end review that neither has taken responsibility, because a bill is still not out. question_text: You are a fundraising assistant at a charity. You and your colleague Callum jointly prepare the monthly donor report. For three months he has sent you his figures late on the afternoon they are due, leaving you to reconcile them in a rush, and last month an error reached the trustees. Today he has done it again. He is friendly and busy, and has never been told this causes a problem. The next report is due in four weeks. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Reconcile the figures again without saying anything, and build in extra checking time next month so that a late hand-off cannot produce another error in the trustee report.
Copy your line manager into your reply to Callum today, noting that the figures have arrived late for the fourth month running and that this caused last month's error in the trustee report.
Reply to Callum today setting out that you will not be able to include his figures in future if they arrive after midday on the due date, so that the deadline is unambiguous from now on.
Reconcile today's figures, then speak to Callum this week, explain what the late hand-off costs at your end, and agree a date each month by which his figures will reach you.
explanation: A: Avoids the difficult conversation: absorbing it silently for a fourth month guarantees a fifth, hides from Callum that his habit has consequences, and leaves the trustees relying on you never having a bad day. Silence is the failure here, not the extra checking. B: Escalates prematurely: Callum has never been told there is a problem, so the first he hears of it is in front of his manager. That makes an ally into a defendant over something a direct conversation has not yet been given the chance to fix. C: Personalises the conflict: it opens with a sanction rather than a conversation, and a donor report missing his figures punishes the trustees for a problem between the two of you. The most effective response is to reconcile today’s figures, then speak to Callum this week and agree a date each month by which his figures will reach you: this month’s report still has to be right, and the recurring cause needs raising with the person who can fix it, directly and once the immediate work is done. Agreeing a date turns a grievance into a working arrangement. It beats copying your line manager into the reply today, because Callum has never been told there is a problem, and involving his manager first turns a fixable habit into a formal complaint. It beats replying that you will exclude his figures in future if they arrive late, because leading with that threat makes the trustees pay for a disagreement between two colleagues. The least effective response is reconciling again in silence and building in extra checking time: it is the only response where Callum never learns anything is wrong, so the pattern is guaranteed to continue, and the trustees’ report stays safe only for as long as your extra checking holds. That is worse than the other two, which are clumsy about how they raise it but do raise it. The principle: fix today’s report, then have the conversation with the person whose behaviour causes it, before involving anyone else.

question_text: You are a graduate in a Barclays technology team. Every incident gets a timeline entry, and the team’s monthly reliability figure counts only incidents that ran over thirty minutes. This morning’s outage ran forty minutes from the first alert. In the review, a colleague says the clock should really start when the alert was acknowledged, which would put the outage at twenty-five minutes, and he asks you to update the entry because you wrote it. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Agree with the colleague that the clock should start at acknowledgement from now on, leave this morning's forty minutes exactly as recorded, and settle the new basis between the two of you.
Leave the entry as it was recorded, and put the question of when the clock starts to the whole team, so any change to the rule applies to every incident rather than this one.
Leave the incident timing exactly as it was, and stay out of the review discussion, since the monthly reliability figure belongs to the team leader rather than to you.
Amend the timeline entry so the outage records as twenty-five minutes, and tell the colleague it is done before the monthly figures are pulled tomorrow morning.
explanation: A: Settles a shared rule between two people: the timing basis feeds a measure the whole team is judged on, so a definition agreed privately with the person who asked for it is not a definition the team has adopted. C: Sits out a question the team is actually asking: when the clock should start is a fair thing to settle, and the person who wrote the entry is the one with something useful to say. D: Alters a record so a measure clears its threshold: the outage lasted forty minutes whatever the entry now says, and the reliability figure stops describing the month it is reporting on. The most effective response is to leave the entry as recorded and put the question of when the clock starts to the whole team. The measure only means something if the rule is the same for every incident, and a definition worth changing is worth changing in the open and in advance. It beats agreeing the new basis privately with the colleague and leaving this morning’s forty minutes as recorded, because a rule two people settle between themselves is not a rule the team has adopted. It beats leaving the timing exactly as it was and staying out of the discussion, because the question of when the clock starts is a reasonable one and you are the person who wrote the entry. The least effective response is to amend the entry so the outage records as twenty-five minutes. Agreeing the change between yourselves and saying nothing are both weak, but neither makes the record untrue, whereas an amended entry means the monthly figure no longer describes what happened. The principle: argue about the rule in front of the team, and never settle the argument by editing the record it is measured from.

question_text: You are an analyst on a Barclays transaction team. Another analyst and you have produced different working capital figures for the same client pack, and she has told you flatly that yours is wrong and that she is not changing hers. The associate wants one figure in the deck for a client call in an hour. Neither of you has been back through the assumptions behind the two versions, and you and she are on this deal together for another month. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Present the two figures as settled to the associate and put her number in the deck, so that the argument does not reach him in the hour before the client call.
Go through the two models with her on the assumptions where they differ, settle what the client's own numbers support, and take anything still unresolved to the associate before the call.
Ask the associate to choose between the two figures now, explaining that you and she disagree and that the assumptions behind each version have not been compared yet.
Use her number in the deck for now, and go back through the two versions properly after the client call, when there is time to work through the assumptions.
explanation: A: States as fact something neither of you has checked: the associate is told the difference is closed when nobody has opened it, and the number goes to the client with a reconciliation behind it that never happened. C: Hands a technical difference upward as a dispute: the associate can pick a number but cannot know which assumptions are right, so an hour that could have closed the gap is spent choosing sides. D: Defers the reconciliation past the moment it counts: the figure the client hears is the one that mattered, and reopening it afterwards costs more than an hour of work now. The most effective response is to go through the two models with her on the assumptions where they differ, settle what the client’s own numbers support, and take anything still unresolved to the associate. It treats the disagreement as a question about assumptions rather than about who is right, it uses the hour that exists, and it leaves the associate a real decision if one is still needed. It beats asking the associate to choose between the two figures now, because he can pick a number but cannot know which assumptions stand behind it. It beats using her number for now and going back through the versions after the call, because the figure the client hears is the one that counts and unpicking it later is dearer than an hour today. The least effective response is to present the two figures to the associate as settled and put her number in the deck. Escalating early and deferring the work are both weaker uses of the hour, but neither tells anybody something untrue, whereas calling a difference closed that nobody has looked at puts an unchecked number in front of a client on your word. The principle: close a disagreement on the assumptions, and never close it by saying it is closed. Excellence, one of Barclays’ values, sets high standards for what we do, and an unreconciled figure in a client deck does not meet them.

question_text: You are a research analyst at Boston Consulting Group, three weeks into a benchmarking study for a retail client. A figure you put in the draft came from a source you have now found is five years out of date. The draft goes to the client tomorrow morning, and the figure is what the study’s main recommendation rests on. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Add a footnote to the draft saying the figure comes from an older source, and leave the recommendation itself exactly as it stands.
Leave the figure in the draft, and if the client asks about it, say it was checked against a current source.
Tell the manager running the study today, saying which figure it is and what is wrong with the source, so that the recommendation can be looked at again before the draft goes out.

Spend tonight looking for a current source that gives the same figure, and mention the problem to the manager in the morning only if you have not managed to find one that supports the study's recommendation by then.
explanation: A: Substitutes your own judgement for the manager's: a footnote records the weakness and quietly decides, on their behalf, that it does not change what the study recommends. B: Gives an assurance you cannot back: the other three leave the client able to find out what the figure rests on, and this one closes that off with a statement you know is untrue. D: Delays the decision: if tonight does not produce a source, the first anybody hears is on the morning the draft goes out, with no time to look at the recommendation again. The most effective response is to tell the manager running the study today which figure it is and what is wrong with the source. The figure is what the recommendation rests on, the manager owns that recommendation, and there is a day left in which it can be looked at again. It beats spending tonight looking for a current source and raising it in the morning only if you fail, because if tonight produces nothing then the problem surfaces on the morning the draft goes out, when nobody can do anything with it. It beats adding a footnote about the older source and leaving the recommendation as it stands, because a footnote decides for the manager that a weak source does not change the conclusion, which is exactly the judgement they should be making. The least effective response is leaving the figure in and telling the client it was checked against a current source: the other three all leave the client able to find out what the figure rests on, and this one shuts that off with a statement you know to be untrue, so a recommendation the client will act on is protected by a false assurance rather than by evidence. The principle: put a weakness in front of the person who owns the conclusion while they can still use it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Đếm số lượng đỉnh hoặc số lượng góc nhọn khi các hình có hình dạng biến thiên phức tạp.

question_text: You are a shared services administrator at Ashmere Trust. You process staff mileage claims. Last month you approved a claim of four hundred and twenty pounds when the correct figure, on the rates in force, was two hundred and ten; you used last year’s rate. The money has been paid. The claimant has not noticed. Nobody audits approved claims. Your team leader is in the office. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Email the claimant directly to explain the overpayment and ask them to repay the difference, without involving anybody else in the team.
Tell your team leader today what you approved and how it happened, and ask how the overpayment should be raised with the claimant.
Amend the claim record to show two hundred and ten pounds, and let the difference sit as an unexplained variance in next month's figures.
Correct the rate table you were working from and leave the paid claim alone, on the view that a single overpayment is not worth the trouble.
explanation: A: Acts alone on somebody else's money: a demand for two hundred and ten pounds arriving from one administrator, with nobody in the team aware, gives the claimant nothing to check it against. C: Amends a record to match what should have happened: the claimant keeps two hundred and ten pounds the rates do not allow, and the file now shows a correct claim that was never paid. D: Fixes the cause and ignores the effect: the rate table is right from now on, and public money that was overpaid stays overpaid because nobody would have noticed. The most effective response is to tell your team leader today what you approved and how it happened, and ask how the overpayment should be raised with the claimant: the error is yours, the money has gone, and how it is recovered from a member of staff has rules attached that she knows and you do not. It beats emailing the claimant directly to explain and ask for repayment, because a demand from one administrator gives them nothing to check it against. It beats correcting the rate table and leaving the paid claim alone, because a corrected table does nothing about money already paid. The least effective response is amending the claim record to show two hundred and ten pounds and letting the difference sit as a variance: the record shows the claim that should have been made rather than the one that was paid, so the overpayment becomes invisible to everybody. That makes it worse than the direct email, which is irregular but honest, and worse than fixing the table, which conceals nothing. The principle: correct the record to what happened, and take the consequence to whoever owns the rules for dealing with it.

question_text: You are a reporting analyst. A figure you circulated on Monday has been corrected, and the new number is materially lower. Two teams have been building next quarter’s plans on the old one since Tuesday, and one of them presents on Thursday. Correcting it publicly will be awkward for the colleague whose data caused the error. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Send both teams the corrected figure today with a short note on what changed, so the team presenting on Thursday can rework its plan before it stands up.
Send the corrected figure only to the team presenting on Thursday, and let the other team come across the change when they next look at the underlying report.
Tell both teams that the original figure came from your colleague's data and that this is the second time their numbers have caused a problem like this one for you.
Raise the correction at the reporting meeting next week, when the change can be explained properly to everybody who uses the figure at the same time.
explanation: B: Tells half the audience: both teams are planning on the same wrong number, and the one without a deadline is the one that will build on it for longest. C: Blames a colleague in front of the people who need the number: the teams still do not know what the corrected figure is, and the correction becomes an argument about who is at fault. D: Delays the decision: Thursday comes first, so the team with the deadline presents a plan built on a number you already know is wrong. The most effective response is to send both teams the corrected figure today with a short note on what changed: the correction is only useful before Thursday, both teams are exposed, and the note lets each of them judge what to redo. It beats sending it only to the team presenting on Thursday, because the other team is planning on the same wrong figure with more time to invest in it. It beats raising the correction at next week’s reporting meeting, because that is after the presentation the correction exists to protect. The least effective response is telling both teams the original figure came from your colleague’s data and that this is the second time: it turns a correction into an accusation, in front of people who still do not have the right number, and the thing they need never arrives. That is personalising it rather than communicating it badly. The principle: get the corrected number to everybody using it, in time to be worth having.

question_text: You are a stock control assistant at Cargill. The same line has shown a discrepancy at count on four occasions in six weeks, always in the same direction and always in the same area. Each time it has been written off as a counting error. You have now checked and the counts were done correctly. Discrepancies of this size and pattern are supposed to be reported to the loss prevention team. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Hand the four counts to the colleague who covers that area on Thursdays, since he knows the line better than you do, and consider your part in it finished.
Keep watching the line for another two counts to be sure the pattern is real, since four occasions could still turn out to be an unfortunate run of coincidences.
Raise it with your supervisor and let her decide whether it goes any further, without mentioning that the counts themselves have now been checked and are sound.
Report the four counts to the loss prevention team today with the checking you have done, since a pattern like that is what the reporting route exists for, and tell your supervisor.
explanation: A: Passes a reportable pattern on without owning it: the colleague has no idea it is four occurrences or that it should be reported, so the one person who knew both facts has stepped out of it. B: Waits for certainty that a report does not require: two more counts is three more weeks, and the threshold for reporting was passed some time ago. C: Escalates without the fact that changes the decision: she is asked to judge a pattern while the one thing that rules out a counting error is left out. The most effective response is to report the four counts to the loss prevention team today with your checking attached, and tell your supervisor you have done it: the pattern is exactly what the reporting route exists for, your checking is what makes it more than a suspicion, and nobody is surprised later. It beats waiting for two more counts, because the threshold was passed weeks ago and waiting adds three weeks. It beats raising it with your supervisor while leaving out that the counts were checked, because that is the fact the decision turns on. The least effective response is handing the four counts to the Thursday colleague and treating your part as finished: he does not know it is four occurrences or that it is reportable, so the only person holding both facts has stepped out, which is a different kind of wrong from waiting too long or from telling somebody too little. The principle: when something crosses a reporting line, take it there yourself, with what you know attached.
tip: Mẹo MT: Đếm số lượng đỉnh hoặc số lượng góc nhọn khi các hình có hình dạng biến thiên phức tạp.

question_text: You are a purchasing assistant at Campbell Soup Company. A supplier has rung to query a set of volumes that a colleague of yours prepared. You can see that your colleague’s numbers are right and that the supplier has misread the layout. He is impatient, has queried her figures before, and says he would rather deal with you from now on because she takes days to reply. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell him her figures are often unreliable and that he should bring the numbers to you in future, so that at least the queries get answered quickly.
Show him where the layout misled him, say the figures are right, and tell him you will pass on his point about reply times to her and your manager.
Answer the query yourself and agree to be his contact for volumes from now on, since he is clearly not going to deal with her and somebody has to answer him.
Tell him the volumes are her work and that he should take the query back to her, since it is her supplier and answering it yourself would cut across her.
explanation: A: Undermines a colleague to an outsider: her numbers were right, and a supplier is now told by her own team that her work cannot be trusted. C: Solves a relationship problem by rearranging it: she loses her own supplier contact without being consulted, and nobody addresses the reply times. D: Applies the boundary and ignores the customer: he is sent back to somebody he says takes days, holding a misreading you could have cleared up in a minute. The most effective response is to show him where the layout misled him, confirm the figures are right, and say you will pass his point about reply times to her and your manager: the query is answered on the spot, your colleague’s work is defended because it is correct, and the real complaint goes somewhere it can be dealt with. It beats agreeing to become his contact, because that quietly takes her supplier away without asking her. It beats sending him back to her with his misreading intact, because it costs a minute to clear up. The least effective response is telling him her figures are often unreliable: they were right, and a supplier has been told by her own team not to trust her, which is a different kind of wrong from over-accommodating him or from standing on the boundary. The principle: defend a colleague’s correct work to an outsider, and take the criticism of her that has substance to her and your manager instead.
tip: Mẹo MT: Loại trừ nhanh các phương án vi phạm quy tắc xoay góc chiều kim đồng hồ.

question_text: You are a relationship support assistant. In a client meeting your colleague gives a figure you know is a month out of date. The client writes it down. The meeting has twenty minutes left and the figure matters to what the client decides today. Correcting it means saying so while they are both sitting there. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Correct the figure by blaming his preparation in front of the client, saying that this is exactly why the numbers ought to be checked before anybody walks into a meeting.
Say plainly that the figure has moved since then, give the current one, and take up how it came to be quoted with your colleague after the meeting.
Pass your colleague a note about the figure and leave it entirely to him to decide whether he corrects it in front of the client or not.
Say nothing at all while the meeting is still running and send the client a corrected figure by email afterwards, so that nothing has to be said in front of your colleague.
explanation: A: Makes a stale figure a verdict on a colleague in front of a client: the correction lands, and what the client remembers is that your firm's people do not trust each other. C: Gives the decision to the person least able to take it: he has just given the number and would have to unsay it himself, mid-meeting. D: Leaves the client deciding on a stale number: they have twenty minutes and a decision, and the email arrives after both. The most effective response is to say plainly that the figure has moved since then, give the current one, and take up how it came to be quoted after the meeting: the client is about to decide on it, a month-old figure is a fact rather than a fault, and taking the preparation up afterwards keeps it between the two of you. It beats saying nothing and emailing the client a corrected figure afterwards, because the decision happens inside the twenty minutes. It beats passing him a note and leaving it to him to correct in front of the client, because asking him to unsay it himself in the room is the hardest possible way to fix it. The least effective response is correcting it by blaming his preparation in front of the client: the number is fixed and the firm looks divided. That is personalising it rather than mistiming it or misrouting it. The principle: correct the fact in the room, and take the person outside it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Đếm số lượng đỉnh hoặc số lượng góc nhọn khi các hình có hình dạng biến thiên phức tạp.

question_text: You are a new enquiries adviser. A colleague on the same desk has twice taken enquiries that were passed to you while you were on another call, and both became instructions credited to him. He says he was only keeping the callers from waiting. The team’s figures are reviewed monthly. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Speak to him directly, say what you have noticed on both occasions, and agree between you what should happen to a transferred enquiry when the person it was passed to is busy.
Ask two others on the desk, behind his back, whether he has done the same to them, so that you know whether this is a pattern before you decide what to do about it.
Let it go on the basis that his explanation is reasonable, and make a point of getting to transferred calls faster yourself so that the situation does not come up again.
Raise it with your team leader before the monthly review and ask her to look at how the two enquiries were credited, given what was happening when each of them came in.
explanation: B: Canvasses colleagues behind his back: it collects a view of a person from people who were not involved, so by the time he is asked anything the desk has already made up its mind about him. C: Prioritises harmony over honesty: it accepts an explanation without testing it and puts the whole remedy on you, so the same thing happens the next time you are on a long call. D: Escalates before speaking to him: it turns a two-person question into a management one without him ever being asked, and does so shortly before the figures that make it worth something to you. The most effective response is to speak to him directly, say what you noticed on both occasions, and agree what should happen to a transferred enquiry when the person it went to is busy. There is a real question about transferred enquiries and a real question about credit, and both are answerable in one conversation. It beats letting it go and getting to transferred calls faster yourself, because his explanation has not been tested and the remedy it accepts is entirely yours. It beats raising it with your team leader before the monthly review, because a manager is the right destination only once he has been asked. The least effective response is asking two others on the desk whether he has done the same to them: it gathers opinion about him from people with no part in it, so the desk forms a view before he has said a word. That is a different kind of wrong from the other two, neither of which involves anybody who was not already in the situation. The principle: ask the person first, and never build a case about them among people who were not there.
tip: Mẹo MT: Loại trừ nhanh các phương án vi phạm quy tắc xoay góc chiều kim đồng hồ.

question_text: You are a disclosure assistant. Your team records the number of documents each person reviews per day and reports the totals to the client each Friday. You have been slower this week because a batch you were given is unusually complex. Your team leader asks you for your figures before she sends the report. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Give her the number and tell her why it is lower this week, so that whatever she sends the client carries the reason along with the figure.
Record a higher figure for the last two days than you actually reviewed, since you will make the difference up next week and the client only ever sees the weekly total.
Give her the number without comment, on the basis that she has the same view of the batches as you do and can see for herself why the week looks like this.
Ask her to leave your figures out of this week's report until the complex batch is finished, so that the client sees a fair picture rather than an unusual week.
explanation: B: Alters a record: it puts a number into the client's report that describes work nobody has done, and it does so in the one system anybody would later use to check. C: Assumes the context is obvious: she is about to send the figure onwards and may not have looked at what was in your batch, so the reason travels only if you send it with the number. D: Removes the awkward data: a report with a person missing invites exactly the question it was meant to avoid, and it treats an unusual week as something to be hidden rather than explained. The most effective response is to give her the number and tell her why it is lower this week, so whatever she sends the client carries the reason along with the figure. It beats giving her the number without comment because she can see the batches herself, since she is the person sending it on and cannot supply a context she has not been given. It beats asking her to leave your figures out of this week’s report, because leaving a name out is more conspicuous than a low number with an explanation. The least effective response is recording a higher figure for the last two days than you actually reviewed: it changes what the record says happened, which is a different kind of wrong from the other two because both of those report a true number badly and this one reports a false one. The principle: send the number with its reason, and never make the number say something else.
tip: Mẹo MT: Kiểm tra quy luật cộng/trừ hình (XOR pattern) theo hàng ngang trước, nếu không thỏa mãn thì xét theo cột dọc.

question_text: You are a compliance assistant. Your team reports each month how many new files had their checks completed before work started. One of this month’s files had its check completed the day after work began, because the fee earner was told the wrong thing by somebody else. Your team leader asks for the figures. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Record the check as completed before work started, since the check was done and the reason it was a day late had nothing to do with the fee earner or with the compliance team.
Give her the figure with the exception shown, and leave the explanation to whoever asks about it, since the numbers are what the report is for.
Give her the figure with the exception shown and a line explaining that the fee earner was given wrong information, so the report carries the cause as well as the count.
Ask her whether the one late file needs to be in the figures at all, given that it was caused by something outside the process the report is meant to measure.
explanation: A: Marks a file as compliant when it was not: the whole point of the figure is that it counts checks done before work began, and a file recorded as fine removes the only trace of what went wrong. B: Reports the number without its cause: the exception will be read as a fee earner ignoring a check, and the thing that actually needs fixing is somebody giving out wrong information. D: Invites the data to be trimmed: the report measures whether checks were done before work started, and this one was not, whatever the reason. The most effective response is to give her the figure with the exception shown and a line explaining that the fee earner was given wrong information. The figure is what it is, and the one line is what turns an apparent breach into something the firm can act on. It beats giving her the figure with the exception shown and leaving the explanation to whoever asks, because an unexplained exception will be read as the wrong kind of failure. It beats asking whether the one late file needs to be in the figures at all, because the measure is about what happened, not about whose fault it was. The least effective response is recording the check as completed before work started: it records the file as compliant when it was not, which is a different kind of wrong from the other two because both of those leave the exception visible. The principle: report the exception and its cause together, and never make the record say the exception did not happen.
tip: Mẹo MT: Loại trừ nhanh các phương án vi phạm quy tắc xoay góc chiều kim đồng hồ.

question_text: You are a reporting analyst. A return that goes to the firm’s largest client is due at noon, and the contract charges the firm for a late or incomplete one. One figure is still missing. The approved route is a signed data extract from another team, which takes a day. The figure is also on a dashboard that is not an approved source for this return. Your manager is in a meeting until 11:30. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Put a note to your manager now setting out the gap, the two routes and the noon deadline, so they can decide at 11:30 with everything in front of them.
Submit the return at noon with the figure left blank, and follow up with the missing number once the signed extract arrives tomorrow.
Interrupt your manager's meeting now to get a decision, since a regulator deadline at noon outranks whatever else is being discussed in there this morning.
Take the figure from the dashboard and put it in the return, since the number will be the same either way and the deadline is the thing that actually matters here.
explanation: B: Files an incomplete return without asking: whether a gap or a late charge is the better outcome on a contracted return is a decision above your level. C: Escalates before there is anything to decide with: the meeting ends at 11:30, which still leaves half an hour, and the options can be set out first. D: Decides which rules count: an approved-source rule exists precisely so a regulator-facing figure can be traced, and a deadline is not a reason for one person to set it aside alone. The most effective response is to put a note to your manager now setting out the gap, the two routes and the noon deadline, so she can decide at 11:30 with everything in front of her: the decision is genuinely hers, 11:30 leaves time, and a written note means she decides on the facts rather than a doorway summary. It beats submitting the return at noon with the figure left blank, because choosing a gap over a late charge is not a junior call. It beats interrupting her meeting now to get a decision, because half an hour is enough and the interruption buys nothing. The least effective response is taking the figure from the dashboard and putting it in the return: an unapproved source goes into a return the client relies on, on one person’s judgement that the number is probably the same. That is setting aside a stated control rather than escalating badly. The principle: when the only route to the deadline breaks a rule, the deadline is somebody else’s decision.
tip: Mẹo MT: Loại trừ nhanh các phương án vi phạm quy tắc xoay góc chiều kim đồng hồ.

question_text: You work in an HR shared service team. It is Wednesday. Three things are outstanding: a new starter’s contract must go out today or she cannot begin on Monday, a manager wants a report on absence figures by Friday, and a colleague has asked you to review her draft policy whenever you have time. The contract takes an hour, the report three hours. You have five hours left today. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Work through all three in the order they were asked for, and let your manager know at the end of the day if anything has not been finished.
Start the absence report because it is the longest job, then do the contract at the end of the day once the bulk of the report is behind you.
Do the contract and the policy review first because they are the two shorter jobs, then start the absence report and continue it tomorrow morning.
Send the new starter's contract first, then work on the absence report, and tell your colleague you will review her policy tomorrow.
explanation: A: Hides the problem / silent deadline slip: the contract is the one item that cannot slip, and reporting at the end of the day is after the point at which anyone could rescue it. Reporting a missed deadline once it is missed is not communication. B: Delays the decision: it leaves an hour-long task with a today-or- never deadline to the end of a five-hour day, so any overrun on the report costs the new starter her start date. C: Splits effort so nothing finishes: it fits the favour in ahead of a report with a named Friday deadline, and pushes three hours of work into a day that already has other demands. The most effective response is to send the new starter’s contract first, then work on the absence report, and tell your colleague the policy review waits until tomorrow: only the contract has a deadline of today with a consequence attached, a start date, and it takes one of the five hours available. That leaves four hours for a three-hour report due Friday, and the policy review has no deadline at all. It beats starting the absence report first because it is the longest job, since that puts a fixed, unrecoverable deadline behind an open-ended one. It beats doing the contract and the policy review first as the two shorter jobs, because that fits an unscheduled favour ahead of a report with a stated deadline. The least effective response is working through all three in the order they were asked for and reporting at the end of the day: it works to the order things were asked in rather than to their deadlines, and reports the failure only once the new starter’s Monday cannot be saved. That is worse than the other two, which sequence badly but at least do the contract today. The principle: identify the task that cannot slip, do it first, and say early which of the others will move.
tip: Mẹo MT: Kiểm tra quy luật cộng/trừ hình (XOR pattern) theo hàng ngang trước, nếu không thỏa mãn thì xét theo cột dọc.

question_text: You are a stock control assistant at Boots. A weekly count shows three hundred units fewer than the system expects on one line. The trading team needs a figure this afternoon to decide what to order for next week, and they have asked you whether the count can be relied on. Investigating the gap properly means pulling the movement history, which takes about two hours. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Give the trading team the counted figure with the gap stated alongside it, say the cause is not yet known, and start on the movement history straight away.
Assure the trading team that the counted figure is sound and the gap is a scanning error, and look at the movement history later in the week if anybody comes back to you.
Hold the figure back until the movement history is finished, and tell the trading team they will have something reliable by the end of the day.
Give the trading team the figure the system holds rather than the counted one, since the system is what their ordering tool reads from in any case.
explanation: B: Gives an assurance you have not earned: nothing yet distinguishes a scanning error from three hundred missing units, and next week's order is placed on a cause that was invented to close the question. C: Delays the decision: the order has to be placed this afternoon, so a reliable number tomorrow is worth less to them than an honest one now. D: Substitutes the convenient source for the checked one: the count is the only evidence anybody has looked at, and it is the number being set aside. The most effective response is to give the trading team the counted figure with the gap stated alongside it and start on the movement history at once: they get a number in time to order, they know exactly how much weight it carries, and the work that settles the cause begins immediately. It beats holding the figure until the history is finished, because the decision is this afternoon and an honest number now beats a certain one tomorrow. It beats handing over the system figure instead, because the count is the only thing anybody has actually observed. The least effective response is assuring them the count is sound and the gap is a scanning error: no work has been done that could support either claim, and stating a cause you have not established is a different kind of wrong from being slow or from choosing the wrong source. The principle: report what you know and what you do not, rather than supplying the certainty the person asking would prefer.
tip: Mẹo MT: Đếm số lượng đỉnh hoặc số lượng góc nhọn khi các hình có hình dạng biến thiên phức tạp.

question_text: You are a purchasing assistant at Boots. A supplier has rung to query a set of volumes that a colleague of yours prepared. You can see that your colleague’s numbers are right and that the supplier has misread the layout. He is impatient, has queried her figures before, and says he would rather deal with you from now on because she takes days to reply. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell him her figures are often unreliable and that he should bring the numbers to you in future, so that at least the queries get answered quickly.
Show him where the layout misled him, say the figures are right, and tell him you will pass on his point about reply times to her and your manager.
Answer the query yourself and agree to be his contact for volumes from now on, since he is clearly not going to deal with her and somebody has to answer him.
Tell him the volumes are her work and that he should take the query back to her, since it is her supplier and answering it yourself would cut across her.
explanation: A: Undermines a colleague to an outsider: her numbers were right, and a supplier is now told by her own team that her work cannot be trusted. C: Solves a relationship problem by rearranging it: she loses her own supplier contact without being consulted, and nobody addresses the reply times. D: Applies the boundary and ignores the customer: he is sent back to somebody he says takes days, holding a misreading you could have cleared up in a minute. The most effective response is to show him where the layout misled him, confirm the figures are right, and say you will pass his point about reply times to her and your manager: the query is answered on the spot, your colleague’s work is defended because it is correct, and the real complaint goes somewhere it can be dealt with. It beats agreeing to become his contact, because that quietly takes her supplier away without asking her. It beats sending him back to her with his misreading intact, because it costs a minute to clear up. The least effective response is telling him her figures are often unreliable: they were right, and a supplier has been told by her own team not to trust her, which is a different kind of wrong from over-accommodating him or from standing on the boundary. The principle: defend a colleague’s correct work to an outsider, and take the criticism of her that has substance to her and your manager instead.
tip: Mẹo MT: Loại trừ nhanh các phương án vi phạm quy tắc xoay góc chiều kim đồng hồ.

question_text: You are a stock control assistant at Boots. A recount you asked for turned up a mistake in your own figures, and the colleague who did it said, in front of two others, that he had wasted an afternoon on your arithmetic. It stung and he was largely right. The next count is due on Thursday and it needs two people, one of whom is normally him. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Ask your supervisor to put somebody else on Thursday's count, since working alongside him this week would be uncomfortable for both of you after what was said.
Refuse to work with him on Thursday's count after the way he spoke to you, and say you would rather do it on your own or not at all.
Acknowledge to him that the figures were wrong and say what you have changed, and do Thursday's count with him as planned since the count needs two people.
Say nothing about it, do Thursday's count as planned, and let the remark fade rather than reopening something that was fair comment anyway.
explanation: A: Redesigns the rota around one awkward afternoon: the count is harder to staff, and the two of you have to work together again the week after in any case. B: Withdraws from a job that needs two people after a disagreement: Thursday's count is put at risk to answer a remark made about an afternoon. D: Lets an unrepaired working relationship stand: the count happens and he has no reason to think the mistake will not simply repeat. The most effective response is to acknowledge that the figures were wrong, say what you have changed, and do Thursday’s count with him: the criticism was largely fair, saying so is what restores the working relationship, and the count that needs two people gets them. It beats asking for somebody else on Thursday, because the rota is rearranged around one bad afternoon and you will work together next week anyway. It beats letting the remark fade, because he has no reason to expect anything different next time. The least effective response is refusing to work with him on Thursday: a count that needs two people is put at risk to answer a remark, which is a different kind of wrong from avoiding him or from staying silent. The principle: when the criticism is fair, own it and stay in the work with the person who made it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Loại trừ nhanh các phương án vi phạm quy tắc xoay góc chiều kim đồng hồ.

question_text: You are a shared services administrator at Ashmere Trust. You process staff mileage claims. Last month you approved a claim of four hundred and twenty pounds when the correct figure, on the rates in force, was two hundred and ten; you used last year’s rate. The money has been paid. The claimant has not noticed. Nobody audits approved claims. Your team leader is in the office. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Email the claimant directly to explain the overpayment and ask them to repay the difference, without involving anybody else in the team.
Tell your team leader today what you approved and how it happened, and ask how the overpayment should be raised with the claimant.
Amend the claim record to show two hundred and ten pounds, and let the difference sit as an unexplained variance in next month's figures.
Correct the rate table you were working from and leave the paid claim alone, on the view that a single overpayment is not worth the trouble.
explanation: A: Acts alone on somebody else's money: a demand for two hundred and ten pounds arriving from one administrator, with nobody in the team aware, gives the claimant nothing to check it against. C: Amends a record to match what should have happened: the claimant keeps two hundred and ten pounds the rates do not allow, and the file now shows a correct claim that was never paid. D: Fixes the cause and ignores the effect: the rate table is right from now on, and public money that was overpaid stays overpaid because nobody would have noticed. The most effective response is to tell your team leader today what you approved and how it happened, and ask how the overpayment should be raised with the claimant: the error is yours, the money has gone, and how it is recovered from a member of staff has rules attached that she knows and you do not. It beats emailing the claimant directly to explain and ask for repayment, because a demand from one administrator gives them nothing to check it against. It beats correcting the rate table and leaving the paid claim alone, because a corrected table does nothing about money already paid. The least effective response is amending the claim record to show two hundred and ten pounds and letting the difference sit as a variance: the record shows the claim that should have been made rather than the one that was paid, so the overpayment becomes invisible to everybody. That makes it worse than the direct email, which is irregular but honest, and worse than fixing the table, which conceals nothing. The principle: correct the record to what happened, and take the consequence to whoever owns the rules for dealing with it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân tích theo từng thuộc tính độc lập: Hướng xoay góc (90°/45°), số lượng nét, màu sắc (Đen/Trắng), và vị trí.

question_text: You are a trainee solicitor. Checking a draft agreement before it goes to the client, you notice a figure that does not match the one in the instructions on the file. Your supervisor is in a meeting for another hour and the draft is due to go out at noon, which is in forty minutes. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Correct the figure in the draft to match the instructions on the file, since the instructions are what the client asked for and the draft is plainly the one that has gone wrong.
Send the draft out at noon and say nothing about the difference, since the deadline was given for a reason and the figure can be corrected in the next version if it turns out to be wrong.
Hold the draft, and use the forty minutes to look through the file for anything that explains which of the two figures is the right one.
Get a note into your supervisor's meeting saying the draft has a figure that does not match the instructions, and ask whether to hold it past noon or send it as it is.
explanation: A: Substitutes own judgement for the supervisor's: the instructions may be the thing that is out of date, and a figure changed by somebody who has not been told which is right is a guess in a document. B: Withholds information somebody needed: the client receives a figure nobody has checked, and the one person who noticed the discrepancy has decided the deadline matters more than the doubt. C: Delays telling anybody: the search is sensible and it uses up the whole margin without your supervisor knowing there is a question, so she comes out of her meeting to a missed deadline. The most effective response is to get a note into your supervisor’s meeting saying the draft has a figure that does not match the instructions, and ask whether to hold it past noon. You cannot resolve the discrepancy and she can, and a note into a meeting takes seconds where forty minutes of searching may take you nowhere. It beats correcting the figure in the draft to match the instructions on the file, because you do not know which figure is right. It beats holding the draft and searching the file for forty minutes, because searching without telling her spends the whole margin on your own. The least effective response is sending the draft at noon and saying nothing about the difference: it sends the client a figure known to be doubtful and tells nobody, which is a different kind of wrong from the other two because both of those keep the problem inside the firm. The principle: when you cannot resolve it and somebody can, the time you have is for reaching them.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân tích theo từng thuộc tính độc lập: Hướng xoay góc (90°/45°), số lượng nét, màu sắc (Đen/Trắng), và vị trí.

question_text: You are a paralegal. You have been asked to complete two schedules by five today. At two you realise the second one needs a figure from the client, who does not usually reply the same day. The fee earner who asked for them is in the building. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Finish both schedules using an estimate for the missing figure, and mark that figure clearly as provisional until the client confirms it.
Email the client asking for the figure, finish the first schedule, and let the fee earner find out at five which of the two is ready and which is not.
Ring the client repeatedly through the afternoon until you get the figure, leaving the first schedule until you have it so that both can be finished together.
Email the client, finish the first schedule, and tell the fee earner now that the second depends on a reply that may not come today.
explanation: A: Fills a gap with a number nobody gave you: a schedule containing an estimate is not the schedule that was asked for, and a provisional marking is easy to lose once it is passed on. B: Leaves somebody to discover it at the deadline: he is in the building all afternoon, and at five the options he had at two, including asking the client himself, have all gone. C: Stakes everything on the uncertain half: the schedule you could certainly deliver is put at risk for one that depends on somebody who may not answer today. The most effective response is to email the client, finish the first schedule, and tell the fee earner now that the second depends on a reply that may not come today. Everything you can do is done, the client is asked, and he learns at two rather than five, when he can still chase them himself. It beats finishing both schedules using an estimate for the missing figure, because an estimated figure is not the figure. It beats ringing the client repeatedly and leaving the first schedule until you have the number, because that risks the one that was certain. The least effective response is emailing the client, finishing the first schedule, and letting him find out at five: it produces the same work as the best answer and tells him nothing, so he discovers it when nothing can be done. That is a different kind of wrong from the other two, both of which at least leave him with something at five. The principle: when a commitment starts to depend on somebody else, say so while there is still afternoon left.
tip: Mẹo MT: Kiểm tra quy luật cộng/trừ hình (XOR pattern) theo hàng ngang trước, nếu không thỏa mãn thì xét theo cột dọc.

question_text: You are a billing assistant. Your team reports to the partners each month how many bills went out within five days of the month end. Two of yours went out on the seventh day because a fee earner was away. Your team leader asks you for your figures for the report this afternoon. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Record the two bills as sent on the fifth day, since the delay was not anything you did and the figure would otherwise say something about you that is not true.
Give her the real dates and the reason for the two late ones, so she can decide whether the report should say anything about fee earners being away.
Give her the real dates without any explanation, since she can see the absences on the team calendar and will work out why those two sat waiting.
Ask her to leave your figures out of this month's report, so that two unrepresentative bills do not distort what the partners see about the team's performance.
explanation: A: Alters the record: the report will then describe two bills that went out on a day they did not, and the reason the delay is worth knowing about disappears with the correction. C: Assumes the context travels: the calendar is not in front of her when she writes the report, so the two late bills reach the partners as two late bills and nothing else. D: Removes the awkward data: a report with a name missing raises the question it was meant to avoid, and the absence that caused the delay stays invisible either way. The most effective response is to give her the real dates and the reason for the two late ones, so she can decide whether the report should mention fee earners being away. The dates are what they are, and whether they are read fairly depends on the reason travelling with them, which is her decision rather than yours. It beats giving her the real dates without any explanation, because a team calendar is not in front of somebody writing a report. It beats asking her to leave your figures out this month, because taking a name out is more conspicuous than explaining two days. The least effective response is recording the two bills as sent on the fifth day: it changes what the record says happened, which is a different kind of wrong from the other two because both of those report true dates badly. The principle: report the number with its reason, and never make the number say something else.

question_text: You are a trading assistant at Compass Online. A large account has queried a charge on last month’s invoice. You have pulled the figures and can see the charge is correct, but the reason it changed is a contract term you do not fully understand. The account manager is out today. The customer wants an answer before the end of the week, and it is Wednesday. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Reply with the figures you have checked and what they show, say that the contract point needs the account manager, and book time with him for tomorrow morning.
Explain the contract term to the customer as best you understand it, and say you will confirm it with the account manager tomorrow.
Send the query on to the account team without the figures you have already checked, and let them start the contract point again from the beginning.
Reply to the customer that the charge is correct and leave the reason for the account manager to explain when he is back in the office tomorrow.
explanation: B: Answers outside what you actually know: an approximate account of a contract term is the thing most likely to be quoted back at the business later. C: Passes the problem on stripped of the work already done: the account team starts from nothing, the day you have spent on it is wasted, and Friday is two days away. D: Answers the easy half only: the customer did not ask whether the charge was right, they asked why it changed, and that is the part being deferred. The most effective response is to reply with the figures you have checked and what they show, say the contract point needs the account manager, and book time with him for tomorrow: the customer sees progress and an honest boundary, the checking work is used, and Friday is still comfortably reachable. It beats explaining the contract term as best you understand it, because an approximation about a contract is exactly the sentence that gets quoted back later. It beats replying that the charge is correct and leaving the reason to the account manager, because the reason is what was asked. The least effective response is sending the query on without the figures you have already checked: the next person starts from nothing, a day of work disappears, and the deadline is two days out, which is a different kind of wrong from over-reaching or from answering only half. The principle: escalate the part you cannot answer, with the part you can attached to it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Đếm số lượng đỉnh hoặc số lượng góc nhọn khi các hình có hình dạng biến thiên phức tạp.

question_text: You are a reporting analyst. A figure you circulated on Monday has been corrected, and the new number is materially lower. Two teams have been building next quarter’s plans on the old one since Tuesday, and one of them presents on Thursday. Correcting it publicly will be awkward for the colleague whose data caused the error. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Send both teams the corrected figure today with a short note on what changed, so the team presenting on Thursday can rework its plan before it stands up.
Send the corrected figure only to the team presenting on Thursday, and let the other team come across the change when they next look at the underlying report.
Tell both teams that the original figure came from your colleague's data and that this is the second time their numbers have caused a problem like this one for you.
Raise the correction at the reporting meeting next week, when the change can be explained properly to everybody who uses the figure at the same time.
explanation: B: Tells half the audience: both teams are planning on the same wrong number, and the one without a deadline is the one that will build on it for longest. C: Blames a colleague in front of the people who need the number: the teams still do not know what the corrected figure is, and the correction becomes an argument about who is at fault. D: Delays the decision: Thursday comes first, so the team with the deadline presents a plan built on a number you already know is wrong. The most effective response is to send both teams the corrected figure today with a short note on what changed: the correction is only useful before Thursday, both teams are exposed, and the note lets each of them judge what to redo. It beats sending it only to the team presenting on Thursday, because the other team is planning on the same wrong figure with more time to invest in it. It beats raising the correction at next week’s reporting meeting, because that is after the presentation the correction exists to protect. The least effective response is telling both teams the original figure came from your colleague’s data and that this is the second time: it turns a correction into an accusation, in front of people who still do not have the right number, and the thing they need never arrives. That is personalising it rather than communicating it badly. The principle: get the corrected number to everybody using it, in time to be worth having.
tip: Mẹo MT: Đếm số lượng đỉnh hoặc số lượng góc nhọn khi các hình có hình dạng biến thiên phức tạp.

question_text: You are a brand assistant at CVS Online. A campaign you have worked on for six weeks goes live on Friday. This morning the insight team found that the headline figure it quotes is wrong. Your manager, who signs the copy off, is away until Thursday, and the printer needs final wording by Wednesday lunchtime. You have never had to unpick something this late and you feel out of your depth. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Ask the printer to hold the slot for a week so the figure can be checked properly, and tell the insight team that the campaign date has moved.
Take the error to your manager's manager first thing, before you have spoken to the insight team, so that somebody senior owns the decision about the wording.
Leave the copy as it stands until your manager is back on Thursday, on the grounds that approving the wording belongs to them rather than to you.
Agree the corrected figure with the insight team this morning and send the amended wording for approval today, so that the print deadline is met with a figure that is right.
explanation: A: Delays the decision: the campaign has a fixed live date on Friday, and moving the print slot spends a week the schedule does not have. B: Escalates prematurely: the correction is an afternoon's work with the insight team, and taking it upwards first turns a fixable error into a decision nobody senior needs to make. C: Waits for an authority four days away: the Wednesday cut-off passes while nothing happens, and the wrong figure reaches customers because nobody decided anything at all. The most effective response is to agree the corrected figure with the insight team this morning and send the amended wording for approval today: the error is fixable inside the two days that are left, and doing it now protects both the print cut-off and your manager’s sign-off. It beats asking the printer to hold the slot for a week, because the campaign has a live date on Friday and the schedule cannot absorb a week. It beats taking the error to your manager’s manager first thing, because a correction the insight team can make in an afternoon does not need a senior decision, and going upwards first spends time the Wednesday cut-off does not have. The least effective response is leaving the copy as it stands until Thursday: it is the only response that lets the cut-off pass with nothing done, so the wrong figure goes out by default. Waiting for the usual signatory is a decision here, and it is the one that cannot be undone afterwards. The principle: when the pressure is real and the fix is inside your reach, act inside the time you have rather than wait for the person who normally decides.

question_text: You are a procurement graduate at CVS Online. Working through delivery notes for a different piece of work, you find that one supplier’s notes have been recording pack sizes that do not match what is actually arriving, and have done for at least six weeks. Nobody has raised it. The supplier is being reviewed in a fortnight, and the pack sizes feed the figures that review uses. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Correct the pack sizes in the figures yourself for the six weeks that you can see, so that the review in a fortnight at least starts from numbers that match what was delivered.
Pass the whole thing to the manager who owns the supplier relationship without mentioning the review in a fortnight, and treat your part as finished.
Raise it at the review itself in a fortnight, when the supplier and the manager are both in the room and the pack sizes are on the agenda anyway.
Take it to the manager who owns the supplier today with the six weeks set out, say what it does to the review's figures, and offer to check how far back it goes.
explanation: A: Alters figures nobody asked you to alter: the numbers stop matching the notes that produced them, and the recording fault that caused it is now invisible to the person accountable for the supplier. B: Hands a finding on without what makes it urgent: the manager receives six weeks of notes with no mention of the review that is about to use them. C: Times the disclosure for the meeting it should have preceded: the review is prepared on figures everybody now knows are wrong, and the correction lands as a surprise. The most effective response is to take it to the manager who owns the supplier today with the six weeks set out, say what it does to the review’s figures, and offer to check how far back it goes: it reaches the person who can act while a fortnight is still enough time, and it carries the consequence rather than only the observation. It beats passing it across without mentioning the review, because the manager cannot act on a deadline nobody has told him about. It beats raising it at the review, because the preparation everybody does beforehand is built on figures already known to be false. The least effective response is correcting the pack sizes in the figures yourself: the numbers stop matching the notes behind them, the supplier carries on recording the wrong sizes, and the person accountable for that supplier can no longer see any of it, which is a different kind of wrong from handing the finding on bare or from raising it too late. The principle: something you found outside your own remit is carried to somebody who can act on it, with what it means attached, and never quietly repaired.
tip: Mẹo MT: Kiểm tra quy luật cộng/trừ hình (XOR pattern) theo hàng ngang trước, nếu không thỏa mãn thì xét theo cột dọc.

question_text: You are a billing assistant. Two fee earners have each told you the other is responsible for a bill that has not gone out, and each has asked you to say so if the month-end figures are queried. The bill is now three weeks late and the client has asked about it. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell the month-end review, if it comes up, that neither of them has taken responsibility, so that the record shows what actually happened rather than either account.
Ask them both for ten minutes, put the client's question and the three weeks in front of them, and ask which of them will get the bill out this week.
Draft the bill yourself and send it to both of them for approval, since the client is waiting and somebody has to break the stalemate before month end.
Blame each of them to the other in front of the billing team, so that they both understand the position and can settle who is responsible between themselves.
explanation: A: Answers a question nobody has asked yet: it prepares a position for a meeting instead of getting the bill out, and the client is still waiting either way. C: Works around the stalemate: the bill may go out and the question of who owns it is left exactly as it was, so the next one stalls the same way. D: Carries private remarks between colleagues: it makes the argument about the two of them rather than about a bill the client is waiting on, and neither can unhear what the other said. The most effective response is to ask them both for ten minutes, put the client’s question and the three weeks in front of them, and ask which of them will get the bill out this week. Those are facts neither disputes, and putting both in front of them together turns a blame exchange into a decision. It beats drafting the bill yourself and sending it to both for approval, because drafting round them leaves ownership unresolved. It beats telling the month-end review that neither has taken responsibility, because a bill is still not out. The least effective response is blaming each of them to the other in front of the billing team: it relays each account to the other, so a late bill becomes a quarrel. That is a different kind of wrong from the other two, neither of which repeats anything anybody said. The principle: put the shared fact in front of both, and never carry remarks between them.
