question_text: You are a disclosure assistant. Your team records the number of documents each person reviews per day and reports the totals to the client each Friday. You have been slower this week because a batch you were given is unusually complex. Your team leader asks you for your figures before she sends the report. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Give her the number and tell her why it is lower this week, so that whatever she sends the client carries the reason along with the figure.
Record a higher figure for the last two days than you actually reviewed, since you will make the difference up next week and the client only ever sees the weekly total.
Give her the number without comment, on the basis that she has the same view of the batches as you do and can see for herself why the week looks like this.
Ask her to leave your figures out of this week's report until the complex batch is finished, so that the client sees a fair picture rather than an unusual week.
explanation: B: Alters a record: it puts a number into the client's report that describes work nobody has done, and it does so in the one system anybody would later use to check. C: Assumes the context is obvious: she is about to send the figure onwards and may not have looked at what was in your batch, so the reason travels only if you send it with the number. D: Removes the awkward data: a report with a person missing invites exactly the question it was meant to avoid, and it treats an unusual week as something to be hidden rather than explained. The most effective response is to give her the number and tell her why it is lower this week, so whatever she sends the client carries the reason along with the figure. It beats giving her the number without comment because she can see the batches herself, since she is the person sending it on and cannot supply a context she has not been given. It beats asking her to leave your figures out of this week’s report, because leaving a name out is more conspicuous than a low number with an explanation. The least effective response is recording a higher figure for the last two days than you actually reviewed: it changes what the record says happened, which is a different kind of wrong from the other two because both of those report a true number badly and this one reports a false one. The principle: send the number with its reason, and never make the number say something else.
tip: Mẹo MT: Loại trừ nhanh các phương án vi phạm quy tắc xoay góc chiều kim đồng hồ.

question_text: You are a knowledge assistant. A directory submission closes at noon tomorrow and the partner who signs off every submission is in a hearing all day. The firm’s rule is that no submission goes out without her approval. You have a complete draft and one figure you are unsure of. Missing the deadline means no entry this year. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Send the submission yourself before noon, since the draft is finished and the rule about approval exists to catch problems rather than to lose the firm its entry for a whole year.
Ask the partner's assistant to approve it on her behalf, so that somebody in her office has signed it off and the submission can go before the deadline.
Accept that the deadline will be missed, and put a note in the file explaining that the partner was unavailable so the firm knows why there is no entry this year.
Send the partner the draft now with the doubtful figure flagged and a note that you need ten minutes of her time before noon, and tell her assistant it is waiting.
explanation: A: Breaches a stated control: it decides for yourself which rules are worth keeping, and the one thing approval exists to catch is the sort of figure you have just said you are unsure of. B: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholder's: an assistant is not the person the rule names, so this manufactures an approval that looks like the real one and is not. C: Gives up before trying: the partner is in a hearing rather than uncontactable, and a hearing has breaks, so the note records a defeat that nobody has yet established was unavoidable. The most effective response is to send the partner the draft now with the doubtful figure flagged and a note that you need ten minutes before noon, and tell her assistant it is waiting. It does everything that can be done without her, puts the one real question in front of her in a form she can answer in a break, and uses her assistant for what an assistant can actually do. It beats asking the assistant to approve it on her behalf, because it seeks her approval rather than a substitute for it. It beats accepting that the deadline will be missed and noting why in the file, because nobody has yet tried to reach her and a hearing is not a closed door. The least effective response is sending the submission yourself before noon: it sends unapproved work carrying the exact uncertainty the approval exists to catch. That is a different kind of wrong from the other two, which both stay inside the rule even where they misjudge it. The principle: when a rule stands between you and a deadline, work the rule faster rather than around it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Đếm số lượng đỉnh hoặc số lượng góc nhọn khi các hình có hình dạng biến thiên phức tạp.

question_text: You are a fundraising assistant at a charity. You and your colleague Callum jointly prepare the monthly donor report. For three months he has sent you his figures late on the afternoon they are due, leaving you to reconcile them in a rush, and last month an error reached the trustees. Today he has done it again. He is friendly and busy, and has never been told this causes a problem. The next report is due in four weeks. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Reconcile the figures again without saying anything, and build in extra checking time next month so that a late hand-off cannot produce another error in the trustee report.
Copy your line manager into your reply to Callum today, noting that the figures have arrived late for the fourth month running and that this caused last month's error in the trustee report.
Reply to Callum today setting out that you will not be able to include his figures in future if they arrive after midday on the due date, so that the deadline is unambiguous from now on.
Reconcile today's figures, then speak to Callum this week, explain what the late hand-off costs at your end, and agree a date each month by which his figures will reach you.
explanation: A: Avoids the difficult conversation: absorbing it silently for a fourth month guarantees a fifth, hides from Callum that his habit has consequences, and leaves the trustees relying on you never having a bad day. Silence is the failure here, not the extra checking. B: Escalates prematurely: Callum has never been told there is a problem, so the first he hears of it is in front of his manager. That makes an ally into a defendant over something a direct conversation has not yet been given the chance to fix. C: Personalises the conflict: it opens with a sanction rather than a conversation, and a donor report missing his figures punishes the trustees for a problem between the two of you. The most effective response is to reconcile today’s figures, then speak to Callum this week and agree a date each month by which his figures will reach you: this month’s report still has to be right, and the recurring cause needs raising with the person who can fix it, directly and once the immediate work is done. Agreeing a date turns a grievance into a working arrangement. It beats copying your line manager into the reply today, because Callum has never been told there is a problem, and involving his manager first turns a fixable habit into a formal complaint. It beats replying that you will exclude his figures in future if they arrive late, because leading with that threat makes the trustees pay for a disagreement between two colleagues. The least effective response is reconciling again in silence and building in extra checking time: it is the only response where Callum never learns anything is wrong, so the pattern is guaranteed to continue, and the trustees’ report stays safe only for as long as your extra checking holds. That is worse than the other two, which are clumsy about how they raise it but do raise it. The principle: fix today’s report, then have the conversation with the person whose behaviour causes it, before involving anyone else.
tip: Mẹo MT: Kiểm tra quy luật cộng/trừ hình (XOR pattern) theo hàng ngang trước, nếu không thỏa mãn thì xét theo cột dọc.

question_text: You are a resourcing coordinator at a recruitment agency. A candidate you placed in a temporary warehouse role two weeks ago rings to say his shifts have been changed to nights without notice and he cannot do them because of childcare. Your agency’s contract with the client says shift patterns are agreed in advance. Your account manager, who owns the client relationship, is in a pitch until 4pm. The candidate is due on a night shift this evening. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Get the details from the candidate, check the agreed pattern on the contract file, and put the facts to your account manager before 4pm so she can raise it with the client before tonight's shift.
Tell the candidate that shift changes are between him and the site supervisor and that he should raise it there, since the agency only placed him and does not run the client's rotas.
Ring the client's site supervisor yourself, point out that the contract requires shift patterns to be agreed in advance, and ask for the candidate to be put back on days from tonight.
Tell the candidate not to attend tonight's night shift, since the change breaches the agreed pattern, and confirm to him that the agency will sort it out with the client afterwards.
explanation: B: Passes responsibility to others: the agreed pattern is in your agency's own contract, so this is exactly the agency's business. Sending a temporary worker to argue it alone with the site abandons the person you placed. C: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholder's: your account manager owns this relationship and a contractual challenge to the client is hers to frame. Making it yourself commits the agency to a position she has not seen. D: Acts on assumptions without checking: it tells a worker to miss a shift before anyone has confirmed the pattern or spoken to the client, which risks his placement on a reading of the contract nobody senior has looked at. The most effective response is to get the details, check the agreed pattern on the contract file, and put the facts to your account manager before 4pm: this is a contractual point the agency owns, it needs the person who owns the client relationship, and there is time to reach her before the shift. Gathering the facts first means she can act rather than investigate. It beats ringing the client’s site supervisor yourself, because a challenge to a client about their contract is the account manager’s to make, and pre-empting it commits the agency to a position she has not agreed. It beats telling the candidate not to attend tonight, because that risks his placement on your reading of a contract, before anyone has checked the agreed pattern or spoken to the client. The least effective response is telling him shift changes are between him and the site supervisor: it is the only response that denies the agency has any part in this, when the agreed pattern sits in the agency’s own contract, and it leaves a temporary worker to argue his own case against the site. That is worse than the other two, which are both wrong about who acts, but at least act. The principle: when something is genuinely yours to own, take it to the person who owns the relationship, with the facts, in time for them to use them.
tip: Mẹo MT: Đếm số lượng đỉnh hoặc số lượng góc nhọn khi các hình có hình dạng biến thiên phức tạp.

question_text: You are a delivery coordinator. You compile the weekly figures showing how the team’s hours split across three projects. This week roughly a third went on unplanned support, which has no project to sit against and makes the delivery figure look poor. Your manager has said she would rather the report did not raise questions from the programme board this month. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Show the support hours as their own line and add a note saying they were unavoidable, so that the delivery figure is read with that caveat attached.
Show the support hours as their own line and say nothing about them unless somebody asks, since the figures speak for themselves either way.
Show the support hours as their own line, and tell your manager the figure will raise questions, so that she has the answer ready before the board asks it.
Record the support hours as covered by the nearest project. The delivery figure then holds up properly, and the board is not distracted by an odd line item this month.
explanation: A: Softens the number with a label: unavoidable is your judgement rather than a fact, and it invites the board to discount a third of the week. B: Reports accurately and abandons the explanation: a third of the week appears without a cause, which is exactly what will generate the questions. D: Records effort against work it was not spent on: a third of the week now appears as project delivery in a report the board uses to allocate people. The most effective response is to show the support hours as their own line, and tell your manager the figure will raise questions. The figures should say what happened, and the honest way to handle her concern is to warn her what the question will be and hand her the answer. It beats showing them as their own line with a note saying they were unavoidable, because that is an opinion added to a fact and it encourages the board to set the week aside. It beats showing the line and saying nothing unless somebody asks, because a large unexplained line is precisely what produces the questions she is worried about. The least effective response is recording the support hours as covered by the nearest project: it is worse than either of the other two, because both leave the hours visible, spun or bare, while this moves a third of the week into project delivery in a report used to allocate people. The principle: report the number as it is and prepare the person who will be asked about it, rather than changing the number so the question is never asked.

question_text: You are a reporting analyst. A return that goes to the firm’s largest client is due at noon, and the contract charges the firm for a late or incomplete one. One figure is still missing. The approved route is a signed data extract from another team, which takes a day. The figure is also on a dashboard that is not an approved source for this return. Your manager is in a meeting until 11:30. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Put a note to your manager now setting out the gap, the two routes and the noon deadline, so they can decide at 11:30 with everything in front of them.
Submit the return at noon with the figure left blank, and follow up with the missing number once the signed extract arrives tomorrow.
Interrupt your manager's meeting now to get a decision, since a regulator deadline at noon outranks whatever else is being discussed in there this morning.
Take the figure from the dashboard and put it in the return, since the number will be the same either way and the deadline is the thing that actually matters here.
explanation: B: Files an incomplete return without asking: whether a gap or a late charge is the better outcome on a contracted return is a decision above your level. C: Escalates before there is anything to decide with: the meeting ends at 11:30, which still leaves half an hour, and the options can be set out first. D: Decides which rules count: an approved-source rule exists precisely so a regulator-facing figure can be traced, and a deadline is not a reason for one person to set it aside alone. The most effective response is to put a note to your manager now setting out the gap, the two routes and the noon deadline, so she can decide at 11:30 with everything in front of her: the decision is genuinely hers, 11:30 leaves time, and a written note means she decides on the facts rather than a doorway summary. It beats submitting the return at noon with the figure left blank, because choosing a gap over a late charge is not a junior call. It beats interrupting her meeting now to get a decision, because half an hour is enough and the interruption buys nothing. The least effective response is taking the figure from the dashboard and putting it in the return: an unapproved source goes into a return the client relies on, on one person’s judgement that the number is probably the same. That is setting aside a stated control rather than escalating badly. The principle: when the only route to the deadline breaks a rule, the deadline is somebody else’s decision.
tip: Mẹo MT: Kiểm tra quy luật cộng/trừ hình (XOR pattern) theo hàng ngang trước, nếu không thỏa mãn thì xét theo cột dọc.

question_text: You are an analyst at a market-research agency. A client’s marketing director is building a product-launch presentation for Thursday around survey results you are producing. Today, Tuesday, you find your fieldwork supplier has so far delivered only half the promised responses; the remainder arrive tomorrow night, and the headline figures may shift once they are in. The marketing director has just emailed asking for the figures today so she can start building her presentation. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Send the preliminary figures now, stating clearly they are based on half the sample and flagging which headline numbers may move when the remaining responses arrive tomorrow night.
Hold the figures back until the full sample has arrived and been checked tomorrow night, so the marketing director only ever sees numbers that will not change.
Reply that the results are in good shape, and send the figures today without mentioning the missing half of the sample, since the final numbers will probably be close.
Raise the problem with your own account manager first and leave it to them to decide what, if anything, the client should be told about the sample.
explanation: B: Delays the message: the marketing director has asked for the figures today to start building a Thursday presentation, and withholding everything until tomorrow night costs her a full day of preparation when a clearly-caveated interim answer would serve her now. C: Falsely reassures the stakeholder: telling the client her results are in good shape while knowingly omitting that half the sample is missing is dishonesty about reliability. She may lock claims you know are unstable into a launch presentation, a different kind of wrong from being slow or indirect. D: Tells the wrong audience first: briefing the account manager is sensible, but leaving the whole decision with them delays a straightforward factual caveat the marketing director needs today, while her request for the figures sits unanswered. The most effective response is to send the preliminary figures now, stating clearly that they rest on half the sample and flagging which headline numbers may move: the marketing director asked for figures today, and a plainly caveated interim answer lets her start building the presentation without locking in claims that could change tomorrow night. It beats holding everything back until the full sample is checked, because that costs her a full day of preparation against a Thursday deadline when a clearly caveated answer meets her stated need now. It beats routing the issue through your account manager first, because that delays a simple factual caveat the client needs today, and her request goes unanswered in the meantime. The least effective response is telling her the results are in good shape and sending the figures without mentioning the missing half: unlike holding them back, which is slow but honest, and unlike escalating internally, which at least surfaces the problem to someone, it assures the client of a reliability you know the numbers do not have. If the headline figures shift tomorrow night, she has built her launch on numbers you knew were unstable. The principle: give stakeholders what they need on time, with an honest statement of how reliable it is, never certainty you do not have.
tip: Mẹo MT: Loại trừ nhanh các phương án vi phạm quy tắc xoay góc chiều kim đồng hồ.

question_text: You are a receptionist at a dental practice. Part of your job is logging each patient’s arrival time, which the practice uses to report waiting times to the health board. A patient arrives forty minutes late for a check-up and is seen straight away. Your colleague on the desk, who joined the practice last month, says the waiting figures are already poor and suggests offhand that you log the arrival as on-time, since the patient was not kept waiting. She has never suggested anything like it before. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Log the correct arrival time and tell the practice manager that your colleague asked you to record it falsely so that she can deal with it as she sees fit.
Log the arrival as on-time as your colleague suggests, since the patient was seen immediately and an accurate entry would make the practice's figures look worse than the service it actually gave.
Leave the arrival time blank rather than enter either figure, so that the record is not falsified and the practice's monthly waiting figures are not dragged down by one late patient.
Log the actual arrival time, and tell your colleague you are not willing to record something you know is untrue, whatever it does to this month's figures.
explanation: A: Escalates prematurely: the entry is right and the point is made by making it. Turning a colleague's bad suggestion into a report before telling her what you think skips the conversation that would probably settle it. B: Falsifies a business record: the log is the practice's evidence to the health board, and entering a time you know is wrong is a deliberate misstatement. That is dishonesty, not a judgement call about presentation. C: Hides the problem: a blank is a quieter way of removing an inconvenient fact. The health board's figures still end up wrong, and nobody can see that a decision was taken. The most effective response is to log the actual arrival time and tell your colleague you are not willing to record something untrue: the log is a record the health board relies on, so it gets the true time, and saying so plainly settles the matter where it arose. It beats logging it correctly and telling the practice manager your colleague asked you to falsify it, because the record is already correct and the disagreement is one sentence away from being resolved; going straight to the manager makes a formal matter of something a direct answer handles. It beats leaving the arrival time blank, because an empty field achieves the same distortion your colleague asked for, only without leaving fingerprints, so the figures are still wrong and nobody can tell why. The least effective response is recording the arrival as on-time because the patient was seen immediately: it is the only response that puts a figure you know to be false into a record the practice reports externally, and the reasoning offered for it, that the service was fine, is exactly the reasoning that makes small falsifications easy. That is worse than the blank field, which at least refuses to write the lie, and worse than going to the manager, which is clumsy rather than dishonest. The principle: record what happened, and say plainly that you will not record what did not.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân tích theo từng thuộc tính độc lập: Hướng xoay góc (90°/45°), số lượng nét, màu sắc (Đen/Trắng), và vị trí.

question_text: You are a compliance assistant. Your team reports each month how many new files had their checks completed before work started. One of this month’s files had its check completed the day after work began, because the fee earner was told the wrong thing by somebody else. Your team leader asks for the figures. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Record the check as completed before work started, since the check was done and the reason it was a day late had nothing to do with the fee earner or with the compliance team.
Give her the figure with the exception shown, and leave the explanation to whoever asks about it, since the numbers are what the report is for.
Give her the figure with the exception shown and a line explaining that the fee earner was given wrong information, so the report carries the cause as well as the count.
Ask her whether the one late file needs to be in the figures at all, given that it was caused by something outside the process the report is meant to measure.
explanation: A: Marks a file as compliant when it was not: the whole point of the figure is that it counts checks done before work began, and a file recorded as fine removes the only trace of what went wrong. B: Reports the number without its cause: the exception will be read as a fee earner ignoring a check, and the thing that actually needs fixing is somebody giving out wrong information. D: Invites the data to be trimmed: the report measures whether checks were done before work started, and this one was not, whatever the reason. The most effective response is to give her the figure with the exception shown and a line explaining that the fee earner was given wrong information. The figure is what it is, and the one line is what turns an apparent breach into something the firm can act on. It beats giving her the figure with the exception shown and leaving the explanation to whoever asks, because an unexplained exception will be read as the wrong kind of failure. It beats asking whether the one late file needs to be in the figures at all, because the measure is about what happened, not about whose fault it was. The least effective response is recording the check as completed before work started: it records the file as compliant when it was not, which is a different kind of wrong from the other two because both of those leave the exception visible. The principle: report the exception and its cause together, and never make the record say the exception did not happen.

question_text: You are a disclosure assistant. Your team records the number of documents each person reviews per day and reports the totals to the client each Friday. You have been slower this week because a batch you were given is unusually complex. Your team leader asks you for your figures before she sends the report. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Give her the number and tell her why it is lower this week, so that whatever she sends the client carries the reason along with the figure.
Record a higher figure for the last two days than you actually reviewed, since you will make the difference up next week and the client only ever sees the weekly total.
Give her the number without comment, on the basis that she has the same view of the batches as you do and can see for herself why the week looks like this.
Ask her to leave your figures out of this week's report until the complex batch is finished, so that the client sees a fair picture rather than an unusual week.
explanation: B: Alters a record: it puts a number into the client's report that describes work nobody has done, and it does so in the one system anybody would later use to check. C: Assumes the context is obvious: she is about to send the figure onwards and may not have looked at what was in your batch, so the reason travels only if you send it with the number. D: Removes the awkward data: a report with a person missing invites exactly the question it was meant to avoid, and it treats an unusual week as something to be hidden rather than explained. The most effective response is to give her the number and tell her why it is lower this week, so whatever she sends the client carries the reason along with the figure. It beats giving her the number without comment because she can see the batches herself, since she is the person sending it on and cannot supply a context she has not been given. It beats asking her to leave your figures out of this week’s report, because leaving a name out is more conspicuous than a low number with an explanation. The least effective response is recording a higher figure for the last two days than you actually reviewed: it changes what the record says happened, which is a different kind of wrong from the other two because both of those report a true number badly and this one reports a false one. The principle: send the number with its reason, and never make the number say something else.
tip: Mẹo MT: Kiểm tra quy luật cộng/trừ hình (XOR pattern) theo hàng ngang trước, nếu không thỏa mãn thì xét theo cột dọc.

question_text: You are a billing assistant. Your team reports to the partners each month how many bills went out within five days of the month end. Two of yours went out on the seventh day because a fee earner was away. Your team leader asks you for your figures for the report this afternoon. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Record the two bills as sent on the fifth day, since the delay was not anything you did and the figure would otherwise say something about you that is not true.
Give her the real dates and the reason for the two late ones, so she can decide whether the report should say anything about fee earners being away.
Give her the real dates without any explanation, since she can see the absences on the team calendar and will work out why those two sat waiting.
Ask her to leave your figures out of this month's report, so that two unrepresentative bills do not distort what the partners see about the team's performance.
explanation: A: Alters the record: the report will then describe two bills that went out on a day they did not, and the reason the delay is worth knowing about disappears with the correction. C: Assumes the context travels: the calendar is not in front of her when she writes the report, so the two late bills reach the partners as two late bills and nothing else. D: Removes the awkward data: a report with a name missing raises the question it was meant to avoid, and the absence that caused the delay stays invisible either way. The most effective response is to give her the real dates and the reason for the two late ones, so she can decide whether the report should mention fee earners being away. The dates are what they are, and whether they are read fairly depends on the reason travelling with them, which is her decision rather than yours. It beats giving her the real dates without any explanation, because a team calendar is not in front of somebody writing a report. It beats asking her to leave your figures out this month, because taking a name out is more conspicuous than explaining two days. The least effective response is recording the two bills as sent on the fifth day: it changes what the record says happened, which is a different kind of wrong from the other two because both of those report true dates badly. The principle: report the number with its reason, and never make the number say something else.
tip: Mẹo MT: Kiểm tra quy luật cộng/trừ hình (XOR pattern) theo hàng ngang trước, nếu không thỏa mãn thì xét theo cột dọc.

question_text: You are a delivery coordinator. You compile the weekly figures showing how the team’s hours split across three projects. This week roughly a third went on unplanned support, which has no project to sit against and makes the delivery figure look poor. Your manager has said she would rather the report did not raise questions from the programme board this month. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Show the support hours as their own line and add a note saying they were unavoidable, so that the delivery figure is read with that caveat attached.
Show the support hours as their own line and say nothing about them unless somebody asks, since the figures speak for themselves either way.
Show the support hours as their own line, and tell your manager the figure will raise questions, so that she has the answer ready before the board asks it.
Record the support hours as covered by the nearest project. The delivery figure then holds up properly, and the board is not distracted by an odd line item this month.
explanation: A: Softens the number with a label: unavoidable is your judgement rather than a fact, and it invites the board to discount a third of the week. B: Reports accurately and abandons the explanation: a third of the week appears without a cause, which is exactly what will generate the questions. D: Records effort against work it was not spent on: a third of the week now appears as project delivery in a report the board uses to allocate people. The most effective response is to show the support hours as their own line, and tell your manager the figure will raise questions. The figures should say what happened, and the honest way to handle her concern is to warn her what the question will be and hand her the answer. It beats showing them as their own line with a note saying they were unavoidable, because that is an opinion added to a fact and it encourages the board to set the week aside. It beats showing the line and saying nothing unless somebody asks, because a large unexplained line is precisely what produces the questions she is worried about. The least effective response is recording the support hours as covered by the nearest project: it is worse than either of the other two, because both leave the hours visible, spun or bare, while this moves a third of the week into project delivery in a report used to allocate people. The principle: report the number as it is and prepare the person who will be asked about it, rather than changing the number so the question is never asked.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân tích theo từng thuộc tính độc lập: Hướng xoay góc (90°/45°), số lượng nét, màu sắc (Đen/Trắng), và vị trí.

question_text: You are a procurement graduate at Hilton. Working through delivery notes for a different piece of work, you find that one supplier’s notes have been recording pack sizes that do not match what is actually arriving, and have done for at least six weeks. Nobody has raised it. The supplier is being reviewed in a fortnight, and the pack sizes feed the figures that review uses. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Correct the pack sizes in the figures yourself for the six weeks that you can see, so that the review in a fortnight at least starts from numbers that match what was delivered.
Pass the whole thing to the manager who owns the supplier relationship without mentioning the review in a fortnight, and treat your part as finished.
Raise it at the review itself in a fortnight, when the supplier and the manager are both in the room and the pack sizes are on the agenda anyway.
Take it to the manager who owns the supplier today with the six weeks set out, say what it does to the review's figures, and offer to check how far back it goes.
explanation: A: Alters figures nobody asked you to alter: the numbers stop matching the notes that produced them, and the recording fault that caused it is now invisible to the person accountable for the supplier. B: Hands a finding on without what makes it urgent: the manager receives six weeks of notes with no mention of the review that is about to use them. C: Times the disclosure for the meeting it should have preceded: the review is prepared on figures everybody now knows are wrong, and the correction lands as a surprise. The most effective response is to take it to the manager who owns the supplier today with the six weeks set out, say what it does to the review’s figures, and offer to check how far back it goes: it reaches the person who can act while a fortnight is still enough time, and it carries the consequence rather than only the observation. It beats passing it across without mentioning the review, because the manager cannot act on a deadline nobody has told him about. It beats raising it at the review, because the preparation everybody does beforehand is built on figures already known to be false. The least effective response is correcting the pack sizes in the figures yourself: the numbers stop matching the notes behind them, the supplier carries on recording the wrong sizes, and the person accountable for that supplier can no longer see any of it, which is a different kind of wrong from handing the finding on bare or from raising it too late. The principle: something you found outside your own remit is carried to somebody who can act on it, with what it means attached, and never quietly repaired.
tip: Mẹo MT: Kiểm tra quy luật cộng/trừ hình (XOR pattern) theo hàng ngang trước, nếu không thỏa mãn thì xét theo cột dọc.

question_text: You are a stock control assistant at Home Depot. A recount you asked for turned up a mistake in your own figures, and the colleague who did it said, in front of two others, that he had wasted an afternoon on your arithmetic. It stung and he was largely right. The next count is due on Thursday and it needs two people, one of whom is normally him. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Ask your supervisor to put somebody else on Thursday's count, since working alongside him this week would be uncomfortable for both of you after what was said.
Refuse to work with him on Thursday's count after the way he spoke to you, and say you would rather do it on your own or not at all.
Acknowledge to him that the figures were wrong and say what you have changed, and do Thursday's count with him as planned since the count needs two people.
Say nothing about it, do Thursday's count as planned, and let the remark fade rather than reopening something that was fair comment anyway.
explanation: A: Redesigns the rota around one awkward afternoon: the count is harder to staff, and the two of you have to work together again the week after in any case. B: Withdraws from a job that needs two people after a disagreement: Thursday's count is put at risk to answer a remark made about an afternoon. D: Lets an unrepaired working relationship stand: the count happens and he has no reason to think the mistake will not simply repeat. The most effective response is to acknowledge that the figures were wrong, say what you have changed, and do Thursday’s count with him: the criticism was largely fair, saying so is what restores the working relationship, and the count that needs two people gets them. It beats asking for somebody else on Thursday, because the rota is rearranged around one bad afternoon and you will work together next week anyway. It beats letting the remark fade, because he has no reason to expect anything different next time. The least effective response is refusing to work with him on Thursday: a count that needs two people is put at risk to answer a remark, which is a different kind of wrong from avoiding him or from staying silent. The principle: when the criticism is fair, own it and stay in the work with the person who made it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Loại trừ nhanh các phương án vi phạm quy tắc xoay góc chiều kim đồng hồ.

question_text: You are a trading assistant at Home Depot. A large account has queried a charge on last month’s invoice. You have pulled the figures and can see the charge is correct, but the reason it changed is a contract term you do not fully understand. The account manager is out today. The customer wants an answer before the end of the week, and it is Wednesday. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Reply with the figures you have checked and what they show, say that the contract point needs the account manager, and book time with him for tomorrow morning.
Explain the contract term to the customer as best you understand it, and say you will confirm it with the account manager tomorrow.
Send the query on to the account team without the figures you have already checked, and let them start the contract point again from the beginning.
Reply to the customer that the charge is correct and leave the reason for the account manager to explain when he is back in the office tomorrow.
explanation: B: Answers outside what you actually know: an approximate account of a contract term is the thing most likely to be quoted back at the business later. C: Passes the problem on stripped of the work already done: the account team starts from nothing, the day you have spent on it is wasted, and Friday is two days away. D: Answers the easy half only: the customer did not ask whether the charge was right, they asked why it changed, and that is the part being deferred. The most effective response is to reply with the figures you have checked and what they show, say the contract point needs the account manager, and book time with him for tomorrow: the customer sees progress and an honest boundary, the checking work is used, and Friday is still comfortably reachable. It beats explaining the contract term as best you understand it, because an approximation about a contract is exactly the sentence that gets quoted back later. It beats replying that the charge is correct and leaving the reason to the account manager, because the reason is what was asked. The least effective response is sending the query on without the figures you have already checked: the next person starts from nothing, a day of work disappears, and the deadline is two days out, which is a different kind of wrong from over-reaching or from answering only half. The principle: escalate the part you cannot answer, with the part you can attached to it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Kiểm tra quy luật cộng/trừ hình (XOR pattern) theo hàng ngang trước, nếu không thỏa mãn thì xét theo cột dọc.

question_text: You are a duty coordinator at a courier depot. At 3pm three things need you. A driver has broken down with a vehicle full of next-day parcels and needs a recovery arranged. Your manager wants the weekly performance figures before he leaves at 4pm. And a customer is holding on the phone about a parcel that has been missing for a week. The recovery firm’s cut-off for same-day attendance is 3.30pm. The figures take twenty minutes. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Take the customer's call first since she is already holding and has been waiting a week, then arrange the recovery and do the figures if there is time before 4pm.
Ask the driver to arrange his own recovery while you handle the customer and the figures, since he is at the roadside and knows the vehicle better than you do.
Arrange the recovery before the 3.30pm cut-off, take the customer's number and promise a call back, then do the figures for your manager before 4pm.
Do the performance figures first so your manager has them before he leaves at 4pm, then arrange the recovery and return the customer's call afterwards.
explanation: A: Ignores the closing window: her parcel has been missing a week and will still be missing in ten minutes, while the recovery cut-off passes at 3.30pm and strands a van of next-day parcels overnight. B: Passes responsibility to others: the depot holds the recovery account and the cut-off, not the driver at the roadside. Handing him a task he cannot complete means the cut-off passes with nobody having acted. D: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholder's: it puts a reporting deadline ahead of a van of next-day parcels whose recovery window shuts in thirty minutes, and your manager has not been told the two clash. The most effective response is to arrange the recovery before the 3.30pm cut-off, take the customer’s number and promise a call back, then do the figures before 4pm: only the recovery has a window that shuts, and missing it strands a van of next-day parcels overnight. Once it is arranged, twenty minutes of figures still fits and the customer gets a call back today. It beats taking the customer’s call first because she is already holding, since a parcel missing for a week is not made worse by ten more minutes, while the cut-off cannot be recovered once passed. It beats doing the performance figures first so your manager has them before he leaves, because that treats a reporting deadline as outranking a closing operational window, without telling him the two clash. The least effective response is asking the driver to arrange his own recovery from the roadside: it hands it to the one person who cannot arrange it, since the depot holds the account, so the cut-off passes with nobody having acted. That is worse than the other two, which sequence badly but keep the work with someone able to do it. The principle: do the thing whose window is closing first, then fit the rest around it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Đếm số lượng đỉnh hoặc số lượng góc nhọn khi các hình có hình dạng biến thiên phức tạp.

question_text: You work in an HR shared service team. It is Wednesday. Three things are outstanding: a new starter’s contract must go out today or she cannot begin on Monday, a manager wants a report on absence figures by Friday, and a colleague has asked you to review her draft policy whenever you have time. The contract takes an hour, the report three hours. You have five hours left today. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Work through all three in the order they were asked for, and let your manager know at the end of the day if anything has not been finished.
Start the absence report because it is the longest job, then do the contract at the end of the day once the bulk of the report is behind you.
Do the contract and the policy review first because they are the two shorter jobs, then start the absence report and continue it tomorrow morning.
Send the new starter's contract first, then work on the absence report, and tell your colleague you will review her policy tomorrow.
explanation: A: Hides the problem / silent deadline slip: the contract is the one item that cannot slip, and reporting at the end of the day is after the point at which anyone could rescue it. Reporting a missed deadline once it is missed is not communication. B: Delays the decision: it leaves an hour-long task with a today-or- never deadline to the end of a five-hour day, so any overrun on the report costs the new starter her start date. C: Splits effort so nothing finishes: it fits the favour in ahead of a report with a named Friday deadline, and pushes three hours of work into a day that already has other demands. The most effective response is to send the new starter’s contract first, then work on the absence report, and tell your colleague the policy review waits until tomorrow: only the contract has a deadline of today with a consequence attached, a start date, and it takes one of the five hours available. That leaves four hours for a three-hour report due Friday, and the policy review has no deadline at all. It beats starting the absence report first because it is the longest job, since that puts a fixed, unrecoverable deadline behind an open-ended one. It beats doing the contract and the policy review first as the two shorter jobs, because that fits an unscheduled favour ahead of a report with a stated deadline. The least effective response is working through all three in the order they were asked for and reporting at the end of the day: it works to the order things were asked in rather than to their deadlines, and reports the failure only once the new starter’s Monday cannot be saved. That is worse than the other two, which sequence badly but at least do the contract today. The principle: identify the task that cannot slip, do it first, and say early which of the others will move.

question_text: You are a junior data engineer. A supplier who provides a daily data feed has told you their file will be late every day for the next fortnight while they move systems. Tell the publishing team that the feed may be late occasionally over the next two weeks, without going into the supplier's system move or the full fortnight.
Tell the publishing team today that the feed will be late every day for a fortnight, and ask what they need from you to protect their nine o'clock commitment.
Put a note in the shared channel about the supplier's system move, so that anybody depending on the feed can see it and plan around it themselves.

question_text: You are a trading assistant at Harrods Online. A figure you produced for a weekly pack rests on an assumption about supplier lead times that changed on Friday. options: Rework the figure quickly this afternoon with an estimate of the new lead times, and put the estimated version in the pack instead of the one you can support.
Put the figure in the pack as it stands, without flagging that the lead times behind it changed on Friday, since the rework cannot be done before this afternoon in any case.
Put the figure in with a clear note that the lead times changed on Friday and what that does to it, and tell the manager before the pack goes out so nothing surprises him.
Leave the figure out of the pack altogether and explain in its place that the number is being reworked after a change to supplier lead times.

question_text: You are a lettings negotiator at an estate agency. At 1pm three things need you. A viewing is booked at 1.30 across town and the applicant is meeting you there. Do the viewing figures first while you are at your desk, then travel to the viewing and email the landlord in the evening.
Leave now for the 1.30 viewing, then reply to the landlord and do the viewing figures before your manager leaves at 5pm.
Let the applicant wait outside the property while you finish the work at your desk, and apologise for the late arrival once you eventually get there.
explanation: A: Delays the decision: the journey takes twenty minutes and it is already 1pm, so any time spent on email first risks arriving after an applicant who is meeting you there. The landlord’s update has until the end of the day and the figures until 5pm. It beats replying to the landlord first because he has asked for an update today, since answering email risks arriving after the applicant, and the update has hours of room. It beats doing the viewing figures first while you are at your desk, because half an hour of reporting due at 5pm should not precede an appointment with someone waiting across town. The least effective response is letting the applicant wait outside the property while you finish the desk work: it leaves her standing there hearing nothing until you arrive. That is worse than the other two, which sequence the work badly but still turn up. The principle: keep the appointment someone else has committed to, then use the remaining hours for the work with slack in it.

question_text: You are a production coordinator at a print and mail house. At 11am three things need you. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?

Work on the renewals and the inserter together, moving between them, and do the headcount figures if the mailing is finished before the 2pm collection.
Do the fifteen minutes of headcount figures for the noon meeting, then give the renewal mailing your full attention until the 2pm collection, and pass the inserter to another operator.
Start the renewal mailing immediately and tell your manager the headcount figures will have to wait until after the 2pm collection.
explanation: A: Abandons own committed work: an unquantified machine fix is taken on ahead of a ninety-minute job with a 2pm legal deadline, which leaves no margin if the jam takes longer than expected. B: Splits effort so nothing finishes: a mailing with a legal notice period is left to compete for attention with a machine fault, which risks missing a deadline that cannot be recovered and is the most costly of the four outcomes. D: Splits the wrong thing: it protects the deadline that matters and sacrifices a fifteen-minute task that fits inside the margin anyway, so the manager goes into a noon meeting without figures for no gain. The most effective response is to do the fifteen minutes of headcount figures for the noon meeting, then give the renewal mailing your full attention until the 2pm collection, and pass the inserter to another operator: there are three hours, the mailing needs ninety minutes of them and has a legal deadline, and the figures are needed at noon. Both fit if the short one goes first, and the machine fault is work someone else can take. It beats starting the mailing immediately and telling your manager the figures must wait, because that protects the same deadline while needlessly sacrificing a fifteen-minute task that comfortably fits. It beats helping your colleague with the jammed inserter first, because taking on a machine fault of unknown length ahead of a legally timed mailing risks the one deadline that cannot be moved. The least effective response is moving between the renewals and the inserter and fitting the figures in afterwards: it lets a mailing with a legal notice period compete for attention with a machine jam, which is the most likely way to miss the collection entirely. That is worse than the other two, which mis- sequence but keep the mailing whole. The principle: check what actually fits in the time, protect the deadline that cannot move, and hand off what someone else can do.

question_text: You are a stock control assistant at Ikea. The same line has shown a discrepancy at count on four occasions in six weeks, always in the same direction and always in the same area. Each time it has been written off as a counting error. You have now checked and the counts were done correctly. Discrepancies of this size and pattern are supposed to be reported to the loss prevention team. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Hand the four counts to the colleague who covers that area on Thursdays, since he knows the line better than you do, and consider your part in it finished.
Keep watching the line for another two counts to be sure the pattern is real, since four occasions could still turn out to be an unfortunate run of coincidences.
Raise it with your supervisor and let her decide whether it goes any further, without mentioning that the counts themselves have now been checked and are sound.
Report the four counts to the loss prevention team today with the checking you have done, since a pattern like that is what the reporting route exists for, and tell your supervisor.

The most effective response is to report the four counts to the loss prevention team today with your checking attached, and tell your supervisor you have done it: the pattern is exactly what the reporting route exists for, your checking is what makes it more than a suspicion, and nobody is surprised later. It beats waiting for two more counts, because the threshold was passed weeks ago and waiting adds three weeks. It beats raising it with your supervisor while leaving out that the counts were checked, because that is the fact the decision turns on. The least effective response is handing the four counts to the Thursday colleague and treating your part as finished: he does not know it is four occurrences or that it is reportable, so the only person holding both facts has stepped out, which is a different kind of wrong from waiting too long or from telling somebody too little. The principle: when something crosses a reporting line, take it there yourself, with what you know attached.

question_text: You are a paralegal. You have been asked to complete two schedules by five today. At two you realise the second one needs a figure from the client, who does not usually reply the same day. The fee earner who asked for them is in the building. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Finish both schedules using an estimate for the missing figure, and mark that figure clearly as provisional until the client confirms it.
Email the client asking for the figure, finish the first schedule, and let the fee earner find out at five which of the two is ready and which is not.
Ring the client repeatedly through the afternoon until you get the figure, leaving the first schedule until you have it so that both can be finished together.
Email the client, finish the first schedule, and tell the fee earner now that the second depends on a reply that may not come today.

The most effective response is to email the client, finish the first schedule, and tell the fee earner now that the second depends on a reply that may not come today. Everything you can do is done, the client is asked, and he learns at two rather than five, when he can still chase them himself. It beats finishing both schedules using an estimate for the missing figure, because an estimated figure is not the figure. It beats ringing the client repeatedly and leaving the first schedule until you have the number, because that risks the one that was certain. The least effective response is emailing the client, finishing the first schedule, and letting him find out at five: it produces the same work as the best answer and tells him nothing, so he discovers it when nothing can be done. That is a different kind of wrong from the other two, both of which at least leave him with something at five. The principle: when a commitment starts to depend on somebody else, say so while there is still afternoon left.

question_text: You are a billing assistant. Two fee earners have each told you the other is responsible for a bill that has not gone out, and each has asked you to say so if the month-end figures are queried. The bill is now three weeks late and the client has asked about it. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell the month-end review, if it comes up, that neither of them has taken responsibility, so that the record shows what actually happened rather than either account.
Ask them both for ten minutes, put the client's question and the three weeks in front of them, and ask which of them will get the bill out this week.
Draft the bill yourself and send it to both of them for approval, since the client is waiting and somebody has to break the stalemate before month end.
Blame each of them to the other in front of the billing team, so that they both understand the position and can settle who is responsible between themselves.
explanation: A: Answers a question nobody has asked yet: it prepares a position for a meeting instead of getting the bill out, and the client is still waiting either way. C: Works around the stalemate: the bill may go out and the question of who owns it is left exactly as it was, so the next one stalls the same way. D: Carries private remarks between colleagues: it makes the argument about the two of them rather than about a bill the client is waiting on, and neither can unhear what the other said. The most effective response is to ask them both for ten minutes, put the client’s question and the three weeks in front of them, and ask which of them will get the bill out this week. Those are facts neither disputes, and putting both in front of them together turns a blame exchange into a decision. It beats drafting the bill yourself and sending it to both for approval, because drafting round them leaves ownership unresolved. It beats telling the month-end review that neither has taken responsibility, because a bill is still not out. The least effective response is blaming each of them to the other in front of the billing team: it relays each account to the other, so a late bill becomes a quarrel. That is a different kind of wrong from the other two, neither of which repeats anything anybody said. The principle: put the shared fact in front of both, and never carry remarks between them.
tip: Mẹo MT: Loại trừ nhanh các phương án vi phạm quy tắc xoay góc chiều kim đồng hồ.

question_text: You are a purchasing assistant at John Lewis. A supplier has rung to query a set of volumes that a colleague of yours prepared. You can see that your colleague’s numbers are right and that the supplier has misread the layout. He is impatient, has queried her figures before, and says he would rather deal with you from now on because she takes days to reply. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell him her figures are often unreliable and that he should bring the numbers to you in future, so that at least the queries get answered quickly.
Show him where the layout misled him, say the figures are right, and tell him you will pass on his point about reply times to her and your manager.
Answer the query yourself and agree to be his contact for volumes from now on, since he is clearly not going to deal with her and somebody has to answer him.
Tell him the volumes are her work and that he should take the query back to her, since it is her supplier and answering it yourself would cut across her.
explanation: A: Undermines a colleague to an outsider: her numbers were right, and a supplier is now told by her own team that her work cannot be trusted. C: Solves a relationship problem by rearranging it: she loses her own supplier contact without being consulted, and nobody addresses the reply times. D: Applies the boundary and ignores the customer: he is sent back to somebody he says takes days, holding a misreading you could have cleared up in a minute. The most effective response is to show him where the layout misled him, confirm the figures are right, and say you will pass his point about reply times to her and your manager: the query is answered on the spot, your colleague’s work is defended because it is correct, and the real complaint goes somewhere it can be dealt with. It beats agreeing to become his contact, because that quietly takes her supplier away without asking her. It beats sending him back to her with his misreading intact, because it costs a minute to clear up. The least effective response is telling him her figures are often unreliable: they were right, and a supplier has been told by her own team not to trust her, which is a different kind of wrong from over-accommodating him or from standing on the boundary. The principle: defend a colleague’s correct work to an outsider, and take the criticism of her that has substance to her and your manager instead.
tip: Mẹo MT: Kiểm tra quy luật cộng/trừ hình (XOR pattern) theo hàng ngang trước, nếu không thỏa mãn thì xét theo cột dọc.

question_text: You are a stock control assistant at John Lewis. A recount you asked for turned up a mistake in your own figures, and the colleague who did it said, in front of two others, that he had wasted an afternoon on your arithmetic. It stung and he was largely right. The next count is due on Thursday and it needs two people, one of whom is normally him. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Ask your supervisor to put somebody else on Thursday's count, since working alongside him this week would be uncomfortable for both of you after what was said.
Refuse to work with him on Thursday's count after the way he spoke to you, and say you would rather do it on your own or not at all.
Acknowledge to him that the figures were wrong and say what you have changed, and do Thursday's count with him as planned since the count needs two people.
Say nothing about it, do Thursday's count as planned, and let the remark fade rather than reopening something that was fair comment anyway.
explanation: A: Redesigns the rota around one awkward afternoon: the count is harder to staff, and the two of you have to work together again the week after in any case. B: Withdraws from a job that needs two people after a disagreement: Thursday's count is put at risk to answer a remark made about an afternoon. D: Lets an unrepaired working relationship stand: the count happens and he has no reason to think the mistake will not simply repeat. The most effective response is to acknowledge that the figures were wrong, say what you have changed, and do Thursday’s count with him: the criticism was largely fair, saying so is what restores the working relationship, and the count that needs two people gets them. It beats asking for somebody else on Thursday, because the rota is rearranged around one bad afternoon and you will work together next week anyway. It beats letting the remark fade, because he has no reason to expect anything different next time. The least effective response is refusing to work with him on Thursday: a count that needs two people is put at risk to answer a remark, which is a different kind of wrong from avoiding him or from staying silent. question_text: You are a trading assistant at John Lewis. A large account has queried a charge on last month’s invoice. You have pulled the figures and can see the charge is correct, but the reason it changed is a contract term you do not fully understand. The account manager is out today. The customer wants an answer before the end of the week, and it is Wednesday. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Reply with the figures you have checked and what they show, say that the contract point needs the account manager, and book time with him for tomorrow morning.
Explain the contract term to the customer as best you understand it, and say you will confirm it with the account manager tomorrow.
Send the query on to the account team without the figures you have already checked, and let them start the contract point again from the beginning.
Reply to the customer that the charge is correct and leave the reason for the account manager to explain when he is back in the office tomorrow.
explanation: B: Answers outside what you actually know: an approximate account of a contract term is the thing most likely to be quoted back at the business later. C: Passes the problem on stripped of the work already done: the account team starts from nothing, the day you have spent on it is wasted, and Friday is two days away. D: Answers the easy half only: the customer did not ask whether the charge was right, they asked why it changed, and that is the part being deferred. The most effective response is to reply with the figures you have checked and what they show, say the contract point needs the account manager, and book time with him for tomorrow: the customer sees progress and an honest boundary, the checking work is used, and Friday is still comfortably reachable. It beats explaining the contract term as best you understand it, because an approximation about a contract is exactly the sentence that gets quoted back later. It beats replying that the charge is correct and leaving the reason to the account manager, because the reason is what was asked. The least effective response is sending the query on without the figures you have already checked: the next person starts from nothing, a day of work disappears, and the deadline is two days out, which is a different kind of wrong from over-reaching or from answering only half. The principle: escalate the part you cannot answer, with the part you can attached to it.

question_text: You are a stock control assistant at Mars Online. A weekly count shows three hundred units fewer than the system expects on one line. The trading team needs a figure this afternoon to decide what to order for next week, and they have asked you whether the count can be relied on. Investigating the gap properly means pulling the movement history, which takes about two hours. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Give the trading team the counted figure with the gap stated alongside it, say the cause is not yet known, and start on the movement history straight away.
Assure the trading team that the counted figure is sound and the gap is a scanning error, and look at the movement history later in the week if anybody comes back to you.
Hold the figure back until the movement history is finished, and tell the trading team they will have something reliable by the end of the day.
Give the trading team the figure the system holds rather than the counted one, since the system is what their ordering tool reads from in any case.
explanation: B: Gives an assurance you have not earned: nothing yet distinguishes a scanning error from three hundred missing units, and next week's order is placed on a cause that was invented to close the question. C: Delays the decision: the order has to be placed this afternoon, so a reliable number tomorrow is worth less to them than an honest one now. D: Substitutes the convenient source for the checked one: the count is the only evidence anybody has looked at, and it is the number being set aside. The most effective response is to give the trading team the counted figure with the gap stated alongside it and start on the movement history at once: they get a number in time to order, they know exactly how much weight it carries, and the work that settles the cause begins immediately. It beats holding the figure until the history is finished, because the decision is this afternoon and an honest number now beats a certain one tomorrow. It beats handing over the system figure instead, because the count is the only thing anybody has actually observed. The least effective response is assuring them the count is sound and the gap is a scanning error: no work has been done that could support either claim, and stating a cause you have not established is a different kind of wrong from being slow or from choosing the wrong source. The principle: report what you know and what you do not, rather than supplying the certainty the person asking would prefer.
tip: Mẹo MT: Đếm số lượng đỉnh hoặc số lượng góc nhọn khi các hình có hình dạng biến thiên phức tạp.

question_text: You are an insight analyst at Infosys, running the weekly figures a client’s regional managers open every Monday at eight. On Saturday evening you look at your phone and see that Friday night’s data load failed, so Monday’s figures will be empty. Nobody else on the engagement is working this weekend. The regional managers plan their week from those figures. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Rerun the load tonight, check the figures yourself, and message the manager running the engagement so that somebody knows what happened before Monday morning at eight.
Rerun the load tonight and say nothing about it, since the figures will be there at eight and nobody will have noticed that anything went wrong on Friday night.
Assume somebody on call has already picked the failure up, and look at it first thing on Monday when you are back at your own desk.
Message the manager running the engagement now to say the load failed, and wait for them to tell you whether they want it rerun.
explanation: B: Removes the evidence of a fault that will repeat: the load failed for a reason nobody now looks at, so it fails again next Friday night. C: Declines to check something only you can see: nobody else is working this weekend, so the regional managers open empty figures at eight with no warning at all. D: Waits for permission you do not need: rerunning a load that failed is the job itself, and Saturday night goes by waiting on somebody who is not working. The most effective response is to rerun the load tonight, check the figures and message the manager about what happened. It puts the figures back before the deadline that matters, it checks them rather than assuming the rerun worked, and it leaves somebody other than you knowing that Friday night failed. It beats messaging the manager now and waiting for them to say whether they want it rerun, because the rerun is the work itself and Saturday night is spent waiting on somebody who is not there. It beats rerunning the load and saying nothing because nobody will have noticed, because a fault nobody records is a fault nobody fixes, and the same load fails next week. The least effective response is assuming somebody on call has already picked the failure up: the other three all put the figures back before eight, whereas this one rests on a person you already know is not working, so the regional managers plan a week from an empty screen. The principle: when you are the only one who can see it, you are the one who acts on it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Kiểm tra quy luật cộng/trừ hình (XOR pattern) theo hàng ngang trước, nếu không thỏa mãn thì xét theo cột dọc.

question_text: You are a process analyst at Infosys, measuring the time saved by a change a client made to how they handle claims. Your measurement so far puts the saving at about a third of the figure the client’s own managers have been quoting to their teams for the past month. Two of the eight sites are still to be measured and will not move the picture much. The client’s programme sponsor asks you on Thursday how it is going. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Give the sponsor the number on Thursday without saying anything about the figure their managers have been using, and leave the two of them to meet somewhere later.
Wait until the last two sites are measured next week and then send the sponsor the full picture in writing, rather than a partial answer on Thursday.
Tell the sponsor on Thursday what the measurement shows so far, that two sites are still to come, and that the figure their managers are using looks about three times too high.
Say nothing about the gap on Thursday and keep it to yourself until the last two sites have been measured, in case the figure improves once they are in.
explanation: A: Reports the fact and not the collision: the sponsor gets a number and is left to find out on their own that their organisation is briefing a different one. B: Waits for a completeness nobody asked for: the last two sites will not move the answer, and a week of briefings goes out while the report is being tidied. D: Hides an unwelcome result: another month of briefings goes out on a number you have measured and know to be wrong, and you are the only person in a position to say so. The most effective response is to tell the sponsor on Thursday what the measurement shows and that the managers’ figure looks three times too high. The sponsor has asked, the gap is the single most useful thing you know, and saying it on Thursday gives their organisation the chance to stop quoting a figure it cannot support. It beats giving the sponsor the number without saying anything about the managers’ figure, because a number handed over without the comparison leaves the sponsor to collide with their own managers’ version later and in public. It beats waiting until the last two sites are measured and sending the full picture next week, because the outstanding sites will not change the answer, so the wait buys tidiness at the cost of another week of wrong briefings. The least effective response is saying nothing about the gap on Thursday and keeping it to yourself until the last two sites are measured: the other three all put something true in front of the sponsor this week, whereas this one keeps a measured result out of their hands entirely on the hope that it moves, so the client goes on telling its own people a figure you know is three times too big. The principle: an unwelcome measurement is worth most on the day somebody asks for it.

question_text: You are a trading assistant at L’Oreal. A figure you produced for a weekly pack rests on an assumption about supplier lead times that changed on Friday. With the new lead times the figure would be materially different. The pack goes to a manager this afternoon and the meeting that uses it is tomorrow. Reworking the figure properly takes half a day, which you do not have. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Rework the figure quickly this afternoon with an estimate of the new lead times, and put the estimated version in the pack instead of the one you can support.
Put the figure in the pack as it stands, without flagging that the lead times behind it changed on Friday, since the rework cannot be done before this afternoon in any case.
Put the figure in with a clear note that the lead times changed on Friday and what that does to it, and tell the manager before the pack goes out so nothing surprises him.
Leave the figure out of the pack altogether and explain in its place that the number is being reworked after a change to supplier lead times.
explanation: A: Substitutes a guess for a stale fact: neither number has been checked, and the estimate carries none of the working the original at least had. B: Withholds the fact that decides what the number is worth: tomorrow's meeting uses a figure whose basis is known to be out of date by the only person who knows it. D: Removes the evidence rather than qualifying it: tomorrow's meeting loses a usable number and gains nothing it can decide with. The most effective response is to put the figure in with a clear note on the lead time change and what it is likely to do, and tell the manager before the pack goes out: the meeting keeps a number it can use, everybody knows what it rests on, and the manager can decide whether tomorrow needs the rework. It beats reworking it quickly on an estimate, because an unchecked guess replaces a number whose working at least exists. It beats leaving the figure out, because the meeting is then deciding with nothing. The least effective response is putting the figure in without flagging the lead time change: the only person who knows the basis has changed says nothing, and the meeting treats a stale figure as current, which is a different kind of wrong from guessing or from withdrawing the number. The principle: when you cannot fix a number in time, publish what is wrong with it to the person who is about to rely on it.
