question_text: You are a procurement graduate at L’Oreal. Working through delivery notes for a different piece of work, you find that one supplier’s notes have been recording pack sizes that do not match what is actually arriving, and have done for at least six weeks. Nobody has raised it. The supplier is being reviewed in a fortnight, and the pack sizes feed the figures that review uses. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Correct the pack sizes in the figures yourself for the six weeks that you can see, so that the review in a fortnight at least starts from numbers that match what was delivered.
Pass the whole thing to the manager who owns the supplier relationship without mentioning the review in a fortnight, and treat your part as finished.
Raise it at the review itself in a fortnight, when the supplier and the manager are both in the room and the pack sizes are on the agenda anyway.
Take it to the manager who owns the supplier today with the six weeks set out, say what it does to the review's figures, and offer to check how far back it goes.
explanation: A: Alters figures nobody asked you to alter: the numbers stop matching the notes that produced them, and the recording fault that caused it is now invisible to the person accountable for the supplier. B: Hands a finding on without what makes it urgent: the manager receives six weeks of notes with no mention of the review that is about to use them. C: Times the disclosure for the meeting it should have preceded: the review is prepared on figures everybody now knows are wrong, and the correction lands as a surprise. The most effective response is to take it to the manager who owns the supplier today with the six weeks set out, say what it does to the review’s figures, and offer to check how far back it goes: it reaches the person who can act while a fortnight is still enough time, and it carries the consequence rather than only the observation. It beats passing it across without mentioning the review, because the manager cannot act on a deadline nobody has told him about. It beats raising it at the review, because the preparation everybody does beforehand is built on figures already known to be false. The least effective response is correcting the pack sizes in the figures yourself: the numbers stop matching the notes behind them, the supplier carries on recording the wrong sizes, and the person accountable for that supplier can no longer see any of it, which is a different kind of wrong from handing the finding on bare or from raising it too late. The principle: something you found outside your own remit is carried to somebody who can act on it, with what it means attached, and never quietly repaired.

question_text: You are a reporting analyst. A return that goes to the firm’s largest client is due at noon, and the contract charges the firm for a late or incomplete one. One figure is still missing. The approved route is a signed data extract from another team, which takes a day. The figure is also on a dashboard that is not an approved source for this return. Your manager is in a meeting until 11:30. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Put a note to your manager now setting out the gap, the two routes and the noon deadline, so they can decide at 11:30 with everything in front of them.
Submit the return at noon with the figure left blank, and follow up with the missing number once the signed extract arrives tomorrow.
Interrupt your manager's meeting now to get a decision, since a regulator deadline at noon outranks whatever else is being discussed in there this morning.
Take the figure from the dashboard and put it in the return, since the number will be the same either way and the deadline is the thing that actually matters here.
explanation: B: Files an incomplete return without asking: whether a gap or a late charge is the better outcome on a contracted return is a decision above your level. C: Escalates before there is anything to decide with: the meeting ends at 11:30, which still leaves half an hour, and the options can be set out first. D: Decides which rules count: an approved-source rule exists precisely so a regulator-facing figure can be traced, and a deadline is not a reason for one person to set it aside alone. The most effective response is to put a note to your manager now setting out the gap, the two routes and the noon deadline, so she can decide at 11:30 with everything in front of her: the decision is genuinely hers, 11:30 leaves time, and a written note means she decides on the facts rather than a doorway summary. It beats submitting the return at noon with the figure left blank, because choosing a gap over a late charge is not a junior call. It beats interrupting her meeting now to get a decision, because half an hour is enough and the interruption buys nothing. The least effective response is taking the figure from the dashboard and putting it in the return: an unapproved source goes into a return the client relies on, on one person’s judgement that the number is probably the same. That is setting aside a stated control rather than escalating badly. The principle: when the only route to the deadline breaks a rule, the deadline is somebody else’s decision.

question_text: You are a support analyst. The monthly figure for tickets resolved first time looks about twenty points too high, and the only way it could be that high is if a colleague has been closing and reopening tickets. The figure goes into a board pack tomorrow. You have a full queue and a difficult history with that colleague. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Rebuild the whole month's figure from the raw ticket data yourself tonight, and take a finished alternative number to whoever compiles the pack tomorrow.
Leave it alone and get on with the queue. The figure is not yours to police, and raising it would mean an awkward conversation about somebody else's numbers.
Send a note to whoever compiles the pack saying the figure looks high and that they may want to check it before tomorrow, without saying why you think so.
Ask your colleague today how the figure got so high, and if the answer does not explain it, tell whoever compiles the pack what you have found before tomorrow.
explanation: A: Spends a night proving what a question would settle: the pack goes tomorrow either way, and one conversation this afternoon would have resolved it. B: Avoids the difficult conversation: a board reads a first-time-fix rate tomorrow that only you have any reason to doubt, and the queue was never the reason. C: Flags a doubt without its reason: they cannot check a number without knowing what to check, so the warning arrives too vague to act on. The most effective response is to ask your colleague today how the figure got so high, and if the answer does not explain it, tell whoever compiles the pack before tomorrow. The one thing that settles this is a question only he can answer, it takes minutes, and there is still time to warn the compiler. It beats rebuilding the whole month’s figure from the raw ticket data tonight, because a night of that produces a rival number without establishing whether the first was wrong. It beats sending the compiler a note saying the figure looks high without saying why, because they have no way to check it. The least effective response is leaving it alone and getting on with the queue: it is worse than either of the other two, because both put something in front of somebody before the pack goes, while this lets a board read a figure only you have reason to doubt. The principle: when the fastest route to the truth is a conversation you would rather avoid, the discomfort is the cost of the check, not a reason to skip it.

question_text: You are an improvement analyst at LEK Consulting, reviewing how a distribution centre handles returns. Last week the site manager asked you how long the checking step takes on average, and you told them eleven minutes. Working through the rest of your observations, you have found that you left a whole shift out, and the real figure is nearer eighteen. The site manager has been building eleven minutes into their staffing plan. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Wait until the review is finished and set the eighteen minutes out in the final report, where the change and the shift you missed can be shown together.
Use eighteen minutes in your own written report at the end of the review, and keep it to yourself that the answer you gave last week was wrong.
Tell the site manager today that the eleven minute figure was wrong, give them the corrected eighteen, and say which parts of their plan it changes.
Send the site manager the corrected figure on its own, and leave out where the difference came from so that the plan simply gets the right number.
explanation: A: Delays a correction that is already costing: the staffing plan is being built this week on a number you already know to be seven minutes short. B: Hides your own mistake: the site manager keeps building on eleven minutes and finds out weeks later from a report, if they happen to compare the two numbers at all. D: Leaves the reader to work it out: the site manager holds two figures with no reason attached and cannot tell which of their assumptions to revisit. The most effective response is to tell the site manager today that the eleven minute figure was wrong and give them the corrected one. It reaches the person who is actively using the wrong number, it arrives while their plan can still be changed cheaply, and it says what the error was so they can judge how far it spreads. It beats sending the corrected figure on its own and leaving out where the difference came from, because a new figure with no explanation leaves the site manager guessing whether their own assumptions or your work moved. It beats waiting until the review is finished and setting eighteen minutes out in the final report, because a plan is being built this week and the report is weeks away. The least effective response is using eighteen in the final report and keeping it to yourself that last week’s answer was wrong: the other three all put the right number in front of the client at some point, whereas this one protects you rather than the plan, so a client keeps staffing a step at eleven minutes when you know it takes eighteen and the only person who could tell them has decided not to. The principle: a wrong answer you gave is corrected to the person you gave it to, as soon as you know.

question_text: You are an insight analyst at LEK Consulting, building reports on a client’s test system. While changing a setting this morning you deleted a table that two of the client’s own analysts use for their weekly figures. Nobody has mentioned it, and their weekly run is on Monday. Putting the table back would need the client’s technical team, who would ask how it was lost. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Ask the client's technical team to put the table back this morning without saying how it was lost, then get on with building the reports before Monday.
Tell the client's two analysts directly that their table has gone, and let them raise it with their own technical team.
Rebuild the table from the copy on your own machine and keep it to yourself, so that nothing has to be said.
Tell the manager running the engagement now and ask the client's technical team to restore the table, saying plainly that you deleted it this morning.
explanation: A: Leaves out the part that matters: the table returns, and the people who decide who may change that system are missing the fact that it was you. B: Sends it round the wrong way: the analysts cannot say how the table was lost, and your own engagement first hears of the problem from the client. C: Conceals your own fault: the client's analysts run Monday's figures from a table nobody has checked, and the one person who knows what happened to it has decided not to say. The most effective response is to tell the manager now and ask the client’s technical team to restore the table, saying you deleted it. It gets the table back through the people who own the system, it does so before Monday, and it puts your own account of what happened on the record before anybody has to ask. It beats telling the client’s two analysts directly and leaving them to raise it, because the analysts cannot explain a loss they did not cause, and your engagement then learns about it from the client. It beats asking the technical team to put the table back without saying how it was lost, because a restore without the reason leaves the client unable to judge whether the same thing can happen again. The least effective response is rebuilding the table from the copy on your own machine and keeping it to yourself: the other three all end with the client’s own people knowing their table was lost, whereas this one substitutes your private copy for the real thing and closes the matter without anyone else ever knowing, so Monday’s figures rest on something no one has checked. The principle: your own mistake is the one you say out loud, and quickly.

question_text: You are a purchasing assistant at Lowe’’s. A supplier has rung to query a set of volumes that a colleague of yours prepared. You can see that your colleague’s numbers are right and that the supplier has misread the layout. He is impatient, has queried her figures before, and says he would rather deal with you from now on because she takes days to reply. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell him her figures are often unreliable and that he should bring the numbers to you in future, so that at least the queries get answered quickly.
Show him where the layout misled him, say the figures are right, and tell him you will pass on his point about reply times to her and your manager.
Answer the query yourself and agree to be his contact for volumes from now on, since he is clearly not going to deal with her and somebody has to answer him.
Tell him the volumes are her work and that he should take the query back to her, since it is her supplier and answering it yourself would cut across her.
explanation: A: Undermines a colleague to an outsider: her numbers were right, and a supplier is now told by her own team that her work cannot be trusted. C: Solves a relationship problem by rearranging it: she loses her own supplier contact without being consulted, and nobody addresses the reply times. D: Applies the boundary and ignores the customer: he is sent back to somebody he says takes days, holding a misreading you could have cleared up in a minute. The most effective response is to show him where the layout misled him, confirm the figures are right, and say you will pass his point about reply times to her and your manager: the query is answered on the spot, your colleague’s work is defended because it is correct, and the real complaint goes somewhere it can be dealt with. It beats agreeing to become his contact, because that quietly takes her supplier away without asking her. It beats sending him back to her with his misreading intact, because it costs a minute to clear up. The least effective response is telling him her figures are often unreliable: they were right, and a supplier has been told by her own team not to trust her, which is a different kind of wrong from over-accommodating him or from standing on the boundary. The principle: defend a colleague’s correct work to an outsider, and take the criticism of her that has substance to her and your manager instead.

question_text: You are a trading assistant at Lidl. A figure you produced for a weekly pack rests on an assumption about supplier lead times that changed on Friday. With the new lead times the figure would be materially different. The pack goes to a manager this afternoon and the meeting that uses it is tomorrow. Reworking the figure properly takes half a day, which you do not have. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Rework the figure quickly this afternoon with an estimate of the new lead times, and put the estimated version in the pack instead of the one you can support.
Put the figure in the pack as it stands, without flagging that the lead times behind it changed on Friday, since the rework cannot be done before this afternoon in any case.
Put the figure in with a clear note that the lead times changed on Friday and what that does to it, and tell the manager before the pack goes out so nothing surprises him.
Leave the figure out of the pack altogether and explain in its place that the number is being reworked after a change to supplier lead times.
explanation: A: Substitutes a guess for a stale fact: neither number has been checked, and the estimate carries none of the working the original at least had. B: Withholds the fact that decides what the number is worth: tomorrow's meeting uses a figure whose basis is known to be out of date by the only person who knows it. D: Removes the evidence rather than qualifying it: tomorrow's meeting loses a usable number and gains nothing it can decide with. The most effective response is to put the figure in with a clear note on the lead time change and what it is likely to do, and tell the manager before the pack goes out: the meeting keeps a number it can use, everybody knows what it rests on, and the manager can decide whether tomorrow needs the rework. It beats reworking it quickly on an estimate, because an unchecked guess replaces a number whose working at least exists. It beats leaving the figure out, because the meeting is then deciding with nothing. The least effective response is putting the figure in without flagging the lead time change: the only person who knows the basis has changed says nothing, and the meeting treats a stale figure as current, which is a different kind of wrong from guessing or from withdrawing the number. The principle: when you cannot fix a number in time, publish what is wrong with it to the person who is about to rely on it.

question_text: You are a management accounts assistant. Every month you rekey the same figures between two systems, which takes half a day and causes errors. You could write a small spreadsheet tool that does it automatically. Tools that move data between these systems have to be registered and reviewed by the systems team first. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Build a prototype, show your manager the half-day saving, and ask them to put it to the systems team for registration before anybody uses it for real.
Ask the systems team to build the tool themselves, since they own the registration process and will know how it should be done.
Carry on rekeying each month and raise the idea at the next systems team forum in three months, when there is a proper slot for suggestions like this one.
Build the tool and start using it for this month's close, and register it with the systems team afterwards once it has proved that it works properly.
explanation: B: Hands away the part you are best placed to do: you know the process and the failure modes, and their queue is long. C: Delays the decision for a quarter: three more months of half-days and known errors, to wait for a meeting. D: Builds a workaround around a control: a month's reported figures come out of an unreviewed tool, and registration afterwards cannot undo that they already have. The most effective response is to build a prototype, show your manager the half-day saving, and ask him to put it to the systems team for registration before anybody uses it for real: the prototype makes the case concrete, he owns the priority, and registration happens before anything real depends on it. It beats carrying on rekeying and raising the idea at the systems forum in three months, because three months of known errors is a real cost. It beats asking the systems team to build the tool themselves, because handing it to a long queue loses the knowledge that makes it work. The least effective response is building the tool, using it for this month’s close, and registering it afterwards: a month’s figures are produced by a tool that the review exists to look at before it is trusted. That is going around a stated control rather than moving too slowly or too fast. The principle: build it, show it, and get it approved before anything real runs on it.

question_text: You are a proposal analyst at McKinsey & Co, writing a section of a bid that is due on Thursday. You also promised the client team at Kelmarsh Foods a summary of last month’s figures on the same day, and you only noticed this morning that the two land together. Both were your own commitments, and nobody else knows the dates collide. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Tell the manager running the bid this morning that the two dates collide, say what you can finish by Thursday, and ask which of the two should move.
Keep it to yourself, work late on both, and let the bid section arrive a day late with no explanation of what caused the delay.
Ask the client team at Kelmarsh Foods whether their summary can wait until Monday, and say nothing about the clash to anybody on the bid.
Split Thursday between the two, sending a shortened bid section and an outline of the summary so that something arrives for each of them.
explanation: B: Hides your own oversight: the bid section is late for a reason nobody is told, and the one person who could have moved a date is left to find out afterwards. C: Moves a client's date without asking your own team: the bid is the piece with the fixed date, and the manager running it never learns the two collided. D: Splits the day so neither finishes: the bid goes in short and the client gets an outline, when one of the two could have been done properly. The most effective response is to tell the manager running the bid that the dates collide and ask which of the two should move. The clash is yours to surface, the manager owns which of the two moves, and Thursday is still three days away. It beats asking the client team whether their summary can wait until Monday, because moving the client’s date is a decision your own team never hears about, and the bid is the piece with the fixed date. It beats splitting Thursday between the two and sending a shortened section and an outline, because half a day on each produces a short bid section and an outline when one of the two could have been finished properly. The least effective response is keeping it to yourself and letting the bid section arrive a day late: the other three all put the collision in front of somebody who can act on it, whereas this one keeps a problem you created out of sight until the bid is already late. The principle: a clash you made is still a clash, and the person who owns the dates cannot move one they do not know about.
tip: Mẹo MT: Đếm số lượng đỉnh hoặc số lượng góc nhọn khi các hình có hình dạng biến thiên phức tạp.

question_text: You are a stock control assistant at McDonalds. A recount you asked for turned up a mistake in your own figures, and the colleague who did it said, in front of two others, that he had wasted an afternoon on your arithmetic. It stung and he was largely right. The next count is due on Thursday and it needs two people, one of whom is normally him. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Ask your supervisor to put somebody else on Thursday's count, since working alongside him this week would be uncomfortable for both of you after what was said.
Refuse to work with him on Thursday's count after the way he spoke to you, and say you would rather do it on your own or not at all.
Acknowledge to him that the figures were wrong and say what you have changed, and do Thursday's count with him as planned since the count needs two people.
Say nothing about it, do Thursday's count as planned, and let the remark fade rather than reopening something that was fair comment anyway.
explanation: A: Redesigns the rota around one awkward afternoon: the count is harder to staff, and the two of you have to work together again the week after in any case. B: Withdraws from a job that needs two people after a disagreement: Thursday's count is put at risk to answer a remark made about an afternoon. D: Lets an unrepaired working relationship stand: the count happens and he has no reason to think the mistake will not simply repeat. The most effective response is to acknowledge that the figures were wrong, say what you have changed, and do Thursday’s count with him: the criticism was largely fair, saying so is what restores the working relationship, and the count that needs two people gets them. It beats asking for somebody else on Thursday, because the rota is rearranged around one bad afternoon and you will work together next week anyway. It beats letting the remark fade, because he has no reason to expect anything different next time. The least effective response is refusing to work with him on Thursday: a count that needs two people is put at risk to answer a remark, which is a different kind of wrong from avoiding him or from staying silent. The principle: when the criticism is fair, own it and stay in the work with the person who made it.

question_text: You are a stock control assistant at M&S. A weekly count shows three hundred units fewer than the system expects on one line. The trading team needs a figure this afternoon to decide what to order for next week, and they have asked you whether the count can be relied on. Investigating the gap properly means pulling the movement history, which takes about two hours. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Give the trading team the counted figure with the gap stated alongside it, say the cause is not yet known, and start on the movement history straight away.
Assure the trading team that the counted figure is sound and the gap is a scanning error, and look at the movement history later in the week if anybody comes back to you.
Hold the figure back until the movement history is finished, and tell the trading team they will have something reliable by the end of the day.
Give the trading team the figure the system holds rather than the counted one, since the system is what their ordering tool reads from in any case.
explanation: B: Gives an assurance you have not earned: nothing yet distinguishes a scanning error from three hundred missing units, and next week's order is placed on a cause that was invented to close the question. C: Delays the decision: the order has to be placed this afternoon, so a reliable number tomorrow is worth less to them than an honest one now. D: Substitutes the convenient source for the checked one: the count is the only evidence anybody has looked at, and it is the number being set aside. The most effective response is to give the trading team the counted figure with the gap stated alongside it and start on the movement history at once: they get a number in time to order, they know exactly how much weight it carries, and the work that settles the cause begins immediately. It beats holding the figure until the history is finished, because the decision is this afternoon and an honest number now beats a certain one tomorrow. It beats handing over the system figure instead, because the count is the only thing anybody has actually observed. The least effective response is assuring them the count is sound and the gap is a scanning error: no work has been done that could support either claim, and stating a cause you have not established is a different kind of wrong from being slow or from choosing the wrong source. The principle: report what you know and what you do not, rather than supplying the certainty the person asking would prefer.
tip: Mẹo MT: Kiểm tra quy luật cộng/trừ hình (XOR pattern) theo hàng ngang trước, nếu không thỏa mãn thì xét theo cột dọc.

question_text: You are a relationship support assistant. In a client meeting your colleague gives a figure you know is a month out of date. The client writes it down. The meeting has twenty minutes left and the figure matters to what the client decides today. Correcting it means saying so while they are both sitting there. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Correct the figure by blaming his preparation in front of the client, saying that this is exactly why the numbers ought to be checked before anybody walks into a meeting.
Say plainly that the figure has moved since then, give the current one, and take up how it came to be quoted with your colleague after the meeting.
Pass your colleague a note about the figure and leave it entirely to him to decide whether he corrects it in front of the client or not.
Say nothing at all while the meeting is still running and send the client a corrected figure by email afterwards, so that nothing has to be said in front of your colleague.
explanation: A: Makes a stale figure a verdict on a colleague in front of a client: the correction lands, and what the client remembers is that your firm's people do not trust each other. C: Gives the decision to the person least able to take it: he has just given the number and would have to unsay it himself, mid-meeting. D: Leaves the client deciding on a stale number: they have twenty minutes and a decision, and the email arrives after both. The most effective response is to say plainly that the figure has moved since then, give the current one, and take up how it came to be quoted after the meeting: the client is about to decide on it, a month-old figure is a fact rather than a fault, and taking the preparation up afterwards keeps it between the two of you. It beats saying nothing and emailing the client a corrected figure afterwards, because the decision happens inside the twenty minutes. It beats passing him a note and leaving it to him to correct in front of the client, because asking him to unsay it himself in the room is the hardest possible way to fix it. The least effective response is correcting it by blaming his preparation in front of the client: the number is fixed and the firm looks divided. That is personalising it rather than mistiming it or misrouting it. The principle: correct the fact in the room, and take the person outside it.

question_text: You are a duty coordinator at a courier depot. At 3pm three things need you. A driver has broken down with a vehicle full of next-day parcels and needs a recovery arranged. Your manager wants the weekly performance figures before he leaves at 4pm. And a customer is holding on the phone about a parcel that has been missing for a week. The recovery firm’s cut-off for same-day attendance is 3.30pm. The figures take twenty minutes. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Take the customer's call first since she is already holding and has been waiting a week, then arrange the recovery and do the figures if there is time before 4pm.
Ask the driver to arrange his own recovery while you handle the customer and the figures, since he is at the roadside and knows the vehicle better than you do.
Arrange the recovery before the 3.30pm cut-off, take the customer's number and promise a call back, then do the figures for your manager before 4pm.
Do the performance figures first so your manager has them before he leaves at 4pm, then arrange the recovery and return the customer's call afterwards.
explanation: A: Ignores the closing window: her parcel has been missing a week and will still be missing in ten minutes, while the recovery cut-off passes at 3.30pm and strands a van of next-day parcels overnight. B: Passes responsibility to others: the depot holds the recovery account and the cut-off, not the driver at the roadside. Handing him a task he cannot complete means the cut-off passes with nobody having acted. D: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholder's: it puts a reporting deadline ahead of a van of next-day parcels whose recovery window shuts in thirty minutes, and your manager has not been told the two clash. The most effective response is to arrange the recovery before the 3.30pm cut-off, take the customer’s number and promise a call back, then do the figures before 4pm: only the recovery has a window that shuts, and missing it strands a van of next-day parcels overnight. Once it is arranged, twenty minutes of figures still fits and the customer gets a call back today. It beats taking the customer’s call first because she is already holding, since a parcel missing for a week is not made worse by ten more minutes, while the cut-off cannot be recovered once passed. It beats doing the performance figures first so your manager has them before he leaves, because that treats a reporting deadline as outranking a closing operational window, without telling him the two clash. The least effective response is asking the driver to arrange his own recovery from the roadside: it hands it to the one person who cannot arrange it, since the depot holds the account, so the cut-off passes with nobody having acted. That is worse than the other two, which sequence badly but keep the work with someone able to do it. The principle: do the thing whose window is closing first, then fit the rest around it.

question_text: You are a data analyst at Mercer. In your review the manager tells you that your work is accurate but that you go quiet when a client questions it, and that this has to change. You have a client workshop on Thursday where two of your figures are certain to be challenged. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Ask a colleague who is good in workshops to field the questions on Thursday, so that the session goes well while you keep working on it for later.
Ask the manager to take the workshop themselves on Thursday, and offer to sit in and write up what the client says.
Ask the manager for an example of where it went wrong and what they would have said instead, then work out how you will answer the two challenges you expect on Thursday.
Go back through your figures in as much detail as you can, so that nothing on Thursday can catch you out, and leave how you handle the room to the day.
explanation: A: Avoids the thing the feedback was about: the workshop runs smoothly and Thursday teaches you nothing, so the same conversation happens again after the next one. B: Hands the problem to somebody else: the feedback was about a thing you do in the room, and the only occasion in the diary for doing it differently is given away. D: Acts on the wrong problem: the manager said the work is accurate, so more checking answers a criticism nobody made and leaves the real one untouched. The most effective response is to ask the manager for an example and what they would have said, then prepare for Thursday. It turns a general remark into something specific enough to act on, it takes the answer from the person who made the criticism, and it aims all of that at the occasion two days away where it will be tested. It beats asking a colleague to field the questions on Thursday, because a colleague fielding the questions makes Thursday go well and leaves you exactly where you started. It beats going back through the figures in detail and leaving the room to the day, because the manager said the figures are right, so more checking is effort spent on the one thing that was not the problem. The least effective response is asking the manager to take the workshop themselves on Thursday: the other three all leave you in the room on Thursday, whereas this one gives the occasion away entirely and turns a piece of development feedback into a reason to do less, which is the opposite of what it was for. The principle: get feedback specific enough to practise, then use the next occasion to practise it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Kiểm tra quy luật cộng/trừ hình (XOR pattern) theo hàng ngang trước, nếu không thỏa mãn thì xét theo cột dọc.

question_text: You are a stock control assistant at Next. The same line has shown a discrepancy at count on four occasions in six weeks, always in the same direction and always in the same area. Each time it has been written off as a counting error. You have now checked and the counts were done correctly. Discrepancies of this size and pattern are supposed to be reported to the loss prevention team. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Hand the four counts to the colleague who covers that area on Thursdays, since he knows the line better than you do, and consider your part in it finished.
Keep watching the line for another two counts to be sure the pattern is real, since four occasions could still turn out to be an unfortunate run of coincidences.
Raise it with your supervisor and let her decide whether it goes any further, without mentioning that the counts themselves have now been checked and are sound.
Report the four counts to the loss prevention team today with the checking you have done, since a pattern like that is what the reporting route exists for, and tell your supervisor.
explanation: A: Passes a reportable pattern on without owning it: the colleague has no idea it is four occurrences or that it should be reported, so the one person who knew both facts has stepped out of it. B: Waits for certainty that a report does not require: two more counts is three more weeks, and the threshold for reporting was passed some time ago. C: Escalates without the fact that changes the decision: she is asked to judge a pattern while the one thing that rules out a counting error is left out. The most effective response is to report the four counts to the loss prevention team today with your checking attached, and tell your supervisor you have done it: the pattern is exactly what the reporting route exists for, your checking is what makes it more than a suspicion, and nobody is surprised later. It beats waiting for two more counts, because the threshold was passed weeks ago and waiting adds three weeks. It beats raising it with your supervisor while leaving out that the counts were checked, because that is the fact the decision turns on. The least effective response is handing the four counts to the Thursday colleague and treating your part as finished: he does not know it is four occurrences or that it is reportable, so the only person holding both facts has stepped out, which is a different kind of wrong from waiting too long or from telling somebody too little. The principle: when something crosses a reporting line, take it there yourself, with what you know attached.

The most effective response is to build a prototype, show your manager the half-day saving, and ask him to put it to the systems team for registration before anybody uses it for real: the prototype makes the case concrete, he owns the priority, and registration happens before anything real depends on it. It beats carrying on rekeying and raising the idea at the systems forum in three months, because three months of known errors is a real cost. It beats asking the systems team to build the tool themselves, because handing it to a long queue loses the knowledge that makes it work. The least effective response is building the tool, using it for this month’s close, and registering it afterwards: a month’s figures are produced by a tool that the review exists to look at before it is trusted. That is going around a stated control rather than moving too slowly or too fast. The principle: build it, show it, and get it approved before anything real runs on it.

question_text: You are a lettings negotiator at an estate agency. At 1pm three things need you. A viewing is booked at 1.30 across town and the applicant is meeting you there. A landlord has emailed asking for an update by the end of the day. And your manager wants the week’s viewing figures, which take half an hour, before she leaves at 5pm. Travel to the viewing takes twenty minutes. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Reply to the landlord first since he has asked for an update today, then travel to the viewing and do the figures afterwards.
Do the viewing figures first while you are at your desk, then travel to the viewing and email the landlord in the evening.
Leave now for the 1.30 viewing, then reply to the landlord and do the viewing figures before your manager leaves at 5pm.
Let the applicant wait outside the property while you finish the work at your desk, and apologise for the late arrival once you eventually get there.
explanation: A: Delays the decision: the journey takes twenty minutes and it is already 1pm, so any time spent on email first risks arriving after an applicant who is meeting you there. B: Substitutes own judgement for the stakeholder's: half an hour of internal reporting due at 5pm is put ahead of a viewing at 1.30 with an applicant already committed to being there. D: Leaves someone waiting with no word: she is standing outside a property you arranged to meet her at, and she is left there while desk work that fits comfortably later is finished. Letting a person wait unheard is a different order of wrong from mis-ordering the tasks. The most effective response is to leave now for the 1.30 viewing, then reply to the landlord and do the viewing figures before your manager leaves at 5pm: the journey takes twenty minutes and an applicant is meeting you there, so leaving now is the only sequence that keeps the appointment. The landlord’s update has until the end of the day and the figures until 5pm. It beats replying to the landlord first because he has asked for an update today, since answering email risks arriving after the applicant, and the update has hours of room. It beats doing the viewing figures first while you are at your desk, because half an hour of reporting due at 5pm should not precede an appointment with someone waiting across town. The least effective response is letting the applicant wait outside the property while you finish the desk work: it leaves her standing there hearing nothing until you arrive. That is worse than the other two, which sequence the work badly but still turn up. The principle: keep the appointment someone else has committed to, then use the remaining hours for the work with slack in it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Phân tích theo từng thuộc tính độc lập: Hướng xoay góc (90°/45°), số lượng nét, màu sắc (Đen/Trắng), và vị trí.

question_text: You are a production coordinator at a print and mail house. At 11am three things need you. A mailing of 20,000 renewal notices must reach the Royal Mail collection at 2pm or the legal notice period is missed. A colleague needs help fixing a jammed inserter on a different job. And your manager wants headcount figures for a meeting at noon. The renewal job needs ninety minutes of your attention. The headcount figures take fifteen minutes. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Help your colleague with the jammed inserter first, since a stopped machine is costing time on the floor, then do the renewals and the headcount figures.
Work on the renewals and the inserter together, moving between them, and do the headcount figures if the mailing is finished before the 2pm collection.
Do the fifteen minutes of headcount figures for the noon meeting, then give the renewal mailing your full attention until the 2pm collection, and pass the inserter to another operator.
Start the renewal mailing immediately and tell your manager the headcount figures will have to wait until after the 2pm collection.
explanation: A: Abandons own committed work: an unquantified machine fix is taken on ahead of a ninety-minute job with a 2pm legal deadline, which leaves no margin if the jam takes longer than expected. B: Splits effort so nothing finishes: a mailing with a legal notice period is left to compete for attention with a machine fault, which risks missing a deadline that cannot be recovered and is the most costly of the four outcomes. D: Splits the wrong thing: it protects the deadline that matters and sacrifices a fifteen-minute task that fits inside the margin anyway, so the manager goes into a noon meeting without figures for no gain. The most effective response is to do the fifteen minutes of headcount figures for the noon meeting, then give the renewal mailing your full attention until the 2pm collection, and pass the inserter to another operator: there are three hours, the mailing needs ninety minutes of them and has a legal deadline, and the figures are needed at noon. Both fit if the short one goes first, and the machine fault is work someone else can take. It beats starting the mailing immediately and telling your manager the figures must wait, because that protects the same deadline while needlessly sacrificing a fifteen-minute task that comfortably fits. It beats helping your colleague with the jammed inserter first, because taking on a machine fault of unknown length ahead of a legally timed mailing risks the one deadline that cannot be moved. The least effective response is moving between the renewals and the inserter and fitting the figures in afterwards: it lets a mailing with a legal notice period compete for attention with a machine jam, which is the most likely way to miss the collection entirely. That is worse than the other two, which mis- sequence but keep the mailing whole. The principle: check what actually fits in the time, protect the deadline that cannot move, and hand off what someone else can do.

question_text: You are a delivery coordinator. You compile the weekly figures showing how the team’s hours split across three projects. This week roughly a third went on unplanned support, which has no project to sit against and makes the delivery figure look poor. Your manager has said she would rather the report did not raise questions from the programme board this month. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Show the support hours as their own line and add a note saying they were unavoidable, so that the delivery figure is read with that caveat attached.
Show the support hours as their own line and say nothing about them unless somebody asks, since the figures speak for themselves either way.
Show the support hours as their own line, and tell your manager the figure will raise questions, so that she has the answer ready before the board asks it.
Record the support hours as covered by the nearest project. The delivery figure then holds up properly, and the board is not distracted by an odd line item this month.
explanation: A: Softens the number with a label: unavoidable is your judgement rather than a fact, and it invites the board to discount a third of the week. B: Reports accurately and abandons the explanation: a third of the week appears without a cause, which is exactly what will generate the questions. D: Records effort against work it was not spent on: a third of the week now appears as project delivery in a report the board uses to allocate people. The most effective response is to show the support hours as their own line, and tell your manager the figure will raise questions. The figures should say what happened, and the honest way to handle her concern is to warn her what the question will be and hand her the answer. It beats showing them as their own line with a note saying they were unavoidable, because that is an opinion added to a fact and it encourages the board to set the week aside. It beats showing the line and saying nothing unless somebody asks, because a large unexplained line is precisely what produces the questions she is worried about. The least effective response is recording the support hours as covered by the nearest project: it is worse than either of the other two, because both leave the hours visible, spun or bare, while this moves a third of the week into project delivery in a report used to allocate people. The principle: report the number as it is and prepare the person who will be asked about it, rather than changing the number so the question is never asked.
tip: Mẹo MT: Đếm số lượng đỉnh hoặc số lượng góc nhọn khi các hình có hình dạng biến thiên phức tạp.

question_text: You are a customer service adviser. A colleague tells you she gave a customer the wrong charges figure last week, that the customer accepted it, and that she has decided not to raise it because “it worked out fine”. She asks you not to mention it. The team logs pricing errors weekly. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Agree to keep it between the two of you and leave the weekly log alone, since the customer accepted the figure and no harm has come of it in the end.
Tell her the log exists for exactly this and that you would rather she entered it herself, and say plainly that you will raise it if she does not.
Say nothing to her about it at all and enter the error in the weekly log yourself later on, since the log needs to be accurate whatever she has decided to do about it.
Tell your team leader today what she has told you, without giving her the chance to enter it in the log herself first.
explanation: A: Joins a decision to hide it: the log's only purpose is counting errors like this one, and two people have now agreed it will not be counted. C: Logs it behind her: she asked you directly, and finding her own error in the log without warning is worse for both of you. D: Escalates before asking: she may well log it if asked plainly, and going straight up makes an error into a conduct question. The most effective response is to tell her the log exists for exactly this, that you would rather she entered it herself, and that you will raise it if she does not: it gives her the chance to put it right, is completely clear about what happens if she does not, and protects the log either way. It beats entering the error in the weekly log yourself without saying anything to her, because logging it silently is the same ambush with extra steps. It beats telling your team leader today what she has told you, because she has not yet been asked. The least effective response is agreeing to keep it between you and leave the log alone: the weekly log is deliberately left wrong by two people who both know it, so a pricing error that happened is recorded as one that did not. That is agreeing to conceal it rather than raising it clumsily. The principle: give them the chance, and say what you will do if they decline it.
tip: Mẹo MT: Loại trừ nhanh các phương án vi phạm quy tắc xoay góc chiều kim đồng hồ.

question_text: You are a support analyst. The monthly figure for tickets resolved first time looks about twenty points too high, and the only way it could be that high is if a colleague has been closing and reopening tickets. The figure goes into a board pack tomorrow. You have a full queue and a difficult history with that colleague. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Rebuild the whole month's figure from the raw ticket data yourself tonight, and take a finished alternative number to whoever compiles the pack tomorrow.
Leave it alone and get on with the queue. The figure is not yours to police, and raising it would mean an awkward conversation about somebody else's numbers.
Send a note to whoever compiles the pack saying the figure looks high and that they may want to check it before tomorrow, without saying why you think so.
Ask your colleague today how the figure got so high, and if the answer does not explain it, tell whoever compiles the pack what you have found before tomorrow.
explanation: A: Spends a night proving what a question would settle: the pack goes tomorrow either way, and one conversation this afternoon would have resolved it. B: Avoids the difficult conversation: a board reads a first-time-fix rate tomorrow that only you have any reason to doubt, and the queue was never the reason. C: Flags a doubt without its reason: they cannot check a number without knowing what to check, so the warning arrives too vague to act on. The most effective response is to ask your colleague today how the figure got so high, and if the answer does not explain it, tell whoever compiles the pack before tomorrow. The one thing that settles this is a question only he can answer, it takes minutes, and there is still time to warn the compiler. It beats rebuilding the whole month’s figure from the raw ticket data tonight, because a night of that produces a rival number without establishing whether the first was wrong. It beats sending the compiler a note saying the figure looks high without saying why, because they have no way to check it. The least effective response is leaving it alone and getting on with the queue: it is worse than either of the other two, because both put something in front of somebody before the pack goes, while this lets a board read a figure only you have reason to doubt. The principle: when the fastest route to the truth is a conversation you would rather avoid, the discomfort is the cost of the check, not a reason to skip it.

question_text: You are a trading assistant at Procter & Gamble. A large account has queried a charge on last month’s invoice. You have pulled the figures and can see the charge is correct, but the reason it changed is a contract term you do not fully understand. The account manager is out today. The customer wants an answer before the end of the week, and it is Wednesday. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Reply with the figures you have checked and what they show, say that the contract point needs the account manager, and book time with him for tomorrow morning.
Explain the contract term to the customer as best you understand it, and say you will confirm it with the account manager tomorrow.
Send the query on to the account team without the figures you have already checked, and let them start the contract point again from the beginning.
Reply to the customer that the charge is correct and leave the reason for the account manager to explain when he is back in the office tomorrow.
explanation: B: Answers outside what you actually know: an approximate account of a contract term is the thing most likely to be quoted back at the business later. C: Passes the problem on stripped of the work already done: the account team starts from nothing, the day you have spent on it is wasted, and Friday is two days away. D: Answers the easy half only: the customer did not ask whether the charge was right, they asked why it changed, and that is the part being deferred. The most effective response is to reply with the figures you have checked and what they show, say the contract point needs the account manager, and book time with him for tomorrow: the customer sees progress and an honest boundary, the checking work is used, and Friday is still comfortably reachable. It beats explaining the contract term as best you understand it, because an approximation about a contract is exactly the sentence that gets quoted back later. It beats replying that the charge is correct and leaving the reason to the account manager, because the reason is what was asked. The least effective response is sending the query on without the figures you have already checked: the next person starts from nothing, a day of work disappears, and the deadline is two days out, which is a different kind of wrong from over-reaching or from answering only half. The principle: escalate the part you cannot answer, with the part you can attached to it.

question_text: You are a relationship support assistant. In a client meeting your colleague gives a figure you know is a month out of date. The client writes it down. The meeting has twenty minutes left and the figure matters to what the client decides today. Correcting it means saying so while they are both sitting there. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Correct the figure by blaming his preparation in front of the client, saying that this is exactly why the numbers ought to be checked before anybody walks into a meeting.
Say plainly that the figure has moved since then, give the current one, and take up how it came to be quoted with your colleague after the meeting.
Pass your colleague a note about the figure and leave it entirely to him to decide whether he corrects it in front of the client or not.
Say nothing at all while the meeting is still running and send the client a corrected figure by email afterwards, so that nothing has to be said in front of your colleague.
explanation: A: Makes a stale figure a verdict on a colleague in front of a client: the correction lands, and what the client remembers is that your firm's people do not trust each other. C: Gives the decision to the person least able to take it: he has just given the number and would have to unsay it himself, mid-meeting. D: Leaves the client deciding on a stale number: they have twenty minutes and a decision, and the email arrives after both. The most effective response is to say plainly that the figure has moved since then, give the current one, and take up how it came to be quoted after the meeting: the client is about to decide on it, a month-old figure is a fact rather than a fault, and taking the preparation up afterwards keeps it between the two of you. It beats saying nothing and emailing the client a corrected figure afterwards, because the decision happens inside the twenty minutes. It beats passing him a note and leaving it to him to correct in front of the client, because asking him to unsay it himself in the room is the hardest possible way to fix it. The least effective response is correcting it by blaming his preparation in front of the client: the number is fixed and the firm looks divided. That is personalising it rather than mistiming it or misrouting it. The principle: correct the fact in the room, and take the person outside it.

question_text: You are a reporting analyst. A figure you circulated on Monday has been corrected, and the new number is materially lower. Two teams have been building next quarter’s plans on the old one since Tuesday, and one of them presents on Thursday. Correcting it publicly will be awkward for the colleague whose data caused the error. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Send both teams the corrected figure today with a short note on what changed, so the team presenting on Thursday can rework its plan before it stands up.
Send the corrected figure only to the team presenting on Thursday, and let the other team come across the change when they next look at the underlying report.
Tell both teams that the original figure came from your colleague's data and that this is the second time their numbers have caused a problem like this one for you.
Raise the correction at the reporting meeting next week, when the change can be explained properly to everybody who uses the figure at the same time.
explanation: B: Tells half the audience: both teams are planning on the same wrong number, and the one without a deadline is the one that will build on it for longest. C: Blames a colleague in front of the people who need the number: the teams still do not know what the corrected figure is, and the correction becomes an argument about who is at fault. D: Delays the decision: Thursday comes first, so the team with the deadline presents a plan built on a number you already know is wrong. The most effective response is to send both teams the corrected figure today with a short note on what changed: the correction is only useful before Thursday, both teams are exposed, and the note lets each of them judge what to redo. It beats sending it only to the team presenting on Thursday, because the other team is planning on the same wrong figure with more time to invest in it. It beats raising the correction at next week’s reporting meeting, because that is after the presentation the correction exists to protect. The least effective response is telling both teams the original figure came from your colleague’s data and that this is the second time: it turns a correction into an accusation, in front of people who still do not have the right number, and the thing they need never arrives. That is personalising it rather than communicating it badly. The principle: get the corrected number to everybody using it, in time to be worth having.

question_text: You work in an HR shared service team. It is Wednesday. Three things are outstanding: a new starter’s contract must go out today or she cannot begin on Monday, a manager wants a report on absence figures by Friday, and a colleague has asked you to review her draft policy whenever you have time. The contract takes an hour, the report three hours. You have five hours left today. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Work through all three in the order they were asked for, and let your manager know at the end of the day if anything has not been finished.
Start the absence report because it is the longest job, then do the contract at the end of the day once the bulk of the report is behind you.
Do the contract and the policy review first because they are the two shorter jobs, then start the absence report and continue it tomorrow morning.
Send the new starter's contract first, then work on the absence report, and tell your colleague you will review her policy tomorrow.
explanation: A: Hides the problem / silent deadline slip: the contract is the one item that cannot slip, and reporting at the end of the day is after the point at which anyone could rescue it. Reporting a missed deadline once it is missed is not communication. B: Delays the decision: it leaves an hour-long task with a today-or- never deadline to the end of a five-hour day, so any overrun on the report costs the new starter her start date. C: Splits effort so nothing finishes: it fits the favour in ahead of a report with a named Friday deadline, and pushes three hours of work into a day that already has other demands. The most effective response is to send the new starter’s contract first, then work on the absence report, and tell your colleague the policy review waits until tomorrow: only the contract has a deadline of today with a consequence attached, a start date, and it takes one of the five hours available. That leaves four hours for a three-hour report due Friday, and the policy review has no deadline at all. It beats starting the absence report first because it is the longest job, since that puts a fixed, unrecoverable deadline behind an open-ended one. It beats doing the contract and the policy review first as the two shorter jobs, because that fits an unscheduled favour ahead of a report with a stated deadline. Sit down with your colleague today and work through both counts against the same data until you can see where they part, then take one agreed number into tomorrow's session.

Tell the client's two analysts directly that their table has gone, and let them raise it with their own technical team.
Rebuild the table from the copy on your own machine and keep it to yourself, so that nothing has to be said.
Tell the manager running the engagement now and ask the client's technical team to restore the table, saying plainly that you deleted it this morning.

question_text: You work in an HR shared service team. It is Wednesday. Start the absence report because it is the longest job, then do the contract at the end of the day once the bulk of the report is behind you.

question_text: You are a trading assistant at Philip Morris. A large account has queried a charge on last month’s invoice. Explain the contract term to the customer as best you understand it, and say you will confirm it with the account manager tomorrow.

Reply to the customer that the charge is correct and leave the reason for the account manager to explain when he is back in the office tomorrow.

question_text: You are an analyst at a market-research agency. A client’s marketing director is building a product-launch presentation for Thursday around survey results you are producing. Hold the figures back until the full sample has arrived and been checked tomorrow night, so the marketing director only ever sees numbers that will not change.
Reply that the results are in good shape, and send the figures today without mentioning the missing half of the sample, since the final numbers will probably be close.
Raise the problem with your own account manager first and leave it to them to decide what, if anything, the client should be told about the sample.

She may lock claims you know are unstable into a launch presentation, a different kind of wrong from being slow or indirect. D: Tells the wrong audience first: briefing the account manager is sensible, but leaving the whole decision with them delays a straightforward factual caveat the marketing director needs today, while her request for the figures sits unanswered. The most effective response is to send the preliminary figures now, stating clearly that they rest on half the sample and flagging which headline numbers may move: the marketing director asked for figures today, and a plainly caveated interim answer lets her start building the presentation without locking in claims that could change tomorrow night. It beats holding everything back until the full sample is checked, because that costs her a full day of preparation against a Thursday deadline when a clearly caveated answer meets her stated need now. The least effective response is telling her the results are in good shape and sending the figures without mentioning the missing half: unlike holding them back, which is slow but honest, and unlike escalating internally, which at least surfaces the problem to someone, it assures the client of a reliability you know the numbers do not have. Say plainly that the figure has moved since then, give the current one, and take up how it came to be quoted with your colleague after the meeting.
Pass your colleague a note about the figure and leave it entirely to him to decide whether he corrects it in front of the client or not.

question_text: You are a junior data engineer. A supplier who provides a daily data feed has told you their file will be late every day for the next fortnight while they move systems. The team that publishes the morning figures depends on that feed and has committed to a customer deadline of nine o’clock each day. Nobody outside your inbox knows. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Keep pressing the supplier every day to deliver on time. It is their commitment to meet, and chasing them is the fastest route back to a nine o'clock file.
Tell the publishing team that the feed may be late occasionally over the next two weeks, without going into the supplier's system move or the full fortnight.
Tell the publishing team today that the feed will be late every day for a fortnight, and ask what they need from you to protect their nine o'clock commitment.
Put a note in the shared channel about the supplier's system move, so that anybody depending on the feed can see it and plan around it themselves.
explanation: A: Passes the problem on without owning it: the supplier has already said a fortnight, and the team promising nine o'clock still does not know it is at risk. B: Softens a warning until it cannot be planned with: occasionally and a fortnight every day are different problems and only one of them can be prepared for. D: Publishes to nobody in particular: the team with the nine o'clock commitment has no reason to be reading that channel this morning. The most effective response is to tell the publishing team today that the feed will be late every day for a fortnight, and ask what they need to protect their nine o’clock commitment. A fortnight of late files against a daily deadline is their problem to solve, and they can only solve it knowing the shape of it. It beats telling them the feed may be late occasionally over the next two weeks, because that produces no plan and every day for two weeks is a different problem. It beats putting a note in the shared channel about the supplier’s system move, because that is not the same as telling the people with a customer commitment. The least effective response is pressing the supplier every day to deliver on time: it is worse than either of the other two, because both put something in front of the affected team, while this spends a fortnight chasing a supplier who has already given their answer. The principle: when a supplier’s problem lands on somebody else’s promise, tell the people who made the promise first.

question_text: You are a build engineer. Last week you told the programme office that the average build takes nine minutes. Since a change on Monday it takes twenty-six. The programme office is publishing a paper this afternoon that uses the nine-minute figure to argue against buying more capacity. Your team lead is in interviews all day and has asked not to be disturbed. Which response below would be most effective, and which would be least effective?
options: Say nothing to anybody until your team lead is out of interviews, and raise the corrected figure with her then rather than going round her to the programme office.
Send the corrected figure to the programme office now and copy your team lead, so that the paper is written on twenty-six minutes rather than on nine.
Interrupt the interviews to tell your team lead, since a paper going to the programme board on a wrong figure is more urgent than an hour of an interview.
Send the programme office a note saying the figure may have moved and that they should check it before publishing anything this afternoon.
explanation: A: Stays silent while waiting for a route: the paper publishes this afternoon and the interviews run until the end of the day. C: Escalates past a stated instruction when a direct route exists: the programme office can be told without disturbing anybody. D: Hedges a fact you are certain of: you know it is twenty-six, and may have moved leaves them deciding whether to believe their own paper. The most effective response is to send the corrected figure to the programme office now and copy your team lead. They own the paper, they can be reached directly, and the copy means nothing is done behind her back while she is unavailable. It beats interrupting the interviews to tell her, because that is unnecessary when the people publishing the paper can be told in one email. It beats sending the programme office a note saying the figure may have moved, because you are certain it is twenty-six, and that passes your certainty on as doubt. The least effective response is saying nothing until she is out of interviews: it is worse than either of the other two, because both reach somebody before the paper publishes, while this waits for a route that will not open until after the argument has been made on a figure you know is wrong. The principle: when a decision is being taken this afternoon on a number you know has changed, go to whoever holds the document and copy the people who should know.
